units.title: Indus Valley Civilization, Vedic Age, Mahajanapadas, Jainism & Buddhism, Magadha, Mauryas, Foreign Invasions, Kushanas, Satavahanas, Sangam Age, Sungas, Gupta Empire

rows.title: Sources of ancient Indian history - archaeological, literary, foreign accounts; dating methods
sub: Group-II S1-1: Sources of ancient Indian history - archaeological, literary and foreign accounts

secs.t: Sources — earliest references to Andhras and FIRSTs

x: The Aitareya Brahmana gives the earliest literary reference, the Mahabharata associates the Andhras with the Kauravas, and Buddhist texts use the term Andhakaratta.

Both are correct: Pali texts give the first definite references to coins (kahapana, nikkha, kamsa, kakanika), and punch-marked coins corroborate them archaeologically. '1 only' and '2 only' each leave out a true statement, and 'Neither' is wrong.

secs.t: Religious texts → what they reveal (Buddhist, Jain, Smriti)

x: The Sri Lankan chronicles illuminate Mauryan history, Andhra Buddhism and Sangam chronology, while Jain texts and Smritis provide information on Andhra traditions and Gupta-age social and legal institutions.
Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa
are Sri Lankan Pali chronicles that provide the Gajabahu-Senguttuvan synchronism used in dating the Sangam age.
Nayadhammakahao
contains the Andhra traditions concerning Yashodhara and his son Dhanada.

secs.t: Books → authors (secular and Puranic literature)

x: Exam angle: "Rajatarangini was composed by" - match work with author and dynasty.
Gunadhya composed Brihatkatha in Paisachi, and it provides information about the Satavahana age.
Arthashastra belongs to the Mauryan context, Gathasaptasati to the Satavahana period, Harshacharita to the age of Harsha, and Rajatarangini to the 12th century.
Kalhana
composed Rajatarangini in the 12th century on the kings of Kashmir.
Gathasaptasati is attributed to the Satavahana king Hala and is in Maharashtri Prakrit.

secs.t: Foreign travellers → work, ruler visited and content

x: Exam angle: arrange travellers chronologically; match work - author - language.
Exam angle: "pair not correctly matched" - the wrong pair both in 2018 and 2019 was
I-Tsing - Ashoka
I-Tsing was a Chinese traveller of the late seventh century who studied at Nalanda and wrote about Buddhist monastic life.
The correct sequence is Megasthenes, Fa-Hien, Hiuen Tsang and Al-Biruni, moving from the Mauryan period through the Gupta and Harsha periods to the eleventh century.
Deimachus, Dionysius, Ptolemy and Strabo
are among the Greek or Roman writers associated with ancient accounts of India.
Ptolemy’s Geography identifies Masolia, generally associated with Machilipatnam, for textiles and Ben Ra, associated with Vengi, as a trade centre.
Hiuen Tsang’s 7th-century account states that the
Sriparvata vihara lacked patronage
The Periplus was written in Greek by an anonymous Greek sailor, Geography by Ptolemy, and Natural History by Pliny in Latin.

secs.t: Scripts → region, direction and decipherment

x: The earliest decipherable Indian inscriptions are Ashokan edicts, generally written in Prakrit using the Brahmi script.
Kharosthi was a right-to-left north-western script, represented in the Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra edicts, and its decipherment drew on bilingual Indo-Greek coins.
Tamil-Brahmi or Tamizhi is dated to approximately
the 3rd century BCE
, supporting the early chronology of the Sangam corpus.

secs.t: Inscriptions → issuer, language and record

x: Exam angle: wrong pair in APPSC 2012 was
Rudradaman - Nanaghat
(correct: Junagadh).
The
Hathigumpha inscription
of Kharavela of Kalinga records his campaigns and mentions Tamil kingdoms.
The Nasik Prashasti is by Gautami Balashri and hails Gautamiputra Satakarni as destroyer of Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas.
The
Naneghat inscription
, issued by Queen Naganika, is an important source for the early history of the Satavahana family.
The
Myakadoni inscription
of Pulumavi III provides the basis for the Karnataka-homeland theory of the Satavahanas.

secs.t: Coins → series and features

x: Punch-marked coins were recently found at Balirajgarh in
Madhubani district of Bihar
Ship-motif coins, evidence of maritime trade, are associated with Vasishthiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri Satakarni.
The ship motif, including the ship with an anchor, is regarded as evidence of
maritime trade
The Kushanas were notable for large-scale gold coin issues, while the Guptas issued the largest number of gold coins, known as dinaras.

secs.t: Archaeologists, historians and persons → contributions

x: John Marshall
, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of the Indus Valley Civilisation in 1924.
The Bhattiprolu stupa was excavated by Alexander Rea; Robert Sewell wrote A Forgotten Empire on Vijayanagara.
The correct order is Brahmi decipherment in 1837, Walter Elliot’s Amaravati work in 1845, discovery of Nagarjunakonda in 1926, and Wheeler’s Arikamedu excavation in 1945.

secs.t: Dating methods → principle

x: Radiocarbon dating measures C-14 decay in organic remains (a-iii); dendrochronology counts annual tree rings (b-i); thermoluminescence measures light released on heating pottery or burnt material (c-ii).
Counting annual tree rings is the principle of dendrochronology, not stratigraphy.
Thermoluminescence
dates pottery or burnt material by measuring radiation accumulated since the last firing.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Megasthenes, the Periplus, Ptolemy and Pliny all provide information relevant to ancient Andhra; the associated references are about 30 Andhra forts, Koddura, Masulia and Satavahana Andhra respectively.
The Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions from Egypt record trader names including
Cikai Korran, Kopan and Catan
, and date from the 1st to 3rd centuries CE.

rows.title: Sources for the history of Andhra - inscriptions, coins, literature and foreign accounts
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-1

secs.t: Literary sources on Andhra → text, author and content

x: The Matsya Purana mentions 30 Satavahana kings and a period of 456 years.
Kharavela was defeated by the Asmaka king Satakarni, so the account is of Satakarni defeating Kharavela.
Hala's Gathasaptasati is in Prakrit, has 700 verses and records early Telugu words.
Both Kashikhandam and Haravilasam, associated with Srinatha, reveal sea trade during the Reddi period.

secs.t: Inscriptions of Andhra → dynasty, language and record

x: Exam angle: Manchikallu + Mayidavolu = Pallavas; Alluru = multiple gifts (Karle, Veerapuram, Ramagiri were the distractors, G2 2017).

The Nagarjunakonda inscription records Santamula’s foundation of the kingdom; Alluru records donations and feudatory status; Manchikallu records the Pallava conquest; Mayidavolu records Pallava rule over Andhrapatha.
Jaggayyapeta records Buddhist donations, Gurazala belongs to the dynasty’s last phase, and Manchikallu records Simhavarman’s conquest of Vijayapuri.

secs.t: Ikshvaku succession, copper-plate grants and terms

x: Copper-plate grants generally record a king granting a village or land to Brahmins, together with tax exemptions.
Vishnukundin grants measured land in ‘
nivartanas
Simhavarman defeated Rudrapurushadatta; after the fall, the Pallavas controlled the territory south of the Krishna and the Brihatpalayanas the territory to its north.

secs.t: Sites and Roman coin hoards → place and finding

x: Salihundam, Guntupalli and Jaggayyapeta are stupa sites.
Gudiwada Dibba is a habitation mound showing occupation from the Mauryan to the Satavahana period.
Kondapur is identified both as a habitation mound and as the location of a mint.
Attirala (Kadapa) and Vinukonda (Guntur) yielded Roman gold coins.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Satavahana history rests on the Puranas, Prakrit inscriptions and coins.
Arikamedu is identified as a Roman trade centre on the east coast, while Rajghat at Varanasi is associated with punch-marked coins and Greek-inscribed seals.

rows.title: Stone Age cultures - Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, Chalcolithic sites of India

secs.t: Stone Age phases → technique, tools and sites

x: The Middle Palaeolithic is characterized by flake tools, prepared cores such as the Levallois technique, scrapers, borers and points.
Patne
, along with Kurnool caves, Jwalapuram and Baghor I and III, is associated with Upper Palaeolithic blades and bone tools.
The Levallois prepared-core technique belongs to the
Middle Palaeolithic
flake industry, and Sembur (TN) is a Middle Palaeolithic site (PYQ 2023).

secs.t: Mesolithic sites and microlith centres → region

x: Langhnaj is located in Gujarat.
Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama are Mesolithic sites in the
Ganga plain of Uttar Pradesh
, particularly the Pratapgarh region.
Lekhahia and Baghai Khor are rock-shelter sites in the Vindhyas of Uttar Pradesh.

secs.t: Rock art sites → features

x: Bhimbetka shows continuous habitation from the Lower Palaeolithic to medieval times.

Bhimbetka contains Upper Palaeolithic art in about 300 caves and shelters, while its Mesolithic art includes hunting and basket-carrying scenes and later became more static after contact with Malwa's Chalcolithic farmers.
Borra Caves are in Visakhapatnam and Kethavaram in Kurnool.
Petroglyphs are carved representations, not painted ones.

secs.t: Neolithic sites → region and distinctive find

x: Mehrgarh is associated with early farming and mud-brick houses, Burzahom with pit dwellings and dog burials, Chirand with bone and antler tools, and Utnoor with ash mounds.
Mehrgarh was located in Baluchistan, Burzahom in Kashmir, Koldihwa in Uttar Pradesh and Utnoor in Telangana.
Eastern Neolithic sites are associated with
pointed-butt celts and shouldered axes
, showing links with South-East Asia.

secs.t: Chalcolithic cultures → date, pottery and type site

x: Ahar-Banas is represented by Ahar, Kayatha by Kayatha, Malwa by Navdatoli, and Jorwe by Inamgaon.
Jorwe culture is associated with painted red ware.
The approximate starting dates are Ahar-Banas (2800 BCE), Kayatha (2450 BCE), Malwa (1900 BCE) and Jorwe (1400 BCE).
Daimabad
had a fortified settlement and copper objects and is identified as the southernmost Harappan site.

secs.t: Megaliths → types, terms and AP districts

x: A cist is a stone-slab box chamber; a dolmen is a table-like chamber; a sarcophagus is a clay or terracotta coffin; and a menhir is an upright memorial stone.
Megaliths are graves with weapons, tools and pottery, surrounded by big stones (PYQ 2018); they belong to the Iron Age with black-and-red ware.

secs.t: AP Stone Age sites → phase and district

x: Billasurgam caves in Kurnool district belong to the Palaeolithic phase and have yielded stone tools, rare bone tools and animal fossils.
Kurnool caves and Jwalapuram are Upper Palaeolithic sites, Nagarjunakonda has Lower Palaeolithic tools and microliths, and Yerragondapalem has quartzite blades.
Keesarapalli is located in Krishna district and is associated with Chalcolithic copper tools.

secs.t: Archaeologists → discoveries

x: Robert Bruce Foote, pioneer of AP prehistory, worked at Billasurgam and the Pennar.
The AP microlith centres were discovered by Robert Bruce Foote; N. R. Banerji is the leading researcher of megaliths.
H. D. Sankalia associated the first harvesting of rice in Andhra with the Iron, or Megalithic, Age.

secs.t: FIRST evidence → site and region

x: Mayiladumparai in Krishnagiri district
of Tamil Nadu has yielded the earliest AMS-dated iron evidence in India, dated to 2172 BCE.
Lehuradeva in Uttar Pradesh provides evidence of early rice cultivation dating to about
6500 BCE
; Koldihwa is another associated site.
Hathnora in the Narmada valley yielded the earliest human fossil ('Narmada Man').

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Karivalamvanthanallur shows occupation passing directly from the Microlithic to the Iron/Early Historic age, without a Neolithic or Chalcolithic phase.
Panayal in
Kasaragod, Kerala
, is associated with a megalithic rock-cut burial chamber.
Giddaluru, Nagarjunakonda and Kondapur are Andhra microlith centres, and their discovery is associated with Robert Bruce Foote.
Anthropomorphic megaliths are associated with Tirupati, where the largest collection is found.

rows.title: Pre-historic cultures of Andhra - Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic and Megalithic sites
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-2

secs.t: Palaeolithic sites of Andhra → district and discoverer

x: Robert Bruce Foote discovered the relevant Palaeolithic tools and also found Palaeolithic tools at Pallavaram near Chennai.
The Billa Surgam caves are in Kurnool district, now Nandyal, and have yielded stone and bone tools.
The
Kurnool caves and Muchatla Chintamani Gavi
are identified as the only Indian Upper Palaeolithic bone-tool sites in this context.

secs.t: Tools by stage → type and raw material

x: Lower Palaeolithic tools were handaxes, cleavers and choppers; Middle Palaeolithic tools included flakes and scrapers; Upper Palaeolithic tools included blades and bone tools; Mesolithic tools were microliths.

The sequence proceeds from quartzite and limestone in the Lower Palaeolithic through chert-based materials, silica-rich stone and bone, Mesolithic microlithic materials, and finally copper in the Chalcolithic.

secs.t: Mesolithic / Microlithic implement centres

x: Giddaluru (Prakasam) is the key microlithic centre, with Nagarjunakonda, Kondapur and Khammam.

secs.t: Neolithic-Chalcolithic sites → district/state and feature

x: Utnur is in Mahbubnagar, Palavoy in Anantapur, Ramapuram in Kurnool, and Sanganakallu–Tekkalakota in Bellary, Karnataka.
All three pairs are correctly matched.
Patapadu
is the standard site associated with Chalcolithic evidence in Andhra Pradesh, particularly painted pottery.

secs.t: Megalithic phase → pottery, grave goods and sites

x: The Megalithic culture in this context is identified with the Iron Age, and black-and-red ware is its characteristic pottery.
Glass mirrors
were not included in the list.
Nagarjunakonda
was identified as a centre among the Megalithic habitation sites.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: AMS dating at Mayiladumparai has placed the Iron Age in South India at approximately
2100 BCE
, earlier than the Gangetic Iron Age.
Upper Palaeolithic
quartz tools and petroglyphs
have been reported from Manchirevula near Hyderabad.

rows.title: Pre-Harappan and Early Harappan cultures - Mehrgarh, Amri, Kot Diji, Kalibangan-I

secs.t: Early farming sites → region and FIRSTs

x: Mehrgarh lies in Baluchistan near the Bolan Pass and gives the earliest evidence of agriculture, domestication and pottery.
Mehrgarh shows Stone Age-to-Harappan continuity, Kili Gul Muhammad lies in the Quetta valley, and Rana Ghundai lies in the Zhob-Loralai valley.
Damb Sadaat in the Quetta valley is identified as an Early Harappan-phase village.

secs.t: Mehrgarh periods → crops, animals, crafts and burials

x: Period I, the aceramic Neolithic phase around 7000 BCE, yielded barley and wheat along with sheep, goats and cattle.
At Mehrgarh, the dead were often buried under or near houses in a flexed position, accompanied by ornaments, tools and sometimes goats as grave goods.

secs.t: Early Harappan cultures → type site and pottery

x: The Early Harappan phase is 3300-2600 BCE and corresponds to the Hakra phase.
Kot Diji
in Sindh was a fortified pre-Harappan settlement destroyed by fire and yielded many stone implements.
Mitathal
is associated with the pre-Harappan, Mature Harappan and Late Harappan phases.
The Early Harappan phase had distinct regional traditions, while Mature Harappan pottery became more uniform.

secs.t: Kalibangan-I → features

x: Kalibangan is located in Rajasthan on the
Ghaggar
The pre-Harappan level at Kalibangan yielded the earliest known ploughed field, whose criss-cross furrows indicate mixed cropping.
The Mature-phase fire altars came later, not in the earlier pre-Harappan level.
B.
B. Lal and B. K. Thapar
excavated Kalibangan from 1961 to 1969.

secs.t: Scholars → excavations and views

x: John Marshall proposed indigenous evolution; E. J. H. Mackay suggested migration from Sumer; Mortimer Wheeler supported diffusion from West Asia; regional evolution from Mehrgarh is the current consensus.
Kot Diji was associated with Ghurye’s discovery and F. A. Khan’s 1955 work; Banawali with R. S. Bisht; Mitathal with Suraj Bhan; and Rana Ghundai with E. J. Ross.

secs.t: Early to Mature Harappan transition → features and debates

x: Pottery and buildings at Kalibangan and Kot Diji anticipate Mature Harappan forms, supporting gradual and internal urbanisation.
All three statements are correct and indicate technological, architectural and symbolic continuity before the Mature Harappan phase.
The gap between Neolithic Mehrgarh and the later urban phase remains an open problem.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Rakhigarhi covers approximately 550 hectares and shows continuous occupation from the
Early to the Mature Harappan phase
Evidence from Mehrgarh and Early Harappan sites supports local growth and regional evolution, rather than an exclusively Mesopotamian origin.

rows.title: Indus Valley Civilization - discovery, chronology, geographical extent, boundary sites
sub: Group-II S1-2: Salient features of the Indus Valley Civilization - extent, chronology and major sites

secs.t: IVC — names, ancient names and site nicknames

x: Lothal is known as Mini Harappa, not the City of the Dead.
The term Harappan is preferred because Harappa was the first site found and the civilisation extended well beyond the Indus valley.
Mohenjodaro
means ‘Mound of the Dead’.
Meluha
is the Mesopotamian name for the Indus region.

secs.t: IVC sites → discovered / excavated by

x: Exam angle: "Excavator of Lothal" -
S.R. Rao
R. D. Banerji
excavated Mohenjodaro in 1922; later work was associated with Mackay, K. N. Dikshit and Marshall.
N. G. Majumdar excavated Chanhudaro, Y. D. Sharma Ropar, J. P. Joshi Surkotada and R. S. Bisht Banawali.
Charles Masson described the ruins during 1826–38, railway ballast use occurred in 1857, J. Fleet published seals in 1912 and Sahni found Harappa in 1921–22.
The excavation years were Harappa—1921, Mohenjodaro—1922, Chanhudaro—1931 and Lothal—1954.

secs.t: IVC chronology → phases and dates

x: Kot Diji, Amri and Sothi-Siswal are Early Harappan (3300-2600 BCE) village settlements.
John Marshall proposed 3250–2750 BCE on the basis of cross-dating with Mesopotamian evidence.
D. P. Agrawal's radiocarbon-based dating placed the civilisation approximately in
Dholavira was inhabited approximately from 3000 to 1800 BCE.

secs.t: Scholars → origin theories; non-Aryan debate

x: Mackay supported the migration-from-Sumer theory.
The current consensus emphasises indigenous regional development from the Mehrgarh tradition, rather than complete external replacement.
The Mature Harappan culture was urban, whereas the Rigvedic culture was predominantly pastoral.
The stated comparison is: Indus Valley—urban, Rigvedic—pastoral, Later Vedic—agrarian and Medieval—landlordism.

secs.t: Geographical extent — boundary sites and area

x: The
Ghaggar–Hakra system
had the highest concentration of settlements, with about 250 sites, of which six were cities.
Manda is the northern site, Daimabad the southern site, Alamgirpur the eastern site and Sutkagendor the western site.
Alamgirpur
in western Uttar Pradesh is the standard eastern boundary site.
Sutkagendor is located on the Makran coast in Balochistan, in present-day Pakistan.

secs.t: IVC sites → river and present state — Site → river → location

x: Lothal lies at the Bhogava–Sabarmati confluence in Ahmedabad district of Gujarat, near the head of the Gulf of Cambay.
Kalibangan is in Hanumangarh, Rajasthan; Ropar is on the Sutlej in Punjab; and Alamgirpur is on the Hindon in Meerut, Uttar Pradesh.
Rakhigarhi is in Hisar district, Banawali in the Hisar–Fatehabad region, Mandi in Muzaffarnagar and Dholavira in Kutch.

secs.t: IVC sites → river and present state — Indian sites by state

x: Harappan sites in Pakistan:
Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Chanhudaro, Kot Diji, Amri, Sutkagendor, Balakot (Kot Bala)
PYQ keys:.
Indian site among Harappa, Kot Bala, Lothal, Mehrgarh =
Lothal.
UP sites =
Mandi and Hulas.
Exam angle: "Kalibangan is located in" - answer
Hanumangarh

secs.t: Harappan vs non-Harappan sites

x: Surkotada is a fortified Harappan site in Kutch associated with horse bones; the interpretation is disputed.
A, B and D are correct.
Kot Diji
has both pre-Harappan and Harappan levels.

secs.t: IVC sites → findings

x: Lothal
has yielded rice husks, fire altars, a Persian Gulf seal and an ivory scale, in addition to its bead-making activity.
Chanhudaro
is distinguished by its bead-making factory, absence of a citadel, ink-pot and cart with a seated driver.
Mohenjodaro
has yielded the bronze Dancing Girl, the Priest-King, the Pashupati seal, the Great Bath, the Great Granary and an assembly hall.

secs.t: Largest sites, UNESCO and protected sites

x: Harappa was discovered in 1921, Mohenjo-daro became a UNESCO site in 1980, Dholavira later became the first IVC site on the UNESCO list, and Tighrana and Mitathal were protected in June 2026.
Dholavira
is the first (and so far only) IVC site in India on the World Heritage List; Rakhigarhi remains on the tentative list.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The civilization is significant for representing the first urbanisation in India and for being the largest Bronze Age civilization by area.
The Rakhigarhi skeletons were transferred by the Archaeological Survey of India to the Anthropological Survey of India at Kolkata under an MoU.
The Harappan Civilization was the largest of the contemporary Bronze Age civilizations—Egypt and Mesopotamia—when compared by area.

rows.title: IVC town planning - grid layout, citadel and lower town, drainage, Great Bath, granaries
sub: Group-II S1-3: IVC town planning, drainage, granaries and the Great Bath

secs.t: Town planning features — streets, houses and wells

x: The Harappan grid plan consisted of north–south and east–west streets crossing at right angles, dividing cities into blocks; main streets were about 30 feet or 10 metres wide.
Banawali
is the only Harappan city with radial streets; Mohenjodaro and Harappa show the typical grid layout with streets crossing at right angles.

secs.t: Sites → layout — citadel, lower town, three-part plan

x: Kalibangan had a fortified lower town, Lothal had both divisions in one enclosure, and Sutkagendor had a citadel and lower city.
The western citadel stood on a raised, fortified platform and contained public buildings, while the eastern lower town was associated with commoners’ houses.
Dholavira is described as the only Indus Valley city divided into three parts: citadel, middle town and lower town.

secs.t: Building materials — bricks, ratio and statement traps

x: Exam angle: statement questions - "same size bricks for all constructions" and "houses mostly single-storey" are both
false
Burnt bricks were common, while mud bricks were used for fillings, platforms and at Kalibangan.
Some Dholavira reservoirs were partly cut into the rock, and sandstone and limestone blocks were used for major construction.

secs.t: Drainage — features

x: The planned drainage system
is regarded as the most advanced feature of Indus Valley Civilization towns.
Covered drains had manholes for maintenance, were built with burnt bricks and terracotta pipes, and used street slopes for natural flow.
Planned drainage existed even in small settlements.

secs.t: Great Bath — site, size, materials, purpose

x: The Great Bath was situated
on the citadel mound
of Mohenjodaro.
The Great Bath was built with burnt bricks set in gypsum mortar and was waterproofed with a layer of bitumen.
The Great Bath had flights of steps at its north and south ends.

secs.t: Granaries and special structures → site

x: Exam angle: "The great granary has been found at" -
Mohenjodaro
Lothal
had a warehouse on a raised platform beside the dock; seal impressions were also associated with the warehouse.
Harappa
had two rows of six granaries (12 units) near the river, with circular working platforms and barracks.
The largest inscription is the ten-sign signboard found at the
North Gate of Dholavira

secs.t: Dholavira → water harvesting and other features

x: Dholavira had giant reservoirs supplied through bunds, check-dams and channels, along with dams and embankments.
Dholavira was occupied through seven stages from approximately 3000 to 1500 BCE.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Standardisation of bricks, grid planning and drainage points to civic authority and considerable early engineering skill.
The absence of clearly identified palaces or temples does not disprove civic authority; standardised urban planning instead suggests it.

rows.title: Major Harappan sites and their signature finds - Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Chanhudaro, Lothal, Dholavira, Kalibangan, Banawali, Rakhigarhi, Surkotada, Rangpur

secs.t: Largest Harappan cities and their current status

x: The genetic finding has been interpreted as pointing towards indigenous ancestry and challenging the Aryan-invasion view.
Rakhigarhi
is on the Tentative List, whereas Dholavira is the only Harappan site on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
The DNA of a Rakhigarhi female skeleton was reported to show no Steppe Pastoralist gene.

secs.t: Seals and sculptures → site

x: The Bronze Dancing Girl is one of the best-known sculptures discovered at
Mohenjodaro
Cylindrical seals are associated with Kalibangan, and a cylindrical seal indicating a Mesopotamian link was found at Mohenjodaro.
The Pashupati seal is from Mohenjodaro, the ship on a seal from Lothal, carts with seated drivers from Chanhudaro, and the red sandstone male torso from Harappa.

secs.t: Water management and ports → site

x: The National Maritime Heritage Complex is being developed at Lothal in Gujarat.
Dholavira
had 16 reservoirs, dams, embankments and stepwells cut in sandstone, demonstrating an elaborate water-management system.
Allahdino in Sindh is associated with well irrigation, an example of
Harappan water-management practice
Lothal's tidal dockyard is the standard reading, with an irrigation-tank view as an alternative.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Rakhigarhi Mound 7:
56 skeletons
in all, incl. a ~4,600-year-old woman.
Latest dig: five complete skeletons (aged 30-40) + three fragmentary burials (23 Jun 2026)

rows.title: IVC economy - agriculture, crops, domesticated animals, internal and external trade, Meluhha
sub: Group-II S1-4: IVC economy - agriculture, crafts, trade, seals, weights and measures

secs.t: Crops → site of evidence; FIRSTs

x: Wheat is evidenced at Harappa and Mehrgarh, barley at Banawali, rice at Lothal and Rangpur, and garlic at Balu.
Wheat, barley, peas, sesame and mustard
are among the crops cultivated by the Harappans.
The Indus Valley Civilization is associated with the first cotton cultivation, Lothal with the world's earliest tidal dockyard, and Kalibangan with the earliest ploughed field.

secs.t: Agriculture — ploughing, irrigation, surplus

x: Terracotta plough models were found at Banawali and Bahawalpur, a clay plough at Rakhigarhi, well irrigation at Allahdino, and reservoirs at Dholavira.
Wells at Allahdino, reservoirs at Dholavira and flood irrigation are evidenced, whereas conclusive evidence of canal irrigation is absent.
Kalibangan
has yielded the earliest ploughed field with furrows indicating mixed cropping.

secs.t: Animals → domesticated, wild and unknown

x: Exam angle: "Which animal was not known to the Indus people" → Horse.
Exam angle: "Which animal is not depicted on Harappan seals" → Horse.
The humped bull, or zebu, was the most represented animal on Harappan seals and served both draught and milk purposes.
Camel bones were found at Kalibangan, a dog was buried with a human at Ropar, and rhinoceros remains occurred at Amri.

secs.t: Crafts and industries → centre

x: Bead-making was concentrated at Chanhudaro, Lothal and Kalibangan; shell work at Nageshwar, Balakot and Lothal; copper and bronze work at Harappa, Mohenjodaro and Lothal; and spinning and weaving at Mohenjodaro and Chanhudaro.
Chanhudaro had factories producing beads, bangles, shell ornaments, metal objects, seals and toys.
The Dancing Girl is a bronze object made by lost-wax casting.

secs.t: Metals and raw materials → source region

x: Exam angle: "Which metal has not been found at Harappan sites" → Iron.
Copper came from Khetri and Oman, tin from Afghanistan, gold from Kolar and Afghanistan, and lapis lazuli from Badakhshan through Shortughai.
Stone tools continued alongside metal tools, and chert blades from Rohri illustrate this.
The Harappans pioneered the use of silver and cotton

secs.t: External trade — ancient names → region, goods

x: Exam angle: "In ancient times the Indus region was known as" → Meluhha; distractors Dilmun, Makan, Surkotada.
Records of Sargon of Akkad, around 2300 BCE, mention ships coming from Meluhha, the Indus region.
Harappan seals, beads and weights are reported from Oman, Bahrain, Iraq (Mesopotamia) and Iran.
The cylinder seals at Mohenjodaro and reserved slip ware at Harappa are evidence of Mesopotamian contacts.

secs.t: Ports → location and role

x: Lothal
is the site associated with trade with West Asia, supported by its dockyard and the Persian Gulf-type seal.
Sutkagendor on the Makran coast of Baluchistan, near the Iran border, is regarded as the
westernmost Harappan site
The Lothal dockyard was brick-lined, about 218 m x 37 m, and sluice gates controlled the water, so 1 and 2 are correct.

secs.t: Seals → form, motifs, find sites abroad

x: Exam angle: bull seal → Mohenjodaro.
The unicorn is the most common motif; square seals combine animals and inscriptions, rectangular seals carry only inscriptions, and a button seal was found at Lothal.
The Pashupati seal, showing a seated yogic figure surrounded by animals, was found at Mohenjodaro.
A cylindrical steatite seal with an alligator motif and five Harappan characters was reported from
Rakhigarhi

secs.t: Weights and measures → site

x: Exam angle: "In which IVC city was a scale discovered" -
Lothal
The ivory scale or balance was found at Lothal, the shell scale at Mohenjodaro, the copper scale at Harappa, and the shell angle-measuring object in Saurashtra.
The widespread uniformity of scales and weights points to
central regulation of trade
across the Indus region.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Farm surplus, trade networks, craft specialisation and standard weights together created the economic conditions for urbanisation.
The Rig Vedic economy was pastoral, and cotton, rice and wheat are not mentioned in the Rig Veda.
The second Dilmun temple, dated to approximately 1900–1800 BCE, was found on
Failaka Island in Kuwait

rows.title: IVC seals, weights and measures, Harappan script (undeciphered features)

secs.t: Seals and sealings — material, shapes, uses

x: Exam angle: long-distance communication → "seals and sealings"; distinctive feature of IVC → seals.
Since the Harappan script remains unread, seals are regarded as the most distinctive artefacts and an important source of information about Harappan society.
Seals and sealings
served as a means of long-distance communication, in addition to their commercial and identity-related functions.

secs.t: Weights — material, shape, binary-decimal system

x: Lower denominations followed the binary sequence 1:2:4:8:16:32:64, after which decimal multiples such as 160, 320 and 640 were used.
The distribution of similar weights over about 8,00,000 square kilometres suggests
central regulation and standardized trade
practices.
Ivory weight balances are associated with Mohenjodaro and Lothal, chert trade weights have been reported from Rakhigarhi, and Harappan weights were generally cubical.

secs.t: Harappan script — features, numbers and FIRSTs

x: Harappan inscriptions were generally written from
right to left
, as indicated partly by cramped spacing at the left end.
J. Fleet
noticed seals with unknown symbols in 1912.
The Dholavira signboard is famous for its inscription of
10 large signs
The Harappan script is pictographic, has approximately 400 signs and remains undeciphered.

secs.t: Scholars → decipherment hypotheses

x: The Proto-Dravidian hypothesis is associated with Iravatham Mahadevan and Asko Parpola; the Indo-Aryan view with S.R. Rao; Proto-Munda has weak linguistic support; and the isolate view considers decipherment impossible for now.
The Harappan script is still undeciphered because no bilingual text (like the Rosetta Stone) has been discovered.
The language underlying the undeciphered script remains debated, particularly between Dravidian and Indo-Aryan interpretations.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Uniform seals and weights indicate
standardisation and regulated trade
across the Harappan cultural region.

rows.title: IVC society and polity - social stratification debate, burial practices, absence of temples/palaces

secs.t: Social stratification — evidence

x: Differences in the quantity and quality of burial goods and ornaments suggest differentiation in social status.
The western citadel contained public and elite areas, while the eastern lower town was associated with commoners' houses.
The three broad building types mentioned are residential buildings, larger buildings and public buildings.
The four-fold division is only a speculative reading of material remains.

secs.t: Views on the polity → basis

x: The priest-rule interpretation draws on the citadel, Great Bath and steatite Priest-King.
Trade-driven uniformity, together with the absence of identifiable kings and palaces, has been used to argue for merchant elites or civic administrators.
The
construction of walls, platforms and reservoirs
indicates the mobilisation and coordination of labour on a considerable scale.

secs.t: Absence of palaces and temples; weapons

x: One interpretation is that worship occurred in domestic or open-air settings and that political power was not personalised in a king.
The Great Bath
, along with structures such as granaries and pillared halls, is interpreted as a civic public structure.
The huddled skeletons at Mohenjodaro were once read as massacre victims but are now interpreted as representing
multiple burials

secs.t: Daily life — dress, ornaments, cosmetics, pastimes → site

x: Harappan ornaments used materials such as gold, silver, ivory, copper, lapis lazuli, carnelian and faience.
Chanhudaro is associated with lipstick, while bronze mirrors, ivory combs and collyrium sticks were used as cosmetic or grooming items.
All four are included among the proposed Harappan pastimes and cultural activities, although hunting and fishing are specifically regarded as speculative.

secs.t: Burial types → site

x: Exam angle: double burial → Lothal; Sanauli → human burials.
Pottery, ornaments and mirrors in graves indicate a belief in an afterlife and differences in status.
The burials at Rakhigarhi Mound 7 followed a standard north-south orientation and were accompanied by pots containing provisions.
Female skeletons at Rakhigarhi were found with jasper and agate beads and shell bangles.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The skeletal remains were handed by the ASI to the Anthropological Survey of India in Kolkata for scientific study under an MoU.
Harappan social and political interpretations are inferred mainly from material remains, and the script has not supplied the names of rulers.
Harappan polity is characterised as corporate in comparison, while the Later Vedic polity is described as a hereditary monarchy with declining Sabha and Samiti.

src: Sources: CDI (Block01 IVC - 7. Social Life, 8. Religious Life (funerary practices), 9. Political Organisation; Block01 Vedic - Key Scholars); APP (Indian History Part 1 > IVC > Burial Practices, Food, Dress; Important Sites; Town Planning); UPSC (Ancient History p.22; Art & Culture p.8); TH 23 Jun 2026; LENS Jun 2026 p.117

rows.title: IVC art and craft - bronze Dancing Girl, Priest-King, terracotta figurines, bead-making, pottery

secs.t: IVC craft techniques — terms, processes and FIRSTs

x: Perforated jars had a large hole at the base and several small holes over the wall, probably for straining liquor.
In the lost-wax process, a wax model is coated with clay, heated to remove the wax, filled with molten metal, and finally freed by removing the clay mould.
Faience was used for
beads, bangles and glazed ware
, and its association with mosaic glass provides an early clue to glass-making.

secs.t: Pottery and seals — colour, motifs, material

x: Indus pottery was wheel-made; red pottery with black painted designs was typical, alongside plain red and painted red-and-black varieties.
The
unicorn
was the most common animal motif on Indus steatite seals; bull, elephant, tiger and rhinoceros were also represented.
Indus seals were commonly made of steatite, displayed animal and Pashupati motifs, and carried short script lines.

secs.t: Metal and terracotta objects → site + material

x: The clay mask of a horned god is from
Gujarat and Kalibangan
, and the lifelike bearded terracotta males are grouped with it.
The dog chasing a deer is a bronze object from Harappa; the dog and bird are copper objects from Lothal; the bull or ox is from Kalibangan; and the larger animal group is from Daimabad.

secs.t: Bead, shell and gem centres → evidence + materials

x: Exam angle: bead industry located at → Chanhudaro.

Chanhudaro had a bead-making factory, Lothal had bead workshops and exported carnelian beads, Kalibangan was a bead-making centre, and Rakhigarhi had a gemstone factory with over 3,000 semi-precious stones.
Indus bead-makers used
carnelian, agate, jasper, steatite, lapis lazuli, faience and gold
Carnelian came from Saurashtra, carnelian beads were exported to Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf, and Lothal had bead workshops associated with this trade.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: NCERT is to restore the original image of the Dancing Girl in its new Class 9 Art textbook.
The naturalistic quality of bronze and stone sculpture indicates advanced metallurgical skill and craft specialisation.

rows.title: IVC religion - Pashupati seal, Mother Goddess, tree and animal worship, fire altars
sub: Group-II S1-5: IVC society, religion, art and the Harappan script

secs.t: Harappan religion — nature and features

x: The civilization is described as predominantly secular, with religious elements present but not dominant.
No temple has been found in the Harappan archaeological record.

All four statements are supported: figurines and images indicate idol worship; the Great Bath suggests ritual purification; yoga and meditation were practised; and belief in ghosts and evil forces is indicated.

secs.t: Pashupati seal and Mother Goddess — features and identification

x: Exam angle: the Indus people worshipped → Shiva.
A horned deity on a terracotta cake was found at
Kalibangan
; a clay mask of a horned god is also associated with Kalibangan and Gujarat.
The terracotta female figurines are associated with fertility symbolism and are interpreted as evidence of
a fertility cult
Mother Goddess figurines have been found at Harappa, Kot Diji, Kalibangan and sites in Gujarat.

secs.t: Animals, trees and symbols worshipped → meaning

x: Exam angle: tree shape found on Indus seals → Pipal.
The humped bull, mythical unicorn, elephant and tiger are identified as sacred animals in the Harappan religious tradition.
The
pipal
is the most depicted tree on Indus seals and appears in ritual scenes with human figures.
Lingam and yoni symbols and round or pierced stones at Harappa are interpreted as fertility objects and possible early Shaivite elements.

secs.t: Ritual and burial practices → site

x: Charms and amulets point to a belief in
ghosts and evil forces
, against which they were presumably worn for protection.
The placement of pottery, ornaments, mirrors, beads and food with the dead indicates a belief in an afterlife and also reflects status differences.
Sonauli is associated with burials containing coffins and chariots, belonging to the Late Harappan or Copper Hoard phase.

secs.t: Art → site + material (Dancing Girl, Priest-King, toys)

x: Exam angle: "Dancing Girl is made of" -
bronze
(the recorded key "1" is a key-position error).
The Priest-King is from Mohenjodaro; the nude male torso and dog chasing a deer are from Harappa; and the copper dog and bird are from Lothal.
Terracotta cart
s, whistles, rattles, birds, animals, gamesmen and discs are among the known Harappan toys and game objects.

secs.t: Polity and classes — UPSC 2013 claims

x: Planned cities and drains suggest municipal governance, while the exact political structure remains uncertain.
No horse-drawn chariots have been found as clear evidence of Harappan warfare, and the proposed four-fold division is speculative.
Fortified citadels suggest the presence of some ruling group, but its nature—possibly priestly or merchant—is not conclusively established.

secs.t: Continuities in later Hinduism and contrast with Vedic religion

x: Harappan religion was nature- and fertility-oriented and included the Mother Goddess, pipal and animals.
The association of Kalibangan fire altars with Vedic yajna remains debated and is not definitive.
Rig Vedic religion featured male nature gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna and open-air yajnas, with no temples or idols.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Both statements are true, and the undeciphered nature of Harappan records is a principal reason why the proto-Shiva interpretation remains debated rather than proven.
Rakhigarhi is noted as the only Harappan site with ancient DNA in the cited account, along with evidence of a gold foundry and gemstone factory.
The label ‘priest-king’ applied to the bearded Mohenjodaro figure is an interpretation, not a proven identification supported by a deciphered inscription.

rows.title: Decline of the IVC - competing theories; Late Harappan cultures (Cemetery-H, Jhukar, Rangpur)
sub: Group-II S1-6: Decline of the Indus Valley Civilization - theories and Late Harappan cultures

secs.t: Decline theories → proponent / study

x: Mortimer Wheeler
proposed the Aryan invasion explanation in 1947; the theory is now generally rejected.
Wheeler, Childe and Piggott are linked with the invasion theory.
The fall in Mesopotamian demand around 1900 BCE is cited as an economic or trade-decline explanation.
The current consensus rejects a single sudden catastrophe and favours a gradual, multi-causal decline.

secs.t: Mortimer Wheeler's invasion theory — evidence and rejection

x: The skeletons are now read as evidence of multiple burials rather than conclusive proof of invasion.
Wheeler cited skeletons found at Mohenjodaro and Indra’s epithet Purandara, meaning ‘fort-breaker’, in support of the invasion theory.
All three statements are among the major grounds for rejecting Wheeler’s invasion explanation: lack of archaeological evidence, the later date of the Rig Veda and reinterpretation of the skeletons.

secs.t: Evidence → theory (floods, rivers, ecology, climate)

x: Exam angle: IIT Kharagpur study group - continuous low rainfall for
900 years
The shifting Indus flooded and then left settlements like Mohenjodaro abandoned.
All four factors are cited: deforestation, soil salinity, overgrazing, and exhaustion of copper and timber resources.
A malaria outbreak has been detected at
Mohenjodaro
and is cited among the evidence relevant to the decline.

secs.t: De-urbanisation and the Late Harappan phase — features

x: Post-urban settlement shifts were mainly
eastward towards the Ganga-Yamuna Doab and southward towards Gujarat and the Deccan
The decline of cities was accompanied by the emergence of smaller rural settlements and movement towards the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, Gujarat and the Deccan.
Late Harappan cultures used stone and copper tools, lacked complicated-casting metal objects, and developed varied regional pottery styles.

secs.t: Late Harappan sites and cultures → region / period

x: Exam angle: Dadheri is a Late Harappan site of → Punjab.
Cemetery H corresponds to the Harappa region of Punjab; Jhukar to Sindh; Rangpur to Gujarat; and the Ganga-Yamuna Doab phase to Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
The Ganga-Yamuna Doab phase is identified in the table with
Ochre Coloured Pottery
(OCP).

secs.t: Continuity — OCP, Copper Hoards, Harappan traits and Vedic links

x: Copper Hoards are often found with OCP in the
Ganga-Yamuna Doab
, forming the basis of their commonly proposed association.
The identification of Ghaggar-Hakra with the Rigvedic Sarasvati is an argument used by scholars supporting continuity between Late Harappan and Vedic cultural traditions.
Ritual bathing is regarded as a possible Harappan continuity reflected in later
temple tanks and ghats

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Copper-age remains in Andhra Pradesh are noted at Patapadu in Kurnool and in
Krishna district
The 4.2 ka aridity event is also linked with the fall of
Akkad
in Mesopotamia.
The debate includes invasion versus internal decline, migration versus continuity, and climate as a sole cause versus a multi-causal explanation.

rows.title: Aryan question - Original Home theories (Max Muller, Tilak, Avinash Chandra Das); archaeological correlates

secs.t: Terms → meaning (Arya, Dasa, Dasyu, Pani)

x: Exam angle: options "ethnic group / nomadic people / speech group / superior race" - answer: speech group.
'Aryan' is primarily a linguistic label: the Vedic Aryans were speakers of Indo-Aryan (Indo-European) languages, so they form
a speech group
The Dasyus were regarded as original inhabitants who possibly practised phallus worship and did not raise cattle for dairy.

secs.t: Linguistic and epigraphic evidence — Indo-European family, Boghazkoi, Avesta

x: Exam angle: "Which inscription names Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatyas?" - Boghazkoi (distractors: Mansehra, Shahbazgarhi, Junagadh, Ecbatana, Behistun).
Vedic Sanskrit belongs to the
Indo-European
language family, whose geographical spread includes Europe, Asia and the Middle East.
The Boghazkoi treaty invokes the Vedic deities
Indra, Mitra, Varuna and Nasatyas
The inscription provides evidence of Vedic-speaking people or deities in West Asia and is used in support of a Central Asian homeland and movement towards Iran and India.

secs.t: Original home → proponent → book

x: Exam angle: match-the-following of homeland, scholar and book (Tilak-Arctic is the favourite pair).
Dayananda Saraswati associated the homeland with Tibet, Penka with Europe or Germany on physical type, and P. Giles with Hungary and the Danube valley on linguistic grounds.
Max Muller proposed Central Asia, B. G. Tilak the Arctic region, Dayanand Saraswati Tibet and A. C. Das the Sapta Sindhu theory.

secs.t: Archaeological cultures → region + link

x: Harappans are described as using solid wheels, while spoked-wheel chariots form part of the archaeological argument associated with Aryan migration.
Horse remains and new burial practices
are associated with the Gandhara Grave culture, which is often correlated with early Indo-Aryans.
The relationship between Painted Grey Ware archaeology and Later Vedic textual geography remains an open question; Vedic archaeology is not settled on this issue.

secs.t: Migration vs indigenous debate → proponents and arguments

x: Romila Thapar and Upinder Singh represent a synthesis in which small groups migrated, achieved elite dominance and underwent cultural assimilation, without a simple invasion or replacement model.
The reported absence of a Steppe Pastoralist gene in the Rakhigarhi skeleton has been cited against
invasion theories and in favour of indigenous ancestral continuity

secs.t: Aryan–Harappan relationship — chronology and comparison

x: Harappan settlements were urban and planned, while the Rigvedic horse was domesticated and important in warfare.
The horse was central to Rigvedic warfare, while no evidence of such awareness is attributed to the Harappan civilization.
The Harappan civilisation declined first; the Early Vedic culture that followed (c. 1500-1000 BCE) was pastoral, mobile and warrior-like rather than urban.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The racial conception of the Aryan was a colonial idea.
Rakhigarhi, the largest known Harappan settlement, lies in Hisar district, Haryana, on the seasonal Drishadvati.

rows.title: Rig Vedic (Early Vedic) period - geography of Sapta Sindhu, rivers, tribes, Battle of Ten Kings

secs.t: Sapta Sindhu places → feature (rivers, mountains, terms)

x: Yamuna is mentioned three times, while Ganga is mentioned once, in the Tenth Mandala of the Rigveda. ⚠ Sources differ: standard exam fact: Ganga once, in Mandala 10 (Nadistuti); a scholarly reading also counts 'gangya' in RV 6.45.31.
Himavant denotes the Himalayas, Mujavant is a Hindu Kush mountain associated with Soma, Dhanva means desert land and Rigvedic Samudra can mean a collection of water.

secs.t: Rig Vedic tribes — Panchajana grouping and odd-one-out

x: Exam angle: "Which tribe is not in the Panchajana?" - Kikata.
The name Bharatavarsha is traced to the Bharata tribe.
The five tribes of the Panchajana were
Yadus, Turvasas, Anus, Druhyus and Purus

secs.t: Dasarajna (Battle of Ten Kings) — site, persons, outcome

x: The battle may reflect actual competition among tribal confederacies, but the Rigveda is religious poetry rather than a straightforward chronicle.
The traditional explanation identifies the rivalry between the priests
Vasishtha and Vishvamitra
as the cause of the conflict.
The Battle of Ten Kings was fought on the banks of the Parushni, the Rigvedic name of the Ravi, where Sudas of the Bharatas defeated the confederacy.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sapta Sindhu geography places the Early Vedic heartland in Punjab, Haryana and adjoining north-western areas before the later eastward movement.
The Early Vedic core lay in Punjab–Haryana, while the Later Vedic core shifted eastward to the Ganga–Yamuna Doab, eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, including Kosala and Videha.

rows.title: Early Vedic polity - rajan, sabha, samiti, vidatha, gana; nature of tribal chiefdom
sub: Group-II S1-7: Early Vedic (Rig Vedic) age - geography, tribes, polity (sabha, samiti, rajan)

secs.t: Early Vedic polity — nature, units, Early vs Later Vedic

x: The early Vedic hierarchy proceeded from Jana, the tribe, to Vis, the clan, Grama, the village, and Kula, the family.
The term Janapada is absent in the Rigveda, reflecting the predominantly tribal rather than territorial character of early Vedic polity.
Jana is mentioned approximately
275 times
in the Rigveda, underlining the importance of the tribe in early Vedic political organisation.

secs.t: Rajan — titles, selection debate, duties

x: Monarchy was the usual form and succession often passed within the family, but the office was not strictly hereditary and the Samiti had a role in selection.
Kingship was generally not considered divine, but the Puru king Trasadasyu was exceptionally described as ardhadeva, or demi-god.
The Rajan was called Gopati or Gopajanasya, protected the tribe and cattle, led in war and maintained order.

secs.t: Vedic assemblies → composition and function

x: Exam angle: "judicial assembly" = Sabha; "earliest/most-mentioned assembly" = Vidatha; "daughters of Prajapati" and "Veda treating Sabha and Samiti as separate" = Atharvaveda (not Rigveda).
In the later Vedic period, Vidatha disappeared; Sabha and Samiti continued but became more restricted under chiefs and nobles, and women were excluded.
Women participated in the Sabha and Vidatha, female members of the Sabha were called Sabhavati, and the Atharvaveda records women's participation in the Samiti.

secs.t: Officials, army and revenue terms → meaning

x: Purohita was the chief priest and adviser, Senani the army commander, Vrajapati the pasture officer and Spasa the spy.
Sena was a temporary militia organised into units such as
Sardha, Vrata and Gana
‘Gavishti’ literally refers to the
search for cows
and denotes cattle raids, which were a common form of warfare in the Rig Vedic period.

secs.t: Tribes, wars and weapons

x: Early Vedic conflicts included intra-Aryan struggles as well as wars against the Dasas and Dasyus.
The five tribes of Panchajana were
Anu, Druhyu, Yadu, Turvasa and Puru
The Bharatas were associated with Bharatavarsha, while Tritsus, Krivis and Srinjayas were other tribes; Divodasa defeated Sambara and Panis were associated with cattle concealment.

secs.t: Rig Vedic rivers and Sapta Sindhu — ancient → modern names

x: Exam angle: pairs of ancient/modern names; Vitasta-Chenab and Asikni-Jhelum are classic wrong pairs.
The standard Sapta Sindhu list comprises
Sindhu, Vitasta, Asikni, Parushni, Vipas, Sutudri and Sarasvati
The Sapta Sindhu region extended over eastern Afghanistan, north-western areas including present Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab, Haryana and the fringes of western Uttar Pradesh.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The assemblies are considered early democratic or proto-participatory elements because they contained traces of elective participation within a tribal order.
The Later Vedic period saw hereditary territorial kingship, the ratnins, regular taxation and royal sacrifices including Rajasuya, Vajapeya and Ashvamedha.
‘Andhra’ first appears later in the Aitareya Brahmana, in connection with the Sunahshepa story; it does not appear first in the Rig Veda.

rows.title: Early Vedic society and economy - pastoralism, gavishti, varna origins, position of women
sub: Group-II S1-8: Early Vedic society, economy and the position of women

secs.t: Pastoral economy — cow terms → meaning, food and pastimes

x: Exam angle: "Aghanya refers to - cows"; "most valuable property in early Rigvedic period - cow".
Gomat = wealthy man owning many cattle (iii); Godhuli = dusk, when cattle return (iv); Gavyuti = measure of distance (ii); Duhitri = daughter, 'one who milks the cow' (i).
The
cow
(gau) was the most valuable property and the standard unit of value, mentioned about 176 times in the Rigveda.

secs.t: Agriculture terms → meaning — crops, implements, irrigation

x: Exam angle: match crop terms (RPSC 2021 paired Yava with "millet" as the only option left - the standard meaning is barley).
Mudga means mung bean, Godhuma means wheat, Ikshu means sugarcane and Vrihi means rice.
Sita = furrow (iii), Datra = sickle (iv), Supra = winnowing fan (ii), Titau = sieve (i).

secs.t: Craftsmen → terms and metals

x: Takshan was a carpenter, Karmara a metal worker, Hiranyakara a goldsmith and Bhishak a physician.
Charmamna referred to a tanner, while Bhishak was the physician.
Ayas in the Rigveda referred to
copper or bronze
Weaving was known, with women undertaking much of it.

secs.t: Exchange, trade and tribute terms → meaning

x: Nishka was a gold ornament in the Rigveda and later came to denote a unit of value or gold piece.
Bali was a voluntary offering or tribute by tribesmen to the rajan and could include war booty.
In the Later Vedic period, bali became compulsory and existed along with bhaga, the one-sixth share of produce, and shulka.

secs.t: Social units and varna origins — FIRSTs and features — FIRSTs

x: The Purusha Sukta is Rigveda 10.90, a late addition and the first statement of the four-fold varna.
The Purusha Sukta describes Brahmana as originating from the mouth, Kshatriya from the arms, Vaishya from the thighs and Shudra from the feet.
Vaishyas were described as emerging from vis, meaning the mass of the people or tribespeople.

secs.t: Social units and varna origins — FIRSTs and features — Nature of early society

x: Arya and Dasa varna reflected a cultural, linguistic and partly colour-based distinction between Vedic groups and conquered local groups; it was not yet a rigid caste system.
Gotra as a lineage institution is absent in the Rigveda (where the word means cow-pen), appears in that sense in the Atharvaveda, and gotra exogamy is a Later Vedic development.

secs.t: Women — status, seers and marriage customs

x: Exam angle: "Which is not Rig Vedic?" - Gargi.
Gargi
was a later Vedic scholar associated with Upanishadic dialogue, whereas Apala, Ghosha and Vishvavara were Rigvedic women seers.
The Aitareya Brahmana reflects the later patriarchal attitude by describing daughters as
a source of misery
Early Vedic society was patriarchal and preferred sons, yet women received education, participated in sacrifices and assemblies, and could own cattle.

secs.t: Rig Vedic gods → role and epithets

x: Exam angle: statement sets - "Prithvi was mother of all gods" is wrong (that is
Aditi
); Dyaus = Zeus/Jupiter is right.
Rig Vedic worship involved hymns and yajnas in the open air and aimed mainly at material benefits such as cattle, sons and victory.
Dyaus was the sky or celestial father and corresponded to
Greek Zeus and Roman Jupiter

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The shift from a cattle-based tribal economy to an agrarian territorial society contributed to the emergence of territorial kingship and a more established varna hierarchy.
Early Vedic society was largely tribal and egalitarian, and occupations were not rigidly determined by birth.
The evidence is mixed: texts praise women seers, and education and assembly rights existed, but society remained patriarchal and displayed son-preference.

rows.title: Later Vedic period - eastward expansion, iron (krishna ayas), Painted Grey Ware culture
sub: Group-II S1-9: Later Vedic age - eastward expansion, iron, rise of kingship and rituals

secs.t: Later Vedic texts → content

x: The Samaveda contains musical versions of Rigvedic hymns; the Yajurveda gives ritual procedures; the Atharvaveda contains spells and charms; and the Upanishads discuss Atman, Brahman, Karma and Moksha.
The Yajurveda gives ritual procedures in prose, is connected with the Adhvaryu priest, and has Krishna and Shukla branches.
The Upanishads are placed approximately in the period
; 13 are regarded as principal among a traditional total of 108.

secs.t: Eastward expansion — legend, places and kings

x: The movement proceeded from Punjab into the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, including Kurukshetra and the Delhi-upper Doab, and then towards Kosala, Kashi and Videha by about 600 BCE.
Kuru-Panchala occupied the Delhi-Meerut area, had Hastinapur as its capital, formed the cultural centre of the Aryan world, and the Kurus resulted from the Bharata-Puru union.

secs.t: Iron — terms, sites and earliest dates — Vedic metal terms

x: Iron technology in North India is dated approximately to 1000–800 BCE, was common at most Painted Grey Ware sites, and increased the importance of smiths and smelters after 1000 BCE.
Iron weapons and horse-drawn chariots
helped the eastward expansion of Later Vedic people.
The Videgha Madhava legend is connected with the clearing of Ganga-region forests through the use of iron axes and fire.

secs.t: Iron — terms, sites and earliest dates — Earliest iron — new dates from South India

x: Exam angle: BPSC 2022 asked when iron use began, with options 6,000/9,000/12,000 years ago (range 6,000-12,000); the key was "none of the above".
The Mayiladumparai date of 2172 BCE and the Sivagalai date of about 2953 BCE push the evidence for Indian iron use far earlier than the Gangetic date of about 1000 BCE.

secs.t: Agriculture, settlements, crafts and trade — features

x: Rice and wheat became chief crops, rice had ritual importance, barley continued, and double cropping was mentioned.
Land was held in common by the clan or vis, while the household head, the Grihapati, held it at the household level.
True towns emerged after the Vedic period during the Northern Black Polished Ware phase, including Shravasti, Kausambi and Hastinapur.
Iron-working, copper work, weaving, leatherwork, pottery and carpentry expanded.

secs.t: Pottery — PGW sites and the protohistoric sequence — Later Vedic pottery

x: The four Later Vedic wares are
Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware and Red Ware
Painted Grey Ware is grey pottery with linear painted designs, mostly bowls and dishes, of the Later Vedic period (c. 1000-600 BCE).
Copper found at the Painted Grey Ware sites was possibly obtained from
Khetri in Rajasthan

secs.t: Pottery — PGW sites and the protohistoric sequence — PGW sites → region

x: Exam angle: "Pottery of 1000-600 BC in the Gangetic plain" = Painted Grey Ware; list questions exclude NBPW.
The sequence is Ochre Coloured Pottery, Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware, Red Ware and Northern Black Polished Ware.
Black and Red Ware occurs from the Chalcolithic period onwards, is known in the Later Vedic context, and is associated with the Megalithic or Iron Age cultures of South India.

secs.t: Ratnins and revenue officials → function; taxes

x: Exam angle: "Bhagadugha" = revenue collector (distractors: gambling officer, messenger, forest officer).
The
Ratnahavimshi
rite involved offerings at the houses of the Ratnins and honoured the king’s twelve functionaries.
The APP list of twelve Ratnins includes
Parivakti
along with Purohita, Rajan, Mahishi, Senani, Bhagadugha, Sangrahitri, Suta, Kshata, Govikartana, Gramani and Akshavapa.

secs.t: Later Vedic gods → rise and decline

x: Pushan became associated with cattle and was regarded as the god of the Shudras.
Indra and Agni lost prominence, while Prajapati became supreme.
Vishnu
rose as the preserver in the later Vedic period, despite being a minor deity in the Rigveda.
Both statements are true, and the increasing ritualism of Later Vedic worship explains the emergence of the Upanishadic critique.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In Andhra Pradesh, the Iron Age is associated with the Megalithic culture and Black and Red Ware pottery.
The extent to which Painted Grey Ware archaeology corresponds to the geography described in Later Vedic texts remains an open question.
The Rajghat material included pre-NBPW pottery about 3,000 years old and supports dating Varanasi’s urban origins to about 800 BCE.

rows.title: Later Vedic polity - rise of territorial kingship; rajasuya, ashvamedha, vajapeya; the ratnins

secs.t: Territorial kingship — terms and titles

x: The term
rashtra
, meaning territory, first appears in this political context and reflects the rise of territorial kingship.
The Aitareya Brahmana names Rajya, Bhojya, Swarajya, Vairajya and Samrajya.
The eastern ruler was called Samrat, the southern Bhoja, the western Svarat, and the northern Virat.
The ruler of the Middle Country was called
Raja
and represented hereditary Kshatriya kingship.

secs.t: Kingdoms → region

x: The Kuru–Panchala alliance dominated the upper Ganga valley, while Kosala, Kashi and Videha rose in the east.
King Janaka was associated with
Videha
, located in North Bihar beyond the Sadanira or Gandak.
Kashi corresponded to the Varanasi region and Kosala to eastern UP; Videha was in North Bihar and Kuru (not Panchala) in the Delhi-Meerut region.

secs.t: Texts → theory of divine origin of kingship

x: The Aitareya Brahmana gives an early account in which the gods, suffering defeat at the hands of the Asuras, selected a king as their war leader.
The Shatapatha Brahmana linked the king to Prajapati, the creator god.
Royal rituals such as Rajasuya and Vajapeya helped connect kingship with divine sanction and legitimacy.

secs.t: Royal sacrifices → purpose and titles

x: Rajasuya was a consecration conferring supreme power, Ashvamedha involved a horse sacrifice and asserted supremacy over other kings, while Vajapeya included a chariot race against the king’s kinsmen.
The royal rituals discussed here are mentioned in the
Aitareya and Shatapatha Brahmanas
Large Shrauta sacrifices required numerous priests and substantial dakshina, thereby increasing Brahmanical influence and strengthening the ritual basis of royal power.

secs.t: Assemblies, army and taxes — fate and nature

x: The sources present two textbook views: one notes emerging standing elements such as chariot warfare, iron weapons and professional warriors, while another records the continued raising of tribal levies and absence of a fully standing army.
Bali became a regular tribute, Bhaga was the king’s share of produce, and Shulka was a customs duty or toll.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The shift to hereditary territorial monarchy during the Later Vedic period prepared the political ground for the rise of the
Mahajanapadas
in the 6th century BCE.
Ratnins were associated with the Later Vedic polity.
Ashvamedha, Rajasuya and Vajapeya were performed to proclaim sovereignty, not to indicate its decline.

rows.title: Later Vedic society - four varnas, ashrama system, gotra, decline in the status of women
sub: Group-II S1-10: Later Vedic society - varna system, ashramas, changing status of women

secs.t: Varnas → role; groups outside the varna order — The fourfold order

x: The Purusha Sukta in the Tenth Mandala of the Rigveda contains the first statement of the fourfold varna order.
The Aitareya Brahmana described the Shudra as ‘
a servant of another
’ and stated that he could be expelled or struck at will.
Upadhyaya was a teacher who taught the Veda or Vedanga for a livelihood, not the head of a Vaishya gana.

secs.t: Varnas → role; groups outside the varna order — Rigidity and emergence of caste

x: Exam angle: "caste as a new form of social organisation" questions test that varna rigidified after the Rig Vedic phase.
Vratyas and Nishadas
were groups placed outside the formal four-varna order.
Later Vedic society witnessed discrimination against Shudras and Chandalas, but untouchability as a formal rule is associated with the post-Vedic Dharmasutras.

secs.t: Gotra and kinship terms → meaning

x: Kula, Vamsha and Gotra are kinship terms, whereas
Kosa
means treasury.
Gotra exogamy prohibited intra-gotra marriage, while caste endogamy and sapinda restrictions formed additional elements of the North Indian kinship pattern.
Irawati Karve
analysed sapinda and gotra rules and divided India into four kinship zones in Kinship Organization in India, published in 1953.

secs.t: Ashramas and purusharthas — stages, duties and goals

x: Exam angle: "Pancha Mahayajna performed in which ashrama?" - Grihastha.
Brahmacharya involved Vedic study, Grihastha involved household duties, Vanaprastha involved gradual withdrawal, and Sannyasa involved complete detachment.
The Pancha Mahayajnas were daily duties of the
Grihastha
, or householder, Ashrama.
Dharma, Artha and Kama formed the earlier trivarga in the Later Vedic-Sutra phase.
Dharma means duty, Artha wealth, Kama desire and Moksha liberation.

secs.t: Samskaras and upanayana → purpose

x: Exam angle: "mantra in the Kshatriya upanayana" = Trishtubh.
Upanayana was the sacred-thread initiation into Vedic study and was available to the Brahmana, Kshatriya and Vaishya varnas, but not to Shudras and women.

Pumsavana is to procure a male child (iii), Simantonnayana is for the safety of the child in the womb (iv), Jatakarma is at birth before cutting the cord (i), and Chudakarma is tonsure in the third year (ii).

secs.t: Marriage — eight forms and types

x: Exam angle: "marriage by purchase of bride" =
Asura
; capture = Rakshasa.
In the Arsha form,
the groom gave a token cow and bull to the bride’s father
Fraternal polyandry is associated with the Khas, sororal polygyny concerns sisters, group marriage involves several men and women, and polygyny is permitted for Muslims.

secs.t: Teachers and priests → terms

x: In the gurukula system, pupils
lived with the guru
An Acharya initiated the pupil through upanayana and taught the whole Veda without accepting a fee.
The Hotri recited the Rigveda, whereas the Udgatri chanted the Samaveda.

secs.t: Women — texts → statements on status

x: The Aitareya Brahmana calls the daughter a source of misery (iii); the Maitrayani Samhita lists liquor, dice and women as three evils (iv); the Shatapatha Brahmana says the wife is half her husband (i); the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad records Gargi's debate with Yajnavalkya (ii).
References to
child marriage and sati
appear in accounts of the declining status of women in Later Vedic society.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Later Vedic period witnessed the fixing of Varna and gotra rules rather than their absence.
Later Vedic society fixed Varna, gotra, samskaras and ashramas, forming the basis of later Dharmashastra society.
The social order of Satavahana Andhra was connected with the varna-ashrama framework and was not completely free from social differentiation.

rows.title: Vedic literature - four Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads, Vedangas, Sutras
sub: Group-II S1-11: Vedic literature - Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads, Vedangas

secs.t: Four Vedas — content, priests, Upavedas and FIRSTs

x: The Rigveda was recited by the Hotri, Samaveda chanted by the Udgatri, Yajurveda executed by the Adhvaryu and Atharvaveda supervised by the Brahman priest.
The
Samaveda
consists mainly of Rigvedic hymns set to melodies called saman and is regarded as the root of Indian music.
The
Samaveda
borrows almost all its verses from the Rigveda (about 1,549 verses, all but about 75 from the Rigveda), setting them to melody.

secs.t: Rigveda — mandala → content, family books, dating

x: The Early Vedic period is generally placed around
, although some comparative tables use the narrower range 1500–1100 BCE.
Mandala VI is associated with Bharadvaja, Mandala VII with Vasishtha and the Battle of Ten Kings, Mandala IX with Soma and Mandala X with the Purusha Sukta and Nasadiya hymn.
The Gayatri Mantra occurs in the
Third Mandala
of the Rigveda and is attributed to Vishvamitra in praise of Savitri.

secs.t: Veda → recensions, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads

x: C: the Krishna (Black) Yajurveda mixes mantras with prose, while the Shukla (White) Yajurveda contains mantras only.
The Shatapatha Brahmana belongs to the
Shukla Yajurveda
, while the Taittiriya Brahmana belongs to the Krishna Yajurveda.
The Shatapatha Brahmana narrates the eastward movement to Videha, mentions the Great Flood and gives the first reference to money-lending.

secs.t: Vedic layers, Vedangas and Sutras → meaning

x: Aranyakas are ‘forest texts’, generally concluding parts of the Brahmanas and forming a bridge from ritualism to philosophical speculation.
Shiksha is phonetics, Kalpa is rituals, Chandas is metrics and Jyotisha is astronomy.
Shrauta Sutras deal with
public rituals and large sacrifices
Grihya, Dharma and Sulba Sutras respectively concern domestic rites, law and social practice, and altar construction.

secs.t: Upanishads — number, teaching, saying → source

x: The Upanishads are anti-ritualistic philosophical texts that teach Atman–Brahman identity and discuss karma, samsara and moksha.
The prayer beginning ‘Asato ma sadgamaya’ and ‘Tamaso ma jyotirgamaya’ occurs in the
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
'Satyameva Jayate' comes from the
Mundaka Upanishad
(some sources wrongly say Mandukya).
Both 'Tat tvam asi' and Satyakama Jabala belong to the
Chandogya Upanishad

secs.t: Authors → works: grammarians, Sulba, Darsanas, Epics, Smritis

x: Nyaya is associated with Gautama, Vaisheshika with Kanada, Sankhya with Kapila and Purva Mimamsa with Jaimini.
Baudhayana
’s Sulbasutra contains the rule corresponding to the theorem now known as the Pythagoras theorem.
The Ramayana contains approximately 24,000 verses and is described as having been composed in five stages beginning from the 5th century BCE.
Manusmriti is regarded as the earliest Smriti, and Vijnaneshwara’s Mitakshara is a commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti.

secs.t: Earliest literary references to the Andhras — text → reference

x: Exam angle: "first literary reference to Andhras" = Aitareya Brahmana; "Andhakaratta" = Jain texts.
The Mahabharata, Arthashastra and Rajatarangini provide these respective references to the Andhras.
Megasthenes’ Indica describes the Andhras as possessing
30 fortified towns and a large army
Ashoka's
Rock Edict XIII
names the Andhras among the peoples within his empire.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Rigvedic hymns are invocations addressed to the devas, whereas Yajurvedic mantras are connected with the conduct of yajna.
The Eastern Chalukya inscriptions from Cheepurupalli and Nidamarru praise Brahmin scholars learned in the Vedas and Vedangas.
The Harappan script is undeciphered, while the Later Vedic cultural tradition is textually documented through oral transmission.
