rows.title: Vedic religion, ritual and philosophy; the six orthodox schools (shad-darshanas)

secs.t: Rigvedic gods → domain, hymn counts, parallels

x: Dyaus was the celestial father and sky deity, comparable to Jupiter or Zeus in Greek and Roman traditions.
Soma was associated with a plant and ritual drink, and
the entire Ninth Mandala of the Rigveda is devoted to Soma hymns
Mitra corresponds to Mithra, while Rita has the Iranian parallel Asha.

secs.t: Vedic rituals and Upanishadic concepts → terms and meaning

x: The
Grihya Sutras
governed domestic rites.
The Upanishadic teaching identifies Atman, the self, with Brahman, the cosmic principle.
The
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
introduced the doctrine of transmigration, connected with the cycle of rebirth.
Both statements are true, and the criticism of mechanical sacrifice explains the Upanishadic turn towards meditation and instruction through a guru.

secs.t: Six orthodox schools → founder, text, core idea, path

x: The traditional pairs are Nyaya–Vaisheshika, Samkhya–Yoga and Mimamsa–Vedanta.
All three statements correctly describe the core orientations of Nyaya, Vaisheshika and Purva Mimamsa.
Samkhya teaches liberation through discriminating Purusha from Prakriti, while Yoga provides the practical discipline and method for achieving it.
Yama, niyama, asana, pranayama and pratyahara are the five bahiranga limbs.

secs.t: Exponents → school

x: Shankaracharya was associated with Advaita; Ramanuja was the first true exponent of Vishishtadvaita and worshipped Narayana and Lakshmi; Ramananda brought the movement to the north.
Narahari Tirtha, a disciple of Madhva, spread
Dvaita
in Andhra-Kalinga, beginning from Srikurmam.
Kumarila Bhatta defended Vedic ritual (karma-kanda) and opposed Buddhist doctrines; Vishishtadvaita was founded by Ramanuja.

secs.t: Doctrine → school; astika vs nastika

x: Exam angle: odd-one-out lists mix one nastika school (Charvaka/Ajivika) among the six astikas.
Satkaryavada is a principal doctrine of
Samkhya
, holding that the effect pre-exists in the cause.
Astika
denotes the systems that accept Vedic authority, including the six orthodox darshanas.
Charvaka, Buddhism, Jainism and Ajivika
reject the authority of the Vedas and are classified as nastika traditions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Upanishadic concepts formed the philosophical and spiritual basis of later Hinduism.
Vivekananda's Neo-Vedanta reworked and presented the
Advaita
Vedanta tradition in a modern form.
The oldest Shivalinga mentioned is located at
Gudimallam in Chittoor district
The Ikshvaku king
Santamula
performed Ashvamedha, Rajasuya, Vajapeya and Agnistoma; an Ashvamedha altar exists at Nagarjunakonda.

src: Sources: APP (Indian History Part 1 > Vedic Age > Six Schools; Rig Vedic Religion; Vedic Deities; AP History > Satavahana Religion); UPSC (Ethics p.106; Ancient History p.36); CDI (Block01 Vedic Culture > Early Vedic Religion; Later Vedic; Block06 Vedanta); CDX (AP History pp.51, 65); APHQ (aph2012_11, aph2019_67); PYQ keys (APPSC-G1 2022/2023, APPSC-GS 2018, MPPSC 2025)

rows.title: The sixteen Mahajanapadas - list, capitals, monarchies vs ganasanghas (Anguttara Nikaya)
sub: Group-II S1-12: Causes for the rise of heterodox sects; the sixteen Mahajanapadas and the rise of Magadha

secs.t: Mahajanapadas → capital, region; sources

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G1 2024 - Avanti-Ujjain, Kosala-Shravasti, Vatsa-Kaushambi, Anga-Champa; Assaka capital =
Bodhan
Kashi was associated with the Ganga–Varuna confluence, Kosala with the Sarayu, Vatsa with the Yamuna and Avanti with the Sipra.
The Jain Bhagavati Sutra gives a different list and includes eastern and southern names such as
Vanga, Malava and Ladha
or Radha.
All four are correct (APPSC-G1 2024): Avanti's capital was Ujjain (Ujjayini), Kosala's Shravasti, Vatsa's Kaushambi and Anga's Champa.
The Suttanipata refers to
sage Bavari’s ashram on the Godavari in Assaka
, providing an early Andhra-region link in Buddhist literature.

secs.t: Monarchies vs gana-sanghas — features and clans

x: Vajji and Malla were gana-sanghas, and Kamboja was regarded as a later republic in the Arthashastra tradition.
Clan chiefs of a gana-sangha met in an assembly hall called the
santhagara
to conduct public affairs.
The Shakyas were associated with Kapilavastu, the Mallas with Kusinara and Pava, Buddha's parinirvana with Kusinara, and Mahavira's death with Pava.

secs.t: Rulers → kingdom and contributions — Buddha's age to the Nandas

x: Exam angle: "Bimbisara's dynasty" = Haryanka; "contemporary of Buddha" = Bimbisara.
Bimbisara, Prasenajit, Udayana and Pukkusati were associated with Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Gandhara respectively.
Chanda Pradyota of Avanti rivalled Bimbisara of Magadha and Udayana of Vatsa.
Udayin built Pataliputra, Ajatashatru defeated the Vajjis, and Kalashoka was associated with the Second Buddhist Council.
The Hathigumpha inscription states that a canal dug by Nandaraja, identified with Mahapadma Nanda, was extended by Kharavela.
Bimbisara
(544-492 BCE) is treated as the founder of the Haryanka dynasty (APPSC-GS 2018, BPSC 2024).

secs.t: Rise of Magadha — causes, rivalries, capitals

x: Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti were the four dominant powers of the period.
Kosala first annexed Kashi; Magadha subsequently acquired it through dowry and war.
Magadha benefited from fertile agriculture, iron resources, elephants and rivers.
Urban growth and metallic money increased economic activity and helped the state raise revenue.
Magadha became the most powerful Mahajanapada during the 6th to 4th centuries BCE.

secs.t: Foreign invasions — Persian and Alexander → events, years

x: The Persian presence contributed to the spread of the Kharosthi script in the north-western region.
Alexander crossed the Indus in 326 BCE, fought Porus at the Hydaspes, faced his army’s refusal beyond the Beas, and died at Babylon in 323 BCE.
Magadha was then ruled by the Nandas under
Dhana Nanda
, the last Nanda king.

secs.t: Causes for the rise of heterodox sects

x: Costly rituals, animal sacrifice, Sanskrit-centred religious practice and dissatisfaction with ritualism encouraged the rise of heterodox sects.
Mahavira and Buddha were Kshatriyas, and Kshatriya resentment of Brahmin dominance was one factor behind the rise of heterodox movements.
Vaishyas enriched by trade and money-lending sought higher social status and religious teachings that did not disapprove of their economic activities.

secs.t: Heterodox teachers → doctrine — Ajivikas, Charvaka

x: Exam angle: "philosophy of the Charvakas" = Lokayata.
The Ajivikas followed Niyati, or strict fatalism, and rejected karma and free will.
Ajita Kesakambali, Purana Kassapa and Pakudha Kaccayana were teachers of the period.
Ashoka and Dasharatha
gifted the Barabar caves to the Ajivikas.
The Charvaka philosophy is called
Lokayata
(APPSC 2025); it is materialist and accepts only perception.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Rajghat artefacts indicate that Varanasi’s urban origins date to approximately
800 BCE
Rajghat was the capital of Kashi, which was ruled by the Brahmadatta dynasty until Kosala annexed it.
The Mahajanapadas and the rise of Magadha were linked with the second urbanisation, the emergence of the first large Indian state and the rise of heterodox sects amid economic change.

src: Sources: Group-I: CDI (Block01 Mahajanapadas > Sixteen Mahajanapadas, Classification, Significance); UPSC (Ancient History pp.66-67, 72); CDX (AP History p.91 Anguttara Nikaya); APP (Mauryan Empire > Magadha's Rise); LENSD 8 Sep 2026; LENS Aug 2026 p.117; PYQ keys (APPSC-G1 2024, APPSC G2 2012, UPSC 2025, UPPSC 2020/2021, MPPSC 2019)

CURRENT lane for this row: no passages.

rows.title: Second urbanisation - NBPW, punch-marked coins, guilds (shreni), growth of towns

secs.t: Causes of second urbanisation — factor → effect

x: All four factors contributed to the second urbanisation: iron technology, agricultural surplus, expanding trade and monetisation, and the formation of states with administrative capitals.
New merchant classes, especially Vaishyas, supported
Buddhism and Jainism
during the period of expanding towns, trade and state formation.

secs.t: Chronology and FIRSTs of the economy

x: Iron ploughshares and axes in the Ganga valley belong to the
Later Vedic period, c. 1000-600 BCE
, which helped forest clearance and agriculture.
Punch-marked coins appeared around the 6th-5th century BCE, while large numbers of gold coins came only with the Kushanas (1st-2nd century CE).
Pali texts
provide the first definite literary references to coins, including kahapana, nikkha, kamsa and kakanika.

secs.t: Towns and sites → region and feature

x: NBPW, dated approximately to 700–200 BCE, followed Painted Grey Ware and served as a hallmark of the second urbanisation.
Rajghat has pre-NBPW levels about 3,000 years old, along with punch-marked coins and Greek-inscribed seals.
More than 60 towns flourished during the period from 600 to 300 BCE, including Pataliputra, Rajagriha, Shravasti, Varanasi, Vaishali, Champa, Kaushambi and Ujjayini.

secs.t: Punch-marked coins — features and coin terms

x: Punch-marked coins were called panas or karshapanas, carried various punched symbols and followed standard weights.
Karshapana or kahapana denoted a standard silver or copper punch-marked coin.
Satavahanas initially used inherited punch-marked coins and subsequently issued die-struck coins in lead, potin, copper and silver.

secs.t: Trade, merchant and banking terms; routes

x: Guild deposits at fixed interest, particularly those recorded in the Nashik inscription, demonstrate that guilds performed banking functions.
Gahapati, Vanija and Setthi are correctly matched.
Sarthavaha meant a caravan/convoy of merchants or its leader (UPPSC 2008).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Kotilingala, Dhulikatta and Kondapur were Satavahana trade centres, Sarthavahas were foreign-trade merchants, and Yajnasri Satakarni issued ship-mast coins.
Vaishya Tekri near Ujjain (Avanti's capital on the Sipra) is a BCE stupa bigger than Sanchi; it yielded punch-marked and cast Avanti coins, and its excavation is to resume after about 90 years.

src: Sources: CDI (Block01 Mahajanapadas > Urbanisation, Coinage, Introduction); UPSC (Ancient History p.44); CDX (AP History pp.21, 45-46); APP (AP History > Satavahana economy); APHQ (aph2019_36, aph2012_5); LENSD 8 Sep 2026, 23 Aug 2026; LENS Aug 2026 p.117; APPCA Jun 2026; PYQ keys (UPSC 2012/2026, RPSC 2018, UPPSC 2008/2010)

rows.title: Rise of Magadha - Haryankas (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru), Shishunagas, Nandas; causes of supremacy

secs.t: Causes of Magadhan supremacy — factor → effect

x: Iron, river transport and eastern elephants contributed to Magadhan power.
Magadha's society was relatively unorthodox, with little Vedic hold.
Nearby iron ore supplied material for weapons and tools.
Alluvial soil and ample rainfall supported agriculture, while the Ganga and Son aided transport and trade.

secs.t: Haryanka persons — queens, succession, physician

x: Kosaladevi belonged to Kosala, Chellana to the Lichchhavi clan of Vaishali, and Khema to Madra in Punjab.
Bimbisara's marriage with Kosaladevi (Mahakoshala) of Kosala brought Kashi as dowry, giving Magadha its revenue.
Buddhist texts preserve a patricide chain involving Bimbisara, followed by Ajatashatru and then Udayin.
Jivaka, the royal physician, was sent by Bimbisara to treat
Pradyota of Avanti
for jaundice.

secs.t: Capitals → who and why

x: Rajagriha was fortified by five hills, whereas Pataliputra functioned as a river fort.
Pataliputra stood at the confluence of the
Ganga and Son
, with the Gandak nearby.
Vaishali is associated with Shishunaga.

secs.t: Rulers → contributions, titles and FIRSTs

x: Bimbisara conquered Anga, Ajatashatru defeated the Vajji confederacy, Udayin shifted the capital to Pataliputra, and Kalashoka is associated with the Second Buddhist Council.
Bimbisara conquered Anga, entered into matrimonial alliances, and was a contemporary of both Buddha and Mahavira.
Ajatashatru fought the Vajji confederacy for
sixteen years
and ultimately defeated it.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Magadha's rise created the territorial and political base for the Mauryan Empire.
Kashi was associated with Brahmadatta and with Rajghat in present-day Varanasi.
The Nandas are described as the first non-Kshatriya dynasty and India's first empire-builders.

src: Sources: CDI (Block01 Mahajanapadas > Rise of Magadha factors; Haryanka; Ajatashatru; Udayin); UPSC (Ancient History pp.1, 73); APP (Mauryan Empire > Magadha's Rise; Factors; Buddha; Mahavira); LENSD 8 Sep 2026; PYQ keys (APPSC-GS 2018/2025, APPSC-G1 2022, BPSC 2024)

rows.title: Jainism - Tirthankaras, life of Mahavira, Triratna, Panchamahavratas, anekantavada and syadvada
sub: Group-II S1-13: Emergence of Jainism - Mahavira, doctrines, Triratna, Panchamahavratas

secs.t: Tirthankaras → symbol, nirvana place; FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: "24th Tirthankara" and "20th Tirthankara - Munisuvrat Swami" are direct one-liners; "24th / 20th / 1st Tirthankara was..." and symbol-matching.
The Rig Veda refers to Rishabha and Arishtanemi, while the Yajur Veda names Rishabha, Ajitanatha and Arishtanemi.
Parshvanatha renounced worldly life at the age of 30, not 40.
Rishabhadeva was the 1st, Neminatha the 22nd, Parshvanatha the 23rd and Mahavira the 24th Tirthankara.
Rishabhadeva is associated with the bull, Munisuvrata with the tortoise, Neminatha with the conch and Vasupujya with the buffalo.

secs.t: Mahavira — life events → detail; titles

x: Mahavira was born at Kundagrama near Vaishali, was the son of Siddhartha, and belonged to the Jnatrika clan.
Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana at Jrimbhikagrama, on the bank of the Rijupalika river, under a sal tree.
Mahavira's birth is traditionally placed
c. 599 BCE
at Kundagrama near Vaishali (the date is debatable; some sources give 540 BCE).

secs.t: Persons → association with Mahavira and Jain thought

x: Exam angle: two traps - "preacher of Syadvada" = Kundakundacharya; "title Syadvadachala Simha" = Somadeva Suri.
Jina, Kevalin, Nirgrantha, Mahavira and Arhat are titles associated with Mahavira.
Makkhali Gosala was Mahavira’s companion for some years and later founded the Ajivika sect.
Kundakundacharya
, the great Digambara philosopher, is the answer for 'who preached Syadvada' (APPSC 2008).

secs.t: Jain philosophy — terms and doctrines → meaning

x: Exam angle: questions test which set belongs to which religion.
Jiva refers to the conscious soul, whereas Ajiva denotes non-conscious matter or non-living reality.
In Jainism, karma is understood as material bondage clinging to the soul and causing rebirth.
Jain liberation involves stopping the inflow of karma and shedding accumulated karma, or nirjara, through penance, ultimately leading to Kevala Jnana and the Siddha state.
Jainism is associated with Anekantavada, Syadvada and Nayavada; Buddhism with anatta and pratityasamutpada; Ajivikas with niyati; and Charvaka with materialism.

secs.t: Panchamahavratas, Anuvratas and Jain practices — vows, rituals, Sallekhana

x: Exam angle: "Santhara is a ritual of fasting to death amongst - Jains".
Paryushana is the Jain festival, its last day Samvatsari is the day of forgiveness, Pratikramana is introspection, and Sallekhana is the ritual fast unto death.
Because Jain ahimsa extends to all forms of life, strict followers avoided agriculture since ploughing and related activities could injure organisms in the soil.

secs.t: Jainism and Buddhism compared

x: Jainism regards the soul as eternal and karma as material bondage.
Jainism follows a stricter interpretation of ahimsa, extending even to thought.
All four statements correctly describe the monastic traditions and textual languages or collections associated with Jainism and Buddhism.
Jainism uses the concept of kevala jnana, while Buddhism refers to nirvana or Buddhahood.

secs.t: Jainism in Andhra — places → feature, royal patrons

x: Vaddamanu or Vardhamanapuram is located in Guntur and is associated with a basadi or vihara built by Samprati in Mahavira's name.
Danavulapadu is a Jain kshetra at Jammalamadugu in YSR Kadapa district, associated with Rashtrakuta ruler Indra III.
The Bhadrabahu–Chandragupta route to Shravanabelagola passed through Kurnool and Anantapur
, supporting the description of Rayalaseema as a Jain corridor.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Anekantavada recognises the many-sided nature of reality and is therefore cited as a basis of pluralism and tolerance.
Jain
ahimsa
significantly influenced Gandhi's philosophy and his emphasis on non-violence.
Jainism's severe austerities limited its mass appeal, while loss of royal patronage and the Digambara–Svetambara split contributed to its later decline.

src: Sources: Group-I: CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.82-83, 193); CDI (Block01 Jainism - key terms, comparison, personalities); APP (Indian History Part 1 > Jainism: Origins, Teachings, Doctrines table); UPSC (Ancient History pp.46-47, 64); APHQ (aph2011_3, aph2008_23, aph2025_53); LENS Apr 2025 pp.18-19

Sources: Group-II S1-13: CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.82-83); CDI (Block01 Jainism - teachings, key terms, decline, comparison); APP (Indian History Part 1 > Jainism: Teachings, Origins, Spread); UPSC (Ancient History pp.46, 64); LENS Apr 2025 pp.18-19

rows.title: Jain councils, Digambara-Svetambara split, Jain literature (Angas), spread and royal patrons
sub: Group-II S1-14: Jain councils, sects, literature, spread and royal patronage

secs.t: Jain councils → place, year, president, outcome

x: Sthulabhadra
presided over the first Jain council at Pataliputra.
The first council arranged the canon into twelve Angas and is traditionally associated with the first Jain split.
Vallabhi, 512 CE, Maitraka patronage.
The Jain conference at Venkatathatipuri during the Satavahana era was presided over by
Arhabali

secs.t: Digambara vs Svetambara → leader, dress, beliefs; sub-sects

x: Digambaras are sky-clad, Svetambaras wear white robes, Sthanakvasis oppose idol worship, and Terapanthi was founded by Acharya Bhikshu.
Digambara doctrine holds that women must be reborn as men before attaining moksha; Svetambaras accept the possibility of liberation for women.
The sectarian division is traditionally linked with a twelve-year famine in Magadha under Chandragupta Maurya, during which Bhadrabahu led a southern migration.

secs.t: Jain canon — terms → meaning

x: Exam angle: odd-one-out - Jain texts (Acharanga, Bhagavati, Kalpasutra) vs Buddhist (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa, Divyavadana, Milindapanho).
The Svetambara canon includes twelve Angas, while Digambaras maintain that all the original Angas were lost and follow a separate canon.
Acharanga Sutra (monks' code of conduct), Bhagavati Sutra (doctrines) and Kalpasutra are Jain texts.

secs.t: Jain books → authors

x: Exam angle: Samayasara (asked 2008 and 2019), Yogasara (2017) - all Kundakundacharya.
The Tattvartha Sutra, associated with Umasvati, presents core Jain doctrines and is accepted in versions by both the Digambara and Svetambara traditions.
Samayasara (like Yogasara, Pravachanasara and Panchastikaya) is by
Kundakundacharya
, who founded the Saraswati gachcha at Konakondla in Anantapur.

secs.t: Royal patrons → dynasty and Jain link

x: Kharavela's influence extended to the areas corresponding to present-day
Srikakulam and Vizianagaram
districts.
Chandragupta Maurya is traditionally described as a disciple of Bhadrabahu who migrated south and ended his life by sallekhana at Shravanabelagola.
Simuka or Srimukha is identified as the first Satavahana Jain patron; the Kalpa Pradeepa attributes 52 Jain temples to his 52 army chiefs.
Indra III built a Jain kshetra at Danavulapadu in Kadapa, not the Gommateshwara statue at Shravanabelagola.

secs.t: Spread and Jain sites → region

x: The famine tradition states that Bhadrabahu, the sixth Thera, travelled south with Chandragupta to
Shravanabelagola
in Karnataka.
Dilwara is at Mount Abu in Rajasthan, Shravanabelagola is in Karnataka, Udayagiri-Khandagiri is in Odisha, and Sammed Shikhar is in Jharkhand.
Sammed Shikhar or Shikharji is situated on
Parasnath Hill
in Jharkhand and is associated with the nirvana of Parsvanatha.

secs.t: Jainism in AP — FIRSTs, centres, patrons, decline

x: Danavulapadu is associated with Rashtrakuta Indra III; Vijayawada with Ayyana Mahadevi’s Nedumbasadi; Munugodu with Pudvithilakavasati; and Ramatirtham with the Eastern Chalukya period.
Ganapatideva’s persecution is mentioned in Siddeshwara Charitra, while the flight of a Jain monk to Hanamkonda from Rajaraja Narendra’s persecution is recorded in the Orugallu Kaifiyat.
Mailama, wife of the Kakatiya minister Betana
, built the Kadalalaya Basadi (1117 CE Padmakshi inscription).

secs.t: Contributions of Jainism — language, literature, social base

x: Early Jains used popular Prakrit instead of Sanskrit, which helped their spread.
Strict ahimsa made agriculture problematic because ploughing and related activities could injure living organisms.
Jainism challenged birth-based hierarchy, emphasised conduct and action, and promoted vegetarianism in accordance with ahimsa.
In Andhra under the Eastern Chalukyas,
Shudras
adopted Jainism as a means of social advancement.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The factors identified were loss of royal patronage, sectarian split, severe austerity, lack of missionary zeal and rival Bhakti revival.

The stated regional tradition associates Kalamukha/Vira Shaiva hostility with the persecution of Jains by Ganapatideva at Anmakonda, while Anmakonda also served as a refuge from Eastern Chalukya persecution.
The Samrat Samprati Museum was inaugurated at
Koba in Gujarat
to highlight Jain heritage.

rows.title: Buddhism - life of the Buddha, Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, Pratityasamutpada, Sangha
sub: Group-II S1-15: Emergence of Buddhism - Buddha's life, Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path

secs.t: The Buddha's family and life → persons and ages

x: All four statements correctly describe Siddhartha Gautama's clan, parents, foster mother, wife and son.
Mahapajapati Gautami was Buddha's foster or step-mother, not a teacher of his austerities.
Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta were his teachers.
Buddha did not name an individual successor; the Dhamma and Vinaya were to be the teacher after his death.

secs.t: Events of the Buddha's life → place and present-day site

x: Exam angle: "first sermon" = Sarnath; birth-enlightenment-sermon-death match.
Dhammachakra Pravartana, the first sermon at Sarnath, expounded
the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path
The five former companions were
Kondanna, Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahanama and Assaji
; they became arhats after the first sermon.
Buddha attained Mahaparinirvana at Kusinara at the age of 80, traditionally dated to 483 BCE; some accounts give an approximate alternative date.
Birth = Lumbini (Rumindei, Nepal); Enlightenment = Bodh Gaya (Uruvela); First sermon = Sarnath (Deer Park, Rishipatana); Mahaparinirvana = Kushinagar (Kusinara).

secs.t: Epithets, disciples and royal followers → persons

x: Ananda was the personal attendant and recited the Sutta Pitaka; Upali recited the Vinaya Pitaka; Mahakassapa presided over the First Council; Subhadda was the last convert.
Sariputta and Mahamoggallana were chief disciples, and their relics are associated with
Sanchi
Bimbisara and Ajatashatru ruled Magadha, Prasenajit ruled Kosala and Udayana ruled Kausambi.

secs.t: Core teachings — terms → meaning

x: The Middle Path avoids both the extreme of severe asceticism and the opposite extreme of sensual indulgence.
Anicca means impermanence, while Anatta teaches that there is no permanent, unchanging self or atman.
Buddhist karma is intention-based morality; the present state is linked to past actions, and rebirth continues until nirvana.

secs.t: Doctrines asked as lists — Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, twelve nidanas

x: Samudaya identifies the cause of suffering, especially craving, ignorance and attachment.
Samma-ditthi means Right View, Sankappa means Right Intention, Vaca means Right Speech and Samadhi means Right Concentration.
Both statements are true, and the identification of Magga as the path to cessation directly explains why the Eightfold Path has this role.
Pratityasamutpada
is the doctrine of dependent origination, according to which phenomena arise through causal conditions.

secs.t: Triratna and the Sangha — rules and monastic terms

x: Parivrajaka means wandering ascetic, Shramana means an ascetic outside the Vedic fold, Upasaka means lay follower and Uposatha is the confession and rule-recitation observance.
Pravrajya means leaving lay life or going forth; Upasampada denotes full ordination.
Women were admitted after requests associated with
Ananda and Mahapajapati Gotami
, who became the first nun.
Shaved heads, yellow/saffron robes and daily alms marked monastic life.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Anagarika Dharmapala
founded the Maha Bodhi Society in 1891 to work for the restoration of Bodh Gaya to Buddhist control.
All four statements correctly describe the rational, moderate and socially accessible nature of Buddhism, its rejection of Vedic ritual and caste, and the role of the organised Sangha in its spread.

rows.title: Buddhist councils (four), Hinayana-Mahayana-Vajrayana, Tripitakas and Pali literature
sub: Group-II S1-16: Buddhist councils, Hinayana-Mahayana-Vajrayana, Tripitakas and the spread of Buddhism

secs.t: Buddhist councils → year, place, patron, president

x: Exam angle: council-president matching and chronological order of venues.
The Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka was held on the advice of the monk
Parsva
and dealt with Sarvastivada disputes in Kashmir and Gandhara.
First Council (Rajagriha) - Mahakassapa; Second (Vaishali) - Sabakami; Third (Pataliputra) - Moggaliputta Tissa; Fourth (Kundalvana) - Vasumitra, with Ashvaghosha as deputy.
Rajagriha (483 BCE, First), Vaishali (383 BCE, Second), Pataliputra (c. 250 BCE, Third), Kundalvana in Kashmir (1st c. CE, Fourth).

secs.t: Tripitakas and the five Nikayas → content

x: Patimokkha, Vibhanga and Khandhaka
are sub-texts of the Vinaya Pitaka, which deals with monastic discipline.
Long discourses and the Mahaparinibbana Sutta are in the Digha Nikaya; the Anguttara is arranged by number and lists the 16 Mahajanapadas.
The Anguttara Nikaya is arranged numerically and includes the list of the sixteen Mahajanapadas.

secs.t: Non-canonical Buddhist texts → language, author, tradition

x: Milindapanha is framed as a dialogue between the Indo-Greek ruler Menander, called Milinda, and the Buddhist monk Nagasena.
Divyavadana
is a Sanskrit collection of Buddhist legends and is associated with the Mahayana tradition.
Aryamanjushrimulakalpa
is a Sanskrit Mahayana-Vajrayana text containing historical data.
Mahavamsa is a Pali Sri Lankan chronicle written by
Mahanama

secs.t: Sects — Hinayana, Mahayana, Vajrayana → features

x: The Arhat ideal of individual liberation belongs to Hinayana/Theravada.
Myanmar
is traditionally associated with Hinayana or Theravada.
Vajrayana developed approximately in the
8th century CE
Vajrayana is linked with
Padmasambhava
The six paramitas are dana, sila, kshanti, virya, dhyana and prajna.

secs.t: Philosophical schools → founder and doctrine

x: Madhyamika philosophy is based on Sunyata, or emptiness, and seeks a middle position between the extremes of existence and non-existence.
Vaibhashika or Sarvastivada expresses the view that all exists, meaning that dharmas exist in the past, present and future.
Mahasanghika, which adopted relatively relaxed rules, is described as the parent of the
Chaitika and Mahayana
traditions.

secs.t: Nagarjuna → school, works, titles, patron

x: The Maha Vihara, also called Parvata Vihara, at Sriparvata is associated with Satavahana ruler
Yajna Sri Satakarni
, who was contemporary and friendly with Nagarjuna.
Suhrlekha was a letter to a Satavahana king, I-tsing noticed its memorisation, and tradition connects Nagarjuna with the Fourth Council and 32 sects in Andhradesha.
The philosophical Nagarjuna founded Madhyamika and Sunyavada, whereas Siddha Nagarjuna is distinguished as the founder of Vajrayana at Sriparvata and is described as a Telugu native.

secs.t: Buddhist scholars → school and work

x: Vasubandhu
wrote Abhidharmakosa and was the brother of Asanga.
Buddhaghosha was born near Guntur (Kota Nemapuri).
Dignaga wrote
Pramana Samuccaya
and is regarded as the father of Indian logic.
Dharmakirti
is known as the “Kant of India” and wrote Pramana Vartika and Nyaya Bindu.
Bhavaviveka
, author of the Tarkajvala, was an acharya at Sriparvata (APPSC G2 2019).

secs.t: Andhra angle — Mahadeva Bhikshu, sect centres, Andhra path

x: Mahadeva's five questions at the Vaishali council triggered the schism.
The
Vinayavatthu
mentions the 'Andhra path' (APPSC G2 2019).
In Andhra, Hinayana was associated with Amaravati, Mahayana with Sriparvata and Vajrayana with Salihundam.
Purvasaila was at Amaravati, Aparasaila at Nagarjunakonda and Siddhadhika at Gudivada.

secs.t: Stupa architecture — terms, types, major stupas

x: A
chaitya
is a Buddhist prayer hall, whereas a vihara is a monastery or residence for monks.
Sanchi was built by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE, encased in stone under the Shungas, and received UNESCO World Heritage status in 1989.
The four toranas of Sanchi are associated with the
Satavahanas
, although the stupa had earlier origins under Ashoka and was later encased under the Shungas.

secs.t: Spread abroad and decline in India → causes

x: Ashoka’s mission to Sri Lanka is associated with
Mahendra and Sanghamitra
The Kushan-era Silk Route and sea trade facilitated the spread of Buddhism.
Mahayana entered Tibet in the seventh century and later merged with Vajrayana and the indigenous Bon tradition.
Nalanda was sacked by
Bakhtiyar Khalji
during the Turkish raids.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Odisha’s Buddhist Diamond Triangle consists of
Ratnagiri, Udayagiri and Lalitagiri
in the Jajpur-Cuttack region.
China insists on
the 1793 Golden Urn rule
in the Dalai Lama succession controversy.
The Tibetan Buddhist canon is associated with the
Kangyur and Tengyur
All the named figures—Nagarjuna, Aryadeva, Buddhaghosha, Dinnaga and Bhavaviveka—are identified with Andhra’s Buddhist intellectual tradition.

rows.title: Spread and decline of Buddhism; Buddhist and Jain architecture - stupa, chaitya, vihara

secs.t: Patrons and hostile rulers → role in spread and decline

x: Veerapurushadatta was the Ikshvaku king who rebuilt the Nagarjunakonda Maha Chaitya and Sriparvata University; Vikramashila was a Pala (Dharmapala) Vajrayana centre, so A is the wrong pair.
Upasika Bodhisri rendered outstanding service in the reign of the Ikshvaku king
Ehuvala Chantamula
Pushyamitra Shunga, Shashanka and Mihirakula
are identified as hostile rulers associated with the decline of Buddhism.

secs.t: Stupa parts → meaning; types; stupa vs chaitya vs vihara

x: Chhatri refers to the umbrella or umbrellas placed above the stupa, symbolising royalty and protection.
Dhatugarbha contains bodily relics, Paribhogika contains objects used by Buddha, and Uddeshika is memorial in character.
An Arama was a larger Buddhist complex containing
a stupa, vihara, chaitya and school
Ayaka pillars or Ayakapata are a distinctive
Andhra
feature; the Purna Kumbha is among their associated symbols.

secs.t: Aniconic symbols → event in the Buddha's life

x: The Bodhi tree and the empty seat symbolise the
enlightenment
of Buddha.
The horse Kanthaka represents renunciation, the Dharmachakra represents the first sermon, and footprints, along with the stupa, represent parinirvana.
The first human-form representations of Buddha appeared in the 1st century CE, particularly in the Gandhara and Mathura schools.

secs.t: Major stupas → builder, period, FIRSTs and largest

x: Piprahwa
in Uttar Pradesh, identified with ancient Kapilavastu, has an inscribed relic vessel linked to the Buddha’s kin and is dated among the earliest stupas, around the fifth century BCE.
Vaishya Tekri is believed to contain a Mauryan third-century BCE stupa associated with Ashoka’s wife Devi and possibly identified with Kanakagiri Vihara.

secs.t: Buddhist and Jain caves → state and sect

x: Bhaja is in Maharashtra, Bagh in Madhya Pradesh, Udayagiri-Khandagiri in Odisha and Sittanavasal in Tamil Nadu.
Karle, with its great chaitya, received a village from Pulumavi II for the Mahasanghikas.
Ajanta has 25 viharas and four chaityas.
Ellora has 34 caves, comprising 17 Hindu, 12 Buddhist and five Jain caves.

secs.t: Monasteries and universities → patrons, scholars

x: Nalanda
is associated with a Gupta foundation under Kumaragupta I. Vikramashila and Odantapuri were associated with the Palas, while Vallabhi was associated with the Maitrakas.
Vikramashila was associated with Dharmapala, Valabhi with the Maitrakas, Odantapuri with Gopala, and Dhanyakataka/Sriparvata with Nagarjuna and Bhavaviveka.
Vikramashila
in Bihar was a major Vajrayana centre patronised by the Pala ruler Dharmapala.

secs.t: Buddhist sites in Andhra → district, features

x: Nagarjunakonda was an Ikshvaku capital, is situated on an island in the Nagarjuna Sagar, and contains over thirty stupas including evidence of a Sinhala vihara.
Guntupalli in West Godavari district is regarded as
the only rock-cut cave temple and the oldest chaitya in Andhra Pradesh
Thotlakonda and Bavikonda are hilltop monasteries in Visakhapatnam district and are linked with Sri Lanka–Southeast Asia trade connections.

secs.t: Ancient names → present site; Andhra sect centres

x: The Buddhist literary name
Siddharthaka Chaitya
is identified with Guntupalli.
Hiuen Tsang found Sriparvata without patronage in the seventh century CE.
Vijayapuri was a Buddhist centre during the
3rd–4th centuries CE
Per the APPSC G2 2012 key, Purvasaila was at Dhanyakataka (Amaravati), and both Aparasaila and Rajagirika at Sriparvata (Nagarjunakonda).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sarnath was on the UNESCO
Tentative List
since 1998 and was nominated for the UNESCO list in 2025–26.
The ‘Discover Andhra’ campaign focused on the Buddhist circuit comprising Amaravati, Bavikonda and Thotlakonda.
Srinatha’s
Haravilasam
describes sea trade under the Reddi kings.

rows.title: Other heterodox sects - Ajivikas (Makkhali Gosala), Charvaka/Lokayata materialism

secs.t: Heterodox teachers and founders → doctrines

x: Akriyavada, associated with Purana Kassapa, held that actions have no moral consequence; even killing or charity produces neither merit nor demerit.
Nigantha Nataputta is the name used for
Mahavira
in the account of the contemporary heterodox teachers.
Gautama Buddha was the teacher of Buddhism, Makkhali Gosala led the Ajivika tradition, Ajita Kesakambalin represented materialism and Sanjaya Belatthiputta was associated with skepticism.

secs.t: Ajivikas → doctrine and features

x: Exam angle: statement-sets - determinism
and
austerity true; "order of rebirth can be changed" false; caste discrimination false.
Ajivikas believed in determinism, denied free will and held that beings were powerless before fate.
Gosala spent about six years as Mahavira's companion before breaking away to lead the Ajivikas.
The
Majjhima Nikaya
records debates involving the Buddha, Jains and Ajivikas.

secs.t: Rulers → patronage, Barabar caves, survival and decline

x: The Barabar caves are
among the earliest rock-cut caves in India
and were donated by Ashoka to the Ajivikas.
The Seventh Pillar Edict of Ashoka, associated with Delhi-Topra, names the Ajivikas along with
Brahmanas, the Sangha and Nirgranthas
The Ajivikas survived for nearly 2,000 years and disappeared around
the 14th century CE
in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

secs.t: Charvaka/Lokayata → names, tenets, aphorism

x: Exam angle: name-matching (Lokayata, Barhaspatya) and "which school accepts only perception".
Charvaka identifies the conscious body with the soul and denies the survival of a separate soul after death.
Charvaka accepts perception but rejects both inference and the authority of the Vedas.
The aphorism expresses the
Charvaka
rejection of an afterlife and its emphasis on material enjoyment during the present life.

secs.t: Texts and inscriptions → sources on the sects

x: The Samannaphala Sutta, contained in the Digha Nikaya, presents Ajatashatru’s report of the views of the six teachers to the Buddha.
The
Bhagavati Sutra
, a Jain Anga, provides the fullest account of Gosala and his quarrel with Mahavira.
Ashokan edicts, Barabar cave inscriptions, the Bhagavati Sutra and the Samannaphala Sutta all provide evidence for the study of heterodox sects, including the Ajivikas.

secs.t: Heterodox schools compared → karma, soul, fate, Vedas

x: Jainism accepts an eternal jiva in all things.
Jainism treats karma as material bondage removable by penance, Buddhism views it through intention, and Ajivikas deny its power to alter destiny.
The Shramana reaction, including Jainism, Buddhism, Ajivika and Charvaka currents, arose amid
urbanisation and Magadhan patronage
in the sixth century BCE.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Charvaka accepts only perception.
These sects reflect the intellectual ferment of the sixth century BCE and the religious pluralism of the Mauryan period.

rows.title: Persian and Macedonian invasions - Alexander's campaign, Battle of Hydaspes, effects on India

secs.t: Achaemenid (Persian) rulers → Indian territory

x: Cyrus
, the founder of the Achaemenid Empire, was the first Achaemenid ruler to campaign into the Indian north-west, particularly the Gandhara region.
Darius I
annexed Punjab and Sindh west of the Indus.
Herodotus described the Indian satrapy as the most populous and fertile.

secs.t: Persian influence → script, edicts, pillars, administration

x: Kharosthi was written from right to left.
Ashokan edicts reflect the Darius model through the terms lipi or dipi and the stylistic movement from third-person opening to first-person expression.
Ashokan pillars resemble Persian pillars in polished surfaces and animal capitals.

secs.t: Political situation on the eve of invasion → causes of Alexander's success

x: The huge army of the Nanda kingdom deterred Alexander from advancing farther east.
Alexander's success was attributed to the absence of a central power, his superior army and assistance from traitorous Indian rulers.
Greek writers called
Dhana Nanda
'Agrammes' or 'Xandrames'; his huge army deterred Alexander, though he was unpopular for heavy taxation.

secs.t: Alexander and Indian rulers → submitted or resisted

x: Exam angle: "which people's women fought Alexander" = Massaga; "first to submit" = Ambhi.
The Malloi or Malavas
and other gana-sanghas fought Alexander during his retreat.
The Assakenoi (Ashvakas), with their capital at Massaga in the Swat valley, resisted fiercely, and their women took up arms after heavy losses (UPPSC 2013).

secs.t: Events → year: route, Hydaspes, retreat, death

x: Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush in 327 BC and entered India through the Khyber Pass in 326 BC.
War weariness, homesickness, disease and fear of the Nanda army contributed to the refusal.
Hyphasis was the Greek name for the
Beas
, beyond which Alexander's army refused to advance.
The campaign lasted about 19 months; he died at Babylon in 323 BCE.

secs.t: Rivers and places → feature

x: The Hydaspes was the Jhelum, called Vitasta in Sanskrit.
Alexander founded Bucephala, named after his horse, and Nicaea near the Hydaspes battlefield.

secs.t: Effects of the invasion → satrapies, contact, politics

x: The invasion opened direct contact between Greece and India and encouraged new land and sea routes.
The accounts of Onesicritus and Nearchus recorded observations on
Indian geography and society
The invasion destroyed several small north-western states and cleared the way for Chandragupta, who expelled the Greek satraps with Porus, also called Parvataka, as an ally.

secs.t: Writers → accounts of Alexander's campaign

x: Nearchus
, Alexander's admiral, accompanied him and left a first-hand account.
Arrian
was a later writer who reconstructed the campaign.
Deimachus was
a later envoy of Antiochus I to Bindusara
and did not accompany Alexander.
Greek writers used the name Sandrokottas for
Chandragupta Maurya
, helping establish the chronology of the early Mauryas around 322 BCE.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Alexander's invasion is regarded as the first dated event of Indian history, and Greek accounts help fix the chronology of the Mauryas.
Persian contact during the sixth–fifth centuries BC left lasting influences on script and art, while Alexander's nineteen-month campaign left almost no lasting political mark.

rows.title: Sources for the Mauryas - Arthashastra, Indica of Megasthenes, Mudrarakshasa, edicts

secs.t: Arthashastra → author, rediscovery, subject

x: Kautilya is also known as Chanakya and Vishnugupta.
It was published in 1909; 1837 is the year James Prinsep deciphered the Ashokan edicts.
Both works are commonly compared for their realist approach to politics and their emphasis on ends-justify-means reasoning.
Kautilya's
Arthashastra
deals with administration, economy, espionage and taxation.

secs.t: Indica of Megasthenes → observations and errors

x: Megasthenes referred to Pataliputra as
Palibothra
, also rendered in some accounts as Polibrotha.
Megasthenes described seven classes and noted endogamy and hereditary occupations.
Both are known errors of the Indica tradition.
Megasthenes
' Indica is the first foreign work to mention the Andhras, with 30 fortified towns and 1,00,000 infantry besides cavalry and elephants.

secs.t: Literary works → author and content

x: The drama deals with the overthrow of the Nandas and the rise of Chandragupta Maurya.
Mamulanar's Sangam reference concerns the
southward push
of the Mauryas.
The Puranas provide Mauryan king lists and genealogies, with the
Vishnu Purana
being the one usually cited.
Vamsatthapakasini
is identified as a commentary on the Mahavamsa.

secs.t: Buddhist and Jain texts → ruler each covers

x: Parishishtaparvan, a Jain work by Hemachandra, describes Chandragupta's conversion to Jainism under Bhadrabahu and his subsequent renunciation.
Jain sources associate Chandragupta with Bhadrabahu, Jainism and his death at
Shravanabelagola
Mahavamsa and Dipavamsa concern Ashoka and Buddhism in Lanka; Divyavadana and Ashokavadana contain Ashokan legends; Parishishtaparvan describes Chandragupta's Jain end; the Puranas give genealogies.

secs.t: Inscriptions and archaeological sites → Mauryan facts

x: The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I is dated approximately to 150 CE and records the construction of the Sudarshana lake during Chandragupta Maurya's reign by the governor Pushyagupta.
The ruins of the 80-pillared hall of Pataliputra are located at
Kumrahar near Patna
The wide distribution of punch-marked coins and Northern Black Polished Ware indicates the
spread of Mauryan material culture

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Indica is regarded as the first foreign work to mention the Andhras, and Ashoka's Thirteenth Major Rock Edict names them.

rows.title: Chandragupta Maurya and Bindusara - conquests, treaty with Seleucus, Chanakya
sub: Group-II S1-17: Mauryan Empire - sources, Chandragupta, Bindusara and Ashoka

secs.t: Persons → other names, titles and Greek names

x: Sandrocottus or Sandrokottas, used by Greek writers, refers to
Chandragupta Maurya
Sir William Jones
made the identification in 1793.
The identification fixed an important point in early Indian chronology and placed Chandragupta around
322 BCE
, contemporaneous with Alexander.
Amitraghata means ‘
slayer of foes
’ or ‘slayer of enemies’; the Greek form was Amitrochates.

secs.t: Chandragupta Maurya → origin, Chanakya and the overthrow of the Nandas

x: Brahmanical sources connect the name Maurya with Mura, while Buddhist and Jain traditions identify Chandragupta with the Kshatriya Moriya clan.
The tradition describes Chanakya as raising an army, eliminating the Greek satraps, allying with Porus and finally besieging Pataliputra.
Chandragupta Maurya took the Magadhan throne in 321 BC from
Dhana Nanda
, with the assistance of Chanakya.

secs.t: Chandragupta's conquests → army, regions, governors

x: Chandragupta expelled the Greek satraps, won four provinces from Seleucus up to Afghanistan, Mamulanar refers to the Mauryas' southward expansion, and Jain tradition places him at Shravanabelagola.
Chandragupta became ruler in 321 BC, defeated Seleucus in 305 BC, later died at Shravanabelagola, and Sudarshana lake was repaired by Rudradaman I much later.

secs.t: Treaty with Seleucus Nicator, c. 305 BCE → provisions

x: Seleucus I Nicator
, a general of Alexander, attempted to recover the north-west but was defeated by Chandragupta.
The ceded territories were Aria, Arachosia, Paropanisadai and Gedrosia.
Chandragupta gave Seleucus
500 war elephants
as part of the treaty arrangement.
The treaty tradition states that
Seleucus’s daughter Helena was married to Chandragupta Maurya

secs.t: Chandragupta and Jainism → Bhadrabahu, famine, Sallekhana

x: Chandragupta is described in Jain tradition as a disciple of
Bhadrabahu
, the sixth Jain Thera.
Jain tradition states that Chandragupta abdicated, became an ascetic and died by Sallekhana, or fasting to death, at Shravanabelagola.
The famine tradition is linked with the division between the Digambara tradition associated with Bhadrabahu and the Svetambara tradition associated with Sthulabhadra.

secs.t: Bindusara → reign, family, foreign contacts, revolts

x: Bindusara (birth name Simhasena) was the son of Chandragupta and Durdhara.
Bindusara requested sweet wine, dried figs and a philosopher.
Bindusara is generally described as a patron of the
Ajivikas
, although some traditions indicate an inclination towards Jainism.
Taxila revolts were directed against oppressive officials; Susima failed, Ashoka was then sent, and Kunala handled another revolt during Ashoka’s reign.

secs.t: Greek envoys → sent by and court; Megasthenes' Indica

x: Exam angle: "Who first mentioned Andhra forts?" = Megasthenes.
Megasthenes
was sent by Seleucus I Nicator to Chandragupta’s court and wrote Indica.
The original Indica has not survived; it is known through quotations by
Strabo, Arrian and Diodorus
Megasthenes claimed that India had no slaves, but the Arthashastra and Ashokan edicts indicate that slavery did exist.

secs.t: Mauryan rulers → religion

x: Bindusara is associated with Ajivika beliefs.
Samprati
is known as the 'Ashoka of Jainism' and is associated with Jainism.
The Barabar caves in Bihar are the oldest surviving rock-cut caves and are carved in granite.
Ashoka and Dasharatha dedicated the Barabar caves to the
Ajivikas
, the sect also patronised by Bindusara.

secs.t: Extent of the empire → southern limits and Andhra sites

x: Yerragudi has major and minor edicts.
Rock Edict XIII names the Andhras among peoples following Ashoka's Dhamma within his domain; the edict is dated approximately to 256 BCE.
The Satavahanas began as Mauryan feudatories, and the Andhras are described as already Buddhist by the time of Rock Edict XIII.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Megasthenes
was the first Greek envoy to an Indian court and visited the court of Chandragupta Maurya.
Mauryan rule reached the Deccan.
Samprati
is associated with the spread of Jainism in Andhra.

rows.title: Ashoka - accession, Kalinga War, Dhamma and its content, Dhamma Mahamatras

secs.t: Ashoka → titles, early career, accession and sources

x: Ashoka used Devanampiya in the sense of beloved of the gods and Piyadasi in the sense of of pleasing looks.
The Ashokavadana or Divyavadana, written in Sanskrit, associates Ashoka with Upagupta, the Taxila campaign and the legend of Chandashoka becoming Dharmashoka.
The Mahavamsa and Dipavamsa are Sri Lankan Pali accounts associated with Nigrodha and Mahinda, and the Mahavamsa depicts early Ashoka as cruel.

secs.t: Kalinga War → motive, year, edict, policy shift

x: The Kalinga War took place around 261 BCE, in Ashoka's eighth regnal year.
RE XIII records the Kalinga War and Ashoka's remorse.
Ashoka described a shift from Bherighosha, the sound of the war drum, to Dhammaghosha, the proclamation of Dhamma.
Ashoka's empire extended from the Hindukush to Bengal and included Afghanistan and Baluchistan.

secs.t: Regnal year → Buddhist acts and Dhamma measures

x: Ashoka acceded around 272 BCE, visited Bodh Gaya in the 11th regnal year, enlarged the Kanakamuni stupa in the 14th year and visited Lumbini in the 21st year.

The appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras is recorded in Rock Edict V. The Dhammayatra is associated with Rock Edict VIII, the quinquennial tours with Rock Edict III, and judicial authority to rajukas with Pillar Edict IV.

secs.t: Third Council and missionaries → region

x: Mahinda and Sanghamitta went to Sri Lanka, Sona and Uttara to Suvarnabhumi, Majjhantika to Kashmir-Gandhara and Mahadeva to Mahishamandala.
Chandragupta is associated with Jainism, Bindusara with the Ajivika tradition, and Ashoka with Buddhism.
The Third Buddhist Council was held at
Pataliputra
under Ashoka, and missions such as Mahinda's to Sri Lanka and Mahadeva's to Mahishamandala followed.

secs.t: Dhamma → nature, virtues, source and debate

x: Pillar Edict II defines Dhamma as few faults and many good deeds (mercy, charity, truthfulness, purity).
Ashoka was personally Buddhist, but his Dhamma incorporated ideas common to several sects and was therefore broader than sectarian Buddhism.
The Bhabru Edict shows Ashoka's personal devotion to the Three Jewels, and non-violence together with religious toleration formed the central idea.

secs.t: Dhamma officials and welfare measures → edict

x: Rock Edict II mentions treatment for people and animals, medicinal plants, wells and roadside trees.
Pillar Edict V, issued in Ashoka's 26th year, mentions restrictions on killing specified animals and burning forests, prohibition of cattle branding, and prisoner releases.
Pillar Edict IV granted condemned prisoners
a three-day respite
before execution.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Mahadeva went to
Mahishamandala
after the Third Buddhist Council.
Ashoka is regarded as the first Indian king to address his people directly through inscriptions, which were written in Prakrit.
RE XIII names Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Magas, Antigonus Gonatas and Alexander of Epirus.

rows.title: Ashokan inscriptions - Major and Minor Rock Edicts, Pillar Edicts, sites, scripts, James Prinsep
sub: Group-II S1-19: Ashoka's Dhamma, edicts and their locations; Kalinga War

secs.t: Decipherment, FIRSTs and titles → edicts naming Ashoka

x: The expression ‘engraved by command of King Piyadassi’ occurs in Major
Rock Edict XIV
The Mahastupa at Kanaganahalli contains a portrait slab of Ashoka with his queen, bearing the label ‘Raya Asoko’.
The Maski edict, found in 1915, named Ashoka and thereby confirmed the identification of Devanampiya Piyadasi with Ashoka.
The name Ashoka occurs in the Maski (Raichur, Karnataka) and Gujarra (Madhya Pradesh) minor rock edicts (APPSC-G1 2022).

secs.t: Scripts and languages → region

x: Brahmi was used in most of India, Kharosthi in the north-west, Greek in Afghanistan, and Aramaic at Kandahar and Laghman.
Kharosthi was written from right to left and was used in the north-west, including Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra in present-day Pakistan.
Shar-i-Kuna is at
Kandahar
in Afghanistan and contains a bilingual Greek–Aramaic edict.

secs.t: Edict sites → present state

x: Exam angle: "Where has a Major Rock Edict been found?" - Girnar (Barabar has cave inscriptions; Allahabad and Delhi are pillar sites).
The Major Rock Edicts at
Shahbazgarhi
, and also at Mansehra, were written in Kharosthi script.
Girnar contains the fourteen Major Rock Edicts, and the same rock later bears Rudradaman's inscription.
Girnar
near Junagadh in Gujarat carries the 14 Major Rock Edicts.

secs.t: Edict number → subject (Major Rock and Pillar Edicts)

x: RE III = quinquennial tours of officials (iii); RE VI = Pativedakas, king available at all times (i); RE VIII = Dhammayatras replace pleasure tours (ii).
Rock Edict XII
advocates welfare of all sects and honouring the essence of all doctrines, expressing religious tolerance.
Major Rock Edict XIII records remorse for the Kalinga War, advocates Dhammavijaya, names Greek kings and mentions the Andhras.

secs.t: Kalinga War and Dhamma → as told in the edicts

x: At Dhauli and Jaugada, the Separate Kalinga Edicts replace Major
Rock Edicts XI–XIII
and address officers of Tosali and Samapa.
Dhamma promoted kindness and charity and condemned violence, cruelty, anger, pride and jealousy.
Kalinga controlled important land and sea routes along the eastern coast, contributing to the strategic importance of its conquest.
Major Rock Edict XIII records approximately 1,00,000 killed, 1,50,000 taken captive, and many more deaths from famine and disease.

secs.t: Minor Rock Edicts → AP/Karnataka sites and Buddhism in Andhra — Edict sites

x: Exam angle: Bhattiprolu and Dhanyakataka are distractors - they are not Ashokan edicts.
Erragudi is associated with instruction in Dhamma, Rajula Mandagiri with the guru-disciple relationship, Maski with the name Ashoka, and Kanaganahalli with the ‘Raya Asoko’ portrait label.
The Andhra inscriptions were in Prakrit and Brahmi, mention Rajukas in relation to welfare and uniform justice, and support the conclusion that the Mauryan administration extended into Rayalaseema.

secs.t: Minor Rock Edicts → AP/Karnataka sites and Buddhism in Andhra — Buddhism in Andhra

x: At Amaravati, Ashoka enlarged a stupa first built by Mahadeva and enshrined relics in it.
Dharanikota sculptures are described as older than the sculptures of Sanchi and Bharhut.
Major Rock Edict XIII lists the Andhras among the
peoples following Dhamma
‘Andhra-bhrityas’ is a Puranic term, and one interpretation identifies the Andhras of Rock Edict XIII with Satavahanas serving as Mauryan feudatories.

secs.t: Pillars → site, content and who moved them

x: The Nigali Sagar inscription records the enlargement of the
Kanakamuni
stupa in the fourteenth year.
The Schism Edict orders that dissenting monks and nuns be
expelled from the Sangha
Firoz Shah Tughlaq
shifted the Topra pillar from Ambala to Delhi and installed it at Firozabad.
The Kosam pillar was traditionally shifted by Akbar, and
Jahangir
later added his own inscription to it.

secs.t: Buddhist missionaries and RE XIII rulers → region

x: The missions followed the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra under Moggaliputta Tissa.
Rakkhita was associated with Vanavasi, Yona Dhammarakkhita with Aparanta, Mahadhammarakkhita with Maharashtra, and Sona and Uttara with Suvarnabhumi.
Major Rock Edict XIII names Antiochus II of Syria, Ptolemy II of Egypt, Magas of Cyrene, Antigonus Gonatas of Macedonia and Alexander of Epirus.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The geographical spread of Ashokan edict sites is the principal evidence for determining the extent of his empire.
Rajatarangini
refers to Kashmir in connection with Ashoka’s son Jalauka.
The form of the edicts shows a comparative relationship with the Persian inscriptions of Darius, including the change from third-person to first-person expression and the use of ‘lipi’ or ‘dipi’.

rows.title: Mauryan administration - central, provincial and local; espionage, judiciary, revenue system
sub: Group-II S1-18: Mauryan administration - central, provincial, revenue, espionage and judiciary

secs.t: Mauryan state — nature, Saptanga elements and checks

x: The Mantriparishad, paura-janapada assemblies and public opinion acted as checks on the king’s authority.
The standard order is Swami (4), Amatya (1), Janapada (5), Durga (2), Kosha (3), Danda/Bala (7), Mitra (6), i.e.
Janapada denotes territory and people, Kosha the treasury, Danda or Bala the army or force, and Mitra an ally.

secs.t: Central officers (eighteen tirthas) → departments

x: Sannidhata was the treasurer and keeper of state stores.
Dandapala was the head of
the army department
in Kautilya’s Mauryan list of tirthas.
Pradeshtri was associated with criminal justice and presided over kantakashodhana courts.
In the Mauryan list, Antapala was the frontier officer and warden of marches.
Tirthas and Adhyakshas together ran approximately 26 departments.

secs.t: Adhyakshas (superintendents) → departments

x: Pautavadhyaksha handled weights and measures, Sitadhyaksha crown lands and agriculture, and Panyadhyaksha commerce or state trade.
Lakshanadhyaksha was associated with the mint and seals.
Panyadhyaksha was in charge of commerce, Akaradhyaksha of mines, Koshadhyaksha of the treasury and Lavanadhyaksha of salt.

secs.t: Provinces, capitals, governors and settlement units

x: Pataliputra was the capital of Magadha/Prachya, Taxila of Uttarapatha, Ujjain of Avantirashtra and Suvarnagiri of Dakshinapatha.
Chandragupta had four provinces, these were ruled by Kumaras (royal princes) or governors helped by Mahamatras, and districts were called Vish or Ahara.
Sthaniya consisted of 800 villages, Dronamukha 400, Kharvatika 200 and Sangrahana 10; therefore.

secs.t: Local, city, army and spy officers → roles

x: Gopa was the accountant over 5-10 villages (ii); Sthanika the tax collector over a larger division (iii); Gramika the village head, probably elected (i).
Rajukas handled land survey and assessment and had judicial powers, while Yuktas served as subordinate revenue or secretarial officers.
The municipal organisation handled sanitation, water supply, roads and buildings, and comprised six committees with five members each.
Megasthenes attributed to Chandragupta an army of approximately 6,00,000 foot soldiers and 30,000 cavalry.

secs.t: Judiciary — courts, judges and penalties

x: The judicial ladder proceeded from the village court to Sangrahana, Dronamukha, Janapada and finally the king.
Punishments included fines, amputation, mutilation and death, and their severity varied by varna.
Civic offences such as
dumping dirt on roads
and creating public nuisance attracted fines.
Pradvivaka was the chief judicial adviser or judge (APPSC G2 2019:
judicial system

secs.t: Revenue terms → meaning and sources

x: Sita was income from crown land (iii); Pranaya the emergency tax or 'gift of affection' (ii); Vivita pasture land and its dues (i).
Hiranya was a cash tax, Setu covered income from gardens, orchards and root crops, and Vana was income from forests.
Megasthenes reported that evasion of the sales tax could attract the
death
penalty.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Census-taking and standardised measures were features associated with Mauryan centralisation.
Suvarnagiri was the southern capital of the Mauryan Empire.
The Arthashastra is understood to describe an ideal or normative administrative system.
Kautilya’s statement indicates that effective government cannot depend on the king alone.
The Eastern Chalukyas (Ashtadasha Tirthas) and the Kakatiyas used the Saptanga and 18 Tirthas model.

rows.title: Mauryan economy, society and urban life; Mauryan art and architecture (pillars, Sarnath capital, Barabar caves, Didarganj Yakshi)
sub: Group-II S1-20: Mauryan socio-economic and religious conditions
Group-II S1-21: Mauryan art and architecture - pillars, capitals, caves and sculpture

secs.t: Agriculture, state monopolies and taxes — terms

x: Sita was crown land cultivated for the state, under the supervision of the Sitadhyaksha, often using slaves and hired labourers.
The Mauryan state exercised monopoly or strong control over mining, forestry, salt, liquor, arms and metallurgy.
Bhaga was generally between one-fourth and one-sixth of the produce and was collected directly by royal officials, according to Megasthenes.

secs.t: Crafts, guilds, credit and coins

x: Exam angle: "Mauryan silver coin was called" - Pana (not Niska, Kakini or Shatamana).
The state supervised the sale of goods, usury prevailed in the absence of banking, and NBPW was typical Mauryan pottery.
Mauryan imperial currency consisted mainly of punch-marked silver coins, often carrying symbols such as peacocks and hills.

secs.t: Trade routes, ports and partners → places

x: Uttarapatha was the northern highway running from
Taxila through Pataliputra to Tamralipti
Dakshinapatha was the great southern trade route, and the Andhra region, including the Krishna–Godavari delta, was a node on it.
All three routes—Shravasti–Rajgir, Shravasti–Pratishthan and Rajgir–Sindhu–Sauvira—are identified as northern routes.
Diamonds, pearls, muslin and fine textiles were among the commodities exported during the period.

secs.t: Megasthenes' Indica → observations on society

x: Megasthenes described
seven
classes: philosophers, farmers, herdsmen or hunters, artisans, soldiers, overseers and councillors.
Megasthenes described hereditary occupations and endogamy and stated that India had no slavery.
Megasthenes was the Greek envoy of
Seleucus
at Chandragupta's court and wrote the Indica.

secs.t: Arthashastra on society — castes, learning, slaves and women

x: Bhadrabahu's Kalpasutra belongs to the Mauryan age, the same period in which Taxila, Ujjain and Varanasi flourished as centres of learning.
The Arthashastra used the term moksha for divorce in certain circumstances and permitted widow remarriage.
The Arthashastra recognised moksha for a wife deserted by her husband, permitted widow and long-deserted-wife remarriage, and records both anuloma and pratiloma inter-varna marriages.

secs.t: Religions → followers and patrons

x: Mauryan religious conditions were broadly liberal and tolerant, allowing freedom of faith, while the state continued to protect the institutions of varna and ashrama.
Chandragupta Maurya
followed the Jain teacher Bhadrabahu to Shravanabelagola.
Ashoka and Dasaratha donated the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves to the Ajivikas.
Chandalas and Shvapakas, untouchable groups, grew in number.

secs.t: Art streams and popular figures → findspots

x: Exam angle: "which of these are Mauryan" - Dhauli elephant, Didarganj Yakshi, Sanchi stupa, Kumrahar hall were all correct (APPSC G1 2024: all four).
All four are Mauryan: the Dhauli rock-cut elephant near Bhubaneswar, the polished Didarganj chauri-bearer Yakshi, Ashoka's brick stupa at Sanchi and the 80-pillared hall at Kumrahar.

secs.t: Pillars — material, parts, capitals → sites, Persian debate

x: Exam angle: "Persian influence" questions - similar in polish and edict idiom, different in base, shaft and lotus.
Mauryan pillars were monolithic, free-standing and circular, generally made of Chunar sandstone and finished with the characteristic Mauryan polish.
The four-lion capital with the Dharmachakra is from Sarnath, the bull from Rampurva, the single lion from Lauriya Nandangarh and the elephant from Sankisa.

secs.t: Stupas built by Ashoka → sites

x: The Sanchi monument had an Ashokan brick stupa core that was later stone-cased by the Sungas.
Tradition states that Ashoka redistributed the Buddha’s relics from the original eight stupas into 84,000 stupas.
Bharhut is noted for its sculpted railings containing
narrative scenes
The Dharmarajika stupas mentioned are located at
Sarnath and Taxila

secs.t: Pataliputra palace and city → excavated sites

x: Pataliputra was mainly a wooden city, although polished stone pillars were used in important structures.
Bulandibagh
yielded remains of the wooden palisade associated with the city of Pataliputra.
According to Megasthenes, the city administration consisted of six committees, each having five members.
Kumrahar
near Patna yielded the 80-pillared hall (8 rows of 10 polished pillars).

secs.t: Barabar and Nagarjuni caves — donor, sect, caves, inscriptions

x: Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha constructed the caves primarily as shelters for Ajivika ascetics.
Lomas Rishi and Karna Chopar belong to Barabar, while Gopika belongs to Nagarjuni.
The Lomas Rishi entrance has the earliest known stone ogee, or horseshoe-shaped, arch.
The
Barabar caves
in Bihar, dedicated by Ashoka to the Ajivikas in the 3rd century BCE, are India's oldest surviving rock-cut caves.

secs.t: FIRSTs, oldest structures and chronology

x: Exam angle: "which was made earliest" and "which of these are Mauryan" sets.

Bharhut is called the most ancient stupa in India, while Bhattiprolu is called the most ancient stupa in Andhra. ⚠ Sources differ: the 'most ancient stupa' title goes to different sites in different texts (Bharhut, Sanchi, Piprahwa).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Barabar caves are identified as the earliest rock-cut architecture, while Lomas Rishi is associated with the earliest stone ogee arch.
The Mauryan rainfall records are significant because they predate Korea’s Cheugugi gauge, which dates to 1441 CE.
Vaishya Tekri may contain a third-century BCE stupa larger than Sanchi and has yielded punch-marked and cast Avanti coins.

rows.title: Decline of the Mauryan Empire - competing explanations
sub: Group-II S1-22: Decline of the Mauryan Empire

secs.t: Later Mauryan rulers → contributions and division of the empire

x: Kunala and later Samprati were associated with the western part, while Dasharatha through Brihadratha ruled the eastern part.
Dasharatha dedicated the Nagarjuni caves to the
Ajivikas
Samprati, another grandson of Ashoka, is described as a patron of
Jainism
The Indo-Greeks had virtually replaced the western later Mauryas by about
180 BC

secs.t: End of the dynasty — Brihadratha, Pushyamitra's coup, year

x: Pushyamitra Sunga
founded the Sunga dynasty after overthrowing the Mauryas.
Pushyamitra, the Mauryan commander-in-chief, killed Brihadratha during a military review, thereby carrying out a military coup.
The Sunga dynasty is generally dated to
187 BC
, though some accounts give approximately 185 BCE.
Brihadratha ruled the eastern half of the declining Mauryan Empire from
Pataliputra

secs.t: Foreign invaders and breakaway regions → powers

x: Antiochus III crossed the Hindu Kush around 206 BC and took tribute from the local ruler
Subhagasena
The Great Wall diverted Scythian tribes towards the west and south, increasing pressure on regions near India while Mauryan frontier defence weakened.
The Satavahanas, earlier Mauryan feudatories, emerged as the breakaway power in the Andhra or Deccan region.

secs.t: Historians → theories of decline, and the evidence

x: Exam angle: match theory with historian; "which is NOT a cause" type.
Romila Thapar explained the decline through over-centralisation and the absence of national consciousness: the administration depended on the king, so weak successors meant collapse.
The increased alloy content in later punch-marked silver coins has been interpreted as evidence of fiscal strain and debasement.

secs.t: Successor dynasties — Sungas and Kanvas

x: Divyavadana describes Pushyamitra as a persecutor of Buddhists, but the growth of Sanchi and Bharhut under Sunga rule complicates that claim.
Malavikagnimitram records that
Vasumitra
, the grandson of Pushyamitra, defeated a Yavana army on the Sindhu river.
Vasudeva Kanva, a Brahmana minister, killed
Devabhuti
, the last Sunga, and seized power.

secs.t: Kharavela of Kalinga — Hathigumpha inscription

x: It is a year-by-year record of Kharavela's reign.
Kharavela was a Jain ruler of the Chedi, or Mahameghavahana, line.
Kharavela raided Magadha and recovered the Jina image the Nandas had taken.
Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription is in the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves of Odisha.

secs.t: Rise of the Satavahanas — origin, founder, titles

x: Simuka, also known as Srimukha, is regarded as the founder of the Satavahana dynasty.
The Satavahanas began as Mauryan feudatories, are called Andhra-bhrityas in the Puranas, and united the Krishna-Godavari region.
Bhojas, Maharathis and Rashtrikas
were feudatory chiefs who rose in the Deccan.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Historians do not accept one single explanation; contemporary interpretations stress structural weakness and weak successors, while also debating religious explanations.
Ashokan edicts at
Erragudi and Rajula Mandagiri
in Kurnool demonstrate Mauryan rule in Andhra.
At the end of Mauryan rule, the Andhra feudatories declared independence, enabling the rise of the Satavahanas.

rows.title: Early historic Andhra - Andhras in literature, Mauryan contact, early Buddhist centres
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-38

secs.t: Texts → references to Andhra

x: Exam angle: "Which text mentions Andhra Path?" - Vinayavatthu, not Suttanipata or the Jatakas.
The Rigveda has no reference to the Andhras, while the Mahabharata associates them with the Kaurava side and the Vayu Purana places them in the Deccan.
The Chulla-Kalinga Jataka records the Kalinga-Assaka conflict, in which the king of Assaka defeated
the king of Kalinga
; the other options are much later rulers.

secs.t: Persons → contributions in early Andhra

x: Bavari was a Brahmin teacher from
Kosala
who settled on the Godavari in Assaka territory.
The Bavari legend indicates that
Buddhist ideas had reached the Godavari region before Mauryan expansion
, showing early contact between the region and Buddhism.
Megasthenes stated that the Andhras possessed 30 forts, described as walled towns, and that they lived in towns.

secs.t: Asokan edicts in Andhra → site and content

x: Erragudi (Kurnool, now Nandyal) is in Prakrit and Brahmi.

secs.t: Places → ancient names, janapadas and excavations

x: Assaka had its capital at Bodhan; Mulaka had its capital at Pratishthana; Andhra lay on the Dakshinapatha trade route; and Asmaka was another name for Assaka.
Gudiwada Dibba
in Krishna district is an early historic mound showing continuous occupation from Mauryan to Satavahana times.
The Serivanija Jataka refers to Andhapura or Andhakapura, a city reached by crossing the river
Telavaha

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Both A and R are true and R explains A. Andhra appears as a people or region in the Aitareya Brahmana, Buddhist and Jataka texts, Megasthenes' Indica and Ashoka's 13th Rock Edict, and in sites such as Gudiwada Dibba and the Nagarjunasagar valley, all before the Satavahanas.
The Madhya Pradesh government is to resume digging at Vaishya Tekri near Ujjain, where a possible Mauryan stupa larger than Sanchi has been identified.
