rows.title: Sungas and Kanvas - Pushyamitra Sunga, Bharhut and Sanchi, Patanjali, the Besnagar pillar

secs.t: Sources → author → what they record

x: The
Gargi Samhita
records the Yavana advance on Saketa, Panchala, Mathura and Pataliputra.
Patanjali
authored the Mahabhashya, which contains references to the Yavana sieges of Saketa and Madhyamika.
Kalidasa's
Malavikagnimitram
presents Agnimitra as its principal hero and also refers to the Vidarbha conflict and Vasumitra's victory.
Mudrarakshasa concerns Chandragupta Maurya and the establishment of Mauryan power, not the Yavana invasion during Pushyamitra's reign.

secs.t: Dynasties → period, founder and end

x: The sequence is Maurya, Sunga, Kanva and Kushana.
Devabhuti was killed by his minister Vasudeva, who founded the Kanva dynasty.
The Puranas state that the Satavahanas defeated the Sunga and Kanva dynasties.
The Sungas were Brahmins.
The Sungas broadly kept Mauryan administrative institutions.

secs.t: Sunga rulers and scholars → contributions

x: All three pairs are correctly matched.
Agnimitra is noted for
fighting Yajnasena of Vidarbha
He killed Brihadratha c. 187 BC.
The Sunga court encouraged a revival of classical Sanskrit, in contrast to Ashoka's prominent use of Prakrit.

secs.t: Pushyamitra and Buddhism — the persecution debate

x: Buddhist art continued to flourish at Sanchi, Bharhut and Bodh Gaya.
Merchants and guilds kept funding Buddhism.
One tradition attributes destruction of the original Bodhi Tree to Pushyamitra and also records a similar act by Shashanka of Gauda in the seventh century CE.

secs.t: Besnagar (Heliodorus) pillar — Bhagavatism

x: Heliodorus was the ambassador of
the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas
at the court of the Sunga king Bhagabhadra.
The Besnagar monument is a
Garuda-dhvaja dedicated to Vasudeva
, and Heliodorus describes himself as a Bhagavata.
The pillar is early inscriptional evidence of Bhagavatism, an early form of Vaishnavism, and shows the assimilation of a foreigner into an Indian religious tradition.

secs.t: Sunga art sites → features

x: Sunga art marks a significant movement from earlier wood and ivory traditions towards stone architecture and sculpture.
Bharhut's inscriptions mention guilds of ivory workers and stone carvers who contributed to its construction and decoration.
Mathura sculpture began under the Sungas, but Gupta temple architecture did not begin there under the Sungas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Sunga period is associated with Brahmanical revival, the rise of Bhagavatism and the development of stone Buddhist art.
Satakarni I
is said to have defeated Pushyamitra Sunga.
Simuka is said to have ended the Kanva dynasty.

src: Sources: CDI (CDI Kushans Sunga Kanauj Contributions - Literary, Religious, Cultural, Political dimensions; persecution debate; Block02 Satavahanas); UPSC (Ancient History p.2, p.94); APHQ (2003 Q3); APP (Mauryan Empire After Ashoka; AP History Satavahana Dynasty); CDX (AP History p.20, p.34, p.58); APPCA 1 Jun 2026 (NextGenIAS)
see: See also Group-II S1-22 (Decline of the Mauryan Empire), merged under A-38.

rows.title: Indo-Greeks - Menander and Milindapanho, Indo-Greek coinage and its significance

secs.t: Bactrian Greeks — origin, entry and places raided

x: Scythian (Saka) pressure pushed them south.
Bactria was situated in
north Afghanistan
, where Greek settlers established themselves after Alexander’s campaigns.
The raids are described as reaching Saketa and Madhyamika and extending towards Pataliputra.
The Sakas replaced the Indo-Greeks first, followed by the Parthians or Pahlavas, and finally the Kushanas.

secs.t: Indo-Greek rulers → contributions

x: Exam angle: "Sankarshana + Vasudeva on coins" = Agathocles, not Kushana or Gupta rulers.
Menander I
, also known as Milinda, is regarded as the greatest Indo-Greek ruler and is associated with the spread of Hellenistic culture.
Hermaius
was the last ruler of the line, and his defeat ended Greek supremacy south of the Hindu Kush.

secs.t: Menander → Milindapanho, evidence and matches

x: Sixteen coins of Menander were found at
Bairat
Gandhara art is associated with the Kushanas, the Junagadh rock inscription with Rudradaman I, Milindapanho with Menander, and the Taxila copper plate with Patika.

secs.t: Indo-Greek coinage — FIRSTs, legends, metals, deities

x: The Indo-Greeks were among the first rulers to issue definitively attributable royal coins and the first to issue gold coins in India.
Indo-Greek coins commonly carried Greek legends on the front and Kharoshthi, representing Prakrit, on the back.
Indo-Greek coins are noted for realistic royal portraits, often showing rulers wearing helmets or diadems.

secs.t: Terms and envoys → administration, culture and diplomacy

x: Hellenistic art contributed to the development of the Gandhara school, which flourished later under the
Kushanas
Megasthenes was associated with Seleucus I, Daimachos with Antiochus I’s mission to Bindusara, and Heliodorus with Antialcidas’s mission to Bhagabhadra.
Rock Edict XIII refers to Hellenistic kings and is evidence of
earlier Greek–Mauryan contacts

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Indo-Greek period is associated with Greek–Indian synthesis in Gandhara art, religious interaction through Heliodorus, and philosophical exchange through Milindapanho.
Indo-Greek coinage is especially noted for royal portraits and bilingual legends, while Kushana coinage is associated with large-scale gold and numerous deities.
The Kushanas issued gold coins on a large scale; Vima Kadphises was the first to do so.

src: Sources: UPSC (Ancient History p.105-107); CDI (CDI Kushans Sunga Kanauj Contributions - Political and Religious dimensions; Block02 Megasthenes); APP (AP History Satavahana Dynasty; Mauryan Empire After Ashoka; Chandragupta/Bindusara); CDX (AP History p.34)

rows.title: Shakas, Parthians and Western Kshatrapas - Rudradaman I and the Junagadh inscription, Saka era

secs.t: Foreign invaders → sequence and FIRST king

x: The sequence is Indo-Greeks, Sakas, Parthians and Kushanas.
Maues, also known as Moga, is regarded as the first prominent Saka king, around 80 BC.

secs.t: Shaka branches → region and rulers

x: The Kshaharatas were associated with the Western Deccan, whereas the Kardamakas ruled around Ujjain, Malwa and Kathiawar.
Chashtana
belonged to the Kardamaka branch.
Rajuvula and Sodasa belonged to the Mathura branch.
Mathura
, Ujjain and Girnar were important centres of Saka rule.
The Sakas were often at war with the
Satavahanas
, especially in western and upper Deccan regions.

secs.t: Rulers → contributions and conflicts

x: Ptolemy
records the clash between Chashtana and the Satavahana ruler Vasishthiputra Pulumavi.
The Jogalthembi hoard contains silver coins of Nahapana restruck by Gautamiputra Satakarni.
The Nasik Prashasti was issued by
Gautami Balashri
, mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni.
Rudradaman defeated Satakarni twice but spared him because of their close relationship, and Rudradaman’s daughter married Vasishthiputra Satakarni.

secs.t: Inscriptions → issuer and content

x: Exam angle: "repaired Sudarshana lake in a 2nd-century Sanskrit rock inscription" =
Rudradaman
Ushavadatta was Nahapana's son-in-law, his Nasik record deposits 2,000 karshapanas with the weavers' guild at Govardhana at 12% a year, and it gives 1 suvarna = 35 karshapanas.
The Junnar record, a gift of a cave or mandapa dated year 46, was issued by Ayama, Nahapana's amatya (APPSC G2 2017 key).

secs.t: Terms → administration, economy and contributions

x: Numerous silver coins have been found in western India, and Kardamaka silver coins carried dates in the Saka era.
These foreign ruling groups patronised the artistic centres of
Sanchi, Mathura and Gandhara
Trousers, long coats, helmets and boots
were features shared by the Shakas and Kushanas, along with a stronger cavalry tradition.
The Shakas, Parthians and related foreign groups were absorbed into society as
Vratya Kshatriyas

secs.t: Eras → starting year + founder; Saka era as the national calendar

x: The Saka Era is commonly associated with Kanishka, while the Salivahana tradition credits Gautamiputra Satakarni.
The Common Era year is obtained by adding 78 to the Saka year: 125 + 78 =
203 CE
In a leap year, 1 Chaitra falls on
21 March
; in a normal year it falls on 22 March.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gautamiputra Satakarni
defeated Nahapana, the Kshaharata ruler, and restruck his coins as an assertion of Satavahana power.
Following Rudradaman I's defeat of Pulumavi, the Satavahana centre shifted from Pratishthana, or Paithan, to Amaravati.
The Satavahana–Kshatrapa relationship included
a marriage alliance

src: Sources: CDI (Block02 Satavahanas; Block01 Chandragupta - Expansion in Western India); APP (AP History Ancient Parts 1-2 > Satavahana Dynasty, economy and coinage); UPSC (Ancient History p.96, p.100); CDX (AP History p.24, p.36, p.59); APHQ (2000 Q3; 2008 Q16; 2017 Q8); APPCA 1 Jun 2026 (NextGenIAS)

rows.title: Kushanas - Kujula Kadphises, Kanishka, era of 78 CE, Fourth Buddhist Council, Kushana coinage

secs.t: Kushana rulers → contribution and titles

x: Kujula Kadphises
, also known as Kadphises I, united the five Yuezhi clans and occupied the Kabul valley and Kashmir.
Devaputra reflected Chinese influence, Shaonano Shao Persian influence, Kaisara the Roman Caesar tradition, and Maharaja the Indian tradition.
Vima Kadphises
(Kadphises II), a Shiva devotee, called himself Maheshvara and Sarvaloka Ishvara (RPSC 2024).

secs.t: Kanishka → capitals, extent, inscriptions

x: Purushapura
, identified with Peshawar, was Kanishka's main or winter capital.
Kanishka's empire extended from the Oxus to the Ganga and included Kashgar, Khotan and Yarkand in the Tarim Basin.
The Rabatak inscription gives the succession as Kujula Kadphises, Vima Taktu, Vima Kadphises and Kanishka.

secs.t: Era of 78 CE — founder debate and later name

x: Although the 78 CE era is commonly credited to Kanishka, some accounts credit
Gautamiputra Satakarni
with starting the Salivahana era.
The era became known as the Saka era because the Western Kshatrapas, who were Sakas, used it on their records and coins.
The era is also called Salivahana Saka and became India's national calendar in 1957.

secs.t: Fourth Buddhist Council — place, patron, president

x: The council formalised the Mahayana–Hinayana division, addressed Sarvastivada disputes, and used Sanskrit instead of the earlier Pali or Prakrit practice.
The correct sequence is the First Council at Rajagriha, the Second at Vaishali, the Third at Pataliputra and the Fourth at Kashmir.
Vasumitra
presided over the Fourth Council at Kundalvana, Kashmir, and compiled the Mahavibhasha; Ashvaghosha was vice-president.

secs.t: Court scholars → works

x: Ashvaghosha
of Pataliputra composed Buddhacharita in Sanskrit and was also vice-president of the Fourth Buddhist Council.
Nagarjuna
is associated with Madhyamika philosophy and Suhrllekha, a letter addressed to a Satavahana king.
Charaka
served as the court physician and is associated with the Charaka Samhita.
I-tsing recorded that he saw students in India memorising Nagarjuna's Suhrllekha.

secs.t: Mahayana and Buddha images → schools of art

x: Mahayana made Buddha images and worshipped him as a god.
Buddhism spread to Central Asia, China, Korea and Japan in this period.
Gandhara art shows strong Greek influence and commonly depicts the Buddha standing in pleated robes.
The first Buddha images date to the 1st century CE and are associated with the Gandhara and Mathura styles.

secs.t: Kushana coinage — FIRST large-scale gold, deities, portraits

x: The dinara followed the Roman standard of about 8 g (120 grains) and was 22-23 carat gold.
Kushana coins depicted more than thirty deities from Greek, Iranian and Indian traditions, including Helios, Mithra and Shiva.
Kanishka is shown standing in a peaked helmet, long coat and boots and making a sacrifice at an altar.
Vima Kadphises
first issued gold coins on a large scale (BPSC 2018).

secs.t: Items introduced by Shakas and Kushanas — dress and cavalry

x: The Shakas and Kushanas improved cavalry and promoted the wider use of saddles and reins in riding.
Some UPSC/NCERT notes also list turbans, but for APPSC follow the key, so every option with 5 is wrong.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Kushanas acted as Silk Road intermediaries connecting
Han China, Rome and India
Kushana trade promoted a second wave of urbanisation involving centres such as Mathura, Taxila, Ujjain and Shravasti.
Nagarjuna of the Madhyamika school is associated with
Sriparvata and the Satavahana court
in Andhra.

src: Sources: UPSC (Ancient History p.101, p.105); CDI (CDI Kushans Sunga Kanauj Contributions - Political, Religious, Economic dimensions; Block01 Buddhist Councils); APP (Buddhism > Sangha and Councils, Buddhist Writers; AP History Satavahana Dynasty); CDX (AP History p.58, p.88, p.91); VIS PT365 Updated Part 1 (Apr 2026) p.100

rows.title: Schools of art - Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati compared

secs.t: Buddha image — FIRSTs and the origin debate

x: Before anthropomorphic representation, the Buddha was worshipped aniconically through symbols including the throne, footprints, wheel, tree and stupa.
Standing Buddha images became prominent in the
Gupta phase
of the Mathura school.
The first human statues worshipped in India were those of
the Buddha
, made from the Kushana period onward (RPSC 2010).

secs.t: Gandhara and Mathura schools → region, patron, features

x: Exam angle: "Indian + Greek features = ?" → Gandhara; "flourished under which dynasty?" → Kushanas.
The Gandhara school developed in the north-western frontier region, particularly around Peshawar, Taxila and the Swat Valley in present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan.
Gandhara art reflects Hellenistic
Greek, Roman and Persian
influences in combination with Indian artistic traditions.
The Mathura school produced the earliest surviving iconic images of several Hindu deities, Jain Tirthankaras and Yaksha-Yakshi figures.

secs.t: Amaravati school → AP sites, FIRSTs and legacy

x: The Amaravati centre is associated with
Dharanikota and Dhanyakataka
, on the bank of the Krishna in the old Guntur district.
The first depiction of Sati in Indian art is found in an Amaravati-school sculpture belonging to the Ikshvaku period.
Amaravati art influenced Sri Lanka, particularly Anuradhapura, South-East Asia and later Gupta art.

secs.t: Persons and terms → Amaravati art

x: Amaravati is a 'living art' for its human feelings and the only art depicting all important events of the Buddha's life.
James Fergusson
publicised Amaravati art through his work Tree and Serpent Worship and called it the ‘Epitome of Indian architecture’.

secs.t: Mudras of the Buddha → event depicted

x: Bhumisparsha
mudra shows the right hand touching the earth, symbolising enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and calling the earth to witness against Mara.
Abhaya is the raised right palm (fearlessness, protection) = iii; Dhyana is hands in the lap (meditation) = i; Varada is the lowered open palm (boon-giving) = ii.

secs.t: Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati compared — patron, material, theme, depiction

x: Gandhara is linked with the Kushanas; Mathura with the Kushanas and later Gupta age; Amaravati with the Satavahanas and Ikshvakus; and its mature phase with the Ikshvakus and Mahayana themes.
Gandhara sculpture is marked by heavy, toga-like robes with deep folds, while Mathura sculpture commonly shows a transparent, clinging garment.
Mathura
is characterised by frontal, single icons, unlike Gandhara’s standing Buddha in Greek attire and Amaravati’s crowded narrative compositions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Amaravati, or Dhanyakataka, is associated with the belief that the Buddha first taught
Kalachakra
there.
The Amaravati sculptures are divided between
the Amaravati Museum and the British Museum
Gandhara is foreign-influenced and Buddhist, Mathura is indigenous and multi-religious, while Amaravati is indigenous and narrative in the Satavahana-Ikshvaku context.

src: Sources: CDI (Block01 Kushans; Block02 Guptas; Block09 Buddhism in Andhra; Block09 Satavahanas Art); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.58, 78, 88); APP (Indian History Part 1 > Gupta Art; AP History Ancient Part 1 > Satavahana, Ikshvaku); UPSC (Art & Culture pp.18-19; Ancient History p.105); APHQ (2001_4, 2002_3, 2019_29); VIS PT365 Apr 2026 p.92; APPCA Feb 2026, May 2026

rows.title: Satavahanas - origin debate, Simuka, Gautamiputra Satakarni, Nasik Prasasti, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
sub: Group-II M1-A-5: Satavahanas - origin, chronology and political history from Simuka to Yajnasri Satakarni
Group-II M1-A-6: Gautamiputra Satakarni and the Nasik Prasasti; Satavahana-Saka conflict

secs.t: Satavahana names, FIRSTs and dynastic sequence

x: The Satavahanas are described as having initially served as Mauryan feudatories and having established independence in the Deccan after the decline of the Mauryas.
After the Vakatakas and other immediate successors, the later sequence mentioned is Chalukyas followed by Rashtrakutas.
The Satavahanas were the first kings to issue inscriptions in Andhra itself, but Ashoka’s inscriptions were earlier in time.

secs.t: Scholars → theories on origin

x: Exam angle: scholar → theory matching; "not the same" = Sukthankar.
All three statements correctly represent the views attributed to D.C. Sircar, K.A. Nilakanta Sastri and R.S. Sharma respectively.
B.S.L. Hanumantha Rao
held that the Satavahanas belonged to the original Andhra janapada.
The APPSC 2017 key credits
R.G. Bhandarkar
with the Bellary (Myakadoni) view.

secs.t: Puranas, books and foreign accounts → authors and content

x: The Puranic long chronology places Simuka approximately in 230–207 BCE
, while another chronology places the dynasty broadly from the first century BCE to the third century CE.
The
Matsya Purana
contains the longest and most systematic list of Satavahana kings and is the principal Puranic basis for their political history.
Pliny wrote Natural History, Megasthenes recorded that the Andhras lived in towns, Ptolemy wrote Geography, and Somadeva Suri composed Kathasaritsagara.

secs.t: Inscriptions → issuer, ruler and findspot

x: The Naneghat inscription was issued by Devi Naganika, wife of Satakarni I. It records his victories, Vedic sacrifices, gifts to Brahmins and a Maharathi marriage connection.
Myakadoni, also called Mekadoni, is associated with the period of Pulumavi III and reflects the
final phase of Satavahana power in the Bellary region
The Kanheri record is associated with
the queen of Vasishthiputra Satakarni
, who is described as the daughter of the Kshatrapa Rudradaman.
The Junagadh record states that Rudradaman defeated Satakarni twice but spared him because Satakarni was a near relative.
The earliest Satavahana inscriptions, such as Naneghat and Kanha's Nasik record, come from
Maharashtra

secs.t: Capitals, AP places and regions conquered

x: Pratishthana is identified with
Paithan in Maharashtra
and was the principal western capital of the Satavahanas on the Godavari.
The eastern centre was shifted to Dhanyakataka or Amaravati under
Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
after the attacks of Rudradaman.
Aparanta was North Konkan, Vidarbha was Berar, Akara was East Malwa and Avanti was West Malwa.

secs.t: Rulers → period → contribution

x: Pulomavi III was defeated by the Ikshvaku Srisantamula and spent his last days at Myakadoni (Bellary).
Yajna Sri Satakarni
is described as the greatest of the later Satavahana rulers.
Satakarni I is identified as a contemporary of
Kharavela
Pulumavi III is identified as the last ruler in the Puranic sequence, whereas revival of maritime power and ship coins are associated with Yajna Sri Satakarni.
Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
issued ship-motif coins and extended Satavahana rule into coastal Andhra.
Ptolemy records clashes with Chashtana, while the Sanskrit Junagadh inscription identifies Satakarni as lord of Dakshinapatha.
Yajnasri Satakarni
later won back territory that had been lost by the Satavahanas.

secs.t: Gautamiputra Satakarni and the Nasik Prasasti

x: The Nasik Prasasti is in Prakrit prose and Brahmi script and records Gautamiputra’s expeditions, victories, empire and titles, including his destruction of Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas.
Gautamiputra Satakarni was the
23rd king
, the last of the early Satavahanas (rulers 1-23). '28th', found in some sources, is an error; the 17th king was Hala and the 30th and last was Pulomavi III.

secs.t: Royal titles → ruler and meaning

x: Satakarni I
bore the titles Dakshinapathapati and Apratihatachakra.
Kavivatsala was the title of Hala.
Shakasanhari was one of the titles of
Gautamiputra Satakarni
, reflecting his association with the defeat of the Shakas.
The first three pairs are correct.
‘Trisamudradhipati’ is associated with Yajna Sri Satakarni, not Hala.
Vasishthiputra Pulumavi bore the titles ‘Dakshinapatheshwara’ and ‘
Navanagaraswami

secs.t: Queens and metronymics

x: Devi Naganika acted as guardian and regent during the minority of her son.
Gautami Balasri was the mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni.
Metronymics reflected the high status of royal women and respect for the mother, but Satavahana succession continued to be patriarchal.
Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra and Halamiputra
are maternal-gotra names prefixed to Satavahana kings' names.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Satavahana homeland and chronology remain debated, while the Nasik Prasasti is the main source for Gautamiputra’s reign.
Gautamiputra is credited in the tradition with the Salivahana era of AD 78, but that attribution conflicts with the dates c. 106–130 CE assigned to his reign.
Simuka is placed around c. 230–207 BCE, Gautamiputra around c. 106–130 CE, Rudradaman’s Junagadh inscription around 150 CE, and Yajnasri’s recovery occurred later.

rows.title: Satavahana administration, economy, coinage and Prakrit literature (Hala's Gathasaptasati)
sub: Group-II M1-A-7: Satavahana administration and the feudatory system
Group-II M1-A-8: Satavahana socio-economic conditions - varna, guilds, trade, ports and coinage
Group-II M1-A-10: Satavahana literature - Prakrit, Hala's Gathasaptasati, Gunadhya's Brihatkatha

secs.t: Satavahana kings and queens → titles and contributions

x: Satavahana rulers used
matronymics
, or names derived from the mother’s lineage or gotra.
Chaturvarna operated, and the absorption of Sakas and Yavanas indicates social mobility despite continuing Brahmanical ideology.
Gautamiputra Satakarni called himself
Ekabrahmana and Varnasankarya nirodhaka
, the stopper of the mixing of varnas.
Lilavati Parinayam mentions Satavahana patronage of Nagarjuna, and Harshacharita gives Yajna Sri the title Trisamudradhipati, meaning lord of three seas.
Hala
, the 17th king and compiler of the Gathasaptasati, was called Kavivatsala, 'fond of poets' (G2 2008).

secs.t: Inscriptions → issuer and content

x: Gautami Balasri issued the Nasik inscription during the reign of her grandson Pulumavi.

Sanskrit became prominent under the Ikshvakus; Rudradaman’s Junagadh inscription is the first complete Sanskrit inscription, while Nagabu and Vepuru occur in the Amaravati and Myakadoni inscriptions respectively.

secs.t: Officers and council → roles (TERMS @ administration)

x: Heranika was the treasurer, Rajjugahaka the land surveyor, and the Akshapatakas wrote and kept records of the king's orders.
Hereditary village offices encouraged feudal tendencies, while vetti referred to forced labour owed by villagers.

The Gulmika (Gaulmika) was a village headman heading a Gulma, a cluster of villages, and kept law and order - the G2 2008 key answer, from the Myakadoni inscription (not 'Maski', as one PYQ wrongly says).

secs.t: Administrative and urban units → terms

x: Distant Aharas were entrusted to Mahasenadhipatis, a Gramani could oversee five or ten villages, and a cluster of villages was called a Gulma.
An Ahara was governed by
an Amatya
(or Mahamatra), called a Kumaramatya when a prince held it.
The Nigama Sabha, the urban council that administered towns, is referred to in the
Bhattiprolu inscription
(one PYQ-book explanation cites Naneghat, which is not an option here).

secs.t: Feudatories → titles and grading

x: Maharathis were hereditary tax-collecting feudatories of the western Deccan.
The omission of the emperor’s name suggests that the Mahabhojas enjoyed a
near-independent position
within the Satavahana political structure.
The indicated order was Raja, followed by Mahabhoja, followed by Senapati.
Mahatalavaras or Mahasenadhipatis were generals entrusted with border provinces and later developed into feudal lords.

secs.t: Army → strength and camp terms

x: Exam angle: "Katakas and Skandhavaras mean..." with distractors like tax-free monk villages or rock-cut areas.
Amaravati sculptures show infantry in front, cavalry and elephants on the flanks, and archers at the rear.
Katakas (permanent camps/garrisons) and Skandhavaras (temporary campaign camps) both served as administrative centres when the king stayed there - the APPSC G1 2024 key.

secs.t: Taxes and tax-free land grants → terms and FIRSTs

x: The Satavahanas made tax-free grants of villages or land to
Brahmanas and Buddhist monks
Tax-free land grants created rights and immunities that later formed a basis of
the early-medieval feudal order
At Naneghat, Satakarni I gave land, cows or godhana, and gold to Brahmanas.
The Nasik grants provided immunities from entry by royal officers and soldiers, salt-digging, district police and royal dues.

secs.t: Agriculture and guilds → crops, crafts and banking — Agriculture and crops

x: Ghatiyantras used for lifting water were made by the
Udayantrika guild
Shrenis organised traders and artisans of a particular craft and regulated work, quality, prices, wages and conduct.
Tailika denotes the oil guild, Kulara the potters, Gandhika the perfume traders and Sarthavaha the long-distance traders.
Kolika were weavers, Tilapishaka oil-pressers and Udayantrika made water-machines.

secs.t: Agriculture and guilds → crops, crafts and banking — Guild banking

x: Exam angle: rate of interest (12%), which inscription (Nasik), which guild (Kolika = weavers; Padhika = butchers).
Guilds acted as banking institutions: they accepted deposits and paid interest, including payments benefiting monasteries.
The Nashik inscription records deposits of 2,000 karshapanas at 1% monthly interest and 1,000 karshapanas at three-fourths of 1% monthly interest.

secs.t: Trade centres and routes → goods

x: The inland route from Ujjain to Bharuch passed through Paithan and Tagara.
Pratishthana or Paithan was the capital and an inland trade centre situated on the
Godavari
Tagara was an important emporium linked to coastal ports.
Mahapatha nirmatalu
means builders or makers of great roads and is associated with the Satavahanas.

secs.t: Ports → ancient name and modern place

x: Bharuch or Barygaza came under Satavahana control after
Nahapana
was defeated.
Maisolia was identified with Machilipatnam, Kantakossyla with Ghantasala, Koddura with the Gudur area, and Dhanyakataka with Amaravati/Dharanikota.
Bharukachha, Sopara, Kalyan and Vyjayantipura
were the west-coast ports associated with Satavahana maritime expansion.
Bhavaviveka is described as the acharya at the
Sriparvatam vihara

secs.t: Indo-Roman trade → sources, exports, imports, decline

x: Pliny, writing in Latin in Natural History, referred to the drain of Roman gold and fine cloth.
The anonymous Greek Periplus described Arikamedu as the “market street of the Romans.”.
Wootz steel
was among the exports.
Roman coins have been found at
Bhattiprolu and Nagarjunakonda
Roman trade declined after the Satavahanas

secs.t: Coins → metals, issuers, motifs and FIRSTs — Metals and denominations

x: Lead was the most common coin metal.
Iron coins with a copper coating are attributed to
the Shalankayanas
, not the Satavahanas.
The silver coin was called a karshapana, and one suvarna was equivalent to 35 karshapanas.

secs.t: Coins → metals, issuers, motifs and FIRSTs — Coin type → issuer

x: The bilingual silver portrait coins carried Prakrit on one side and a Dravidian language on the other.
Satavahana coin legends were generally in Prakrit and written in Brahmi script.
The cited account associates ship-motif coins with Vasishthiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri Satakarni and states that no later ruler issued them.

secs.t: Coins → metals, issuers, motifs and FIRSTs — Motifs, shapes, technique and mint

x: The Kondapur mint in Medak is associated with the legend ‘Siri Chimuka Sata’.
A
lotus throne
is not included in this group.
The Ujjain symbol is described as
a cross with four circles
and appears on the reverse of Satavahana coins.

secs.t: Language and script → Prakrit, Sanskrit and FIRST Telugu words

x: The common people spoke
Desi bhasha
, while Prakrit served as the royal, administrative and inscriptional language.
Kuntala Satakarni
, regarded as the thirteenth Satavahana king, is associated with making Sanskrit the royal language.
Prakrit
, written in Brahmi, was the royal, administrative and inscriptional language of the Satavahanas (APPSC 2011).
Atta, Addam, Potta and Pilla are among the early Telugu words associated with Gathasaptasati.

secs.t: Society and women → evidence

x: Independent donations by women, without naming husbands or fathers, are recorded at
Bharhut, Sanchi and Amaravati
The evidence includes women artisans and merchants, women poets in the Gathasaptasati, and the Kamasutra's reference to vetti or forced labour performed by women.
All four features—sugar and jaggery, Brundagana, house-wall paintings and hanging of criminals—are included in the social picture associated with Gathasaptasati.

secs.t: Books → authors

x: Brihatkatha is associated with Gunadhya, Katantra with Sarvavarma, Lilavati Parinayam with Kutuhala, and Harivijaya with Sarvasena.
Brihatkatha formed the basis of Kathasaritsagara by Somadeva Suri and Brihatkatha Manjari by Kshemendra.
The G2 2017 key attributes the Yogasara to
Kundakundacharya
, who also wrote the Jain Samayasara.

secs.t: Gathasaptasati, Brihatkatha and Katantra → features

x: Gathasaptasati, or Sattasai, is an anthology of 700 gathas in Maharashtri Prakrit, dealing chiefly with love, rural life and nature.
Anulakshmi, Anupalabdha, Reva or Revati, and Madhavi are identified as women contributors to Gathasaptasati.
All three statements form the traditional account: Gunadhya lost the dispute with Sarvavarma, wrote in Paishachi, and began burning the work after the king ignored it.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The newly found Satavahana-era Prakrit-Brahmi inscriptions were discovered in Gundaram Forest in Jayashankar Bhupalpally district of Telangana.
In the context of the Deccan-Roman routes (Ujjain-Paithan-Tagara-Bharuch), the ship coins are credited to
Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
The Desi words in the Gathasaptasati are regarded as
the earliest traces of Telugu
, and the Satavahana period laid the foundation of the language.
Gathasaptasati and Brihatkatha are literary works, whereas the Naneghat and Nasik records are inscriptions used as sources for Satavahana social history.

rows.title: Satavahana art and architecture - Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda, rock-cut caves (Karle, Bhaja, Nasik)
sub: Group-II M1-A-4: Buddhist sites of Andhra - Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu, Salihundam, Ghantasala
Group-II M1-A-11: Satavahana art and architecture - Amaravati school, stupas and rock-cut caves

secs.t: Stupas → types, relics and size FIRSTs

x: All four pairings are correct in the stated descriptions: Sanchi is the largest stupa in India, Kesariya the largest brick stupa, Bharhut the most ancient stupa in India and Amaravati the largest in Andhra Pradesh. ⚠ Sources differ: 'largest' and 'most ancient' stupa claims vary by source (Sanchi, Bharhut, Piprahwa and Kesariya each get superlatives).

secs.t: Stupa features and Buddha symbols → terms

x: The lotus represents birth, the horse the Great Departure, the Bodhi tree enlightenment and the wheel the first sermon.
Ayaka platforms and pillars are identified with the Andhra sites of Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Ghantasala, Bhattiprolu and Jaggayyapeta.
The chaitya hall has an apsidal (horseshoe) plan with pillared aisles and a stupa at the apse end.

secs.t: Amaravati Mahachaitya → patrons, phases, size and themes

x: Amaravati Mahachaitya was built under Satavahana ruler Pulumavi II and was later enlarged by the Ikshvakus.
The final enlargement is attributed to the Ikshvakus, while Acharya Nagarjuna is associated with construction of the enclosing wall or prakara.
Vasishthiputra Satakarni
is credited with enlarging the Amaravati stupa, adding limestone sculptures and a stone railing (APPSC 2001 key).

secs.t: Discoverers and excavators → site and year

x: Colin Mackenzie discovered the Amaravati stupa in 1797 and was the first Director General of the Survey of India.
James Fergusson
featured Amaravati in Tree and Serpent Worship and called its sculptures the 'Epitome of Indian architecture'.
The correct order is Mackenzie’s identification in 1797, Sewell’s excavations in 1877, Rea’s Bhattiprolu excavation in 1892, and Longhurst’s Nagarjunakonda work in 1927.

secs.t: Nagarjunakonda → names, Ikshvakus, sects and submergence

x: The
Ikshvaku queens
are specifically noted as major donors to Buddhist establishments at Nagarjunakonda.
Yajna Sri Satakarni built the 1,500-room
Sriparvata Sangharama
for Acharya Nagarjuna.
Vijayapuri was submerged by the Nagarjunasagar dam, while monuments were rebuilt on a hilltop.
The
Golden Temple
(Swarna Devalayam) at Nagarjunakonda bears the first Sanskrit inscription of Andhra and South India, of Ehuvala Shantamula.

secs.t: Other Andhra sites → features

x: Bhattiprolu is associated with the oldest stupa in Andhra; Jaggayyapeta with a relic stupa and the Mandhata sculpture; Ghantasala with Kantakossyla; and Nagarjunakonda with the Ikshvaku centre and over 30 stupas.
Nelakondapalli is associated with a post-Satavahana mahastupa, bronze and marble Buddhas in the Amaravati style, and a sculptor’s workshop identified with V. V. Krishna Sastry.

secs.t: Ancient names and Buddhist sects → centres

x: Siddharthaka chaitya is associated with Guntupalli, not Nagarjunakonda.
Purvasaila, Aparasaila, Uttarasaila, Rajagirika and Siddharthika were five Chaitika branches of
the Mahasanghikas
, associated with Mahadeva Bhikshu.
Purvasaila was centred at Dhanyakataka (Amaravati) and Aparasaila at Sriparvata (Nagarjunakonda).
The G2 2019 key places Bhavaviveka's vihara at
Sriparvatam
; some sources say Dhanyakataka, but the exam key is Sriparvatam.

secs.t: Buddhist acharyas → contributions

x: Nagarjuna was associated with Sriparvata/Nagarjunakonda and is linked with Madhyamika and Shunyavada.
Aryadeva, a disciple of Nagarjuna, is associated with Chittasuddhi Prakaranam.
Dinnaga
is identified as the father of Buddhist logic and is associated with work in the Andhra country.
Aryasangha is associated with Yogachara, Maitreyanatha with Vijnanavada, and Padmasambhava with the transmission of Vajrayana to Tibet.

secs.t: Rock-cut caves → site and feature

x: Karle has the largest chaitya hall; Bhaja has early Buddhist caves; Nasik has viharas with Satavahana inscriptions; and Bedsa has a chaitya with bell-capital pillars.
Rock-cut work peaked in
the Sahyadris of the western Deccan
, including sites such as Nasik, Naneghat, Karle, Bhaja, Kanheri, Junnar and Ajanta.
Ajanta Cave 10, a Satavahana-era chaitya, carries the painting of the
Shwetagaja (Chhadanta) Jataka

secs.t: Patrons and donors → gifts

x: ‘Tambaya Danamu’ is an inscriptional donation term found at
a Buddhist site in the Krishna district
Merchants, guilds, Yavanas and artisans
, including an artisan named Dimikudu, are recorded as donors.
Women donors dominate the records: Satavahana queens (e.g.

secs.t: Art schools → region, material, phases and comparison

x: All four features are characteristic of the Amaravati school: narrative Buddhist reliefs, movement, emotional expression, floral and vegetal decoration, and the Buddha seated on a lotus in padmasana.
The early phase is aniconic, using the Bodhi tree, empty throne, footprints, wheel and stupa; the later phase depicts the Buddha in human form, seated on a lotus with dancing Gandharvas and Yakshas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Buddhavanam is a 279-acre Buddhist theme park at
Nagarjuna Sagar in Nalgonda, Telangana
The Ikshvakus
built the earliest structural Hindu temples, while Satavahana chaitya-vihara forms provided an architectural base for later Hindu temple architecture.
Amaravati is described as a Satavahana capital, the site of the Mahachaitya, the modern capital of Andhra Pradesh, and one of India’s three major ancient art schools.

rows.title: Satavahana religious conditions - Buddhism, Brahmanism and royal patronage
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Inscriptions → issuer and religious content

x: The Naneghat inscription of Devi Naganika was in Prakrit; she was the wife of Satakarni I and daughter of Maharathi Tranakayiro.
The inscription combines Vedic deities such as Indra, Yama and Varuna with Bhagavata deities Vasudeva and Sankarshana.
The Alluru inscription of the
Ikshvaku Virapurushadatta
records donations to many communities and institutions.

secs.t: Gods and temples → Bhagavata religion and Shiva worship

x: The Parasurameswara temple is at
Gudimallam
in the present Chittoor, now Tirupati, district, and contains the oldest Shivalinga of the Satavahana period.
Bhagavata religion was founded by Vasudeva-Krishna and centred at Mathura.
Bhagavata religion reached Andhra under Krishna, became the Vasudeva religion by Hala’s time, and Bhagavata symbols are noted in Gautamiputra’s inscriptions.

secs.t: Buddhism in Andhra → arrival, sects and centres

x: Mahadeva Bhikshu, the first Buddhist acharya in Andhra, founded the Chaityaka sect.
Buddhism reached Andhra in the sixth century BC, and its local form came to be called Andhra Buddhism.
Tibetan tradition states that the Buddha preached at Amaravati at the request of King
Subendran
Kielhorn
identified Sri Parvataswamy as the Buddha (G2 2019 key).

secs.t: Kings, queens and donors → faith and gifts

x: The rulers associated with yajnas are
Satakarni I, Satakarni II, Gautamiputra and Yajna Sri
Gautami Balasri donated
a cave vihara at Nasik for the Bhadrayaniya sect
, reportedly for the recovery of her son.
Donors included kings, queens, officials, merchants, guilds such as ivory workers and coral dealers, artisans and independent women.

secs.t: Acharyas → works, philosophy and place (Nagarjuna, Kundakunda)

x: Nagarjuna's Suhrullekha ('friendly letter') was addressed to his patron and close friend
Yajna Sri Satakarni
All three titles—‘Second Buddha’, ‘Indian Martin Luther’ and ‘Indian Einstein’—are associated with Acharya Nagarjuna.
Kathasaritsagara states that Nagarjuna was killed by a Satavahana prince, whereas Lilavati Parinayam refers to his patronage by a Satavahana king.
Kundakundacharya was a Jain teacher associated with Konakondla and preached
Syadvada

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The period is characterised by religious pluralism, including Brahmanical practices such as the Ashvamedha and Buddhist centres such as Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda.
The principal Andhra anchors are
Amaravati/Dhanyakataka, Sriparvata and Gudimallam
Prakrit, described as the people’s language, helped Buddhism communicate beyond elite circles and become a mass movement.

rows.title: Ikshvakus - political history, Vasishthiputra Chamtamula and Virapurushadatta
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Scholars → theories of Ikshvaku origin

x: Rapson and Buhler supported a North Indian origin; Vogel a Kannada origin; D.R. Bhandarkar a Kshatriya or mixed Kshatriya-Brahmin origin; and Gopalachari a Telugu/Andhra origin.
Southern names and the southern custom of cross-cousin marriage are cited as evidence supporting the Andhra origin of the Ikshvakus.
The link to the Solar/Ayodhya line is made by tradition and scholars from the name, not by their own inscriptions (G2 2025 key).

secs.t: Ikshvaku rulers → period and contributions

x: The Puranas list 7 Ikshvaku kings, while inscriptions confirm 4 (some sources say 8 and 5). '4 and 7' reverses the figures, and '8 and 3' and '30 and 7' match neither source.
Chamtamula invited Brahmins from northern regions, and the family worshipped Virupakshapati, identified with Shiva, and Mahasena, identified with Kartikeya.

secs.t: Ikshvaku titles, names and deities → meaning

x: The Puranas refer to the
Ikshvakus
as Sri Parvatiyas or Sri Parvatiya Andhras and as Andhrabhrityas.
The lion was the Ikshvaku symbol and Prakrit was their royal language.
Sri Parvatadhipati was a title of Virapurushadatta, while Gosatasahasra and Halasatasahasra were titles of Chamtamula.

secs.t: Ikshvaku FIRSTs and LASTs

x: Machilipatnam
is the 16th–17th century handloom port; it should not be confused with the Ikshvaku-period ports Motupalli and Ghantasala.
Rudrapurushadatta
was the last Ikshvaku ruler.

secs.t: Capital, sites and ports → features

x: Vijayapuri, identified with modern Nagarjunakonda, lies in the Nagarjuna Sagar valley and was excavated by R. Subrahmanyam.
Excavations at Vijayapuri revealed an amphitheatre, possibly built with Roman help, and an Ashvamedha platform.
Motupalli and Ghantasala
are identified as ports associated with the Ikshvaku period.
Many Roman coins have been found at
Nagarjunakonda
, indicating long-distance commercial connections.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Ikshvakus are regarded as a bridge dynasty that brought the Amaravati school to its peak, built the first temples and moved Andhra towards an agrarian, Puranic order.

src: Sources: APP (AP History Ancient Parts 1-2, Ikshvaku dynasty); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.62, 64-65, 100); CDI (Block09 Ikshvaku Dynasty - introduction, conclusion); APHQ (G2 2017 Q11, 2019 Q5, 2025 Q3)

rows.title: Ikshvaku socio-economic conditions; role of royal women as donors
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Royal women donors → monuments and gifts

x: Exam angle: "the woman who served Buddhism most" =
Bodhisiri
(Bapisiri, Chantisiri, Adavi Chantisiri are the distractors).
Bapisri and Chatisri, queens of Virapurushadatta, made
independent pillar dedications at the Mahachaitya
Rudradhara Bhattarika, a queen of Virapurushadatta, was the daughter of
Kshatrapa Rudrasena of Ujjain
Bhatti Mahadevi was the chief queen of Virapurushadatta and the mother of
Ehuvala Santamula
Upasika
Bodhisri
is ranked first among women donors and represents non-royal patronage.

secs.t: Donative inscriptions → features

x: Chamtisri held the titles
Mahatalavari and Mahadanapatni
, the latter referring to her position as wife of Pugiya chief Skandasri.

secs.t: Economic terms, guilds and titles → meaning

x: Bhaga was the land tax and amounted to one-sixth of the produce.
The title
Goshatasahasra Halashatasahasra
denotes the giver of hundreds of thousands of cows and ploughs.
Guilds were called
Nigamalu
; the spelling Negimalu also occurs.
Parnika Sreni consisted of betel-leaf traders, Poosika Sreni of sweetmeat traders, Sale of weavers and Telika of oil pressers.

secs.t: Agrarian economy — Chamtamula's gifts and use of revenue

x: Santamula brought Brahmins from the north and granted them agraharas.
Santamula performed the Ashvamedha, Vajapeya and Agnistoma sacrifices, and an Ashvamedha altar has been found at Nagarjunakonda.
The four specified allocations were administration and army, temples and festivals, poets and scholars, and gifts to religious bodies.

secs.t: Trade, ports, exports-imports and coins

x: Roman trade was lower than under the Satavahanas.
Roman gold and silver coins found at Nagarjunakonda and a Roman-style amphitheatre at Vijayapuri indicate foreign contact.
Motupalli and Ghantasala
are identified as ports in the relevant records.
Exports included
spices
, iron, coconuts and cotton textiles.
Ikshvaku coins were of lead and copper.

secs.t: Society — varna order, clans and marriage customs

x: Varna rules became stricter, Brahmadeya grants supported Brahmins, Shudras were the majority and a new landlord class emerged.
The alliances linked the Ikshvakus with the
Kshatrapas of Ujjain and the Chutus
The inscriptions record the practice of sati, the use of matronymics such as Vasishthiputra and names derived from the grandfather, such as Ehuvala Santamula.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Ikshvaku period marks Andhra's movement from the Satavahana trade economy towards an agrarian, agrahara-based early medieval order.
The Buddhist heritage circuit
is placed first in the AP 'Discover Andhra' campaign, and Nagarjunakonda is identified as a key site.
The debate holds that women's general status declined, even though royal women continued to exercise religious and economic agency, including through patronage and donations.

src: Sources: CDI (Block09 Satavahanas-Ikshvakus... Socio-Economic; Block09 Jainism and Buddhism in Andhra; Block02 Early Educational Institutions); CDX AP History Complete Notes pp.64-77; APP (AP History Ancient Parts 1-2 > Ikshvaku Dynasty); APHQ 2019, 2025; APPCA Feb 2026

rows.title: Ikshvaku religious conditions - Buddhism at Nagarjunakonda, Brahmanical temples
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Ikshvaku kings → religious policy

x: Exam angle: greatest patronage =
Veerapurushadatta
; Bodhisri's service = reign of
Ehuvala Chamtamula
. Some notes list Bodhisri under Virapurushadatta; the APPSC key follows Ehuvala.
The sculptures at Nagarjunakonda show a Shivalinga trampled underfoot, reflecting the strong Buddhist orientation associated with Virapurushadatta's reign.
The Ikshvaku pattern was one of dual patronage: most kings performed Vedic sacrifices, while royal women and wealthy lay women supported Buddhist stupas and viharas.

secs.t: Persons → statements on Nagarjuna and Sriparvata

x: Hiuen Tsang found the Sriparvata vihara
neglected
during his seventh-century visit.
Sriparvata refers to Nagarjunakonda or Vijayapuri, while Sriparvataswami was the family deity of the Vishnukundins and is identified with Srisaila Mallikarjuna.
Kielhorn identified Sri Parvataswamy of the Ikshvaku records with the Buddha (G2 2019 key; a one-liner wrongly credits N. Venkataramanayya).

secs.t: Monasteries → Buddhist sects

x: The Maha Chaitya belonged to the Aparamahavinaseliya tradition; Bhatti Mahadevi or Ehuvala Santamula's vihara to the Bahushrutiyas; Kodabalisri's vihara to the Mahishasakas; and Bodhisri's Sinhala Vihara to the Mahaviharavasins.
Purvasailiya, Rajagirika and Siddharthika were among the Mahasanghika branches or related sects named.
Purvasailiya was centred at Amaravati, Aparasailiya at Nagarjunakonda, and Rajagirika at Sriparvatam (APPSC 2012 key).

secs.t: Mahachaitya — relic stupa, builders, inscriptions

x: The Maha Chaitya was a Dhatugarbha, or relic stupa, built over the Buddha's bodily relics.

Chamtisri rebuilt the Paravata Mahachaitya in Virapurushadatta's sixth year, and the structure had nine Ayaka pillars; the earlier monument was associated with Yajnasri Satakarni and Acharya Nagarjuna.
Kantakasala is identified with
Ghantasala

secs.t: Bodhisri's inscription → countries and foreign links

x: Bodhisri built viharas for foreign monks from Sinhala, Kashmir, China and Gandhara, and seven viharas at Papili.
Ceylonese monks made Nagarjunakonda their base for Hinayana, strengthening the Sri Lankan Buddhist connection.

secs.t: Brahmanical temples and deities → builders

x: Puranic Shaivism, Vaishnavism and Shakti worship all flourished
under the Ikshvakus.
Skanda was identified with Kartikeya; Vishnu was worshipped as Narasimha; Hariti protected children; and Ganapati was the elephant-headed deity.
The Pushpabhadraswami shrine was a Shaiva shrine with an elephant-back plan, begun by Virapurushadatta and completed by Ehuvala.
The Ashtabhuja Narayanaswami shrine was built by Shivasena, the commander of the Abhira king Vasusena.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Bodh Gaya is associated with Hinayana, while Sriparvata is associated with Mahayana.
In April 2026, the Palnadu Collector visited the Nagarjunakonda Museum, proposed a Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam boat service and pushed Swadesh Darshan works.
Ashtabhuja Narayanaswami is regarded as the first Vaishnava temple in Andhra, while the Ikshvakus represented the last royal Buddhist zenith in Andhra.

Religious Conditions; Block09 Jainism and Buddhism in Andhra); APP (AP History Ancient Parts 1-2 > Ikshvaku Dynasty; Satavahana Buddhism); APHQ 2008, 2012, 2019; TH 2 Apr 2026; LENS May 2025 p.16; APPCA Feb 2026

rows.title: Ikshvaku art, architecture and literature
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Ikshvaku art FIRSTs and sculptures → significance

x: Nagarjunakonda panels commonly depicted episodes from the Buddha's life and Jataka stories.
The Mandhata sculpture at Jaggayyapeta is regarded as the most important Ikshvaku sculpture and the
first depiction of a Chakravarti in Indian art
The carving of sculptors' names is associated with the
beginning of the Sculptor's Style
; Badantacharya at the Mahavihara is an example.

secs.t: Stupa and temple terms → meaning

x: Excavations revealed
more than 30 stupas
, along with many viharas and apsidal chaityas, in a small valley.
The major stupas had a wheel-shaped or spoked plan, with Ayaka platforms in the four directions.
Garbhagudi, antarala, mantapa, dhvajastambha and prakara are components of the Agamic temple plan.
The Pushpabhadraswami temple followed a Gajaprishtha plan, meaning an apsidal or elephant-back plan.

secs.t: Secular structures at Vijayapuri → purpose

x: The Kreeda Vedi was a sports arena, thought to have been built with Roman assistance, and it has been described as having no parallel elsewhere in India.
The
acoustic building
was designed on principles of sound and is regarded as the most unique find at the site.
Kummakundam denotes
water tanks or bathing pools
excavated at Vijayapuri.

secs.t: Inscriptions → language

x: Early Ikshvaku inscriptions were in Prakrit, which remained the court language initially.
The earliest Sanskrit inscription of Andhra and South India is at the Swarna Devalayam, or Golden Temple, at Nagarjunakonda.
Sanskrit replaced Prakrit in Ikshvaku inscriptional usage from the fourth century CE.
Bapi, Remmanaka, Adavi, Ehuvala and Anikki are Telugu words found in Ikshvaku records.

secs.t: Books → authors (literature linked to Nagarjunakonda)

x: Suhrllekha, along with Madhyamika works, is associated with
Acharya Nagarjuna
Sutralankara, in Sanskrit, is attributed to
Aryasangha
Visuddhimagga is a Pali work attributed to Buddhaghosha.
The eighth-century Kuvalayamala records the presence of foreign students at
Dhanyakataka and Nagarjunakonda

secs.t: Excavations → year and excavator

x: The correct sequence is 1926 discovery, 1927–31 work of A. H. Longhurst, 1938 work of T. N. Ramachandran, and the 1954–60 rescue excavation.
R. Subrahmanyam
was among the excavators involved in the large rescue excavation of 1954–1960.
The habitation at Nagarjunakonda extends from the
Palaeolithic period up to 1960 CE

secs.t: Nagarjuna Sagar project (1955) — relocation and island museum

x: Jawaharlal Nehru
laid the foundation stone of the Nagarjuna Sagar Project on 10 December 1955.
The Archaeological Survey of India used
salvage archaeology
to dismantle and rebuild monuments before submergence.
The monuments relocated to Anupu and Nagarjunakonda island are called
transplanted monuments
Jawaharlal Nehru laid the foundation stone on 10 December 1955 (G2 2012).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Ikshvakus laid the base of
Dravida temple architecture
The Palnadu Collector
reviewed the Nagarjunakonda Museum and the Swadesh Darshan works.

src: Sources: CDX AP History Complete Notes pp.64, 75-81; CDI (Block09 Satavahanas-Ikshvakus... Language and Literature, Art and Architecture; Block09 Jainism and Buddhism in Andhra); APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Ikshvaku Dynasty; Satavahana Roman trade; Ancient Part 2 one-liners); APHQ 2002, 2011, 2012, 2019; LENS May 2025 p.16; TH 2 Apr 2026

rows.title: Vishnukundins - political history, Madhava Varma I and II
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Scholars → Vishnukundin origin

x: Most historians regard the Vishnukundins as Brahmins belonging to the Vishnukundina gotra, although alternative caste theories have also been proposed.
B.V. Krishna Rao regarded them as Brahmins; K. Gopalachari proposed an Agnikula Kshatriya origin; N. Venkataramanayya described them as Brahmins who adopted Kshatriya ways.
Early records and forts at Amrabad, Keesaragutta and Indrapalanagara point to Telangana as the original home.

secs.t: Dynasty succeeded — post-Ikshvaku order

x: Exam angle: G2 2008 order question - answer
a, d, c, b
(Ikshvakus, Brihatpalayanas, Salankayanas, Vishnukundins).
After the Ikshvakus came the Brihatpalayanas or Pallavas in the relevant territories, followed by the Salankayanas, Vishnukundins and Eastern Chalukyas.
The Salankayana capital was Vengi or Pedavegi, they followed Vaishnavism, and Madhava Varma II conquered them.

secs.t: Vishnukundin rulers → period and contribution

x: Indravarma
, who ruled from 358 to 370 CE, is described as the founder of the Vishnukundin dynasty and a Vakataka vassal.
These activities are associated with
Govinda Varma I
, whose rule also saw expansion into the Krishna-Godavari region and both sides of Sriparvata.
Vikramendra Varma I was the son of Madhava Varma II and a Vakataka princess, while Indrabhattaraka Varma was defeated by Ishanavarma and killed in the Kalinga war.

secs.t: Vishnukundin rulers → period and contribution — Madhava Varma II — sacrifices and conquests

x: Prithvi Maharaja broke away at Pishtapuram during the rule of
Vikramendra Varma II
, as recorded in the Tandivada inscription.
Pulakeshin II of the Badami Chalukyas
defeated Manchana Bhattaraka at Kunala near Kolleru in 624 CE, ending Vishnukundin rule.
Kubja Vishnuvardhana, the brother of Pulakeshin II, founded the
Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
after the Vishnukundin defeat.

secs.t: Vishnukundin capitals → ruler and location

x: Exam angle: "Amarapuri → Denduluru" =
Madhavavarma
Indrapalanagara is Tummalagudem in Telangana, was built by Indravarma (Tummalagudem inscription) and was the capital of Madhava Varma I and Govinda Varma.
Madhava Varma II
shifted the capital from Amarapuri to Denduluru because of constant Pallava wars and fortified Amarapuri.
The Vishnukundins carved the Indrakeeladri and Mogalrajapuram caves at
Bezawada
, present-day Vijayawada.

secs.t: Vishnukundin titles → ruler

x: Madhava Varma II acquired the title Trikuta-Malayadhipati after defeating
the Anandagotrikas
Govinda Varma was Shadabhigna, Vikramendra Varma I was Mahakavi, and Indrabhattaraka Varma bore the title Satyasraya.
Trisamudradhipati belonged to Madhava Varma II; Shadabhigna to Govinda Varma; Paramamaheshwara to Indrabhattaraka Varma; and Sakala Bhuvana Rakshabharanaikashraya to Vikramendra Varma II.

secs.t: Vishnukundin inscriptions → ruler

x: The Ipur plates, found at Tenali, are associated with Madhava Varma I and bear Lakshmi and conch symbols.
The Tummalagudem records include associations with Govinda Varma I and Vikramendra Varma II, a grant to Paramabhattarika’s vihara, and the first Sanskrit inscription found in Telangana.
The Khanapur plates record Madhava Varma II’s marriage with a daughter of Vakataka ruler Prithvisena II.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Vishnukundins link the Ikshvaku age with the Eastern Chalukyas.
The wrong pair is C. The Khanapur plates come from Satara district in Maharashtra, and Ramatirtham is Indravarma's record, so neither belongs to the Guntur region.
Differences among sources concern the founder, numbering of rulers, dates and certain title attributions.

src: Sources: CDX AP History Complete Notes pp.94, 100-106; APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Vishnukundin Dynasty); CDI (Block09 Salankayana Dynasty; Vishnukundin Dynasty); APHQ 2008, 2011, 2025

rows.title: Vishnukundin society, religion, administration and coinage
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Administration — units and officers → function

x: The hierarchy was Kingdom, Vishaya, Rashtra and Grama.
Akshapataladhikrita kept records, Rajjuka measured land with ropes, Gulmika supervised border areas, and Phaladara measured grain and fixed the king's share.
Amrabad was described as
the biggest fort in the Telugu country
, with walls of about 200 kilometres.

secs.t: Military, revenue and land terms → meaning

x: Hastikosa was the elephant corps, Veerakosa was the infantry commander and Chhata was a spy.
The Polamuru plates record divine ordeals, Bhaga was one-sixth, and Vishti was forced labour, later called vetti in Telugu.

secs.t: Coinage and trade → metal, symbols, find-spots

x: Lion, Nandi, ship, trishula, conch and Sriparvata were mentioned as symbols;
lotus
was not included in the list.
Ship-marked coins and the title Trisamudradhipati point to the importance of
sea trade
A Roman gold coin of Constantine was found at
Kudali Sangameswaram near Alampur
Fa-hien
reported the use of cowrie shells, or gavvalu, as money.

secs.t: Gods, sacrifices and FIRSTs in Vishnukundin religion

x: Dantamukha Swami was installed at
Velpuru
in the 33rd year of Madhava Varma II.
Bhutagrahaka Swami was associated with Yama, Ramalingeswara temples were recorded at the four named places, and Dharmapuri became a Narasimha kshetra.
Madhava Varma II performed
11 Ashvamedhas and 16 Rajasuyas
, and about 1,000 yagas in all.

secs.t: Buddhist viharas and Jainism → donors and decline

x: Govinda Varma I founded the Govinda Vihara; Prithvimula and Harivarma were associated with the Gunapashapuram viharas; Vikramendra Varma II granted Irundhera; and the queen of Govinda Varma I founded the Paramabhattarika Mahadevi Vihara.
Jainism declined as Kapalika Shaivism rose; Jain shrines such as Srisailam were converted, and Kumarilabhatta attacked Jainism.

secs.t: Grants → donees (agraharas)

x: The Ipur plates name Agnisarma and Easwarasarma as donees; Indravarma and Agnivarma received Mutukali.
Agraharas also functioned as
centres of Vedic learning
The feudalisation interpretation holds that tax-free Brahmadeyas with administrative rights created
a landed intermediary class

secs.t: Education — Ghatikas and scholar-kings

x: Ghatikas were higher Sanskrit and Vedic colleges concerned with advanced Brahmanical learning.
The inscriptions of
Indrabhattaraka Varma
provide the first mention of Ghatikas in Andhra.
Indrabhattaraka Varma is credited with the Ghatikeshwara temple at
Keesara
The Ghatikas taught fourteen vidyas: four Vedas, six Vedangas, Mimamsa, Nyaya, Dharmashastra and Puranas.
Govinda Varma was known by the title Shadabhigna.

secs.t: Books → authors and language

x: The work is associated with Madhava Varma II through the title Janasraya, while an alternative view credits the poet Gunaswami with composing it in the king's name; its subject is prosody.
The Chikkulla plates contain the expression “Vijaya rajya samvatsarambul”, and village names were Telugu, showing Telugu's entry into the records.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The period witnessed a Vedic-Puranic revival, the temple and agrahara economy, and the first Hindu cave temples.
The period is described as one in which varna rules hardened, women's status declined, and practices such as child marriage and sati increased.

src: Sources: CDX AP History Complete Notes pp.100-109; APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Vishnukundin Dynasty: Administration, Economy, Society, Religion, Education); CDI (Block09 Vishnukundin Dynasty); APHQ 2025

rows.title: Vishnukundin art and architecture - Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram and Bhairavakonda caves
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Cave temples → dynasty, deity, location and FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: APPSC GS 2019 asked where Undavalli is; the key is
Vijayawada
. Its revenue district is Guntur.
The
Guptas
at Udayagiri in Madhya Pradesh are credited with the earliest Hindu cave temples in India, whereas the Vishnukundins are associated with the first Hindu cave temples in the Telugu states.

secs.t: Undavalli caves — features

x: Exam angle: Aug 2026 test - "built by the
Cholas
as a Hindu temple, later Buddhist" is
false
; the true statements are the Krishna-bank location and the Ananta Padmanabha statue.
The Undavalli caves are in Guntur on the Krishna and feature Vishnukundina adaptation of Gupta rock-cut architecture, including the five-metre reclining Ananta Padmanabha Vishnu.

secs.t: Mogalrajapuram and Bhairavakonda caves — features

x: APP and CDX credit Madhava Varma I of the Vishnukundin dynasty, whereas APHQ dates the caves to the Pallava period of the seventh–eighth centuries CE.
Bhairavakonda closely resembles the
early Pallava caves of Mahabalipuram
, which is why some sources (APHQ) date it to the Pallava period of the 7th–8th c., although most notes credit Madhava Varma I of the Vishnukundins.

secs.t: Architecture terms → meaning

x: The typical plan consists of a pillared mandapa or ardhamandapa in front of one or more garbhagriha cells cut into the rock.
Dwarapalas, or door guardians, flank the entrances to the shrine spaces, a feature also seen in contemporary Pallava caves.
The style is described as a blend of
Ikshvaku and Vakataka traditions
, with additional influence borrowed from the Pallavas.

secs.t: Vishnukundin vs Pallava (Mahendravarman) caves

x: The Vishnukundin caves are generally dated to the fourth–sixth centuries, with Undavalli in the fourth–fifth century, while Mahendravarman I’s Pallava caves belong to the seventh century.
The Vishnukundin style had a Gupta–Vakataka base but also borrowed from or imitated Pallava forms.
The Pallava (Mahendravarman I) cave style of the 7th c. was later taken up by the
Telugu Chodas and Eastern Chalukyas

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Minister
Kandula Durgesh
announced at the close of the festival that it would become an annual festival held in every region.
The AP government's two-day Telugu Mahotsavam at the Undavalli Caves was held on 25–26
July 2026
, so July 2026 is right; the April and 2025 dates are distractors.
Undavalli Caves lie inside the Amaravati capital area, specifically in Tadepalli mandal.

src: Sources: CDI (Block09 Vishnukundin Dynasty > Art and Architecture; Block09 Pallavas Andhra Context; Block03 Pallavas... Legacy); CDX AP History Complete Notes pp.102, 108-109; APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Vishnukundin Dynasty > Architecture); APHQ 2012, 2019, 2025; LENSD 29 Jul 2026; LENS Aug 2026 pp.117, 124; CDCA Jul 2026 p.65; APPCA 15 Jul 2026; TH 17 Apr, 25-27 Jul 2026, 28 Apr 2026

rows.title: Andhra society and culture in the early period - varna, women, education and festivals
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Varna, caste terms and marriage types — Satavahana varna order

x: The social structure of ancient Andhra was predominantly influenced by the Vedic varna system, and the Satavahanas played a crucial role in it.
Satavahana kings were associated with the enforcement of varna-dharma, granted tax-free villages to Brahmins, and the Nanaghat inscription mentions Brahmins trained in Vedic learning and ritual.
Greeks, Sakas, Pahlavas and Kushanas
adopted Indian names and faiths and were assimilated into the Kshatriya order.

secs.t: Varna, caste terms and marriage types — Occupational castes → term

x: Exam angle: statement pairs on "Vedic caste system + Satavahana role"; match sub-caste name → occupation.
A Nagarjunakonda sculpture depicts a woman committing sati, and the Greek writer Strabo also noted the practice.
Anuloma was a higher-caste man–lower-caste woman union producing offspring termed Ugra, while Viloma or Pratiloma was the reverse union producing offspring termed Chandala.

secs.t: Queens and women → marriages, titles, patronage

x: Exam angle: Ikshvaku woman patron of Buddhism (Bodhisiri); matronymics; female poets of the Gathasaptasati.
The society was patriarchal and organised around joint families, yet women enjoyed considerable respect and participated in festivals, assemblies and public life.
Gautami Balasri funded a cave-vihara at Nasik, Bodhisiri was the greatest woman patron of Buddhism, and Chantisiri built the Mahachaitya at Nagarjunakonda.

secs.t: Education and religion — centres, scholar-kings, titles, deities

x: Indrabhattaraka Varma
is associated with the expression ‘Ghatika Vapta punyasancharya’ and was credited with founding ghatikas.
Vasishthiputra Chantamula, an Ikshvaku king, performed the
Asvamedha and Vajapeya
sacrifices.
Nagarjunakonda contained Buddhist establishments as well as Brahmanical shrines, including Pushpabhadraswami.
Amaravati reliefs show the worship of
nagas, yakshas and sacred trees
alongside Buddhist symbols.

secs.t: Sources → festivals, amusements, dress and ornaments

x: Exam angle: "most important literary source of Satavahana society" → Gathasaptasati (not Puranas, Aitareya Brahmana or Dharmasutras).
Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda reliefs show men wearing a lower cloth and turban, while women are depicted with heavy anklets, bangles, girdles and necklaces.
Hala's
Gathasaptasati
, about 700 verses in Maharashtri Prakrit on family, marriage, agriculture, trade and festivals, is the most important literary source for Satavahana society (APPSC 2019).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Early Andhra combined the Vedic varna order with strong Buddhist patronage, and women played a major role in that patronage.

src: Sources: APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 - Satavahana and Vishnukundin society, religion, education); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.42-43); APHQ (aph2019_1, aph2019_3); CDCA 31 Jul 2026 p.61; TH 22 Apr 2026

rows.title: Sangam Age - the three Sangams, sources; Tolkappiyam, Ettuthogai, Pattupattu, Pathinenkilkanakku

secs.t: Three Sangams → place, scholar, chronology

x: The traditional account places the first Sangam at Then Madurai, the second at Kapatapuram and the third at Madurai; all are described as being under Pandya patronage.
The Sangam corpus is generally placed between approximately the 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE, or
300 BCE–300 CE
The legendary account of three Sangams and two submerged cities is traditional rather than historically established.

secs.t: Sangam literature — terms, corpus and anthologies

x: Exam angle: statement questions - "devoid of material culture / no warrior ethic" are false.
Sangam literature is rich in material culture and refers to polity, trade, cities, wars, economy and the warrior ethic.
Pathinenkilkanakku comprises eighteen minor works, mainly on ethics and morals, includes Tirukkural and is largely regarded as post-Sangam.

secs.t: Tamil works → authors and subjects

x: Tolkappiyam was written by Tolkappiyar, Tirukkural by Tiruvalluvar, Silappadikaram by Ilango Adigal and Manimekalai by Sittalai Sattanar.
Tolkappiyam
, attributed to Tolkappiyar, is the earliest extant Tamil work on grammar and poetics and also contains material on society and polity.
Manimekalai relates how
the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi becomes a Buddhist nun
and reflects Buddhist philosophy.

secs.t: Foreign writers and inscriptions → what they record

x: The anonymous Greek work
Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
provides information on ports, Muziris, pepper and Arikamedu.
Pliny’s Natural History refers to Chera spices, Pandya pearls, Chola muslin and the outflow or drain of Roman gold.
Ashokan inscriptions identify the
Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas
as southern neighbours of the Mauryan Empire; Satiyaputras and Keralaputras are also mentioned in Rock Edict II.

secs.t: Archaeological sites → findings

x: Arikamedu
, near Puducherry, was an Indo-Roman trading settlement and is described in the Periplus as the ‘market street of the Romans’.
Kaveripattinam or Puhar was a Chola port described in Pattinappalai as cosmopolitan and containing Yavana settlements.
Keezhadi is considered the most important Sangam urban excavation and indicates
South Indian urbanisation contemporary with the Gangetic Second Urbanisation

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In February 2026 about 30 Indian inscriptions, mostly Tamil-Brahmi, of the 1st–3rd c. CE were documented in the Theban tombs of Egypt, showing the mobility of Indo-Roman trade; a July 2025 Tamil Nadu excavation yielded Tamil-Brahmi potsherds, carnelian beads and weaving tools.
Sangam Age sources are significant because they offer
the earliest detailed picture of South Indian society, economy and polity

src: Sources: CDI (Block02 Sangam Age - sources, literature, post-Sangam works); UPSC (Ancient History pp.130-131, 135); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.28, 47); APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Satavahana - literary sources on trade); APPCA (NextGen History CA 2026, Jun 2026); LENS Jul 2025 p.18; LENS Feb 2026 p.107

rows.title: Sangam kingdoms - Cheras, Cholas, Pandyas; Karikala, Senguttuvan, Nedunjeliyan

secs.t: Muvendar → capital, port, emblem, river

x: The Chola heartland was the
Kaveri delta, extending from Tiruchi up to southern Andhra
Chera, Chola and Pandya rulers were collectively called the
Muvendar
, meaning the three crowned kings.
The
Pallava
s were not a Sangam dynasty; they rose from the fourth century CE.
The Cheras traded with Rome and are said to have built a temple of Augustus near Muziris.

secs.t: Polity terms → meaning; chieftains

x: Ko, Kon, Mannan and Vendan were terms used for the
king
Aimperunkulu was a
five-member advisory body
consisting of ministers, priests, commanders, envoys and spies.
Avai was the royal court, in which poets were also present.
Army commanders bore the title
Enadi
The seven great patrons were Pari, Kari, Ori, Pegan, Ay, Athiyaman and Nalli.

secs.t: Sangam rulers → contributions and titles

x: Senguttuvan, known as the Red Chera, founded the Pattini cult centred on Kannagi.
Udiyanjeral was an early
Chera
ruler; the pair 'Udiyanjeral - Chola' was the wrong pair in UPSC 2026.
Arya Padai Kadantha Nedunjeliyan was the Pandya ruler who executed Kovalan.
Nedunjeliyan of the Pandyas won at Talaiyalanganam and gained control over the Tamil country.
Ugra Peruvaludhi
was the last renowned Sangam Pandya.

secs.t: Battles, Kallanai, Pattini cult and Pandya decline

x: Karikala Chola
won the Battle of Venni, defeating the Cheras, Pandyas and eleven chieftains.
The remains were found in the Kollidam, a distributary of the Kaveri that branches off at the Upper Anicut or Mukkombu.
The Pattini cult centred on Kannagi, regarded as the
ideal wife
The Sri Lankan king Gajabahu is said to have attended the consecration of the Pattini idol.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The seal shows the
Chola tiger with the Pandya two fish and the Chera bow
, marking Chola victory over both the Pandyas and Cheras.
Rivalry among the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, together with Roman trade, shaped early Tamil political organisation.
The Renati, Pottapi and Nellore Choda families claimed descent from
Karikala Chola

src: Sources: UPSC (Ancient History pp.135-136); CDI (Block02 Sangam Age - political organisation); IYB 2026 p.627; CDX (AP History Complete Notes p.150); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Telugu Chodas); APPCA (NextGen History CA 2026, Jun 2026); LENSD 15 Aug 2026; TH 18 May 2026

rows.title: Sangam society and economy - tinai concept, Indo-Roman trade, ports, religion; the Kalabhra interregnum

secs.t: Tinai → landscape, occupation, deity

x: Kurinji was associated with Murugan, Mullai with Mayon, Marutam with Vendan and Neidal with Varunan.
Marutam was associated with agriculture in riverine plains.
The Tolkappiyam gives the five-fold division, including Kurinji, Mullai and Palai with their respective landscapes and deities.

secs.t: Social groups and customs → terms

x: Exam angle: "Vellalars were rich peasants who formed the fourth caste"; distractors were poets, labourers and forest tribes.
The Tolkappiyam lists Arasar, Anthanar, Vanigar and Vellalar, with Vellalar as the fourth group.
Kalavu denotes
pre-marital or secret love
, whereas Karpu denotes married life or wedded chastity.
Avvaiyar, Nachchellaiyar and Kakkaipadiniyar are identified as women poets of Sangam literature.

secs.t: Religion — deities, hero stones, burial

x: Seyon, identified with Murugan, was regarded as the chief Tamil deity in the Sangam tradition.
Murugan's six sacred abodes are known collectively as
Arupadai Veedu
Korravai, not Varunan, was associated with war and victory.
Nadukal were set up for warriors who fell in battle and could contain carvings of their deeds and inscriptions.

secs.t: Ports → kingdom, coast, classical name

x: Exam angle: Korkai, Poompuhar and Muchiri were
ports
Muziris
, also known as Musiri, was a Chera port on the west or Malabar coast.
Korkai was a Pandya port on the east coast, noted for pearl fishing and the export of pearls and shells.
Puhar or Kaveripattinam was a Chola east-coast port where cotton, muslin and silk were traded and a Yavana quarter prospered.

secs.t: Indo-Roman trade — items, terms, coins and hoards

x: Yavanapriya meant black pepper, Rome's most prized Indian import.
An amphora was a tall, double-handled jar used for carrying wine and oil.
The Roman coin finds include gold and silver coins of
Augustus, Tiberius and Nero
The Pandya embassy to Augustus is regarded as the best-known Indian embassy to the Roman Empire.

secs.t: Excavators and writers → Indo-Roman evidence

x: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, composed around 60 CE, is attributed to
an anonymous Greek merchant
and is a major source for Indo-Roman trade.
Tamil-Brahmi potsherds have been found at
Berenike, Quseir al-Qadim and the Valley of the Kings
in Egypt.
Pliny, in his Natural History, said Rome lost 55 million sesterces a year to India.

secs.t: Kalabhras — period, religion, dark age debate, end

x: The Kalabhras ruled the Tamil country after the Sangam age, approximately from the 3rd to the 6th century CE.
The period was called a dark age because later Brahmanical records depicted the Kalabhras negatively and surviving sources are scarce.
The Kalabhra interregnum ended in the late sixth century through the efforts of the Pandya ruler Kadungon and the Pallava ruler Simhavishnu.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Indo-Roman trade peaked during the Satavahana-Sangam age, broadly from the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE.
The Pattanam excavations in Ernakulam have been used by the KCHR to identify Pattanam with the ancient trading centre of
Muziris
All four are Roman coin find-spots in Andhra, along with Vijayawada and Nagarjunakonda; Attirala is in Kadapa and Salihundam in Srikakulam.

rows.title: Gupta Empire - sources, Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and the Allahabad Prasasti (Harishena)
sub: Group-II S1-23: Gupta Empire - sources, Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II

secs.t: Gupta sources → ruler, author, record

x: Devichandraguptam narrates the episode involving
Ramagupta, Dhruvadevi and Chandragupta II
Mudrarakshasa, written by Vishakhadatta, is a political drama concerning Chanakya and Chandragupta Maurya.
Gupta coins, mostly gold, depict rulers, deities and rituals and thereby reveal royal titles, religious ideas, ritual practices and the prosperity of the period.
The Junagadh, or Girnar, inscription records that Parnadatta repaired the Sudarshana lake while serving as Skandagupta’s governor.

secs.t: Allahabad Prasasti — Harishena, language, the pillar

x: The pillar bearing the Allahabad Prasasti also carries an inscription of Jahangir, along with Ashoka’s edicts and the Queen’s edict.
The Allahabad Prasasti celebrates Samudragupta’s military conquests, while Ashoka’s inscriptions on the same pillar convey a message associated with peace and dhamma.
Samudragupta's conquests are recorded in the Allahabad Pillar (Prayaga) prashasti by Harishena (APPSC 2025 key).

secs.t: Gupta origin and Chandragupta I — FIRSTs

x: The Guptas are described as originally Vaishyas who were later treated as Kshatriyas by Brahmanas; a Brahmana origin has also been proposed on the basis of the Dharana gotra.
Chandragupta I
, who ruled approximately from 319 to 335 CE, is regarded as the real founder of the Gupta Empire.
The first Gupta gold coins issued by Chandragupta I are the
King-Queen type
, depicting Chandragupta I and Kumaradevi in association with the Lichchhavis.

secs.t: Gupta kings → queens

x: Exam angle: king-queen matching (UPPSC 2019: 3-1-2-4).

secs.t: Samudragupta's campaigns — four-fold policy

x: Samudragupta annexed territory in the north, restored southern rulers as tributaries, received tribute from frontier rulers and subdued forest kingdoms.
Kushanas and Sakas paid homage, while rulers of Southeast Asia and Ceylon sent tribute.

secs.t: Southern campaign (Dakshinapatha) → king and kingdom

x: Mahendra was associated with Kosala, Vishnugopa with Kanchi, Hastivarman with Vengi and Swamidatta with Kottura.
Mahendragiri was associated with
Pishtapura
, identified with present-day Pithapuram in the Kakinada region.
The Allahabad Prasasti refers to
twelve
southern kings who were defeated and subsequently released and reinstated as tributaries.
The Dakshinapatha campaign proceeded along the eastern coast towards Kanchi.

secs.t: Samudragupta — Ashvamedha, coin types, minister, foreign contacts

x: Meghavarman, the Buddhist ruler of Sri Lanka, sent a mission to Samudragupta for permission to build a monastery and rest house at Bodh Gaya.
Chandragupta II's sea trade reached Europe via Egypt, indicating wide-ranging maritime commercial contacts.
The
lyrist or veena-player type
depicts Samudragupta as a poet-musician and supports the association of the title Kaviraja with him.

secs.t: Gupta titles and epithets → ruler

x: Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja and Paramabhattaraka were imperial titles associated with the Gupta tradition. ‘
Dharmamahamatra
’ was an administrative designation associated with the Mauryan period, not a common Gupta imperial title.
V.A. Smith called Samudragupta the Napoleon of India; Vikramaditya is Chandragupta II (APPSC-G2 2008); Mahendraditya is Kumaragupta I; the Allahabad prashasti calls Samudragupta Lichchhavi-dauhitra.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Gupta Era (Gupta Samvat) began in
, the date of Chandragupta I's accession.
Samudragupta’s empire extended from Nepal and Punjab to Kanchi, while his influence reached Simhala.
The inscription is a chief source for information about the fourth-century Andhra regions and rulers of
Vengi, Pishtapura, Avamukta and Devarashtra
