rows.title: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya, Kumaragupta, Skandagupta; the Hunas and Gupta decline
sub: Group-II S1-29: Decline of the Guptas; the Huna invasions

secs.t: Gupta rulers → period (chronology)

x: Exam angle: Samudragupta → Chandragupta II → Kumaragupta I → Skandagupta.
Sri Gupta
, who ruled approximately from 240 to 280 CE, is regarded as the founder of the Gupta dynasty and bore the title ‘Maharaja’.
Vishnugupta was the last ruler of the main line and ruled approximately from 540 to 550 CE; the other named rulers belonged to the later Gupta succession.

secs.t: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya → accession, titles, conquests, alliances, court — Ramagupta episode and accession

x: Chandragupta II bore the title
Vikramaditya
Chandragupta II issued
lion-slayer coins
and used the title Simhavikrama.
The Ramagupta episode is narrated in
Devichandraguptam
, attributed to Vishakhadatta.

All three statements describe the traditional Ramagupta episode: the elder brother agreed to surrender Dhruvadevi, after which Chandragupta II killed the Saka king, killed Ramagupta and married Dhruvadevi.

secs.t: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya → accession, titles, conquests, alliances, court — Sakas and second capital

x: Chandragupta II defeated the Saka ruler Rudrasimha III and annexed western Malwa and Gujarat, thereby reaching the western sea.
The silver coins of Chandragupta II were modelled on Saka silver coins and were issued after the Saka conquest, making them strong evidence of that victory.
Chandragupta II married Kuberanaga, a Naga princess; his daughter Prabhavati married Vakataka ruler Rudrasena II; Dhruvadevi was married after Ramagupta’s killing.

secs.t: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya → accession, titles, conquests, alliances, court — Fa-Hien and court

x: Fa-Hien was a Buddhist pilgrim, and he did not name the reigning king because his focus was Buddhism rather than political history.
Fa-Hien
was a visiting Buddhist pilgrim, not one of the traditional Navaratnas.

secs.t: Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta → titles and contributions

x: Kumaragupta I
issued new gold coin types showing Kartikeya and the king feeding a peacock.
Skandagupta’s gold coins depict him with
a bow and arrow, the Garuda standard and Lakshmi
The Bhitari pillar records
Skandagupta
's victories over the Pushyamitras and the Hunas; he is the Gupta ruler who defeated the Hunas (UPPSC 2015).

secs.t: Huna invasions → leader, Gupta reign, opponent

x: Exam angle: Kumaragupta I = first attack; Skandagupta = repulsed; Yashodharman = defeated Mihirakula.

C is correct: Toramana occupied Malwa and central India (up to Eran) but no Indian ruler is recorded as defeating him, while Mihirakula was defeated by Yashodharman of Malwa and Narasimhagupta Baladitya.

The Saka conquest of Chandragupta II preceded the first Huna attack in late Kumaragupta I’s reign; later Huna waves occurred under Skandagupta, followed by Toramana’s advance under the weaker successors.

secs.t: Inscriptions → what they record

x: The Damodarpur copper plates indicate that guilds could act as
banks
The Eran boar inscription was built in Toramana's first regnal year and records Huna rule over Eran.
Banabhatta's Harshacharita also mentions the Hunas.
The Eran inscription of Bhanugupta's general Goparaja (510 CE) is the earliest record of sati.

secs.t: Causes of Gupta decline — factor → effect

x: Hereditary governors contributed to the growth of autonomous feudatories rather than strengthening centralised imperial control.
The absence of Gupta coins and inscriptions after Skandagupta in western Malwa and Saurashtra is evidence that these areas were no longer under effective Gupta control.
Later Gupta gold coins were debased, with less gold and more alloy, and coins gradually disappeared as payments shifted to land.

secs.t: Successor powers and regional kingdoms → region

x: The Later Guptas were associated with Magadha, the Maitrakas with Valabhi, the Pushyabhutis with Thanesar and later Kannauj, and the Aulikaras with Mandsaur.
Madhava Varma II was the greatest Vishnukundin ruler, ruled around 440–495 CE, won over 100 battles and performed 11 Ashvamedhas.
The
Jaunpur inscription
of Uttar Pradesh records the defeat of Indrabhattaraka Varma by the Maukhari ruler Ishanavarma.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The break-up of Gupta authority marked a movement from a single empire to regional kingdoms and a more feudal political order.
The Kushans declined under pressure from the Sasanians together with the rise of an Indian power, while the Guptas similarly faced external invasions and the rise of regional powers.

rows.title: Gupta administration - feudalism debate, land grants, agraharas, revenue and local bodies
sub: Group-II S1-24: Gupta administration, land grants, revenue and the feudalism debate

secs.t: Gupta kingship — titles, divine claims and decentralisation

x: Gupta rulers used the exalted titles Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja and Paramabhattaraka and made divine claims about kingship.
Samudragupta was equated with Kubera or Dhanada, Varuna, Indra and Yama or Antaka.
Gupta kingship was hereditary, but there was no firm rule of primogeniture.
Gupta administration relied substantially on feudatories and grantees, and it was considerably less centralised than Mauryan administration.

secs.t: Officials → functions; judicial system

x: Kumaramatyas were senior or high-cadre officers, ranked with princes; ministers and commanders were chosen from them.
The period witnessed a clearer distinction between civil and criminal law; theft and adultery were criminal matters, while property disputes were civil matters.
Harishena
, the court poet of Samudragupta, held all three top titles: kumaramatya, sandhivigrahika and mahadandanayaka.

secs.t: Administrative units → officers; town and district councils

x: Exam angle: "Kayastha" = scribes.
The
Prathama kulika
represented the chief artisans or craft guilds on the town board.
The
Nagarashreshthi
, the chief banker or merchant, served as chairman of the town council or adhikarana.
Kayasthas were associated with scribal and official work; the Prathama kayastha represented the chief scribes on the town board.

secs.t: Revenue terms → meaning

x: Bhoga consisted of periodic supplies in kind, including fruits, firewood and flowers, made to the king.
Udranga and uparikara were additional or new taxes, with uparikara probably associated with temporary tenants.
The broad trend was an increase in land taxes accompanied by a decline in trade taxes.
Bhaga was the king's share of produce and the main land revenue; the law books prescribed
one-sixth

secs.t: Land terms and measures → meaning

x: Exam angle: Kuliyavapa and Dronavapa = land measurement.
Kshetra means cultivated or fertile land, Khila means untilled waste land, Vastu means habitable house-site land, and Aprahata denotes uncultivated forest land in this classification.
Aprahata is generally taken as
uncultivated forest or jungle land
in the standard classification used for this period.

secs.t: Land grants → grantee, rights, tenures and effects

x: Brahmadeya was granted to Brahmanas singly or collectively, agrahara was tax-free land or a village given to Brahmanas, devagrahara was assigned to temples and monasteries, and secular grants went to officials or feudatories in lieu of salary.
Nivi dharma meant a trust, nivi dharma akshayana a perpetual endowment, aprada dharma enjoyment of income without alienation, and bhumichchhidranyaya ownership by the first reclaimer of waste land.

secs.t: Historians → positions on Indian feudalism

x: R.S. Sharma
argued that Indian feudalism crystallised through land grants, sub-infeudation, vishti, decline of trade and urban decay.
The evidence cited included the seventh-century
decline in long-distance trade and gold coinage
, shrinking towns and a closed village economy.
The essential elements are power based on control of land, lord–vassal ties and weak central authority.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The debate centres on R. S. Sharma’s land-grant thesis and the criticism that the absence of serfdom makes the European model of feudalism unsuitable or limited for India.
The Mauryan state was centrally regulated, whereas Gupta administration relied more on feudatories and grantees; therefore; .
Satavahana and Ikshvaku brahmadeya grants barred royal officials from interfering in the granted areas.

rows.title: Gupta society and economy - varna and jati, position of women, Fa-Hien's account, trade decline
sub: Group-II S1-25: Gupta socio-economic conditions - Fa-Hien's account, trade, caste and women

secs.t: Fa-Hien (traveller) → ruler, route and observations

x: Fa-Hien travelled overland through Central Asia and Gandhara and returned by sea through Sri Lanka, including the port of Tamralipti on his return route.
Fa-Hien states that the Chandalas lived outside towns or settlements and struck a piece of wood to warn others of their approach.
Cowries were used in daily exchange, Hindus and Buddhists lived in harmony, and the people were described as peaceful and prosperous.

secs.t: Castes and social groups → status

x: The asserted social order of the period was expressed through the concept of
Varnashram Dharma
Both statements are true, and the absorption of foreigners and tribes through land-grant processes explains the multiplication of jatis.
Chandalas were outside the four-varna order and lived outside settlements; untouchability intensified in relation to them.

secs.t: Women — marriage, property, education; earliest sati inscription

x: Women generally had no property rights, but they could control stridhana, consisting of marriage gifts.
The evidence indicates the absence of purdah rather than its general prevalence.
The Eran inscription (510 CE) records the sati of the wife of
Goparaja, a general of Bhanugupta
; it is the earliest sati inscription, though sati was rare under the Guptas.

secs.t: Land types and irrigation — Amarakosha, Sudarshana lake

x: Amarakosha lists 12 types of land.
Urvara means fertile, usara barren, maru desert, and aprahata fallow land.
The lake was first built by Pushyagupta under Chandragupta Maurya, repaired by Rudradaman, and repaired again under Skandagupta by Parnadatta.
The Sudarshana lake was located at
Girnar

secs.t: Crafts and guilds — centres, features, terms

x: Exam angle: "NOT a feature of guilds" - the wrong option is always "non-autonomous bodies".
Silk weaving flourished in Lata in Gujarat until
the weavers moved to Mandsaur in Malwa
Guilds undertook charitable activities such as constructing temples, rest houses, assembly halls and gardens;
appointment of provincial governors
was not their function.

secs.t: Inscriptions → guild and trade content

x: Exam angle: MPPSC 2024 and 2021 - Dashpur = first advertisement; composer is not "Bhava".
The
Damodarpur copper plates
mention guilds acting as banks for loans and deposits.
The Dashpur inscription concerns the silk-weavers’ guild and Sun temple; the Indore copper plate concerns the oil-men’s guild and temple lamp; the Damodarpur plates describe banking functions.

secs.t: Ports → region; exports and imports

x: Tamralipti
, identified with Tamluk, was the chief eastern port in Bengal.
Bharuch or Barygaza was situated in
Gujarat
and was the largest port on the west coast.
All four pairs are correctly matched.
Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul handled foreign trade, and Bharuch was the largest west-coast port.
Gems, spices and textiles
were the main exports.

secs.t: Coins → metal, name and use

x: The Gupta gold coins were called
dinaras
, and the Guptas issued them in the largest numbers.
Rupaka or rupyaka was a silver coin used mainly for local exchange.
Copper issues were few, later dinaras contained less gold, gold coins became scarce after the Gupta period, and cowries were used for ordinary exchange.

secs.t: Trade decline and urban decay — causes, effects, timing

x: Exam angle: statement-type questions on the post-Gupta decline of trade and towns.
R. S. Sharma’s urban decay interpretation links the shrinking of commercial towns with rural self-sufficiency and scarcity of gold coins.

Eastern Roman trade continued until about 550 CE; decline became visible in the post-Gupta period, stagnation is associated with c. 750–1000 CE, and recovery came with the Arab empire from the 10th century.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Odisha's Baliyatra festival honours
Sadhaba mariners who sailed to Southeast Asia
Ghantasala and Kadura in Krishna district were Andhra's east-coast ports, while the Satavahana weavers' guild was known as Kolika Shreni.
Peasant obligations, including vishti or forced labour, formed the basis of
the urban decay and feudalism critique
of the Gupta economy.

rows.title: Gupta religion - Bhagavatism, Vaishnavism, Saivism; beginnings of temple architecture (Deogarh, Bhitargaon)
sub: Group-II S1-26: Gupta religious conditions - Vaishnavism, Saivism, Buddhism and Jainism

secs.t: Bhagavatism and Vaishnavism — origin, persons, royal titles, FIRSTs

x: Chandragupta II

is credited in most notes as the first Gupta ruler to take the title 'Parama Bhagavata' (his coins carry it), marking devotion to Vishnu. ⚠ Sources differ: UPPSC keys (2009, 2015) name Samudragupta as the first, so read the options and the exam's key.
The colossal Varaha panel at Udayagiri was carved under
Chandragupta II
, and the cave functioned as his personal temple.

secs.t: Puranic Hinduism, Shaktism and Tantrism — texts and practices

x: Hinduism became increasingly theistic and devotional, while temple-based idol worship became common and the earlier dominance of sacrificial Brahmanism declined.
There are 18 Mahapuranas (APPSC G2 2011 key), among them Vishnu, Bhagavata, Matsya, Vayu, Brahmanda, Markandeya, Shiva and Kurma.
Tantrism spread from the fifth century, emphasised ritual and feminine energy, admitted women and Shudras, and affected all four named religious traditions.

secs.t: Saiva sects → founder and features; linga sites

x: Exam angle: both APPSC Kapalika keys exist - read the options (Pashupata vs Misra).
Kalamukha followers were linked to Kalanana, and the sect had associations with Simha Parishat in Andhra and Shakti Parishat in Karnataka.
The
linga, trident and bull
appeared as sectarian symbols on Gupta coins and seals.
Ekamukhalinga, showing one face of Shiva, is exemplified by
Udayagiri Cave 4 and Khoh
in Madhya Pradesh.

secs.t: Buddhism under the Guptas — rulers, scholars → works

x: Kumaragupta I
, also known as Shakraditya, is credited with founding Nalanda.
Asanga was a Yogachara teacher, Vasubandhu wrote the Abhidharmakosa, Dinnaga founded Buddhist logic and Buddhaghosa wrote the Visuddhimagga.
Mahayana images flourished in Gupta art.

secs.t: Jainism and religious tolerance — council, centres, records

x: The Sanchi inscription of Chandragupta II’s officer Amrakardava records a grant to a Buddhist vihara, demonstrating tolerance toward another faith.
The Kahaum pillar inscription of the Skandagupta period records Jain images, providing evidence of the continued presence and acceptance of Jainism.
Fa-Hien noted cordial Hindu-Buddhist relations during the Gupta period, despite observing decay at certain Buddhist centres.

secs.t: Temple architecture — stages → examples, features, FIRSTs

x: The architectural sequence was first-stage Sanchi and Tigawa, second-stage Nachna and Bhumara, and third-stage Deogarh and Bhitargaon.
The second stage (Nachna, Bhumara) is marked by a roofed ambulatory, raised platform and two storeys; the shikhara comes only in the third stage.
The Gupta temples established the square garbhagriha, pillared mandapa, pradakshina path and raised jagati platform.

secs.t: Religion → founder, text, symbol, centre (matching)

x: Exam angle: APPSC G2 2025 match - Jainism-Triratna, Buddhism-Ashtanga Margam, Saivism-Linga, Animism-Nature worship.
Jainism is associated with Mahavira and the Agamas, Buddhism with Gautama Buddha and the Tripitaka, Ajivika with Makkhali Gosala, and Saivism with the Linga.
Jainism is associated with Triratna, Buddhism with Ashtanga Marga, Vaishnavism with chakra, shankha and Garuda, and Saivism with the linga.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Statement 3 reverses the change: Mauryan religion was Vedic plus Shramana, and the Gupta shift was from sacrifice to temple and bhakti.
The Salankayanas followed Vaishnavism, but their rulers also used Shaiva titles such as Parama Mahesvara.
Nandivarman II’s Pedavegi inscription is regarded as the first inscription in Andhra Pradesh concerning
Vishnu temples

rows.title: Gupta art, literature, science and technology - Kalidasa, Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Ajanta, Mehrauli pillar
sub: Group-II S1-27: Gupta art and architecture - temples, Ajanta, sculpture and coins
Group-II S1-28: Gupta literature, science and technology - Kalidasa, Aryabhata, Varahamihira

secs.t: Gupta age — FIRSTs, earliest and the classical-age label

x: Aryabhata is regarded as the first Indian scholar to treat mathematics as a distinct subject; Aryabhatiya contains a separate Ganitapada.
The Sankheda copper plate is dated 594 CE (cited by some sources as the earliest dated place-value numeral); 876 CE is the Gwalior inscription.
Arab contact
carried the Indian decimal place-value notation to the Islamic world and subsequently to Europe.
The criticism highlights rigid caste distinctions, forced labour, declining trade and towns, and the falling status of women, showing that benefits were unevenly distributed.

secs.t: Navaratnas of Chandragupta II → fields

x: All four pairs are correctly matched.
Amarasimha was a lexicographer associated with the Amarakosha.
The Navaratna list is a traditional association.

secs.t: Scientists and physicians → works and contributions

x: The Brahmasphutasiddhanta is by Brahmagupta; Varahamihira wrote the Panchasiddhantika, Brihat Samhita and Brihat Jataka.
Brahmagupta formulated rules of arithmetic involving
zero and negative quantities
Bhaskara II belonged to the twelfth century and authored Siddhanta Shiromani, in addition to Lilavati.
Aryabhata is credited with using zero and place value, while Brahmagupta formalised arithmetic involving zero.

secs.t: Scientists and physicians → works and contributions — Varahamihira's texts

x: Varahamihira's works range across several branches of knowledge, and Greek astronomical influence is considered possible.
Romaka Siddhanta is an astronomical work summarised by Varahamihira and reflects Roman-Greek influence, comparable to the Paulisa tradition.
Ancient physicians used iron and mercury preparations, performed operations such as lithotomy, and Navanitakam was a medical manual concerning metallic preparations.

secs.t: Kalidasa → works, plots and wrong attributions

x: Exam angle: "which is NOT by Kalidasa" - Mudrarakshasa, Mrichchhakatika, Kiratarjuniya are the usual distractors.
Abhijnana Shakuntalam
is a play, not one of these five Mahakavyas.
Abhijnana Shakuntalam and Vikramorvashiyam are dramas; Kumarasambhava is a Mahakavya; and Meghaduta is a lyric poem.
Malavikagnimitram portrays the love of Agnimitra, a
Shunga king of Vidisha
, and Malavika.

secs.t: Other Gupta books → authors (drama, fables, polity, grammar, law)

x: Devichandraguptam is attributed to
Vishakhadatta
and deals with events connected with Ramagupta and Dhruvadevi.
Hitopadesha is a later work based on the Panchatantra, while Bhasa predates Kalidasa and Charudatta is his best-known play in this context.
Amarakosha was written by Amarasimha, Chandra Vyakarana by Chandragomin, Prakrit Prakasha by Vararuchi, and Katantra by Sharvavarman.
The Panchatantra is attributed to
Vishnu Sharma
and is placed in the Gupta period (APPSC 2012).

secs.t: Mehrauli pillar and sculpture → ruler, site, feature

x: The pillar is now at Mehrauli, was originally erected at Udayagiri near Vidisha, and its inscription records victories or authority in the North-West and Bengal.
The high-phosphorus iron is associated with the formation of a protective layer, helping the pillar resist corrosion for more than fifteen centuries.
The seated Buddha at Sarnath is characteristically shown in the
Dharmachakra mudra
, symbolising the turning of the wheel of the Dharma.

secs.t: Gupta structural temples → site, deity, material, stage

x: Bhitargaon = 5th-6th c. brick temple (UPPSC 2021, both statements true).
The Deogarh Dashavatara Temple is a stone temple dedicated to Vishnu, with a shikhara and panchayatana plan.
Bhitargaon in Kanpur district is a Brahmanical brick temple of the 5th–6th century CE and is noted for its terracotta panels.
Sanchi 17 has a flat roof and four-pillar porch; Nachna has a covered ambulatory; Bhumara has flanking shrines; and Deogarh has a shikhara with a panchayatana plan.
The Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal (like the Malegitti Shivalaya) is Dravida in style (UPSC 2026).

secs.t: Ajanta → location, phases, patrons, panels, technique — Ajanta - basics

x: The Ajanta caves were recorded by the British officer John Smith in 1819 while he was hunting tigers.
Ajanta has about 30 caves; Caves 9 and 10 contain the earliest paintings, and the later phase received Vakataka patronage under Harishena.
The Chhaddanta Jataka is in
Cave 10
, one of the earliest (Satavahana-era) painted caves (APPSC G2 2012).

secs.t: Ajanta → location, phases, patrons, panels, technique — Themes, panels and technique

x: The Dying Princess is associated with Cave 16.
Padmapani and Vajrapani are Bodhisattvas, and the Mother and Child panel is associated with Cave 17.
Ajanta contains themes from Jataka tales, secular life, Bodhi-tree worship and group dances.
Lapis-lazuli blue is in fact used at Ajanta, though some sources claim otherwise.

secs.t: Udayagiri, Bagh and other caves → site, feature

x: The Udayagiri caves near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh comprise twenty caves, including nineteen Hindu and one Jain cave, with Varaha and Shiva representations.
The Bagh caves in Dhar district of Madhya Pradesh comprise nine Buddhist viharas, generally dated to the fifth–sixth centuries CE, and their paintings include secular and local themes.

secs.t: Gupta coins → type and ruler

x: The silver coins introduced after the Saka conquest were modelled on
Saka silver issues
The Kartikeya / king feeding peacock type (and an Ashvamedha type) belongs to Kumaragupta I. So A is incomplete and C and D include pair 2.
The king-queen type belongs to Chandragupta I; tiger-slayer to Samudragupta; lion-slayer to Chandragupta II; and Garuda standard to Skandagupta.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Works such as the Romaka and Paulisa Siddhantas show Greek input into Indian science.
The earliest Ajanta paintings, especially those in Caves 9 and 10, are associated with the Satavahana period and are linked to the Amaravati style.
The gift was a Sarnath Buddha in Dhyan mudra presented to Thailand's King in April 2025.

rows.title: Vakatakas; Harshavardhana - sources (Harshacharita, Hiuen Tsang), Kannauj and Prayag assemblies, administration
sub: Group-II S1-30: Harshavardhana - sources, rise to power and conquests
Group-II S1-31: Harsha's administration, religion, patronage and the accounts of Hiuen Tsang and Banabhatta

secs.t: Vakataka rulers → contributions

x: Pravarasena I was Vindhyashakti’s son, the only Vakataka ruler to take the title Samrat, and performed Vajapeya and Ashvamedha sacrifices.
She married Rudrasena II; Pravarasena I was the son of the founder Vindhyashakti.
Pravarasena II
wrote the Prakrit work Setubandha.
Harishena patronised Ajanta
Caves 16 and 17
through his minister Varahadeva.

secs.t: Vardhana rulers → lineage, titles and capitals

x: Harsha died without an heir in 647 CE, bringing the Pushyabhuti line to an end.
Prabhakaravardhana was their father, Yashomati became sati in 605 CE, and Rajyavardhana was killed by Sasanka.
Harsha bore the title
Siladitya
(APPSC G1 2012) and also Sakalottarapathanatha, lord of all North India.
The line is called the
Pushyabhuti
dynasty after its founder Pushyabhuti (BPSC 2022 key); its rulers were once Gupta feudatories.

secs.t: Harsha's conquests → allies, rivals and vassals

x: Dhruvasena II of Valabhi was made a vassal of Harsha and married Harsha's daughter.
The Maukharis were associated with Grahavarman, Gauda with Sasanka, Kamarupa with Bhaskaravarman and Valabhi with Dhruvasena II.
Sasanka of Gauda was Harsha’s enemy and was responsible for the killing of Rajyavardhana.
Nepal, Kashmir and Kamarupa acknowledged Harsha's authority or sent tribute.
Both statements are true, and Pulakesin II's victory explains why Harsha's southward advance stopped at the Narmada.

secs.t: Books, inscriptions and court poets → authors — Literary works

x: Exam angle: "not written by Harsha" =
Harshacharita
Exam angle: "Which is NOT written by Harsha?" - the answer is
Harshacharita
(by Bana) or Kadambari; Bana is paired with Harsha, not the Guptas or Kanishka.
Harshacharita, written by Banabhatta, is
a semi-historical biography of Harsha
and an important literary source for his reign.
Banabhatta
, Harsha's court poet, wrote Kadambari, one of the earliest Sanskrit novels, as well as Harshacharita.

secs.t: Books, inscriptions and court poets → authors — Inscriptions

x: The Madhuban plate, Sonpat seal and Banskhera inscription are all sources for Harsha's reign; the Banskhera record is noted for bearing Harsha's signature.
Harshacharita is a literary Sanskrit biography, Si-Yu-Ki is a foreign account, Banskhera bears Harsha's signature and the Madhuban plate is an epigraphic land-grant record useful for chronology.
The
Aihole inscription
is a Chalukyan epigraphic source recording Pulakesin II's victory over Harsha on the Narmada.

secs.t: Harsha's religion and the Kannauj and Prayag assemblies

x: The Kannauj assembly honoured Hiuen Tsang and propagated Mahayana, while the Prayag assembly was primarily a charitable gathering held periodically.
The Prayag assembly was held every five years, Harsha distributed his treasury while retaining only his clothes, and Hiuen Tsang attended the sixth assembly.
Harsha was converted to Mahayana Buddhism under the influence of
Hiuen Tsang
; the influence of his sister Rajyashri is also noted.

secs.t: Harsha's administration → revenue, officials, punishments

x: The four parts were assigned to the king's own use or state administration, public servants, scholars and religious activities including charity to Brahmanas and Buddhist monks.
Officials were commonly remunerated through land grants rather than cash, while samantas acknowledged Harsha's authority by sending tribute.
Prisoners could be left to languish in dungeons; they were not always released after a short period.

secs.t: Nalanda in Harsha's time → founder, head, curriculum

x: Exam angle: statement sets mixing "founded by Harsha" / "Hiuen Tsang was chancellor" with the correct one (Silabhadra).
Nalanda had a difficult entrance examination, used Sanskrit as the medium of instruction and encouraged debate over lectures.
Nalanda accommodated about 10,000 students with free boarding; Hiuen Tsang studied and taught there; and Harsha built a multi-storied monastery at the institution.

secs.t: Hiuen Tsang → profile and observations

x: Hiuen Tsang was a Chinese Buddhist monk popularly called the ‘
Prince of Pilgrims
’; some accounts also refer to him as the ‘King of Travelers’.
Si-Yu-Ki is regarded as
the longest and most detailed account of Central and South Asia
among the works associated with Hiuen Tsang.
Hiuen Tsang mentioned rigid caste distinctions, untouchables, the declining position of women and the rise of Brahmanism.

secs.t: Hiuen Tsang's places → what he found (incl. Andhra)

x: Hiuen Tsang referred to Andhra as An-to-lo and identified
Vengi
as its capital.
Vengi had about 20 viharas and Dhanyakataka had about 20 Mahasanghika viharas.
The account records decline at Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda, degeneration of some monasteries and lack of patronage at Sriparvata.
The tradition recorded by Hiuen Tsang stated that Buddha first visited Salihundam and then Dharanikota, identified with Dhanyakataka.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Hiuen Tsang visited Andhra in
, during the time of Kubja Vishnuvardhana.
Hiuen Tsang's Andhra account is the principal evidence, while the cited explanation attributes the decline to Shaiva propaganda and associates Kumarila Bhatta with it.
Harsha's court at Kannauj was an intellectual centre, and his rule represented the last great unified empire of ancient northern India before the Rajput age.

units.title: Kanauj and their Contributions; South Indian Dynasties - Badami Chalukyas, Eastern Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Kalyani Chalukyas, Cholas, Hoysalas, Yadavas, Kakatiyas, Reddis

rows.title: Tripartite struggle for Kanauj - Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas; causes and outcome

secs.t: Kannauj → ancient names and causes of the struggle

x: Mahodaya
, also expressed as Mahodaya Shri, was an ancient name associated with Kannauj.
After Harsha, Kannauj became a symbol of imperial sovereignty and was associated with the title of Samrat of North India.
Kannauj commanded the agrarian wealth of the Gangetic Doab and access to Arabian Sea trade through Gujarat, thereby bypassing the Arab-held Indus delta.

secs.t: Contending dynasties → base, rulers, distractors

x: Mihira Bhoja was a Gurjara-Pratihara ruler who held Kannauj in the later phase; the Pala rulers were Dharmapala, Devapala and Mahipala I. So A is incomplete and C and D include statement 3.
Vatsaraja, Dharmapala and Dhruva belonged respectively to the Pratihara, Pala and Rashtrakuta dynasties.
The correct sequence is Pallava Mahendravarman I, Pala Gopala, Pratihara Bhoja and Chola Parantaka I.

secs.t: Phases → Kannauj rulers installed and removed

x: The struggle began when Gurjara-Pratihara ruler
Vatsaraja
, around 780–800 CE, clashed with Dharmapala and Rashtrakuta ruler Dhruva.
The sequence was Vatsaraja's occupation, Dharmapala's installation of Chakrayudha, Nagabhata II's ousting of Chakrayudha, and the later Pratihara control under Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala I.
Dharmapala removed the Pratihara nominee
Indrayudha
and installed Chakrayudha as his puppet ruler at Kannauj.

secs.t: Rashtrakuta rulers → northern campaigns (defeated whom)

x: Dhruva defeated Vatsaraja and Dharmapala, took booty and returned south.
Rashtrakuta ruler Indra III sacked Kannauj around 916 CE after defeating Pratihara ruler
Mahipala I
The Rashtrakuta campaigns brought booty and prestige, but the Rashtrakutas did not retain lasting control over the northern territories.
Govinda III defeated Nagabhata II.

secs.t: Inscriptions → dynasty and content

x: The Sanjan plates, issued during the reign of Rashtrakuta ruler Amoghavarsha I in 871 CE, describe
Govinda III's Himalayan campaign
The
Gwalior prashasti
of Mihira Bhoja records Nagabhata II's victories over Chakrayudha and Dharmapala.
The Khalimpur plates state that Dharmapala installed Chakrayudha at Kannauj with the approval of the northern kings.

secs.t: Outcome → winner, duration, effects

x: Kannauj was finally held by the Pratiharas under Bhoja and Mahendrapala I, but no single power permanently retained it for a long period.
The exhaustion of the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas, along with Pratihara decline after Indra III's raid, opened the way for new Rajput states such as the Chandelas and Chauhans.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The struggle demonstrates the shift of power to regional kingdoms during early medieval India.
Rashtrakuta ruler
Dhruva
defeated Vishnuvardhana IV of the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, showing the parallel Deccan dimension of Rashtrakuta expansion.
Kannauj's primacy began under Harsha; Hiuen Tsang observed that Pataliputra had lost its earlier place to Kannauj.

rows.title: Palas of Bengal - Gopala, Dharmapala, Devapala; Nalanda and Vikramshila, Pala art

secs.t: Pala rulers → achievements, and the Sena successors

x: Dharmapala (c. 770-810) installed the puppet Chakrayudha at Kannauj, was defeated by Dhruva and by Nagabhata II near Monghyr, and founded Vikramashila.
Mahipala I
, whose reign is placed around c. 977–1027, revived Pala power and was defeated by Rajendra Chola.
The order is Gopala (elected founder, mid-8th c.), Devapala, Mahipala I (c. 977-1027) and Ramapala (c. 1072-1126), the last strong Pala ruler.

secs.t: Acharyas and foreign contacts → institution, Tibet, Southeast Asia

x: Pala-style bronze images found in Southeast Asia indicate maritime cultural exchange across the Bay of Bengal.
Shilabhadra was associated with Nalanda in Harsha's time; Shantarakshita went to Tibet and founded Samye; Atisha was linked with Vikramashila; and Sakya Sri Bhadra was associated with Jagaddala.
Kautilya
was not a Nalanda acharya (BPSC 2025 trap).

secs.t: Pala-era mahaviharas → founder, present location

x: Somapura Mahavihara is located at Paharpur in Naogaon district of present-day Bangladesh.
Odantapuri was situated at Bihar Sharif in Nalanda district of Bihar and is described as having accommodated approximately 12,000 monks.
The destruction is generally placed around
Taxila
was an ancient centre in Gandhara and does not belong to the early-medieval Pala group.

secs.t: Pala art and books → artists, authors

x: Pala art is known for bronze and black-stone or basalt sculpture and illustrated Buddhist manuscripts written on palm leaves.
Somapura had rich terracotta ornamentation and Vikramashila had terracotta panels on its walls.
Ramacharita was written by
Sandhyakar Nandi
and deals with Ramapala and the Kaivarta peasant revolt.
Buddhist texts were compiled at Nalanda under Dharmapala, while Jagaddala became associated with translating books into Tibetan.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Palas were the last major royal patrons of Buddhism in India and supported its transmission to Tibet and Southeast Asia through institutions, teachers and maritime contacts.
Andhra's Dharmakirti taught at Nalanda and studied under the Nalanda head Dharmapala of Kanchi.
Kumaragupta I founded Nalanda, Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura, and Ramapala founded Jagaddala.

rows.title: Gurjara-Pratiharas - Nagabhata I and II, Mihira Bhoja; resistance to Arab expansion

secs.t: Pratiharas → name, origin and capitals

x: The dynasty claimed descent from Lakshmana, who was regarded as Rama's
door-keeper
brother.
The Agnikula legend associates the
Pratiharas, Chaulukyas, Paramaras and Chauhans
with birth from the fire-pit at Mount Abu.
The sequence was Bhinmal in early Rajasthan, followed by Ujjain or Avanti, and later Kannauj, also known as Mahodaya, from the time of Nagabhata II.

secs.t: Pratihara rulers → period and achievement

x: Vatsaraja took Kannauj and defeated Dharmapala, but was later defeated by the Rashtrakuta ruler Dhruva, marking the beginning of the tripartite struggle.
Nagabhata II ousted Chakrayudha, beat Dharmapala near Monghyr, was himself defeated by Rashtrakuta Govinda III, and made Kannauj the Pratihara capital.
Mihira Bhoja
, also known as Bhoja I, ruled approximately from c. 836 to c. 890, when the dynasty reached its zenith.

secs.t: Mihira Bhoja → title, parentage, capital, extent

x: Mihira Bhoja was the son of
Ramabhadra
and therefore the grandson of Nagabhata II.
Mihira Bhoja bore the title
Adivaraha
, reflecting his devotion to Vishnu; Adivaraha also appeared on his coins.
Kannauj was the capital of Mihira Bhoja's kingdom and was also known as Mahodaya.
Early defeats by Palas, Rashtrakutas and Kalachuris were followed by a comeback.

secs.t: Arab travellers → what they said of the Pratiharas

x: The Teli-ka-Mandir at Gwalior is associated with
Mihira Bhoja
Sulaiman (mid-9th century) called him Juzr/Al-Juzr.
Sulaiman praised the Pratihara cavalry, while he named Amoghavarsha of the Rashtrakutas as one of the four great kings of the world.

secs.t: Rajashekhara → patrons and works

x: Prabandhachintamani
was written by Merutunga, whereas Kavyamimamsa, Karpuramanjari and Viddhasalabhanjika were works of Rajashekhara.
Kavyamimamsa is a work on poetics, Karpuramanjari is a Prakrit play and Viddhasalabhanjika is by Rajashekhara.
Rajashekhara was the court poet of Mahendrapala I and was also associated with the court of Mahipala I.

secs.t: Decline → raids and successor Rajput states

x: All three developments weakened the Pratihara power: Indra III raided Kannauj, Mahmud of Ghazni attacked it in 1018, and several feudatories became independent.
The
Chandelas, Chauhans, Paramaras and Chaulukyas
broke away as the Pratihara feudatory structure weakened.
The Pratihara temple style is stated to have peaked at
Khajuraho
, built by the Chandelas (originally Pratihara feudatories) and now a UNESCO site.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Gurjara-Pratiharas were the principal power that helped keep Arab rule confined to Sindh.

rows.title: Rashtrakutas - Dantidurga, Govinda III, Amoghavarsha (Kavirajamarga), Krishna I

secs.t: Rashtrakuta rulers → period, capital and contribution

x: Dantidurga, whose reign is placed around 753–756 CE, was contemporary with Eastern Chalukya
Vijayaditya I
Dhruva was the first Rashtrakuta ruler to move north, defeated Vatsaraja and Dharmapala, and subdued the Eastern Chalukyas and the Gangas of Talakad.
The sequence is Dantidurga, Dhruva, Govinda III and Amoghavarsha I. Their approximate reign periods were 753–756, 780–793, 793–814 and 814–878 respectively.

secs.t: Battles and conflicts → victor: Vengi, Takkolam

x: The Rashtrakuta–Vengi conflict continued for approximately 200 years and involved repeated struggles with the Eastern Chalukyas.
Dhruva acted through Vemulavada Arikesari I to beat Vishnuvardhana IV, who then gave his daughter Shila Mahadevi to Dhruva; Amoghavarsha I won at Vingavalli and took the title Viranarayana.
At Takkolam in 949 CE, Krishna III defeated the Cholas under Parantaka I, and the Chola prince Rajaditya was killed.

secs.t: Titles → ruler

x: Balhara, or Vallabharaja, was a title generally used for Rashtrakuta kings, not exclusively for Govinda III.

secs.t: Literary works → authors; court poets → patrons

x: Pampa wrote a Kannada Adipurana, Jinasena wrote a Sanskrit Adipurana, and Pampa is described as Telugu-origin or Telugu-born.
Pampa was patronised by Arikesari II, Ponna by Krishna III, Ranna by Tailapa II, and Swayambhu was an Apabhramsha poet linked to the court.
The Kannada Ratnatraya consisted of
Pampa, Ponna and Ranna
, the three celebrated Kannada poets associated with major royal patrons.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pampa wrote Vikramarjuna Vijaya in Kannada, modelled Arjuna on Arikesari II, and is noted as a Telugu-born or Telugu-origin poet.
The Rashtrakuta period is described as a golden age of Kannada and as the zenith of rock-cut art, represented by the Kailasa temple at Ellora and Elephanta.
Sulaiman visited the court of
Amoghavarsha I
and considered him one of the four great kings of the world.

src: Sources: CDI (Block03 Rashtrakutas - Literature, Exam Value Additions; Block09 Rashtrakutas Literature; Block02 Sulaiman); UPSC (Medieval History p.8, 9, 44); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Eastern Chalukyas); CDX (AP History Complete Notes p.110, 116, 117)

rows.title: Rashtrakuta administration, trade and religion; Kailasa temple at Ellora; Al-Masudi's account

secs.t: Rashtrakuta administration → founder, capital, units and officers

x: Rashtra was headed by the Rashtrapati, Vishaya by the Vishayapati, Bhukti by the Bhogapati and Grama by the Gramakuta or gavunda.
Nad-gavundas were hereditary local officers of the nadu and assisted in the collection of revenue.
Manyakheta, known as Malkhed and located in Karnataka, was the Rashtrakuta capital.
Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakuta power by overthrowing the Badami Chalukya Kirtivarman II.

secs.t: Trade, ports and Arab travellers → accounts

x: Sulaiman
, who visited during the reign of Amoghavarsha I, ranked the Rashtrakuta king among the four great kings along with the Caliph, the Chinese emperor and the Byzantine emperor.
Control of major trade routes
brought prosperity to the Rashtrakutas and connected them with Gujarat, the Arabian Peninsula and South India.

secs.t: Religion → patronage; court works → authors

x: Jainism
reached a high point under Amoghavarsha I, who was a devout Jain and is described as having renounced the throne.
Rashtrakuta religious policy included Shaiva royal affiliation, patronage of Vaishnavism and Buddhism without persecution, and accommodation of Muslim Arab merchants in ports.
Trivikrama
(Trivikrama Bhatta) composed Nalachampu, the first Champu.

secs.t: Cave sites → location, groups, patron: Ellora and Elephanta — Ellora - caves, location and setting

x: Charanandri hills, Aurangabad district, near the Elaganga.
Caves 13–29 constitute the Hindu group.
Cave 10 is the only chaitya, Cave 14 is Ravan ki Khai, Cave 16 is Kailasa and Cave 32 is Indra Sabha.
Ellora has 34 caves (APPSC-GS 2024): Buddhist 12 (Caves 1-12), Hindu 17 (Caves 13-29) and Jain 5 (Caves 30-34).

secs.t: Cave sites → location, groups, patron: Ellora and Elephanta — Ellora - chronology and patronage

x: Exam angle: cave count, the 12-17-5 split, and ordering of named caves.
Elephanta is near Mumbai, its patronage is debated with many historians favouring the sixth-century Kalachuris, and its famous image is the Trimurti.
The MPPSC 2021 key attributes Ellora and Elephanta to the
Rashtrakutas
, though many historians date Elephanta's main cave to the 6th-century Kalachuris.

secs.t: Kailasa temple (Ellora Cave 16) → ruler, technique, features

x: Exam angle: "carved during the reign of" - Krishna I, not Dantidurga or Amoghavarsha.
The temple was excavated downward and inward from one basalt cliff and is the largest monolithic rock excavation, larger in surface area than the Parthenon.
The temple contains panels such as Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa, Mahishasuramardini and Shiva Nataraja, along with Ramayana, Mahabharata and Purana scenes.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The twinning agreement signed by India and Jordan concerned
Petra and Ellora
, both UNESCO sites.
The Rashtrakuta era raised Kannada to a classical medium and gave Ellora its Hindu peak.
Krishna III helped Danarnava kill Ammaraja II in 970 CE and seize Vengi.
The Rashtrakutas declined by the late tenth century under Chalukya-Chola pressure.

rows.title: Badami (Vatapi) Chalukyas - Pulakesin I, Pulakesin II, Aihole inscription of Ravikirti

secs.t: Badami Chalukya rulers → period and achievement

x: Pulakesin I fortified Vatapi, as recorded in the Badami cliff inscription dated to
543 CE
After exile, Pulakesin II attacked and killed Mangalesha at
Elapattu-Simbige in the Bana territory
around 609-10 CE.

Pulakesin I founded the independent kingdom; Kirtivarman I expanded it and became the ‘night of doom’; Mangalesha ruled as regent and extended the territory; Vikramaditya I restored power after Pallava occupation.

secs.t: Pulakesin II → reign, titles and FIRST

x: Pulakesin II ruled from 609 to 642 CE.
Dakshinapatheshwara contrasts with Harsha's Uttarapatheshwara.

secs.t: Pulakesin II → conquests, Vengi and foreign contacts

x: Pulakesin II conquered Kosala and Kalinga, marched to Vengi, defeated the Durjayas and appointed Kubja Vishnuvardhana there.
Embassies were exchanged with Khusrau II.
The account of China–India relations under the Chalukyas is credited to
Ma Twan-lin
, also rendered in some references as Matwalin.

secs.t: Aihole inscription → author, language, date, poets, victories

x: Ravikirti, a Jain poet, wrote this Sanskrit verse prasasti.
The Aihole inscription refers to the celebrated poets
Kalidasa and Bharavi
Kirtivarman I is described as the ‘night of doom’ to the
Nalas, Mauryas and Kadambas

secs.t: Other inscriptions → Andhra place names and events

x: Exam angle: "Which inscription of Pulakesin II calls Mangalagiri Mangalapura?"
The
Satara inscription
of 617 CE records Pulakesin II's appointment of his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana as viceroy of Vengi.
The inscriptions at Chipurupalli, Kopparam, Chejarala and Timmapuram are associated with Kubja Vishnuvardhana, and Timmapuram uses the titles ‘Maharaja’ and devotee of Vishnu.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pulakesin II's Vengi conquest led to the Eastern Chalukya line, with Vishnuvardhana's appointment in 617 CE, independence in 624 CE and Pithapuram as capital.
The Pune copper plates of Eastern Chalukya
Vishnuvardhana II
, dated 669 CE, contain the first epigraphic reference to Guntur as Kumturu.
The Badami Chalukyas are significant for bridging North and South India, while the Aihole inscription is an important dated prasasti for their history.

src: Sources: UPSC (Medieval History p.25-26); CDI (Block03 Badami Chalukyas intro and exam table; Religious synthesis); CDX (AP History p.110-111, 113); APP (Indian History Part 1 > Harsha; AP History Ancient Part 1 & 2 > Eastern Chalukyas, cross-era fragments); APHQ (G2 2019); TH 25 Aug 2026

rows.title: Chalukya-Harsha and Chalukya-Pallava conflicts; Chalukya administration

secs.t: Battles → place, date, victor and source

x: Pulakesin II of the Badami Chalukyas
stopped Harsha's southward expansion on the Narmada.
The Aihole inscription of Pulakesin II, composed by Ravikirti, and Hiuen Tsang’s account confirm the conflict.
Narasimhavarman I defeated Pulakesin II at Manimangala around 642 CE.
Paranjoti
was the Pallava general associated with Narasimhavarman I’s sack of Vatapi.

secs.t: Chalukya-Pallava rivalry → rounds and rulers

x: C is wrong: Nandivarman II was the Pallava ruler whose Kanchi Vikramaditya II took three times and spared; he did not overthrow the Rashtrakutas.
Vikramaditya II entered Kanchi around 740 CE during Nandivarman II’s reign and left a Kannada inscription on a pillar.
Lokamahadevi’s
Virupaksha temple
at Pattadakal commemorates Vikramaditya II’s victory and copies the Kailasanatha temple of Kanchi.

secs.t: Titles won in these wars → ruler

x: Pulakesin II was styled
Dakshinapatheshwara
, meaning lord of the south, in opposition to Harsha’s title Uttarapatheshwara.
Narasimhavarman I
assumed the title Vatapikonda, meaning conqueror of Vatapi, after capturing the Chalukya capital.

secs.t: Chalukya administration → units, agraharas, feudatories

x: Vishayapati
was the official heading a Rashtra or Vishaya.
Agraharas were Brahmin land grants run by mahajanas.
The Alupas, Gangas and Sendrakas were feudatories.
In Rayalaseema, the Renati Chodas were initially feudatories of the early Pallavas and subsequently became feudatories of the Badami Chalukyas.

secs.t: Women in administration → queens and princesses

x: Vijayabhattarika, also known as Vijaya-mahadevi, was the queen of Chandraditya and governed while issuing land grants in her own name.
Lokamahadevi and Trailokyamahadevi
, queens of Vikramaditya II, commissioned the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples at Pattadakal.
Akkadevi, a Kalyani Chalukya princess, governed the province of Kisukad.
The
Chalukyas
frequently gave ladies high administrative positions (UPPSC 2007 key).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The wars stimulated political activity in Rayalaseema, including
the rise of the Renati Chodas, Banas and Vaidumbas
The Pitikayagulla inscription indicates
post-Badami Chalukya influence in Rayalaseema
and is written in early Telugu script.
The rivalry lasted about a century and influenced Deccan and Tamil politics as well as temple art.

src: Sources: APP (Indian History Part 1 > Harsha's conquests, timeline); UPSC (Medieval History p.25-26, 29); CDI (Block03 Badami Chalukyas intro, Pattadakal; SOUTH INDIAN DYNASTIES); CDX (AP History p.111, 150); APPCA Jun 2026; TH 14 Jun 2026

rows.title: Badami Chalukya art - Aihole, Badami, Pattadakal (UNESCO); origin of the Vesara style

secs.t: Epithets, FIRSTs and UNESCO status

x: K. A. Nilakanta Sastri described Aihole as the “
Cradle of Indian temple architecture
Percy Brown credited the Chalukyas with being the first to break the monopoly of the rock-cut tradition in the Deccan.
Pattadakal was a royal coronation site, is associated with the coronation stone, represents the mature phase and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

secs.t: Persons → patronage and craft

x: Ravikirti was the
poet and composer
named in the Aihole Meguti inscription, not the architect of the temple.
The Virupaksha temple inscriptions name the architects
Gunda Anivaritachari and Sarvasiddhi Acharya

secs.t: Sites → features: Badami, Aihole, Pattadakal, Alampur

x: Badami has four principal sandstone caves dating broadly to the 6th–7th centuries; the earliest were made under Mangalesha, and the fourth cave is Jain.
Pattadakal displays Nagara and Dravida temple forms side by side and represents the mature phase of Chalukyan architecture.
Pattadakal is noted for Nandi mandapas, narrative friezes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Panchatantra, and polished pillars.

secs.t: Temple → site → shikhara style

x: Lokamahadevi's Virupaksha commemorates the victory over the Pallavas and copies Kailasanatha, Kanchi.
Ravana Phadi is a rock-cut cave at Aihole without a tower.
Papanatha at Pattadakal is associated with the Nagara style.
Huchimalligudi at Aihole and the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh have Nagara shikharas (UPSC 2026 key).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The sequence proceeds from the rock-cut caves of Badami to the experimental structural temples of Aihole and finally to the mature architectural phase at Pattadakal.
Bikkavolu and Draksharama
are cited as Andhra examples of the Vesara or Chalukyan style carried by the Eastern Chalukyas.
The Virupaksha temple is Dravida, not Nagara.

src: Sources: CDI (Block03 Badami Chalukyas - Vesara style, Pattadakal, exam table; SOUTH INDIAN DYNASTIES); UPSC (Art & Culture p.37, 44; Medieval History p.31); APP (Indian History Part 1 > temple styles, Lad Khan; Chola > Dravida; AP History Ancient Part 2 > Eastern Chalukyas); APHQ (G2 2008 Navabrahma)

rows.title: Pallavas - Simhavishnu, Mahendravarman I, Narasimhavarman I Mamalla, Nandivarman II

secs.t: Pallavas → origin, territory, period and capital

x: Kanchipuram was the Pallava capital, and the Pallava dynasty is generally placed approximately between 275 and 897 CE.
The major theories mentioned are Parthian or Pahlava origin, Andhra origin and local Tamil origin in Tondaimandalam.
The Andhra-origin theory draws support from early Prakrit charters found in the Krishna-Guntur region and the Pallavas’ replacement of the Ikshvakus there.

secs.t: Inscriptions and charters → ruler and point

x: The Mayidavolu plates were issued by Sivaskandavarman as yuvaraja, the Hirahadagalli plates record his sacrifices, and the Manchikallu inscription is associated with Simhavarman’s conquest of Vijayapuri.
Pallava
Simhavarman
defeated the last Ikshvaku ruler Rudrapurushadatta, an event associated with the establishment of Pallava rule in the Krishna valley.
Mahendravarman I lost the Krishna-Godavari region to the Chalukya ruler
Pulakesin II
, as indicated by the Maruturu and Kopparam inscriptions.

secs.t: Pallava rulers → period and political event

x: Sivaskandavarman is linked with Kanchi coming under Pallava control; Vishnugopa faced Samudragupta; Simhavishnu defeated the Kalabhras; and Narasimhavarman I took Vatapi.
Narasimhavarman I defeated and killed Pulakesin II at Manimangala in 642 CE and captured or sacked Vatapi through his general Paranjoti.
Aditya I Chola
killed Aparajita, bringing the Pallava dynasty to an end around 897–898 CE.

secs.t: Titles → ruler

x: Mamalla and Vatapikonda were his titles.

secs.t: Books → authors; Kanchi as a centre of learning

x: Mahendravarman I
(c. 600-630) wrote the Mattavilasa Prahasana (APPSC-G1 2012), and Mattavilasa was also one of his titles.
A Ghatika was a higher learning centre where scholars gathered, generally attached to temples.
According to the Talagunda inscription, Mayurasharman, a Brahmin student at
the Kanchi Ghatika
, was insulted by a Pallava horseman and subsequently took up arms and founded the Kadamba kingdom.

secs.t: Religion and temple building → ruler

x: The
Mandagapattu
cave temple carries the celebrated claim that it was constructed without brick, timber, metal or mortar.
Mandagapattu, Mahendravadi and Dalavanur are associated with Mahendravarman I’s cave temples.
He was a Vaishnavite who built Vaikuntha Perumal, Kanchi.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pallava rule was important for Dravida temple architecture, the spread of Grantha-derived scripts, and the growth of Alvar and Nayanar Bhakti traditions.
The Mayidavolu and Manchikallu records are associated with Andhra, and the Renati Chodas are identified as early Pallava feudatories.

src: Sources: CDI (Block03 Pallavas intro, 4 stages; Block09 Pallavas Andhra - Religion, Rathas); UPSC (Medieval History p.26, 31-32); APHQ (G2 2019, 2025, 2000); APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Ikshvakus - Rudrapurushadatta; Part 2 > fragments); CDX (AP History p.108, 111, 147, 150)

rows.title: Pallava art and architecture - Mandagapattu inscription, Mahabalipuram rathas, Shore Temple, Kailasanatha

secs.t: Phases of Pallava architecture → ruler → example

x: Pallava architecture evolved from rock-cut pillared mandapas to monolithic rathas and mandapas, and subsequently to structural temples.

The Mahendra phase is represented by Mandagapattu and Mahendravadi; the Mamalla phase by the Pancha Rathas; the Rajasimha phase by the Shore Temple and Kailasanatha; and the later phase by Vaikuntha Perumal.
The Nandivarman/Aparajita phase is associated with smaller structural temples such as Vaikuntha Perumal, not the earliest rock-cut cave temples.

secs.t: FIRSTs, largest, smallest, oldest

x: The inscription is associated with
the beginning of rock-cut cave temples in South India
under Mahendravarman I.
Dvarapalakas
, or guardian figures, are found at the entrance and later became common in South Indian temples.
Arjuna's Penance or the Descent of the Ganga is the largest open-air rock relief in India and is associated with Bhagiratha's penance.

secs.t: Monuments → patron → key fact: Mahabalipuram and Kanchi

x: The Pancha Rathas, Varaha Mandapa and Mahishasuramardini Cave are attributed to
Narasimhavarman I
, also known as Mamalla.
The Pancha Rathas are monolithic granite monuments named after the five Pandavas and Draupadi, and their forms imitate earlier wooden and structural traditions.
Vaikuntha Perumal is a Vishnu temple with a storeyed sanctum and panels depicting Pallava history.

secs.t: UNESCO sites → year: Mahabalipuram vs Ajanta

x: The Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram received UNESCO World Heritage status in 1984.
Ajanta was inscribed in 1983, contains 25 viharas and 4 chaityas, has Jataka paintings, and was found in 1819 by John Smith.
Ajanta consists mainly of cave paintings and rock-cut monasteries in a cliff, whereas Mahabalipuram is noted for open-air reliefs, monolithic rathas and a structural temple.

secs.t: Sculpture and painting → site

x: Pallava sculpture evolved from rigid forms towards graceful, dynamic and naturalistic representations and included narrative panels.
Jain cave in Pudukkottai with lotus-pond murals.
Panamalai contains a Rajasimha-period painting of
Parvati
in the Talagirishvara Temple.

secs.t: Pallava-style rock-cut caves in Andhra → location, attribution

x: The caves at Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram and Bhairavakonda are attributed to the
Vishnukundins
, who imitated the Pallava cave style in the Telugu lands.
Undavalli is a multi-storeyed Vishnukundin complex on the Krishna in Guntur district with a monolithic reclining Anantasayana Vishnu; its attribution is not Chola.
APPSC keys place Bhairavakona in
Nellore
district (one source, CDI, says Prakasam).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pallava rathas contributed the vimana and ardhamandapa forms to early Andhra temples, while Vishnukundin caves imitated Pallava style.
The Pallavas are regarded as pioneers of Dravida temple architecture.
The Pattadakal Virupaksha temple was modelled on the Pallava Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi.
Undavalli is a 4th-5th century monolithic complex on the Krishna.

src: Sources: CDI (Block03 Pallavas - Art & Sculpture, 4 stages, Mains value addition; Block09 Pallavas Rathas, Vishnukundin rock-cut caves); UPSC (Art & Culture p.35, 45, 48); APHQ (G2 2000, 2008, 2012, 2025); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > fragments; Indian History Part 1 > Ajanta); CDX (AP History p.58, 108); LENS Aug 2026 p.124

rows.title: Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi - Kubja Vishnuvardhana, dynastic history, patronage of Telugu (Nannaya)
sub: Group-II M1-A-19: Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi - Kubja Vishnuvardhana and the dynastic history

secs.t: Eastern Chalukyas — origin, period, identity and FIRSTs

x: The Eastern Chalukyas were founded as a branch of the
Badami Chalukyas
after Pulakeshin II conquered the Vengi region.
Pulakeshin II
conquered Vengi and appointed his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana as its viceroy.
The matronymic Hariti-putra was also used by the
Satavahanas, Ikshvakus and Kadambas
, indicating a southern cultural connection.
Gunaga Vijayaditya III
(Tripura Martya Maheshwara) is regarded as the greatest ruler of the line (APHQ 2011).

secs.t: Rulers → titles

x: Exam angle: title-to-king matching; the Kiranapuram/Achalapuram/Kandukur triplet is the favourite distractor trap.
Chalukya Bhima was associated with Kollabhiganda, Saktivarma I with Chalukya Chandra, Vimaladitya with Rajamartanda, and Rajaraja Narendra with Rajarajanarayana.
The key (G2 2012) credits Kollabhiganda to
Chalukya Bhima I
. Some sources give it to Vijayaditya IV, who ruled six months after Bhima: that is the trap.

secs.t: Rulers → contributions

x: All three statements are associated with Chalukya Bhima I: the 360 battles, a 30-year reign and the construction of the Pancharamas.
Panduranga, the commander of
Gunaga Vijayaditya III
, issued the Addanki inscription.
Rajendra Chalukya ousted Vijayaditya VII in 1070 CE and later became known as Kulottunga I.
Kubja Vishnuvardhana used Pithapuram as the first capital, Jayasimha Vallabha I used Vengi, and Rajamahendravaram was associated with Amma I and Rajaraja Narendra.

secs.t: Wars, defeats and marriage alliances — Rashtrakuta wars → ruler

x: Vishnuvardhana IV supported Govinda III, was defeated by Dhruva, and strengthened the relationship through Dhruva's marriage to Sheela Mahadevi.
Vijayaditya II is traditionally said to have fought 108 battles in 12 years.
Chalukya Bhima I repelled Krishna II's forces at
Niravadyapura and Peruvanguru

secs.t: Wars, defeats and marriage alliances — Later rivals - Telugu Chodas and Kalyani Chalukyas

x: The Telugu Choda ruler
Jatachoda Bhima
killed Danarnava and seized Vengi until Danarnava’s sons recovered it with Chola assistance.
Coins of
Saktivarman I
have been found in Arakan, present-day Burma.
After 973 CE, the
Kalyani Chalukyas
emerged as the principal rival of the Eastern Chalukyas.
Saktivarma I defeated Bayyalanambi with Chola help in 1006 CE.

secs.t: Wars, defeats and marriage alliances — Marriages and succession war

x: The events occurred in 624 CE, 1006 CE, 1022 CE and 1070 CE respectively.
Vimaladitya married both Kundavva and Melama, while Rajaraja Narendra married Ammanga Devi, the daughter of Rajendra Chola.
Rajaraja Narendra, the son of Kundavva, was supported by
Rajendra I
. Vijayaditya VII, the son of Melama, was supported by Kalyani Jayasimha II.
Ahavamalla Someshwara
killed Rajadhiraja I at Koppam in 1053.

secs.t: Capitals, towns and other names

x: Vijayaditya III, or Gunaga Vijayaditya, developed Kandukuru as another Bejawada.
Jayasimha Vallabha I
shifted the capital from Pithapuram to Vengi, identified with Pedavegi.
Ammaraja I made Rajamahendravaram his capital and Rajaraja Narendra ruled from it and made it famous (the G2 2008 key says he 'built Rajahmundry').
Dandin calls Vengi '
Andhra Nagaram

secs.t: Inscriptions and copper-plate grants → ruler

x: The Nandampudi inscription records Rajaraja Narendra's grant to Narayana Bhattu, written by Nannaya, and the Korumelli plates are also associated with Rajaraja Narendra.
The Chekurru copper-plate grant is associated with
Ammaraja I
. Vipparla is associated with Jayasimha I and Kopparam with Kubja Vishnuvardhana.
The Kopparam copper plates (631 CE) were issued by
Pulakesin II
; in these same plates Kubja Vishnuvardhana appears only as Yuvaraja.
The
Kalamalla inscription
, dated approximately to 575 CE and associated with Renati Choda Dhananjaya, predates Nannaya.

secs.t: Temples → builder and style

x: Exam angle: "108 Shaivalayas" → Vijayaditya II, not Kubja or Vishnuvardhana III/IV.
The Bikkavolu Shiva temples of
Mukteshwara, Vijayeshwara and Chandrashekhara
are attributed to Gunaga Vijayaditya III.
The Bhimeswara temples at Draksharama and Samalkot, also called Chalukya Bhimavaram, are associated with
Chalukya Bhima I
The
Vijayeshwara temple
is noted for its carved figures of the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna.

secs.t: Religion, queens and Jain patronage

x: Chamekamba
, a courtesan during the reign of Ammaraja II, secured the Kaluchumbarru grant for a Jain temple.
Kushmandini was the mother goddess of the Eastern Chalukyas (APPSC G2 2019 key).
The 2025 key makes Ayyana Mahadevi the queen of
Kubja Vishnuvardhana

secs.t: Poets, books and court figures → works and titles

x: Nannaya Bhattaraka is regarded as Adi Kavi because Andhra Mahabharatamu is considered the first major Telugu literary work.
Nannaya's Andhra Mahabharatamu follows the Champu style, which combines verse and prose.
Nannaya composed the Nandampudi inscription, which records the agrahara granted to his collaborator Narayana Bhattu under Rajaraja Narendra.
Pavuluri Ganitamu renders
Mahaviracharya's Ganitasarasangraham
in Telugu verse.

secs.t: Andhra dynasties → period

x: The Eastern Chalukyas ruled approximately from 624 to 1075 CE.
The 2019 key credits the Kesari Samudra lake to
Rudradeva

secs.t: Universal angles

x: A major significance of the Eastern Chalukyas was that they helped turn Telugu into a literary language and laid the foundation for Telugu literature.
The core territory was the Krishna-Godavari doab, known as Venginadu.
The 1075 CE date excludes the later Chalukya-Chola phase, whereas the 1189 CE interpretation includes that phase in the dynastic reckoning.

src: Sources: Group-I: APHQ (2002, 2017, 2019, 2025 PYQs); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Unit 1 Eastern Chalukyas); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.110-112, 122-123, 134, 205); CDI (Block03 Eastern Chalukyas; Block09 Literature); UPSC (Medieval History pp.24, 27)

Sources: Group-II M1-A-19: CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.110-111, 118, 121-122); APP (AP History Ancient Parts 1-2 > Eastern Chalukyas); CDI (Block03 Eastern Chalukyas); APHQ (PYQs 2011, 2012, 2017, 2019, 2025); UPSC (Medieval History p.27)
see: See also Group-II M1-A-21 (Growth of the Telugu language under the Eastern Chalukyas - Nannaya and the Andhra Mahabharatam), merged under A-82.

rows.title: Eastern Chalukya administration, society and religious conditions
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-67

secs.t: Administration — units and terms → meaning

x: The kingdom followed the Saptanga idea and had Ashtadasa Tirthas, meaning eighteen offices.
The council of ministers was called Tirthulu, and the Samaharta was the chief among its members.
The state was organised into Vishayas or Mandalas under a Vishayapati or Mandaleswara.
The village head was known as
Grameyaka
, Gramani or Urgavunda.
Vanneyus were toll collectors, whereas the Sthanadhipati managed temple affairs.

secs.t: Society and economy — agraharas, guilds and overseas trade

x: Eastern Chalukya society followed a varna-based order with Brahmin privilege, and kings often granted tax-free villages called agraharas to Brahmins.
Brahmins receiving tax-free agraharas performed
Hiranyagarbha and Bahusuvarna
rituals.
Panduranga
subdued the Boyas, while Jayasimha II is associated with the assimilation of the Koya Kottalu.
Saktivarma’s coins have been found in Arakan, Burma, and trade with the eastern islands continued under Rajaraja Narendra.

secs.t: Rulers → religious patronage

x: Vimaladitya built the Ramakonda cave temple for
his Jain guru Trikala Yogi Siddhanta Deva
, as recorded in the Ramateertham inscription.
Vishnuvardhana III granted Mushikonda village to Jains, while Ammaraja II made the Kaluchumbarru grant at the request of Chamekamba.
Queen
Ayyana Mahadevi
built the Nedumba Vasati (APPSC G2 2025; the key makes her the wife of Kubja Vishnuvardhana).

secs.t: Religious sects and centres → features

x: Parama Maheshwara, Parama Brahmanya and Parama Bhagavata were royal religious titles.
Andhra Mahavishnu at Srikakulam, Ahobilam and Bhavanarayana at Narsavaram were Vaishnava shrines.
The Shaiva sects of the period were
Kapalika, Kalamukha and Pasupata
Potlacheruvu was a famous Jain centre, not Buddhist.

secs.t: Temple arts — music, dance and sculpture

x: Kings and vassals made land endowments, while musicians and dancers such as Chellavva were attached to temples and courts.
Hallisaka, or Kolatam, was
a popular dance
associated with the cultural life of the period.
Bhairavakona in Nellore preserves sculptures of the
veena, mridangam and cymbals

secs.t: Education — Ghatikas, subjects and scholars

x: Ghatikas were
advanced Sanskrit schools attached to agraharas or temples
The heads of Ghatikas were called
Ghatika Samanyulu
Mandasharma was the head of the
Asanapura Ghatika in Kammanadu
Ghatikas taught subjects such as Vedas, Vedangas, Dharmashastras, Tarka, Vyakarana, Arthashastra, Dhanurveda and Ayurveda.
Jain pupils began their studies with the expression “
Om Namah Siddham

secs.t: Court scholars and artists → title, work and patron

x: Chellavva
, also called Challavva, held the title “Gandharva-vidya-visarada” and served as a court singer and dancer.
Ugradityacharya
composed Kalyanakaraka, a medical treatise of the Eastern Chalukya period.
The respective royal titles were Kavi Pandita Kamadhenu, Kavigayaka Kalpataru and Kavyageetha Priyudu.
Chellavva was patronised by Chalukya Bhima I, who gave her Attili village and two kandikas of land.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sanskrit was the official language, and patronage of Jainism, Buddhism and Hinduism indicates religious tolerance.
The Uma Dharmalingeswara Temple at Panchadarla has Eastern Chalukya and fifteenth-century inscriptions.
The ASI recorded 17 inscriptions at Panchadarla in 1899, published in South Indian Inscriptions Vol.

src: Sources: CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.118, 129-134); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Eastern Chalukyas; Medieval > Kakatiyas); CDI (Block03 Cultural Contributions); APHQ (PYQs 2011, 2017, 2025); UPSC (Medieval History p.29); CDCA Aug 2026 p.39

rows.title: Eastern Chalukya art and architecture - Biccavolu, Draksharama and Samalkot temples
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-67

secs.t: Vengi / Chalukya-Chola style — names, influences and materials

x: The Eastern Chalukyas mainly followed the Dravida style, combining Pallava and Badami Chalukya influences with local Andhra features.
Some accounts describe the style as Vesara or Chalukya style and explain it as a blend of the Dravidian vimana form with Buddhist art.
The
Draksharama Bhimeswara temple
exemplifies the Chalukya-Chola style (APPSC G2 2025 key, asked twice).

secs.t: Temples → builder

x: Chalukya Bhima I
is associated with building the Pancharamas or establishing them as Shaiva kshetras.
Bhimeswara is at Draksharama, Kumararama at Samalkot, Kumaraswamy at Chebrolu and Someswara at Gunupudi near Bhimavaram.
The group belongs to Gunaga Vijayaditya's time (9th c.); Chalukya Bhima I built the Bhimeswara temples at Draksharama and Samalkot.

secs.t: Pancharama kshetras → place, district and plan

x: Ksheerarama is the exception to the two-storeyed form, and the Skanda Purana and Srinatha's Bhimeswara Puranam are associated literary sources.
Chalukya Bhimavaram is
Samalkot
(Kumararama); Palakollu is Ksheerarama and Gunupudi (Bhimavaram) is Somarama.
Draksharama and Samalkot share a closely similar two-storeyed plan, while Samalkot's gopuram is a later addition and both were later renovated by the Reddis.

secs.t: Debates and exam traps

x: The 2025 key marked '
Rajaraja Narendra built the Rajarajeswara temple at Biccavole
' as incorrect, though some sources credit him with a Rajaraja temple there; follow the key.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Badami Chalukyas developed Vesara in Karnataka, while the Vengi line transmitted a Dravida-based regional style into the Chalukya-Chola phase.
The pillars at Panchadarla temple carry Eastern Chalukya inscriptions, and the Archaeological Survey of India recorded 17 inscriptions there in 1899.
The nine Navabrahma temples at Alampur were built by the
Badami Chalukyas
during the 7th–8th centuries CE.

src: Sources: CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.118, 134); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Eastern Chalukyas > Architecture, Religion); CDI (Block09 Eastern Chalukyas > Art and Architecture; Block03 Vengi School; Block10 Reddi Architecture); APHQ (PYQs 2012, 2019, 2025); UPSC (Medieval History p.31); CDCA Aug 2026 p.39

rows.title: Andhra Cholas / Telugu Cholas - Renati Cholas and their inscriptions
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-67

secs.t: Renati Cholas — ancestry, territory, capital and period

x: The Renati Cholas claimed Suryavamsa Kshatriya descent from Karikala Chola, although their culture and administration were Telugu.
Renadu was also called Renadu Saptasahasra, referring to
7,000 villages
Renadu lay where
Kadapa, Kurnool and Chittoor
meet, in the upper Pennar basin.
The Renati Cholas ruled from the
fifth to the eighth centuries CE

secs.t: Renati Chola rulers → titles and contributions

x: Nandivarma
is identified as the progenitor of the Renati Chola line.
Dhanunjaya Varma was the founder, son of Nandivarma, and ruled from Chimbapuram.
Satyaditya
bore the titles Chola Maharaja and Chola Mahadhiraju, and the decline began after his reign.
Punyakumara
(625-650 CE), with titles such as Pormukharama and Prithvivallabha, was the greatest Renati Chola ruler.

secs.t: Inscriptions → ruler and the FIRST of Telugu

x: CDX lists 33 Renati Chola Telugu inscriptions, most of which are donation records or dana sasanalu.
The Renati Cholas gave Telugu official and legislative status, and the period from 575 to 848 CE saw Telugu used in complete prose sentences.
The
Kalamalla inscription of Dhanunjaya
(Erikal Mutturaju Dhananjaya), dated 575 CE, is the first Telugu inscription (G2 2012 key).

secs.t: Overlords, successors and legacy

x: The Renati Cholas were first feudatories of the Pallavas, later of the Badami Chalukyas; the Pallava–Chalukya conflict produced the three Rayalaseema states, after which the Banas and Vaidumbas ruled the area.
Purushartha Saramu
by Sivadevayya records the Kakatiya-period rule that a woman's property passed to her daughters and daughters' daughters.

secs.t: Telugu Choda families → region, and Nellore Choda persons

x: The
Nellore Chodas
, associated with Vikrama Simhapuri, were regarded as the foremost Telugu Choda clan.
The Velanati Choda line ended when
Kakatiya Ganapatideva killed Mummadi Rajendra Chola
Tikkana Choda, also called Tikkabhupati, was the son of Manumasiddhi I and took the title Chola Sthapanacharya after helping Rajendra Chola ascend the throne.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The 25 inscriptions (2nd to 16th century CE) copied in the June 2026 Nallamala survey include Pottapi Chola, Eastern Chalukya and Kakatiya records.
The Renati Cholas gave Telugu its first royal dignity, approximately five centuries before Nannaya, by using it in royal and legislative records.
The inscriptions belonged broadly to
the 2nd to 16th centuries CE
, covering a long span of Andhra history.

src: Sources: CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.150-151, 310); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Successor and vassal dynasties); CDI (Block09 The Renati Cholas); APHQ (PYQs 2012, 2019); TH 14 Jun 2026

rows.title: Political overview of Andhradesa, 11th to 16th centuries
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-67

secs.t: Dynasties → period, founder and capital

x: Exam angle: arrange dynasties chronologically; "which dynasty founded Berar" → Imad Shahis.
Vijayanagara emerged in 1336, the Bahmani kingdom in 1347, the Gajapatis in 1435 and the Imad Shahis in 1490.
The
Satavahanas, Kakatiyas and Qutb Shahis
are identified respectively as the first, second and third unifiers of all Telugu lands.

secs.t: Bahmani break-up and Qutb Shahis — founders and FIRSTs

x: Mahmud Gawan was executed in 1482, after which the Bahmani kingdom split into the five Deccan Sultanates.
The five successor sultanates were Qutb Shahi, Adil Shahi, Nizam Shahi, Barid Shahi and Imad Shahi.
The Qutb Shahi state was Shia, used Persian officially, had Telugu-speaking people, and ended under Abul Hasan Tana Shah.

secs.t: Feudatory families → kingdoms

x: The Musunuri Nayakas, Reddis and Velamas were three of Prataparudra's generals who survived the Kakatiya collapse in 1323 and established independent kingdoms.
Ambadeva led the Kayastha revolt in the Kadapa region in 1272 with Pandya support.
The Qutb Shahis were Bahmani tarafdars, or governors, of Telangana from 1496 and became independent in 1518.

secs.t: Contested regions and battles → year and sides

x: At the accession of Krishnadevaraya,
the Adil Khan of Bijapur
held the Raichur Doab.
Kapaya Nayaka ceded Golconda fort to Bahmani ruler Muhammad I after the death of his son Vinayaka in 1361.
Rakshasi-Tangadi was fought on 26 January 1565, Raichur in 1520, Muttukur in 1263 and Palnadu in the 12th century.

secs.t: Regional succession — predecessor → immediate successor

x: The Telangana sequence was Kakatiyas, Delhi Sultanate in 1323, Musunuri Nayakas, Velamas/Bahmanis and finally the Qutb Shahis.
In Rayalaseema, the sequence was Kakatiyas through Kayastha chiefs, followed by Vijayanagara and then the Qutb Shahis or later powers.
Singama was associated with the Velamas, Prolaya Vemareddy with the Reddis, Harihara-Bukka with Vijayanagara and Hasan Gangu with the Bahmani formation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The fall of the Kakatiyas in 1323 ended Telugu imperial unity; the Telugu lands stayed divided among Musunuris, Reddis, Velamas, Vijayanagara, Bahmanis and Gajapatis until the Qutb Shahis reunited the region.
The new Seshachalam inscriptions are dated to the 16th century and linked to
the Tuluva or early Aravidu period
of Vijayanagara.

rows.title: Minor dynasties of Andhradesa - Chalukya-Cholas, Kona Haihayas, Matsyas, Pusapati and others
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-67

secs.t: Kulottunga I and the Chalukya-Chola merger — FIRSTs and viceroys

x: Kulottunga I took the Chola throne in 1070 and Vengi in 1075, after the death of Vijayaditya VII, the last Eastern Chalukya.
Jayangondar
wrote Kalingattuparani, which describes Kulottunga I’s conquest of Kalinga by sea.
Velanati Gonka I was the Samasta Senadhipati of Vengi and fought off the Kalyani Chalukyas and Kalingas.

secs.t: Minor dynasties → region and capital

x: The Palnadu Haihayas were associated with Gurajala, the Gona Haihayas with Vardhamanapuram, and the Panchadhara Haihayas with the Visakhapatnam-Yelamanchili region.
The Pithapuram inscription of the Velanati Choda Prithvisvara names
Kolleru Lake
(APPSC 2017).
The Matsyas of Oddadi were northern Andhra chieftains of
the upland Srikakulam-Vizianagaram zone
All three statements describe the Matsyas of Oddadi: their early Telugu records, hero-stones and small temples, and bilingual Telugu-Kalinga border culture.

secs.t: Kota chiefs → rulers, territory and overlords

x: Bhimaraju II was associated with the 1182 Palnadu war, absorbed Kondapadamati, and bore the title Dannala Kota Padaveshtita Kadana.
A Kota chief married Ganapamba, daughter of
Kakatiya Ganapatideva
; some sources name him Bhimaraju II.
The Kota chiefs were successively subordinate to the Chalukya-Cholas, the Velanati Chodas and finally the Kakatiyas.

secs.t: Palnadu war (Palnati Yuddham), 1182 — site, factions and persons

x: The Palnadu war, or Palnati Yuddham, was fought at
Karempudi
in 1182 CE.
Brahmanaidu led the Malideva faction; Nagamma was on Nalagamaraju's side and opposed his reforms.
The
Velamas
were described as intruders into Reddi-dominated Palnadu and were driven out in the Battle of Karempudi.
Srinatha’s
Palnati Veera Charitra
is the epic account associated with the Palnadu war.

secs.t: Minor dynasty inscriptions → ruler

x: The Draksharama inscription identifies the place as the coronation seat of
a Chalukya-Chola viceroy
The Satrasala inscription is the founder’s record of Palnadu Haihaya Betaraju I.
Potladurthi is associated with Renati Choda Punyakumara.
The Kalamalla inscription of the Renati Chodas, dated to 575 CE, is regarded as the first Telugu inscription.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Post-Eastern Chalukya Andhra was a web of nadus under vassals.
The Velanati Chodas were not related to the Telugu Chodas.

rows.title: Kalyani (Western) Chalukyas - Tailapa II, Vikramaditya VI; Bilhana's Vikramankadevacharita, Vijnaneswara's Mitakshara

secs.t: Kalyani Chalukya rulers → period and contributions

x: Exam angle: reign period of Vikramaditya VI -
Someshvara I killed Rajadhiraja I at Koppam, assumed the title Vengi Purveshwara and granted Hanamkonda to Prola I. The Chalukya-Vikrama era was founded by Vikramaditya VI.
Vikramaditya VI was the greatest Kalyani Chalukya ruler, ruled for 50 years, bore the title Tribhuvanamalla and brought the Vengi feudatories under his authority.

secs.t: Books → authors (Kalyani-age literature)

x: Bilhana’s Vikramankadevacharita is a historical mahakavya dealing with the life and conquests of Vikramaditya VI.
Bilhana was a Kashmiri poet at Vikramaditya VI’s court and likened the ruler’s reign to Ramarajya.
Someshvara III
, who ruled from 1126 to 1138 CE, was the author of Manasollasa or Abhilashitartha Chintamani.
Manasollasa (Abhilashitartha Chintamani) is a 100-chapter Sanskrit encyclopaedia covering statecraft, agriculture, medicine, astronomy, music, dance and cuisine.

secs.t: Mitakshara vs Dayabhaga and medieval jurists

x: Mitakshara is a commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti, not the Manusmriti.
Bengal
was associated with the Dayabhaga school.
The principal distinction is that Mitakshara recognises the sons’ right in ancestral property by birth, while Dayabhaga recognises it only after the father’s death.
Rajasekhara was a poet-dramatist, not a jurist.

secs.t: Art and temples → place and feature

x: The style is mature Vesara (Gadag style).
The Itagi Mahadeva temple is popularly known as the “
Emperor among temples

secs.t: End of the dynasty and successor feudatory powers → region

x: These powers emerged in different regions after the weakening of Kalyani Chalukya authority.
Kalachuri ruler Bijjala seized the throne at Kalyani around 1156 CE.
The dynasty ended around 1189 CE, while successor powers expanded and the Chalukya–Chola hold over Vengi weakened.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Kalyani Chalukyas checked Chola expansion towards the north, while the Mitakshara tradition associated with their court shaped Hindu inheritance law for about a millennium.
The broad periods are Badami from the sixth to eighth centuries, Vengi from the seventh to eleventh centuries, and Kalyani from the late tenth to twelfth centuries.
