rows.title: Imperial Cholas - Vijayalaya, Rajaraja I, Rajendra I; Gangaikonda title and the naval expeditions
sub: Group-II S1-32: The Cholas - political outline: Vijayalaya, Rajaraja I and Rajendra I

secs.t: Imperial Chola rulers → succession and contributions

x: Exam angle: "Identify the incorrect statement" sets on founder / successor / title pairs.
Maduraikonda was the title of Parantaka I, not Kulottunga I. Rajaraja I was known as Mummadi Chola, Rajendra I as Gangaikondachola, and Rajadhiraja I as Yanai-mel-thunjina Devar.
The
defeat of the Sailendra ruler at Kadaram
was achieved by Rajendra I in his 1025 CE expedition.
All three statements correctly describe Rajaraja I, also known as Arumolivarman, whose reign is dated 985–1014 CE and marked major expansion of the Chola state.

secs.t: Titles → Chola ruler

x: Madurai-konda was associated with Parantaka I's capture of Madurai; Mummudi Chola and Ulakalanda Perumal were titles of Rajaraja I; and Gangaikonda Chola was assumed by Rajendra I after the Ganga expedition.
Mummudi Chola was a title of Rajaraja I, associated with northern Sri Lanka being named Mummadichola Mandalam.

secs.t: Conquests and naval expeditions → ruler

x: Exam angle: "Who led the campaign against Srivijaya?" -
Rajendra I
(asked by UPSC 2025 and the APPSC Group-II papers).
Rajendra I's 1025 CE naval expedition was against the revived
Srivijaya
empire: he defeated the Sailendra king and took Kadaram (Kedah) in Malaya and parts of Sumatra.
Chola-Sailendra ties, once cordial, soured when Srivijaya
blocked Indian traders on the China route
; Rajendra I's 1025 CE expedition cleared these obstacles and widened Chola trade with China.

secs.t: Capitals, constructions and places → association

x: Uraiyur was the early (Sangam) Chola capital, not a city built by Rajendra I; his new capital after the Ganga expedition was Gangaikondacholapuram.
Rajendra I
dug the Chola Gangam tank at his new capital Gangaikondacholapuram after the Ganga expedition.
Amma I made Rajamahendravaram the capital, Rajaraja Narendra made it famous, and it was an important centre in the Vengi administration.

secs.t: Battles for Vengi → participants and result

x: The wars arose mainly from succession disputes in Vengi, with each side backing a claimant, and from the wider struggle for supremacy in the Deccan.
Takkolam was won by the Rashtrakutas under Krishna III; at Koppam Rajendra II claimed victory after Rajadhiraja I’s death; Virarajendra won at Kudalasangamam; Rajendra I’s army won at Kalidindi.

secs.t: Chola–Eastern Chalukya marriages and Vengi viceroys → persons

x: Madhurantaki married Rajendra Chalukya, who became Kulottunga I. Kundavai married Vimaladitya, Ammanga Devi married Rajaraja Narendra, and Saktivarman I was Vimaladitya's elder brother who ruled Vengi with Rajaraja I's help.
Vira Chola, who served twice as viceroy of Vengi, was crowned at
Jagannathapuram
Rajaraja Chola Ganga is associated with the
Tekkali inscription
and exercised authority up to Mahendragiri.

secs.t: Kulottunga I → parentage, FIRSTs and achievements

x: After Virarajendra and Adhirajendra died around 1070–71, Rajendra Chalukya took the Chola throne as Kulottunga I.
After Vijayaditya VII’s death in 1075, Kulottunga I
merged Vengi with his Chola dominions
and ruled both regions, giving rise to the Chalukya-Chola association.
Kulottunga I was the son of Rajaraja Narendra and Ammanga Devi, was also called Rajendra Chalukya, and took the Chola throne in 1070 CE.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Cholas are described as the first Indian power with overseas naval campaigns, and their activities spread Dravidian art to Southeast Asia.
Tamil Nadu began the third phase of underwater exploration off
Poompuhar
, identified as an early Chola capital.
Vengi was central to Chola–Chalukya rivalry; Kulottunga I united the Tamil and Andhra kingdoms; and the Mandalika Yugam followed from 1076 to approximately 1210.

rows.title: Chola local self-government - the Uttaramerur inscriptions, ur, sabha, nagaram, variyams
sub: Group-II S1-34: Chola local self-government - Uttaramerur inscriptions, ur, sabha, nagaram, variyams

secs.t: Village autonomy — dynasty identification and comparison

x: Pallava institutions provided an earlier base, the Cholas elaborated them, Badami Chalukya administration was highly centralised, and Rashtrakuta village assemblies had a significant administrative and dispute-related role.
Nilakanta Sastri
regarded the Chola system as a remarkable example of grassroots democracy.
The segmentary-state interpretation stresses the persistence of local autonomy, particularly at the periphery, rather than uniform central control.

secs.t: Assemblies → village type and composition

x: Ur was the general assembly in ordinary non-brahmadeya, or vellanvagai, villages.
Sabha or Mahasabha was the Brahmin-only assembly of agraharas or brahmadeya villages, with membership based on property, family, learning and conduct.
The nattar was the nadu assembly of leading vellala landholders and dealt with revenue collection and disputes above village level.

secs.t: Uttaramerur inscriptions → ruler, year, qualifications and election

x: The two Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I are dated 919 and 921 CE.
The
Uttaramerur inscriptions
provide detailed information about Chola village government and administration.
Qualifications: 1/4 veli of land, age 35-70 and Vedic knowledge (an own house was also needed).
Owning a residence
was a qualification, whereas failure to submit accounts, committing sins and stealing property were disqualifications.

secs.t: Variyams → function, and powers of assemblies

x: Samvatsara variyam dealt with annual works, eri variyam with tanks and water distribution, pon variyam with gold and finance, and thotta variyam with gardens.
The Uttaramerur record refers to committees dealing with
irrigation, gardens, justice and finance
The assembly was absolute proprietor of village and newly acquired lands, could raise loans and levy taxes, and could auction defaulters' land.

secs.t: Terms → meaning (APPSC match)

x: Exam angle: this exact four-term match was asked in
APPSC-G1 2022 and 2023
- key a-IV, b-I, c-II, d-III.
Kudavolai was the selection procedure in which names written on palm leaves were placed in a pot and drawn by lot.
Kudumbu means ward, perumakkal means a member of the village assembly, and variyapperumakkal means elected committee members.

secs.t: Chola assembly vs 73rd Amendment → Articles

x: The 73rd Amendment does not prescribe Vedic learning; qualifications for PRI elections operate within the constitutional and state-law framework.
The intermediate tier is optional below the twenty-lakh population threshold, Panchayats normally have five-year terms, and elections after dissolution are to be completed within six months.
The Chola system had no quota for women, while Article 243D reserves one-third of seats (and chairperson posts) for women.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The kudavolai, or ballot-pot system, was cited as evidence of
India’s early democratic traditions
The system was not based on universal adult franchise; eligibility was restricted by property, learning and other conditions.
Kakatiya and Velanati inscriptions
refer to village mahajana assemblies in Andhra, forming a weaker parallel to the Chola institutions.

rows.title: Chola central and provincial administration, land classification, revenue and irrigation
sub: Group-II S1-33: Chola central and provincial administrative system
Group-II S1-35: Chola revenue administration, land classification, army and navy

secs.t: Chola kingship → succession, titles and image

x: Exam angle: "Which dynasty's king declared his successor during his own tenure?" -
Chola
Ko, Perumal, Raja-rajadhiraja and Ko-konmai kondan were all inscriptional titles associated with Chola kingship.
The Chola king was presented in divine and royal terms: royal images could be placed beside deities, and inscriptions praised his military, cultural and social-religious roles.

secs.t: Central officials and departments → terms

x: The bureaucracy expanded from the reign of Rajaraja I and weakened after
Kulottunga I
as local chieftains gained greater power.
The
tirumandira-olai
was the royal secretary who recorded the king’s oral orders on palm leaf.
Perundaram and sirudaram represented higher and lower officials respectively; Shrikaranam was the revenue department and Dharmasana the royal court of justice.

secs.t: Administrative divisions and provincial government → units

x: Mandalam was the provincial unit, the empire had eight such provinces, and they were administered by viceroys or governors, often princes or nobles.
Each mandalam was governed by
a viceroy or governor, often a royal prince or noble
; offices were paid by land assignments.
A Samanta was a defeated king restored on condition that he accepted overlordship, paid tribute and provided military help.

secs.t: Army and navy → terms and rulers

x: Exam angle: "Which South Indian state was famous for naval power?" -
Chola
; "Which king started the navy?" -
Rajaraja I
Rajendra I's 1025 CE Srivijaya expedition took Kadaram (Kedah) and parts of Sumatra.
The Kalingattuparani describes Kulottunga I’s conquest of Kalinga as being carried out with
great naval power

secs.t: Land survey, revenue and tax terms → meaning

x: Antarayam was a cash rural tax, Eccoru was the obligation to feed officials, Nettal was compulsory labour and Kasu was a gold coin.
Rajaraja I
conducted a detailed land survey and assessment, and such surveys were repeated periodically.
Kulottunga I
was called Sungam Tavirtta Chola, meaning the Chola who abolished tolls.

secs.t: Land classification and land rights → terms

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2016 pair-matching - Eripatti (tank land) and Ghatikas (colleges) correct; Taniyurs described as "villages donated to a single Brahmin" is wrong.
Pallichchandam was land donated to Jaina institutions; temple land was devadana.
Karanmai = right to cultivate, mitachi = superior possessory right.

secs.t: Irrigation and the temple → functions

x: The
eri variyam
was the tank committee responsible for managing tanks and distributing water to fields.
The Grand Anicut on the Kaveri was built by
Karikala, the Sangam Chola
, and was maintained by later Cholas.
Rajaraja I directed the Sabhas of Cholamandalam to perform services for the
Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur

secs.t: Inscriptions and copper plates → ruler and content

x: The
Anbil plates
contain a Sanskrit genealogy and are associated with the Leiden grant; they were issued under Sundara Chola.
The Tiruvalangadu plates of Rajendra I provide Chola genealogy and accounts of conquests.
The smaller plates contain three sheets and record Kulottunga I’s extension of the grant after two Javanese envoys appealed to him.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Vengi administration had the Ashtadasha Tirthas, or 18 departments; the Yuvaraja participated as a partner in governance; and councils were called Varagoshti.

Andhra Pradesh launched the Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain pilot, providing a unique digital ID for each land parcel, with statewide expansion planned from November; the State also runs Mee Bhoomi-Mee Hakku re-survey and passbook camps.

rows.title: Chola economy and merchant guilds - Ayyavole, Manigramam; overseas trade with China and Srivijaya

secs.t: Merchant guilds → base, activity and organisation

x: Exam angle: "Which institution belonged to foreign trade?" - UPPSC 2018 key accepts
Nanadesis or Manigramam
Ayyavole-500 originated from Aihole and operated widely; Manigramam was a foreign-trade corporation; Ubhaya Nanadesi handled both domestic and foreign trade; Nagaram was a market-town assembly.
Merchant guilds had emblems and private militias, settled disputes, acted as bankers, donated to temples and became more independent as the Cholas declined.

secs.t: Places → ports and guild inscriptions abroad

x: Takua Pa names Manigramam, Pagan has a Nanadesi Vishnu temple inscription, Sri Lanka has many Ayyavole and Nanadesi inscriptions, and Barus has the 1088 Ayyavole-500 inscription.
Nagapattinam
was the main Chola port and the location of the Chudamani Vihara.
Mahabalipuram was a Pallava-era port.

secs.t: Exports, imports and the temple economy

x: The principal exports included textiles, pepper and precious stones.
Temples functioned as major economic institutions: they were large landholders, employers and lenders and received guild donations and royal grants.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Netherlands returned them at The Hague in May 2026.
Ayyavole and Manigramam were active in Andhra, especially around Penugonda, while Nakaras headed by Shreshthis traded under the Eastern Chalukyas.
The guild networks extended Chola commerce and Dravidian cultural influence across the Bay of Bengal.

rows.title: Chola art - Brihadeshwara temple, Dravida style elements, Chola bronzes (Nataraja), Tamil literature
sub: Group-II S1-36: Chola economy, trade guilds, art, architecture and Tamil literature

secs.t: Dravida style — temple terms, Nagara vs Dravida vs Vesara and the Chola shift — Chola shift to structural temples

x: Garbhagriha literally denotes the womb-house and houses the principal deity or icon of the temple.
Mandapa is a pillared hall, antarala is the intervening vestibule and jagati is a raised platform.
Gopuram
refers to the imposing entrance gateway tower characteristic of South Indian temples.
Shikhara
denotes the topmost, dome-like crowning portion of the vimana; the monolithic shikhara of the Thanjavur temple is especially noted.

secs.t: Dravida style — temple terms, Nagara vs Dravida vs Vesara and the Chola shift — Temple styles - Nagara, Dravida, Vesara

x: The Nagara style is associated with North India and is identified from about the 5th century CE.
Vesara blends Dravida vimana tiers with the Nagara curvilinear profile.
Elaborate prakara walls and gateways are characteristic of Dravida temples, whereas Nagara temples usually lack such elaborate enclosures.
The Teli temple at Gwalior has a pinnacle in the Dravida style (UPPSC 2016 key).

secs.t: Chola temples → builder, site, features, chronology and UNESCO

x: Exam angle: builder-temple matching and 4-temple chronological order mixing Pallava and Chola monuments.
The Chit Sabha of the
Thillai Nataraja Temple at Chidambaram
contains carvings of 108 classical dance poses.
All three are Chola temples (APPSC-GS 2018 key): Thanjavur's Brihadeeswara by Rajaraja I, Gangaikondacholapuram by Rajendra I, and the Thillai Nataraja temple at Chidambaram enlarged by Chola kings.

secs.t: Chola bronzes, frescoes and sculpture — Nataraja iconography

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2021 - "four hands" and "man's earring right, woman's left" are
both correct
Chola bronzes were worshipped icons, distinguished by fine craftsmanship, intricate jewellery and expressive faces.
Murals are known at Gangaikondacholapuram, Narthamalai paintings show Shiva and Parvati, and notable Dakshinamurthy panels occur at Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram.

secs.t: Chola rulers → inscriptions, temple life and foreign missions

x: The inscriptions mention about 400 temple dancing women and also refer to musicians and other staff who were paid through grants.
Chola–Srivijaya relations began amicably, but obstruction of Indian traders led to Rajendra I’s 1025 expedition to Kadaram.
Rajaraja I sent a mission in 1015, Rajendra I in 1033 and Kulottunga I in 1077.

secs.t: Tamil literature — work → author, and the Tirumurai

x: Kamba Ramayanam or Ramavataram was composed by
Kamban
and is a Tamil adaptation of the Ramayana, not merely a translation of Valmiki.
Kalingattupparani was written by Jayamkondar, Moovar Ula by Ottakuthar, Nalavenba by Pugalendi and Nannul by Pavanandhi.
Nambi Andar Nambi compiled the Tirumurai in Rajaraja I's time; it is the Saiva canon of Nayanar hymns in 12 books, the Periya Puranam being the 12th.

secs.t: Ports, trade partners and economic terms

x: The
Cholas
were the South Indian dynasty particularly known for maritime trade with Southeast Asia and links with China, Srivijaya, Sri Lanka and the Arab world.
Arab trade on the west coast prominently involved horses and spices, while Anjuvannam was associated with foreign merchants.
Kaveripattinam, not Nagapattinam, was the early Chola capital and a port at the mouth of the Kaveri.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Draksharama Bhimeswara temple shows an independent Chalukya-Chola style combining
Pallava and early Chalukya elements
The comparison states that the Pallavas laid the foundation of Dravidian art, while the Cholas built its monumental culmination.
Tamil Nadu
began the third phase of underwater exploration off Poompuhar or Kaveripattinam.
Earlier finds at Poompuhar included wharves, fourth-century BCE pottery and a lighthouse.

rows.title: Hoysalas - Vishnuvardhana and Ramanuja; Belur, Halebid and Somanathapura temple architecture

secs.t: Hoysala capitals — Belur, Dwarasamudra and the modern name Halebid

x: Belur
was the earlier capital of the Hoysalas, before Dwarasamudra became their capital.
Dwarasamudra, the Hoysala capital, is modern
Halebid
(Halebidu, 'old city'), a name it took after the Delhi armies sacked it (UPPSC 2003, 2014 keys).

secs.t: Hoysala rulers → contributions, and Vishnuvardhana's conversion

x: Veera Ballala II
defeated Yadava Bhillama and made the Hoysalas independent; his reign is given as 1170–1220.
Ballala III ruled from 1295 to 1342, defeated Ramachandra’s forces in 1305, and was later defeated by the Kakatiya commander Pedarudru after 1316.
Vishnuvardhana defeated the
Cholas at Talakad
and assumed the title Talakadugonda.

secs.t: Hoysala conflicts → Yadavas, Pandyas, Malik Kafur and the end

x: The Hoysalas were involved in constant wars with the Yadavas of Devagiri and the Pandyas.
Malik Kafur took Dwarasamudra in 1311, before the Hoysala kingdom’s space passed to Vijayanagara.
Ballala III died in 1342, and the political space of the Hoysala kingdom subsequently passed to Vijayanagara.

secs.t: Hoysala temples → builder, deity, site and UNESCO listing

x: The Keshava Temple at Somanathapura is dedicated to Vishnu and was built in 1268 by Somanatha, the general of Narasimha III.
The Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage property in 2023.
The three components are Chennakeshava Temple at Belur, Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebid and Keshava Temple at Somanathapura.

secs.t: Hoysala style — features, terms and sculptors

x: Hoysala architecture is generally classified as
Vesara
in examination keys, although it is also described as an evolution of the Dravida style.
Hoysala temples commonly have stellate plans on raised jagati platforms, and the form reached its peak under the Hoysalas in the twelfth century.
Hoysala temples used chloritic schist, commonly called soapstone, which allowed intricate, jewel-like carving.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The hero stone, unearthed on 28 June 2026, may help settle the long-disputed date of Vishnuvardhana’s death.
Vijayanagara architecture followed the
Hoysala and Pandya styles
according to the comparative assessment.

rows.title: Yadavas of Devagiri - Bhillama, Singhana, Hemadri and the Hemadpanti style

secs.t: Yadava rulers → contributions, Bhillama V to Harapaladeva

x: Singhana II

, who ruled from 1200 to 1247, was regarded as the greatest Yadava ruler and bore the title ‘Teluguraya Sthapanacharya’. ⚠ Sources differ: Singhana II's reign is given as 1200-1247 in some sources and c.1210-1246 in others.
Shankaradeva died during Malik Kafur’s invasion in 1313, and Harapaladeva was killed during Mubarak Khalji’s invasion in 1317–18.

secs.t: Scholars and saints → works (books → authors)

x: Sangita Ratnakara was written by
Sarngadeva
, the court musician of Singhana II.
The Sangita Ratnakara is considered a basic text for both Hindustani and Carnatic music.
Hemadri served
Mahadeva and Ramachandra
as Shrikaranadhipa, the head of the secretariat or records.
Chaturvarga Chintamani is a Sanskrit encyclopaedia dealing with
dharma, rituals, charity, pilgrimage and vratas

secs.t: Hemadpanti style — features

x: Hemadri is credited with the
Hemadpanti style
of temple architecture.
Hemadpanti construction used local black basalt and interlocked dressed stones without mortar, a technique known as dry masonry.

secs.t: Delhi Sultanate raids and Kakatiya conflicts — events by year

x: The 1295 raid by Alauddin (for Jalaluddin) made the Yadavas Delhi vassals.
The sequence was the 1295 first invasion, Malik Kafur’s 1307–08 campaign, Shankaradeva’s death in 1313, and Harapaladeva’s death in 1317–18.
In 1295, Alauddin Khalji, acting for Sultan Jalaluddin, defeated Ramachandra at Devagiri and took Ellichpur.
After 1323, Devagiri’s vizier Malik Burhanuddin was placed in charge of conquered Andhra.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Devagiri was the first southern kingdom to fall to Delhi, opening the road to Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai.
The rivalry included Jaitugi’s killing of Rudradeva, Singhana’s claim to be the installer of the Telugu king, and Rudramadevi’s repulse of Mahadeva’s attack.

rows.title: Kakatiyas - origins, Beta I, Rudradeva, Ganapatideva; Kakatiya-Yadava-Hoysala relations
sub: Group-II M1-A-27: Kakatiyas - origin, Beta I, Prola II, Rudradeva and Ganapatideva

secs.t: Kakatiya origins — progenitor, overlords, caste, emblem and religion

x: The progenitor is identified in different traditions as Kakara Gundana of Magallu or Venna Bhupati of Bayyaram.
Samanta 956-1162, sovereign 1163-1323.
Kakatamma, or Kakati Devi, was associated with the Jain Kushmandini before being absorbed into Hindu tradition.
The early Kakatiya base was
Hanamkonda Vishaya
, corresponding broadly to modern Karimnagar, Warangal and Khammam areas.

secs.t: Kakatiya rulers → period and contribution, Gundana to Ganapatideva

x: Beta II built Shivapura and Betesvaralayam, Durgaraja made donations to the Betesvara temple, and Prola II erected a victory pillar at Srisailam.
Ganapatideva ruled for 63 years, issued the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam in 1244, and Ramappa temple was built during his reign by Recherla Rudra.
The order is Beta II (1076–1108), Prola II (1116–1157), Rudradeva (1158–1195), and Mahadeva (1195–1199).

secs.t: Kakatiya rulers → period and contribution, Gundana to Ganapatideva — Ganapatideva - release and accession

x: Ganapatideva married Pinnachodi's daughters Narama and Perama, and appointed their brother Jayapa as Gajasahani, the chief of the elephant forces.
Ganapatideva bore the title
Andhra Deshadhiswara
and is associated with the unification of Telugudesam.
Kupama Devi
, Rudrama Devi’s mother, guided her training when she was being raised as a son.

secs.t: Kakatiya capitals — Hanamkonda to Orugallu (Warangal)

x: Orugallu is the ancient name of Warangal and means ‘
single rock
Andhranagari was used under Ganapatideva, and Sultanpur was the name given after the conquest of 1323.
Prola II developed Hanamkonda.
Rudradeva shifted the capital and began fortifying Orugallu.

secs.t: Tanks, temples and Jain shrines → builder

x: Exam angle: match tank → builder and ruler → temple.
Ramappa temple was built during Ganapatideva’s reign by
Recherla Rudra
Ramappa temple, the Lakkavaram and Ghanapur tanks, and the grant of Ganapavaram villages are associated with Ganapatideva’s reign.
Recherla Rudra saved the kingdom during Ganapati’s captivity and is associated with the Ramappa temple and tank at Palampet.

secs.t: Kakatiya wars → Yadavas, Hoysalas, Velanati Chodas, Kalachuris, Pandyas

x: Prithviswara was killed in 1210, the joint title was adopted by Ganapatideva and Choda Tikka, and the Velanati kingdom ended in that year.
The poet
Tikkana
went as an envoy to request Ganapatideva’s intervention on behalf of Manumasiddhi II.
Rudramadevi repulsed Yadava Mahadeva, and Prataparudra’s commander Pedarudru defeated Hoysala Ballala III after 1316.

secs.t: Kakatiya feudatories → member and title

x: All four pairs are correctly matched.
Kamasani belonged to the
Viriyala
family and made Garuda Beta a Chalukya vassal, as recorded in the Gudur inscription.

secs.t: Kakatiya inscriptions → issuer, year and fact

x: The Draksharamam inscription of 1158 was issued by
Minister Inangala Brahma Reddi
and records Rudradeva's accession.
The Bayyaram tank inscription of 1219 was issued by Mailamba, Ganapatideva's sister, and provides the best genealogy of the early Kakatiyas.
These inscriptions respectively refer to Jain Juddha Mallajinalaya, the Ramappa temple, Jalakaranda and Kolleru Lake.

secs.t: Titles of Kakatiya rulers → holder

x: Mahamandaleswara was a feudatory title used by the Samanta Kakatiyas under the Kalyani Chalukyas.
Prola I
bore the title Samadhigata Panchamahashabda, along with Arigajakesari.
Rudramadevi
bore the title Rayagajakesari for her victory over the Yadavas of Devagiri.
Recherla Rudra
is credited with the title Kakati Rajya Sthapanacharya, the founder of the Kakatiya kingdom.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Kakatiyas are described as the second dynasty after the Satavahanas to unite the Andhra region and the first to rule all Telugu-speaking regions.
The Ramappa Temple at Palampet became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 and is noted for its star-shaped platform and floating bricks.
Prataparudra II
is identified as the last ruler of the Kakatiya dynasty.

rows.title: Rani Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra; Marco Polo's account; fall to the Delhi Sultanate
sub: Group-II M1-A-28: Rani Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra; the fall of Warangal

secs.t: Rudrama Devi → accession, reign, family and FIRSTs

x: Rudrama began co-regency in 1258, the 1266 inscription retained the vassal description, and her full coronation followed Ganapatideva’s death in 1262.
Rudrama Devi is regarded as the second great woman ruler of medieval India after
Razia Sultana
Visveshwara Shivacharya
was Rudrama Devi’s royal guru and was associated with the Mandaram agrahara.

secs.t: Rudrama Devi → revolts, wars and death in 1289

x: The revolt of Harihara and Murari was suppressed with the assistance of Prasadaditya Kayastha, Gona Gannareddy, Jannigadeva and other commanders.
Vengi was occupied in 1262 and recovered in 1278 after Poti Nayaka and Prolinayaka defeated Virabhanudeva.
The
Chandupatla inscription
(Nalgonda district), set up by her servant Puvvula Mummadi, records that she died fighting the rebel Ambadeva in 1289.

secs.t: Marco Polo → visit and observations of the Kakatiya kingdom

x: Marco Polo reported that merchants were not subjected to oppressive taxes; he also noted sea trade, textiles, diamonds and rice.
Marco Polo described prosperity, efficient administration and a woman ruler of martial ability; his account is regarded as the first foreign reference to a female ruler in India.
The APPSC G2 2011 key places Marco Polo's visit, when he landed at Motupalli, in
Rudramadevi
's reign.

secs.t: Prataparudra II → succession, campaigns and the Nayankara system

x: The Nayankara system assigned principalities and forts to military officers known as Nayakas, who maintained troops and paid fixed tribute.
Prataparudra’s economic measures included land reclamation, waterworks and founding villages; oppressive merchant taxation was contrary to the account of the period.
Prataparudra was Rudrama’s grandson through Mummadamma, was trained by her, and was crowned in 1289.

secs.t: Khalji and Tughlaq invasions of Warangal, 1303 to 1323 — year, commander, outcome

x: Exam angle: "first Muslim attack on Orugallu" →
Exam angle: captor =
Ulugh Khan
(not Malik Kafur, not Alauddin).

Khusrau Khan's 1318 expedition, sent by Mubarak Khalji, ended in a fresh treaty and tribute: Prataparudra was defeated again and renewed his vassalage, so D is the only option that fits (the invading army was not routed).
The first invasion occurred in 1321–22 under Ulugh Khan; the second occurred in 1323 under Juna Khan; Orugallu was renamed Sultanpur; and Malik Burhanuddin was placed in charge of Andhra.
Ulugh Khan
(Juna Khan, later Muhammad bin Tughlaq) took Prataparudra captive after the 1323 siege (APPSC G2 2019 key).

secs.t: Books and sources → authors (court scholars, Persian and Telugu sources)

x: Amir Khusrau called Prataparudra 'Ravaddar Dev'; Rayagajakesari is Rudrama Devi's title for her victory over the Yadavas of Devagiri.
Ekamranatha’s
Prataparudra Charitramu
records Kakatiya traditions, including the Jaitugi–Ganapati marriage.
Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi was written by
Barani
and records Delhi’s southern campaigns.
Prataparudra Charitramu was written by Ekamranatha, Siddheswara Charitra by Kase Siddhappa, Khazain-ul-Futuh by Amir Khusrau and Futuh-us-Salatin by Isami.

secs.t: Titles → ruler and event commemorated

x: Amir Khusrau used Ravaddar Dev for Prataparudra II; Ganapatideva was known as Andhra Deshadhiswara; and Rudradeva Maharaja was Rudrama Devi’s male regnal name.
Two APPSC keys (GS 2018, G2 2017) give Rayagajakesari to
Rudrama Devi
for repulsing the Yadavas of Devagiri; one PYQ book key gives it to Prataparudra, so read the options.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The fall of Warangal in 1323 ended Kakatiya rule and was followed by the Musunuri-led liberation movement, which produced the Musunuri and Reddi states.
Rudrama Devi is a leading example of
a woman monarch in medieval South India
The comparative sequence is the Nayankara system, followed by the Vijayanagara Amaranayakas and later the Poligars.

rows.title: Kakatiya administration - Nayankara system, tank irrigation, trade, Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam
sub: Group-II M1-A-29: Kakatiya administration - Nayankara system, revenue and military organisation
Group-II M1-A-30: Kakatiya economy - agriculture, tank irrigation, trade and the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam

secs.t: Administrative units, departments and officers → terms

x: Rashtra or Mandala was the largest province, followed by Nadu or Bhumi, Sthala and finally Grama.
Karanam was the
village accountant
The Ayagars were
twelve
village functionaries (APPSC G2 2012 key), paid by shares of produce and service lands.
The central departments were called 72 Niyogas and were supervised by the
Bahattara Niyogadhipati

secs.t: Persons → roles and statements

x: Malyala Hemadri Reddi
served as prime minister under Ganapatideva.
The three surviving generals named are
Prolaya Nayaka, Racherla Singama and Prolaya Vemareddy
Jayapa Senani held the position of Gaja Sahini under Ganapatideva.
Padmanayakas were Recherla Velama chiefs and key Kakatiya commanders.

secs.t: Nayankara system and military organisation — features

x: Exam angle: statement questions on "who introduced the Nayankara system" → Prataparudra II.
A Nayaka retained a share of revenue for maintaining troops, paid a fixed annual sum to the king and remitted the balance.
Nayakas received villages called
Nayakasthalam
instead of a regular salary, drawing revenue from them to meet their obligations.
Baddena's Neeti Sastra Muktavali and Ekamranatha's Pratapa Charitra are cited as sources for the Nayankara system.

secs.t: Sources → authors (books and inscriptions)

r: licensed for Pakanadu, Vengi and Hanumakonda

secs.t: Agriculture and tax terms → meaning — Land classes and crops

x: Magani denoted irrigated wet land, generally used for food crops, while Metta denoted rain-fed dry land.
Maize is excluded because it reached India only after 1500.

secs.t: Agriculture and tax terms → meaning — Taxes and cesses

x: Land revenue, referred to as bhaga or Ari, was generally
one-sixth
of the produce.
Dashabandhamu referred to lands connected with tank maintenance.
Ari denoted land revenue or Bhumi sistu.
Pellipannu was a wedding tax, not a cattle tax.
Pullari, Kanika and Alam are correctly matched.

secs.t: Tanks → builders, tank terms

x: Samudrams were large tanks, Golusukattu cheruvulu formed linked chains, surplus flowed to lower tanks, and Dashabandhamu was tax-free land for upkeep.
The Porumamilla tank inscription dates to 1369 and was issued by Bhaskara, son of Vijayanagara ruler Bukka I. It belongs to the Vijayanagara period and lists twelve requisites of a good tank.

secs.t: Crafts and trade — places → products

x: Ratna kambalu was associated with Warangal, knives with Nirmal and diamonds with the Golconda region.
Marco Polo is said to have described the extremely fine cloth of the region in this manner; the material is identified as
fine muslin
The recorded trading partners included China, Persia, Arabia, Ceylon and the East Indies.

secs.t: Merchant guilds and samayas → terms and functions

x: The Virabanajam guild was licensed for
Pakanadu, Vengi and Hanumakonda
, as recorded in the Tripurantakam inscription of 1282.
Guilds maintained seals or emblems, settled disputes and kept private military forces, but they did not possess an exclusive royal monopoly over all trade.
Guild members came from several communities, including Settis, Reddis, Nayakulu, Boyas, Dasaris and Vaishyas.

secs.t: Ports, Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam and coins

x: Exam angle: "Abhaya" = assurance of safety; issuer Ganapatideva, not Rudrama.
Ganapatideva issued the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam in
at Motupalli.
The charter protected foreign merchants, remitted arbitrary taxes and promised compensation for losses from shipwreck or theft.
The 1416 Motupalli Dharma Sasanam belonged to Vijayanagara ruler Deva Raya I, not Ganapatideva.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Burton Stein’s interpretation is associated with the term ‘segmentary state’, while Romila Thapar used the expression ‘metropolitan state’.
The Kakatiya arrangement was called Nayankara, the comparable Vijayanagara arrangement was Amaranayaka, and the Mughal parallel was the jagir linkage between land and military duty.
Motupalli was among the Vishnukundin-era ports and also appears among Vijayanagara’s Andhra ports, along with Pulicat and Machilipatnam.

rows.title: Kakatiya society and religion - Veerashaivism, Jainism, temple institutions
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-78

secs.t: Castes and samayas → groups and terms

x: Ashtadasha kulas denotes the 18 occupational groups that lived inside Warangal fort, as mentioned in Kreedabhiramam.
Reddis, Kammas and Velamas
, also referred to as Padmanayakas, emerged as Sudra warrior-peasant groups.
The Kakatiyas, described as Sudras of originally Pulinda origin who adopted the Varna order, represented
the culmination of the non-Brahmanical trend

secs.t: Persons → religious roles and contributions

x: Betaraja and Durgaraja were disciples of a Kalamukhacharya belonging to the Srisailam Shila matha.
Prataparudra II endowed the Chennakeshava temple in 1321, while his queen Lakshmidevi endowed the Ramanatha temple at Yelledu.
Royal women of the Kakatiya period made donations to
temples and tanks
, contributing to both religious institutions and public water works.

secs.t: Books → authors

x: Purushartha Saramu records that a woman's property passed to her
daughters and daughter's daughters
, indicating a comparatively progressive legal outlook.
Niti Shastra Muktavali is associated with Baddena, not Sivadevayya.
Purushartha Saramu also describes the 72 Niyogas, or departments, and the daily routine of the king's council.

secs.t: Sects → founders, traits and tenets

x: Exam angle: "Kapalikas arose from which doctrine" and "popular religion of the Reddi Rajas" - both answer Pasupata.
The decline of Jainism was associated with hostility from Kalamukha and Veerashaiva groups and persecution by certain Kakatiya authorities.
The Kakatiyas supported orthodox Brahmin sects through grants but did not persecute Lingayats and generally did not take sides among these sects.

secs.t: Religious centres and temple institutions

x: The period witnessed widespread
superstition, animal sacrifice and self-sacrifice by devotees of Shiva
Viragallu were memorial stones for warriors who died in battle or during cattle raids.
Temples functioned as
landed corporations
, possessing lands and employing organised staff.
Temples included monasteries and feeding houses, Kalamukhas supported food charity, and Kalavatis sustained dance and music.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Kakatiya age is called the
Shaiva era
because Shaivism had a prominent position during the period.
The legal framework comprises the AP Endowments Act, 1987 and Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution, in relation to State powers over interim management of old religious endowments.
Srisailam, Alampur and Draksharama
remained important centres of the Shaiva-Shakta axis of Andhra during the period.

rows.title: Kakatiya art - Thousand Pillar Temple, Ramappa/Rudreshwara (UNESCO 2021), Warangal Fort
sub: Group-II M1-A-33: Kakatiya art and architecture - Thousand Pillar Temple, Ramappa, Warangal Fort, Kakatiya Kala Thoranam

secs.t: Rulers and patrons → religious patronage

x: The conflicts began under Rudradeva, Ganapatideva was a Shaivite, and Gangadhara built the Prasanna Keshava Temple at Hanamkonda.
The recorded figures are 1,300 Vaishnava temples, 2,400 Mallara Devudu temples, 4,400 Bhairava/Durga/Ganesha temples and 52 villages endowed to Srisailam Mallikarjuna.
Recherla Rudra, the Kakatiya general, built the Ramappa temple around 1213 during Ganapatideva's reign; he also built the Ramappa tank.

secs.t: Temples → builders → places, FIRSTs

x: The Hanamkonda Thousand Pillar Temple is a Trikuta temple, while the Palampet Ramappa Temple is associated with floating bricks and is named after its sculptor Ramappa.
Ghanapur, also known as Kota Gullu, is in Jayashankar Bhupalpally and contains a group of Kakatiya-period temples.
Ramanujapuram
in Mulugu, near Palampet, is noted for the only Panchakuta temple of the Kakatiya era.

secs.t: Kakatiya style — features, terms and influences

x: Floating bricks lighten the tower, stellate plans increase sculptural surface, ekasila refers to monolithic carving, and Kirtimukha means the face of glory.
Kakatiya temples show the influence of the
Western Chalukyas of Kalyani
, especially in carved pillars, star-shaped platforms, ornate doorways and sculptured ceilings.
Kakatiya temples commonly feature a raised star-shaped platform on a sandbox foundation, polished lathe-turned pillars and projecting madanika or bracket figures in dance poses.

secs.t: Thousand Pillar and Ramappa temples — features

x: Exam angle: builder-ruler-place matching, the UNESCO year, and "floating bricks / sandbox" statements.
The Trikuta temple is dedicated to Rudreshwara or Shiva, Vasudeva or Vishnu, and Surya.
Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) built it in 1163 on a Trikuta plan with a star-shaped platform.
The Ramappa Temple was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on
25 July 2021

secs.t: Treatises and literary works → authors

x: Exam angle: "Jayapa's main profession" has been asked, and the answer is Gajasahini, not dancer.
The madanika poses at Ramappa follow Jayapa Senani's
Nritta Ratnavali
Perini Shiva Tandavam was danced by male warriors
before battle to invoke Shiva
The translation 'A Lover's Guide to Warangal' is by David Shulman and Velcheru Narayana Rao; Jayapa Senani wrote Nritta Ratnavali.

secs.t: Warangal Fort and Kakatiya Kala Thoranam — features

x: Warangal had three concentric defensive lines, with Puttakota as the innermost enclosure and Kalukota as the outer stone fort.
The Kala Thoranam comprises four ornate stone gateways situated around the Swayambhu Shiva temple inside Warangal Fort.
The
Kakatiya Kala Thoranam
is the official emblem of Telangana State.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Archaeological Survey of India completed restoration of the Kalyana Mandapam, or dance pavilion, of the Thousand Pillar Temple in May 2026.
Kakatiya painting at Pillalamarri is regarded as having paved the way for the later Vijayanagara painting style seen at Lepakshi.
The sandbox foundation of Ramappa is cited as an example of heritage engineering because it helped the temple withstand earthquakes.

rows.title: Temple architecture styles of Andhradesa between the 11th and 16th centuries
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-79

secs.t: Temple components and orders → terms

x: The basic components include the garbhagriha, mandapa, northern shikhara or southern vimana, and the axially placed vahana and dhvaja pillar before the sanctum.
Nagara architecture is marked by a curvilinear shikhara with the sanctum under the tallest tower; Mukhalingam and Simhachalam represent the Kalinga variant on the north coast.
The Dravida order is marked by a
pyramidal vimana, enclosure walls and gopurams

secs.t: Styles by dynasty → features and examples

x: Eastern Chalukya temples followed a Dravidian idiom influenced by Pallava and Badami Chalukya forms, while gradually acquiring local characteristics.
Kakatiya architecture is associated with star-shaped platforms, sandbox foundations, floating bricks and basalt carving; exclusive use of wooden superstructures is incorrect.
Kakatiya builders filled foundation pits with sand, stone chips and earth to cushion temples on black cotton soil, which is why Ramappa survived earthquakes.

secs.t: Rulers and builders → temple contributions

x: The temple is the Rudreswara Temple, was built by Rudradeva in 1163, and was dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu and Surya.
At
Siddhavatam in Kadapa
, a 1233 CE Tamil-Grantha inscription of Chola Rajendra III records the western gopuram.
Nataraja Ramakrishna
revived the Perini Shiva Tandavam using the dance panels of Ramappa Temple.
Prolaya Vema Reddy
completed the steps to Patalaganga at Srisailam in 1346.

secs.t: Temple sculpture — features

x: Exam angle: treatise → temple → author matching (Nrittaratnavali - Jayapa - Ramappa).
The madanika bracket figures at Ramappa were carved in dance postures based on Jayapa Senani's Nrittaratnavali.
Nrittaratnavali is the dance treatise, Jayapa Senani was associated as Ganapatideva's commander, Ramappa is at Palampet, and Ganapatideva was the patron under whom it was built.

secs.t: Places → temples and features

x: The Thousand Pillar Temple dates to 1163, Ramappa to 1213, the Siddhavatam inscription to 1233, and the Mangalagiri gopuram to the nineteenth century.
ASI completed restoration of the Kalyana Mandapam of the Thousand Pillar (Rudreswara) temple at Hanamkonda, the trikutalaya built by Rudradeva in 1163.
Draksharama was built by Chalukya Bhima I, later received Reddi renovation and endowments, and is regarded as the most architecturally significant Pancharama.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The copied inscriptions date from the 2nd to the 16th centuries and span the Satavahana period to the Vijayanagara period, including the Kakatiyas and Reddis.
The plan includes master plans for 22 major temples.
Simhachalam, Annavaram, Srikalahasti and Kanipakam were all among the temples for which master plans had been done.

rows.title: Reddi kingdoms of Addanki, Kondavidu and Rajahmundry - Prolaya Vema Reddi, Kumaragiri Reddi
sub: Group-II M1-A-35: Reddi kingdoms of Addanki-Kondavidu - Prolaya Vema Reddi to Kumaragiri Reddi
Group-II M1-A-36: Rajahmundry Reddis and the end of Reddi rule
Group-II M1-A-37: Reddi society, religion, economy and administration
Group-II M1-A-38: Reddi literature and art - Errana, Srinatha and temple building

secs.t: Reddi dynasty — period, lineage, capitals and forts

x: The Reddis belonged to the Panta vamsam, were also associated with the Deseti kula, used the Bull as their emblem, worshipped Mula Guramma and used Sanskrit as the royal language.
Prolaya Vema Reddi is credited with building 74 forts, including Kondaveedu, Kondapalli and Dharanikota.
Kondaveedu replaced Addanki as the capital and later saw conflict between the Gajapatis and Vijayanagara; Kondapalli was a strategic Krishna-region fort later held by the Gajapatis.

secs.t: Kondavidu Reddi rulers → period → contribution

x: Anavota Reddi revived the Motupalli port, abolished the tax on gold and bore the title ‘Dweepa Vijetha’.
Prolaya Vema Reddi had served in Prataparudra's court and expelled Tughluq forces from coastal Andhra around 1325, with one account placing the event in 1324.
Prolaya Vema built steps to Patala Ganga at Srisailam in 1346, constructed steps to Ahobilam hill and restored agraharas to Brahmins.

secs.t: Kondavidu Reddi rulers → period → contribution — Prolaya Vema Reddi - rise

x: Kumaragiri settled the succession opposition by assigning Pedakomati Vema the Chandolu feudatory position and heirship, and later divided the kingdom by creating a separate Rajahmundry division.
Rajahmundry was first placed under Anavota, later under Kataya Vema in 1395, and Pedakomati Vema seized Kondavidu in 1402 before Kumaragiri died in refuge at Rajahmundry.

secs.t: Rajahmundry (Rajamahendravaram) rulers → period → contribution

x: Kumaragiri Reddi
carved out the Rajahmundry division from the eastern conquests made by his brother-in-law and commander Kataya Vema, and placed it first under his son Anavota and then under Kataya Vema (1395).

Allada Reddi was regent (1414-c.1420) for Veerabhadra; Veerabhadra was the nominal king, restored in 1423 and 1429; his brother Vema (Veda) Reddi was prime minister and de facto ruler; Kataya Vema was killed at Kakaraparthi (1414) by Gajaraju Tippa.

secs.t: Battles, conquests and the end of Reddi rule → defeated / conquered by — Anavema Reddi - conquests

x: Anavema Reddi took Nidadavolu, Rajahmundry, Pithapuram, Simhachalam and Konaseema.
After taking Nidadavolu, Anavema Reddi gave it to
Choda Bhima

secs.t: Battles, conquests and the end of Reddi rule → defeated / conquered by — Wars by opponent

x: The Reddis resisted Bahmani attacks at Motupalli and Kambhammetta, repelled the Kandukur attack in 1398, and later Deva Raya I annexed the Kandukuru Reddis.
Kataya Vema defeated Harihara II, Annadevu took parts of Vengi with Velama help, Anavota halted the Kalinga Gangas on the Krishna, and Pedakomati Vema recovered lost land from Vijayanagara in 1404.

secs.t: Battles, conquests and the end of Reddi rule → defeated / conquered by — Gajapati and Vijayanagara rivalry over Rajahmundry, 1420-1448

x: The correct sequence is 1420, 1423, 1429 and 1446–48: Ganga Ganapati's capture, recovery by Veerabhadra and Vema, Veerabhanu's occupation, and Kapileswara's annexation.
Deva Raya II
expelled Veerabhanu Deva up to Simhachalam and restored the Reddis as Vijayanagara feudatories.
After the death of Racha Vema Reddi, Kondavidu passed to Vijayanagara under
Deva Raya II

secs.t: Administration and taxes → terms → meaning

x: Exam angle: "Which Reddi king levied Puriti Pannu?" - Rachavema (not Kumaragiri or Anavema).
The
Karnam, Reddi and Talari
collectively held village judicial and police powers, following an inherited Kakatiya administrative pattern.
Kanika meant presents or gifts; Pullari was the cattle-grazing tax; Illari was the house tax; and Ari was the land tax in Kakatiya usage.
Racha Vema Reddi
(1420-1424), the last Kondaveedu Reddi ruler, levied the Puriti Pannu (a tax on childbirth) and was killed by the public (APPSC G2 2019; PYQ 2018).

secs.t: Motupalli port → trade, Abhaya Sasanam, literary source

x: Anavota abolished the gold tax, while his minister Somaya issued the Abhaya Sasanam at Motupalli to encourage trade.
Anavota developed the Motupalli dock, Somaya was his minister, and Srinatha’s Haravilasam describes Reddi-period imports and exports.
Mallareddi
, the brother of Prolaya Vema Reddi, took Motupalli from Hasan Gangu of the Bahmani Sultanate.

secs.t: Society, women, festivals and dance → persons — Castes

x: The merchant
Avachi Tippayya Setti
funded the Vasantotsavams; this patronage is recorded in Srinatha's Haravilasam.
Lakumadevi was the celebrated Bharatanatyam dancer at
Kumaragiri Reddi
's court.
The
Komatis
were mainly engaged in inland and coastal trade.
The Brahmin-warrior-merchant order survived into Gajapati rule.

secs.t: Society, women, festivals and dance → persons — Queen Surambika and her tank

x: Exam angle: read the options. If only one of Govardhana Samudram or Santana Sagaram is offered, that is the answer.
Devadasis were trained in music, dance and ritual and were respected performers at Shiva temples, including the Pancharamas.
According to the APPSC G2 2019 key, Surambika's tank was
Govardhana Samudram
(the APPSC GS 2018 key calls it Santana Sagaram), and her son Racha Vema cut the Jaganobbaganda canals to feed it.

secs.t: Religion and temples → built by

x: Reddi donations reached Srisailam, Simhachalam and Ahobilam, and the Pancharama Shiva temples received renovations and land grants.
Prolaya Vema Reddi
built the pilgrim rest-houses at Ahobilam and Srisailam and rebuilt the ramparts of Ahobilam and Mahanandi.
Vallaya Vemana
, the minister of Anavota Reddi, restored the Amareswara temple at Amaravati after Bahmani damage.

secs.t: Books → authors (ruler-authors and court poets)

x: Srngara Dipika
was authored by Pedakomati Vema Reddi and deals with Amaru Shatakam.
Pedakomati Vema Reddi wrote Saptasati Saratika (on Gatha Saptashati) and Bhava Dipika, Sivalinga Reddi of Kandukuru wrote Tatva Prakashika, and Vinukonda Vallabhamatya wrote the Telugu Kridabhiramam.
Pedakomati Vema Reddi
, the scholar-king (1402-1420), wrote Sangeeta Chintamani (PYQ 2011, 2019) as well as Sahitya Chintamani and Srngara Dipika.
Errana is associated with Aranya Parva shesham, Harivamsam and Nrusimha Puranam.
Singabhupala II was a Recherla Velama ruler of Rachakonda, not a Reddi ruler, and he wrote Sangeeta Sudhakaram.

secs.t: Court poets → patron, titles, contributions

x: Errana was the last of the Kavitrayam and completed the Telugu Mahabharata by translating the remaining portion of the Aranya Parva.
Errana was associated with Prolaya Vema, Bala Saraswati with Anavota, and both Srinatha and Vamana Bhatta Bana were associated with Pedakomati Vema.
Vamana Bhatta Bana, at Pedakomati Vema Reddi's court, held the titles Sahitya Samrajya Dhurandhara and Sahitya Chudamani.
Srinatha (Kavi Sarvabhauma) was Vidyadhikari, the minister of education, at Pedakomati Vema Reddi's court, and he composed Pedakomati's Sanskrit inscriptions.

secs.t: Titles → ruler

x: Dharma Pratishtana Nagarudu was Prolaya Vema Reddi’s title; Dweepa Vijetha belonged to Anavota Reddi; Karpura Vasanta Rayalu to Kumaragiri Reddi; and Sarvajna Chakravarti to Pedakomati Vema Reddi.
Veeranna Pothu belonged to Anavota Reddi, Andhra Suratrana and Vasantaraya were associated with Anavema Reddi, Karpura Vasantaraya with Kumaragiri, and Bharatamata Patanga with Sivalinga Reddi.
The APPSC G2 2017 key gives Rachuru Durga Vibhala to
Anavema Reddi
, who also bore Rajashri Ramani and Andhra Suratrana.

secs.t: Inscriptions and records → ruler / content

x: Anitalli issued the Kaluvacheru inscription in 1423 after
the recapture of Rajahmundry
The 1346 Srisailam record refers to the Patala Ganga steps built by Prolaya Vema Reddi.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Bikkavolu temples, Draksharama Bhimesvara and Samarlakota Kumararama are identified as Godavari-region sites carrying Reddi-era renovations.
Rajahmundry was associated with all three works: Srinatha’s Kashikhandam, Sivaleka Kommana’s Sivalila Vilasamu and Vinnakota Peddana’s Kavyalankara Chudamani.
Literary patronage gave the Reddis political legitimacy, while their Shaiva devotion was expressed through the restoration and endowment of Pancharama shrines.

rows.title: Musunuri Nayaks and the Velama (Racherla) chiefs of Rachakonda-Devarakonda
sub: Group-II M1-A-34: Musunuri Nayaks - Prolaya Nayaka, Kapaya Nayaka and the recovery of Andhradesa
Group-II M1-A-39: Velama (Racherla) kingdoms of Rachakonda and Devarakonda

secs.t: Fall of Warangal (1323) and the liberation movement — FIRSTs, leader, chiefs

x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq renamed Warangal Sultanpurti and placed Andhra under Malik Burhanuddin, with Malik Maqbul assisting him.
The other sets include rulers outside it, such as Devaraya II, Ganapati Deva, Kumaragiri, Pedakomati Vema, Rajaraja Narendra and Kulottunga Chola.
Musunuri Prolaya Nayaka
led the liberation confederacy, the Vimochanodyamam (APPSC GS 2018; G2 2019).

secs.t: Musunuri rulers → origin, capital, contribution, titles — Prolaya Nayaka - capital Rekapalli

x: Warangal fell in 1323, the Vilasa grant was issued in 1330, Orugallu was captured in 1336, and the Battle of Bhimavaram occurred in 1367–68.
In 1336, Kapaya Nayaka,
Hoysala Veera Ballala III, Prolaya Vema Reddi and Singama
took Warangal from Malik Maqbul.
Kapaya recovered Warangal, Singama cleared Nalgonda and Mahabubnagar, and Prolaya Vema Reddi cleared Kammanadu and Pakanadu south of the Krishna.

secs.t: Musunuri rulers → origin, capital, contribution, titles — Kapaya Nayaka - administration

x: Exam angle: "first borne by" → Kapaya; "popular title of" with Anavema in the options → Anavema Reddi.
Kapaya Nayaka appointed his nephew
Anapotha Nayaka
to govern Vengi.
Kapaya Nayaka extended his authority to Kaulas in the Bidar region.
Musunuri
Kapaya Nayaka
was the first to bear Andhra Suratrana (APPSC GS 2019).

secs.t: Kapaya and the Bahmanis → losses, truce, Battle of Bhimavaram

x: At Bhimavaram, near Orugallu, Kapaya Nayaka was defeated and killed by the Recherla Velamas led by Anapota Nayaka, after which Telangana passed to the Velamas of Rachakonda.
Kapaya Nayaka helped Hasan Gangu, also known as Zafar Khan, establish the Bahmani kingdom at Gulbarga in 1347.
Warangal was recovered in 1336, the Bahmani kingdom was founded in 1347, Bhuvanagiri was lost in 1356, and Golconda was lost in 1364–65.

secs.t: Recherla Velama rulers → origin, founder, contribution

x: The Recherlas initially served as feudatories of the early Kakatiyas, and their kingdom is dated approximately from 1325 to 1475, a period of about 150 years.
Sultan Quli Qutb Shah
, who ruled at Golconda from 1518 to 1543, defeated the Velama chiefs and annexed Rachakonda and Devarakonda.
Singama Nayaka I was killed fighting the chiefs of Jallipalli, whereas Anapota Nayaka defeated Kapaya at Bhimavaram.

secs.t: Velama battles and alliances → defeated / allied with — Velama-Reddi conflicts

x: Kapaya’s decline enabled the Reddis to take coastal Andhra, while the Velamas absorbed Musunuri Telangana.
Madanayudu and Naganayudu defeated Anavota Reddi at
Dharanikota
, also called Dannala Kota.
After the victory over Anavota Reddi at Dharanikota, the titles
Jagadabbaganda and Rayavesa Bhujanga
were associated with the victors.
The battle of Bhimavaram took place in 1367–68, where Anapota Nayaka defeated Musunuri Kapaya.

secs.t: Velama battles and alliances → defeated / allied with — Alliances → power

x: The Velamas allied with the Bahmanis and Gajapatis against
Vijayanagara and the Reddis
Velama support enabled Annadevu to capture parts of Vengi from Kataya Vema.
Pedakomati Vema Reddi died fighting the Velamas in 1420.
Bahmani minister Mahmud Gawan put down the Telangana revolts with Velama assistance.
Lingamanidu of Devarakonda
sought Gajapati help against a Bahmani attack.

secs.t: Velama court culture → books, authors

x: Sarvagna Singa Bhupala was a Sanskrit scholar-king and composed
Rasarnava Sudhakara
, a work on dramaturgy.
Sangeeta Sudhakaram is a musical work associated with Singabhupala II and serves as
a commentary on Sarngadeva’s Sangita Ratnakara

secs.t: Capitals and forts → dynasty, architecture

x: The architecture is associated with high adhisthanas, carved pillars, toranas, and lotus and swan motifs.
Rachakonda and Devarakonda served as the twin capitals and strongholds of the Velamas.
The Recherla Velamas shifted their capital from
Amanagallu to Rachakonda
under Anapota.
In 1336 CE, Kapaya Nayaka, together with Prolaya Vema Reddi, Recherla Singama and Hoysala Ballala, took Orugallu from Malik Maqbul.

secs.t: Velama families → region ruled

x: The Pithapuram line was associated with the Pithapuram estate in the Godavari region, not Rachakonda.
Under the Poligar system, Velama, Reddi and Raju landed families became zamindars.
The Recherla Velamas ruled Telangana from these centres for about
150 years
, approximately from 1325 to 1475.

secs.t: Sources → content

x: The Vilasa grant of 1330 records Prolaya Nayaka’s rise and the atrocities committed under the Tughluq rule.
Polavaram, Ganapeshwaram and Palasamarri are associated with
Kapaya Nayaka
Ferishta’s work is a Persian source, calls Telangana ‘Tilang’ and describes the wars between the Bahmanis and Kapaya Nayaka.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The loss of Kakatiya unity gave rise to the Musunuri, Recherla Velama and Reddi successor states.
The Vilasa grant was issued in 1330, Vijayanagara was founded in 1336, the Bahmani kingdom arose in 1347, and the Golconda truce occurred in 1364–65.
Damerla, Velugoti, Bobbili and Pithapuram carried the Velama line into the zamindari era in Andhra Pradesh.

rows.title: Gajapatis of Orissa in Andhra; Bahmani incursions into Andhradesa
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-81

secs.t: Bahmani kingdom — founder, capitals, FIRSTs

x: Hasan Gangu, or Zafar Khan, founded the Bahmani kingdom in 1347.
The Bahmani kingdom later split into Golconda,
Bijapur
, Ahmadnagar, Bidar and Berar; Bijapur was the first to break away, in 1489.
Ahmad Shah I
moved the Bahmani capital from Gulbarga to Bidar (PYQ G2 2003).

secs.t: Bahmani sultans → incursions into Andhradesa

x: Muhammad Shah I burned Kapaya's son Vinayaka alive in 1361.
All three are correct.
Muhammad III and Mahmud Gawan suppressed Telangana revolts from 1453; Gawan subdued Orugallu and took Kondaveedu, pushing into Odisha in 1471.
The Bahmani kingdom reached its greatest extent under Mahmud Gawan.

secs.t: Gajapati rulers → campaigns and conquests in Andhra

x: Kapilendra preceded Purushottama, and Prataparudra followed Purushottama in the Gajapati succession and campaigns in Andhra.
Kapilendra attacked Tiran Andhra in 1448 and captured Kondaveedu around 1450.
Kapilendra took Bellamkonda, Velugodu, Addanki and Srisailam, besides Kondaveedu.
Kondaveedu was under Vijayanagara until 1449, fell to the Gajapatis around 1450, and was approached by Rajamahendra with Velama support.

secs.t: Gajapati administration → officer titles

x: Exam angle: the title for southern revenue officers is Naidu.
Naidu was the title used for revenue officers in the southern Andhra regions of the Gajapati Empire.
Nayakas and samantas collected revenue and maintained order, and the Reddi-era social order continued.
Devadanas and brahmadeyas were land endowments made to
scholars and temples
, including institutions at Puri, Srisailam and coastal shrines.

secs.t: Gajapati-Vijayanagara conflict → battles, marriage, peace terms

x: Saluva Narasimha
drove the Gajapatis out of south-eastern Andhra by about 1470 and extended his occupation up to the Godavari.
Krishnadevaraya's campaign lasted from 1513 to 1519, and the settlement is best placed around
The campaign proceeded through Udayagiri, Kondaveedu, Kondapalli and Bejawada, followed by the march to Cuttack in 1518.

secs.t: Sources → content

x: Ferishta wrote a Persian history of the Deccan sultans, making his account especially significant for the Bahmani side.

The Penugonda inscription records Kapileswara's attack on Tiran Andhra in 1448; the Anantavaram inscription records the defeat and tribute of the Virupaksharayas; the Draksharama inscription records Vijayanagara help to the Reddis; and the victory pillars commemorate Krishnadevaraya's triumph over the Gajapatis.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Andhra Pradesh sites associated with the Gajapati wars are
Udayagiri, Kondaveedu, Kondapalli, Rajahmundry and Simhachalam
The Gajapati rule is dated approximately from 1434 to 1541.
Uttarandhra culture shows the influence of the Gajapatis.

rows.title: Telugu language and literature to the 14th century - Nannaya, Tikkana, Errana, Palkuriki Somanatha
sub: Group-II M1-A-21: Growth of the Telugu language under the Eastern Chalukyas - Nannaya and the Andhra Mahabharatam
Group-II M1-A-24: Origin and evolution of the Telugu language - earliest inscriptions (Kalamalla, Erragudi), scripts
Group-II M1-A-32: Kakatiya literature - Palkuriki Somanatha, Tikkana and the Siva Kavis
Group-II M1-A-48: Growth of Telugu literature, 11th to 16th centuries - Kavitrayam and the Prabandha age

secs.t: Telugu language — family, names, epithets and literary ages — Family and status

x: The Trilinga theory refers to
Srisailam, Kaleshwaram and Draksharama
as the three Shaiva centres of Trilinga desa.
No derivation of Telugu 'by all scholars exclusively from Tamil' is given; Telugu is said to have grown out of the Desi bhasha (Paisachi) of Prakrit, and its name is traced to Trilinga.

secs.t: Telugu language — family, names, epithets and literary ages — Epithets of Telugu → coined by

x: The Venetian traveller
Niccolo de' Conti
, who visited in the fifteenth century, is associated with the epithet “Italian of the East” for Telugu.
The Srinatha age is followed by the Prabandha or Rayala age in the 16th century, the Dakshinatya or southern Nayaka age in the 17th–18th centuries and the Modern age from the 19th century onward.

secs.t: Earliest Telugu words in Prakrit records and script stages

x: ‘Vepuru’ appears in the Myakadoni inscription. ‘Andhrapatha’ belongs to the Mayidavolu plates, ‘Nagabu’ to Amaravati, and ‘-ambul’ to Vishnukundin plates.
The sequence is Bhattiprolu Brahmi variant, common Old Kannada–Telugu script, differentiation during the Rashtrakuta–Eastern Chalukya age, and separate Telugu script in the 11th–14th centuries.
Hala's Gatha Saptasati, a Prakrit work, contains Telugu words such as atta, addam, potta, tuppu, padi, pandi and pilla.

secs.t: Inscriptions → ruler, dynasty and metre; court language — Earliest Telugu inscriptions → issuer

x: The
Erragudipadu inscription
of Punyakumara of the Renati Cholas is regarded as the first fully available Telugu inscription and uses a song or geya style.
Pitikayagulla is associated with the eighth century and post-Badami Chalukya influence, particularly in relation to early Telugu script; it is not the first Telugu poetic inscription.

secs.t: Inscriptions → ruler, dynasty and metre; court language — Poetic inscriptions → issuer and metre

x: Addanki is linked with Taruvoja and the first Telugu poetic inscription; Bezawada with the first Madhyakkara poem; Sataluru with Champakamala and prasa; and Kandukur–Dharmavaram with Seesa and Ataveladi.
The Chebrolu inscription is noted for showing
the Marga and Desi forms
The Addanki inscription in Taruvoja metre was issued by Panduranga (Pandaranga), commander of the Eastern Chalukya king Gunaga Vijayaditya III.

secs.t: Inscriptions → ruler, dynasty and metre; court language — Pre-Nannaya literature - claims and evidence

x: The inscriptions demonstrate that written Telugu, including Telugu verse, existed before Nannaya; however, no pre-Nannaya literary text survives in the evidence described.

secs.t: Kavitraya → patrons, parvas and philosophy

x: Tikkana dedicated his work to Hariharanatha, taught the unity of Shiva and Vishnu through Harihara Advaita, and had Ketana as a disciple.
Indra Vijayam and Chamundika Vilasam are associated with Nannaya, while Andhra Shabda Chintamani is the grammar treatise associated with Nannaya.
Krishna Satakam
is an independent work of Tikkana, along with Nirvachanottara Ramayanam and Kavi Vakbandham.
Tikkana preached Harihara Advaita (the unity of Shiva and Vishnu; some sources say Harihara Dvaitam).
Errana
wrote Narasimha Puranam, the first Kshetra-mahatmya kavya in Telugu (APPSC G2 2017 key); he also wrote Harivamsam.

secs.t: Nannaya and Narayana Bhattu → contributions and the Nandampudi grant — Nannaya → contribution

x: Nannaya translated the Adi and Sabha Parvas and 142 padyas of the Aranya Parva.
Nannaya pioneered the Champu style.
Andhra Shabda Chintamani is a Sanskrit grammatical work dealing with Telugu grammar.
Nannaya was court poet, teacher and adviser of the Eastern Chalukya king Rajaraja Narendra (r.

secs.t: Nannaya and Narayana Bhattu → contributions and the Nandampudi grant — Narayana Bhattu - assistant in the translation

x: Nandampudi agrahara was associated with Narayana Bhattu, while Navakhandavada agrahara was granted to Pavuluri Mallana.
The
Nandampudi donation inscription
is cited as evidence of Narayana Bhattu's assistance in the translation.
Narayana Bhattu was a polyglot familiar with eight languages, held the title Ashtabhasha Kavisekhara, and represented Someshwara I at Rajamahendravaram.

secs.t: Shiva Kavis and Palkuriki Somanatha → works and desi metres

x: Panditaradhya Charitra, by Palkuriki Somanatha, narrates the life of Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya and is described as the first Telugu encyclopedia.
Basava Puranam was composed by Palkuriki Somanatha, is in dwipada form, deals with the life of Basava and is described as the first Telugu Purana.
Somanatha was hailed as Prathama Andhra Viplava Kavi, belonged to the Veerashaiva tradition and was a native of Palakurthi in Janagama district.

secs.t: Kakatiya-age poets → works (Pavuluri Mallana, Ketana, Marana and others) — Pavuluri Mallana - first Telugu mathematics book

x: Pavuluri Mallana is dated to approximately 1100 CE, and his agrahara, Navakhandavada, was granted by Rajaraja Narendra.
Pavuluri Mallana's Sara Sangraha Ganitam (Pavuluri Ganitam), from Mahaviracharya's Ganita Sara Sangraha, is the first mathematics book and first scientific kavya in Telugu (G2 2019 key).
Ketana, known as Mula Ghatika, dedicated his work to Tikkana and is credited with the early use of the words Tenugu and Telugu.

secs.t: Kakatiya-age poets → works (Pavuluri Mallana, Ketana, Marana and others) — Vijnaneswaram vs Purushartha Saramu

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2019 asked about the woman's-property rule. The answer is Purushartha Saramu by Sivadevayya, not Ketana's Vignaneswaram.
Purushartha Saramu
, composed by Sivadevayya, contains the stated rule regarding the succession of a woman's property.
Most notes credit Ketana with Vijnaneswaram, but the APPSC G2 2012 key gave
Shivadevayya
, who is otherwise known for Purushartha Saramu.

secs.t: Kakatiya-age poets → works (Pavuluri Mallana, Ketana, Marana and others) — Other poets and scholars → work, title

x: Jinendra Kalyanabhyudayamu was composed by
Appayacharya
, also known as Appayaryudu, and is associated with Jain literature.
Marana, a disciple of Tikkana, wrote
Markandeya Puranam
and belonged to the Kakatiya period.
Ranganatha Ramayanam, by Gona Budda Reddy, is described as the first Telugu Ramayana and the first dwipada kavya.
Baddena is associated with Sumati Satakam and
Nitisastra Muktavali

secs.t: Early Telugu grammar and prosody → author

x: Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam
by Ketana is regarded as the first grammar written in Telugu and contains 196 padyas.
Kavijanasrayam, the first Telugu work on prosody, was authored by
Malliya Rechana
Andhra Shabda Chintamani is traditionally ascribed to Nannaya; Kavi Vakbandham is by Tikkana; Kavyalankara Chudamani is by Vinnakota Peddana; and Appakaviyam is by Kakunuri Appakavi.

secs.t: Kakatiya court — Sanskrit authors → works; Kreedabhiramam

x: Vidyanatha wrote Prataparudra Yashobhushanam; Jayapa Senani wrote the three Ratnavali works; Sakalya Mallabhattu is named among the Sanskrit authors.
Ravipati Tripurantakudu is credited with the Sanskrit Niroshthya Ramayanam, but an APP fragment attributes Niroshtya Ramayana and Udara Raghavam to Takavelli Mallikarju Bhattu.
Kreedabhiramam is regarded as a Telugu rendering of Ravipati Tripurantakudu’s Sanskrit play
Premabhiramam
, creating an attribution issue alongside its credit to Vallabharaya.

secs.t: Literary FIRSTs — genre → first example — Genres → first example

x: Nannaya's Bharatam uses verse and prose in champu form; Errana is identified as the first prabandha writer, while Nannechoda began the eight descriptions.
Dasakumara Charitra is a story kavya, Markandeya Puranam is a Purana, Nrusimha Puranam is a Kshetra-mahatmya, and Raghavapandaviyam is a dvyarthi kavya.
The Bhakti poets brought a native Telugu idiom into literature in opposition to the heavily Sanskritised marga style.

secs.t: Literary FIRSTs — genre → first example — FIRST/LAST - revision list

x: Andhra Mahabharatamu is identified as the first Telugu book, Andhra Shabda Chintamani as the first Telugu grammar in Sanskrit, and Ganita Sara Sangraha as the first Telugu mathematics book.
Ketana dedicated Dasakumara Charitra to Tikkana Somayaji, making Tikkana the first Telugu poet to have a work dedicated to him.

secs.t: Srinatha and the Prabandha age — works, patrons, features

x: Srinatha was titled
Kavi Sarvabhauma
and is regarded as the bridge between the Kavitraya and the Prabandha age.
Errana is credited as the first Prabandha writer in one classification, while Srinatha is identified as a pioneer through works such as Sringara Naishadham and Haravilasam.
Veerabhadra Vijayam
is by Bammera Potana, a common distractor.
The APPSC-GS 2019 key gave the
Vijayanagara
Empire, where the Prabandha style peaked with the Ashtadiggajas at Krishnadevaraya's court.

secs.t: Translations and epic versions → translator, language

x: Errana translated Harivamsa, Marana translated Markandeya Puranam, Srinatha rendered Naishadham as Sringara Naishadham and Ketana translated Dasakumara Charitra.
Manchena rendered
Viddhasalabhanjika
as Keyurabahu Charitra in Telugu.
Pampa composed Vikramarjuna Vijaya in Kannada, Kamban composed Ramavataram in Tamil, Sarala Dasa composed the Mahabharata in Odia, and Kasirama Das composed the Mahabharata in Bengali.

secs.t: Vijayanagara-age works → authors and APPSC match-list pairs

x: Manucharitra was written by Allasani Peddana, Parijatapaharanam by Nandi Timmana, Panduranga Mahatmyam by Tenali Ramakrishna and Vasucharitra by Ramaraja Bhushana.
Pingali Surana
was the author of both Kalapurnodayam and Raghavapandaviyam.
Tirumalamba
wrote the Sanskrit work Varadambika Parinayam.
Madhura Vijayam was written in Sanskrit by Gangadevi, not by Pingali Surana.
Bhadraparinayamu is by Allamaraju Subrahmanya Kavi (APPSC-GS 2022).

secs.t: Poets' titles → holder

x: Tikkana was Kavibrahma, Errana was Sambhudasa, Allasani Peddana was Andhra Kavita Pitamaha and Srinatha was Kavisarvabhauma.
Potana held the title Sahaja Panditya.
Ketana was called Abhinava Dandi for his Telugu Dasakumara Charitra, which he rendered from Dandin.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Telugu Mahabharata was completed over three successive eras: the Eastern Chalukya, Kakatiya and Reddi periods.
Nannaya's Bharatam helped fix the grammar and literary register of classical Telugu and began the tradition of the Kavitrayam.
29 August, Telugu Language Day, is the birth anniversary of
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy
; Telugu Language Awards are given the same day.

rows.title: Arab conquest of Sindh (712 CE); Ghaznavid and Ghurid invasions - Mahmud, Muhammad Ghori, Battles of Tarain

secs.t: Invaders and Indian rulers → role, reign and FIRSTs — Invaders → role

x: The Ghaznavid line was founded by Alptigin, while Sabuktigin is considered its real founder.
Mahmud of Ghazni undertook 17 raids between 1000 and 1027.
Qutbuddin Aibak
, Ghori's slave and Master of Stables, founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206.
Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji
was the real founder of Turk rule in Bihar.

secs.t: Invaders and Indian rulers → role, reign and FIRSTs — Indian rulers and resisters → role

x: Muhammad bin Qasim captured Debal, Nirun, Sehwan, Brahmanabad and Multan.
The Chachnama, an Arabic chronicle of the conquest of Sindh, was rendered into Persian by
Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi
Chandela ruler Vidyadhara
resisted Mahmud of Ghazni.
The Chaulukya ruler
Bhimdev II
defeated Muhammad Ghori near Mount Abu at Kayadara in 1178.

secs.t: Raids and battles → year, target, victor — Arab conquest of Sindh (712 CE)

x: Mahmud first encountered the Hindushahis in 1001–1008, attacked Nagarkot in 1009, Thanesar, Mathura and Kanauj in 1014–1018, and Somnath in 1025.
Mahmud attacked Somnath in 1025, when the Solanki Bhima I ruled Gujarat.
Ghori took Multan in 1175, Peshawar around 1179, Sindh around 1182, and Punjab and Lahore around 1190.

secs.t: Raids and battles → year, target, victor — Tarain battles → year, opponent, victor

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2011: Prithviraj defeated Ghori at
Tarain
(the first battle).
The
Second Battle of Tarain
in 1192 was the turning point that opened North India to Ghori.
Bakhtiyar Khalji sacked the Buddhist centres of
Nalanda, Vikramashila and Odantapuri
during approximately 1193–1203.
The Buddhist centres were sacked around 1193–1203; Nadia was attacked in 1204, Lakshmana Sena was driven out, and Bakhtiyar then ruled from Lakhnauti.

secs.t: Books and court scholars → author / work

x: Firdausi wrote the commissioned Shahnama, Utbi wrote Tarikh-i-Yamini, and Al-Biruni composed an objective account of eleventh-century India.

secs.t: Causes, effects and debates

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G1 2018 asked why Ghori won. Key:
superior war technology of the Turks
Indian mathematics, especially
the decimal and place-value systems
, along with astronomy and medicine, passed to the Islamic world and later to Europe.
Turkish armies used
mobile cavalry and mounted archers
, whereas Indian armies relied heavily on elephants.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Mahmud of Ghazni is characterised mainly as a plunder-seeking raider, while Muhammad Ghori pursued conquest and established a lasting political presence in North India.
The Arab contact beginning with the conquest of Sindh in 712 CE helped Indian scientific knowledge move westward and subsequently reach the Islamic world and Europe.

src: Sources: CDI (Block04 Advent of Islam, Phases II-IV); UPSC (Medieval History pp.54-55); APP (Indian History Part 1, Mamluk dynasty - Aibak; Delhi before the Sultanate); LENS Jan 2026 p.113

rows.title: Rajput states and society; Chandella (Khajuraho), Solanki (Dilwara, Modhera), Paramara contributions

secs.t: Rajput origins — theories → proponents

x: The foreign-origin theory, which associates the Rajputs with Scythians, Hunas and Gurjaras, was propounded by Col.

The Agnikula tradition describes the clans as emerging from a sacrificial fire at Mount Abu and is recorded in association with Chand Bardai’s Prithviraj Raso; the four traditional clans are Paramara, Pratihara, Chauhan and Solanki.

secs.t: Rajput dynasties → founder, capital, rulers

x: Mahalakadeva
was the last Paramara ruler mentioned here and was killed in 1305 by the forces of Alauddin Khalji.
The Paramara dynasty was founded by Upendra, also known as Krishnaraja.
The Iron Pillar is
a Gupta work that was only moved to Delhi
; linking its making to Anangapala is a trap.

secs.t: Rajput rulers → contributions (Bhoja, Solanki kings)

x: Bhojpur, near Bhopal, is known for an unfinished Shiva temple containing a huge linga and the Bhojpur lake.
The Udaipur Prashasti gives the Paramara genealogy and praises King Bhoja.
Jayasimha Siddharaja
patronised the Jain scholar Hemachandra and is associated with the Sahasralinga tank at Patan.
The Solankis were Shaivas who also patronised Jainism, not exclusively Buddhist rulers.

secs.t: Temples and monuments → builder, deity, place

x: Vimal Vasahi with Rishabha, Luna Vasahi with Neminatha, Modhera with Surya and Somnath with Shiva.
Maru-Gurjara is a Solanki-associated Nagara sub-style of Gujarat and Rajasthan, broadly dated to the eleventh–thirteenth centuries, and combines the Maha-Maru and Maha-Gurjara traditions.
Rana Kumbha built the Vijaya Stambha at Chittor to commemorate his victory over
Mahmud Khalji of Malwa

secs.t: Nagara temple style — terms → meaning, regional schools

x: Latina, also called Rekha-prasada, is characterised by
a single curvilinear tower
The Maru-Gurjara style, associated with the Solanki tradition of Gujarat and Rajasthan, often includes a
Kirti-torana

secs.t: Rajput court literature → work and author

x: ‘Prithviraj Raso’ was authored by
Chand Bardai
and is associated with Prithviraj Chauhan.
Jagnik
is credited with ‘Alha Khand’, which is associated with Chandela Paramardi.
‘Navasahasanka Charita’ was written by Padmagupta, not Someshvara. ‘Samarangana Sutradhara’ was written by Bhoja.
Samarangana Sutradhara
’ is Bhoja’s work on architecture. ‘Siddha-Hema’ is associated with Hemachandra, while ‘Alha Khand’ and ‘Kirtikaumudi’ have different authors.

secs.t: Rajput society and warfare — feudalism, strategy, women

x: Land grants carried revenue, judicial and police rights.
Rajput warfare emphasised direct combat and personal valour, with chivalry and clan honour receiving great importance.
Jauhar was self-immolation by women to avoid capture.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Madhya Pradesh High Court relied on ASI findings in declaring Bhojshala a Hindu temple; the survey was ordered in 2024, while the 2003 arrangement provided for worship by the two communities on separate days.
Modhera was fully solarised under an MNRE scheme (6 MW plant with 15 MWh storage), inaugurated on 9 October 2022.
