rows.title: Sources for medieval India - Persian chronicles, inscriptions, travellers' accounts

secs.t: Persian and Arabic chronicles → authors, reign covered (chronological order)

x: Exam angle: match author to work (Al-Biruni: Tahqiq-i-Hind; Minhaj: Tabaqat-i-Nasiri; Barani: Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; Ibn Battuta: Rihla); arrange the works in chronological order.
Futuh-us-Salatin was written by
Isami
at the Bahmani court around 1350 and covers the period from the Ghaznavids to Muhammad bin Tughlaq, including the Tughlaq campaigns against Warangal.

secs.t: Regional, Sanskrit and Deccan texts → authors

x: Ramacharitam was written by Sandhyakara Nandi and deals with the life of Pala king Ramapala.
Madhura Vijayam, written by Gangadevi, describes
Kampana’s conquest of Madurai and conditions under Tughlaq rule
Siddhesvara Charitam is a Telugu work by Kase Siddhappa that provides information on
Kakatiya-era society and religion
Kalhana
wrote Rajatarangini, the 12th-century history of Kashmir in 8 tarangas (books).

secs.t: Historians and court writers → origin, patron, contribution

x: Al-Biruni came to India around 1030 CE, during the eleventh century, under Mahmud of Ghazni.
Al-Biruni learned Sanskrit and wrote in Arabic on Indian religion, philosophy, astronomy and the caste system.
Al-Biruni recorded
the celebration of Diwali
on Kartika Amavasya.
Al-Biruni observed that Indians were unwilling to share their learning with outsiders.

secs.t: Foreign travellers → origin, ruler visited, what they described

x: Exam angle: "who mentioned 300 ports" (Abdur Razzaq; ⚠ APPSC key said Barbosa), "who mentioned sati" (Abdur Razzaq), traveller → country pairs.
Ibn Battuta
’s account of Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s reign contains observations on espionage, the postal system, sati and slave markets.
Abdur Razzaq
, the Timurid envoy to Deva Raya II's Vijayanagara, is credited with mentioning '300 ports'. ⚠ The APPSC key said Barbosa, so recognise that answer if it appears in an APPSC paper.

secs.t: Inscriptions and coins → place, ruler, what they record

x: The Nizami Mosque inscription at Golconda dates the independence of Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk to 1518.
The Lahore dirhams of Mahmud of Ghazni carry an Arabic legend along with a Sanskrit translation written in Sharada script.
The Palam Baoli inscription, dated 1276, praises
Balban
in Sanskrit.

secs.t: Buildings, calligraphy and painting → terms

x: Sultanate buildings demonstrate the shift from trabeate construction to arcuate construction through the use of
true arches, domes and lime mortar
Naskh was used for Quranic verses, while Nastaliq was used for Persian texts.
The Golconda school of painting was founded by
Mir Hashimi

secs.t: Biases and debates in the sources

x: Ziauddin Barani wrote from an orthodox Sunni viewpoint and also theorised about kingship.
The Telugu sources Pratapa Charitra, Vilasa and Kaluvacheru record eight invasions of Warangal, whereas Muslim sources associated with Amir Khusrau and Wassaf record five.
Firishta's story that Deva Raya kidnapped Nehal is rejected by modern historians.
Foreign accounts supplement Indian textual evidence, but their statements must be cross-verified with inscriptions and archaeological evidence.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Marco Polo is associated with Motupalli, Abdur Razzaq and Barbosa with Vijayanagara, and Tavernier with Golconda.
Al-Biruni, Nicolo Conti and the Ain-i-Akbari are cited as early evidence of Diwali in the referenced UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage discussion.
The Allahabad High Court sought responses from
the Centre and the Archaeological Survey of India

rows.title: Slave/Mamluk dynasty - Qutbuddin Aibak, Iltutmish (iqta, Chalisa, Turkan-i-Chahalgani), Razia Sultan, Balban

secs.t: Mamluk dynasty — lines, period, order of rulers

x: The dynasty is known as the Slave or Mamluk dynasty; the ruling line is also associated with the Ilbari Turks.
The sequence was Mamluk (1206–1290), Khalji (1290–1320), Tughlaq (1320–1414), Sayyid (1414–1451) and Lodi (1451–1526).
Iltutmish (1210-36) was followed, after Ruknuddin Firuz, by Razia (1236-40); after Bahram Shah and Alauddin Masud came Nasiruddin Mahmud (1246-66) and then Balban (1266-86).

secs.t: Qutbuddin Aibak and Iltutmish → career and contributions

x: Aibak rose to the position of
Amir-i-Akhur
, or Master of Stables, and subsequently became a general.
The Second Battle of Tarain occurred in 1192, followed by Ghori's death and Aibak's accession in 1206; Aibak died in 1210.
Iltutmish was an Ilbari Turk, Aibak's slave and son-in-law.
Iltutmish refused shelter to Jalaluddin Mangbarni of Khwarazm.

secs.t: Razia, Nasiruddin Mahmud and Balban → career and contributions

x: The Turkish nobles resented Razia's favour towards
Yaqut, an Abyssinian
Altuniya's revolt was followed by Yaqut's death and Razia's imprisonment; Razia then married Altuniya, marched towards Delhi, and was defeated and killed in 1240.
Balban was captured by the Mongols, bought by Iltutmish, rose from water-carrier to the Forty, and was made Amir-i-Shikar by Razia.

secs.t: Terms → meaning (administration, court, titles)

x: Mamluk is an Arabic term meaning ‘owned’.
The Abbasid Caliph's mansur came in 1229.
Balban held the Sultan to be Zil-i-Ilahi.

secs.t: Monuments → builder

x: The Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque was built at Delhi.
Qutbuddin Aibak began the Qutb Minar and dedicated it to
Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki
Iltutmish built the
Sultan Ghari tomb
and is consequently called the Father of tomb building.

secs.t: End of the dynasty and rise of the Khaljis

x: Balban died in 1286 and was followed by his grandson Kaiqubad, who was murdered.
Jalaluddin Firoz Khalji crowned himself at
Kilokhari
in 1290, thereby ending Mamluk rule and beginning the Khalji dynasty.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The
Slave or Mamluk dynasty
was the first Muslim dynasty to rule North India from Delhi and laid the institutional foundation of the Delhi Sultanate.
The dynasty helped establish the iqta, Forty, tanka-jital and Diwan-i-Arz institutions, while the Qutb complex is now a UNESCO site.
Iltutmish received the first Caliphal investiture in 1229.

rows.title: Khalji dynasty - Jalaluddin; Alauddin Khalji's conquests, Deccan campaigns of Malik Kafur

secs.t: Khalji Sultans → accession, policy, contribution

x: Jalaluddin Khalji was the first Sultan described as having a benevolent attitude towards Hindus, and he was lenient towards rebels including Malik Chhajju.
Jalaluddin crowned himself at Kilokhari, failed in his attack on Ranthambore, and was murdered at Kara by Alauddin in 1296.
Alauddin Khalji raided Devagiri during
, before murdering Jalaluddin and becoming Sultan.

secs.t: Posts, titles and terms → meaning

x: Alauddin was Amir-i-Tuzuk (master of ceremonies).

secs.t: Mongol invasions → leaders, battles, defence

x: The first Mongol threat came under Iltutmish in 1221, when
Chengiz Khan
was the Mongol leader.
Settled converted Mongols were the New Mussalmans.
Alauddin did not abandon the north-western frontier.
Zafar Khan died at Kili.

secs.t: Alauddin's conquests and Malik Kafur's Deccan campaigns → year, ruler defeated, commander

x: Exam angle: chronological order (UPPSC 2022: Gujarat, Ranthambore, Chittor, Warangal); statements on Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan leading the 1299 Gujarat campaign.
Gujarat was associated with Rai Karan, Chittor with Rana Ratan Singh, Warangal with Prataparudra II, and the Malwa campaign was led by Ain-ul-Mulk Multani.
Devagiri (Yadava Ramachandra, 1307-08), Warangal (Kakatiya Prataparudra II, 1309-10), Dwarasamudra (Hoysala Vira Ballala III, 1310-11) and Madurai (Pandya princes, 1311).

secs.t: Chittor and the Padmini legend → text, author, debate

x: Malik Muhammad Jayasi composed Padmavat in
Awadhi
Some scholars treat the Padmini motive as a legend rather than an undisputed historical account.

secs.t: Successors → end of the Khaljis

x: After Alauddin's death in 1316, Malik Kafur set aside Khizr Khan and placed the minor Shihabuddin Umar on the throne.
Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah was Sultan from 1316 to 1320.
Khusrau Khan subdued Warangal again in 1318, which is identified as the third invasion.
Mubarak Shah withdrew, rather than restored, Alauddin Khalji's harsh regulations and price controls.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All four statements correctly describe the major stages of Kakatiya–Delhi relations: the defeat at Upparapalli, the treaty of 1309–10, assistance against the Pandyas in 1311, and the cessation of tribute after 1316.
Alauddin Khalji's reign is called
the imperial period
of the Delhi Sultanate because of its extensive territorial expansion and campaigns.

rows.title: Alauddin Khalji's market control regulations, revenue and military reforms
sub: Group-II S1-38: Alauddin Khalji - conquests, market control and administrative reforms

secs.t: Alauddin Khalji → posts, kingship, titles, Mongol victories

x: Alauddin did revive a harsh and centralised style of rule, but unlike Balban he did not depend on religious sanction for his policies.
The Mongol defeats associated with the four years were Jalandhar in 1298, Kili in 1299, Amroha in 1305 and Ravi in 1306.
Alauddin Khalji
took the title Sikandar-i-Sani, reflecting his dream of world conquest, from which Kotwal Ala-ul-Mulk dissuaded him.

secs.t: Officials and departments → role

x: The Shahna-i-Mandi supervised each market, while the overall system was administered by the Diwan-i-Riyasat under the Naib-i-Riyasat.
The
Diwan-i-Mustakhraj
was established to recover arrears from revenue officials.

secs.t: Military reforms → features and FIRSTs

x: Dagh referred to branding horses and huliya or chehra to the descriptive roll of each soldier.
Alauddin Khalji
created the first standing army paid in cash and introduced dagh and huliya in military administration.
Ferishta puts Alauddin's permanent cavalry at about 4,75,000, recruited by the Ariz-i-Mumalik and paid in cash.

secs.t: Market control → aim, markets, enforcement, supply

x: Exam angle: UPPSC keys call the market control "highly successful"; Barani is the main source.
Mandi dealt with food grains, Sarai Adl with cloth and other specified commodities, the third market with horses, slaves and cattle, and the fourth market with miscellaneous goods.
Alauddin Khalji
's market control kept state granaries stocked and rationed grain during scarcity, regarded as the first public distribution system of the Sultanate.

secs.t: Revenue reforms → terms, share, taxes

x: Alauddin first measured land, using the biswa.
Ghari, the house tax, and charai, the pasture or grazing tax, were added as new taxes.
Unjustified inam and waqf grants were taken back, enlarging the khalisa, or crown-land, area.
Khuts, muqaddams and chaudharis were brought under taxation, and the headman's cess was abolished.

secs.t: Barani's causes of revolt → ordinances

x: Barani identified noble wealth, noble intermarriage and gatherings, a weak intelligence system and drinking as four causes of revolt perceived by Alauddin.
Alauddin reorganised espionage, prohibited liquor and gambling, and confiscated religious grants and free lands.
All three measures belong to
Alauddin Khalji
: his ordinances prohibited liquor and gambling, he regulated the markets, and offenders were punished severely.

secs.t: Malik Kafur and the Deccan campaigns → year, kingdom, ruler

x: Malik Kafur and Khwaja Haji besieged Warangal, obtained Prataparudra's submission and sent the loot to Delhi on 1,000 camels.
The Deccan expeditions were primarily financial ventures intended to secure plunder and tribute for paying the army, rather than to annex the southern states.
Devagiri was ruled by Ramachandra, Warangal by Prataparudra II, Dwarasamudra by Vira Ballala III, and the Pandya kingdom of Madurai was sacked.

secs.t: Effects, reversal and dynasty comparison

x: Mubarak Shah, who ruled from 1316 to 1320, abolished the price controls, restored confiscated lands and withdrew the harsh regulations.
The reforms helped maintain low prices and a strong army capable of resisting the Mongols, but repression and espionage created widespread discontent.
The Lodis were the first Afghan dynasty and Agra was founded under them, so the third pair is wrong.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Potuganti Maili and Recherla Venna
defeated Malik Fakhruddin Juna at Upparapalli during the failed 1303 attack on Warangal.
Mahmud Gawan
of the Bahmani kingdom later introduced dagh and chehra, land measurement and a larger khalisa.
The combination of despotism and extensive espionage weakened the state internally, and the dynasty declined soon after Alauddin’s death in 1316.

rows.title: Tughlaq dynasty - Ghiyasuddin; Muhammad bin Tughlaq's five experiments; Firoz Shah's reforms
sub: Group-II S1-39: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiments and Firoz Shah Tughlaq's reforms

secs.t: Tughlaq rulers → rise, reign, contribution, end — Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (1320-25)

x: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq improved communication by organising a postal system using runners and horsemen.
Ghiyasuddin became Sultan in 1320, Juna Khan attacked Warangal in 1321–22, Warangal fell in 1323, and Ghiyasuddin died in 1325.
Warangal fell in 1323 during
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
's reign and was renamed Sultanpur.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq is credited with
laying about 1,200 gardens

secs.t: Tughlaq rulers → rise, reign, contribution, end — Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351-88)

x: Firoz Shah succeeded
Muhammad bin Tughlaq
at Thatta in 1351 and ruled until 1388.
Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul paid compensation to persons who had suffered during Muhammad bin Tughlaq's rule.
The Tughlaq period began with Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq in 1320 and ended when Khizr Khan took Delhi in 1414.
Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah Tughlaq
, the last Tughlaq, ruled during Timur's invasion of 1398.

secs.t: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's five experiments → cause and result

x: Exam angle: statement questions ("token currency was copper and brass"; "the Doab tax coincided with famine").
The capital was transferred in 1327, token currency was introduced around 1329–30, and the Khurasan and Qarachil experiments followed.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced token currency in copper and brass because of a shortage of silver.
The higher Doab taxation aimed at increasing revenue, but it coincided with famine and led to peasant revolts and flight.

secs.t: Departments, taxes and terms → meaning

x: Taqavi or sondhar loans were agricultural advances intended to help cultivators purchase seed and dig wells.
Ibn Battuta recorded horse couriers called uluq at intervals of four miles and foot couriers called dawa at three stations to every mile.
Diwan-i-Khairat dealt with charity, Diwan-i-Bandagan with slaves, Dar-ul-Shifa was a free hospital, and Diwan-i-Istihqaq provided pensions and grants.

secs.t: Ibn Battuta and historians → statements on MBT

x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq appointed Ibn Battuta Qazi of Delhi and later sent him as an envoy to China in 1342.
Ibn Battuta is identified in this context as the first foreign traveller to visit Vijayanagara during the reign of
Harihara I
Ibn Battuta (Abu Abdullah Muhammad) was a Moroccan, born at Tangiers in 1304.

secs.t: Revolts and new states under MBT → year, leader

x: Kapaya Nayaka
recaptured Warangal in 1336 after the earlier leadership of Prolaya Nayaka.
The Bahmani kingdom was founded by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah.
The order is coastal Andhra liberation around 1325, Madurai Sultanate in 1335, Vijayanagara in 1336 and Bahmani kingdom in 1347.
Harihara and Bukka had been sent by Muhammad bin Tughlaq and later founded Vijayanagara under the guidance of Vidyaranya.

secs.t: Firoz Shah's public works → places

x: Firoz Shah built more canals than any other Delhi Sultan and imposed an irrigation cess called haq-i-sharb.
His canals ran from the Yamuna and Sutlej to Hisar.
Firoz Shah transported Ashokan pillars from Topra in the Ambala region and from Meerut to Delhi.

secs.t: Firoz Shah → revenue, jizya, iqta, books and campaigns

x: Firoz wrote off taqavi loans and state debts, fixed land revenue, retained the four Islamic taxes, and made iqtas hereditary.
Firoz Shah made jizya a separate tax and, following the advice of the ulema, extended it to Brahmins for the first time.
Azizuddin Khalid Khani
translated the Sanskrit texts taken from the Jwalamukhi temple at Nagarkot into Persian.
Ragadarpan
, a work on music, was also translated during Firoz Shah's reign.

secs.t: Delhi Sultans → distinctive measure; cities of Delhi → founder

x: Iltutmish
established the Chahalgani, while Balban later ended its influence.
Branding of horses
, or dagh, was a measure of Alauddin Khalji.
The Zil-i-Ilahi theory was associated with Balban, not Iltutmish.
Siri was founded by Alauddin Khalji and Tughlaqabad by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Malik Maqbul was originally the captured Brahmin Jagannatha Pandit, who converted to Islam and later became Firoz Shah's wazir, Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq is regarded as the first Sultan of Delhi to initiate canal digging, while Firoz Shah undertook canal construction on a much larger scale.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq's schemes were ambitious and often sound in idea, but their poor execution led to failure and instability.

rows.title: Timur's invasion; Sayyid and Lodi dynasties; the First Battle of Panipat, 1526

secs.t: Sayyid and Lodi dynasties → period, founder, succession

x: Khizr Khan, Timur’s viceroy, arrested Daulat Khan Lodi, captured Delhi in 1414 and ruled as Timur’s deputy without using the title Sultan.
Alauddin Alam Shah voluntarily gave up the throne to Bahlol Lodi in 1451.
Bahlol Lodi was succeeded by his son Sikandar Lodi, who was followed by Ibrahim Lodi.

secs.t: Sayyid and Lodi rulers → contributions

x: Tarikh-i-
Mubarak Shah
i was written by Yahiya bin Ahmad Sarhindi in the reign of Mubarak Shah (1421-34).
Sikandar Lodi extended his authority from Punjab to Bihar, subdued Jaunpur and defeated Bengal rulers and Rajput chiefs.
Sikandar Lodi was religiously intolerant in several actions, including destruction of images and temples and imposition of jizya, yet he had a Sanskrit medical treatise translated into Persian.

secs.t: Books, terms and buildings → meaning or author

x: Mubarak Shah’s octagonal tomb is noted for
blue enamelled tiles and guldasta motifs

secs.t: Invasions and battles → year, route, tactics, result

x: Timur crossed the Indus, passed through Punjab via Multan and Bhatnair, and sacked Delhi in December 1398.
Tulughma was a flanking manoeuvre and Araba carts were chained as a defensive line (Rumi device).
Babur’s
field artillery and muskets
were decisive factors in the victory at Panipat.
Babur fought Rana Sanga at Kanwah in 1527 and then fought at Chanderi in 1528.

secs.t: Persons → invitation to Babur; contemporaries of Ibrahim

x: Babur was descended from Timur on his father’s side and from Chengiz Khan on his mother’s side.
The political background included Ibrahim Lodi’s unpopularity, strong Mewar and Marwar, five Deccan Sultanates and Vijayanagara in the south.
Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of Punjab, and Alam Khan, Ibrahim's uncle,
invited or sought Babur's help against Ibrahim Lodi
; Rana Sanga too offered to join him, according to Babur.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The 500th anniversary of the First Battle of Panipat, fought in 1526, was marked on
21 April 2026
The Lodis constituted the first Afghan dynasty and the final ruling dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, while Ibrahim Lodi was its last Delhi Sultan.
Sikandar Lodi
was the Delhi Sultan when Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498.

rows.title: Delhi Sultanate - the five dynasties in outline
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-90

secs.t: The five dynasties → period, founder, origin

x: Exam angle: the rule periods are asked as a match (Tughlaqs 1320-1414, Mamluks 1206-1290, Lodis 1451-1526, Sayyids 1414-1451).
The Mamluks ruled from 1206 to 1290, the Khaljis from 1290 to 1320, the Tughlaqs from 1320 to 1414 and the Sayyids from 1414 to 1451.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Khizr Khan and Bahlol Lodi founded the Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties respectively.

secs.t: Rulers → succession order and reign periods

x: The succession was Qutbuddin Aibak, Aram Shah, Iltutmish, Ruknuddin Firoz and Razia.
The order was Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin Khalji, Shihabuddin, the child set up by Malik Kafur, and Mubarak Shah.

secs.t: Battles, invasions and breakaway kingdoms

x: Chengiz Khan reached the Indus in 1221 while pursuing the fugitive Khwarezm prince
Jalaluddin Mangbarni
Alauddin Khalji
later adopted and completed Balban's policy of strengthening the north-west frontier against the Mongols.
Timur invaded India in 1398 during the reign of
Nasiruddin Mahmud
, the last ruler of the Tughlaq dynasty.
Harihara and Bukka were sent against Deccan rebels, later returned to Hinduism under Vidyaranya, and founded Anegondi, which developed into Vijayanagara.

secs.t: Sultans → titles and epithets

x: Gulrukhi was the pen-name of Sikandar Lodi.
Balban
adopted the titles Zil-i-Ilahi or Zillillah, meaning Shadow of God, and Niyabat-i-Khudai.
Lakh Bakhsh means ‘
giver of lakhs
’, referring to Aibak's generosity.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
was earlier known as Ghazi Malik.
Alauddin Khalji
assumed the title Sikandar-i-Sani.

secs.t: FIRSTs and LASTs → ruler

x: Kaiqubad
was the last effective ruler of the Mamluk dynasty and was killed in 1290.
Sikandar Lodi
was the Delhi Sultan when Vasco da Gama arrived at Calicut.
Bahlol Lodi was the first Afghan ruler of Delhi
; the rulers before him were Turks.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Delhi forces invaded Andhra five times during 1303–1323.
Ulugh Khan was the earlier name of
Muhammad bin Tughluq
, who captured Prataparudra II in 1323.
Qutbuddin Aibak was the first Sultan of Delhi.
Ibrahim Lodi
was the last Sultan of Delhi and was defeated at the Battle of Panipat in 1526.

rows.title: Sultanate central administration - Sultan, wazir, the diwans, nobility, theory of kingship
sub: Group-II S1-40: Delhi Sultanate administration - Sultan, wazir, diwans, iqta and the nobility

secs.t: Sultans → theory of kingship and relations with the Caliph

x: Exam angle: BPSC 2022 asked who "opposed the Khalifa's power". The key was "more than one of the above".
Balban
propounded the concept of the Sultan as Zil-i-Ilahi, or Shadow of God, along with Niyabat-i-Khudai, or divine deputyship.
Balban excluded low-born men from high office, whereas the appointment of non-Turks and low-born men is associated with Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

secs.t: Features of the state — legal basis and nature

x: Sharia covered the civil matters of Muslims, while royal decrees or zawabit supplemented the legal order.
Hindu personal law was retained, criminal law was governed by the Sultan’s rules, and the Sultan combined supreme military and appellate authority.
The Delhi Sultanate combined
Perso-Arabic, Turko-Mongol and Indian elements
and was comparatively centralised.

secs.t: Central departments (diwans) → head, function, founding Sultan

x: Diwan-i-Wizarat dealt with finance and revenue, Diwan-i-Insha with royal correspondence and decrees, and Diwan-i-Qaza with justice.
Diwan-i-Arz, the department dealing with army recruitment and inspection, was set up by
Balban
Diwan-i-Riyasat was the department of
market control
, functioning under the Naib-i-Riyasat, during Alauddin Khalji's reign.
The Sadr-us-Sudur supervised
religious affairs and endowments
; the Chief Sadr was also the Chief Qazi.

secs.t: Central officials → duty

x: The Naib ranked next to the Sultan and in practice controlled all departments.
The Dabir-i-Khas headed the Diwan-i-Insha and dealt with royal correspondence and the drafting of decrees.
Qazi-ul-Quzat was the Chief Justice, Barid-i-Mumalik headed intelligence, and Wakil-i-Dar supervised the court and royal household.

secs.t: Wazirs and key nobles → Sultan served

x: Imad-ul-Mulk served Balban, Malik Kafur was the Naib Malik of Alauddin Khalji, and Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul was the wazir of Firoz Tughlaq.
Nizam-ul-Mulk Junaidi
served as the wazir of Iltutmish.
The wizarat reached its heyday under
Firoz Tughlaq
, when Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul effectively ran the government.
Ain-ul-Mulk Multani
conquered Malwa for Alauddin Khalji in 1305.

secs.t: Changes in the nobility — the Chalisa to the Lodis

x: Balban introduced sijda, paibos and the Persian festival Nauroz.
The Khalji Revolution opened high office to non-Turks and Indian Muslims, breaking the earlier Turkish monopoly.
Lodi rulers dealt with an Afghan tribal nobility that treated the Sultan as first among equals.
Iltutmish created the Forty, Balban destroyed its power, Jalaluddin Khalji came to power in 1290, and Alauddin later imposed restrictions on the nobility.

secs.t: Local and revenue officials → unit and role

x: The muqaddam or chaudhari headed the village, the chaudhari had a major rural revenue role, and Alauddin abolished the khut’s cess.
A pargana, comprising a group of villages, was placed under an amil for revenue collection.
Mir Bakshi
was a Mughal office and did not exist under the Delhi Sultans.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Sultanate diwans prefigured important Mughal institutions, including the Diwan, Mir Bakshi and Sadr-us-Sudur.
The Peshwa was the Prime Minister, was renamed Diwan under Tana Shah, was last held by Madanna, and the Majumdar served as auditor, mostly from the Hindu community.
The Bahmani Prime Minister was known as the
Wakil-us-Saltanat

rows.title: Sultanate provincial and military administration - iqta system, dagh and huliya, army organisation

secs.t: Iqta system — definition, origin and FIRSTs

x: Fawazil was the surplus revenue left after meeting the muqti’s costs, and it had to be remitted to the treasury.
A muqti maintained troops, collected revenue, preserved law and order, and remitted the surplus to the centre.
Muhammad Ghori granted Hansi (some sources say Kuhram) to Qutbuddin Aibak, the first iqta.

secs.t: Sultans → changes in the iqta and army pay

x: Alauddin Khalji
maintained the first large permanent standing army paid in cash from the royal treasury.
Iltutmish and Balban used iqtas for payment, Alauddin Khalji introduced large-scale cash payment, and Firoz Tughlaq returned to assignment-based payment through the jagir revival.
The jagir revival enabled nobles to control
recruitment, promotion and discipline
, which weakened the efficiency of the army.

secs.t: Army organisation and military technology

x: Alauddin Khalji
introduced dagh, the branding of horses, and huliya, the descriptive roll of each soldier.
Branding horses and maintaining descriptive rolls helped prevent soldiers from bringing inferior horses or sending proxies in their place during inspection.
The Turks introduced or strengthened horse-based warfare, mounted archery, the iron stirrup, armour and stronger fortifications.

secs.t: Postal and intelligence systems → introducer

x: Alauddin Khalji obtained daily market reports from
barids and munhiyans
, the latter functioning as secret spies.
Ghiyasuddin Tughluq
improved the postal system by employing both runners and horsemen.
The horse post, called ulaq, was used to bring fruit from Khorasan to Delhi.
Sher Shah's dak chowki is regarded as a later precursor of the modern postal system.

secs.t: Land assignment terms → meaning and dynasty

x: An iqta was an assignment of land revenue to an officer, usually an iqtadar or muqti, instead of a cash salary.
Khalisa was crown land, iqta was assigned to officials in place of salary, and inam was granted to religious men and institutions.
A is true: Sultanate land was broadly khalisa (crown land) and iqta (revenue assignments).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The iqta system provided the financial basis for maintaining troops while also connecting military service with the administration of assigned territories.

Vijayanagara had the Siddha Sainyam and Amara Nayankara army; the Qutb Shahis had the Siddha Sainyam and Jagirdar Sainyam; Kakatiya royal bodyguards were Lenkas; and Shivaji maintained a cash-paid standing army.

rows.title: Sultanate economy - kharaj, jizya, zakat, khams; agriculture, urbanisation, trade and craft
sub: Group-II S1-41: Sultanate socio-economic conditions - agriculture, revenue, towns and trade

secs.t: Taxes and cesses → nature, payer, Sultan — Sharia taxes and booty

x: Exam angle: "Khams = 1/5 of war booty" and "Zakat = tax on Muslims only" are the standard traps.
Jizya was a protection tax on non-Muslims, zakat was payable by Muslims, and khams was the state’s one-fifth share of booty and treasure-troves.
Firoz Tughlaq abolished the many illegal cesses and kept only the four Sharia taxes:
kharaj, jizya, zakat and khams

secs.t: Taxes and cesses → nature, payer, Sultan — Land revenue and land categories

x: Peasants generally paid one-third of the produce as land revenue, but Alauddin Khalji raised the demand to one-half.
Alauddin Khalji
introduced Ghari, the house tax, and Charai, the grazing tax on milch cattle.
Haq-i-sharb was an irrigation tax on land watered by canals and was approximately one-tenth of the produce.
An iqta was a land assignment made to officials instead of paying them a direct salary.

secs.t: Agriculture — crops, irrigation, agrarian measures

x: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
is regarded as the first canal-builder of the fourteenth century, while Firoz Tughlaq later built the largest number of canals.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq gave taccavi or sondhar loans to cultivators for extending cultivation.
Ibn Battuta observed two harvests a year, rabi and kharif, and noted that rice was sown three times annually.

secs.t: Crafts, industries and Turkish technologies

x: The Turks popularised paper-making, glass-making, the spinning wheel, improved looms, the iron stirrup and better armour.
The availability of paper
strengthened bureaucratic record-keeping
in the Sultanate administration.
Leather work, metal-work and carpet-weaving flourished during the Sultanate period, along with textiles and other crafts.
Royal karkhanas made luxury goods for the court, and
Firoz Shah Tughlaq
ran about 36 of them.

secs.t: Towns → founder; urban centres and ports

x: Devagiri was located in Maharashtra and is presently known as Daulatabad.
Alauddin Khalji founded Siri, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founded Tughlaqabad, Muhammad bin Tughlaq founded Jahanpanah and Sikandar Lodi founded Agra.
Sikandar Lodi founded Agra in 1504.
Many medieval cities developed around forts, administrative centres and military cantonments.

secs.t: Trade — routes, imports, post and trading groups

x: The overland route was Khorasan-Kabul-Multan/Lahore and coastal trade used Cambay and Broach.
Multanis and Khurasanis controlled overseas trade and financing; Gujarati, Marwari and Muslim Bohra merchants dominated inland trade; and Banjaras carried bulk goods such as grain using oxen.
The horse post, or uluq/ulaq, had royal horses stationed about every four miles.

secs.t: Coins → metal and Sultan

x: Iltutmish
first issued the silver tanka and copper jital as standard Arabic coinage.
Firoz Tughlaq introduced the adha, worth one-half of a jital, and the bikh, worth one-fourth of a jital.
The tanka was silver, associated with Iltutmish and weighed 175 grains; the jital was copper; and the shashgani was worth six jitals.

secs.t: Social classes → role

x: Nobles held iqtas, the ulema interpreted religious law, and khuts and muqaddams were involved in collecting revenue from peasants.
Ibn Battuta referred to slave markets, and Firoz Tughlaq maintained a separate department for slaves.
Hindu society retained its caste order, while sati and purdah spread during this period.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Alauddin Khalji's price controls were designed in the context of maintaining the army, showing how military needs shaped economic policy.
Paper strengthened administration and the Persian wheel improved irrigation; both had lasting economic significance.
Amir Khusrau's account of Warangal's diamonds and wealth helps explain why it attracted invasions from Delhi.

Sources: Group-II S1-41: APP (Indian History Part 2 > Administration, Economy and Society); UPSC (Medieval History pp.70, 72); CDI (Block02 Ibn Battuta; Block03 Bahmani revenue); CDX (AP History p.209)

rows.title: Sultanate society - nobility, ulema, position of women, slavery; conversion and syncretism
sub: Group-II S1-42: Sultanate religious conditions - ulema, conversion, jizya and syncretism

secs.t: Social groups → terms and meaning

x: Kulah-daran referred to the Sayyids, who wore the pointed cap called kulah.
Ashraf denoted elite Muslims of foreign descent, including Turks, Persians, Afghans and Sayyids.
The Hindu caste order, with Brahmins at the top, continued.

secs.t: Sultans and the ulema → religious policy — Ulema, qazis and the Islamic character of the state

x: The ulema interpreted Islamic law, qazis administered it, and the Qazi-ul-Quzat served as the chief judge.
Barani regarded the Sultanate as not truly Islamic because the Sultan framed his own regulations (zawabit) to supplement Muslim law.
The Sadr-us-Sudur headed the Diwan-i-Risalat, dealt with religious affairs and grants to mosques and madrasas, and was also the Chief Qazi.

secs.t: Sultans and the ulema → religious policy — Religious policy by Sultan

x: Firoz Tughlaq followed the ulema, adopted theocratic principles, respected the Egyptian Caliph and extended jizya to Brahmins.
Sikandar Lodi was orthodox; he destroyed temples at Mathura, broke the Jwalamukhi images at Nagarkot and imposed jizya.
Hindu gods and goddesses were worshipped in the royal palace during the reign of
Nasiruddin Khusrau Shah

secs.t: Jizya and temple destruction — features

x: Jizya was a protection tax on non-Muslims in place of military service.
The Qutb Shahis of Golconda never imposed jizya.
Temple destruction could be motivated by royal legitimacy and the acquisition of temple wealth, in addition to religious considerations.

secs.t: Position of women — purdah, sati, jauhar, women rulers

x: Sati was prevalent and had documented instances, including Ibn Battuta’s description.
Jauhar was performed at
Ranthambhor in 1301 and Chittor in 1303
during resistance against Alauddin.
Lal Ded
of Kashmir was a female saint who found expression through Bhakti and Sufism.
Razia Sultana
(1236-40) was the only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate and faced resistance because of gender norms.

secs.t: Slavery — sources, markets, Diwan-i-Bandagan

x: Slaves came from war captivity, purchase in markets and among defaulters.
Alauddin Khalji’s third regulated market dealt with horses, slaves and cattle at fixed prices.
Firoz had about 1,80,000 slaves.
Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban were themselves slaves, or bandagan, which explains the association with the name Slave or Mamluk Dynasty.

secs.t: Conversion — theories, causes and debates

x: Current scholarship rejects the sword theory as a colonial trope; coercion was isolated.
Sufi influence was a major factor especially in Bengal and Punjab, and it operated together with agrarian expansion.
Conversion was gradual and multi-causal.
Sufi saints reached lower castes and farming communities through
pirs and dargahs

secs.t: Sufis and scholars → contributions to syncretism

x: Hamiduddin Nagori's Hindi verses equated the Hindu devotional expression Alakh Niranjan with Khuda.
Sheikh Nuruddin founded Kashmir's Rishi movement, echoing Lalla, adopted vegetarianism and served people of all castes.
Sufis, especially the
Chishtis
such as Muinuddin, Nizamuddin Auliya and Baba Farid, communicated with people in Hindavi.
The sitar is traditionally cited as a Hindu-Muslim fusion instrument, and Amir Khusrau is traditionally credited with the sitar and qawwali.

secs.t: Bhakti-Sufi interaction — features, shared rituals, music

x: The Bhakti movement had indigenous roots in the Alvars and Nayanars, while Islam reinforced its egalitarian and anti-ritual tendencies.
Sufi poetry used human love as a metaphor for divine love.
The Deccan developed a mixed culture in which Hindu Nayakas served Sultans and Sultans patronised temples.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In Meenakshipuram in February 1981, 558 Dalits embraced Islam, associated with the social-liberation argument of escaping caste oppression.
Gesu Daraz moved to Gulbarga under Firoz Shah Bahmani and wrote in Persian and early Dakhni, including Mirqat-ul-Ashyaq.
Barani's interpretation presents the state as a theocracy, while another approach sees it as a military state adapting to local realities.

rows.title: Indo-Islamic architecture - arcuate style, Qutb Minar, Alai Darwaza, Tughlaqabad, provincial styles
sub: Group-II S1-43: Sultanate art and architecture - Indo-Islamic style, Qutb complex, Tughlaq architecture

secs.t: Arcuate style — terms → meaning

x: The arcuate style uses arches, domes and vaults, in contrast to the trabeate system based on lintels, pillars and corbels.
A squinch or pendentive helps transform a square chamber into a round or polygonal base capable of supporting a dome.
The decorative vocabulary moved away from human and animal figures towards geometric patterns, arabesque and Quranic calligraphy.

secs.t: Architectural FIRSTs and dynasty → style features

x: Alai Darwaza
is noted for its horseshoe arch with a lotus-bud or spearhead fringe, along with red sandstone and marble inlay.
Battered walls belong to the Tughlaqs, octagonal tombs and double domes to the Lodis, the propylon screen to the Sharqis, and the lotus-bud horseshoe arch to the Khaljis.
Sayyid and Lodi builders reintroduced Hindu-style gates or façades, plaster ornament and external drip-stones.

secs.t: Sultans → monuments built, chronological order

x: Exam angle: match building → Sultan (UPPSC 2022 pairs: Sultan Garhi-Iltutmish, Red Palace-Balban, Jamat Khana-Alauddin, mosque-Aibak).
Alauddin Khalji excavated the tank known as Hauz-i-Alai, while Firoz Shah Tughlaq added the madrasa and tomb.
Quwwat-ul-Islam stands in the Qutb complex at Delhi and Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer; both were built by Aibak.
The Qutb complex World Heritage Site includes the Qutb Minar, Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Alai Darwaza, Iron Pillar, tomb of Iltutmish, Alauddin’s tomb and madrasa, and Imam Zamin’s tomb.

secs.t: Qutb complex, Delhi — site → features

x: The Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.
The Qutb Minar has five tapering storeys, is about 72.5 metres high and is decorated with bands of Quranic calligraphy.
The Iron Pillar is a Gupta-era pillar.

secs.t: Provincial styles — region / dynasty → monuments

x: Bengal architecture is noted for brick construction and curved roofs, with the Adina Mosque and the mosques of Pandua as important examples.
Gujarat
’s provincial style is characterised by strong Hindu-Jain carving, exemplified by the Jama Masjid of Ahmedabad.
The Sharqi style of Jaunpur is marked by massive gateway facades with a propylon screen and no minarets, as in the Atala Masjid.

secs.t: Qutb Shahi Hyderabad and Golconda — places → features

x: The Charminar’s form reflects Persian and Deccani elements, while Mir Momin Astarabadi planned Hyderabad on the model of Isfahan.
The Qutb Shahi Tombs at Ibrahim Bagh contain the seven rulers of the dynasty and are characterised by onion domes resting on square bases.
Naskh
is used for the Quranic verses around the mihrab, while the gateway carries fine Nastaliq calligraphy.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The synthesis of indigenous Indian and Islamic architectural elements during the Sultanate provided the direct foundation for
Mughal architecture
Qutb Shahi architecture combined Persian and Hindu traditions and is described as an Indo-Saracenic blend.
Rajon ki Baoli, known as the stepwell of the masons, was built by Daulat Khan Lodi in 1506 under Sikandar Lodi at Mehrauli Archaeological Park.

src: Sources: Group-I: CDI (Block04 Advent of Islam §8; Block04 Qutub Shahis > calligraphy; Block03 Qutb Shahi Art and Architecture; Block05 Mughal Architecture); APP (Indian History Part 2 > Indo-Islamic Architecture; Firoz Tughluq; AP History Medieval > Qutb Shahis); UPSC (Art & Culture p.53; Medieval History pp.59, 70, 147); CDX (AP History pp.282-285, 301); PYQs APPSC-G1 2024, APPSC-GS 2019, CGPSC 2023, BPSC 2022, UPPSC 2022, JPSC 2021

rows.title: Sultanate literature and culture - Amir Khusrau, Ziauddin Barani, Ibn Battuta, music and Sufi influence
sub: Group-II S1-44: Sultanate language and literature - Persian chronicles, Amir Khusrau, regional languages

secs.t: Indo-Persian histories and travelogues → authors

x: Ibn Battuta’s Rihla is an Arabic travelogue containing observations on the Delhi Sultanate and the Deccan.
Kitab-ul-Hind belongs to about 1030, Prithviraj Raso is traditionally assigned to the late twelfth century, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri to about 1260, and Fatawa-i-Jahandari to the fourteenth century.
Al-Biruni wrote Tahqiq-i-Hind (Kitab-ul-Hind), Minhaj-us-Siraj the Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, Isami the Futuh-us-Salatin, and Ibn Battuta the Rihla.
The Tughluqnama, on the rise of Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, was written by Amir Khusrau, not Ibn Battuta (UPPSC 2019 trap).

secs.t: Barani and Amir Khusrau → patrons, titles and views

x: Both statements are true, and the gap between the ideal of protecting sharia and the practical use of state laws explains Barani’s assessment.
Khusrau wrote in Hindavi, an early form associated with the later development of Hindi–Urdu literary expression.
Amir Khusrau is credited with founding the Indian style of Persian poetry known as
Sabak-i-Hindi
or the Hindustani style.

secs.t: Amir Khusrau's works → subject

x: Khazain-ul-Futuh
describes the conquests of Alauddin Khalji, including his Deccan campaigns.
Miftah-ul-Futuh deals with Jalaluddin Khalji's campaigns.
Ashiqa, or Deval Rani–Khizr Khan, deals with
the romance involving Alauddin Khalji’s son

secs.t: Music — Khusrau's forms, Sufi terms, instruments and treatises → author

x: Tradition credits Amir Khusrau with the sitar, the tabla and forms such as tarana and khayal.
Aiman (Yaman), along with Zilaf and Sazgiri, is a raga traditionally credited to Amir Khusrau.
The Bahmanis brought the
rebab and oud
to the Deccan, where they were combined with the veena and mridangam.

secs.t: Sanskrit-Persian translations → translator and patron

x: Zain-ul-Abidin of Kashmir
is associated with translating the Mahabharata and Rajatarangini into Persian.
Razmnama was the Persian translation of the Mahabharata, whereas Suka Saptati was translated as Tutinama.
Ziya-uddin Nakhshabi
made the Tutinama from the Suka Saptati in Muhammad bin Tughlaq's time (UPPSC 2022).

secs.t: Sufi, premakhyan and Telugu works → author

x: Chandayan, an Awadhi premakhyan composed in 1379, was written by
Mulla Daud
Mrigavati was written by Qutban, Padmavat by Malik Muhammad Jayasi, Padmavati Katha by Damodar Kavi, and Fawaid-ul-Fuad by Amir Hasan Sijzi.
Kase Siddhappa
wrote Siddhesvara Charitam, noted for its description of socio-economic conditions.
Srinatha
wrote Kasi Khandam and Sringara Naishadham during the Reddi period associated with Pedakomati Vema.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Persian became the elite language of administration and culture, while Indo-Persian historiography developed through writers such as Minhaj, Barani, Afif and Isami.
Abdullah Qutb Shah and Abul Hasan Tana Shah
are identified as the first Qutb Shahi rulers to issue farmans in Telugu.
Addanki Gangadhara was the first poet to dedicate a Telugu work, Tapati Samvaranopakhyanam, to a Muslim Sultan, Ibrahim Qutb Shah.

rows.title: Provincial kingdoms - Bahmani Sultanate and Mahmud Gawan; Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa, Jaunpur, Kashmir

secs.t: Provincial dynasties → founder, year and capital (FIRSTs)

x: The Bahmani kingdom was founded in the Deccan, initially ruled from Gulbarga, and ended in 1527 under its last Sultan, Kalimullah.
Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah, also called Hasan Gangu, founded the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347 with Gulbarga as capital.
Jaunpur city was founded by Firoz Shah Tughlaq before the Sharqi dynasty was founded in 1394; Jaunpur fell to Bahlul Lodi in 1479.

secs.t: Rulers → titles and contributions

x: Alauddin
Hussain Shah and his son Nusrat Shah
patronised Bengali translations of the Mahabharata.
Firuz Shah
, who ruled from 1397 to 1422, was regarded as a scholar-king and the Bahmani kingdom reached peak strength during his reign.
Sikandar Butshikan destroyed temples, imposed jizya and drove out Brahmins.
Zain-ul-Abidin was called “Bud Shah”, meaning Great King, and the “Akbar of Kashmir”.

secs.t: Mahmud Gawan → office, reforms and end

x: Mahmud Gawan strengthened the centre, curtailed provincial nobles, divided the four tarafs into eight and placed forts under central commanders.
Mahmud Gawan's madrasa at Bidar was three storeys high, decorated with glazed tiles and had a huge library.
Mahmud Gawan was framed by rival nobles and executed, traditionally dated to 1481; his fall contributed to the break-up of the Bahmani Kingdom.

secs.t: Monuments → builder (Bengal, Bahmani, Jaunpur, Mandu)

x: Atala Masjid and Jama Masjid were associated with Ibrahim Shah Sharqi, while Lal Darwaza Mosque was built by Bibi Raje.
Hoshang Shah began the Jami Masjid, Mahmud Khalji completed it, and Ghiyasuddin Khalji built the Hindola Mahal.
The Jahaz Mahal at Mandu was built by
Ghiyasuddin Khalji
(JPSC 2023 key), who also built the Hindola Mahal.

secs.t: Chronicles → subject and author

x: Mirat-i-Sikandari was written by
Sikandar bin Muhammad
as a Persian history of the Gujarat Sultanate.
Mirat-i-Sikandari concerns Gujarat, Burhan-i-Maasir concerns Ahmadnagar, Riyaz-us-Salatin concerns Bengal, and Riyaz-ul-Insha contains Mahmud Gawan’s letters.
Both statements are correct (UPPSC 2023).

secs.t: Wars, conflicts and annexations

x: Exam angle: "main cause of conflict" = Raichur Doab; "who shifted to Bidar" = Ahmad Shah I.
The Raichur Doab was the main bone of contention with Vijayanagara.
Bahadur Shah annexed Malwa in 1531, attacked Chittor in 1535, was defeated by Humayun and was killed by the Portuguese at Diu in 1537.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Doab was contested in Bahmani-Vijayanagara wars, Telangana saw revolts, and the Qutb Shahi state of Golconda emerged from the Bahmani break-up.
Bidriware developed under the Bahmanis in the fourteenth century, is linked to Bidar, received a GI tag in 2006 and was included among the Prime Minister’s diplomatic gifts on 22 May 2026.

rows.title: The five Deccan Sultanates - Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmednagar, Bidar, Berar; Golconda and Andhra
sub: Group-II M1-A-47: Qutb Shahis of Golconda - Andhra under Qutb Shahi rule; Telugu patronage

secs.t: Five Deccan Sultanates → capital, founder and FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: "Berar was founded by" = Imad Shahis.
Adil Shahi was centred at Bijapur, Nizam Shahi at Ahmadnagar, Imad Shahi at Berar and Barid Shahi at Bidar.
Yusuf Adil Shah founded the Adil Shahi dynasty, Malik Ahmad the Nizam Shahi, Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk the Imad Shahi, and Sultan Quli the Qutb Shahi dynasty.

secs.t: Qutb Shahi rulers → contributions

x: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah was a Dakhni and Urdu poet who used the pen-name
Maani
Muhammad Qutb Shah used Zillullah as his pen-name, Abdullah patronised Kshetrayya, and Abul Hasan made the pact with Shivaji in 1677.
Abdullah Qutb Shah ruled with his mother Hayat Bakshi Begum and had the longest reign among the Qutb Shahi rulers.
Sultan Quli was killed in 1543; 31 years counts back to 1512, the start date some sources give for the dynasty, not 1518 (which gives 25 years).

secs.t: Bijapur and Ahmednagar persons → contributions

x: Ibrahim Adil Shah II was a Dakhni author, invoked Saraswati, received Firishta’s dedication, and married Chand Sultana, Muhammad Quli’s sister.
Malik Ambar
was an Abyssinian regent of the Nizam Shahis and resisted the Mughal emperor Jahangir.
Malik Ambar revived revenue administration on Todar Mal’s lines through survey and fixed assessment, avoided revenue farming and used Maratha guerrilla cavalry.

secs.t: Telugu patronage and literature → author

x: Addanki Gangadhara’s
Tapati Samvaranopakhyanamu
is regarded as the first Telugu poem or kavya dedicated to a Muslim ruler.
Kshetrayya was associated with Abdullah’s court, while Bhakta Ramadasu, or Kancherla Gopanna, was associated with Abul Hasan’s court.
Addanki Gangadhara wrote Tapati Samvaranopakhyanamu, Ponnaganti Telaganarya wrote Yayati Charitra, and Kandukuri Rudrakavi wrote Sugriva Vijayam.
Kandukuri Rudrakavi
wrote Sugriva Vijayam, the first Telugu Yakshagana, and received the Rentachintala agraharam.

secs.t: Qutb Shahi administration — officials → duty

x: Mir Jumla was the finance minister, the Kotwal headed city policing and also ran the mint, and the Havaldar was associated with treasuries and stables.
A Sarkar was headed by a Faujdar, a Pargana by a Tahsildar or Deshmukh, and the village had the Mukaddam as head and Kulkarni as accountant.

secs.t: Qutb Shahi revenue — sources and terms

x: Land revenue was the main source and was collected through tax farming, in which collection rights were auctioned to the highest bidder.
Dasabandhu lands paid only
one-tenth
of the produce or assessment as revenue.
The bidders in the revenue-farming auctions were called
Mustajirs
and were mostly Hindus.
Salt, betel leaf and tobacco
were state monopolies.

secs.t: Madanna and Akkanna → offices, titles and fall

x: Madanna was the Diwan or prime minister, while Akkanna was the Sar Lashkar or army chief.
Podili Linganna was the governor of the Karnatak, while Kancherla Gopanna was the tahsildar of Palvancha.
The brothers were murdered in 1686, shortly before Golconda fell to Aurangzeb in 1687, thereby weakening the state’s administration and defence.

secs.t: Hyderabad, Golconda and Bijapur monuments → builder / feature

x: Charminar is linked with the four Char Kaman gateways, Golconda fort is famous for its acoustics (handclap at the gate heard at the Bala Hisar), and the Qutb Shahi tombs at Ibrahim Bagh have onion domes on square bases with charbagh gardens.
Golconda served as the Qutb Shahi capital from Sultan Quli, Ibrahim built its high walls, and Hussain Sagar was built by Hussain Shah Wali in 1562 during Ibrahim’s reign.

secs.t: Golconda diamonds, travellers and Machilipatnam trade

x: Tavernier visited the mines during the reign of
Abdullah Qutb Shah
Diamonds were traded at Moti Darwaza and polished at Karwan.
The Dutch factory dates to 1605, the English factory to 1611, and Captain Hippon arrived in the ship Globe.
Machilipatnam was famed for
muslin and Kalamkari
, in addition to its importance as a trading centre.

secs.t: Conquests, battles and Mughal annexation

x: The correct order is Ahmadnagar’s capture in 1600, the end of the Nizam Shahis in 1633, Bijapur’s annexation in 1686 and Golconda’s annexation in 1687.
Abul Hasan Tana Shah, the last Qutb Shahi ruler, was imprisoned first at Bidar and then at
Daulatabad
, where he died in 1699; he was buried at Khuldabad.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The revival of Machilipatnam port is linked with the historical
Gilakaladindi port
, which functioned as a transshipment hub under the Golconda dynasty.
Hussain Sagar was named after Hussain Shah Wali, built under Ibrahim, and received the UNWTO designation ‘Heart of the World’ in 2012.
Murari Rao, Jagadeva Rao and Madanna
are identified as Hindus who held high office under the Qutb Shahis.

rows.title: Foundation of Vijayanagara - Harihara and Bukka, Vidyaranya; the Sangama dynasty
sub: Group-II M1-A-41: Vijayanagara Empire - Sangama, Saluva and Tuluva dynasties in the Andhra context

secs.t: Founding of Vijayanagara — year, coronation, emblem and FIRSTs

x: The
Nellore inscription
is regarded as the first inscription to call Harihara I a king; it dates his reign to 1336–1355.
The legend proceeds from the fall of Warangal and conversion in Delhi to the Deccan campaign, meeting Vidyaranya, and return to Hinduism.
The site was considered a place of valour because a hare reportedly
turned on the royal hunting dogs

secs.t: Origin theories → what they say and who backs them

x: Exam angle: APPSC treats the Kakatiya link as the correct answer.
The Kakatiya theory states that Harihara and Bukka served
Prataparudra of Warangal
before being taken to Delhi after 1323.
This is the Kampili version.
Father Heras
, Rice, S. K. Ayyangar, H. Krishna Sastri and P. B. Desai supported the Kannada or Hoysala theory.

secs.t: Places of the founding → feature — Anegondi, Vijayanagara, Hampi, Sringeri

x: Vidyaranya headed the
Sringeri Shankara Math
and is associated with the brothers' return to Hinduism.
Vijayanagara means '
City of Victory

'; it was built on the south bank of the Tungabhadra and its ruins lie at Hampi. 'City of Learning', 'City of Gold' and 'City of the Boar' are not meanings of the name (the boar, Varaha, was the royal emblem, not the city's name).

secs.t: Dynasties of Vijayanagara → span, founder, origin

x: Sangama was founded by Harihara I and Bukka I, Saluva by Saluva Narasimha, Tuluva by Vira Narasimha, and Aravidu by Tirumala Raya.
The APPSC-associated account identifies Vira Narasimha as the founder; he was crowned in 1505 after executing Immadi Narasimha.
Tirumala Raya founded the Aravidu dynasty, whose capitals included Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore.
The
Sangama
dynasty was the longest-ruling dynasty; Devaraya II was regarded as its greatest ruler and Praudha Raya as its last ruler.

secs.t: Sangama rulers → contributions — Harihara I to Devaraya I

x: Bukka I completed the city, conquered Madurai and reconciled Jains and Vaishnavas.
Irugappa
, the minister of Harihara II, built the Ganigitti Jain temple and wrote Navaratnamala.
Devaraya I built a dam and canals, fought Firuz Shah and is recorded as the first Sangama ruler to recruit Muslims into the army.
Bukka I
(1356-77) bore the title Vedamarga Pratishthapaka.

secs.t: Sangama rulers → contributions — Harihara I to Devaraya I — Bukka I — southern conquest and foreign embassy

x: Kumara Kampana
, son of Bukka I, overthrew Sambhuvaraya in 1366 and destroyed the Madurai Sultanate.
Kampana led the conquest, while General Saluva Mangu killed the Sultan and received the title ‘Parapakshi Saluva’.
Madhura Vijayam, a Sanskrit work describing the Madurai conquest, was written by
Gangadevi
, the wife of Kumara Kampana.
Devaraya I’s capture of southern Kondaveedu, including Motupalli, is recorded in the
Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam

secs.t: Devaraya II → army reforms, titles, deeds and patronage

x: Purva-Paschima Samudradhipati
was the title of Harihara I. Devaraya II was known as Gajabetekara, Praudha Devaraya and Ilanti Raikonda.
Devaraya II annexed Kondaveedu, received Sri Lankan tribute through Lakkanna Dandanayaka and repelled the Gajapatis, as recorded at Draksharama.
Devaraya II sent Mallappa Odayar to help
Rajahmundry
, as recorded in the Draksharama inscription of 1444.

secs.t: Scholars and poets → contributions — Sayana, Madhava, Vidyaranya, Gangadevi

x: Sayana (brother of Vidyaranya, minister of Harihara II) wrote the Vedic commentary Vedartha Prakasha; Vidyaranya wrote the Vidyaranya Kalajnana; Nachana Somana, patronised by the first two Sangama kings, wrote Uttara Harivamsam.
The Vedic commentaries were produced under Bukka Raya I and continued under Harihara II, during whose reign Sayana served as minister.

secs.t: Books → authors — modern histories and sources

x: Kampili and Vijayanagara was written by Nelaturi Venkataramanaiah, not Robert Sewell.
Robert Sewell’s A Forgotten Empire: Vijayanagar is an English translation of the Portuguese accounts of Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz.
Ferishta was a Persian chronicler of the Deccan sultans and provides the Bahmani perspective on the wars.
Rayavachakam is by Sthanapati.

secs.t: Foreign travellers → reign

x: Abdur Razzaq described the open diamond bazaars, the large number of ports and the taxation of prostitution.
Nicolo Conti’s visit is dated 1420–21, during Devaraya I, although an APPSC association places him under Devaraya II.
Abdur Razzaq was the Persian envoy of Shah Rukh and visited in 1443 under Devaraya II.

secs.t: Vijayanagara-Bahmani conflicts → battles — Raichur doab, Mudgal, Goa

x: The Raichur Doab, or Raichur Antarvedi, lies between the
Krishna and Tungabhadra
rivers and was the main cause of the recurring wars.
The 1358 Mudgal conflict occurred under Bukka I, who took Mudgal; it is noted as the first Indian war involving artillery, followed by a truce intended to spare civilians.
The correct sequence is Mudgal in 1358, Goa’s loss in 1472, the capture of Gulbarga in 1523, and Talikota in 1565.

secs.t: Saluva Narasimha → end of the Sangamas, the first usurpation

x: Saluva Narasimha was lord of Chandragiri.
The Saluva clan came from Kalyana and Saluva Mangu served Kumara Kampana.
Annamacharya (1408–1503) was a contemporary of
Saluva Narasimha
and is also placed in his court.
Jaimini Bharatam was written by Pillalamarri Pinaveerabhadra and dedicated to Saluva Narasimha.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The copper plates relate to Devaraya I’s coronation, use Sanskrit, Kannada and Nagari, record the grant and renamed village, and contain a full Sangama genealogy.
Udayagiri, Kondaveedu, Penukonda and Chandragiri
are identified as places linking the empire with Andhra Pradesh.
Nicolo Conti came under Devaraya I/II, Abdur Razzaq under Devaraya II (1443) and Domingo Paes under Krishnadevaraya.

rows.title: Saluva and Tuluva dynasties; Krishnadevaraya - conquests, Amuktamalyada, the Ashtadiggajas
sub: Group-II M1-A-42: Krishnadevaraya - conquests in Andhra, Amuktamalyada, Bhuvana Vijayam and the Ashtadiggajas

secs.t: Saluva Narasimha → first usurpation (1485) and rule

x: Saluva Narasimha seized the throne in 1485, an event described as the first usurpation.
Nuniz described Virupaksha II as a drunkard, while Praudha Raya was considered worthless; their weakness contributed to the crisis of the kingdom.
Saluva Narasimha ruled from 1485 to 1491 and shifted the capital from Kalyanapuram to Chandragiri.

secs.t: Tuluva dynasty → origin, second usurpation (1505) and succession

x: The Tuluva dynasty was named after
Tulunadu
, identified with the Mysore region.
Timmaraju was the progenitor, and Kannada was the mother tongue.
Tuluva Narasa Nayaka
, a Saluva general, was the real ruler under Immadi Narasimha.
Vira Narasimha established Tuluva rule after killing Immadi Narasimha at Penugonda in 1505.
The order was Vira Narasimha, Krishnadevaraya, Achyutaraya and Sadasiva.

secs.t: Krishnadevaraya → accession and campaigns (1509-1523)

x: During the
Diwani or Kovilkonda campaign
of 1509–10, the Bahmani jihad was crushed and Yusuf Adil Khan was killed.
After taking Raichur and freeing Sultan Mahmud Shah from Ali Barid, Krishnadevaraya acquired the title Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya.
The sequence is coronation in 1509, Ummattur in 1512–13, Udayagiri in 1513–14, and Raichur in 1520.

secs.t: Kalinga campaign → forts, victory pillars and temple grants (1513-1519)

x: Saluva Timmarusu
, popularly known as Appaji, served as the Prime Minister of Krishnadevaraya.
Krishnadevaraya brought the
Balakrishna idol
from Udayagiri to Hampi, where the Krishna temple was built for it.
Saluva Timmarusu helped capture Kondaveedu by splitting the army of Veerabhadra Gajapati.
Victory pillars were erected at
Potnuru and Simhachalam
after the Kalinga campaign.

secs.t: Relations with the Portuguese → Almeida, Albuquerque, Goa and the horse trade

x: Vira Narasimha allied with Viceroy
Francisco de Almeida
for horses and military training.
Krishnadevaraya backed Albuquerque's capture of Goa through the envoy
Luis
Krishnadevaraya received horses and training and permitted the Portuguese to build a fort at Bhatkal.
João de Castro
made peace after the defeat of Martin de Souza, whose actions had included damaging temples.

secs.t: Krishnadevaraya → titles and towns founded

x: Nagalapuram was named after Krishnadevaraya's mother Nagalamba.
Hospet, or
Tirumaladevi
pattana, was named after Krishnadevaraya's queen Tirumaladevi.
Andhra Bhoja, Sahiti Samarangana Sarvabhauma and Kannada Rajya Rama Ramana were titles of Krishnadevaraya.

secs.t: Krishnadevaraya's works → language — Amuktamalyada and the Sanskrit works — Amuktamalyada

x: Amuktamalyada means “
one who offers the garland she has worn
,” referring to the devotional story associated with Goda Devi or Andal.
The work deals with Goda Devi’s marriage to Ranganatha, includes Yamunacharya Charitra and Maladasari Katha, and gives political advice.
The famous expression praising Telugu among regional languages occurs in the preface to
Amuktamalyada

secs.t: Krishnadevaraya's works → language — Amuktamalyada and the Sanskrit works — Other works

x: Usha Parinayam is among the Sanskrit works attributed to Krishnadevaraya.
Madalasa Charita, Rasamanjari and Jnana Chintamani are Sanskrit works of Krishnadevaraya, so pairs 1-3 are correct.
Jambavati Kalyanam is a
Sanskrit
drama (APPSC G2 2019).

secs.t: Ashtadiggajas → works and titles — Bhuvana Vijayam

x: Vasucharitra, associated with Ramarajabhushana, was dedicated to
Tirumala Raya
Krishnadevaraya personally fixed the Gandapenderam anklet on Allasani Peddana's foot.
Bhuvana Vijayam was the court hall where the
Ashtadiggajas met
The Tippalur inscription calls the Ashtadiggajas a
Kavula Samstha
, or institution of poets.
Allasani Peddana wrote Manucharitramu and was titled Andhra Kavita Pitamaha (APPSC G2 2019).

secs.t: Foreign accounts → Krishnadevaraya's reign — Paes, Barbosa, Nuniz, Babur

x: Barbosa
also visited the court of Krishnadevaraya; Domingo Paes described the Bhuvana Vijayam or House of Victory and the king.
Bhuvana Vijayam is identified as the
House of Victory
and formed part of the royal courtly setting described by travellers.
Domingo Paes described the
palace, festivals, army and markets
along with Bhuvana Vijayam.

secs.t: Achyutaraya and Sadasivaraya → Rama Raya's regency and Talikota (1565)

x: Rama Raya killed Salakam Tirumala in 1543, made Sadasiva a figurehead king, was beheaded at Talikota in 1565, and thereafter Sadasiva and Tirumala fled to Penukonda.
Rama Raya used divide and rule against the
Deccan Sultanates
, which eventually united against him.
The battle of Talikota, also called Rakshasi-Tangadi or Bannihatti, took place in
January 1565

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The first usurpation was by Saluva Narasimha in 1485, the second by Vira Narasimha in 1505, and Sadasiva was the last Tuluva ruler.
The Kalinga campaign is associated with the forts of
Udayagiri, Kondaveedu and Kondapalli
Tirumala has bronze statues of
Krishnadevaraya and his queens
Pedaganjam and Chinaganjam were known for salt, and the salt pans at Pedaganjam were taxed.

rows.title: Vijayanagara administration - Nayankara and Ayagar systems, amaram tenure, revenue and army
sub: Group-II M1-A-43: Vijayanagara administration in Andhra - Nayankara and Ayagar systems, amaram tenure

secs.t: Central administration → officers and departments (Kandachara, Athavane)

x: The king was the supreme head, commander and fountain of justice, but he was expected to act within Dharma and in consultation with ministers.
Athavane, also called Attavana, dealt with revenue and finance.
Kandachara or Kandacharya dealt with military affairs, including the standing army.
Rayavachakam records nine departments, and each department was headed by a Samprati.

secs.t: Amuktamalyada → Krishnadevaraya's political ideas

x: Amuktamalyada advises improving harbours, encouraging imports and treating foreign merchants generously.
The work combines devotion and practical statecraft, stresses Dharma and protection of subjects, and recommends tanks and irrigation.
Amuktamalyada records the genealogy of the dynasty, but it does not record Krishnadevaraya’s campaigns.
Amuktamalyada advises that
Brahmins
should command forts.

secs.t: Provincial administration → units, heads and governors' powers

x: A province was headed by a prince or Durgadhipati, a Nadu by the Nadagauda and Parupatyagar, a Sthala by the Reddi, Gauda or Sthalakaranam, and a village by the Ayagars.
Brahmins were deliberately posted as Dannayakas in border provinces, giving them an important military and administrative role.
Aravidu inscriptions divide the Udayagiri, Penukonda and Hampi Rajyams into
Vanitas

secs.t: Nayankara system → amaram terms, obligations and scale

x: Amaram
was land granted to military chiefs, who were known as Amaranayakas, Nayaks, Palaiyagars or Poligars.
The amaranayakas paid tribute, maintained troops, horses and elephants, and attended court at Mahanavami with gifts.
Amaranayakas collected taxes, maintained law and order, and administered justice within their amarams.
Durgadayam
was collected in the Amara gramalu to meet the expenses of the army.

secs.t: Palegars → from amara-nayakas to the poligars of Rayalaseema

x: The
Amara-nayakas
became the Palegars or Poligars when central authority weakened after the Battle of Talikota.
After Talikota they became hereditary local rulers.
The poligar chiefs of Rayalaseema operated under the nominal authority of
the Nizam of Hyderabad
Military officer Campbell
assisted Thomas Munro in suppressing the poligars of Rayalaseema.

secs.t: Ayagar system → village functionaries, payment and officers

x: Karanam was the accountant, Reddi the village head, Talari the watchman and Purohita the priest.
Ayagars received tax-free Manyam lands, also called Mirasi, Bhattu Vrutti or Jatikattu Manyalu, along with a share of the harvest called Mera.
The Talari had no salary and instead collected Merulu, or gifts in grain, from farmers and merchants at harvest.

secs.t: Land revenue → terms, land classes and share of produce

x: Land tax
constituted the main source of revenue in the Vijayanagara Empire.
Bagayati denoted garden land.
Neerarambamu, also called Magani, was irrigated land and was generally taxed in grain at higher rates.
Adhuvanatantram referred to land-tax documents, rates varied with land quality, and private workshop owners paid an industries tax.

secs.t: Tax terms → meaning, and Krishnadevaraya's tax policy — Tax terms

x: Putrodaya kanuka was a tax on the birth of a son.
Badige was associated with sheep sales.
Siddhaya meant a fixed levy.
The sequence is the remission in some regions by Saluva Narasimha, the recorded attribution to Vira Narasimha, and the empire-wide abolition under Krishnadevaraya.
Meruka was a tax on the
sale and purchase of goods
(APPSC G2 2011 key).

secs.t: Tax terms → meaning, and Krishnadevaraya's tax policy — Tax policy

x: Exam angle: a single-term question ("Meruka was a tax on") or a four-pair match of the tax terms.
The right to collect market taxes was
auctioned to Sunkandarlu

secs.t: Army → wings, firearms, forts and cavalry

x: Nuniz counted approximately 600,000 troops among the Amara-nayaka levies under Achyutaraya.
The Vijayanagara army included several social groups, including Chenchus, Koyas, Boyas and Muslim troops.
Saluva Narasimha
introduced the Samugaris, or gunmen.
The four types of forts were
Giri, Sthala, Jala and Vana
forts.
Horses came via the west-coast ports Goa, Honnavar and Bhatkal.

secs.t: Judicial and police terms → meaning — pradvivaka and the Kavali system

x: Death was prescribed for treason, mutilation for theft, and Brahmins received life imprisonment instead of the death penalty.
Conti
recorded that divine ordeals were used as a means of proof in the judicial system.
The Kavali Daru maintained law and order at the Sthala level, the Peta Kavalidaru watched the towns, and the Talari policed the village.

secs.t: Nayankara compared → Kakatiya, Vijayanagara and Mughal mansabdari

x: The Kakatiya system involved 75 or 77 Nayakas holding mandalams and forts; the Vijayanagara system involved amaram fiefs and about 200 Nayakas; Mughal mansabdars held zat and sawar ranks.
Kakatiya Nayakas retained a share of revenue, held a fort and a quarter of the land, and paid a fixed sum.
After 1565, semi-independent Nayaka kingdoms emerged and some became independent, including those of Madurai, Tanjore and Keladi.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The inscriptions illustrate how revenue assignments and temple grants operated through the transfer of Kaanika taxes and related land grants.
The Nayankara system enabled the empire to maintain a huge army cheaply, but it also facilitated the rise of Nayaka kingdoms that broke away after Talikota.
Burton Stein characterised Vijayanagara as a segmentary state, whereas Nilakanta Sastri described it as a military administration.

rows.title: Vijayanagara society, economy and trade; accounts of Nicolo Conti, Abdur Razzak, Domingo Paes, Nuniz
sub: Group-II M1-A-44: Vijayanagara society, economy and religion in Andhradesa; foreign travellers' accounts

secs.t: Foreign travellers → country, ruler visited and observations

x: Exam angle: questions pair a traveller with a fact (Sati, 300 ports, "large as Rome").
All four statements occur in accounts attributed to Abdur Razzaq: the city’s grandeur, Mahanavami celebrations, the prostitution tax and the absence of purdah.
Robert Sewell translated the accounts of Paes and Nuniz and authored A Forgotten Empire in 1900.
Nicolo de Conti visited in 1420–21, Abdur Razzaq in 1443–44, Domingo Paes in 1520–22 and Caesar Frederick in 1567.
Abdur Razzaq
, Shah Rukh's envoy to Deva Raya II (1443), wrote that the king had 300 ports in his dominions, each equal to Calicut. ⚠ APPSC key said Duarte Barbosa (G2 2019).

secs.t: Who recorded it → fact → traveller

x: Abdur Razzaq
recorded the practice of Sati.
Barbosa recorded that
Christians, Jews and Muslims
lived without interference, indicating a measure of religious tolerance.
Domingo Paes
recorded the sacrifice of 250 buffaloes and 400 goats on the final day of the Mahanavami festival.

secs.t: Castes, communities and social divisions → occupation

x: The society is described as having four varnas and about eighteen castes; Brahmins included priests and officials, while many Sudras became amaranayakas.
Vira Panchalas were artisans; Padmasalis and Kaikkolars were weavers; Settis were traders.
The right-hand and left-hand groupings began during
Chola times
and continued under the Vijayanagara Empire.
Vaidikulu were Brahmin priests, Niyogulu were Brahmin administrators, Vipravinodins were Brahmin performers, and some Shudras became Amaranayakas.

secs.t: Women and social customs → terms and poetesses

x: Devadasis were temple dancers trained in music and dance; many were land-owning and socially respected.
Sati was mainly found among
royal, elite and warrior families
, although it was recorded by several foreign visitors.
Accounts describe the absence of strict purdah and women serving as bodyguards, wrestlers, accountants and judges; both kanyasulkam and dowry existed.

secs.t: Rulers → faith, patronage and religious tolerance

x: Venkatapati Raya II
allowed a church at Chandragiri and extended protection to the Jesuit mission.
Chevvappa Nayaka
permitted the Portuguese to build a church in Thanjavur.
From
Venkatapati II
onward, Venkateswara replaced Virupaksha as the main deity.
Tirupati rose under Saluva Narasimha, Achyutaraya was crowned at Tirumala, and Ahobilam and Kadiri had Narasimha temples.

secs.t: Places → religious centres, ports and production centres

x: Srisailam, Tripurantakam and Srikalahasti
were the Shaiva centres.
Draksharama and Amaravati
were centres where Smarta Shaivism was followed.
The main seat of Vasavi Kanyaka Parameswari is Penugonda in West Godavari (APPSC G2 2019 key).
Gutti and Rayadurg supplied silk, Venkatagiri supplied zari, and diamonds from Kurnool and Anantapur were polished at Vajrakarur.

secs.t: Festivals and performing arts → features

x: The Mahanavami Dibba, on which the Dasara celebrations were held, was built by
Krishnadevaraya
Vasantotsava appears in Jambavati Parinayam.
Burrakatha consists of a lead narrator who plays the burra and is accompanied by
two vantalu or assistants
Tholu Bommalata is leather shadow-puppetry, is mentioned in Panditaradhya Charitra, and later gave rise to Surabhi theatre.

secs.t: Economy — revenue, tanks, temple finance, trade goods and guilds

x: Bukka I is associated with the Siruveru tank near Penukonda.
Devadaya villages and land endowments supported temples, while Sri Bhandara was the temple treasury kept by the Karanam.
Devaraya I belonged to a period earlier than the Portuguese arrival in India in 1498; therefore, crediting them with his dam is chronologically inconsistent.
The
Porumamilla inscription
(Kadapa), issued by Bhaskara Mantri and recording the Anantasagaram tank (1369, Bukka I's time), gives the 12 rules for building a tank (APPSC G2 2012, 2019).

secs.t: Coins → metal, value and symbol

x: The panam, or fanam, was equal to
one-tenth of a pratapa
and was the most used coin.
Hanuman appears on the coins of Harihara and Bukka, Venkateswara and Balakrishna on Krishnadevaraya's, Garuda on Achyutaraya's and Varaha on Tirumala Raya's.
Legends were in Devanagari; the varaha (pagoda) was the largest gold coin; Tar and Pesado were silver; Jital and Kasu were copper.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Foreign accounts are a major source for studying Vijayanagara's economy and society, though they are used alongside works such as Amuktamalyada and Rayavachakam.
Amuktamalyada and Rayavachakam
are mentioned alongside foreign accounts as significant sources for understanding Vijayanagara history.
The accounts differ in details concerning
Sati and the number of ports
, which is why their observations require careful comparison.

rows.title: Vijayanagara art and architecture - Hampi, gopurams, kalyana mandapa, Vitthala temple, painting
sub: Group-II M1-A-45: Vijayanagara art and architecture in Andhra - Lepakshi, Tadipatri, Ahobilam, Srisailam, Tirupati

secs.t: Vijayanagara style — features, terms and scholars

x: Raya gopuram is the towering gateway; kalyana mandapa is the marriage hall; Amman shrine is the goddess's separate shrine; composite pillars carry yalis and charging horses with riders.
The Vijayanagara period introduced secular buildings within temple premises, while also showing Indo-Islamic influence in structures such as the Lotus Mahal and Huzur Daftar.

secs.t: Rulers and patrons → monuments built

x: The Nayaka brothers
Virupanna and Veeranna of Penukonda
built the Lepakshi temple.

secs.t: Hampi temples → popular name, deity and patron

x: Virupaksha is associated with Pampapati, Vitthala with Saptaswara Devalayam, Krishna with the Bala Krishna idol from Udayagiri, and Achyutaraya with the Tiruvengalanatha temple.
The Vitthala Temple is Vaishnava, contains musical pillars and a stone chariot, and was begun under Devaraya II and expanded by Krishnadevaraya.
The Vittala stone chariot appears on the reverse of the
note of the Mahatma Gandhi New Series.

secs.t: Hampi secular structures → feature and style

x: The Lotus Mahal is also called
Chitrangi or Padma Mahal
The Lotus Mahal is lotus-shaped with domes in Indo-Islamic (Indo-Arabic) style.
Huzur Daftar or Diwan Khana was a council chamber in Indo-Persian style and had 40 pillars.
Krishnadevaraya built the Mahanavami Dibba for the Mahanavami/Dasara festival, which is why it is also called the Dasara Dibba.

secs.t: Lepakshi — location, builders and features

x: Exam angle: "stone bull / hanging pillar / frescoes" → Lepakshi.
The temple stands on Kurma Shailam.
The temple belongs approximately to the 1530s and is associated with Achyutaraya's reign.
The Naga linga is carved from a single boulder and is sheltered by a seven-hooded serpent.

secs.t: Painting — centres, themes, technique and source

x: The ceilings depict Ramayana and Mahabharata themes, while the walls contain Shiva-related subjects including Parvati Parinayamu, Tripurasura Samharam, Shiva Tandavam, Bhikshatana and Dakshinamurti.
The Lepakshi murals are regarded as the finest or peak expression of the
Vijayanagara school
of painting.
Mineral pigments were applied on lime plaster, with bold dark outlines, flat colours, elongated figures and energetic movement.

secs.t: Andhra temples → location, deity and additions

x: Krishnadevaraya renovated Srikalahasti, and its gali gopuram collapsed in 2010.
Shanti Lingayya constructed the sculptured prakaram at Srisailam during the reign of Krishnadevaraya.
Krishnadevaraya was associated with the Tirumala Kalyana mandapam, outer prakara and bronze statues of himself with Chinnadevi and Tirumaladevi.
Krishnadevaraya renovated or endowed Srikalahasti, Simhachalam, Amaravati and Kanaka Durga at Bejawada.

secs.t: Forts, palaces and capitals after Talikota

x: Chandragiri served as the Aravidu capital under
Venkatapati Raya II
Chandragiri shows Hindu and Indo-Saracenic elements, Gooty was Aliya Rama Raya’s base, and Mir Jumla looted the idols of Gandikota in 1657.
Udayagiri in Nellore was built by the Vijayanagara rulers, later taken by Golconda, and is associated with the Panchaloha cannon.

secs.t: Performing arts and music under Vijayanagara

x: Tolu Bommalata was the chief rural entertainment.
Veedhi Bhagavatham is a street dance-drama regarded as the
forerunner of Kuchipudi
The Machupalli Kaifiyat records a Kuchipudi troupe performing before
Viranarasimharaya
Sangita Suryodaya was written by Lakminatha, identified as a court musician of Krishnadevaraya.

secs.t: Monument feature → site (quick revision)

x: "gopurams better than Hampi" = Tadipatri.
The gopurams said by art critics to surpass those of Hampi's Vittala temple are at Tadipatri, not Chandragiri.
Ubattu Shilpalu and the painting of Vatapatra Shayi are associated with
Tadipatri
Among these,
Srisailam
is noted for its four entrance gates facing the four directions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The authorship of the Hazara Rama temple is debated among Devaraya I, Devaraya II and Krishnadevaraya, while Lepakshi is variously attributed to Krishnadevaraya or Achyutaraya.
The
Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams
approved a new Kalyana mandapam at Lepakshi in May 2026.
The inscriptions were found on the 50-foot monolithic pillar of the
Somapalayam Chennakesava temple
in Annamayya district.
