rows.title: Folk culture of Andhra - Burrakatha, Harikatha, Veedhi Natakam, Oggu Katha, Tolu Bommalata
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-103

secs.t: Folk forms through the ages — periods, other names and FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: "which folk form was earlier called Jangam Katha" → Burrakatha.
Yakshaganam entertained royal courts and elites, while the leather puppet show was especially popular in rural Andhra.
Late Vijayanagara patronage produced Yakshaganas and Vachana styles.
Someshwara’s Abhilashitartha Chintamani, also known as Manasollasa, records these performances at temple festivals.

secs.t: Persons → contributions to folk performance

x: Burrakatha historical ballads draw upon events such as the
Bobbili War of 1757
, in which Vijayarama Raju of Vizianagaram sought French assistance.
Sheikh Nazar was a Burrakatha artist, received the Best Artist honour of the Andhra Nataka Akademi in 1981 and the Padma Shri in 1986, and is associated with the biography Pinjari.

secs.t: Books and works → authors

x: Jagajyothi and Navarasa Tarangini are his kavyas.
Bengal Karuvu
is associated with Sheikh Nazar.
Palakuriki Somanatha
wrote Panditaradhya Charitra.

secs.t: Harikatha and Burrakatha → form, region, instruments and use

x: Narayana Dasu fused music, story-telling, dance, philosophy and literature into Harikatha.
Burrakatha uses the
Gummata, Burra, Tambura and Ukki
, along with the characteristic chorus phrase ‘Thandana Taana’.
Burrakatha evokes
heroic and tragic rasas
through its narrative and performance style.
Burrakatha narrators communicated news, reform and nationalist messages to unlettered rural populations.

secs.t: Tolu Bommalata, Kathas and Bhagavata Mela → performers, region and format — Tolu Bommalata

x: Tolu Bommalata uses thin, translucent leather figures painted on both sides.
Tolu Bommalata combines leather shadow figures, sung verses and dialogue, movable puppet heads, and themes drawn from major Hindu epics and Puranic traditions.
Shadow puppetry is also found in Odisha, Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu.
Govinda Rao put live actors in place of puppets in Keechaka Vadham.

secs.t: Tolu Bommalata, Kathas and Bhagavata Mela → performers, region and format — Other narrative forms

x: Bhagavatulu are mostly Yadavas, perform Krishna Leelas and are famous in Rayalaseema.
Asadi Katha
is performed by the Asadi sub-caste of Madigas and narrates the story of Ellamma.
Dance around a pillar with Sita-Rama-Lakshmana idols is associated with Bhagavatulu, not Harikatha.
Oggu Katha is the Golla/Kuruma ballad of Telangana sung to the oggu drum.

secs.t: Tolu Bommalata, Kathas and Bhagavata Mela → performers, region and format — Yakshaganam and Kuchipudi

x: Exam angle: Kuchipudi <- Bhagavata Mela <- Siddhendra Yogi; Tana Shah grant.
Andhra Yakshaganam is performed in Telugu, uses elaborate costumes and presents epic or Puranic stories.
Kuchipudi is named after Kuchipudi village in
Krishna district
Kuchipudi is traditionally associated with Siddhendra Yogi and grew out of the Bhagavata Mela dance-drama tradition.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All four statements describe identified challenges: inadequate patronage, only three or four performances annually in some cases, youth disinterest and weak welfare support for veteran artists.
The Centre’s
Kala Sanskriti Vikas Yojana
supports folk festivals.
Folk performance was a living expression of distinct Telugu culture behind the Andhra Movement and helped carry that cultural identity to villages.

rows.title: Folk arts, festivals and fairs of Andhra Pradesh
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-103

secs.t: Folk arts — definitions, songs and FIRSTs

x: Jola patalu are
lullabies
Kolatam kirtanas are sung for
group dance
and are associated with Annamacharya.
The Gathasaptasati records couple and choir dances of rural folk.
The first folk-knowledge theory book was by Biruduraju Ramaraju; Annamacharya wrote Kolatam kirtanas.
World Folk Day is observed on
22 August

secs.t: Persons → association with arts and festivals

x: Lakumadevi was the court dancer of the Reddi king
Kumaragiri Reddy
Kumaragiri Reddy used the title Karpura Vasantarayalu, and merchant Avachi Tippayashetti headed the Sugandhabhandagara that supplied the festival.

secs.t: Kuchipudi → origin, status and vs Bharatanatyam

x: Kuchipudi village is associated with Krishna district, and the dance is among India’s eight classical forms and is regarded as a global ambassador of Indian culture.
Kuchipudi is an Andhra dance-drama tradition, while Bharatanatyam is associated with Tamil Nadu and a solo temple-dance tradition.
Tarangam is a distinctive Kuchipudi feature in which the dancer performs while
dancing on the rim of a brass plate

secs.t: Folk dances → region and feature

x: Shepherd communities perform Tappeta Gullu to
invoke rain and appease Gangamma
The origin of Dhimsa is traced to
Koraput in Odisha
, although it is strongly associated with the tribal women of the Araku and ASR region.
Dommarata = acrobatics, Lambadi = Banjara, Chekka Bhajana = wooden clappers, Keelugurram = dummy-horse dance (Guntur).

secs.t: Festivals → month, region and dynastic origin

x: Sankranti falls in January and features Gangireddulaata, Kolla Pandalu (cockfights) and Pottella Pandalu (ram fights).
Atla Taddi is a women’s festival observed during the
Ashwayuja
month.
Vasantotsavam
was the most popular festival under the Reddi kings (APPSC G2 2019 key); Kumaragiri Reddy styled himself Karpura Vasantarayalu.
Rongali Bihu is celebrated in April, Kongali Bihu in October and Bhogali Bihu in January.

secs.t: State festivals, fairs and temple towns → place

x: Lepakshi Utsav is held at Lepakshi and reflects Vijayanagara heritage; Visakha Utsav is held in Visakhapatnam, and the Kondapalli Toys Festival is to be held annually.
Medieval Tirunallu or Jataralu were held at holy sites, with Kotappakonda and Srikakulam in Krishna district cited as examples.
Gangamma Jatara is associated with Tirupati, Paidithalli Ammavaru with Vizianagaram, Mahanandi fair with Shivaratri, and Jola patalu with lullabies.

secs.t: Handicrafts and GI-tagged arts → place

x: All four pairs are correctly matched.
Farishkhani and Ashunkhani were designs of Eluru carpets that attracted attention at the
London Exhibition of 1851
Per the craft table.
Srikalahasti is known for pen or freehand Kalamkari, while the Machilipatnam-Pedana tradition is block-printed.
Lepakshi (APHDC) is the state handicrafts nodal agency.

secs.t: AP vs Telangana — crafts and markers

x: Dharmavaram sarees
are an Andhra Pradesh tradition.
The other sets contain Andhra Pradesh traditions or mixed associations.
The APPSC-GS 2022 key marks
Bidri work
as the one NOT traditional to AP; Bidri is a Hyderabad craft that came from Bidar in Karnataka.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Kondapalli Toys Festival was made annual, with this development reported in April 2026.
APHDC markets Andhra Pradesh GI crafts through Lepakshi under the theme ‘
Vocal for Local
Kolatam kirtanas
are associated with group dance in the Andhra folk-song context.

rows.title: Battle of Talikota (1565), the Aravidu dynasty and the legacy of Vijayanagara
sub: Group-II M1-A-46: Aravidu dynasty and the Battle of Talikota; the Nayaka successor states

secs.t: Talikota 1565 → date, names, place and sides

x: Sadasiva Raya was the nominal Tuluva king, while Rama Raya was his regent; Rama Raya's brothers Tirumala and Venkatadri fought with him.
Bijapur was ruled by Ali Adil Shah, Ahmadnagar by Hussain Nizam Shah, Golconda by Ibrahim Qutb Shah and Bidar by Ali Barid Shah.
Vijayanagara under Aliya Rama Raya fought the confederacy of the Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar).

secs.t: Aliya Rama Raya → regency, policy and causes of Talikota

x: In 1546-47 Rama Raya backed Ahmadnagar against Bijapur and Bidar and took the Raichur doab, and in 1557-63 he backed Bijapur and razed Ahmadnagar - playing the Sultans against each other.
The coalition is attributed to Rama Raya's diplomacy, interference, earlier attacks and sheltering of Jagadeva Rao; no Bahmani emperor created the coalition.

secs.t: Talikota → course and results

x: The battle initially saw Vijayanagara successes, followed by deceptive peace talks, a surprise attack and the withdrawal of Muslim contingents from the Vijayanagara army.
Hampi was looted for about six months, the destruction was severe but not total, and the Nayakas became autonomous.
Sadasiva and Tirumala fled to Penukonda (Chandragiri became a capital later, under Venkata II).

secs.t: Aravidu dynasty → origin, span, capitals

x: The dynasty was named after Araviti, also called Aravidu, a village in Kurnool district.

secs.t: Aravidu rulers → period and contribution — Rulers

x: Tirumala Raya
founded the Aravidu dynasty and was crowned at Penukonda in 1570.
Venkatapati Raya II, the greatest and longest-ruling Aravidu ruler, was called the
Second Krishnadevaraya
Jagga Raya was killed at Toppur; Mir Jumla later defeated Sriranga III at Vandavasi (1642).
Tirumala used Penukonda, while Venkatapati II shifted the capital first to Chandragiri and then to Vellore in 1600.

secs.t: Aravidu rulers → period and contribution — Venkatapati Raya II (1585-1614)

x: The Vilapakam inscription of 1601 gives the genealogy of the
Tuluva and Aravidu
dynasties.

Venkatapati Raya II was called the 'Second Andhra Bhoja' (and 'Second Krishnadevaraya'), Appayya Dikshita (Shaivarka Mani Dipika) was at his court, his coins bore 'Om Venkateshwaraya Namah', and he defeated Veerappa Nayaka of Madurai at Vallankota.

secs.t: Nayakas and Palegars → terms, places and the grant of Madras

x: The grant was issued through Damarla Venkatadri Nayaka to Francis Day of
the English East India Company's Machilipatnam council
Velugoti Yachama Nayaka and Raghunatha of Tanjore
won the Battle of Toppur in 1616.
Mir Jumla of Golconda
is recorded as having melted temple idols into cannon at Gandikota in 1657.

secs.t: Nayaka kingdoms → founder and contemporary ruler

x: Madurai was founded by Vishwanatha Nayaka, Tanjore by Sevappa Nayaka, Gingee by Krishnappa Nayaka and Mysore by Raja Wodeyar.
Vishwanatha's son Krishnappa Nayaka made Madurai independent c. 1565; Tirumala Nayaka ruled 1623-59.
Madurai fell to Chanda Sahib in 1739.
Chowdappa Nayaka is identified as the founder or key ruler of Ikkeri (Keladi), founded around 1500.

secs.t: Legacy → art, books and rediscovery of Hampi

x: Colin Mackenzie
surveyed and mapped the Hampi ruins in 1800 and later became the first Surveyor General of India.
Robert Sewell’s
A Forgotten Empire
, published in 1900, brought Vijayanagara history to wide notice.
Caesar Frederick
, a Venetian merchant, visited Vijayanagara in 1567 and left an eyewitness account of the ruined capital.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sadasiva Raya
, who ruled during 1542–1570, was the last ruler of the Tuluva dynasty.
The correct sequence is Talikota in 1565, Caesar Frederick’s visit in 1567, and Tirumala’s foundation of the Aravidu line and shift to Penukonda in 1570.
Caesar Frederick was a Venetian merchant who recorded an eyewitness account in 1567; Tirumala, not Caesar Frederick, founded the Aravidu line.

rows.title: Mughal Empire - Babur: Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi, Ghaghra; Tuzuk-i-Baburi

secs.t: Babur → birth, descent, career and invitations

x: Babur was descended from Timur through his father and from Chingiz Khan through his mother.
Babur’s first raid into India took place in 1519 and involved Bajaur and Bhera.
The third inviter was Rana Sanga of Mewar, not Bahadur Shah.
Babur became ruler of Farghana in 1494, experienced repeated success and failure at Samarkand, and captured Kabul in 1504.

secs.t: Panipat I (1526) → tactics, terms and FIRSTs

x: The Rumi method (araba) chained carts as a barrier for matchlockmen and guns; the elephant version is a known error.
Panipat marked the first large-scale use of field artillery in North Indian warfare.
Babur’s force of about 12,000 defeated approximately 1,00,000 troops of Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat.
Lavish distribution earned him the nickname 'Qalandar'; 'Ghazi' was the title he took after Khanwa.

secs.t: Khanwa (1527) → coalition, religious appeal, title

x: Rana Sanga’s coalition included the Afghan
Mahmud Lodi and Hasan Khan Mewati
After Khanwa Babur took the title 'Ghazi'.
Babur used trenches and barricades against the elephants of Rana Sanga.

secs.t: Babur's death and empire → extent and limits

x: At his death, Babur’s dominions extended
from Kabul and Badakhshan through Punjab, Delhi and Agra to the borders of Bihar

D is the answer because Babur set up no administrative system at all (his rule had shallow roots and the treasury was empty), so 'a fully developed administrative system' was not one of his limitations.

secs.t: Books, buildings and coins → Tuzuk-i-Baburi, gardens, mosques

x: Leyden and Erskine produced an English translation in 1826.
Ram Bagh, also called Aram Bagh, at Agra was the first Mughal garden.
The Kabuli Bagh mosque at Panipat commemorates Babur’s victory in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
Babur introduced the charbagh garden and issued silver Shahrukhi coins in the Timurid style.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Panipat I ended the rule of the Lodis, the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, and began Mughal rule in India.
The Mughals did not interfere in the Deccan during Babur’s time
Ibrahim Lodi was the last Delhi Sultan, and Panipat I was the first major field-artillery battle in North India.

rows.title: Humayun and Sher Shah Suri - Sur administration, land revenue, sarais, currency, Grand Trunk Road
sub: Group-II S1-45: Mughal Empire - Babur, Humayun, Sher Shah Suri and the Sur interregnum

secs.t: Babur → origin, memoir, tactics, buildings

x: After Panipat Babur occupied Delhi and Agra.
The Baburnama was written in Chaghatai Turkish (Persian was the Mughal court language).
The Rumi method was Ottoman.
Babur built the Kabuli Bagh Mosque at Panipat to commemorate the events of 1526.

secs.t: Humayun → accession, battles, exile, return, death

x: Humayun's initial problems included his rival brothers, the Afghans, Bahadur Shah of Gujarat-Malwa and an empty treasury.
Humayun defeated the Afghans at Dourah and drove
Mahmud Lodi
from Jaunpur.
When pressed by Humayun in Gujarat in 1535, Bahadur Shah allowed the Portuguese to fortify Diu.
The Safavid Shah Tahmasp of Persia helped him retake Kandahar and Kabul.
He fell from the stairs of the Sher Mandal library in the Purana Qila, Delhi.

secs.t: Sher Shah and the Sur successors → rise, titles, conquests

x: He took the title Sher Shah after Chausa (1539); after Kannauj (1540) he took the throne.
The remark referred to the hard-fought Battle of
Samel against Maldeo
of Marwar.
Jaita and Kumpa were associated with Maldeo of Marwar and fought with great valour against Sher Shah at Samel.
Sher Shah died in 1545 in a gunpowder explosion during the siege of
Kalinjar

secs.t: Sur administration → officers and terms

x: Sher Shah's administration included Hindus in high army posts, reflecting a practical and inclusive policy.
The pargana had a Shiqdar, Amin, Fotedar and Hindi and Persian-writing Karkuns.
Sur officers were frequently transferred, limiting the growth of local personal power and vested interests.
Statement 2 reverses the terms: dagh was horse branding and chehra/huliya the descriptive roll of soldiers.

secs.t: Sher Shah's land revenue → measurement, terms, legacy

x: Sher Shah introduced a uniform system of land measurement using the sikandari gaz, also called
gaz-i-Sikandari
Land was classified as good, middling or bad according to its productivity.
The state share was one-third of average produce (APPSC-G1 2024 key marks 'one-fourth' false).
The Qabuliyat was the peasant's deed of acceptance of the revenue demand, signed by him.

secs.t: Sher Shah's currency, roads and sarais → coins, routes, dak-chowkis

x: Sher Shah's rupiya was a silver coin weighing approximately
178 grains
Sher Shah minted pure gold and silver coins, and the monetary system continued to influence currency after the Sur dynasty ended.
The major road, also called the Grand Trunk Road, ran from Sonargaon in Bengal to the Indus.
Sadak-e-Azam was the Bengal–Indus highway; the remaining pairs reproduce the three other routes correctly.

secs.t: Sur and Humayun monuments → builder and location

x: The tomb at Sasaram is an octagonal monument surrounded by water in a tank.
Rohtas fort is in present-day Pakistan; Sasaram has Sher Shah's tomb.
Humayun's Tomb is considered
the first garden tomb of the Indian subcontinent
Sher Shah built the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque inside the Purana Qila in Delhi; Humayun began the fort and Sher Shah rebuilt it.

secs.t: Mughal-Afghan battles 1526-1576 → year, sides, result

x: Exam angle: "wrong pair" questions - Jahangir-Chausa is wrong.
The order is Panipat I (1526), Khanwa (1527), Chanderi (1528), Ghaghra (1529).
Panipat II was fought in 1556 between Akbar, represented by Bairam Khan, and Hemu.
The Battle of Haldighati in 1576, fought between Man Singh and Maharana Pratap, was
not decisive
Chausa (1539) was fought by Humayun against Sher Khan, so '
Chausa - Jahangir
' is the wrong pair (APPSC G2 2025).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sher Shah used three land classes and a one-third rate, while Akbar’s system used ten-year averages and four classes while retaining the one-third share.
Sultan Quli Qutb Shah ruled Golconda from 1518 to 1543 and was contemporary with the early Mughals and Sher Shah, while Mughal interference in the Deccan had not yet begun.

rows.title: Akbar - conquests, Rajput policy, religious policy, Ibadat Khana, Din-i-Ilahi, Sulh-i-Kul
sub: Group-II S1-46: Akbar - conquests, Rajput policy, religious policy, Mansabdari and revenue system
Group-II S1-50: Mughal religious conditions and policies

secs.t: Akbar's accession and regency → events and persons

x: Akbar was enthroned at Kalanaur in February 1556 at the age of 14.
The term refers to the period from 1560 to 1564 when
Maham Anaga and her son Adham Khan
exercised considerable influence.
At Panipat II (1556)
Hemu
was hit in the eye by an arrow and captured, ending Afghan power.

secs.t: Akbar's conquests → year and ruler opposed

x: Baz Bahadur opposed Akbar in Malwa, Rani Durgavati in Gondwana, Rana Udai Singh at Chittor, and Surjan Rai at Ranthambore.
Gondwana was conquered in 1564, Chittor in 1568, Gujarat in 1572–73 and Kabul in 1581.
Akbar's last campaign was the conquest of Khandesh in 1601, during which the Asirgarh fort was taken from Miran Bahadur.

secs.t: Rajput policy → features, marriages, mansabdars, Mewar

x: Akbar followed a twin policy of
conquest and conciliation
, accepting submission while restoring autonomy and honour in suitable cases.
In 1562, Akbar married the daughter of
Raja Bharmal of Amber
, a Kachhwaha ruler.
Raja Todarmal
was prominent in revenue administration under Akbar, while Man Singh was a leading Rajput military officer.

secs.t: Revenue systems → terms and land classes

x: One account describes the Gaz-i-Ilahi (about 82 cm) used under Zabti as
bamboo
, so C. Other sources say the bamboo item was the jarib, made of bamboo pieces joined with iron rings in place of hemp rope; either way, the material was bamboo, not copper, stone or iron.
Batai involved division of the harvested crop, Kankut estimated the standing crop, and Nasaq relied roughly on the peasant's past payments.

secs.t: Akbar's court → persons, fields and books

x: Faizi, the poet laureate, made the Persian Lilavati (a–iii); Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan, son of Bairam Khan, translated the Baburnama into Persian (b–iv); Badauni wrote the Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh (c–i); Nizamuddin Ahmad wrote the Tabaqat-i-Akbari (d–ii).
Tansen
(Ramtanu Pandey) was the court musician credited with Miyan ki Malhar and Miyan ki Todi.
Akbar's curriculum included ethics, arithmetic, agriculture, geometry, astronomy, government, medicine, logic and history.

secs.t: Religious policy → year and measure

x: Zakat was an alms tax on Muslims, ushr was a land tax on Muslims, khums represented one-fifth of war booty, and jizya was imposed on non-Muslims.
The sequence is abolition of jizya in 1564, construction of the Ibadat Khana in 1575, Mahzar in 1579 and Din-i-Ilahi in 1582.
Akbar
, in keeping with Sulh-i-Kul, issued coins with Rama and Sita and the legend 'Rama-Siya' (UPPSC 2011).

secs.t: Religious contacts → person, title, grant

x: The first Jesuit mission from Goa in 1580 was led by
Rudolf Acquaviva and Antonio Monserrate
The third Jesuit mission, sent in 1595, was under
Jerome Xavier
Hiravijaya Suri was 'Jagat Guru'.
Land granted to Guru Ram Das became associated with the growth of
Amritsar

secs.t: Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi), 1582 → features and members

x: Din-i-Ilahi or Tauhid-i-Ilahi was proclaimed as a
syncretic moral order
Din-i-Ilahi included belief in one God, reverence for the sun and fire, and avoidance of meat-eating.
Birbal
was the only Hindu member of Din-i-Ilahi.
Both statements are true, and the voluntary nature and small membership of Din-i-Ilahi explain why it did not become a mass religion.

secs.t: Orthodox reaction → Sufi orders, founders and doctrines

x: Badauni and the Naqshbandi scholar Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi criticised Akbar's religious innovations, including Din-i-Ilahi and Sulh-i-Kul.
The Naqshbandi order stressed strict adherence to Islamic law, or Sharia.
The Qadiri order is associated with Abdul Qadir Jilani and Dara Shikoh, while the Naqshbandi order was founded by Baha-ud-din Naqshband and had an orthodox Wahdat-ul-Shuhud orientation.

secs.t: Mughal emperors → education, titles and memoirs

x: Akbar
was unlettered, yet he was a great patron of learning, literature and culture.
Jahangir wrote the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri.
Jahangir gave Prince Khurram the title 'Shah Jahan'.

secs.t: Sikh Gurus, Banda Singh Bahadur and the Mughals — Guru → Mughal relation

x: Guru Arjan Dev was executed by Jahangir in 1606 for supporting the rebel prince Khusrau.
Guru Gobind Singh fought 14 wars against Aurangzeb's forces and wrote the Zafarnama, which advocated using the sword only when all other avenues failed.
The Chali Mukte, or 40 liberated ones, died defending Guru Gobind Singh at Muktsar; the event is commemorated as Maghi.

secs.t: Sikh Gurus, Banda Singh Bahadur and the Mughals — Guru Tegh Bahadur

x: Ninth Guru, born Tyag Mal (1621), Guru 1665-75; founder of Anandpur Sahib with 116 hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib; 'Hind-di-Chadar'.
Banda Singh Bahadur captured Sirhind from
Wazir Khan
in 1710 to avenge the killing of Guru Gobind Singh's younger sons.
Banda Singh Bahadur, originally Lachhman Dev, became a disciple of
Guru Gobind Singh

secs.t: Emperor-wise religious policy and Hindu nobles

x: Exam angle: the counter-intuitive answer "Aurangzeb" is the tested fact.
Shah Jahan retained many Hindu nobles, and Aurangzeb had the highest absolute number, including Marathas and Rajputs recruited during the Deccan wars.
Jahangir broadly continued Akbar's tolerant approach, but Guru Arjan Dev was executed for political reasons related to support for rebel prince Khusrau.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sulh-i-Kul and the Rajput partnership broadened support and helped turn the conquest state into a durable empire.
Mansabdari, jagirdari and Zabti
formed the core of Mughal governance for about 150 years.
The jagirdari crisis arose because too many mansabdars chased too few jagirs, which increased pressure on the peasantry.
Baisakhi is associated with the foundation of the Khalsa, not Banda Singh Bahadur’s conquest of Sirhind.

rows.title: Akbar's institutions - Mansabdari system, Todar Mal's bandobast, dahsala, zabti and other revenue systems

secs.t: Raja Todar Mal → service, office and measurement units

x: Todar Mal had earlier served
Sher Shah
and built upon Sher Shah’s survey-based system.
The jarib was made from bamboo pieces joined with iron rings, avoiding the shrinkage or stretching associated with hemp rope.
Todar Mal served as the Diwan, or finance minister, of the empire and was also counted among the Navratnas.

secs.t: Revenue systems → meaning and region

x: Zabti (measurement, cash rates) ran in the core North Indian provinces (a–iii); Batai crop-sharing in areas such as Thatta, Kabul and Kashmir (b–ii); Nasaq mainly in Bengal (c–i); assessment by number of ploughs in parts of the Deccan (d–iv).
The Bandobast system is the Dahsala (Zabti) reform of Todar Mal, introduced in 1580 (JPSC 2013).

secs.t: Revenue terms → meaning (state share, land classes, grants)

x: Polaj was cultivated every year, Parauti remained fallow for one or two years, Chachar for three or four years, and Banjar for five or more years.
Suyurghal was another name for charitable revenue-free grants like madad-i-maash; crown land whose revenue went to the treasury was khalisa.
A jagir was an assignment of the right to collect revenue in lieu of salary; it did not confer ownership of the land.

secs.t: Administrative units → officials

x: The officials associated with a Suba included the Subedar, Diwan, Bakhshi, Sadr and Qazi.

Sarkar had the faujdar (law and order) and amalguzar (revenue) (a–iii); pargana had the shiqdar, amil and qanungo (b–iv); the town had the kotwal for police and municipal order (c–i); the village had the muqaddam, patwari and chowkidar (d–ii).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The mansabdari and zabti-dahsala arrangements together provided the Mughal state with a salaried, transferable nobility and a predictable stream of cash revenue.
Mughal mansabdars combined civil and military functions, held non-hereditary ranks and were paid through jagirs.
Golconda generally took one-third, not one-half.

rows.title: Jahangir and Nur Jahan; Shah Jahan - Deccan and Central Asian policy, the war of succession
sub: Group-II S1-47: Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb - policies and consequences

secs.t: Jahangir's reign → events and years

x: Exam angle: "Which events took place under Jahangir" - Arjan Dev's execution, Mewar's submission and the English arrival are correct; annexation of Kabul-Kandahar is the trap.
Akbar's eldest son Salim was named after Sheikh Salim Chishti and assumed the title
Nur-ud-din Muhammad Jahangir
when he was crowned in 1605.
Nur Jahan's backing of Shahryar provoked Khurram's revolt (1622-26), not Khusrau's revolt of 1606.
Guru Arjan Dev was executed in 1606, Mewar submitted in 1615 and Hawkins (1608) and Roe (1615-19) came during Jahangir's reign, so 1, 2 and 3 are correct (APPSC G1 2022).

secs.t: European envoys → sender and outcome

x: Portuguese intrigue blocked Hawkins's trade farman and he left in 1611; trading rights came later through Sir Thomas Roe (1615-19).
Captain Best's victory over the Portuguese in 1612 preceded the establishment of the English factory at Surat in 1613.
Sir Thomas Roe's embassy resulted in English rights to trade and establish factories.

secs.t: Nur Jahan and the junta → members, titles, FIRSTs

x: Ghiyas Beg was Nur Jahan's father and Jahangir's diwan; Asaf Khan was her brother and Mumtaz's father; Khurram married Arjumand; Nur Jahan's name appeared on coins and farmans.
Mumtaz Mahal was born Arjumand Banu Begum, was the daughter of Asaf Khan (Nur Jahan's brother), married Prince Khurram in 1612, and is entombed in the Taj Mahal.

secs.t: Mughal royal family → relations, titles, fate

x: Shah Jahan was deposed in 1658, confined in Agra Fort and cared for by Jahanara.
Mehrunnisa, widow of Sher Afghan, married Jahangir in 1611, received the title Nur Jahan and was later known as Padshah Begum.
Mumtaz Mahal, born Arjumand Banu Begum, was Asaf Khan's daughter and Shah Jahan's queen, and she is entombed in the Taj Mahal.

secs.t: Shah Jahan's reign → events, monuments and books

x: The Deccan governor
Khan Jahan Lodi
sought shelter with the Nizam Shah.
Shah Jahan's policy was somewhat more orthodox, including the destruction of some new temples, but many Hindu nobles remained in service.
Shah Jahan was crowned at Agra in 1628, faced the stated revolts, and is associated with major architectural works and the Peacock Throne in the Diwan-i-Khas.

secs.t: Deccan policy → treaties and annexations

x: The Nizam Shahi state of Ahmadnagar was extinguished and annexed under Shah Jahan in 1636; 1687 is the annexation of Golconda.
Sambhaji was captured and executed in 1689; Rajaram continued resistance from Jinji, followed by Tarabai, while Shahu was later released by Bahadur Shah I.
The prolonged war against the Marathas proved unwinnable, drained the Mughal treasury and continued until Aurangzeb's death in the Deccan in 1707.
The phases were 1658–68 recovery of Bijapur territory, 1668–84 alliances against the Marathas, 1686–87 annexation, and 1687–1707 war against the Marathas.

secs.t: Central Asian policy → Kandahar and Balkh campaigns

x: The Persian governor
Ali Mardan Khan
surrendered Kandahar to Shah Jahan.
The Balkh-Badakhshan campaign was commanded first by Murad Bakhsh and later by Aurangzeb, not Dara Shikoh.
Aurangzeb's sieges in 1649 and 1652 and Dara Shikoh's siege in 1653 all failed; Kandahar was thereafter lost for good.

secs.t: War of succession → princes, battles, fate

x: Exam angle: chronology - Shuja near Banaras, then Dharmat, then Samugarh, then Deorai.

At Bahadurgarh near Banaras, Dara's son Sulaiman Shikoh beat Shuja (a–ii); at Dharmat near Ujjain, Aurangzeb and Murad beat Jaswant Singh and Qasim Khan (b–i); Samugarh near Agra was the decisive defeat of Dara (c–iv); at Khajwa Aurangzeb beat Shuja (d–iii).

Dara was betrayed by Malik Jiwan of Dadar, executed in 1659 and buried in Humayun's Tomb (a–iii); Murad was imprisoned in Gwalior and executed in 1661 (b–iv); Shuja fled to Arakan (c–i); Shah Jahan was confined in Agra Fort, nursed by Jahanara, till his death in 1666 (d–ii).

secs.t: Revolts against Aurangzeb → region and leader

x: The Jats were associated with Mathura and Gokula; the Satnamis with Narnaul; the Sikhs with Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution; and the Rajputs with Marwar, Mewar and Durgadas Rathore.
The Afghan revolt involved the
Yusufzai and Afridi
tribes of the north-west.
Gokula led the Jat revolt in the
Mathura
region in 1669.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Jahangir–Shah Jahan era is regarded as the Mughal high noon, and the 1636 treaties made the Deccan sultanates tributaries, preparing the way for later annexations.
Jahangir's envoy to Golconda was Mir Makki; Mir Jumla is linked with Aurangzeb's 1656 attack on Golconda.
Aurangzeb's Deccan wars, alienation of the Rajputs and the jagir crisis contributed to the later decline of the Mughal Empire.

rows.title: Aurangzeb - religious policy, Deccan policy; Rajput, Jat, Satnami, Sikh and Maratha resistance

secs.t: Aurangzeb → titles, coronations and FIRSTs

x: Aurangzeb had a hurried first coronation in 1658 after Samugarh and a grand second coronation in 1659 after Deorai.
Roshanara was made Padshah Begum, Jahanara was honoured as Sahibat-uz-Zamani, and Alamgir means World Conqueror.
The
Child's War
of 1686–90 was the first conflict between the English and a Mughal emperor under Aurangzeb.

secs.t: Religious policy → taxes, measures and terms

x: Exam angle: identify the tax on non-Muslims (Jizya vs Zakat, Ushr, Khums).
Aurangzeb reimposed jizya in 1679, banned Navroz, banned music at court and had the Fatawa-i-Alamgiri compiled.
Zawabit were secular regulations issued by the emperor in addition to the provisions of Sharia.
The share of Hindu nobles rose to about 31.6 per cent during 1679–1707
, with many Marathas included.

secs.t: Revolts → leader and region (Jat, Satnami, Rajput)

x: Gokula led the 1669 Jat revolt at Mathura, Rajaram plundered Akbar's tomb, Churaman built Jat power, and the Satnami revolt occurred at Narnaul.
Gokula led the 1669 Jat peasant revolt in the Mathura region, particularly at Tilpat, against
heavy revenue demands
The clumsy handling of Marwar and Mewar broke the Rajput alliance that had been a pillar of Akbar's empire and cost the Mughals considerable influence.

secs.t: Golconda conquest → persons and dates

x: Abdullah Pani was the traitor who opened the gates of Golconda.
The 27-year Deccan war drained the Mughal treasury and was therefore called the 'Deccan Ulcer', in comparison with Napoleon's Spanish Ulcer.
Abul Hasan Qutb Shah, also known as Tana Shah, was Golconda's last ruler and the state became the 21st suba after conquest.

secs.t: Maratha conflict and last years → events and places

x: During his 1666 visit to Agra, Shivaji was insulted and placed under house arrest, from which he escaped in fruit baskets.
Aurangzeb died in 1707 at
Ahmednagar
Aurangzeb was buried in a simple grave at
Khuldabad, near Aurangabad
Shivaji's coronation as Chhatrapati took place at
Raigad

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Golconda fell to Aurangzeb in 1687 and its last ruler Abul Hasan Qutb Shah (Tana Shah) was imprisoned, which ended Qutb Shahi rule over Andhra; Golconda became the 21st Mughal suba.
The conventional criticism refers to the Deccan ulcer and Rajput alienation, while the revisionist view highlights the increased presence of Hindu nobles under Aurangzeb.

rows.title: Mughal administration - mansab (zat and sawar), jagirdari system and the jagirdari crisis
sub: Group-II S1-48: Mughal administration - mansabdari, jagirdari, zamindari and provincial set-up

secs.t: Mansabdari system → introduction, purpose and PYQ features

x: Exam angle: statement sets on "hereditary?", "introduced by Akbar?", "three classes?", "civil officers also mansabdars?".
Exam angle: the system served both army recruitment and revenue/civil administration (BPSC 2019 - "more than one").
Akbar’s mansab ranks ranged from 10 to 10,000, the highest were reserved for princes, and the decimal pattern had Central Asian or Mongol origins.

secs.t: Mansab terms → meaning (zat, sawar, classes)

x: First class had sawar equal to zat, second class had sawar equal to half of zat, and third class had sawar less than half of zat.
Zat represented the mansabdar’s personal rank, status, salary and prestige; sawar indicated the number of cavalrymen to be maintained.
The stated norm required every 10 sawars to bring 20 horses.

secs.t: Emperors → changes in the mansab system

x: Jahangir
introduced du-aspa sih-aspa, under which selected mansabdars maintained additional cavalry without a corresponding increase in zat.
Aurangzeb
introduced mashrut, a temporary increase in the sawar rank connected with a specific assignment.
Under Shah Jahan, a half-yield jagir was called shashmaha and a quarter-yield jagir sihmaha.
Jama represented the estimated revenue, whereas hasil represented the actual yield.

secs.t: Army components and musters → terms

x: Ahadis were gentlemen troopers recruited and paid directly by the emperor.
The Mughal army was not composed exclusively of ahadis.
Dagh was the branding of horses to prevent substitution.
Periodic military musters were conducted under the Mir Bakhshi.

secs.t: Central officials → functions (incl. espionage)

x: The
Mir Bakhshi
headed military and intelligence affairs, supervised recruitment, promotion, pay and musters, and presented candidates to the emperor.
Although the Wakil had traditionally been the chief adviser or regent, the office became largely
symbolic
under Akbar.
Waqia-navis, khufia-navis and harkaras formed complementary channels, intelligence came under the Mir Bakhshi, and Sher Shah had earlier operated an efficient espionage system.

secs.t: Provincial units → officials (ascending order)

x: The administrative order from the lowest to the highest level was village, pargana, sarkar and subah.
A Chakla was a group of parganas placed between the pargana and sarkar levels.
Akbar had 12 subahs in 1580, 15 by the end of his reign, and Aurangzeb had 21, with Golconda as the twenty-first.
The
Shiqdar
performed military and police functions at the pargana level.

secs.t: Jagir types → features; jagirdar vs zamindar

x: A Tankhwah jagir was assigned in lieu of salary, a Watan jagir was hereditary and retained in the homeland, Mashrut was conditional, and Altamgha was a perpetual grant.
Jagirs were revenue assignments in lieu of
salary and military service
; they carried no judicial or police duties (UPSC 2019 key: a statement linking jagirs to judicial/police duties is wrong).

secs.t: Jagir transfers and jagirdari crisis → causes and historians

x: Frequent transfers, usually every three to four years, were intended to prevent mansabdars from establishing local bases and becoming independent feudal lords.
Under Aurangzeb, the number of mansabdars increased, profitable jagirs became scarce, and peasants were subjected to intensified extraction.

Satish Chandra explained the crisis through shortage of jagirs relative to claimants; Irfan Habib stressed agrarian exploitation and revolts; Athar Ali highlighted the influx of Deccani and Maratha nobles.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The mansab-jagir system bound the Mughal nobility to the emperor and helped maintain imperial control over them.
The breakdown of
the jagirdari system
, known as the jagirdari crisis, is a core explanation of Mughal decline.
The British ICS was purely civil and cash-paid, whereas Mughal mansabdars performed mixed civil-military duties and were paid through jagirs.

rows.title: Mughal provincial and local administration; the mansabdari-jagirdari-zamindari linkage

secs.t: Provincial units → heads and number of subas

x: Exam angle: ascending order -
Pargana - Sarkar - Suba
; Mughal "district" =
Sarkar
The state's effective administrative reach generally ended at the Pargana; villages retained substantial self-government.
The
Sarkar
was the Mughal district, headed by the faujdar and amalguzar; in ascending order the units ran Pargana - Sarkar - Suba (UPSC 2021).

secs.t: Provincial and revenue officials → functions

x: A Suba was headed by the Subedar and provincial Diwan, while a Sarkar had the Faujdar and Amalguzar as its principal officials.
The provincial Diwan handled revenue and finance independently of the Subedar, thereby acting as a check on the governor.
Bitikchi prepared assessment and land records; Qanungo maintained pargana-level revenue records; Potdar was the treasurer; and Patwari was the village accountant.

secs.t: Mansabdar-jagirdar-zamindar linkage → flow and zamindar categories

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2019 - "jagirs in lieu of judicial/police duties" and "jagirs hereditary" are both
wrong
(answer: neither).

The Mansabdar got a rank and was paid by a tankhwah jagir; the jagirdar's agents collected the assessed revenue (jama) through the zamindars, who kept a hereditary share, and the peasant paid about one-third of the produce.
Short tenure encouraged Jagirdars to press for higher collections; Zamindars resisted or rebelled, and peasants sometimes fled, producing a local face of the jagirdari crisis.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The separation of the Subedar and Diwan and the Zabti revenue system were important models for later revenue administration.
The Sultanate had Iqtas administered by Muqtis, while the British district collector combined revenue, magisterial and police powers that the Mughals kept separate.
The village officials included the Mukaddam and accountant Kulkarni, while the Desai served as the Pargana accounts officer.

rows.title: Mughal economy - agriculture, karkhanas, trade, silver influx, Indian Ocean commerce
sub: Group-II S1-49: Mughal socio-economic conditions - agriculture, trade, karkhanas, classes

secs.t: Agriculture — crops, marketed share and irrigation

x: Exam angle: "approximately what % was marketed?" - 15%.
Approximately
15 percent
of rural agricultural produce reached the market.
Jins-i-kamil referred to commercial or superior cash crops such as cotton, sugarcane, indigo, oilseeds and opium.
The Shahab Nahr was constructed by restoring the Rajabwah canal of Firuz Shah.
By the eighteenth century agriculture was stagnant and technologically backward.

secs.t: Land revenue terms → meaning — Zabt / Bandobast of Raja Todarmal

x: Polaj was cultivated annually; Parauti remained fallow for one year; Chachar for three to four years; and Banjar was uncultivated.
Patta was a title deed, while Qabuliyat was a deed of agreement issued in the revenue arrangement.
The Zabt system was devised by Akbar's revenue minister Raja Todarmal, and land was measured with the Ilahi Gaz, a bamboo rod joined with iron rings.

secs.t: Agrarian classes and trading communities → role — Agrarian and social classes

x: Exam angle: "traders who carried bulk goods over long distances" =
Banjaras
Banjaras transported grain in bullock caravans and played an important role in internal supply networks.

Seths and Bohras specialised in long-distance trade (a-iv); Baniks were local retail traders (b-ii); Mahajans were moneylenders-cum-merchants (c-i); Sarrafs were money-changers and bankers who issued hundis (d-iii).

secs.t: Agrarian classes and trading communities → role — Trading communities → region

x: Marwaris comprised Oswals, Maheshwaris and Agarwals; Chettis were Coromandel merchants; Muslim merchants dominated Malabar trade; and Gujarati merchants included Hindus, Jains and Muslims.
The
nagarseth
was the head of a merchant community and acted as its representative in dealings with officials.
Merchant strikes are recorded in
Ahmedabad
, illustrating the collective organisation of trading communities.

secs.t: Karkhanas — royal workshops and artisans

x: The Mughal royal karkhanas were supervised by the Mir Saman, also known as Khan-i-Saman.
Mughal karkhanas supplied courtly luxury goods and continued a tradition inherited from the Sultanate karkhanas.
Artisans worked in both state karkhanas and private enterprises and were often organised into guilds; they were not confined exclusively to royal workshops.

secs.t: Credit and coin terms → meaning

x: Exam angle: distractors are Farman (royal order), Parcha, Rokad (cash).
A
hundi
was a letter of credit issued by a shroff against cash deposited at one place and encashed later or elsewhere.
The English East India Company relied on Indian brokers or dalals, shroffs and banians and thus fitted into the existing credit network.

secs.t: Ports and trading centres → feature

x: Surat
was the chief Mughal port on the west coast and was known as the Gateway to Mecca or Bab-ul-Makka owing to its importance for Haj traffic.
The Dutch arrived at Masulipatnam in 1605, the English in 1611, the Portuguese were expelled from Hugli in 1632, and the French arrived at Masulipatnam in 1669.

secs.t: Exports, imports and European firmans → year

x: The Golden Firman of 1636, issued by Abdullah Qutb Shah, granted the
English trade rights
Shah Jahan granted exemptions to the English in 1652 and the Dutch in 1665, while Farrukhsiyar’s firman of 1716/1717 reduced English duties.

secs.t: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce — causes and effects

x: India became a ‘sink of precious metals’ because European companies paid for Indian goods with bullion, causing large inflows of gold and silver.
Careri
, writing around 1690, described the global movement of silver to India.
The decline was associated with Aurangzeb’s Deccan wars, growing insecurity and the loss of Indian shipping.

secs.t: Books → authors on the Mughal economy

x: Exam angle: book-author matching (APPSC-G1 2022: a-IV, b-I, c-II, d-III).

Tapan Raychaudhuri was a co-editor, along with Irfan Habib, of the Cambridge Economic History of India, Volume I. Six Voyages was associated with Tavernier, Early Travels in India with William Foster, and Storia do Mogor with Niccolao Manucci.
*Fall of the Mughal Empire* was written by Jadunath Sarkar.

secs.t: European travellers → accounts of the Mughal economy and society

x: William Hawkins was associated with Jahangir; Pelsaert came during Jahangir's time in 1620; Peter Mundy visited during Shah Jahan's reign; Tavernier visited during the reigns of Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb.
Roe reached Jahangir's court in 1615, Pelsaert came in 1620, Peter Mundy travelled in 1630-34 and Thevenot reached Surat in 1666, so the order is
A, B, C, D
. The order B, A, C, D wrongly puts Pelsaert (1620) before Roe (1615).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Mughal economy was monetised, supported by credit and marked by a trade surplus.
Cash revenue under zabt monetised the rural economy and connected peasants with markets.
Machilipatnam
was the first European trade centre in Andhra, established by the Dutch in 1605.
Bernier did express the view that private property in land did not exist.

rows.title: Mughal society - nobility, peasantry, position of women, urban classes

secs.t: Nobility — groups → reign and changing shares

x: Mughal nobles were wealthy but remained wholly dependent on the emperor’s favour.
Turanis and Iranis were dominant under Babur and Humayun.
M. Athar Ali estimated the Hindu share in the Mughal nobility at about
one-third
under Aurangzeb.

secs.t: Terms → meaning: peasants, court customs and institutions

x: Peasants, or raiyats, were the backbone of the Mughal economy and carried the burden of land revenue.
Firangi Mahal in Lucknow was a madrasa associated with
Muslim jurisprudence
Aurangzeb
ended Jharokha darshan and stopped the celebration of Nauroz.
Sijda meant prostration, while paibos meant kissing the feet; Akbar introduced both practices at court.

secs.t: Persons → statements and contributions on Mughal society

x: Nur Jahan married Jahangir in 1611, became Padshah Begum, had her name inscribed on coins and farmans, and built Itimad-ud-Daula’s tomb.
Jahanara, Shah Jahan’s daughter and Padshah Begum, built the
Jama Masjid at Agra and a sarai at Chandni Chowk
Makhfi is best known as the pen name of Zeb-un-Nissa, Aurangzeb's daughter; some sources give it for Nur Jahan, so 'Nur Jahan alone' is the trap.

secs.t: Urban classes, slavery and women's position → features

x: Merchants such as nagarseths, Marwaris, Bohras and Chettis, along with artisans, formed the middle and lower urban strata.
Akbar stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war in 1562, although slaves and large domestic staffs continued to exist in noble households.
Muslim women were described as strictly veiled and transported in covered palanquins, while Hindu women were reported as moving more freely.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Travellers’ accounts are a major source for Mughal social history, but their observations should be read critically alongside Persian chronicles.
Qutb Shahi Golconda shared Mughal customs such as
Nauroz
Muharram was known as Peerla Panduga in Golconda.

rows.title: Mughal architecture - Fatehpur Sikri, Humayun's tomb, Taj Mahal, Red Fort; garden and tomb traditions
sub: Group-II S1-51: Mughal art and architecture - Fatehpur Sikri, Taj Mahal, gardens and forts

secs.t: Monuments → builder, place and date (Ram Bagh to Bibi ka Maqbara)

x: Exam angle: "built in Akbar's reign" sets and "not built by Shah Jahan" odd-one-out questions.
The order is Humayun's Tomb (1565–1572), Jami Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri (1571–1574), Tomb of Salim Chishti (1580–1581), and Char Minar (1591).
Akbar's Tomb was completed around 1613, followed by the Taj Mahal (1632–1648), Red Fort (1639–1648), and Jama Masjid of Delhi (1650–1656).
Prince Azam Shah built Bibi ka Maqbara during Aurangzeb's reign for his mother,
Dilras Banu Begum
Humayun's tomb (c.1565-72, commissioned by Haji Begum in Akbar's reign), Buland Darwaza (c.1575, for the Gujarat victory) and Salim Chishti's tomb (c.1580-81) all belong to Akbar's reign.

secs.t: Tomb tradition — evolution and FIRSTs

x: The standard answer is Humayun's widow Haji Begum (Bega Begum), who commissioned the tomb in Akbar's reign (c.1565-72).
Humayun’s tomb was the first garden tomb in the subcontinent, introduced the double dome and used red sandstone with white marble inlay.
Sayyid-Lodi tombs incorporated Hindu elements such as Hindu-style gates and facades, plaster ornament and drip-stones.

secs.t: Architectural terms → meaning and where first seen

x: The Persian-Indian synthesis combined
arches and domes with trabeate forms, chhatris and Hindu motifs
, as seen at Fatehpur Sikri and Akbar's tomb.
Akbar's phase is represented by red-sandstone structures such as Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri, while Shah Jahan's phase is dominated by white marble, as in the Taj Mahal.

secs.t: Fatehpur Sikri — buildings → feature

x: Buland Darwaza, meaning the “Gate of Magnificence”, commemorated Akbar's
victory in the Gujarat conquest
The
Ibadat Khana
was the House of Worship used for philosophical debates among scholars of various religions.
Jodha Bai's palace combines Hindu trabeate construction, based on beams and lintels, with Islamic arcuate construction, based on arches and domes.
Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar's planned capital during 1571–1585 and reflects multiple architectural influences, including the Tudor arch introduced by Akbar.

secs.t: Taj Mahal — architect, marble source, historians' views, court case

x: Humayun's Tomb
provided an important design ancestry for the Taj Mahal, particularly through the garden-tomb form and use of a double dome.
Unlike the usual central placement in a charbagh, the Taj Mahal's tomb stands at the river end of the garden, near the Yamuna.
Sulphur dioxide emitted by the Mathura refinery, industries and traffic contributes to yellowing and the deterioration popularly called marble cancer.

secs.t: Forts → builder; Red Fort and Shahjahanabad

x: Agra Fort was begun in 1565, Allahabad Fort was built in 1583, Lahore Fort was rebuilt by Akbar and the Red Fort at Delhi was built by Shah Jahan.
The Jami Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri was built by Akbar, while the Jama Masjid of Delhi and Moti Masjid of Agra Fort were built by Shah Jahan.

secs.t: Places — gardens and emperors' tombs → location

x: Nishat Bagh at Srinagar, on Dal Lake, was built by
Asaf Khan
, the brother of Nur Jahan.
Shah Jahan is buried in the Taj Mahal at Agra beside Mumtaz Mahal.
Aurangzeb was buried in
a simple grave at Khuldabad near Aurangabad
Charminar is in Hyderabad, Akbar's Tomb at Sikandara, Humayun's Tomb in Delhi and the Taj Mahal at Agra.

secs.t: UNESCO Mughal sites → year inscribed

x: Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal were inscribed in 1983, Fatehpur Sikri in 1986, Humayun's Tomb in 1993 and the Red Fort Complex in 2007.
The Taj Mahal was included among the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Mughal architecture is regarded as the peak or zenith of
Indo-Islamic architecture
, combining Persian, Timurid and Indian elements.
The Bahmani Jama Masjid at Gulbarga is notable for its fully covered courtyard, whereas Mughal mosques generally followed an open-court arrangement.
The Allahabad High Court issued notices in connection with the petition challenging the Agra court's refusal to allow a survey of the Taj Mahal.

rows.title: Mughal painting, music, language and literature; Persian-Sanskrit translation movement
sub: Group-II S1-52: Mughal language, literature and painting; decline of the Mughal Empire

secs.t: Mughal painting — emperor → emphasis

x: Exam angle: statement sets. "Jahangir's reign = golden period" is correct; statement pairs on Humayun's Persian masters and Jahangir's golden age.
Humayun is associated with the Persian masters; Akbar with illustrated manuscripts; Jahangir with naturalism; and Shah Jahan with formal court scenes and floral decoration.
Jahangir
's painters introduced the halo or nimbus behind the emperor's head, reflecting the period's refined and naturalistic style.

secs.t: Court painters → reign and title

x: Abdus Samad was a Persian master associated with Humayun and Akbar and was given the title Shirin Qalam.
Ustad Mansur, a painter of Jahangir's court, was renowned for depicting
flora and fauna
Manohar, the son of Basawan, worked in the Akbar–Jahangir period and was known for portraits, while Basawan was a leading Akbar-era master.

secs.t: Regional painting schools → region and features

x: Rajput paintings are known for bold colours, a flat two-dimensional style, and subjects such as Hindu epics, love legends and daily life.
At Golconda,
Mir Hashim
is identified as the founder of the Deccani painting tradition; he was later invited to the Mughal court.
Mughal painting generally displayed muted naturalistic colours, perspective, shading and a cosmopolitan outlook, while Rajput painting was indigenous, vivid and decorative.

secs.t: Musicians and music forms → court

x: Baz Bahadur was the Sultan of Malwa (famed with Rupmati), who served Akbar only after Akbar's forces defeated him in 1561, not from the start of his career.
Tappa was refined by
Shori Miyan
in the late eighteenth-century Awadh–Lucknow milieu.
Although Aurangzeb ended court music, Persian treatises on classical music were produced during his reign, and he played the veena.

secs.t: Languages — Persian, Urdu/Rekhta and Deccani

x: Persian acquired elite official status, while Hindavi developed through the interaction of Perso-Arabic script and indigenous grammar and vocabulary.
Dakhni Urdu served as the common language of Deccan camps and bazaars, became a literary medium under the Qutb Shahis, and Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah is known for the first Urdu poetic diwan.
Urdu mixes Persian, Arabic, Turkic, local Prakrits and Braj, uses the Perso-Arabic script, and retains an indigenous grammar.

secs.t: Persian histories and memoirs — book → author

x: Humayun-nama was authored by
Gulbadan Begum
, the daughter of Babur and sister of Humayun.
The Akbarnama was written by Abul Fazl in three volumes, with the third volume known as the Ain-i-Akbari.
Tabaqat-i-Akbari was written by Nizamuddin Ahmad; Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh by Badauni; Padshahnama by Abdul Hamid Lahori; and Alamgirnama by Mirza Muhammad Kazim.
The Ain-i-Akbari, dated 1590, mentions Diwali and compares it with
Shab-e-baraat

secs.t: Translation movement — Persian work → original → translator

x: The Maktab Khana was created as a translation bureau to
promote cross-cultural understanding among the nobility
Lilavati was Bhaskaracharya's mathematical work, translated into Persian by Faizi during Akbar's reign.
Nizamuddin Panipati
translated the Yoga Vasistha, known as Jog Bashisht, for Prince Salim during Akbar's reign.
The Panchatantra was earlier rendered into Persian under the title
Kalila wa Dimna

secs.t: Persons → contributions: Dara Shikoh and Hindi poets

x: Majma-ul-Bahrain, meaning ‘Mingling of the Two Oceans’, explores the
common ground between Sufism and Vedanta
Anquetil-Duperron
prepared a Latin version of Sirr-i-Akbar, helping take the Upanishads to Europe.
Keshavdas of the Orchha court wrote Ramchandrika, Kavipriya, Rasikpriya and Ratan Bavani, not Ram Rasayan (the MPPSC 2025 trap).
Kavindracharya Saraswati obtained Shah Jahan's remission of the pilgrim tax at Banaras and Prayag and wrote Kavindra-kalpalata in Hindi.

secs.t: Causes of Mughal decline — factor → effect

x: The jagirdari crisis involved too many mansabdars and too few revenue-yielding jagirs, a condition described as be-jagiri, which weakened the mansabdari system.
The decline was also accelerated by weak successors, Turani, Irani and Hindustani noble factions, the rise of regional powers and the Marathas, and invasions by Nadir Shah and Ahmad Shah Abdali.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The interaction of translation, painting and Hindavi-Urdu literature helped create
a composite Indo-Persian culture
The PIL followed the removal of a Maratha Empire map from a revised NCERT textbook.
Golconda was annexed by Aurangzeb on
3 October 1687
and was incorporated as the twenty-first Suba.
Abul Hasan Tana Shah
granted Kuchipudi village to the dancers of the form that grew under Siddhendra Yogi.

rows.title: Decline of the Mughal Empire - causes and historiography; the Later Mughals; regional successor states

secs.t: Later Mughal rulers → reign, events and fate — Rulers in order

x: Farrukhsiyar ruled from 1713 to 1719, was controlled by the Sayyid brothers, executed Banda Singh Bahadur in 1716, and granted the English duty-free trade in Bengal.
Jahandar Shah was called Lampat, was backed by Zulfiqar Khan and remained under the sway of his mistress Lal Kunwar.
Muhammad Shah eliminated the Sayyid influence with Nizam-ul-Mulk’s help, witnessed the autonomy of major provincial rulers and faced Nadir Shah’s invasion in 1739.

secs.t: Later Mughal rulers → reign, events and fate — Traps on dates and patrons

x: Shah Alam II lived at Allahabad under Company protection and returned to Delhi in 1771–72 under Mahadji Scindia’s protection.

secs.t: Titles, epithets, FIRSTs and LASTs

x: Bahadur Shah I, also known as Muazzam, was given the epithet
Shah-i-Bekhabar
Aurangzeb conferred the title Chin Qilich Khan, Farrukh Siyar conferred Nizam-ul-Mulk, and Muhammad Shah conferred Asaf Jah in 1725.

secs.t: Sayyid king-makers and invaders → year and consequence

x: After defeating Muhammad Shah at Karnal and plundering Delhi, Nadir Shah carried away
the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne
Punjab and Multan were ceded to Ahmad Shah Abdali, and his repeated invasions occurred during the reign of Alamgir II.
Both statements are true, and the repeated invasions, military challenges and financial drain explain why Mughal weakness was exposed.

secs.t: Farmans, grants and treaties → year and content

x: The 1719 grant recognised Shahu's claim to chauth and sardeshmukhi from the six Deccan subas through his agent Balaji Vishwanath.
Under the Treaty of Allahabad,
Shah Alam II granted the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
From 1772 Warren Hastings stopped the annual grant and sold Kora and Allahabad to the Nawab of Awadh.

secs.t: Successor states → founder and Mughal post held

x: Saadatullah Khan
, also rendered as Saadullah Khan, founded the Carnatic state of Arcot and named his nephew Dost Ali as successor.
Husain Ali Khan was a Sayyid brother, Murshid Quli Khan was associated with Bengal, Chin Qilich Khan was the Nizam of Hyderabad and Safdar Jung was associated with Awadh.

secs.t: Asaf Jahi Hyderabad → founding, administration and Nizams in sequence

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk helped overthrow the Sayyid brothers and appointed Puran Chand as Diwan.
The order is Asaf Jah I (1724), Nasir Jung (1748), Muzaffar Jung (1750), Salabat Jung (1751), and Nizam Ali Khan (1762).
Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi
founded the Asaf Jahi state and became its first Nizam.
Bahadur Shah Zafar was the last Mughal emperor, while Mir Osman Ali Khan was the last Nizam of Hyderabad.

secs.t: Causes of decline → factor and effect

x: Independent nobles weakened, rather than strengthened, central authority.
Under Aurangzeb the empire reached from Kashmir to Jinji and from the Hindukush to Chittagong.
Religious policies, prolonged warfare, factional noble politics, fiscal crisis and agrarian unrest combined to weaken the empire.

secs.t: Historians → book and view on decline

x: Irfan Habib
explained the decline through an agrarian crisis in The Agrarian System of Mughal India (1963), arguing that over-exploitation of peasants provoked revolts.
Satish Chandra wrote
Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court, 1707–1740
and associated decline with the jagirdari crisis.
Athar Ali argued that the enlarged nobility, including Deccanis and Marathas, intensified the shortage of jagirs.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, obtained in 1765, provided the Company's legal foothold for territorial and fiscal power in India.
Golconda was incorporated as the 21st Mughal suba in 1687, Hyderabad emerged from the Mughal Deccan, and the Nizam accepted the Subsidiary Alliance in 1798.
Ahmad Shah Abdali
's raids, which began from 1748, culminated in the Battle of Panipat in 1761.

rows.title: Rise of the Marathas - Shivaji's career, Ashtapradhan, revenue system, chauth and sardeshmukhi
sub: Group-II S1-57: Shivaji - career, conquests and the Ashtapradhan administration
Group-II S1-58: Shivaji's revenue system, chauth and sardeshmukhi; rise of the Maratha Empire

secs.t: Causes of the Maratha rise → factor and effect

x: The first three statements are correct causes.
Tukaram and Ramdas
are identified with the spiritual and regional unity that aided the Maratha rise.
The prolonged Deccan campaign drained the treasury, while the succession war after 1707 created a political vacuum.

secs.t: Persons around Shivaji → role

x: Tradition names Samarth Ramdas, author of Dasbodh, as Shivaji's guru.
Samarth Ramdas is traditionally named as Shivaji's guru, but the attribution is disputed by historians.
Dadaji Kondadev served as guardian of the Pune jagir and acted as Shivaji’s tutor.
Akkanna was the Sar Lashkar of Golconda.

secs.t: Shivaji's career and conflicts → year and outcome

x: Shivaji took Raigad from the Mores of Javli in 1656, and it later served as his
capital and coronation site
Shivaji killed the Bijapur general Afzal Khan with a wagh nakh at the foot of Pratapgad in 1659.
Torna was captured in 1646, Afzal Khan was killed in 1659, Shaista Khan was attacked in 1663 and the Treaty of Purandar was concluded in 1665.

secs.t: Treaties and Mughal grants → year and terms

x: Exam angle: the 2011 APPSC option "1665 - Raja Jai Singh" is the right pairing.
The coronation at Raigad occurred in 1674, the second raid on Surat occurred in 1670, the treaty with Abul Hasan Tana Shah was made in 1677 and Shivaji died in 1680.
In 1719, Mughal emperor
Farrukhsiyar
granted recognition of Shahu, Swarajya lands, and the rights to chauth and sardeshmukhi in the six Deccan subas.

secs.t: Coronation (1674), titles and FIRSTs

x: Shivaji seized Torna from Bijapur in 1646, and it was his first fort.
Shivaji's coronation took place at Raigad in 1674.
Gaga Bhatt, a learned Brahmin from Banaras or Varanasi, officiated at the coronation with Vedic rites.
The coronation title was "Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati".
Shivaji began the
Rajabhisheka Shaka
after his coronation to assert sovereign status.

secs.t: Ashtapradhan → minister, Persian title and portfolio

x: Exam angle: title-to-portfolio matching.
The Dabir was the Sumant, in charge of foreign affairs and the master of ceremonies who received envoys (APPSC-G1 2024).

Sar-i-Naubat was the Senapati, the military commander (APPSC-G2 2023); Shurnavis (Surnis) was the Sachiv, in charge of royal correspondence and records; Waqia-navis was the Mantri, in charge of intelligence and the king's diary; Dabir was the Sumant, in charge of foreign affairs.

secs.t: Revenue system → terms, units and officials

x: Kathi was a measuring rod, Jirayat denoted dry land and Bagayat denoted irrigated land.
A Prant was administered by a Subedar or Sarsubedar; Pargana and Tarf were associated with Deshmukh and Deshpande; Mauza had the Patil and Kulkarni.
Shivaji divided the kingdom into prants and curtailed the hereditary rights of Deshmukhs and Deshpandes.

secs.t: Chauth and sardeshmukhi → rate, nature and recognition

x: Exam angle: "Maratha revenue claim for protection" =
Chauth
Chauth was generally one-fourth of land revenue, justified as protection against invasion or Maratha raids.
Chauth was levied on
territories outside direct Maratha rule
, including Mughal and Deccan Sultanate territories.
Together, the levies financed military expansion and extended political hegemony without requiring the Marathas to administer every territory directly.

secs.t: Coins, language, records and tactics → meaning

x: Ganimi Kava was the guerrilla hit-and-run method used by Shivaji in the difficult Sahyadri terrain.
The Rajvyavahar Kosh replaced Persian official terminology with Sanskrit terminology.
Shivaji issued the gold Hon and the copper Shivrai.
Marathi and Sanskrit were promoted in official usage over Persian, and the cursive Modi script was used for Marathi administrative records.

secs.t: Military organisation → forts, army and navy

x: Raigad, Pratapgad, Torna and Sinhagad
are hill forts, or Giri Durg.
The hill troops in Shivaji's army were known as
Mavali infantry
Bargirs were state-equipped cavalrymen, whereas Shiledars supplied their own horses; both were cavalry categories.
Shivaji's standing army was paid in cash rather than jagirs so that loyalty remained directly attached to the state.

secs.t: Shivaji's successors → years and role (1680-1749)

x: Exam angle: order is
Sambhaji - Rajaram - Shivaji II - Shahu
; "Maratha woman who fought the Mughals from 1700" = Tarabai.
Tarabai governed as regent, raided Mughal territory, and her line was later settled at Kolhapur under the Treaty of Warna.
Aurangzeb died in the Deccan in 1707, having failed to subdue the Marathas.
Balaji Vishwanath backed Shahu during the civil war and brought Maratha chiefs together in his support.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Maratha Deccan war, especially Tarabai’s raids, seriously weakened and broke Mughal finances.
The stated peak extent of the Maratha Empire ran from Attock to Cuttack and from the Gulf of Khambhat to beyond the Kaveri.
After the 1795 war, the Nizam paid chauth to the Marathas; this pressure contributed to his move towards the British Subsidiary Alliance in 1798.
The PIL concerning the removal of the “Maratha Empire” map from NCERT was reported in the
Bombay High Court

rows.title: Peshwas and the Maratha confederacy; Third Battle of Panipat (1761); three Anglo-Maratha wars
sub: Group-II S1-59: Peshwas, the Maratha confederacy and the Third Battle of Panipat

secs.t: Rise of the Peshwa → causes and shift of power

x: From Balaji Vishwanath’s appointment in 1713, Shahu’s dependence on him and the hereditary character of the office strengthened the Peshwa.
The Sangola agreement of 1750 followed Shahu’s death in 1749 and left the Chhatrapati nominal, thereby consolidating the Peshwa’s position.
Poona
(Pune) was the Peshwas' seat of power (APPSC 2018).

secs.t: Peshwas → tenure, contribution and treaties (1713-1818) — Peshwas in order

x: Balaji Vishwanath obtained the 1719 Mughal grant recognising Shahu’s swarajya and granting the Marathas the right to collect chauth and sardeshmukhi in the Deccan.
Balaji Baji Rao, or Nana Saheb, was Peshwa from 1740 to 1761, during which Maratha power reached its zenith and Maratha forces reached Lahore and Peshawar.

secs.t: Peshwas → tenure, contribution and treaties (1713-1818) — Baji Rao I

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2024 order - Balaji Vishwanath, Balaji Baji Rao, Narayan Rao, Raghunath Rao; APPSC 2025 - Gujarat under
Balaji Baji Rao
Nana Saheb refers to Balaji Baji Rao, not Balaji Vishwanath.
Hindu Pad Padshahi is Baji Rao I's ideology.

secs.t: Maratha leaders beyond the Peshwas → role and title

x: Baji Rao I built the confederacy to maintain unity among Maratha factions and to accommodate older chiefs led by Senapati Dabhade.
Nana Phadnavis led the twelve-member Barabhai council, governed for the infant Madhav Rao II, opposed Raghunath Rao and helped preserve Maratha unity during the First Anglo-Maratha War.
After Nana Phadnavis’s death, Holkar and Scindia competed for influence over the weak Peshwa in 1801–02.

secs.t: Maratha confederacy → houses, seats and administration

x: The confederacy was weakened by rivalries among semi-independent chiefs and their tendency to put regional interests before common Maratha interests.
Saranjam consisted of land assignments made to chiefs for military service and formed the base of the Maratha confederacy.
The Peshwa Daftar at Pune contains Peshwa-era state records that were largely maintained in Modi script.

secs.t: Battles and treaties with the Nizam → year and result (1728-1795)

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2025 - Mungi-Shevgaon was between the
Marathas and the Nizam
The correct order is Palkhed (1728), Udgir (1760), Rakshasbhuvan (1763) and Kharda (1795).
Mungi-Shevgaon was a treaty between
the Marathas and the Nizam
(APPSC 2025), signed after Baji Rao I defeated the Nizam at Palkhed (1728); it conceded chauth and sardeshmukhi of the Deccan.

secs.t: Third Battle of Panipat (1761) → sides, causes and consequences — The battle

x: Balaji Baji Rao
, popularly known as Nana Saheb, was the Peshwa when the Third Battle of Panipat was fought.
Kashiraj Pandit
was an eyewitness chronicler who served Shuja-ud-Daula and recorded an account of the battle.
The Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761) was fought between
the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali
(APPSC-G1 2018).

secs.t: Third Battle of Panipat (1761) → sides, causes and consequences — Causes

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2018 - "Third Battle of Panipat was fought between Ahmad Shah Abdali and the Marathas".
The Marathas did not receive strong support from the Jats and Rajputs; their absence or neutrality contributed to the defeat.
The battle halted Maratha imperial ambitions in the north and caused heavy losses, but Maratha power was not destroyed and recovered within about a decade.

secs.t: Anglo-Maratha wars → treaties, years and Governors-General

x: Raghunath Rao offered Salsette, Bassein and revenue from Surat and Bharuch to obtain British support in the succession dispute.
After their defeat at Talegaon in 1779 the British were forced by the Convention of Wadgaon to give up their gains, but Governor-General Warren Hastings rejected it.
The Peshwaship was abolished, Baji Rao II was pensioned at Bithur and a reduced Satara state was created for Shivaji’s descendant.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Marathas and the Nizam joined the British against Tipu in the Third Mysore War, and the Treaty of Srirangapatnam was concluded in 1792.
Salbai maintained the status quo in 1782, Bassein placed the Peshwa in a position of subsidiary subordination in 1802, and 1818 marked the extinction of the Peshwaship.
The Marathas repeatedly defeated the Nizam at
Palkhed, Udgir and Kharda
, and extracted chauth from the Nizam’s Deccan territories.

rows.title: Bhakti Movement - origins, Alvars and Nayanars, Nirguna and Saguna streams, social base
sub: Group-II S1-53: Bhakti Movement - origin, Nirguna and Saguna streams, principal saints

secs.t: Bhakti → meaning, scriptural roots, origin and spread

x: The word bhakti is derived from the root bhaj, meaning
to share or participate
The Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita and Bhagavata Purana are identified as roots of the Bhakti movement.
The movement first developed in the Tamil region through the Alvars and Nayanars during the sixth–ninth centuries and reached the northern belt by the fifteenth century.

secs.t: Sacred texts → tradition and compiler

x: The Nalayira Divya Prabandham contains 4,000 Alvar hymns, was compiled by Nathamuni and is popularly called the Tamil Veda.
The Tevaram holds the hymns of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar.
The Tirumurai has 12 books compiled by Nambi Andar Nambi.

secs.t: Saints and forerunners → contribution

x: Shankaracharya, born at Kaladi in 788 and deceased in 820, is associated with the philosophy of
Advaita
Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi and opposed
idol worship
Ramananda
is described as the first medieval reformer to denounce caste outright and he admitted disciples from all castes.
Andal and Karaikkal Ammaiyar were women saints.

secs.t: Nirguna, Saguna and Nathpanthi streams → idea and saints

x: The Nathpanthis and Siddhas of the Gorakhnath tradition rejected caste and ritual, used vernacular languages and influenced Kabir's nirguna idiom.
Nirguna worship is directed towards a formless and attributeless God, while Saguna worship accepts God with form, attributes, avatars and personal deities.
Kabir, Guru Nanak, Dadu Dayal and Ravidas
are associated with the Nirguna stream, which worships a formless God.

secs.t: Gurus → disciples and social base

x: The Alvars and Nayanars came from different castes, including high and low social groups, and challenged Brahmanical dominance.
Kabir was a weaver.
Daya Bai was a disciple of
Charandas
Ravidas was Mirabai's guru, Surdas was Vallabhacharya's disciple and Janabai was Namdev's disciple.

secs.t: Causes, beliefs and limits → factor and effect

x: The movement reacted against ritualism, priestly dominance and caste, while the paths of knowledge and action were considered difficult for ordinary people.
Older historians viewed Bhakti as a reaction to Islam, whereas modern scholars emphasise its indigenous Alvar–Nayanar roots and regard Islam as influencing mainly its later egalitarian character.
Monotheism, the guru and salvation through devotion were core beliefs.

secs.t: Language → region and saints

x: Bhakti saints commonly preached in regional languages rather than Sanskrit, contributing to the enrichment of Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati and other literatures.
Basavanna and Akkamahadevi composed vachanas in Karnataka; Tukaram composed abhangas in Maharashtra; Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi; and Chaitanya was associated with kirtans in Bengal.
Namdev
was identified as the most influential saint of the Maharashtra tradition; Eknath, Tukaram and Narhari were also associated with it.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The movement brought Hindus and Muslims closer and weakened caste bondage, but it did not fully achieve lasting Hindu-Muslim unity or completely abolish caste.

All three statements are correct within the stated first/last distinctions: Andal was the only female Alvar, Ramanuja the first true exponent, and Ramananda the first to denounce caste outright in the north.

rows.title: Bhakti saints and their teachings - Ramanuja, Madhva, Nimbarka, Vallabha, Ramananda

secs.t: Vedantic acharyas — chronology, contemporaries and FIRSTs

x: Ramanuja preceded Nimbarka, followed by Ramananda and then Vallabhacharya.
Vallabhacharya (1479–1531) and Chaitanya (1485–1533) were contemporaries.
Shankaracharya taught Advaita or monism and is described as a forerunner or pioneer of the Bhakti cult.

secs.t: Acharyas → school, teaching and deity

x: Exam angle: "which statement is NOT correct" - e.g. Madhva propounded Nirguna bhakti is wrong; Shankara = Advaita.
Ramanuja stressed devoted worship of
Narayana and Lakshmi
as the means of escaping the cycle of birth and death.
Madhvacharya’s Dvaita philosophy maintains that God, identified with Vishnu, and individual souls are eternally distinct.
Vallabha worshipped child Krishna and Radha-Krishna; Ramananda worshipped Rama; Chaitanya worshipped Krishna; and Nimbarka worshipped Radha-Krishna.

secs.t: Acharyas → contributions and disciples

x: Vallabhacharya visited the court of
Krishnadevaraya
, refuted Shaiva propositions and defeated the Dvaita scholar Vyasaraya, also known as Vyasa Tirtha.
Kabir was a weaver of Muslim background, Raidas a shoemaker or leather worker, Sena a barber and Dhanna a Jat cultivator.
Since Ramanuja died in 1137 and Ramananda belonged to a much later period, the description is understood as referring to Ramananda’s following of Ramanuja’s school, not direct contemporaneity.

secs.t: Sects and books → founders and authors

x: Pushtimarga was associated with Vallabhacharya, Ramanandi with Ramananda, Gaudiya Vaishnavism with Chaitanya and Sri Vaishnava with Ramanuja.
Pushtimarga is the Vallabha Sampradaya, means the path of grace and was represented through 84 centres established by Vallabhacharya.
Sri Vaishnavism later split into Vadakalai, associated with the Vedic tradition of Vedanta Desika, and Tengalai.
Tattva Teeka and Nyaya Siddhanjanam are works of
Vedanta Desika

secs.t: Places → acharyas; Ramanuja in Andhra

x: Ramanuja’s main centre was the Srirangam monastery; Madhva’s was the Udupi Krishna Matha; Nimbarka’s was Brindavan; and Ramananda’s was Varanasi.
Brahmanayudu's Veera Vaishnava movement in Palnadu was inspired by Sri Vaishnavism and aimed at creating
a casteless society
Krishnadevaraya's Amuktamalyada, referred to in this context as Mala Dasari Katha, is cited as a prime example of social inclusion.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Ramanuja's 11th–12th-century influence preceded the Vijayanagara period; Vedanta Desika's Andhra activity belongs to the 14th century, while the Hyderabad statue is a modern development.
The acharyas provided a philosophical basis for Bhakti against Advaita and helped open temple worship to lower groups; their teachings were not confined exclusively to elites.

rows.title: Kabir, Guru Nanak, Chaitanya, Mirabai, Tukaram, Namdeva, Surdas, Tulsidas

secs.t: Bhakti saints → period, region and contemporary ruler — Chronological order of Bhakti saints

x: Order:
Namdev (1270-1350) → Kabir (15th c.) → Nanak (1469-1538) → Vallabha (1479-1531) → Chaitanya (1485-1533) → Mirabai (1498-1546) → Surdas/Tulsidas (16th c.) → Tukaram/Ramdas (17th c.)
UPPSC 2025 key: Namdev, Kabir, Nanak, Chaitanya.

secs.t: Bhakti saints → period, region and contemporary ruler — Saint → period, region and contemporary ruler

x: Mirabai was associated with
Rajasthan
and is described as a Rajput princess of Merta.
Tulsidas was associated with Akbar’s time; Chaitanya with Prataparudra Gajapati; Tukaram with Shivaji; and Mirabai with the Rajput and Mewar royal houses.
The sequence is Namdev, Kabir, Guru Nanak and Chaitanya.
Vallabhacharya, Chaitanya, Mirabai and Tukaram belong successively to the late fifteenth–early sixteenth, early sixteenth, sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

secs.t: Saints → teachings and contributions

x: Kabir condemned rituals and idol worship in both communities, opposed caste, worked for Hindu-Muslim unity and is regarded as the greatest saint of the Bhakti cult.
Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi
lived from 1564 to 1624, later than Kabir; therefore, he could not have influenced Kabir.
Ramdas stressed
strength, discipline and devotion to Rama
, and these ideas aided the Maratha political awakening.

secs.t: Sects and terms → meaning

x: Sankirtan means
collective devotional singing
The Varkari sect worships Vitthala, also called Vithoba, at Pandharpur.

secs.t: Guru → disciple lineages

x: Ramananda was associated with Kabir, Raidas with Mirabai, Vallabhacharya with Surdas and Guru Nanak with Mardana.
Kabir, Raidas and Pipa are included in the lineage associated with Ramananda.
Amir Khusrau was a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya.

secs.t: Books → authors and languages

x: Gita Govinda was written by Jayadeva.
Sahitya Lahari is not attributed to Tulsidas in the stated literary associations.
Abhangas are associated with Tukaram and also with Namdev in the Marathi Bhakti tradition.
Surdas used Braj Bhasha, not Rajasthani.
Mirabai’s poetry is associated with Rajasthani, with elements of Braj.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Vemana and Potuluri Veerabrahmam
are identified as Andhra parallels to Kabir in their attack on caste.
These saints enriched several regional literatures and contributed to the early stirrings of both Maratha and Sikh awakening.
Kabir, Guru Nanak and Guru Ravidas are associated with the Nirguna tradition, which emphasises devotion to the formless divine.
