rows.title: Bhakti in Andhra - Annamacharya, Bammera Potana, Vemana, the Tallapaka poets
sub: Group-II S1-54: Bhakti Movement in the South and in Andhra; its social impact
Group-II M1-A-49: Telugu literature - Srinatha, Potana, Annamacharya and the Bhakti stream

secs.t: Acharyas → philosophy preached

x: Ramanuja preached Vishishtadvaita and stressed the worship of Narayana and Lakshmi.
Basavanna founded the Virashaiva movement, and its theology was termed Shakti Vishishtadvaita, according to which the soul and Shiva are fundamentally identical.
Ramanuja's Statue of Equality stands at
Hyderabad
Nimbarka preached Dvaitadvaita, not Vishishtadvaita.

secs.t: Alvars and Nayanars → deity, number, saints, canon

x: Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar and Manikkavachakar
are notable Nayanar saints.
The Alvars and Nayanars used Tamil devotional hymns, while Tirumurai became the major Shaiva canonical collection.
There are traditionally 12 Alvars (Vaishnava, devotees of Vishnu) and 63 Nayanars (Shaiva, devotees of Shiva). '63 and 12' reverses them, and the other two options give both groups the same number.

secs.t: Virashaiva movement → persons, terms and Andhra spread — Person → contribution

x: Virashaivism entered Andhra through
Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya
, after which Pandita reformers helped spread it.
The teachings emphasised equality, devotion to Shiva, dignity of labour and opposition to caste discrimination; compulsory caste hierarchy is contrary to them.
Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya wrote Sivatattvasaram, consisting of about 400 kanda poems, and is regarded as the originator of the Sataka form.

secs.t: Virashaiva movement → persons, terms and Andhra spread — Term → meaning

x: The Anubhava Mantapa at Kalyana was an early religious parliament and the ideas spread through Kannada Vachanas.
Somanatha championed Desi kavita, using
simple native metres such as Dwipada, Ragada, Manjari and Kanda
against the Sanskritised Marga style.
Aradhya Saivism was the moderate Andhra Shaiva tradition associated with Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya; it retained Vedic learning and varna while preaching devotion to Shiva.

secs.t: Srinatha → courts, patrons and titles

x: After Kondaveedu fell in 1424, Srinatha went to Rajahmundry under Veerabhadra Reddy through Bendapudi Anantamatya.
At Vijayanagara, under Devaraya II, Srinatha defeated Gauda Dindima Bhatta and received Kanakabhishekam, Ganda Penderam and the title Kavi Sarvabhauma.
Srinatha was Vidyadhikari at the Kondaveedu court of Pedakomati Vema Reddy and wrote the king's Sanskrit inscriptions.

secs.t: Srinatha's works → dedication and attribution traps

x: Exam angle: "not written by Srinatha" lists; know both the attribution in your notes and the key APPSC used.
Bhimakhandamu, or Bhimeswara Puranam, was composed at the Rajahmundry court of Veerabhadra Reddy, and Kasikhandamu belongs to the same Reddi-period setting.
Veerabhadra Vijayam is regarded by the cited accounts as Potana's first work, written at the request of his guru Ivaturi Somanaradhya, though an older APPSC key attributed it to Srinatha.

secs.t: Annamacharya and the Tallapaka poets → life, works, titles — Annamacharya — life

x: About 32,000 sankirtanas were composed, about 12,000 survive, preserved on copper plates at Tirumala.
Annamacharya is regarded as the father of the Telugu keertana and a pioneer of the padakavita or pada form.
The Kannada saint
Purandara Dasa
is stated to have met Annamacharya.
Annamacharya (1408-1503) was a contemporary of
Saluva Narasimha
(APPSC-G2 2011).

secs.t: Annamacharya and the Tallapaka poets → life, works, titles — Tallapaka family → works

x: Padakavita Pitamaha, Sankirtanacharya and Harikirtanacharya are titles of Annamacharya.
China Tirumalacharya held the title Ashtabhasha Kavi Chakravarti and wrote Ashtabhasha Dandakam (and Sankirtana Lakshanamu).
Chinnanna wrote
Annamacharya Charitra
, a biography of Annamacharya in the Dvipada form, along with Paramayogi Vilasam, Ashtamahishi Kalyanam and Usha Kalyanam.
Sri Venkateswara Satakam is
Annamacharya
's work and the first Telugu Shringara Satakam.

secs.t: Bammera Potana → life, works, patronage debate

x: Potana was known by the titles
Sahaja Panditudu and Nigarva Chudamani
Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu is the Telugu Bhagavata Purana and was offered to Lord Rama.
Potana refused to dedicate the work to Sarvajna Singabhupala and offered it to Sri Rama.
Potana was a contemporary of
Srinatha

secs.t: FIRSTs in Telugu bhakti literature

x: Basava Puranam spread Basava's teachings in simple Telugu, and Vrushadhipa Satakam is the first Telugu satakam with all satakam features.
Both statements are true: Srinatha's writings contain the first reference to paper as writing material in Andhra, and the reference belongs to the fifteenth century.
The first Telugu Dandakam was Potana's Bhogini Dandakam; it should not be attributed to China Tirumalayya.

secs.t: Vemana and Potuluri Veerabrahmam → anti-caste voices

x: Exam angle: Vemana is paired with Potuluri Veerabrahmam (Kaalagnanam) as Andhra's anti-caste voices.
Vemana criticised superstition, empty ritual, idol worship and hypocrisy; he advocated humanism, inner wisdom and equality.
Vemana mainly used the Ataveladi metre, and his verses commonly conclude with the refrain “Vishwadabhirama Vinura Vema.”.
Veerabrahmendra Swamy strongly condemned caste differences and accepted disciples from different castes and faiths, including Siddaiah, a Muslim.

secs.t: Later Andhra composers → deity and works

x: Bhakta Ramadasu (Kancharla Gopanna), a Golconda revenue official under Tana Shah, used state revenue to rebuild the Bhadrachalam Rama temple.
The Carnatic Trinity consists of Tyagaraja, Muthuswami
Dikshitar and Syama Sastri
Bhakta Ramadasu was
Kancherla Gopanna
, a prominent devotee and composer associated with Bhadrachalam.
Bhakta Ramadasu was imprisoned for
12 years
in Golconda Fort by Abul Hasan Tana Shah.

secs.t: Telugu women poets → literary work

x: Tallapaka Timmakka, also called Tirumalamma, was Annamacharya's first wife and is regarded as the first woman poet of the Andhra region.
Gangadevi's Sanskrit work Madhura Vijayam describes her husband Kumara Kampana's conquest of Madurai.
Gangadevi wrote Madhura Vijayam (Veera Kamparaya Charitam) in Sanskrit, so '
Gangadevi — Marichi Parinayam
' is the wrong match (APPSC-G2 2023 and 2025).

secs.t: Places → saints; Palnadu in literature

x: The text records houses decorated with Rama and Krishna avatars and refers to 1,500 painters' houses at Orugallu, making it a source for social life.
Tarigonda Vengamamba is included among the saints associated with
Tirumala
and the Venkateswara tradition.
Narahari Tirtha is associated with Srikurmam and spread the
Dvaita
tradition.

secs.t: Social impact of bhakti — caste critique, vernaculars, spread factors

x: Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam
became important vernacular vehicles that carried Bhakti ideas to common people instead of relying exclusively on Sanskrit.
The
satakam and dwipada
forms helped communicate Bhakti ideas to common people in Telugu-speaking regions.
These traditions challenged caste and Brahmanical dominance rather than uniformly upholding it.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Nannaya was Adikavi, Tikkana was Kavibrahma and Errapragada was Prabandha Parameswara.
Telugu Bhakti poets carried devotional expression through
padams, keertanas, satakas and dvipada compositions
, helping establish the Telugu base of the Carnatic music repertoire.
The Bhakti tradition asserted women's spiritual authority and the dignity of labour through Kayaka; it did not reject devotional poetry.

rows.title: Sufism - doctrines, khanqah, sama; silsilas - Chishti, Suhrawardi, Qadiri, Naqshbandi
sub: Group-II S1-55: Sufi Movement - doctrines, silsilas and major saints

secs.t: Sufism — meaning, origin, FIRSTs and Sufis vs Ulema

x: The ulema were legalistic, the Sufis valued inner experience.
The term Sufi has been explained through Suf, Safa and the Greek word Sophia.
Ali Hujwiri
is considered the first prominent Sufi in India.
‘Kashf-ul-Mahjub’ was written by
Ali Hujwiri
, also known as Data Ganj Bakhsh.
Naqshbandi and Firdausi are Ba-shara orders, while Madaris and wandering Qalandars are Be-shara groups.

secs.t: Sufi terms → meaning

x: A khanqah was a Sufi hospice for the residence and training of disciples, and it also provided food and shelter to the poor.
Fana denotes annihilation of the self or ego in God, while Baqa denotes subsistence in God.
Ba-shara Sufis follow the Shariat, whereas Be-shara Sufis remain outside it; qalandars are given as an example of the latter.

secs.t: Doctrines, stages and practices — Wahdat-ul-Wujud, maqamat, yogic borrowings

x: Amritakund was translated into Arabic and Persian in the
13th century
, after which breath control became important in almost every Sufi order except the Naqshbandis.
The ten maqamat begin with Tauba (repentance) and end with Riza (submission), passing through Wara, Zuhd, Faqr, Sabr, Shukr, Khauf, Raja and Tawakkul.
Wahdat-ush-Shuhud, or Unity of Appearance/Witness, was associated with
Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi
of the Naqshbandi order.

secs.t: Silsilas → founders, saints and centres

x: Exam angle: "which saint belongs to the Chishti order" (Gesudaraz - yes; Bahauddin Zakariya = Suhrawardi; Sirhindi and Baqi Billah = Naqshbandi).
Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi, Burhanuddin Gharib, Gesudaraz and the Chishti Hamiduddin of Nagaur are all associated with the Chishti order.
The Chishti Hamiduddin of Nagaur was a disciple of Moinuddin Chishti, whereas Qazi Hamiduddin Nagori was a Suhrawardi.
The Chishti order developed around Ajmer and Delhi, later reached Deccan centres such as Gulbarga and Bijapur, and gained popularity by adapting to local traditions and vernacular languages.
Abdul Qadir Jilani founded the Qadiri order; it reached India in the fourteenth century in the stated account, and Miyan Mir and Dara Shikoh were Qadiri figures.
Muhammad Ghaus of Gwalior belonged to the
Shattari
order and is identified as Tansen's guide.
The
Suhrawardi
order was concentrated mainly in Sindh, Multan and Punjab, with Multan serving as an important centre.

secs.t: Silsilas → attitude to state patronage, sama and orthodoxy

x: Bahauddin Zakariya received the title
Shaikh-ul-Islam
after backing Iltutmish against Qabacha.
Chishtis encouraged sama and qawwali, Suhrawardis accepted sama and raqs, while Naqshbandis opposed sama.
The Naqshbandis were regarded as the most orthodox, adhered strictly to the Shariat and condemned innovations or bid'at.
Ahmad Sirhindi criticised Akbar’s Sulh-i-Kul and was imprisoned during the reign of
Jahangir

secs.t: Sufi saints → dargahs, dates and titles

x: Verses of
Baba Farid
are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, also called the Adi Granth.
Nizamuddin Auliya’s dargah is in Delhi; he was born at Badaun and was a disciple of Baba Farid.
Salim Chishti
is identified as Akbar’s saint and is associated with Fatehpur Sikri.
Amir Khusrau introduced
Qaul, the opening hymn
of Qawwali.
Aibak dedicated the first storey of the Qutub Minar to
Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki

secs.t: Sufi texts → authors

x: Ali Hujwiri (Data Ganj Bakhsh) wrote it and is considered the first prominent Sufi in India.
‘Maktubat-i-Imam Rabbani’ consists of the
letters of Ahmad Sirhindi
Tazkiras are biographies of saints.
‘Radd-i-Khawafiq’ is an
anti-Shia tract
associated with Ahmad Sirhindi.

secs.t: Sufis in the Deccan and Andhra — places → saints

x: Abul Hasan Tana Shah was a disciple of the Chishti saint
Shah Raju Qattal
Burhanuddin Gharib took the order to Khuldabad, and the migration of Chishtis to Gulbarga followed.
The dargah of Gesudaraz or Bande Nawaz is at
Gulbarga
, where he settled under the Bahmanis.
Golconda witnessed the settlement of Sufi gurus, widespread popularity of Sufism and the development of khanqahs as higher-education centres.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sufism gave Islam in India a tolerant and vernacular character, while khanqahs served as welfare centres.
The adaptation of Chishtis to local language and music helped Sufism serve as a bridge for Indo-Islamic composite culture.
Ali Hujwiri is identified as the first prominent Sufi in India, while Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi is the last great Chishti saint of Delhi.

rows.title: Sufi saints - Moinuddin Chishti, Nizamuddin Auliya, Baba Farid, Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi

secs.t: Sufi saints → contemporary rulers

x: Moinuddin Chishti came with Muhammad Ghori in 1192 and settled at
Ajmer
All four associations are correct.
The statement ‘Hunuz Dilli dur ast’ is associated with
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
in connection with Nizamuddin Auliya.

secs.t: Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi → order, doctrine and opposition to Akbar

x: Sirhindi was a Naqshbandi, a disciple of Baqi Billah, and his letters are the Maktubat-i-Imam Rabbani.
Sirhindi criticised Akbar’s Sulh-i-kul and Din-i-Ilahi and opposed sama and visits to saints’ tombs.
Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi propounded Wahdat-ush-Shuhud in opposition to Wahdat-ul-Wujud.

secs.t: Sufi texts → authors and compilers

x: Fawaid-ul-Fuad records the conversations of
Nizamuddin Auliya
Fawaid-ul-Fuad was compiled by
Amir Hasan Sijzi
Radd-i-Rawafiz is an anti-Shia tract associated with
Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi
Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi was known as
Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All four statements correctly express the contrast: Nizamuddin was a Chishti associated with sama and aloofness from court, while Sirhindi was a Naqshbandi orthodox critic.
The Dargah Committee runs Dargah Khwaja Saheb at Ajmer
The Chishti dargahs at Ajmer and Delhi developed as shared shrines visited by both Hindus and Muslims.

rows.title: Interaction and impact of the Bhakti and Sufi movements on society and language
sub: Group-II S1-56: Impact of the Bhakti and Sufi movements on Indian society and languages

secs.t: Bhakti and Sufi — common principles

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2022 and 2023 both keyed
I, II and III only
(monotheism, asceticism, tolerance) - "accepted idol worship" is the trap.
Nirguna is the Bhakti idea of the formless one God (Kabir, Nanak), and Tawhid is the Sufi doctrine of God's oneness, so '
Bhakti — Nirguna; Sufism — Tawhid
' is right.
Bhakti traditions placed devotion above Vedic ritual and priestly mediation, while Sufism emphasised inner spiritual experience rather than merely formal observance of the Shariat.

secs.t: Persons → contributions to Bhakti-Sufi interaction

x: Hamiduddin Nagori
equated the Nath term 'Alakh Niranjan' with 'Khuda' in Hindi verse.
Sheikh Nuruddin
founded the Rishi movement of Kashmir, which echoed the poetess Lalla (Lal Ded).
Sulh-i-kul means
universal peace
and represented Akbar’s attempt to harmonise diverse beliefs.
Akbar revered Salim Chishti and undertook pilgrimages to Ajmer, reflecting the Sufi influence on his religious outlook.

secs.t: Nathpanthi Hath Yoga — practitioners and Sufi borrowings

x: Exam angle: "Hath Yoga practised by Nathpanthis and adopted by Sufis" -
both correct
The Kanphata Yogis followed the Nath tradition of
Gorakhnath
and were practitioners of Hath Yoga.
The interaction involved spiritual dialogues, meditation and breath-control techniques; it was not confined exclusively to temple rituals.
Both statements are correct (UPPSC 2019).

secs.t: Music → traditions and works

x: Exam angle: UPPSC A-R - both true, but Chishti love of music is
not
the explanation for the translations.
Amir Khusrau
is credited with introducing the Qaul, which became associated with qawwali traditions around Sufi shrines.
Hindustani music absorbed Persian, Bhakti and Sufi influences, including contributions associated with Amir Khusrau and Tansen.

secs.t: Vernacular literature → works and poets by language

x: Ramcharitmanas, composed by Tulsidas, belongs to the Hindi literary tradition, particularly Awadhi.
Punjabi is associated with Baba Farid’s verses, Marathi with Jnaneshwari, Bengali with Padavali kirtans and Telugu with Annamacharya’s sankirtanas.
Vemana
, associated with the seventeenth century, used satire in common Telugu against birth-based inequality.
All three statements describe the vernacular orientation of Bhakti and Sufi preaching and literature.

secs.t: Reformers → impact on caste, including Andhra

x: Basava’s Veerashaivism condemned caste and child marriage and supported widow remarriage and gender equality.
His disciples cut across castes (Siddayya a Dudekula, Kakkaiah a Madiga) and he admitted women, his granddaughter Eswaramma becoming a yogi.
Ramananda
was the first medieval reformer to denounce caste outright; his disciples included Kabir (weaver), Raidas (shoemaker), Sena (barber) and Dhanna (Jat cultivator).

secs.t: Women in the movements

x: Mirabai, Andal, Lal Ded, Janabai and Bahinabai
are the women named for expressing their devotion openly.
Lal Ded or Lalla belonged to Kashmir and inspired the Rishi movement.
Molla
was an Andhra woman poet associated with the Telugu Molla Ramayanam of the sixteenth century.
The Bhakti and Sufi movements created space for women’s open spiritual expression; Veerabrahmam also admitted women to his order.

secs.t: New sects → founders and regions

x: Kabirpanth is associated with North India, Dadupanth with Rajasthan, Mahanubhava with Maharashtra and the Rishi movement with Kashmir.
The Mahanubhava sect was founded by Chakradhara and was associated with Maharashtra.
Basaveswara founded or led the Lingayat/Veerasaiva tradition, which was associated with Karnataka and Andhra.

secs.t: Outcomes, limitations and debates

x: Bhakti-Sufi interaction produced
a composite Indo-Islamic culture
, with shrines and vernacular traditions acting as shared spaces.
In some phases, Veerashaivism spread through physical force, described as the “Sivapasa”, meaning the
sword
The movements later hardened into separate sects and panths, despite their earlier emphasis on broad spiritual and social interaction.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Bulleh Shah prioritised Tariqat over rigid Shariat, followed Wahdat-al-Wujud, used the Kafi form and regarded Shah Inayat Qadiri as his guide.
The Andhra pre-colonial reform line included
Veerashaivism and Srivaishnavism
, along with figures such as Brahmanayudu, Vemana, Veerabrahmam and Nasaraiah.
The movements preached egalitarian ideals, but caste was not dismantled and sects sometimes became new communities.

rows.title: Sikhism - the ten Gurus, Guru Granth Sahib, the Khalsa; Banda Bahadur and Ranjit Singh

secs.t: Sikhism — terms and FIRSTs

x: 'Sikh' means
disciple
, from the Sanskrit shishya. 'Pure' is the meaning of Khalsa; 'warrior' and 'brotherhood' are not the meaning of the word.
Anand Karaj includes
four
circumambulations of the Guru Granth Sahib while the Lavan hymns are sung.
The Panj Pyare were baptised with sacred nectar at its founding.
The Five Ks are Kesh, Kangha, Kara, Kachera and Kirpan.

secs.t: Gurus → contributions — Kabir and Guru Nanak

x: Kabir taught belief in one God known by many names and condemned the rituals of both faiths, advocating Hindu–Muslim unity.
Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi, now known as Nankana Sahib, near the Ravi.
Guru Nanak’s teachings included
Nirguna devotion, Ek Onkar, Naam Simran and Sangat
, while rejecting rituals of both religions.

secs.t: Gurus → contributions — The ten Gurus in order

x: Exam angle: founder, meaning of 'Sikh', successor of Nanak, Guru → contribution matching.
The order is Nanak, Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan Dev, Hargobind, Har Rai, Har Krishan, Tegh Bahadur, Gobind Singh.
Guru Hargobind militarised the Panth and was released from Gwalior Fort in 1619 along with 52 prisoners, an event associated with Bandi Chhor Divas.

secs.t: Guru Granth Sahib → compiler and contributors

x: Sheikh Farid, Namdev and Ravidas contributed to the Guru Granth Sahib.
The Guru Granth Sahib is written in the
Gurmukhi
script.
Guru Arjan
compiled the Adi Granth (APPSC 2019 named Adigranth as the Sikh scripture); Guru Gobind Singh finalised it as the Guru Granth Sahib.

secs.t: Khalsa and sacred places → Guru

x: Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa on Baisakhi, 13 April 1699, at Takht Keshgarh Sahib in Anandpur.
The Panj Pyare were the five volunteers whom Guru Gobind Singh baptised with sacred nectar at the founding of the Khalsa.
Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib at Nanded is associated with the final resting place of Guru Gobind Singh.

secs.t: Banda Bahadur and the Sikh misls — events → year

x: After Banda Bahadur, the Khalsa was organised into 12 misls, including Bhangi, Ahluwalia, Ramgarhia, Kanhaiya, Sukerchakia and Phulkian.
Ranjit Singh
, belonging to the Sukerchakia misl, unified the misls into the kingdom of Lahore.
Banda Bahadur was born Lachhman Dev, and after defeating Wazir Khan at Chappar Chiri and conquering Sirhind in 1710 he founded the first sovereign Sikh state with Lohgarh as its capital.

secs.t: Ranjit Singh → contributions, treaties and successors

x: Exam angle: capital and Treaty of Amritsar are the most-asked facts.
The Treaty of Amritsar, concluded in 1809 with Lord Minto, fixed the
Sutlej
as the boundary between the British and Ranjit Singh's territories.
The order was Kharak Singh, Nau Nihal Singh, Sher Singh and finally the minor Dalip Singh, with Rani Jindan as regent.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Akal Takht asked for the re-amendment of the
Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act, 2026
The 350th martyrdom year of Guru Tegh Bahadur was observed in 2026.
Andhra Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister
Pawan Kalyan
paid tribute at Hazur Sahib, Nanded, during the Shaheedi Samagam.
Banda Bahadur
established the first sovereign Sikh state at Sirhind in 1710.

units.title: European Trading Companies in India - Struggle for Supremacy (Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Mysore, Andhra, Nizam); Governors-General and Viceroys

rows.title: Age of discovery and the sea route to India - Vasco da Gama; motives of European expansion

secs.t: Motives of European expansion → factor and effect

x: Spices, silk, religion, wealth, prestige, rivalry and the desire to break Arab control were stated motives.
Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople in 1453, closing the main overland route through Constantinople and Central Asia to India.
The statement is attributed to
Peter the Great of Russia
and reflects the perceived global importance of Indian commerce.

secs.t: Explorers, navigation and treaties → sponsor, year and provision

x: Bartholomew Dias and Vasco da Gama were sponsored by Portugal, whereas Christopher Columbus was sponsored by Spain.
Pope Alexander VI
issued Inter caetera in 1493, dividing newly discovered lands between Spain and Portugal.
The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 divided newly claimed lands along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, assigning the eastern sphere to Portugal and the western sphere to Spain.

secs.t: Vasco da Gama — voyage, arrival at Calicut, Zamorin, later voyages

x: Exam angle: CGPSC 2022 - only "Zamorin ruled Calicut" was correct; he did not stay a year in India.
The trader
Abdul Majid
is identified as the guide who helped Vasco da Gama reach Calicut from Malindi.
The arrival is associated with the 1497–98 voyage, while both 17 May and 20 May 1498 appear in different date conventions, with 20 May used as the landing date in some examination material.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Cabral reached Brazil in 1500, two years after Vasco da Gama's 1498 arrival in India, and this historical link was recalled in the context of the Prime Minister's visit for the 17th BRICS Summit.
The years 1453 and 1498 are treated as marking the beginning of the Modern Age for India and Andhra, linking the disruption of old routes with the opening of the sea route.

rows.title: Advent of Europeans - Portuguese, Dutch, English, French and Danish
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-128

secs.t: European companies — formation, charter, first factory, order of arrival (FIRSTs)

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 asked the EIC year thrice -
. APPSC 2024 keyed the 1600 Charter as "exclusive trading rights" - not territorial or legislative powers.
The order of arrival is Portuguese (1498), Dutch (first factory Masulipatnam 1605), English (Surat farman 1613), Danes (Tranquebar 1620) and French (Surat 1668).
The States-General granted the VOC sovereign powers, including making war, constructing forts and concluding treaties.
James Lancaster
led the first English East India Company voyage in 1602, which reached Bantam.

secs.t: Persons → contributions (Portuguese governors, English envoys, founders) — Portuguese governors → years → policy

x: Francisco de Almeida
, the first Portuguese viceroy in India, followed the Blue Water Policy, which emphasised naval mastery rather than territorial expansion inland.
Albuquerque reversed Almeida's exclusively naval approach and pursued territorial conquest, including Goa, Malacca and Hormuz.
Francisco de Almeida served first from 1505–09, followed by Afonso de Albuquerque from 1509–15, and then Nino da Cunha.

secs.t: Persons → contributions (Portuguese governors, English envoys, founders) — English envoys and travellers at the Mughal court, in order

x: Francis Day
obtained the site from the Raja of Chandragiri and built Fort St. George at Madras in 1639.
Ralph Fitch visited Akbar in the 1580s, William Hawkins was at Jahangir’s court from 1608 to 1611, Sir Thomas Roe arrived in 1615, and Edward Terry accompanied Roe as chaplain.
William Hawkins came to Jahangir’s court during 1608–11 as the envoy of
James I
. He was given the title ‘English Khan’.

secs.t: Terms, policies and farmans → meaning

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 twice - Blue Water Policy =
Portuguese
Almeida
Cartaz was a naval-pass system used to regulate shipping and enforce the Portuguese maritime monopoly, along with convoys and customs duties.
Abdullah Qutb Shah of Golconda
issued the Golden Farman in 1636, granting trade concessions to the English.

secs.t: Places → power → event (settlements in India and Andhra)

x: The correct sequence is Goa in 1510, Diu in 1535, expulsion from Hooghly in 1632, and the Maratha capture of Salsette and Bassein in 1739.
Bombay formed part of Catherine of Braganza’s dowry to Charles II in 1661 and was transferred by the Crown to the Company in 1668.
Job Charnock settled at Sutanuti in 1690; the three zamindaris were bought in 1698, and Fort William was built in 1700.
Pulicat was initially Portuguese, was captured by the Dutch and became the Dutch headquarters in 1610; pepper and cloth were important commodities there.

secs.t: Battles, contributions and exits — Swally to Operation Vijay

x: Tobacco
is one of the New World crops the Portuguese brought to India, along with potato, chilli, maize, pineapple, papaya, cashew and groundnut.
The English fought the Portuguese at Jask in 1620 and Ormuz in 1622 and emerged victorious; Ormuz was taken for the Shah of Persia.
Travancore, under
Marthanda Varma
, defeated the Dutch at Colachel in 1741.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The British benefited from the steady finances of a private joint-stock company and from using the rivalries among Indian rulers.
The Portuguese naval monopoly ended with the emergence of the Dutch and English as competing maritime powers.
Andhra’s
calico and Kalamkari
were important articles connected with the region’s export trade.

rows.title: Portuguese in India - Almeida's Blue Water Policy, Albuquerque, Estado da India, Cartaz system, decline

secs.t: Portuguese settlements → year → grantor

x: Goa was taken from Bijapur in 1510, Bassein was obtained in 1534, Diu was secured by treaty in 1535 and conquered in 1546, and Daman was obtained in 1559.
Akbar granted the Portuguese permission to establish themselves at
Hugli
Pressed by Humayun, Bahadur Shah of Gujarat permitted Nino da Cunha to build the Diu fort in 1535.

secs.t: Persons → role (rulers, missionaries, Mughal opponents)

x: Almeida defeated the combined fleet of
Gujarat, the Egyptian Mamluks and the Zamorin
at Diu in 1509.
Kannada and Malayalam Bible printing is associated with the Portuguese, Xavier reached Goa in 1542, and his remains are at the Basilica of Bom Jesus.
During Aurangzeb's reign, Bengal governor
Shaista Khan
captured Sondip and Chittagong and suppressed the Arakanese pirates.

secs.t: Terms → meaning (Cartaz, Caes, Inquisition, Budata Keechu)

x: A Cartaz was a Portuguese naval trade licence or pass required for ships sailing in the Indian Ocean.
Ships without the required Cartaz could be
confiscated or sunk
by the Portuguese.
The Cartaz system was backed by the Caes convoy system and customs duties.
The Goa Inquisition in the sixteenth century acted against religious dissent and used state machinery for conversions.

secs.t: Portuguese contributions — New World crops, printing press, forts

x: Tobacco, chilli and tomato (to Telugu soil) are Portuguese introductions.
Vindaloo derives from the Portuguese expression vinha d'alhos.

secs.t: Decline — causes, Hugli piracy, territories lost

x: Portuguese raiders operating from Hugli and Chittagong acted with Arakanese pirates in the Bay of Bengal.
Shah Jahan
captured Hugli in 1632 in response to Portuguese piracy and related activities.
The Portuguese suffered defeat at Swally in 1612, off Jask in 1620, and lost Ormuz in 1622 to the English and the Shah of Persia.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Tomato, chilli and groundnut
were among the New World crops introduced by the Portuguese into the Telugu country.
The Portuguese left India in 1961; 1510 is associated with Goa becoming the first European territory in India since the time of Alexander.
Francisco de Almeida
(1505-09) was the first Viceroy.

src: Sources: CDI (Block05 Advent of Europeans; Block05 Christian Missionaries; Block11 European Trade Establishments); APP (AP History Modern-3, Modern-4; Indian History Part 2 - Portuguese); APHQ (aph2025_58, aph2019_17); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.350-351); UPSC (Modern History p.21; Art & Culture p.81); IYB (pp.580, 647)

rows.title: Dutch in India - VOC, factories (Pulicat, Machilipatnam, Nagapattinam), Battle of Colachel

secs.t: VOC — formation, charter, Asian HQ and Dutch FIRSTs

x: The VOC received sovereign powers to wage war, build forts and sign treaties; it had no power to crown the British monarch.
The VOC primarily focused on the
Spice Islands
, while India was not its central strategic focus.
Pulicat
was the chief Dutch centre until 1690, after which Nagapattinam became the chief factory.

secs.t: Persons → role in Dutch history

x: Philip II’s ban on Lisbon trade formed part of the background to Dutch expansion.

secs.t: Dutch factories → place → year

x: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
of Golconda permitted Van der Haghen to establish the Dutch factory at Machilipatnam.
Draksharama
was one of the subordinate Dutch factories in the Krishna–Godavari weaving belt.
The correct sequence is Surat (1616), Karaikal (1645), Chinsura (1653) and Nagapattinam (1658).
Mahe
was a French centre, although it is sometimes incorrectly included in lists of Dutch centres.

secs.t: Trade → exports, imports and Coromandel ports

x: Pulicat was a hub of the slave trade to Batavia, not a centre of porcelain production.
Silk and porcelain
were imported, whereas gems, diamonds, indigo, cotton, Kalamkari and cloth were among the exports.
The Dutch carried textiles from the Coromandel in exchange for
spices
from the East Indies.

secs.t: Battles, treaties and decline — Colachel (1741), Bedara (1759), Anglo-Dutch Treaty (1824)

x: Travancore under Marthanda Varma defeated the Dutch at Colachel in 1741, ending Dutch ambitions in Malabar.
The English defeated the Dutch at Bedara/Chinsura in 1759, with Francis Forde as commander, after which the Dutch withdrew to Indonesia.
The Dutch prioritised their spice monopoly in Indonesia, while Malabar was less profitable to them than the Coromandel cloth trade.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Dutch network in Andhra extended from Machilipatnam in the south-western part of the network to Bheemunipatnam in the north-east.

src: Sources: APHQ (aph2005_2, aph2017_36, aph2019_17); APP (AP History Modern-3, Modern-4; Indian History Part 2 - The Dutch); CDI (Block05 Advent of Europeans; Block11 European Trade Establishments); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.348-349); UPSC (Modern History pp.23-24)

rows.title: English East India Company - Charter of 1600, Surat, Madras, Bombay, Calcutta; Farman of 1717

secs.t: Charters → year → provision (1600 to 1708)

x: The charter initially granted a fifteen-year monopoly, later made perpetual.
The Company was run by a Governor and a 24-member committee, later known as the Court of Directors.
Charles II and James II delegated powers including coining money, exercising jurisdiction, and making war and peace with non-Christians.
Queen
Elizabeth I
granted the charter on 31 December 1600.

secs.t: Persons → contributions (captains, founders, grantors)

x: Shivaji sacked Surat twice and threatened the English factory located there.
Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
permitted the English to establish their first factory at Machilipatnam in 1611.

secs.t: Factories and Presidencies → year → founder (India and Andhra) — Factories in India

x: Exam angle: first English factory - Surat (India) vs Machilipatnam (Andhra).
Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta are associated respectively with 1612–13, 1639, 1668 and 1690/1700 in the early English settlement chronology.
Francis Day founded Madras in 1639 after obtaining a grant from the Chandragiri ruler Venkatapati Raya III, with the efforts of the Damerla brothers, Venkatadri and Ayyappa.

secs.t: Factories and Presidencies → year → founder (India and Andhra) — English on the Andhra coast

x: The Globe reached Machilipatnam in 1611 under
Captain Anthony Hippon
, marking the establishment of the first English factory in Andhra.
Armagaon was established in 1626 at Dugarajapatnam, now in Tirupati district, and was named after Karanam Armugam Mudali.
Pulicat was the second settlement, was abandoned due to Dutch hostility, Visakhapatnam was established in 1682, and Bhimili became the first municipality in Andhra in 1861.

secs.t: Farmans → ruler → privilege (Golden Farman to the Magna Carta of 1717)

x: The Golden Farman permitted free trade in Golconda ports in return for an annual payment of 500 pagodas.
The Farman of 1717 was issued by Mughal emperor
Farrukhsiyar
and substantially enhanced the Company’s trading privileges.
The Farman granted the Company the right to issue
dastaks
, or passes for duty-free trade in Bengal.

secs.t: Conflicts and trade goods → source

x: The Swally victory occurred in 1612, Jahangir’s farman followed in 1613, and further English victories occurred in 1615, off Jask in 1620 and at Ormuz in 1622.
The main sources of indigo mentioned are
Gujarat and the Coromandel region
Imported bullion
was used to pay for Indian goods in the early period of Company trade.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Company was established as a trading company in 1600 and emerged as a territorial ruling power after the Battles of Plassey in 1757 and Buxar in 1764.
The correct order is establishment of the Company in 1600, Plassey in 1757, Buxar in 1764 and the end of Company rule in 1858.

rows.title: French in India - Colbert, Compagnie des Indes, Pondicherry, Dupleix and his policy

secs.t: French East India Company — founder, nature, FIRST and LAST

x: The company received a 50-year monopoly in the Indian and Pacific Oceans together with rights over Madagascar.
The French East India Company was state-owned and depended on subsidies, making it vulnerable when sustained state support was lacking.
Abdullah Qutb Shah
granted permission for the French trading centre at Machilipatnam.
The French were the third Europeans in Andhra, Yanam was their only territory there, and it is now part of the Union Territory of Puducherry.

secs.t: French settlements → year → founder; enclaves and merger

x: Surat 1668, Pondicherry 1673-74, Yanam 1723, Mahe 1725, Karaikal 1739.
Sher Khan Lodi
, the Bijapur governor of Valikondapuram, gave the land to François Martin in 1673.
After Wandiwash and the Treaty of Paris of 1763, the French retained only the trading enclaves of Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam and Chandernagore.
The Danish company was founded in 1616; Tranquebar was established in 1620, Serampore was another Danish settlement, and the settlements were sold to the British in 1845.

secs.t: French governors and leaders → contributions (Martin to Lally)

x: Dupleix served from 1742 to 1754, Godeheu replaced him and was recalled at the start of the Third Carnatic War, while Lally lost at Wandiwash to Eyre Coote.
Dupleix intervened in the Hyderabad succession between Nasir Jang and Muzaffar Jang and in the Carnatic succession between Anwaruddin and Chanda Sahib.

secs.t: Battles and treaties → year → outcome (Ambur to Treaty of Paris)

x: The sequence is 1693, 1697, 1761 and 1763: Dutch capture, Treaty of Ryswick restoration, British capture and Treaty of Paris restoration.
The battle took place on 24 January 1757; French forces under Bussy supported Vijayaramaraju, Ranga Rao was killed, and Vijayaramaraju was later killed by Ranga Rao’s brother-in-law Tandra Papayya.

secs.t: Northern Circars → grant and loss (1753 to 1788)

x: The Northern Circars granted in 1753 comprised Mustafanagar or Kondapalli, Eluru, Rajahmundry and Chicacole or Srikakulam.
Salabat Jang granted the Northern Circars to the French to pay for Bussy's troops.
Forde captured Machilipatnam in 1759.
The transfer was the first British-Hyderabad agreement.
The other Circars became British in 1768, while Guntur followed in 1788.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Yanam
was the last French enclave on Andhra soil and remained French de facto until 1954 and de jure until 1962.
The Northern Circars grant in 1753 represented
the high point of French power in India
The Battle of Bobbili was fought in 1757, the same year as Plassey, and is among the AP-linked French events.

rows.title: Danish and other minor European settlements (Tranquebar, Serampore)

secs.t: Order of arrival and settlement → power matching

x: Exam angle: match-the-settlement-to-power (UPPSC 2016: Pondicherry-French, Goa-Portuguese, Tranquebar-Danish, Sadras-Dutch).
The Portuguese were the first among these powers to arrive, followed by the Dutch, British, Danish and French.
Pondicherry was founded as a French headquarters in 1673–74 by
Francois Martin
Chinsura was a Dutch settlement, not a Danish one.
Tranquebar and Serampore were Danish, and Chandernagore was French.

secs.t: Danish East India Company — founded (1616), settlements, sale (1845)

x: Serampore
, established in 1699 near Calcutta, became the second major Danish settlement and the focus of Danish activity in Bengal.
The commercial impact of the Danish settlements was negligible, but
their Protestant missionary, educational and linguistic work
was historically important.
The sale of Serampore and Tranquebar to the British in 1845 took place under Governor-General
Hardinge I

secs.t: Missionaries → contributions (Ziegenbalg, Schulz, Serampore Trio)

x: Exam angle: "Who translated the Bible into Telugu in 1746-47?" - Benjamin Schulz.
The Serampore Trio consisted of the Baptist missionaries
William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward
Carey, Marshman and Ward operated from Danish Serampore to bypass the early bans imposed by the East India Company on missionary activity.

secs.t: Missions, books and institutions → founder → year

x: Founded in 1706, the Danish-Halle Mission at Tranquebar was the earliest sustained Protestant mission in
South India
Serampore College was founded by Carey, Marshman and Ward in 1818.
The Telugu Bible was printed at the Serampore press during
, making it the first Telugu Bible printed in India.

secs.t: Ostend and Swedish companies — brief presence

x: The Ostend Company of the Austrian Netherlands was chartered in 1722.
The Ostend Company’s Indian activities were suspended within a decade under British-Dutch pressure.
The Swedish East India Company was established in 1731, focused mainly on trade with China, and had only a negligible presence in India.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Danish legacy was primarily educational and linguistic, reflected in printing, vernacular Bible translation and Serampore College, rather than commercial dominance.
The Danes left in 1845, while the French were the last to arrive in 1664.
Lutheran missions centred on Guntur and Baptist missions on Ongole.

rows.title: Advent of Europeans in Andhra - Portuguese, Dutch, French and English
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-133

secs.t: FIRST and LAST — order of factories at Machilipatnam; Nellore

x: Abdullah Qutb Shah
permitted the French to establish their factory at Machilipatnam in 1669.
The order was Dutch in 1605, English in 1611, French in 1669 and Portuguese in 1670.
Armagaon was located at
Durgarajapatnam
, about 35 miles north of Pulicat.
The Masulipatnam factory of 1611 marked the beginning of the Company's territorial expansion in the south.

secs.t: Policies → power → meaning

x: The Blue Water Policy belonged to the Portuguese, spice monopoly and own coins to the Dutch, and dadni advances and dubashes to the English.
The English gave dadni advances to weavers through local intermediaries known as dubashes.
The Portuguese held the Arabian Sea trade monopoly until the seventeenth century
, and their decline began with the Dutch arrival in 1605.

secs.t: French settlements in Andhra — Machilipatnam (1669) to Yanam (1723)

x: The French Company was established in 1664 under
Colbert
's initiative.
The French established themselves at Surat in 1668, Machilipatnam in 1669 and Pondicherry during 1673–74.
Yanam, acquired in 1723, was
the only French territorial possession in Andhra

secs.t: Battles and events → year → outcome (Anglo-French rivalry in Andhra)

x: Colonel Forde
, who was sent from Bengal, defeated the French forces commanded by Conflans at Chandurthi in 1758.
The correct order is the grant of the Circars to the French in 1753, the Bobbili War in 1757, the Battle of Chandurthi in 1758, and the fall of Masulipatnam in 1759.

secs.t: Missionaries → contributions in Andhra

x: Christian missionaries contributed significantly to education in Andhra and established schools, including the school founded by Rev.
Benjamin Schultze
, a German Lutheran missionary, completed the first Telugu Bible translation around 1732.
Robert Noble founded the Machilipatnam school in 1843 (APPSC 2011).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Dutch, Portuguese and French advanced money and paid fairly, whereas the English paid less while demanding high-quality goods, causing weavers to avoid them.
Machilipatnam attracted all four European powers because of its important chintz and diamond trade.
The
Dutch
were the first to get the right to mint coins in Andhra, granted by local rulers.

rows.title: Trade centres of coastal Andhra - Masulipatnam, Nizampatnam, Bheemunipatnam, Yanam
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-133

secs.t: Exports and imports → centres

x: Saltpetre was exported from Machilipatnam, Narsapur and Pulicat; diamonds came from Golconda and Kollur; indigo from Nagulavancha and Nalgonda; and salt from Pedaganjam and Chinaganjam.
Textiles
were the dominant pre-colonial industry and stood second only to diamonds in the Qutb Shahi economy.
Bullion
brought from Europe financed English purchases of chintz, calico and muslin.

secs.t: Ports and trade centres → period and feature

x: Under
the Qutb Shahis of Golconda
, Masulipatnam was the Sultanate’s main maritime gateway, and its customs revenue contributed to Golconda’s wealth.
The bans imposed by England in 1700 and 1721 did not seriously affect Andhra because other markets remained open.
Motupalli
was an important Kakatiya port, and Ganapatideva’s Abhaya Sasanam protected foreign traders there.

secs.t: European factories → power and year (Yanam, Bheemunipatnam)

x: The Dutch established a factory at Pulicat in 1610.
Madapollam was associated with the English, not the French.
Yanam merged into the Indian Union in 1954, while the de jure transfer occurred in 1962.
A Dutch cemetery
survives at Bheemunipatnam.
Bheemunipatnam had a Dutch subordinate factory, later an English factory, and Bhimili became Andhra’s first municipality in 1861.

secs.t: Merchants, texts and terms of trade → meaning

x: The
Komatis
played the key role among the merchant communities of Masulipatnam.
Mughra and Theliyaneta
were the weaving groups associated with Masulipatnam.
Chintz was glazed and became brighter after washing
The term
odaberam
was used for sea-going ships in the Shuka Saptati.
Haravilasam
, dedicated to Avachi Tippaya Setti, is the Reddi sea-trade text (APPSC 2019 key), not Kashikhandam.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Machilipatnam
is one of the four new ports under construction, the other three being Mulapeta, Ramayapatnam and Kakinada SEZ.
The proposed Nizampatnam and Vodarevu ports are under the PPP-BOOT model and were on hold during a CBI investigation.
Both the assertion and reason are true, and the high Company-era duties explain the adverse effect on Andhra’s domestic and foreign trade.

rows.title: First Carnatic War - causes, Battle of St. Thome, Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle

secs.t: First Carnatic War — belligerents, causes and European link

x: The English navy seized French ships; France retaliated, and the French, using a fleet from Mauritius, captured Madras in 1746.
The First Carnatic War (1746-48) was fought between the English and French East India Companies (APPSC 2018) as an extension of the War of Austrian Succession.

secs.t: Persons → role in the First war

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk sent Anwaruddin as guardian of the minor Nawab Syed Ali.
Anwaruddin opposed fighting in his territory, supported the English, suffered defeat at St. Thome, and was later killed at Ambur in 1749 during the Second Carnatic War.

secs.t: Battle of St. Thome and Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle → date, terms, results

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2020/2025 - "war ended" and "English got back Madras" are both correct.
A small French force under
Captain Paradis
defeated the army of the Nawab of Carnatic at St. Thome.
The battle showed the superiority of disciplined European infantry over a much larger Indian army and opened the way for European interference in Indian politics.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle restored the pre-war position, while the Treaty of Paris in 1763 marked the end of French political power in India.

rows.title: Second Carnatic War - Anwaruddin, Chanda Sahib, Muhammad Ali; Robert Clive at Arcot

secs.t: Trigger and claimants → throne and backer

x: The disputes were triggered by the death of Nizam-ul-Mulk in 1748 and the release of Chanda Sahib, who had earlier been held by the Marathas.
The French backed Muzaffar Jang (Hyderabad) and Chanda Sahib (Carnatic).
Nasir Jang was Nizam-ul-Mulk's son and Muzaffar Jang was his daughter's son.
Anwaruddin was supported by the English and Chanda Sahib by the French.

secs.t: Battles and events → year and outcome

x: Exam angle: CGPSC 2023 - a statement that Ambur was fought in 1752 is wrong; it was
Bussy immediately installed
Salabat Jang
, the fourth son of Nizam-ul-Mulk, after Muzaffar Jang was killed.
Law first surrendered; Chanda Sahib surrendered in June 1752, was executed, and Muhammad Ali subsequently became Nawab of the Carnatic.

secs.t: Persons → role

x: Mysore, Tanjore and the Maratha chief Morari Rao joined the English.
Robert Clive and Stringer Lawrence
relieved Trichinopoly.
Godeheu
succeeded Dupleix in 1754 and made peace with the English.
Dupleix was recalled in 1754, in connection with the settlement of the Second Carnatic War.

secs.t: Rewards to Dupleix and his recall (1754)

x: Dupleix was declared Governor or Nawab of Mughal territory south of the Krishna and received Valapadu as a jagir.
The rewards included Valapadu, Villianur, Bahur, Diviseema and Machilipatnam.
The French Company became alarmed by the heavy expense and failures of Dupleix's interventionist policy, particularly the defeat at Trichinopoly, and recalled him in 1754.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The war centred on Indian political disputes, demonstrated the territorial and revenue advantages of backing claimants, and brought major French gains on the Andhra coast.
Dupleix succeeded in the Deccan, particularly through influence at Hyderabad, but lost the Carnatic struggle at Arcot and Trichinopoly.
The main French territorial gains on the Andhra coast were
Machilipatnam, Diviseema and the Northern Circars

rows.title: Third Carnatic War - Battle of Wandiwash, Treaty of Paris (1763); reasons for English success

secs.t: War → European link, Bengal resources and Treaty of Paris

x: Exam angle: "Third Carnatic War concluded by the Treaty of ___ in 1763" - Paris.
The Third Carnatic War was the Indian theatre of the Seven Years' War, fought from 1756 to 1763.
After Clive's victory at Plassey in 1757 and the capture of French Chandernagore, Bengal revenue helped finance the English Carnatic campaign.

secs.t: Battles and events → date, place, victor

x: The victory at Chandurti
drove the French out of the Northern Circars
and was later described as a small battle with great results.
Eyre Coote led the English victory over Count de Lally at Wandiwash, where Bussy was taken prisoner.
Lally captured Fort St. David at Cuddalore in 1758 but failed before Madras because he lacked money and naval support.

secs.t: Persons → role
Reasons for English success and French failure

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2016 - both "Bengal wealth and manpower" and "naval superiority" are correct reasons.
The English company was privately organised, with a yearly elected board and relatively quicker decision-making.
Both statements are true, and dependence on royal subsidy and a state-controlled structure directly contributed to French financial weakness.
Lally's quarrels with his officers and inadequate understanding of Indian conditions weakened the French effort.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The victories at Chandurti and Machilipatnam gave the English their first foothold in the Northern Circars.
Chandurti is described as the foundation of British rule in Andhra, in a parallel often drawn with
Plassey
as the foundation of British rule in India.
The Battle of Chandurti or Condore took place on
7 December 1758
near Rajahmundry.

rows.title: Anglo-French rivalry - the three Carnatic Wars and the English ascendancy
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-136

secs.t: Wars → years, European context, treaty and participants — Wars, causes and treaties

x: Exam angle: match-the-pair of war and treaty; "Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle ended the First war and returned Madras" - both correct.
Madras was captured in 1746, the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle was signed in 1748, the Treaty of Pondicherry followed in 1754, and the Treaty of Paris was concluded in 1763.
The Third Carnatic War was connected with the
Seven Years’ War
of 1756–63 and began before the Treaty of Pondicherry could be ratified.

secs.t: Wars → years, European context, treaty and participants — Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) - terms

x: The Seven Years' War broke out before the treaty was ratified by England and France, thereby beginning the Third Carnatic War.
Anwaruddin supported the
English
during the First Carnatic War, which was fought between the British and the French.
Nasir Jang was the son and Muzaffar Jang the grandson of Nizam-ul-Mulk.

secs.t: Commanders and governors → side, war and role — Commanders → side and war

x: La Bourdonnais
, the French governor of Mauritius, captured Madras or Fort St. George in 1746.
Colonel
Francis Forde
led the English forces at Chandurti in 1758 and captured Machilipatnam in 1759.
Count de Lally, the French commander and Governor in the Third Carnatic War, captured Fort St. David in 1758 and surrendered Pondicherry on 16 January 1761.

secs.t: Commanders and governors → side, war and role — Admirals

x: Exam angle: Count de Lally = Third Carnatic War; defeated at Wandiwash.
La Bourdonnais agreed to return Madras to the English in return for a ransom, but Dupleix overruled him and kept the city.
d'Ache was the French admiral and Pocock was the English admiral.

secs.t: Battles → year, war and victor

x: During the Second Carnatic War, Clive defeated
Raja Sahib and Chanda Sahib
at Arni and Kaveripak in 1751–52.
Chendurthi was fought on 7 December 1758, Wandiwash on 22 January 1760, Ambur in 1749 and Arcot in 1751.
Eyre Coote defeated Lally at Wandiwash on 22 January 1760 during the Third Carnatic War, and Bussy was taken prisoner.

secs.t: Reasons for English success over the French

x: The English navy defeated
d’Aché’s fleet off Pondicherry
(1759), after which he withdrew to Mauritius.
French difficulties included the recall of Dupleix, Lally’s quarrels and unpaid troops, failures at Madras and Thanjavur, and the withdrawal of Bussy from Hyderabad.
Robert
Clive, Stringer Lawrence and Eyre Coote
were identified as better English commanders who contributed to English success.

secs.t: French in Andhra → places, events and enclaves

x: The Northern Circars were granted to the French in 1753, the Treaty of Charmahal followed the Tumnapalem victory in 1756, the Battle of Bobbili occurred on 24 January 1757, and Chendurthi was fought in 1758.
Yanam, French from 1723, is an enclave inside AP's Godavari delta but is administered as part of Puducherry UT.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The wars showed the military effectiveness of disciplined European infantry and established the English as kingmakers of South India.
Both statements are true, and the military events at Bobbili and Chendurthi and the fall of Machilipatnam explain why the Andhra struggle decided control over the Northern Circars.

rows.title: Bengal - Murshid Quli Khan to Siraj-ud-Daula; Black Hole episode; Battle of Plassey (1757)

secs.t: Nawabs of Bengal → period and key act

x: Murshid Quli Khan wanted the English to pay customs duties, but the English increased their military establishment instead.
Murshid Quli Khan
, Nawab from 1717 and founder of the autonomous Bengal Nawabi, was the last Subahdar of Bengal appointed by the Mughal Emperor.
Alivardi Khan was Deputy Governor of Bihar, opposed the fortification of Calcutta and Chandernagore, and was succeeded by his grandson Siraj-ud-Daula.

secs.t: Terms → meaning (revenue and trade)

x: Ijaradari was revenue farming: contractors called ijaradars collected the land revenue (APPSC 2018), the contract-based collection also called mal jasmani under Murshid Quli Khan.
Conversion of jagir land into khalisa brought the land under direct state control for revenue purposes.
The 1717 farman allowed duty-free Company trade, but Company servants misused dastaks for private trade, causing the Nawab to lose revenue.

secs.t: Siraj-ud-Daula and the English → causes of conflict

x: All three developments intensified the conflict: unauthorised fortification, English refusal to stop it, and asylum to Krishna Das.
Ghaseti Begum and Shaukat Jang of Purnea
were court factions whom the English were perceived to support against Siraj-ud-Daula.

secs.t: Events 1756-57 → date

x: J.Z. Holwell
, one of the survivors, gave the principal account on which the story of the Black Hole largely rests.
The usual account says 146 English prisoners were confined and about 120 died (Holwell's own figure was 123).
Kasimbazar was seized in May 1756, Calcutta fell in June 1756, Clive and Watson recaptured it in January 1757, and the Treaty of Alinagar followed in February 1757.

secs.t: Battles → year; Plassey vs Buxar debate

x: Plassey is generally viewed as a victory of treachery and a political-financial arrangement rather than a prolonged contest between equally matched armies.
Buxar
, fought in 1764, is regarded as the real military test and confirmed the political result achieved at Plassey.
Plassey is commonly called the foundation of British rule, but Buxar is treated in some examination assessments as the most significant or decisive battle.

secs.t: Persons → called as / known as

x: Mir Jafar was the puppet Nawab installed after Plassey.
William Pitt the Elder
called Robert Clive a heaven-born general.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The deal associated with Clive's conspiracy at Plassey involved Jagat Seth, Omichund and Mir Jafar.
Plassey is characterised as a conspiracy, while Buxar is characterised as an open military victory.
The 269th anniversary of Plassey was noted in
June 2026
The numbers associated with the Black Hole episode remain a subject of historical criticism and debate.

rows.title: Mir Jafar, Mir Qasim and the Battle of Buxar (1764); Treaty of Allahabad (1765) and Diwani
sub: Group-II S1-62: Rise of British power - Battle of Plassey, Battle of Buxar and the Diwani of Bengal

secs.t: Terms → meaning (farman, dastak, Diwani, Nizamat)

x: Farrukhsiyar's 1717 farman allowed the Company to trade in Bengal without customs duties for a fixed payment of Rs 3,000 a year.
The 1717 farman granted important trading privileges to the Company and is popularly called the
Magna Carta of the Company
A dastak was a free pass that enabled duty-free trade.

secs.t: Battle of Plassey (1757) — year, location, commanders, conspirators

x: Clive's much smaller force defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey; Siraj was the last independent Nawab and had French support.
The British used the deaths of prisoners in the Black Hole episode as a pretext for launching war against Siraj-ud-Daulah.
After Plassey, the Company obtained the zamindari of the 24 Parganas, duty-free trade in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, and resources to fight the French.

secs.t: Nawabs of Bengal → tenure and acts (Mir Jafar, Mir Qasim, Najm-ud-Daula) — Nawabs of Bengal in sequence

x: Shuja-ud-din was too powerful to heed the court orders of 1735; Sarfaraz Khan was killed by Alivardi; Alivardi stopped the fortifications; and Siraj-ud-Daulah killed Shaukat Jang at Manihari.
Mir Qasim was regarded as a reformer, ruled Bengal from 1760 to 1763 and fought at the Battle of Buxar.
Murshid Quli Khan
(1717-27) was the last Subahdar appointed by the Mughal Emperor (UPPSC 2021 key).

secs.t: Nawabs of Bengal → tenure and acts (Mir Jafar, Mir Qasim, Najm-ud-Daula) — Mir Jafar — two tenures, Dutch intrigue, removal

x: Mir Jafar plotted with
the Dutch
against the English, but Clive defeated the Dutch at Chinsura or Bidara in 1759, after which the Dutch left India.
Mir Jafar was removed in 1760 because he could not meet the increasing demands of the Company.

secs.t: Nawabs of Bengal → tenure and acts (Mir Jafar, Mir Qasim, Najm-ud-Daula) — Mir Qasim — accession, reforms, trade duties and conflict

x: By abolishing internal duties, Mir Qasim placed Indian merchants on an equal footing with English merchants and removed the advantage that Company servants obtained through misuse of dastaks.
Mir Qasim
(1760-63) moved the capital to Monghyr (Munger) in Bihar and abolished all inland duties, so Indian merchants paid the same as the English.

secs.t: Battle of Buxar (1764) — allies, commander, outcome; Buxar vs Plassey

x: Mir Qasim was the deposed Nawab of Bengal, Shuja-ud-Daulah was Nawab of Awadh, Shah Alam II was the Mughal Emperor, and Hector Munro commanded the British forces.

All four statements describe the consequences recorded after the English victory at Buxar: Shuja fled, sought assistance, surrendered, Awadh and Allahabad were occupied, and Shah Alam II joined the English.

secs.t: Treaty of Allahabad (1765), Diwani and treaty chronology — Treaty of Allahabad - parties and terms

x: Under the Dual Government, the Company enjoyed the financial power of Diwani, while the Nawab formally retained Nizamat and associated responsibilities.
Robert Clive returned as
Governor of Bengal for the second time
in May 1765 and concluded the Treaty of Allahabad later that year.
Shuja-ud-Daula paid a war indemnity of Rs 50 lakh and recovered the rest of his dominions, while Kora and Allahabad were given to Shah Alam II.

secs.t: Treaty of Allahabad (1765), Diwani and treaty chronology — Grant of Diwani

x: Exam angle: "Which treaty followed Buxar?" The answer is Allahabad, not Salbai, Bassein or Sugauli.
Buxar (October 1764), Clive's return (May 1765), the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) and Warren Hastings as Governor (1772):
C, D, A, B
. The other orders put Allahabad before Clive's return, Clive before Buxar, or Hastings before Allahabad.

secs.t: Dual Government (1765-72) → division, criticism and end

x: In 1772, Warren Hastings ended the Mughal pretence and ruled Bengal by right of conquest.

secs.t: Robert Clive — titles and record

x: Clive is called the founder of the British Empire in India (APPSC 2019), and William Pitt called him a 'heaven-born general'.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Dual Government separated power from responsibility.
Buxar and Allahabad made the Company the real ruler of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, while the Mughal Emperor became its pensioner.
Control over Bengal's revenue transformed the Company from a trader into a territorial power and provided funds for its subsequent conquests.

rows.title: Dual Government in Bengal and its consequences; the Bengal Famine of 1770

secs.t: Dual Government — basis, structure and terms

x: The Second Treaty of Allahabad in 1765 enabled Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II to grant the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company.
B is the odd one out: the Dual Government arose from a LACK of British manpower for civil administration, not to provide adequate manpower.
The Company did not initially collect revenue itself; it operated through Indian deputies.

secs.t: Persons → roles in Dual Government

x: Exam angle: "The dual system was enforced by" - Robert Clive (not Warren Hastings, who abolished it).
Robert Clive
introduced the Dual Government in Bengal during his second term as Governor of Bengal from 1765 to 1767.
Muhammad Reza Khan was Naib Diwan at Murshidabad, Shitab Rai was Naib Diwan in Bihar, Clive introduced the system, and Hastings abolished it.

secs.t: Abolition (1772), FIRSTs and LASTs

x: Exam angle: BPSC 1996 asked "who abolished Dual Government" - Warren Hastings.
Hastings’ action was described as tearing the mask of Mughal sovereignty and asserting rule over Bengal by right of conquest.
Warren Hastings was the last Governor of Bengal from 1772 to 1773 and became the first Governor-General of Bengal in 1773.

secs.t: Consequences of Dual Government — factor → effect

x: Company agents forced weavers to sell their products at low prices, contributing to the decline of handicrafts.
Mir Qasim abolished internal duties for all traders in protest against the Company servants’ misuse of duty-free dastaks.
In under two decades, Bengal was reduced to
acute poverty, famines and epidemics
despite its earlier wealth.

secs.t: Bengal Famine of 1770 — areas, causes, mortality, Company response

x: Exam angle: "Governor during the 1770 famine" - John Cartier; "Famine and Dual Government" - direct cause-effect.
The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 occurred during
John Cartier
's term as governor, which lasted from 1769 to 1772.
The famine came under the
Dual Government
(1765-72), when the Company held revenue power without responsibility and kept squeezing revenue as the famine spread.

secs.t: Sanyasi-Fakir rebellion and Anandamath — revolt, leaders, book

x: The revolt was caused by
the famine of 1770, Company insensitivity and restrictions on pilgrims
visiting holy places.
The participants included Hindu Sanyasis, Muslim Fakirs, dispossessed zamindars and peasants.
Majnum Shah, Bhawani Pathak and Devi Chaudhurani were associated with the revolt;
Shah Alam II
was not a leader of it.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Both statements are true, and the Company's formal control over revenue provides the basis for tracing the drain of wealth and deindustrialisation to the arrangement.
The Guntur famine of 1832–33 and the Kurnool famine of 1866 were separate Andhra famines, distinct from the Bengal Famine of 1770.

rows.title: Anglo-Mysore Wars I-IV - Haidar Ali, Tipu Sultan, Treaty of Mangalore and Srirangapatnam

secs.t: Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan → contributions

x: Exam angle: statement questions on "French embassy + navy" point to Tipu, not Haidar or the Wodeyars.
Haidar Ali adopted Western military techniques and established a modern arsenal at Dindigul with French help.
Tipu Sultan supported the Jacobin Club at Seringapatam, became a member, used the title ‘Citizen Tipu’ and planted a Tree of Liberty.

secs.t: Other persons → roles in the Mysore wars

x: Velu Nachiyar
of Sivaganga recovered her kingdom with Haidar Ali's help and is called the first queen to wage war against the British (APPSC-G1 2022).
In 1790, Tipu Sultan defeated the British army under
General Meadows
during the Third Anglo-Mysore War.
Arthur Wellesley served in
the campaign of the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War
and later became known as the Duke of Wellington.

secs.t: Battles of the Anglo-Mysore Wars — year, war, result

x: Cornwallis's coalition won at Seringapatam in 1792 and Tipu sued for peace.
Tipu Sultan was killed on
while defending Seringapatam during the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

secs.t: Treaties of the Mysore wars — year and terms

x: The Nizam got the areas from the Krishna to beyond the Pennar (ii), the Marathas got the areas around the Tungabhadra (iii), and the British got Malabar, Coorg, Dindigul and the Bara Mahal (i).
After the Fourth War, Mysore was partitioned, the Hindu Wodeyar dynasty was restored, the boy ruler Krishnaraja Wodeyar III was installed, and the state was placed under a Subsidiary Alliance.

secs.t: Nizam and Marathas — side in each war

x: Haidar Ali used diplomacy to win over the Marathas and detach the Nizam from the British during the First Anglo-Mysore War.
In the First Anglo-Mysore War, the Nizam initially joined the British but was subsequently detached from them by Haidar Ali.
Both the Nizam and the Marathas were with the British in the
Third Anglo-Mysore War
, forming part of the grand alliance.

secs.t: Places → feature — Srirangapatna monuments

x: Daria Daulat Bagh was a summer palace with war murals, the Gumbaz is the mausoleum of Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan, and Jamia Masjid is also known as Masjid-e-Ala.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Third Anglo-Mysore War ended Tipu Sultan's supremacy in the south.
The Fourth Anglo-Mysore War removed the French-backed threat and brought Mysore and Andhra, through the Ceded Districts, under the Company.
The Ceded Districts were
Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur and Bellary

rows.title: The Nizam of Hyderabad, Subsidiary Alliance, and the cession of the Northern Circars
sub: Group-II S1-64: Subsidiary Alliance and the Doctrine of Lapse; annexation policy

secs.t: Nizams → reign and key events

x: After joining the British against Tipu Sultan during 1790–1792, Nizam Ali Khan obtained lands from
the Krishna to beyond the Pennar
After the defeat at Kharda in 1795, Nizam Ali Khan blamed Sir John Shore's neutrality, dismissed his British battalions and relied on French troops under Raymond.
Afzal-ud-Daula
, or Asaf Jah V, ruled from 1857 to 1869, was the Nizam during the Revolt of 1857 and received the title “Star of India” for his loyalty.
Salar Jung I served
Nasir-ud-Daula, Afzal-ud-Daula and Mir Mahbub Ali Khan
, dying in 1883 during the period of the latter's reign.

secs.t: Persons → roles at Hyderabad and in the Circars — British Residents, envoys and rivals

x: Resident
James Kirkpatrick
reported the Nizam's French battalions in the 1790s and pushed him into the Subsidiary Alliance of 1798.
James Kirkpatrick built the Hyderabad Residency building, which was popularly known as the
Koti
Kandregula Jogipantulu
proposed the lease (at Rs 15 lakh, finally Rs 9 lakh in 1766), became Majumdar of Rajamahendravaram and got the title 'Raja Bahadur' (APPSC G2 2019 key).

secs.t: Persons → roles at Hyderabad and in the Circars — 1857 at Hyderabad and the Salar Jungs

x: Turrebaz Khan attacked the Residency on 17 July 1857 in an attempt to free Chida Khan, but Davidson repulsed the attack.

secs.t: Northern Circars and Guntur — grants and treaties → year — Grant and lease

x: Under the 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad, the Northern Circars were leased to the British for military aid or an annual payment of ₹9 lakh.
The Mughal firman granting the Circars to the East India Company was issued by
Shah Alam II
in 1765, though some sources date it to 1766.
Nizam Ali initially refused to accept Shah Alam II's firman and agreed to lease the Circars in 1766.

secs.t: Northern Circars and Guntur — grants and treaties → year — Guntur Circar

x: Exam angle: "Area of conflict between Nizam Ali and the British" =
Guntur Circar
, not the Northern Circars as a whole.
Guntur Circar
was the area of conflict because it was held by Nizam Ali's brother, Basalat Jung.
Basalat Jung died in 1782.

secs.t: Subsidiary Alliance — aims, terms and effects

x: Wellesley designed the system to counter French influence and establish British paramountcy without assuming the cost of direct administration.
Wellesley sought to exclude French influence seen in the Nizam's French battalions under Raymond and Tipu Sultan's French connections.
The alliance reduced sovereignty, imposed financial burdens, caused territorial cessions such as the Nizam's Ceded Districts and increased dependence on the Company.
The disbanded soldiers of allied states were left without work, creating additional social and political discontent.

secs.t: Subsidiary Alliance — order of signing, FIRSTs, refusals

x: Exam angle: "First Indian state to sign the Subsidiary Alliance" = Hyderabad.
Hyderabad accepted in 1798, Awadh in 1801, the Peshwa in 1802 and Scindia in 1804.
Mysore accepted the Subsidiary Alliance in 1799.
Tipu's refusal led to the Fourth Mysore War.
Holkar, Bharatpur, Jodhpur, Jaipur and Bundi
entered into the arrangement in 1818.

secs.t: Ceded Districts (1800) and other Andhra transfers — places

x: The ceded territories of Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur and Bellary were known as Dattamandalalu, or the Ceded Districts.
The Andhra Mahasabha at Nandyal, presided over by
Dr S. Radhakrishnan
, approved the name Rayalaseema proposed by Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao.
The 1801 acquisition of Nellore and Chittoor completed Company control over the Andhra region, which Wellesley merged into the Madras Presidency.

secs.t: Policies towards Indian states → author — Revision table

x: Awadh was developed as a buffer after Buxar (1764) under the 1765 Treaty of Allahabad, and Hastings sold Kora and Allahabad to its Nawab.
Lord Dalhousie
pursued annexation for misgovernment, including the annexation of Awadh in 1856.
Dalhousie's annexation policy (from 1848) is the
Doctrine of Lapse
(APPSC-GS 2018 key).

secs.t: Policies towards Indian states → author — Subordinate isolation and the Rajput alliances (Lord Hastings)

x: Charles Metcalfe
negotiated the treaties with the Rajput states in 1818 under Lord Hastings.
The alliances aimed to protect the Rajput states from the Marathas and Pindaris, bring them under British paramountcy and isolate them from Maratha powers.
Lord Hastings
pursued subordinate isolation during 1813–1823, binding each princely state separately to the paramount Company.

secs.t: Dalhousie's annexations — state → year → ground

x: Punjab annexed 1849
(the key there is blank, but 1849 is correct).
The correct sequence is Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1849), Jhansi (1853) and Nagpur (1854).
Berar was taken from the Nizam in 1853 on account of
arrears
Awadh
was annexed in 1856 on the ground of maladministration, based on Outram's reports.
The Udaipur referred to in the annexation list was Udaipur in
Chhattisgarh
, not the larger princely state of Udaipur in Mewar.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Hyderabad was the first state tied to Wellesley's system, and its territorial cessions were central to the formation of British Andhra.
Telangana
remained under the Nizam, whereas the Northern Circars and Ceded Districts together broadly correspond to Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema.
The annexations and Awadh takeover turned
rulers, taluqdars and sepoys
against the Company, contributing to the revolt.

rows.title: Andhra region under the Company - Machilipatnam, Ceded Districts, early administration and revenue
sub: Group-II M1-A-54: Andhra under the Company - acquisition of the Northern Circars and the Ceded Districts
Group-II M1-A-55: Company administration in Andhra - districts, revenue and judicial arrangements

secs.t: Regions → how they came to the Company — Circars, Ceded Districts, Carnatic — Northern Circars and the Mughal grant

x: Robert Clive secured the firman from
Shah Alam II
; the firman is dated 1765 in the detailed chronology.
Since the Nizam initially refused to accept the firman, the Company negotiated a lease of the Circars from him in 1766.
The territories changed hands during the Mysore conflicts and were finally ceded by the Nizam in 1800 under the Subsidiary Alliance arrangement.

secs.t: Regions → how they came to the Company — Circars, Ceded Districts, Carnatic — Ceded Districts - names

x: Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
suggested the name, which was adopted at the Andhra Mahasabha at Nandyal in 1928 (APPSC G2 2012 key).
Nellore and Chittoor were once under
Aravidu Sriranga Raya III
and later formed part of the Carnatic.
After the Second Carnatic War, the British installed
Muhammad Ali
as Nawab of the Carnatic, though his position became secure only after 1763.

secs.t: Persons → roles in Company Andhra — Company officials

x: Thomas Munro
became the first Collector of the Ceded Districts in 1800, with sub-collectors stationed at Harpanahalli, Kadapa, Adoni and Kurnool.
Munro introduced Ryotwari and surveyed the Ceded Districts during 1802–07.
Thomas Munro was Governor of Madras from 1820 to 1827.
C.P. Brown studied Telugu thoroughly and published Vemana’s verses as well as a Telugu-English dictionary.

secs.t: Persons → roles in Company Andhra — Kandregula Jogipantulu - intermediary in the Circar lease

x: Kandregula Jogipantulu was a prominent dubashi and envoy who acted between the Nizam's court and the Company's men at Machilipatnam.
After the defeat, the minor son Narayana Babu was made zamindar and George Russell was placed in charge of Vizianagaram’s forts.
Tandra Papayya
, brother-in-law of Bobbili Ranga Rao, later killed Vijayaramaraju to avenge the destruction of Bobbili.

secs.t: Treaties and battles → year

x: Salabat Jung's grant belongs to 1759, the Circar lease to 1766, the Treaty of Masulipatnam to 1768 and the Treaty of Hyderabad to 1798.
The Treaty of Masulipatnam allowed the Company to retain the Circars for a reduced annual peshkash of 9 lakh rupees, along with military assistance to the Nizam.

secs.t: Zamindaris → family and status

x: Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram were pre-existing estates brought under the Permanent Settlement
The hereditary zamindari families of the Northern Circars included
Velamas, Reddis and Kshatriya Rajus
Venkatagiri in Nellore was the zamindari of the
Velugoti family
Peddapuram was associated with the Vatsavayi dynasty.

secs.t: Early administration — Chiefs and Councils, Circuit Committee, Collector, Board of Revenue — Factories and the Chiefs and Councils

x: Before acquiring the Circars, the East India Company maintained factories at
Machilipatnam and Visakhapatnam

Provincial Chiefs and Councils at Masulipatnam and Vizagapatnam governed the Circars; the supervising revenue body over these stations is called the 'Board of Revenue' in some sources; and district Collectors replaced the arrangement in 1794, when that body was abolished.

secs.t: Early administration — Chiefs and Councils, Circuit Committee, Collector, Board of Revenue — Collector system

x: From 1794 the Collector handled land revenue, law and order and acted as magistrate.
Collectors lost their judicial powers in 1816, and civil justice remained with District Judges.
The Board of Revenue was at the state level, the Collector at the district level, the Tahsildar at the taluk level and the Karanam and Munsab at the village level.

secs.t: Districts and headquarters → year of formation

x: Exam angle: year of a district's creation (Kadapa 1911 trap), and the count of collectorates by 1856.
The Ceded region functioned as one collectorate centred at
Anantapur
under Munro until 1808.
The five coastal collectorates were Ganjam, Visakhapatnam, Godavari, Krishna and Nellore.
The initial eight collectorates included Ganjam, Bellary and Kurnool, but not Chittoor.

secs.t: Revenue terms → meaning — Moturpha, Peshkash, Haveli, Sayer, Abkari

x: Exam angle: statement pairs. "Moturpha is a salt tax" is false; "Peshcush is the revenue collected from zamindars" is true.
Sayer
was the tax imposed on inland transit and customs duties on goods.
Moturpha was imposed on trades and occupations, including looms, shops and artisans.
The Madras Native Association's petition of 1861 complained about the burden of
Moturpha

secs.t: Revenue systems — Permanent Settlement areas vs Ryotwari areas

x: The Permanent Settlement introduced
a fixed revenue demand
in place of the auctioning of zamindaris.
Zamindari applied to estates such as Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram; Ryotwari dealt directly with the ryot; and Mahalwari involved collection through village headmen.
Ryotwari areas experienced heavy assessment, often exceeding 50 percent of the produce, along with dependence on moneylenders and alienation of land.

secs.t: Judiciary and police — courts, codes, Munro's reforms

x: Munro presided over the Judicial Commission in 1814, whose report was submitted in April 1816 and was largely accepted.
The Madras Regulations of 1816 established Munsiff courts and Panchayat courts in every large village and district as courts of first instance.
Traditional village watchmen continued but were
supplemented by a central police force under a District Superintendent
Munro's changes in 1816 transferred police supervision from
judges to Collectors

secs.t: Chronology of Andhra colonial events (revision)

x: The firman was issued in 1765, the treaty transferring the Circars was concluded in 1766, and the Treaty of Masulipatnam settled the dispute in 1768.
The correct order is Treaty of Masulipatnam (1768), Guntur handed over (1788), Battle of Padmanabham (1794), and Subsidiary Alliance (1798).
The events occurred in 1788, 1794, 1820 and 1948 respectively: Guntur, Padmanabham, extension of Ryotwari, and abolition of zamindari.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Circars came under Company control in 1766, Guntur in 1788, the Ceded Districts in 1800 and Nellore-Chittoor in 1801.
The contrasting development of the Circars and the Ceded Districts later shaped the
Sri Bagh Pact
debate.
The plea invoked
Article 14
and argued that officers without legal training should not adjudicate land-title disputes.
