rows.title: Establishment of British rule in Andhra - administrative consolidation and its effects
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-142

secs.t: Districts and the Collector → year of formation

x: In 1859, Rajahmundry and Machilipatnam were reorganised into Godavari and Krishna districts respectively.
The correct order is 1802, 1859, 1904 and 1925: union of collectorates, reorganisation into Godavari and Krishna, formation of Guntur and East Godavari, and formation of West Godavari.
From 1819, the Collector in Ganjam also acted as Agent to the Governor for the Agency tracts.

secs.t: Administrators, engineers and writers → contributions

x: C.P. Brown contributed to Telugu revival, edited the Madras Literary Journal and served as Curator of the Madras Manuscript Library.

Arthur Cotton built the major anicuts; C.P. Brown contributed to Telugu revival and manuscript work; Colin Mackenzie preserved records; and Thomas Munro introduced ryotwari and suppressed the palegars.
Arthur Cotton reported to the Board of Revenue in 1844, urging the construction of an anicut near Rajahmundry.

secs.t: Anicuts and projects → river, engineer, year

x: The Krishna anicut was on the Krishna, the Penna anicut was at Nellore, the K.C. Canal was associated with the Tungabhadra at Sunkesula, and the Sangam anicut was on the Penna.
Charles Orr built the Krishna anicut on
Arthur Cotton
's plan.
The Krishna anicut at Bezwada was constructed during 1852–55, not in 1872.

secs.t: Railways, ports, canals and economic effects

x: Deindustrialisation occurred because artisans lost traditional patronage and British goods entered duty-free.
Since land revenue had to be paid in cash, farmers increasingly cultivated commercial crops such as tobacco, indigo, cotton and oilseeds.
The shift from food crops to commercial crops reduced food availability and made the region more vulnerable to famines.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The barrage is 5.837 kilometres long, was rebuilt in 1969, and irrigates about 10 lakh acres.
Automated crest-gate telemetry and SCADA were installed at the
Prakasam Barrage
in February 2026.
The Godavari and Krishna deltas are collectively known as the “Rice Bowl of Andhra” because of their importance for rice cultivation.

rows.title: Anglo-Maratha and Anglo-Sikh wars; conquest of Sindh; Doctrine of Lapse and annexations
sub: Group-II S1-63: Consolidation of British power - Anglo-Mysore, Anglo-Maratha and Anglo-Sikh wars

secs.t: Wars of expansion — chronology and order

x: Chronology item: Wandiwash (1760), Nand Kumar hanged (1775), Salbai (1782), death of Tipu (1799).
The Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–1799) preceded the Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1818), which in turn preceded the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–1849).
Wandiwash was fought in 1760, Nand Kumar was hanged in 1775, the Treaty of Salbai was signed in 1782 and Tipu died in 1799, so the order is 2, 4, 1, 3 (BPSC 2025).

secs.t: Anglo-Mysore Wars → years, rulers, causes and outcome

x: The British broke the Treaty of Madras by not helping Haidar Ali against the Marathas, and they also captured Mahe, contributing to the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
Srirangapatnam
, also known as Seringapatam, was the capital of Mysore under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan.
Lord Wellesley feared Tipu Sultan's alliance with Napoleon
, which contributed to the decision to wage the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

secs.t: Anglo-Maratha and Anglo-Sikh Wars → GG, causes and battles — Anglo-Maratha Wars 1775-1818

x: The First Anglo-Maratha War, generally dated 1775–1782, occurred during the tenure of
Warren Hastings
The Third Anglo-Maratha War was set off by Lord Hastings' campaign against the
Pindaris
, followed by the rising of the Peshwa, Bhonsle and Holkar.
The Bhonsle of Nagpur and the Holkar of Indore
joined Baji Rao II after his attack on the British Residency at Poona.

secs.t: Anglo-Maratha and Anglo-Sikh Wars → GG, causes and battles — Anglo-Sikh Wars 1845-49

x: Lord Hardinge
was the Governor-General during the First Anglo-Sikh War, fought in 1845–46.
The First Anglo-Sikh War began when the Sikh army crossed the Sutlej, whose boundary had been fixed by the Treaty of Amritsar of 1809.
It began after the British officers Vans Agnew and Anderson were murdered at Multan, under Dalhousie.

secs.t: Treaties → year, parties and terms

x: Exam angle: the Treaty of Salbai was between the
British and the Marathas
Under the Treaty of Seringapatam, Tipu gave up half his territory, paid Rs 3 crore and handed over two sons as hostages to the British, Marathas and Nizam, who were allied against him.
Bassein was signed by Peshwa Baji Rao II (subsidiary alliance), Deogaon with the Bhonsle of Nagpur, Surji-Arjangaon with Scindia and Rajpurghat with Holkar, so
The Treaty of Salbai restored the status quo, allowed the British to retain Salsette and ushered in approximately twenty years of peace.

secs.t: Governor-Generals → wars and treaties

x: Sir John Shore
, Governor-General from 1793 to 1798, followed a policy of neutrality at Kharda, where the Marathas defeated the Nizam.
The First Anglo-Burmese War occurred from 1824 to 1826 during
Amherst
’s tenure, and the Treaty of Yandabo transferred Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim to the British sphere.
Salbai (1782) was signed under Warren Hastings, Amritsar (1809) with Ranjit Singh under Minto I, and Lahore (1846) after the First Anglo-Sikh War under Hardinge I (APPSC-G2 2023).

secs.t: Battles → war and British commander

x: Arthur Wellesley commanded at Assaye, Lord Lake at Delhi and Laswari, and Sir Hugh Gough at Mudki and Chillianwala.

secs.t: Annexations and ceded territories → year, GG and ground — Nizam of Hyderabad — alliances and Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema)

x: The Nizam blamed Sir John Shore's neutrality at Kharda and hired French battalions under Raymond.
In 1800 the Nizam ceded Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur and Bellary to meet the cost of the subsidiary force.
Sir Charles Napier
used coercive diplomacy against the Amirs and annexed Sindh after the battles of Miani and Dabo.

secs.t: Annexations and ceded territories → year, GG and ground — Other annexations → year and ground

x: Nana Sahib, the adopted son of Baji Rao II, was denied continuation of the Peshwa pension after Baji Rao II died in 1851.
Berar was assigned by the Nizam under the
Berar Treaty
Awadh’s cotton market and agrarian wealth were important motives, while misgovernance was used as the formal justification.

secs.t: Paramountcy — grounds for intervention; Rajputana alliances

x: Misgovernance was cited as a ground for intervention and annexation in
Coorg and Awadh
Lord Hastings
developed subsidiary alliances into the system of British paramountcy and imposed humiliating treaties on the Peshwa and Scindia.
The Rajputana states accepted British protection and surrendered control over their external relations under subordinate alliances in 1818.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The classification is: conquest for Sindh and Punjab, Doctrine of Lapse for Satara to Nagpur, misgovernance for Awadh and Coorg, and abolition of titles for Carnatic and Tanjore.
Nellore and Chittoor were taken from the Carnatic Nawab in 1801 on the charge of
collusion with Tipu Sultan
, an early pretext annexation.

secs.t: The office — titles and FIRSTs

x: The Regulating Act of 1773 created the office of Governor-General of Bengal, with Warren Hastings as its first holder.
Robert Clive was the first Governor of Bengal, Warren Hastings the first Governor-General of Bengal and Lord Canning the first Viceroy and Governor-General.
(APPSC-GS 2019): the office was Governor of Bengal from 1757 to 1772, and Bentinck became the first Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833.

secs.t: Governors-General → tenure (chronological order 1773-1856)

x: Sir John Shore served from 1793 to 1798, and
Wellesley
succeeded him in 1798.
Wellesley served before Cornwallis’s second term; Cornwallis’s second term was followed by Sir George Barlow and then Minto I.
Bentinck served from 1828 to 1835; after the Charter Act of 1833, he held the title Governor-General of India from 1833 onward.

secs.t: Acts, treaties and institutions → year → GG

x: Minto I
concluded the Treaty of Amritsar with Ranjit Singh in 1809.
Bentinck took Coorg in 1834 and took over Mysore’s administration.
The Vellore Mutiny occurred in 1806 during the tenure of
Sir George Barlow
The Charter Act of 1813 was passed at the transition between
Minto I and Marquess Hastings
, whose tenure began in 1813.

secs.t: Governors-General → other measures and policies

x: The Code of Gentoo Laws (1776) was compiled under Warren Hastings, Thuggee was suppressed by Bentinck with Sleeman, the PWD was set up under Dalhousie and the press was liberated by Metcalfe:
The Ring Fence policy treated Awadh as a buffer state to protect British territories from external threats.

secs.t: Impeachment of Warren Hastings — charges and outcome

x: The impeachment trial of Warren Hastings ran from 1788 to 1795 and ended in his acquittal.
The charges included the Rohilla War, the treatment of Chait Singh, the plunder of the Begums of Awadh and the judicial murder of Nand Kumar.

secs.t: Persons → popular titles and real names

x: Lord Wellesley
described himself as the "Bengal Tiger".
All four pairs are correctly matched.
Bentinck is called the Father of Modern Western Education in India.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Under Wellesley, the Subsidiary Alliance with the Nizam was concluded in 1798, the Ceded Districts followed in 1800, and Andhra was merged into Madras in 1801.
The prohibition of human sacrifice in 1845 is associated with Hardinge I. Dalhousie is associated with caste disabilities legislation in 1850 and widow remarriage in 1856.

secs.t: Viceroys 1858-1947 — order, FIRSTs and LASTs

x: Sher Ali Afridi, a convict, murdered Lord Mayo in
the Andamans in 1872
while Mayo was on tour.
The correct order is Canning's Indian Councils Act of 1861, Mayo's 1870 resolution, Lytton's Royal Titles Act of 1876 and Ripon's First Factory Act of 1881.
The Government of India Act, 1858 created the designation Viceroy, and
Lord Canning
became its first holder.

secs.t: Viceroy → key measures, events and memoirs

x: The Second Factory Act was passed during the tenure of Lord Lansdowne in 1891.
Lord Ripon's Local Self-Government Resolution of 1882 is described as the Magna Carta of Local Self-Government.
The INC was founded under Dufferin, the Durand Commission came under Lansdowne, the Chapekar killings under Elgin II and the Frazer Police Commission under Curzon:
Only A is correct: the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh (1919) came under Chelmsford.
The events occurred in 1919, 1931, 1940 and 1945 respectively.
The 1945 Simla Conference failed on Jinnah's stand.
The Viceroy's Journal was written by Wavell.
Mountbatten came after Attlee's 20 February 1947 statement.
The Police Commission of 1902 was appointed by Lord Curzon and functioned under
Andrew Frazer

secs.t: Delhi Durbars, summer capital and the shift to Delhi

x: Exam angle: A-R pairs - the 1911 Durbar was for George V; the Edward VII coronation Durbar was 1903 (true, but not the reason for 1911).
In 1912, Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal attempted to assassinate Lord Hardinge II during his state-entry procession into Delhi.
The anti-partition
Vande Mataram movement
contributed to the revocation of the Partition of Bengal, which was announced through King George V in 1911.

secs.t: Archaeological Survey of India → founder, motto, Viceroy

x: The motto of the Archaeological Survey of India is '
Pratnakirti Apavarini
The ASI was set up in 1861 under Canning, and Cunningham was its founder (APPSC 2012 key: Canning).

secs.t: Acts and commissions → year → Viceroy

x: Exam angle: "match the Act with the Viceroy" - Lytton owns three (Royal Titles, VPA, Arms), Ripon repealed VPA.
The Royal Titles Act was passed in 1876 during
Lord Lytton
's viceroyalty and recognised Queen Victoria as Empress of India.
The famine commission chain was Strachey under Lytton, Lyall under Elgin II and MacDonnell under Curzon.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gadicherla and Bodi Narayana Rao
are identified as the first Telugu political prisoners on 18 July 1908, during Minto II's tenure.
Lytton's reactionary policies, including the Durbar during famine conditions, the Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act, fuelled early nationalist criticism.
The Ilbert Bill controversy revealed the racial discrimination involved in preventing Indian judges from exercising jurisdiction over European British subjects on equal terms.

secs.t: Regulating Act, 1773 — background, committees and FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: "incorrect statement" - it did
not
abolish the Court of Directors.
After the Battle of Buxar in 1764, Shah Alam granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company in 1765.
In 1772, Parliament appointed a Select Committee headed by Burgoyne and a Secret Committee to investigate the Company's affairs.

secs.t: Acts → year → provisions (1773, 1781, 1786, 1793)

x: The Supreme Court at Calcutta, established in 1774, consisted of one Chief Justice and three judges and exercised civil and criminal jurisdiction.
The Act of 1786 was passed to meet Lord Cornwallis's condition for accepting the office of Governor-General.
The Act of 1786 allowed the Governor-General to override his Council in special cases and combined the office with that of Commander-in-Chief.

secs.t: Defects of 1773 → remedies

x: The Governor-General did not possess a veto and could be outvoted by his Council.
The Act of 1786 addressed the defect under which the Governor-General, including Hastings, could be repeatedly outvoted by his Council.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Sadar Adalat and Sadar Faujdari Adalat dealt with
persons other than British subjects
in the Madras Presidency.
The Regulating Act of 1773 began parliamentary control.
The Ministry of Law and Justice traces its origin to the
Charter Act of 1833
, which introduced the Law Member and the first Law Commission.

secs.t: Charter Acts — FIRSTs, LASTs and persons

x: The first Law Commission was established in 1834 under Macaulay and drafted the Indian Penal Code.
Macaulay made this observation in his speech in the House of Commons on the Bill that became the
Charter Act of 1833
Macaulay's Minute on Education was issued in 1835.

secs.t: Trade monopoly and the Company's status → Act

x: Exam angle: CGPSC 2022 - "the 1813 Act abolished the Company's trade monopoly" is marked
not true
because tea and China trade were kept.
Exam angle: the "held in trust" line is fill-in-the-blank bait: answer
Charter Act
(not Regulating Act).
The
Charter Act of 1853
continued the Company's authority over its Indian territories in trust for the British Crown, its heirs and successors.

secs.t: Legislature, centralisation and Agra Presidency → Act

x: The separated territory was placed under the Agra Presidency in 1834 and was renamed the
North-Western Provinces
The Charter Act of 1833 is regarded as the final step towards centralisation and converted the Company into a purely administrative body.
The
Charter Act of 1833
marked the peak of centralisation by vesting exclusive legislative power in the Governor-General-in-Council.

secs.t: Education, missionaries and civil services → Act

x: Under Evangelical pressure and the influence of figures such as William Wilberforce and Charles Grant, the Act allowed missionaries to enter India and propagate Christianity.
Section 87 declared that
religion, place of birth, descent or colour
should not bar an Indian from holding office.
Charles Trevelyan and Robert Lowe
supported the introduction of open competitive examination for the civil services.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Charter Act of 1853 opened the way for a legislature and merit-based recruitment to the ICS; the transfer to the Crown came later through the Government of India Act of 1858.
The Charter Act of 1853 was the last Charter Act, and the Government of India Act of 1858 ended the East India Company's rule by transferring authority to the Crown.

rows.title: Land revenue systems - Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari; areas and effects
sub: Group-II S1-70: Land revenue systems - Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari; economic impact
Group-II M1-A-56: Revenue settlements in Andhra - Permanent Settlement and the Ryotwari system of Thomas Munro

secs.t: Three systems — originator, year, areas and FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: "Ryotwari first introduced in Andhra" = Rayalaseema. "In the Madras Presidency" = Baramahal. A 2018 PYQ stem gave the date as 1808. The answer is still Munro.
Lord Cornwallis planned the Permanent Settlement with
John Shore
The first experiment was conducted in
Baramahal
, comprising areas such as Salem, Krishnagiri, Dharmapuri and Tiruvannamalai.
Baramahal came under Company control in 1792, the Permanent Settlement became permanent in 1793, Regulation VII was issued in 1822 and Regulation IX in 1833.
Mahalwari covered the North-Western Provinces (Agra-Oudh) and parts of Punjab, plus Central India (APPSC 2018).

secs.t: Settlement makers → posts and contributions — Thomas Munro

x: Munro served in the Mysore wars from 1780 to 1792, assisted Read in the Baramahal from 1792 to 1799, and became Collector of South Canara in 1799.
Munro served as Assistant to Read in the Baramahal, Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts, President of the Judicial Commission, and finally Governor of Madras.
Munro suppressed the Palegars with the assistance of officer
Campbell
before bringing the Ceded Districts under Ryotwari settlement.

secs.t: Settlement makers → posts and contributions — Mahalwari officials

x: Holt Mackenzie devised the system, R.M. Bird revised it through survey-based settlement, and James Thomason carried on Bird's settlement in the NWP.
R.M. Bird revised the Mahalwari system through a survey-based settlement under Regulation IX of 1833 during Bentinck's period.

secs.t: Features of each system — Permanent Settlement - features and rationale

x: The rationale included assured income, lower collection costs, a loyal landlord class and the hope that zamindars would improve the land.
Ryotwari revenue was linked to
the actual area cultivated
, so the amount could rise or fall accordingly.
All four statements describe features of the Ryotwari arrangement: individual settlement, land-based assessment, periodic revision and supervision through village officers under the Collector.

secs.t: Features of each system — Mahalwari - features

x: The Mahalwari system covered approximately 30 percent of British India.
Under Mahalwari, the mahal meant a village or estate.
Common ownership arrangements under the Mahalwari framework were called
Bhai Chara or Mahali

secs.t: Terms, regulations and commissions → meaning

x: The regulations of 1799, known as Haftam, and 1812, known as Panjam, enabled zamindars to seize tenants' property.
Moturpha was a tax on
professions, trades and looms
, affecting weavers, artisans and merchants in the Madras Presidency.
Village-lease settlements, in which village headmen acted as lessees, replaced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts after Munro's departure from 1808 onward and lasted until about 1820.

secs.t: Andhra — timeline, regions and systems

x: The Northern Circars were mainly zamindari areas, whereas Haveli lands under direct British control later came under Ryotwari.
The Mahalwari-type arrangement is placed in
Nellore and Chittoor
in the relevant regional account; in some accounts, Nellore alone is specifically mentioned.
The correct sequence is Guntur acquired in 1788, Battle of Padmanabham in 1794, Ceded Districts obtained in 1800, and the 1802 settlements.
In the Battle of Padmanabham in 1794,
Vijayarama Gajapati Raju, the Vizianagaram zamindar
, was defeated.

secs.t: Effects → factor and effect — Zamindari areas

x: Under the zamindari system, the gains from agriculture went to the zamindars, not to the Company.
Many old zamindars lost their estates for arrears, which were purchased by urban merchants and moneylenders, creating a new landed class.
All four were effects of the Permanent Settlement.
Zamindari was associated with rent-racking of tenants and absentee landlordism.

secs.t: Effects → factor and effect — Ryotwari and mahalwari areas

x: The inflexible cash demand continued even during crop failures, forcing ryots to borrow from Mahajans and often mortgage or lose their land.
The Mughal zabt is described as involving a one-third share and taccavi loans, whereas the British demand was rigid and offered no famine remission.
Merchant-landlords became prominent in Zamindari areas, while moneylender-landlords emerged particularly in Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas.

secs.t: Comparison tables — Permanent, Ryotwari and Mahalwari

x: The zamindar was the collector under the Permanent Settlement, the individual farmer under the Ryotwari System, and the village headman or lambardar under the Mahalwari System.
Default under Zamindari could result in forfeiture of the estate under the Sunset Law, while default under Ryotwari could lead to auction of the land.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The three settlements made land transferable, helped create a loyal landlord class and contributed to rural indebtedness, which in turn fed peasant revolts.
Munro is remembered as the first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema and for establishing its direct relationship between the ryot and the state through ryotwari administration.
The three settlements shaped agrarian class relations and structures, which post-1947 land reforms sought to dismantle or modify.

rows.title: Economic impact of colonial rule - drain of wealth, deindustrialisation, commercialisation of agriculture
sub: Group-II S1-71: Economic impact of colonial rule - drain of wealth, deindustrialisation, famines

secs.t: Colonialism — stages, industry FIRSTs and Andhra industries

x: The mercantilist stage from 1757 to 1813 was marked by the Company's trade monopoly, direct plunder and the use of Bengal revenue for purchasing export goods.
The Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company was established in 1854 by
Cowasji Nanabhai Davar
Nellore
district was the world leader in manganese during 1892-1929 (APHQ 2019 key; some sources credit Vizag).

secs.t: Economic nationalists → books and contributions

x: Dadabhai Naoroji
popularised the Drain of Wealth Theory and was known as the Grand Old Man and the father of Indian Nationalism.
Dadabhai Naoroji
coined the expression 'moral drain' while explaining the economic consequences of colonial rule.
Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti reported Andhra famines in his paper The Crescent and founded the Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam.

secs.t: Drain of wealth — meaning, components and effects — Meaning

x: The drain is traced to the grant of the Diwani of Bengal in 1765, after which Indian resources were transferred to England without economic return.
The export surplus financed British expenses and invisible imports rather than providing India with a complete economic return.

secs.t: Drain of wealth — meaning, components and effects — Components (home charges and more)

x: Exam angle: "popularised by" = Naoroji; reason-for-drain options.
A component of the drain was interest on
public debt raised in Britain
and paid out of Indian resources.
Salaries and pensions of British civil and military officials were remitted home and therefore formed part of the drain.
British railway investors were guaranteed a 5 percent return, whether or not the railway lines earned sufficient revenue.

secs.t: Deindustrialisation — chronology, causes and results

x: The
Charter Act of 1813
ended the Company's monopoly, after which British machine-made goods entered India at low duty.
British goods entered India almost duty-free, whereas Indian manufactures faced heavy duties in Britain.
The collapse of handicrafts pushed artisans onto the land, producing overcrowding in agriculture and disguised unemployment.
Marx described Britain as having inundated “the very mother country of cotton with cottons.”.
By 1850, India imported
one-fourth
of all British cotton exports.

secs.t: Andhra textiles → places and products

x: Srikakulam is associated with muslin, Machilipatnam with dyed clothes, Nellore with towels and Eluru with carpets.
Nellore was famous for towels, whereas silk clothes were associated with Peddapuram, Dharmavaram, Adoni and Bellary.
The Dutch set up their first Andhra factory at
Machilipatnam
, the most famous handloom and textile port of the 16th-17th centuries (APHQ 2017).

secs.t: Commercialisation of agriculture — crops → regions, causes and effects

x: Cotton was associated with the Deccan, Gujarat and Berar; jute with Bengal; opium with Bengal-Bihar and Malwa; and tea with Assam.
The triangular trade consisted of Indian opium going to China, Chinese tea and silver going to Britain, and British manufactures going to India.
Both statements are true, and the replacement of food crops by cash crops directly explains the decline in food security and the increased frequency of famines.

secs.t: Acts, commissions and policies → year

x: The cotton excise duty of 1894–96 on Indian mill cloth was imposed to offset the import duty and is a classic example of tariff policy.
The Richard Strachey Commission was appointed in 1880 after the
Great Famine of 1876–78
, during the viceroyalty of Lytton.

Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. A higher rupee-sterling ratio (1s 6d rather than the 1s 4d Indian business wanted) made Indian goods dearer abroad, and that is what hurt exporters.

secs.t: Famines — toll and Andhra famines

x: The Guntur famine of 1832-33 (Dokkala or Nandana Karuvu) was the worst famine in the south, killing about 2 lakh people, roughly half the population.
The late nineteenth century witnessed eleven famines, with 1865–66 described as the most severe.
Budda Vengalareddy of Uyyalawada
fed people during the 1866 Kurnool famine and received a gold medal from Victoria on 1 January 1877.
The Guntur famine helped push irrigation development, including Arthur Cotton's Godavari anicut constructed during 1847–52.

secs.t: Economy on the eve of independence — data and sectors — Colonial legacy and world share

x: British policy contributed to deindustrialisation, industry declined through loss of markets and agriculture remained stagnant with low productivity.
The export surplus generated by India was used for Britain’s office expenses and war expenses, contributing to the drain of wealth.
Maddison's estimate (APPSC-GS 2024 key) is that India's share of world income fell from about 27% in 1700 to about 3% in 1950, reflecting deindustrialisation and drain.

secs.t: Economy on the eve of independence — data and sectors — Sectors

x: More than 75 percent of the workforce depended on agriculture, but the sector contributed only about 50 percent of GDP, indicating low productivity and disguised unemployment.
India exported primary products such as raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo and jute.
Large foodgrain imports and inflation led the First Plan to give top priority to
agriculture, irrigation and power

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Colonial economic change involved the decline of India's manufacturing export position and its transformation into a supplier of raw materials.
The drain theory and the wider economic critique were major contributions of the Moderates and helped provide the basis for Swadeshi and early nationalism.
The comparison holds that IMF–World Bank structural adjustment programmes caused deindustrialisation through sudden tariff removal, reflecting a one-way free-trade logic comparable to colonial India.

rows.title: Famines under colonial rule and famine policy; Famine Commissions

secs.t: Major famines → year, region, mortality and epithets

x: The Doji Bara famine, also called the skull famine, occurred in 1791–92 and affected the Deccan, Hyderabad and the Northern Circars.
The Great Famine of 1876–78 affected Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay and occurred during Lytton’s tenure.
The correct sequence is Great Bengal Famine (1770), Doji Bara (1791–92), Orissa and Ganjam (1865–66), and Great Famine (1876–78).

secs.t: Famine policy — relief, Temple wage and Famine Code 1883

x: The Famine Code of 1883 was framed on the recommendations of the
Strachey Commission
The Famine Code provided for stages of scarcity and famine, relief works for able-bodied persons, gratuitous relief for the old and infirm, and suspension or remission of revenue.
Kautilya’s famine duties included supplying seeds and food, granting tax exemption and undertaking public works.

secs.t: Famine Commissions → chairman, year and Viceroy

x: Campbell was associated with John Lawrence, Strachey with Lytton, Lyall with Elgin II and MacDonnell with Curzon.
The
Lyall Commission
assessed the causes of famine and recommended measures to prevent or mitigate future famines.
The MacDonnell Commission was appointed in 1901 during Curzon’s tenure in relation to the famine of 1899–1900.

secs.t: Persons → famine critique and irrigation response

x: Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt
connected famines with the burden of high land revenue and the drain of wealth.
The Krishna anicut at Bezwada was proposed by Colonel Henry Atlock Lake and supervised by
Charles Orr
Veenam Veeranna
was the Andhra official who helped Cotton build the Godavari dam (APPSC-G2 2019 key).

secs.t: Anicuts → river, place and year

x: Arthur Cotton’s Godavari anicut project was reported in 1844, sanctioned in 1846, begun in 1847 and had its main structure completed in April 1852.
The Godavari anicut had three main canals serving about 6.62 lakh acres initially; the area later rose to 10 lakh acres for two crops.
The Penna anicut at Nellore, dating from 1860, was constructed according to
Arthur Cotton
’s plan.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The five phases progress from Phase 1 Minimal through Phase 2 Stressed, Phase 3 Crisis and Phase 4 Emergency to Phase 5 Catastrophe/Famine.
Modern food security through the PDS is based on
availability, accessibility and affordability
of food.
The Campbell Commission of 1866 was the first famine commission, while the Woodhead Commission of 1944 was the last colonial famine commission.

rows.title: Education policy - Orientalist-Anglicist debate, Macaulay's Minute, Wood's Despatch 1854, Hunter Commission

secs.t: Early institutions → founder and year (1781-1825)

x: Exam angle: institution-founder pairs; "first educational institution in British India" = Calcutta Madrasa (Warren Hastings).
Lord Richard Wellesley
established Fort William College in Calcutta in 1800 to train Company civil servants.
The institutions were founded in the order Calcutta Madrasa (1781), Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784), Sanskrit College, Benaras (1791), and Fort William College (1800).

secs.t: Acts, minutes and committees → year and provision

x: The Charter Act was passed in 1813, the General Committee was established in 1823, the English Education Act followed in 1835, and Wood's Despatch was issued in 1854.
Dalhousie's Minute of 1853 backed vernacular education, and Wood's Despatch followed in 1854.
Wood's Despatch (1854), drafted by Sir Charles Wood under Dalhousie, is called the Magna Carta of English Education in India.

secs.t: Wood's Despatch, 1854 — epithet and provisions

x: The Despatch proposed a hierarchy beginning with vernacular primary schools and progressing through Anglo-vernacular high schools and affiliated colleges to universities.
Wood's Despatch introduced a grants-in-aid system to encourage private, largely missionary, educational enterprise.
Wood's Despatch recommended supervision of vernacular education, teacher training, and a differentiated language policy using English at higher levels and vernacular languages at lower levels.

secs.t: Commissions and plans → year, Viceroy and focus (Hunter 1882 to Sargent 1944)

x: The 1913 Resolution on Education Policy was issued during the Viceroyalty of
Lord Hardinge II
The Sadler Commission recommended a 12-year school course, an intermediate stage, and a three-year degree.
The Hartog Committee examined wastage and stagnation in primary education and continued to support vernacular education.
The 1913 Resolution on Education Policy responded to Gopal Krishna Gokhale's demand for compulsory primary education.

secs.t: Missionaries in Andhra → mission and region

x: Correct: North German Society - Rajahmundry and Eluru (1843); Lutherans under Father Heyer - Guntur; American Baptists - Rayalaseema, Ongole and Nellore; London Missionary Society - Kadapa (centre in 1824).
Western education in Andhra was first spread by
Christian missionaries
(APPSC key), beginning with the London Missionary Society in 1805 and followed by the CMS, North German, Lutheran and American Baptist missions.

secs.t: Andhra and Madras colleges → place, founder and year

x: The Machilipatnam institution founded by Reverend Robert Noble and upgraded in 1864 is now known as
Noble College
Elphinstone's scheme dates to 1839, the regional school to 1854, the second-grade college to 1873 and the degree college to 1877.
The correct order is Central Collegiate Institute (1841), Noble School (1843), Madras University (1857), and the grants-in-aid system linked to results (1877–78).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: English education contributed to the emergence of a reformist middle class in coastal Andhra, represented by Kandukuri Veeresalingam, and also helped create a pan-Indian educated elite.
The
downward filtration
approach was criticised because it prioritised educating a limited section and neglected mass literacy.
The
Hunter and Hartog Commissions
repeatedly emphasised the importance of primary education, especially against the limitations of downward filtration.

rows.title: Development of railways, telegraph, post and the press; the Vernacular Press Act
sub: Group-II S1-72: Changes in the social and cultural sphere - education policy, press, railways and telegraph

secs.t: Railways, telegraph and post — FIRSTs, years and Governor-Generals

x: The first railway in South India ran from Royapuram in Madras to Wallajah Road near Arcot on 1 July 1856.
Dalhousie's Railway Minute of 1853 set out a trunk-line network for military, commercial and administrative purposes.
The first passenger train ran from Bombay (Bori Bunder) to Thane (34 km) on 16 April 1853, run by the Great Indian Peninsula Railway.

secs.t: Railways — guarantee system, motives and effects

x: Companies got a guaranteed 5% return.
Colonial railway construction served military movement, the export of raw materials and the internal distribution of British manufactures.
The unintended effects included a national market, shared travel across castes and faster nationalist mobilisation.
Despite their exploitative colonial purposes, railways were also used to move grain for famine relief.

secs.t: Newspapers → founders and editors

x: Amrita Bazar Patrika was founded by Sisir Kumar Ghosh and Motilal Ghosh; The Hindu by G. Subramania Iyer, M. Veeraraghavachariar and others; The Bengalee by Surendranath Banerjee; and Kesari by Tilak.
James Augustus Hicky
started the Bengal Gazette on 29 January 1780, India's first newspaper.
Sambad Kaumudi was
Raja Ram Mohan Roy
's Bengali paper.

secs.t: Telugu journals → founders, editors and years

x: Vrittanti
was an early Telugu journal published from Madras during 1837–1838.
Satyaduta dates to 1835; it was not the journal published from Masulipatnam in 1848.
Desamata
, associated with Chilakamarti, was among the press publications supportive of the Home Rule movement, along with Andhra Patrika and Krishna Patrika.
Sitarama Sastri of Guntur
wrote the series ‘Telugu Prajala Prasthuta Paristhiti’ in ‘The Hindu’.

secs.t: Press laws → year, Governor-General and provision

x: Charles Metcalfe’s Press Act of 1835 repealed the 1823 restrictions and earned him the description ‘
liberator of the Indian press
The Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act of 1908 was associated with Minto II and enabled magistrates to seize presses of papers inciting violence.
The 1908 Act empowered magistrates to seize presses of newspapers that incited violence and was directed against extremist activities.
Metcalfe’s 1835 measure brought relative freedom, the 1878 Act imposed restrictions, it was repealed in 1882, and repression returned through the 1908 and 1910 measures.

secs.t: Vernacular Press Act, 1878 — Lytton's "Gagging Act": provisions, targets, repeal

x: The Act was passed by Lord Lytton amid public anger over the 1876–77 famine and the lavish Delhi Durbar held in 1877.
Som Prakash
was one of the newspapers targeted by the Vernacular Press Act, along with Bharat Mihir, Dacca Prakash and Samachar.
Amrita Bazar Patrika
became an English paper overnight because the VPA applied only to Indian-language papers.

secs.t: Education — Orientalists, Anglicists and persons → contributions

x: Munro's 1826 survey found
a wide network of vernacular village schools in the Madras Presidency
Thomas Munro supported pathashalas and vernacular schooling, not English-only education in Madras.
Macaulay's Minute of 1835 was approved by
Lord William Bentinck
, who is associated with modern Western education in India.
Anglicists supported Western science and English literature, while Orientalists supported Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian learning.

secs.t: Macaulay's Minute, 1835 — recommendation, remarks, downward filtration

x: Macaulay sought a class Indian in blood and colour but English in taste, opinions, morals and intellect, to act as interpreters between rulers and ruled.
Macaulay made the well-known comparison that
a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia
Wood's Despatch rejected the
downward filtration theory
and asked the Company to take up mass education.

secs.t: Education milestones and Acts → year and Viceroy (revision)

x: Wood's Despatch (1854) planned a ladder from vernacular primary school to Anglo-vernacular high school to university, and universities were set up at
Calcutta, Bombay and Madras
Wood’s Despatch was issued in 1854, the First Factory Act in 1881, the Famine Code in 1883, and the Resolution on Local Self-Government in 1882.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: English education, the press, railways and the telegraph helped create an educated middle class and an all-India public sphere in which nationalism developed.
Telugu journalism is traced to 1835, and Machilipatnam and Rajahmundry were important early centres of education and public activity.
Raja Ram Mohan Roy is associated with Atmiya Sabha in 1814, Hindu College in 1817, an English school in 1822 and Vedanta College in 1825.

rows.title: Administrative changes - civil services, army reorganisation, police, judiciary, local self-government (Ripon)
sub: Group-II S1-69: Changes in administration - civil services, police, judiciary, army and local self-government

secs.t: Civil services — persons → contributions and FIRSTs

x: Cornwallis established a merit-based covenanted civil service, prohibited private trade and acceptance of gifts, and introduced promotion substantially based on seniority.
The maximum age was reduced to 19 in 1878 during the tenure of
Lord Lytton
, and this became an important Indian grievance.
Satyendranath Tagore
became the first Indian in the ICS in 1864 (many texts say 1863).

secs.t: Civil services — Acts, commissions and examinations → year

x: The Indian Civil Services Act of 1861 allowed limited Indian entry, mainly into uncovenanted posts, with conditions including seven years' residence and an examination in the local language.
Lytton's statutory civil service scheme reserved one-sixth of covenanted posts for Indians of high families; it was later abolished.
Aitchison (1886, Dufferin) replaced covenanted/uncovenanted with Imperial, Provincial and Subordinate services.

secs.t: Judiciary — Governor-General → judicial reform

x: Warren Hastings
established the district Diwani Adalats for civil cases and Faujdari Adalats for criminal cases in 1772.
Under
Cornwallis
, the Sadar Diwani and Sadar Nizamat Adalats at Calcutta were presided over by the Governor-General in Council.
The Regulating Act of 1773 created the Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), with
Sir Elijah Impey
as its first Chief Justice.

secs.t: Judiciary — codes, Acts and courts → year

x: The Indian High Courts Act of 1861 provided for High Courts at
Calcutta, Bombay and Madras
; they began functioning in 1862.
The High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras replaced the existing
Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats
The correct sequence is Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), Charter Act and Law Commission (1833), Code of Civil Procedure (1859), and Indian High Courts Act (1861).

secs.t: Police — terms and reformers: Cornwallis, Munro, Police Act 1861

x: The Royal Irish Constabulary model was adopted
for the Police Act of 1861, not for Cornwallis's reorganisation.
Thomas Munro returned in June 1814 as President of the
Judicial Commission
, which reviewed judicial and police administration in Bengal and Madras.
Munro recommended police supervision under the Collector and trial of minor crimes by village officers.

secs.t: Ilbert Bill controversy, 1883 — aim, "White Mutiny", compromise

x: The Ilbert Bill sought to allow Indian
district magistrates and sessions judges to try European British subjects
, removing the racial judicial privilege enjoyed by Europeans.
The fierce European agitation against the Ilbert Bill was popularly described as the “
white mutiny
The controversy revealed British racism, encouraged organised Indian political action and saw the Indian Association support the Bill.

secs.t: Local self-government — year → step; Mayo and Ripon

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 statement set - Cantonments Act 1924, Madras corporation 1688, Ripon as father of LSG -
all three correct

Mayo's Resolution dealt with financial decentralisation; Ripon's Resolution was regarded as the Magna Carta of local self-government; the 1907 Royal Commission stressed village panchayats; and the 1919 Act made local self-government a transferred provincial subject.
The correct sequence is Madras Corporation in 1688, Bombay and Calcutta Corporations in 1726, Lord Mayo’s resolution in 1870, and Lord Ripon’s resolution in 1882.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: NJDG data cited in June 2026 indicated that pending cases across courts had crossed
5 crore
The ICS is the direct ancestor of the IAS, codified laws of IPC-era codes, the 1861 police model of modern police institutions, and Ripon's local bodies of PRIs and ULBs.
The Karnataka Governor suspended the KPSC Chairperson pending inquiry and sought a Supreme Court reference under Article 317(1).

units.title: Indian War of Independence 1857; Religious and Social Reform Movements of the 19th Century; India's Freedom Movement; Revolutionaries in India and Abroad

rows.title: Revolt of 1857 - political causes (annexations, Doctrine of Lapse, subsidiary alliance)

secs.t: Subsidiary alliance, 1798 — terms, states → year, Hyderabad first

x: Awadh accepted the alliance in November 1801, the Peshwa in December 1802 (Treaty of Bassein), Bhonsle of Berar in December 1803 and Scindia in February 1804.
The Nizam ceded the Rayalaseema districts in 1800 to meet the cost of the subsidiary force; these became known as the
Ceded Districts
The Nizam raised French battalions under
Raymond

secs.t: Doctrine of Lapse — Dalhousie, meaning and withdrawal

x: A dependent state without a natural heir
lapsed to the East India Company
under the Doctrine of Lapse.
Under the policy, an adopted son could inherit private property but not the throne.
Lord Dalhousie formulated and applied the Doctrine of Lapse from 1848.
Queen Victoria’s Proclamation, read by Canning at the Allahabad Durbar on 1 November 1858, abolished the policy and recognised adoption.

secs.t: Governor-Generals → titles, pensions and Mughal succession

x: Nana Saheb, the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, was denied the pension of his adoptive father.
Dalhousie declared that Bahadur Shah’s successors would have to leave the
Red Fort and move to the Qutub at Mehrauli
Canning announced that after Bahadur Shah Zafar, his successors would lose the imperial title and would be treated merely as princes.

secs.t: Annexation of Awadh, 1856 — misgovernment, summary settlement, taluqdars and sepoys

x: Nawab
Wajid Ali Shah
was deposed after Awadh was annexed and was exiled to Calcutta.
The settlement was made directly with village proprietors, while taluqdars lost their estates, were disarmed and had their forts demolished.
The Bengal Army drew heavily from Awadh, and the new revenue burden directly affected the families of its sepoys.

secs.t: Leaders of 1857 → personal political grievance (revision)

x: Begum Hazrat Mahal opposed the annexation of Awadh and had her son Birjis Qadr proclaimed ruler.
Denial of Baji Rao II’s pension was Nana Saheb’s grievance.
Rani Lakshmibai’s adopted son, Damodar Rao, was not recognised as heir and
Jhansi
was annexed in 1853.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Fear of further annexations encouraged princely and aristocratic participation and helped transform the sepoy mutiny into a wider revolt.
After 1858, princely states were guaranteed in return for accepting British
paramountcy
Satara
(1848) was the first state annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse.

rows.title: Revolt of 1857 - economic, socio-religious, administrative and military causes
sub: Group-II S1-65: Revolt of 1857 - political, economic, socio-religious, administrative and military causes

secs.t: Political and administrative causes — factor → effect

x: Annexations displaced thousands of officials, retainers and soldiers who had depended on princely courts for employment and patronage.
The adopted son of Rani Lakshmibai was refused succession to the throne of Jhansi under the Doctrine of Lapse.
Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of misgovernance, not the Doctrine of Lapse (which took Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur).

secs.t: Economic causes — peasants, landed classes, artisans

x: The heavy revenue burden pushed peasants into debt, often resulting in the loss of their land to moneylenders and traders.
After the Industrial Revolution, cheap British machine-made goods, especially textiles, entered India duty-free while Indian goods faced heavy tariffs, causing deindustrialisation.
Annexations ended princely patronage, while British machine-made goods, particularly textiles, damaged Indian handicrafts; statement 3 reverses this effect.

secs.t: Socio-religious causes — social laws → year, missionaries

x: Sati was abolished in 1829 under Lord William Bentinck, not Dalhousie.
The Act is of 1850 (1856 is the trap date of the Widow Remarriage Act).
Missionary activity under official protection and the spread of Western institutions created apprehensions about religious conversion and the loss of caste identity.
The
Hindu Widow Remarriage Act
was passed in 1856 and challenged orthodox norms.

secs.t: Military grievances — GSEA, bhatta, discrimination, troop ratio

x: Racial discrimination restricted the highest rank ordinarily attainable by an Indian soldier to
Subedar
There were about 2.3 lakh Indian sepoys and 45,000 European soldiers, giving an approximate ratio of
European troops had been drawn away for the
Crimean and Persian wars
, contributing to the imbalance in troop strength.

secs.t: Earlier sepoy mutinies → date and cause

x: The new dress code, including a turban with a leather cockade and restrictions on caste marks and earrings, caused resentment among the sepoys at Vellore.
The 47th Native Infantry at Barrackpore refused to
go to Burma by sea
during the First Anglo-Burmese War.
The Santhal revolt of 1855–56 was a civil revolt and not a sepoy mutiny.

secs.t: Immediate cause — Enfield rifle, rumours and events of 1857 → date

x: The 19th Native Infantry acted at Berhampur in February, Mangal Pandey acted at Barrackpore on 29 March, and the Meerut rising began on 10 May 1857.
The correct sequence is Vellore mutiny in July 1806, Barrackpore mutiny in November 1824, Berhampur in February 1857 and Mangal Pandey’s attack on 29 March 1857.

secs.t: Writers → books on 1857 and their views

x: P.C. Joshi wrote Rebellion 1857: A Symposium (A-3); G.B. Malleson wrote The Indian Mutiny of 1857 (B-4); Christopher Hibbert wrote The Great Mutiny (C-1); Iqbal Hussain wrote Religion and Ideology of the Rebels of 1857 (D-2).
Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies was written by S.B. Chaudhuri; The Great Rebellion by Ashok Mehta; The Peasant and the Raj by Eric Stokes; and Awadh in Revolt 1857-58 by Rudrangshu Mukherjee.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The revolt brought together the grievances of
rulers, peasants, soldiers and common people
Syed Ahmed Khan is associated with the first Indian-language work on the causes of the Revolt of 1857.
Mangal Pandey
is identified as the first martyr of the Revolt of 1857.
After 1858, the Crown promised religious neutrality and withdrew state patronage from missionary work.

rows.title: Outbreak and spread - Mangal Pandey, Meerut; centres and leaders of the revolt
sub: Group-II S1-66: Revolt of 1857 - outbreak, centres, leaders and suppression

secs.t: Outbreak → events, dates and FIRSTs — Event → date → what happened

x: Mangal Pandey attacked British officers at Barrackpore on
29 March 1857
Mangal Pandey was hanged on 8 April 1857 and his regiment, the 34th Bengal Native Infantry, was disbanded.
The slogan was 'Dilli Chalo' (Delhi Chalo).
After reaching Delhi, the rebels entered the Red Fort and killed Commissioner Simon Fraser.
Lord Canning
was Governor-General when the revolt began.

secs.t: Outbreak → events, dates and FIRSTs — Centre → date the rising began

x: Jhansi was recaptured and Kunwar Singh led a fresh rising in Bihar in April 1858, while Bareilly was recaptured in May 1858.
The rising began at Barrackpore on 29 March, Delhi on 11 May, Lucknow on 4 June and Kanpur on 5 June 1857.
Colin Campbell recaptured Kanpur in December 1857, Lucknow in March 1858, Hugh Rose recaptured Jhansi in April 1858 and Gwalior in June 1858.

secs.t: Centres → leaders — Centre → leader(s)

x: Khan Bahadur Khan proclaimed himself
Nawab Nizam
at Bareilly and commanded an army of about 40,000.
Begum Hazrat Mahal led at Lucknow, proclaimed Birjis Qadr ruler of Awadh, and the administration included both Hindus and Muslims in offices.
Kunwar Singh led at Arrah (Bihar), Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow, Nana Saheb at Kanpur and Bahadur Shah Zafar at Delhi (APPSC-G2 2025).

secs.t: Centres → leaders — Lesser-known and local leaders → area / role

x: All three pairs are correctly matched.
Shah Mal mobilised the chaurasee des, meaning the area of 84 villages, in the Baraut region of Uttar Pradesh.

secs.t: Persons → role, advisers and accounts

x: The proclamations in Bahadur Shah Zafar's name stressed Hindu-Muslim unity, including measures such as a ban on cow slaughter and joint commands, and called for restoration of the Mughal order.
W. H. Russell
, correspondent of The Times, reported on the revolt and British reprisals in My Diary in India.
Azimullah Khan, Nana Saheb’s adviser, went to London to plead Nana Saheb’s pension case.

secs.t: Places → affected, unaffected and loyal areas

x: Bengal, Punjab, and eastern, western and southern India were largely unaffected; British forces for suppression came from several of these regions.
The big princely states of
Hyderabad, Mysore, Scindia and Holkar
largely stayed loyal to the British.
Hyderabad's Nizam and Scindia were loyal, while Scindia's troops defected and the troops of Tonk and Bhopal rebelled despite their rulers' loyalty.

secs.t: Revolt in Andhra and Hyderabad → leaders and places

x: Afzal-ud-Daula remained pro-British, and the Nizam’s loyalty helped keep the Deccan quiet.
Dandasena led the rising at Paralakimidi, while Korukonda Subba Reddy led the rebellion at Errannagudem; both occurred in August 1857.
The chronology asked in APPSC-G1 2022 places Mubariz-ud-Daula's imprisonment in Golconda before Turrebaz Khan's attack on the Residency, so B reverses it.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Participation by all major princes and urban elites was not a limitation because many big princes and urban elites stayed away from the revolt.
The Hindu-Muslim unity associated with the revolt was later cited against the
two-nation theory
Tantia Tope
is regarded as the last major leader of the Revolt of 1857 to be executed.

rows.title: Suppression of the revolt; why it failed; areas that stayed loyal

secs.t: British officers → centres retaken

x: Exam angle: "Which centre was recaptured by the English?" - Delhi.
Maulvi Liyakat Ali led the rebellion at Allahabad and Banaras, which were recaptured by Colonel Neill.
Sir Colin Campbell
was the Commander-in-Chief during the suppression and later became known as Lord Clyde.
Lord Canning served as Governor-General from 1856 to 1858 and became the first Viceroy in 1858, serving until 1862.

secs.t: Rebel leaders → fate and area of operation — Repression measures

x: The repression was harsh;
thousands of rebels were publicly executed after mock trials
, and British troops also committed atrocities.

secs.t: Rebel leaders → fate and area of operation — Leader → centre → end

x: Exam angle: "Bahadur Shah was exiled to - Rangoon".
Khan Bahadur Khan operated in Rohilkhand, Ahmadullah in Faizabad, Kunwar Singh in Bihar, and Tantia Tope continued guerrilla warfare in Central India.
Rani Lakshmibai captured Gwalior with Tantia Tope and died fighting near Gwalior on 17 June 1858 against Sir Hugh Rose's force.

secs.t: Rebel leaders → fate and area of operation — Leaders → area of operation, odd-one-out

x: Azimullah Khan
served as Nana Saheb's adviser and coordinated communication among rebel leaders.
Bakht Khan came from
Bareilly
and reached Delhi on 3 July 1857 (APPSC-GS 2023 key).

secs.t: Areas and groups that stayed loyal

x: The revolt was chiefly of the
Bengal Army
; the Madras and Bombay armies largely remained loyal, while a Gorkha regiment assisted Campbell.
The phrase “breakwaters to the storm” is attributed to
Lord Canning
, although some accounts credit Lord Elgin.
The educated middle class generally saw the revolt as
a backward-looking feudal reaction
and therefore remained neutral.

secs.t: Reasons for failure → factor and effect

x: Exam angle: statement sets (military superiority, no unified programme, lack of support from all sections) - all three correct.
The rebels generally used
swords, spears and old muskets
, whereas the British had Enfield rifles and the electric telegraph.
The revolt suffered because several princes and big zamindars remained loyal and it lacked adequate support from the martial races of the north.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The revolt was suppressed by mid-1858, but its impact was profound because it shook British rule in India to its foundations.
Rani Avantibai Lodhi was the ruler of
Ramgarh in Madhya Pradesh
Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula and Salar Jung I stayed loyal, and the Hyderabad Residency attack of 17 July 1857 was repulsed.

rows.title: Nature of 1857 - the historiographical debate (mutiny, feudal reaction, first war of independence)
sub: Group-II S1-68: Nature of the 1857 Revolt - historiographical debate

secs.t: Schools → labels for the revolt

x: British or imperialist historians
commonly used the labels Sepoy Mutiny or Indian Mutiny and denied the revolt a national character.
Indian nationalist historians commonly used the label
Great Rebellion
, while First War of Independence was especially associated with V.D. Savarkar.
Religious fanaticism and administrative blunders were explanations associated with the British or imperialist interpretation.

secs.t: Historians and contemporaries → statements on 1857 — Contemporary views

x: Disraeli questioned whether the event was merely a military mutiny or a national revolt, and viewed it as
a national rising
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan argued that
the absence of Indians in the Legislative Council
caused the rulers to misunderstand the ruled.
Sir John Lawrence
, along with J.R. Seeley and Charles Raikes, regarded the uprising primarily as a sepoy mutiny and denied it a popular or national character.

secs.t: Historians and contemporaries → statements on 1857 — Indian historians

x: Exam angle: "Who first described 1857 as / first called it the First Indian War of Independence?" -
Savarkar
, with Tilak and Majumdar as distractors.
The feudal-reaction interpretation highlights dispossessed princes and taluqdars such as Nana Saheb, Lakshmibai and Begum Hazrat Mahal, who sought to recover lost positions.
Eric Stokes emphasised local agrarian studies and interpreted the revolt as multiple peasant and elite risings, not as one centrally directed movement.

secs.t: Books → authors on 1857

x: Karl Marx's and Friedrich Engels' articles were compiled as
The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859
S.N. Sen's Eighteen Fifty-Seven was the Government of India-commissioned centenary history.

secs.t: Nature of the revolt → statement-type judgments

x: All four statements are cited as limitations: the revolt lacked a common goal, modern nationalism was not yet developed, its main spread was in North India, and most of India remained neutral.
The revolt began among soldiers but quickly drew in rulers, peasants, soldiers and common people, becoming a wider popular rebellion.

secs.t: Social groups → participation; Hindu-Muslim unity

x: Most princes, including Scindia, Holkar, the Nizam and the rulers of Rajputana
, remained loyal to the British.
The greased cartridges offended the religious sentiments of both Hindus and Muslims, creating a common grievance.
After 1857, the British increasingly pursued a policy of divide and rule in response to the cooperation between Hindus and Muslims.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The revolt damaged the belief in British invincibility and helped create the conditions for later nationalism, although it did not end British rule.
Annapurnayya received 18 months’ rigorous imprisonment for his article *Chicharapidugu*, which dealt with the revolt of 1857.
The RIN revolt began at HMIS Talwar in Bombay on
18 February 1946
Mangal Pandey was a sepoy of the
34th Bengal Native Infantry
at Barrackpore.

rows.title: Consequences of 1857 - Queen's Proclamation, Government of India Act 1858, army reorganisation
sub: Group-II S1-67: Impact of the 1857 Revolt - Government of India Act 1858 and army reorganisation

secs.t: Acts and commissions → year → provision

x: Title:
Act for the Good Government of India.
Exam angle: options mix Charter Acts 1833/1853, Pitt's Act and Indian Councils Act 1861 (ICA 1861) - only the 1858 Act transferred power to the Crown.
Exam angle: APPSC G2 2024 and G2 2025 asked "GG of Bengal designated GG of India by?" The answer is the
Charter Act 1833

secs.t: Offices created in 1858 → Secretary of State, Council of India, Viceroy

x: Lord Stanley
was the first Secretary of State for India under the new Crown administration.
The Secretary of State for India was a member of the
British Cabinet
and exercised the powers of the Crown in relation to India.
The Government of India Act of 1858 created the title Viceroy and Governor-General.

secs.t: Queen's Proclamation, 1858 → promises, kept vs broken — Basics

x: The Proclamation promised religious neutrality, rejected forced conversion and was followed by the withdrawal of state patronage from missionary conversion.
The Queen’s Proclamation is often called the
Magna Carta of the Indian people
because of its wide-ranging assurances concerning rulers, religion, public service, property and land rights.
Lord Canning read the Proclamation at a Durbar in Allahabad on 1 November 1858 (UPPSC 2009).

secs.t: Queen's Proclamation, 1858 → promises, kept vs broken — Kept vs broken

x: Equal employment was not kept; SoS Kimberley said an adequate number of civil servants 'shall always be Europeans'.
The Royal Titles Act 1876 gave Victoria the title, and it was proclaimed at the Delhi Durbar of 1 January 1877 under Lord Lytton.

secs.t: Policy towards princes → end of annexation, adoption, paramountcy

x: Lord Canning
withdrew the Doctrine of Lapse and recognised adoption rights after 1857.
The British recognised the right of childless rulers to adopt heirs, thereby withdrawing the Doctrine of Lapse and ending the annexation policy associated with Dalhousie.
Lord Canning
described the loyal princes as breakwaters to the storm, though some accounts credit Lord Elgin.

secs.t: Army reorganisation → Peel and Eden Commissions

x: Exam angle: "divide and rule" inside the army - the counterpoise principle.
The Peel Commission recommended a greater European share in the army and reserved artillery and key positions for Europeans.
The British increasingly recruited
Sikhs, Gurkhas and Pathans
, describing them as martial races, while reducing dependence on recruits from Awadh and Bihar.

secs.t: Changes after 1857 → end of Mughals and Company, divide and rule, racial attitudes

x: The rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan, after which the British tried and exiled him to Rangoon, ending the Mughal dynasty in practice and form.
The British initially held Muslims chiefly responsible for the revolt and adopted anti-Muslim measures, but later cultivated Muslim support against the rising educated Hindu middle class.
In Awadh, zamindars and taluqdars were restored to proprietary rights and became a conservative and loyal landed class supporting British rule.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The submarine cable introduced in 1870 facilitated faster communication between India and London, strengthening control from Britain.
The Proclamation of 1858 established British policy towards the Indian princes and religion, and this broad policy continued until independence in 1947.
Rani Avantibai Lodhi opposed the Doctrine of Lapse and won the Battle of Kheri during the Revolt of 1857.

rows.title: Andhra and South India in 1857 - limited response; earlier local uprisings (Rampa, Palegar revolts)
sub: Group-II M1-A-57: Early resistance to British rule - Poligar/Palegar revolts and the Vizianagaram rising of 1794
Group-II M1-A-58: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt, 1846-47
Group-II M1-A-59: 1857 Revolt and its impact on Andhra - response, repression and consequences

secs.t: Battle of Bobbili, 1757 → date, parties, outcome

x: All four statements correctly describe the parties, French assistance, fall of the fort, mass self-immolation and the subsequent assassination of Vijayarama Raju.
The Treaty of Aurangabad of 1753 gave the Circars to the French.
The Battle of Tummala
in 1757 confirmed French control.
The play
Bobbili Yuddham
is identified as the primary source associated with the Battle of Bobbili.

secs.t: Battle of Padmanabham, 1794 → background, parties, outcome

x: Exam angle: "Padmanabham decided whose defeat?" = Vijayarama Raju of Vizianagaram, not Bobbili.
Colonel Pendergast
commanded the English East India Company forces at the Battle of Padmanabham.
The battle was fought between the English East India Company and Pusapati Chinna Vijayarama Gajapati Raju II, the Vizianagaram zamindar.
The estate was restored on accepting the Permanent Settlement (1802) and a Rs 6 lakh peshkash; Rs 3 lakh was the earlier tribute demand.
Madhava Bhupati Dev was not the British commander at Padmanabham: the Company forces there were commanded by Col.

secs.t: Zamindars and poligars → place and resistance

x: Bhupayya operated in the Vizag hills with about 2,000 followers, was driven into Nizam's territory and died in 1796.
The Company's 1781 arrangement allowed the Nawab of Arcot to manage the revenues of Tirunelveli and the Carnatic, affecting the rights of the Poligars.
Kattabomman was hanged in 1799, the Marudu brothers were executed in 1801, and Velu Thampi Dalawa was associated with the Kundara Proclamation.

secs.t: Rayalaseema palegars → grievances and revolts of 1800-01

x: Palegars were fortified military chiefs who exercised autonomous power under the nominal suzerainty of the Nizam.
The Palakonda Poligars rebelled against
heavy taxes
and were brutally suppressed.
Guntur was taken in 1788 for Rs 7 lakh, and the four Ceded Districts were ceded by the Nizam in 1800 under the Subsidiary Alliance of 1798.

secs.t: Company officers → suppression of palegars and the Vellore Mutiny, 1806

x: Thomas Munro
, serving as Principal Collector, was chiefly responsible for suppressing the Palegar revolts.

All four measures formed part of the suppression and settlement policy: disarmament proclamations, military action for eighteen months, confiscation of rebel estates and small pensions for loyal heirs.
The new uniform regulations, including changes concerning the turban and a ban on caste marks, hurt the caste and religious sentiments of the sepoys.

secs.t: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy → family, grievances, support base

x: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy belonged to the Palegar family of Uyyalawada in Koilakuntla taluk of
Kurnool
district.
His estate was taken over under Munro, he was offered only a meagre pension, and he was ordered to lay down arms and pay peshkash.
The movement had about 5,000 followers, including
farmers, Yanadis, tribal people and people from the Uyyalawada and Nosam estates

secs.t: Uyyalawada revolt, 1846-47 → events, officers, execution, memorials

x: Captured on 7 October 1846 and sentenced to death by the Faujdari Adalat in January 1847, he was publicly hanged near Koilakuntla on
22 February 1847
The revolt began in July, the treasury was looted on 12 July, the Mundlapadu ambush occurred on 24 July, and the capture took place on 7 October 1846.
Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy, a Kurnool poligar, revolted in the 1840s, looted the treasury at Koilkuntla and was later hanged.

secs.t: Hyderabad in 1857 → persons, risings and their order — Persons → role

x: Afzal-ud-Daula
succeeded Nasir-ud-Daula in 1857 and ruled Hyderabad from 1857 to 1869.
Both the Nizam and Salar Jung I were pro-British.

secs.t: Hyderabad in 1857 → persons, risings and their order — Risings in order

x: The 1st Cavalry came under suspicion and was disarmed; Mir Fida Ali was hanged, whereas Maulvi Allauddin was transported to the Andamans.
Maulvi Allauddin was transported for life to the Andamans; hanging after the Aurangabad outbreak was Mir Fida Ali's fate.
Dandasena rose at Paralakimidi, Korukonda Subba Reddy led the rebellion at Errannagudem, Turrebaz Khan attacked the British Residency, and Mubariz-ud-Daula was imprisoned in Golconda Fort.

secs.t: Andhra leaders of 1857 → area and outcome; places → incidents — Leader → area → outcome

x: Exam angle: matching a leader to an area. A 2024 A/R on Sheikh Peer Sahib's jihad was keyed "both true, R not the explanation".
Buttaigudem Munsab Shankar Swamy
helped the British suppress Korukonda Subba Reddy's rising in the Godavari Agency.
Sheikh Peer Sahib preached jihad at Cuddapah on 28 August 1857 and prayed for the success of the Mughal Emperor; he was later arrested.

secs.t: Andhra leaders of 1857 → area and outcome; places → incidents — Godavari Agency unrest - in the spirit of Nana Saheb

x: A Telugu placard displayed at Visakhapatnam during Muharram called for renaming the town Mohammed Pattanam.
The Faujdari Adalat was the court that tried the Uyyalawada rebel leader; it was not the centre of the Godavari Agency movement.
Korukonda Subba Reddy was the village official of
Karaturu
in Godavari district.

secs.t: Limited response in Andhra → reasons; aftermath → repression, rewards, Crown rule

x: The major background grievances identified were the 1800 cession, the Wahabi conspiracy of 1839 and the 1853 Berar treaty, involving Berar, Raichur and Osmanabad/Dharashiv.
A is false: Andhra did have local leaders and risings, such as Turrebaz Khan, Korukonda Subba Reddy, Dandasena and the attempt at Kadiri.
The Queen's Proclamation was issued in 1858, the IPC arrived in 1860, the CrPC in 1861, and the Madras High Court replaced Company courts in 1862.

secs.t: Rampa and agency rebellions → phases, 1830s to 1924

x: Exam angle: the year of the Rampa revolution is 1879, not Alluri's 1922.
The correct order is Vizianagaram–Visakhapatnam hill unrest in the 1830s, Korra Mallayya and Chinna Bhupathi in 1845–48, Korukonda Subba Reddy in 1857–58, and the Rampa rebellion in 1879.
The hill unrest of the 1830s was directed against
zamindari exactions
and led to the establishment of the Agency system.

secs.t: Events → year: rebellions in Hyderabad State and Andhra

x: The Rampa rebellion occurred in 1879, whereas Mubariz-ud-Daula was associated with the 1839 Wahabi conspiracy.
Korra Mallayya and Chinna Bhupathi
were associated with the Gulugonda/Ganjam Agency rising of 1845–48.
Opposition to the Berar assignment occurred in 1853.
Peshwa Rao, or Ramarao, was associated with the 1862 conspiracy and was caught at Kanpur.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Vellore Mutiny of 1806 is regarded as the first major sepoy mutiny and occurred about fifty years before the Revolt of 1857.
Ranga Rao and Tandra Paparayudu of Bobbili remain enduring symbols of Telugu valour.

The 1800–01 movement involved about 80 palegars and Munro, whereas the 1846 movement was a single-leader guerrilla revolt supported by peasants and tribal groups and was the last major palegar rising before 1857.

rows.title: Raja Rammohan Roy and the Brahmo Samaj; abolition of Sati; Debendranath and Keshab Chandra Sen
sub: Group-II S1-74: Socio-religious reform - Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj and Young Bengal

secs.t: Reformers → life, titles and known-as

x: Mughal emperor Akbar II conferred the title ‘Raja’ on Rammohan Roy and sent him to England as his envoy.
Rammohan Roy is called the Father of Modern India, the Father of the Indian (or Bengal) Renaissance and the first Modern Man of India. '
Maharishi
' was the title of Debendranath Tagore. 'Raja' was given to Rammohan Roy by Akbar II.

secs.t: Books and journals → author, language, year

x: Exam angle: journal-language matching; Mirat-ul-Akhbar = Persian, Sambad Kaumudi = Bengali.
Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin, meaning A Gift to Monotheists, was a Persian book of Rammohan Roy written against idolatry.
Precepts of Jesus — the Guide to Peace and Happiness was written in
English
and presented a rational ethical interpretation of Jesus’s teachings.

secs.t: Rammohan Roy → institutions, campaigns and political demands

x: Rammohan Roy started an English school in 1822, so A is right.
He opposed the Jury Act of 1827 because it brought religious discrimination into the courts.
Rammohan Roy opposed press restrictions and advocated fixed maximum rents for peasants.

secs.t: Reform bodies → founder, place, year

x: Exam angle: "Organisation founded in Poona in 1849 against caste and for women's education" → Paramahansa Mandali.
Debendranath Tagore stressed rejection of idolatry and rituals and advocated worship of the formless God while reviving the Brahmo Samaj.
The Tattvabodhini Sabha was founded in 1839, the Widow Remarriage Act was passed in 1856, the Brahmo Samaj of India emerged in 1866 and the Satyashodhak Samaj was founded in 1873.
The chronological order is Raja Rammohan Roy, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Jyotiba Phule and Swami Dayanand Saraswati.

secs.t: Brahmo tenets and social programme (statement type)

x: The Brahmo Samaj believed in one formless, eternal God and rejected belief in avatars.
The Brahmo Samaj opposed idols, animal sacrifice, priestly ritualism and caste distinctions, and encouraged collective prayer.
The Brahmo Samaj rejected sectarian symbols in its halls.
The Brahmo Samaj opposed polygamy and child marriage and supported widow remarriage, women's education and women's property rights.

secs.t: Abolition of Sati, 1829 → Regulation, Governor-General, dates

x: Exam angle: "Sati was abolished by..." (Bentinck); regulation number XVII.
The Bengal Sati Regulation, 1829, was
Regulation XVII
of the Bengal Code.
It was passed under Lord William Bentinck.
Raja Radhakant Deb founded the orthodox Dharma Sabha in opposition to the Brahmo propaganda and the Sati ban.

secs.t: Keshab Chandra Sen → contributions; splits of 1866 and 1878

x: The Native Marriage Act, also called the Brahmo Marriage Act or Act III of 1872, legalised inter-caste marriage and prescribed minimum marriage ages.
Keshab became Acharya in 1862, formed the Brahmo Samaj of India in 1866, founded the Indian Reform Association in 1870 and introduced Nava Vidhan in 1880–81.
The 1878 split followed Keshab Chandra Sen's marriage of his under-age daughter to the Maharaja or prince of Cooch Behar.

secs.t: Maharashtra reformers → contributions; Andhra centres

x: Exam angle: match founders - Atmaram Pandurang → Prarthana Samaj; Derozio → Young Bengal; Dayanand → Arya Samaj; Rammohan → Brahmo Samaj.
Prarthana Samaj promoted widow remarriage, women's education and inter-caste dining through persuasion rather than confrontation.
Balshastri Jambhekar was associated with Darpan, Karsandas Mulji with Satya Prakash, and Gopal Hari Deshmukh was known as Lokahitawadi.

secs.t: Events → year: reform chronology

x: APPSC-GS 2025 order:
Rammohan Roy → Vidyasagar → Jyotiba Phule → Dayanand Saraswati
(C-A-D-B)

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Brahmo Samaj opposed superstition, supported education and women's rights, and contributed to the intellectual and social foundations of nationalism.
The Andhra Trinity of the Brahma Samaj was
Veeresalingam, Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu and Desiraju Peda Bapaiah
, so A. Mannava Buchayya Pantulu was the first Andhra Brahmo but not one of the Trinity.

rows.title: Prarthana Samaj, Young Bengal Movement (Derozio), Paramahansa Mandali

secs.t: Reform bodies → founder, place, year

x: Paramahansa Mandali was founded by Dadoba Pandurang along with Durgaram Mancharam of the Manav Dharma Sabha of Surat.
Prarthana Samaj was inspired by the visit of
Keshab Chandra Sen
and was established in Bombay in 1867.
The Deccan Education Society was founded in Pune in 1884 by Tilak, Agarkar, Chiplunkar and others, with the support of M.G. Ranade.

secs.t: Reformers → ideas and contributions

x: Young Bengal stood for radical rationalism, opposed idol worship, casteism and decadent customs, and supported women's rights and education.
Bal Shastri Jambhekar
started the Marathi paper Darpan in 1832 and attacked Brahmanical orthodoxy.
Gopal Hari Deshmukh
wrote as Lokahitawadi, and his Shatapatre (hundred letters) appeared in the weekly Prabhakar.
R.G. Bhandarkar was known as a
Sanskrit scholar
and joined the Prarthana Samaj in 1870.

secs.t: Journals → linked to

x: Induprakash, an Anglo-Marathi journal, was linked to M.G. Ranade.

secs.t: Paramahansa Mandali and Prarthana Samaj → nature, aims, agenda

x: Prarthana Samaj was an offshoot of the Brahmo Samaj and functioned as a reform movement within Hinduism.
Uplift of the depressed classes was among its aims, along with inter-dining and inter-marriage.
The exam-safe distinction is that Prarthana Samaj focused more on social reform and did not outright forbid idol worship or abandon caste in the manner described for the Brahmos.

secs.t: Reform body matching → APPSC keys

x: Atmaram Pandurang founded the Prarthana Samaj (Bombay, 1867), so A is right.
Pandita Ramabai's Sharada Sadan was a home for widows, so C is the wrong pair.
The Satyashodhak Samaj was founded by Jyotiba Phule, not Dayananda Saraswati.
Prarthana Samaj pursued reform through persuasion and social work and also supported inter-dining, inter-marriage and the uplift of depressed classes.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Arya Samaj rejected idol worship and ritualism.
Prarthana Samaj was a milder Brahmo-inspired movement, Young Bengal was radical, Paramahansa Mandali was secret, and Satyashodhak Samaj had an anti-Brahmanical, lower-caste focus.
Veeresalingam founded it at
Rajahmundry
in 1878 (APHQ 2019), and K. Seethamma later organised its women's wing.

rows.title: Arya Samaj and Dayananda Saraswati - Satyarth Prakash, shuddhi, Dayanand Anglo-Vedic schools

secs.t: Dayananda Saraswati → life, titles, slogans

x: Dayananda Saraswati’s original name was
Mool Shankar Tiwari
He died at Ajmer in 1883; Lahore was only the later headquarters of the Arya Samaj.
Dayananda Saraswati was born at Tankara in the Kathiawar region of Gujarat.
It was Lala Lajpat Rai who called him the 'Martin Luther of India'.
Dayananda wrote his main work in Hindi and promoted Hindi as a link language.

secs.t: Satyarth Prakash and "Back to the Vedas" → author, language, ideas

x: The slogan expressed the belief that the four Vedas were infallible and constituted the primordial word of God.
Dayananda rejected later Puranic accretions, including myths, ritualism and idol worship, while supporting rational thought and moral action.
Satyarth Prakash presented Dayananda’s religious and social philosophy and criticised Hindu orthodoxy, idolatry, caste by birth and child marriage.

secs.t: Arya Samaj, 1875 → founding, base, programme

x: Exam angle: statement traps - "founded in Calcutta" (wrong; Bombay) and "promotes idol worship" (wrong; rejects it).
Arya Samaj was founded by Swami Dayananda Saraswati at
Bombay
The Ten Principles emphasised truth, rational thought, moral conduct and the well-being of all.
Arya Samaj influenced Lala Lajpat Rai, Swami Shraddhanand and the family of Bhagat Singh, contributing to militant nationalist attitudes.

secs.t: Arya Samaj movements → Shuddhi and the Hyderabad satyagraha

x: Exam angle: "Shuddhi was started by ___" → Arya Samaj (not Brahmo Samaj, Satyashodhak Samaj or Ramakrishna Mission).
Shuddhi was started by Arya Samaj to reconvert converts and admit outsiders into the Hindu fold.
In 1938–39, Arya Samaj conducted a satyagraha in Hyderabad State against the Nizam’s restrictions on religious and civil rights.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Arya Samaj combined revivalism with reform, built Hindu self-confidence and contributed to militant nationalism.
