Kanyasulkam is dated 1892 (written in 1890 and first staged on 13 August 1892) and was revised in 1909, when its second edition was dedicated to Ananda Gajapati.

secs.t: Women reformers of Andhra → organisations and journals

x: Rajyalakshmamma, or Bapamma, married Veeresalingam in 1860 and supported widows and couples involved in the remarriage movement.
Acchamamba founded Stree Samajam in 1902, Hindu Sundari was associated with Ramabai and Shantabai, and Rajyalakshmamma provided shelter and organised marriages.
Acchamamba wrote Abala Sachcharitra Ratnamala, Ramabai and Shantabai were associated with Hindu Sundari, and Muthulakshmi Reddy and Chodagam Ammannaraja worked for the Devadasi Bill.

secs.t: Reform and cultural associations → founder and year

x: The Madras Native Association dates to 1852 and was associated with Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty; the Madras Mahajana Sabha was formed in 1884.
The first widow remarriage in Andhra was in 1881, Stree Samajam at Brundavanapuram and Hindu Sundari both date to 1902, and the Andhra Desa Library Association to 1914.

The correct associations are Social Purity Association–R. Venkataratnam Naidu; Widow Remarriage Association–Veeresalingam; Temperance and Social Purity Sangham–Desiraju Peda Bapayya; and Varthamana Vyavaharikandhra Bhasha Parivartaka Samaj–Gidugu Ramamurthy.

secs.t: Journals → founder and year — Journals → founder

x: Vivekavardhini attacked corruption and superstition, while Satyasamvardhini printed a biography of Raja Rammohan Roy.

Satyaduta was issued by the Bellary Christian Mission; Satyasamvardhini was associated with the Rajahmundry Prarthana Samaj; Janana Patrika concerned women's education; and Chintamani was the first Telugu political journal.
Veeresalingam's
Hasyasanjeevani
, started in 1876, was a satirical reply to Kokkonda Venkataratnam's Hasyavardhini.
Telugu was associated with Gidugu in 1919, Janavani with Tapi Dharma Rao, and the Andhra Sahitya Parishad magazine with Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu.
Satyavahini, also referred to as Satyavadini, was Veeresalingam's reply to Kasibhatta Brahmayya Sastri's Arya Mata Bodhini and is associated with 1905.

secs.t: Journals → founder and year — Conflicting keys

x: Kokkonda Venkataratnam was an orthodox editor of *Andhra Bhasha Sanjeevini* and opposed the reform towards spoken Telugu.

secs.t: Books → authors: Veeresalingam, Brahmo texts and early prose

x: Vedam Venkataraya Sastri wrote
Stree Punarvivaha Durvada Nirvaranam
in 1883, described as the first major anti-remarriage book.
Abhijnana Sakuntalam, Malavikagnimitram and Ratnavali were among the translations through which Veeresalingam rendered classical Sanskrit drama into Telugu for the first time.
Rajasekhara Charitra carried the reform themes of
widow remarriage and education
and helped establish the pattern of Telugu social fiction.
C. P. Brown, Collector of Cuddapah, prepared the first Telugu-English dictionaries and edited Vemana’s verses.

secs.t: Gurajada Apparao → role, works and Kanyasulkam — Role

x: Gurajada Appa Rao worked alongside
Kandukuri Veeresalingam
's reform activities, contributing to literary and cultural renaissance.
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy
and Gurajada Appa Rao were prominent champions of vyavaharika, or spoken, Telugu.
Gurajada Apparao, associated with 1861–1915, and Gidugu Ramamurthy, associated with 1863–1940, are described as twin pioneers.

secs.t: Gurajada Apparao → role, works and Kanyasulkam — Works - genre and social theme

x: Kanyasulkam attacked bride-price and child marriage, Mutyala Saralu introduced a new metre, and Desamunu Preminchumanna is a patriotic song associated with Gurajada Appa Rao.
Saranga Dhara is an English poem written with Shyamala Rao and published in Indian Leisure Hour; it is not a Telugu novel.
A is true: Kanyasulkam is a social play in spoken (vyavaharika) Telugu attacking bride-price, child marriage and the plight of widows.

secs.t: Gurajada Apparao → role, works and Kanyasulkam — Kanyasulkam - characters and dialect

x: Exam angle: assertion-reason - "Kanyasulkam written by Kommaraju Lakshmana Rao" is false; "it is a satirical play on social evils" is true.
Gurajada's line means that
a country is its people, not merely its soil
. ⚠ Sources differ on the poem it comes from: Desamunu Preminchumanna / Desabhakti in most notes, while the APPSC 2025 key says Kanyaka.

secs.t: Gidugu Ramamurthy → life, tribal-language work and Telugu Language Day

x: 29 August is observed as Telugu Language Day in recognition of
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy
, a major champion of vyavaharika Telugu.
Gidugu Ramamurthy was born on 29 August 1863 at Ponduru in the Srikakulam region.
Gidugu created a script, prepared bilingual dictionaries and wrote *A Manual of Savara Language*.
Telugu was granted classical language status by the Government of India in 2008.

secs.t: Vyavaharika vs granthika — terms, bodies and persons

x: Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy led the movement for Vyavaharika Bhasha, opposing
the Sanskritised grandhika style
Orthodox pandits supported Granthika Telugu, while Gidugu and Gurajada led the Vyavaharika cause.
Gidugu founded the Vyavaharika Bhashodyama Samstha after a meeting held at
Visakhapatnam
P. T. Srinivasa Ayyangar
wrote *Life or Death: A Plea for Vernaculars* in support of vernacular language use.
Gidugu, Gurajada, Tapi Dharma Rao and the Navya Sahitya Parishat all supported the movement for spoken-Telugu prose.

secs.t: Titles — called as / known as

x: Gidugu was born in 1863, founded the organisation in 1910, received Kaisar-e-Hind in 1934, and died in 1940.
Gidugu was known as Vyavaharika Bhashodyama Pitamaha and Abhinava Vaganushasanudu, and received the titles Rao Saheb and Kaisar-e-Hind.
M. G. Ranade
called Veeresalingam the ‘Vidyasagar of South India’ in 1898, when Veeresalingam presided over the Indian Social Reform Congress at Madras.

secs.t: Social evils, methods and opponents

x: Paidah Ramakrishnayya supported remarriages at Kakinada, Vedam Venkataraya Sastri wrote the anti-remarriage work, and Kasibhatta Brahmayya Sastri was associated with Aryananda Brundavani Sabha.
Veeresalingam's reform methods included journals, satire, public lectures, schools, co-education, remarriages at his own expense and widow homes.
Nautch
, or the Bhogam system, was one of the social evils targeted by reformers in Andhra.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Kasibhatta Brahmayya Sastri
criticised Rajasekhara Charitra by calling it a mere translation.
Veeresalingam is linked with the Prarthana Samaj and widow remarriage, while Venkataratnam Naidu was associated with the Brahmo Samaj, anti-nautch and social purity reforms.
The reform movement became institutional through
samajs, homes and journals
, enabling it to outlive its individual founders.
The Prarthana Samaj did not reject idol worship or caste outright, whereas the Brahmo Samaj took a more categorical position against them.
Vyavaharika prose made school books, newspapers and nationalist songs accessible to a wider public.

rows.title: Cultural institutions and the Telugu renaissance in the early 20th century
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-168

secs.t: Telugu FIRSTs — book, journal, novel, drama

x: Vavilala Vasudeva Sastri
wrote Seesari Charitra, a Telugu rendering of Julius Caesar, in 1875.
The standard answer is Kandukuri Veeresalingam’s Rajasekhara Charitram, although some scholars have proposed Kokkonda Venkataratnam’s Mahasweta.
The 2011 key names
Tatvabodhini
(1864-70) as the first Telugu magazine from Bellary, although Satyaduta (1835) is also called the first Telugu journal.

secs.t: Colonial scholars of Telugu → contributions

x: The Kavali brothers
—Borraiah, Venkataramaiah and Lakshmaiah—assisted Colin Mackenzie in collecting Kaifiyats.
C.P. Brown edited works of Nannaya, Tikkana, Pothana and other classical poets, helping rescue palm-leaf texts through missionary presses.
The C.P. Brown Memorial Trust Library is at
Kadapa
(Cuddapah), where Brown served as Collector (APPSC G2 2001 and 2005 keys).

secs.t: Places → presses, journals and press laws

x: These measures were press regulations or Press Acts used to impose curbs on the press during colonial rule.
Christian missionaries made the major contribution to education in Andhra
The correct order is Adams Regulation in 1823, Vernacular Press Act in 1878, Press Acts in 1908 and 1910, and the declaration of Telugu as a Classical Language in 2008.

secs.t: Books → authors: modern Telugu works

x: Asamardhuni Jeevayatra was written by
Tripuraneni Gopichand
Musalamma Maranamu was written by Gurajada Apparao, not Tripuraneni Gopichand.
Gabbilam, published in 1941, presents
a bat carrying a Dalit’s prayer to God
Kandukuri Veeresalingam
is known as the Father of the Telugu Renaissance.
Veeresalingam was the first to render Kalidasa’s Shakuntalam and Malavikagnimitram into Telugu.

secs.t: Literary associations and places → Andhra Sahitya Parishat, Rajahmundry, Brown's College

x: Kokkonda Venkataratnam
presided over the Andhra Sahitya Parishat meetings at Rajahmundry on 23 April 1912 and 22 April 1913.
Pattam Parabrahma Sastri, Ravipati Gurumurti Sastri and Juluri Appayya of Brown’s College wrote commentaries on these works.
The Young Men's Association, Rajahmundry, played an active role in Bipin Chandra Pal's Rajahmundry visit (APPSC G2 2017 key).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Telugu Language Day falls on 29 August, marks Gidugu's birth anniversary, and is associated with Telugu Language Awards.
Andhra Pradesh re-introduced Vemana Suktulu lessons in schools, and a Telugu Bhavan was planned in Mumbai.
Penugonda
is the principal kshetra of Goddess Vasavi.
The 2019 key names
Rudra Purushadatta
as the last Ikshvaku ruler.

rows.title: Women's question in the 19th century - widow remarriage, age of consent, education, women's organisations
sub: Group-II S1-73: Social legislation in the colonial period - Sati, widow remarriage, age of consent

secs.t: Early humanitarian laws → year and Governor-General (1795–1870)

x: Regulation XVII of 1829, associated with William Bentinck, prohibited sati and treated participation in it as culpable homicide.
The order is Bengal Regulation XXI of 1795, the Sagar Island measure of 1802, the Female Infanticide Prevention Act of 1870, and the Native Marriage Act of 1872.
The Charter Act of 1833 directed abolition, Act V of 1843 under Ellenborough made slavery illegal, and the IPC of 1860 made the slave trade an offence.

secs.t: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar → contributions and the Widow Remarriage Act, 1856

x: Exam angle: statement pairs "upliftment of women" + "movement for Widow Remarriage Act" → both correct.
The bill was prepared during Dalhousie’s tenure but the Act was enacted in July 1856 under Lord Canning.
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar served as
Head Pandit at Fort William College
As Principal of Sanskrit College, Calcutta, Vidyasagar opened the institution to non-Brahmin students.
Vidyasagar helped
J.E.D. Bethune
establish the Bethune School in 1849, one of the earliest girls’ schools in India.

secs.t: Age-of-consent campaigners and cases → contributions

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2020 asked what the Rakhmabai case was about (age of consent + restitution of conjugal rights).
Bal Gangadhar Tilak
opposed the Bill, including through Kesari, on the ground that it was foreign interference in Hindu custom.
Phulmoni Dasi
, a child bride of about 10-11, died after forced cohabitation (1889-90), and her case pushed the 1891 Act through.

secs.t: Marriage and consent Acts → ages (1872, 1891, 1929 and later) — Native Marriage Act (Civil Marriage Act), 1872

x: Keshab broke the Native Marriage Act he had himself campaigned for by marrying his minor daughter to the Cooch Behar prince, and this split the Samaj in 1878.
The 1891 Act raised the age of consent from 10 to 12, dealt with consummation rather than directly regulating marriage, and was enacted during Lord Lansdowne’s tenure.
BNS 2023 Section 63 retains the age of consent at
18 years
, consistent with the position under POCSO 2012.

secs.t: Marriage and consent Acts → ages (1872, 1891, 1929 and later) — Child Marriage Restraint Act (Sarda Act), 1929

x: The Sarda Act was moved by
Har Bilas Sarda
during the period of Lord Irwin.
The 2021 proposal to raise the women's age to 21 had not become law by January 2026, when the legal age remained 18.
The Sarda Act fixed
14 for girls and 18 for boys
, the same ages as the 1872 Native Marriage Act.

secs.t: Women reformers of western India → FIRSTs, institutions, works

x: Exam angle: matching "Sharda Sadan → a home for widows".
D.K. Karve founded the Widow Marriage Association, Pandita Ramabai founded the Arya Mahila Samaj, and Jyotiba and Savitribai Phule established a girls' school for untouchables.
The Phules opened a girls’ school at Pune in 1848, Savitribai is regarded as India’s first woman teacher, and a home for upper-caste widows was established in 1854.

secs.t: Reform institutions and women's organisations → founder and year

x: Exam angle: institution-founder matching; the 2023 key differs from the textbooks.
Poona Seva Sadan was founded by
Ramabai Ranade and G.K. Devadhar
The Ladies’ Social Conference, also called Bharat Mahila Parishad, was associated with Ramabai Ranade in Bombay in 1904 and functioned under the National Social Conference.
Deva Samaj — Shiv Narayan Agnihotri; Seva Samiti — Hriday Nath Kunzru (Allahabad, 1914); Social Service League — N.M. Joshi (Bombay, 1911); Sharada Sadan — Pandita Ramabai (1889).

secs.t: Andhra — Veeresalingam's work and women reformers → contributions

x: Veeresalingam's first girls' school dates to 1874, the Innispeta school to 1881, and he was the first in Andhra to promote co-education.
Kandukuri Rajyalakshmamma hosted widow remarriages and inter-caste marriages at her home, which also became a shelter for widows and destitute women.
Bandaru Achamamba wrote
Abala Sachcharitra Ratnamala
, dealing with the lives of notable women.
Missionaries ran widow homes in Andhra
as part of the social-support environment associated with reform efforts.

secs.t: Social-reform Acts — year, Governor-General, provision, mover (revision table)

x: Exam angle: Act-year-Governor-General matching, and ages under the 1872, 1891 and 1929 Acts.
Exam angle: "Sati was abolished by" → Bentinck; "Widow Remarriage Act passed in" → 1856.
The correct sequence is the Caste Disabilities Removal Act of 1850, Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act of 1856, Age of Consent Act of 1891, and Child Marriage Restraint Act of 1929.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The age of consent is 18 under POCSO/BNS, while the minimum marriage age under the PCMA 2006 is 18 for women and 21 for men.

The Supreme Court's observation concerns POCSO and consensual adolescent relationships, while the Rajasthan High Court criticised 'Atta Satta' and noted its possible violation of the PCMA, 2006 when minors are involved.

rows.title: Growth of nationalism - factors; pre-Congress political associations

secs.t: Factors of nationalism — causes, reactions and Lytton's measures

x: Exam angle: "Which was NOT a measure of Lytton?" (the Ilbert Bill was Ripon's).

British rule produced political, administrative and economic integration through railways, telegraph, post and uniform laws, but economic exploitation ruined many artisans rather than bringing them prosperity.
Economic exploitation, racial arrogance, Lytton’s policies, the Ilbert Bill controversy and foreign nationalist movements stimulated nationalism.

secs.t: Nationalist literature → authors and years

x: Bankim wrote Anandamath in 1882, and Tagore first sang Vande Mataram at the Calcutta INC of 1896.
The Telugu translation of Vande Mataram was made by
Y. Doraiswamayya and M. Ramarao
'The Cry of Mother India' appeared in
Krishna Patrika on 15 December 1905
and was regarded as the first nationalist song in Andhra.

secs.t: Newspapers and Telugu journals → founders and years

x: Amrita Bazar Patrika was founded in 1868 and changed into an English newspaper overnight in 1878 to escape the Vernacular Press Act.
Sisir Kumar Ghosh
was the founder-editor of Amrita Bazar Patrika.
Kasinadhuni Nageswara Rao
founded Andhra Patrika in 1908.
Tanguturi Prakasam
founded the English daily Swarajya at Madras in 1922 (APPSC G2 2011 key).

secs.t: Persons → contributions: Surendranath Banerjee and Gazula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty

x: The reduction from 21 to 19 was viewed as a measure to exclude Indians from the ICS, and Surendranath Banerjee campaigned against it.
Surendranath Banerjee convened the Indian National Conference in 1883 and 1885; it subsequently merged with the Indian National Congress.
S. N. Banerjee toured in 1878 on behalf of the
Indian Association
, stimulating political sentiment.

secs.t: Pre-Congress associations of Madras and Andhra → founders, years and activities — Madras Native Association

x: Gazula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty founded the Association on 26 Feb 1852, was its first president, and had started Crescent in 1844.
The Sabha was founded on 16 May 1884 and demanded larger councils with more Indian representation.
The Kakinada Literary Association demanded that the ICS age limit be raised and that the examinations be held simultaneously.

secs.t: Pre-Congress associations of Madras and Andhra → founders, years and activities — Krishna District Association

x: Agricultural banks at Angalur were associated with a Krishna District Association conference in 1900, not the Madras Native Association.
The conferences were held at Guntur in 1892, Machilipatnam in 1893, Eluru in 1894 and Angalur in 1900.
The Krishna District Association, formed in 1892 following the INC’s suggestion, was
the first district association in the Madras Presidency

secs.t: Universal angles

x: These associations trained educated Indians in constitutional political methods such as petitions and memorials and promoted all-India coordination, leading to the formation of the INC in 1885.
The early associations were largely led by landlords or the urban elite and were regional in character.
The Krishna District Association was modelled on the Indian National Congress’s advice to establish district-level political bodies.

rows.title: Foundation of the Indian National Congress 1885 - A.O. Hume, the safety-valve theory
sub: Group-II S1-79: Rise of nationalism and the founding of the Indian National Congress, 1885

secs.t: Causes of nationalism — Lytton, Ilbert Bill and books → authors

x: Lord Lytton
was Viceroy from 1876 to 1880 and enacted both the Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act in 1878.
Dinabandhu Mitra’s Neel Darpan portrayed
the oppression of indigo cultivators
Lord Lytton
(1876-80) held the lavish Delhi Durbar in 1877 amid the famine of 1876; he also passed the Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act (1878).

secs.t: Pre-Congress associations → founders and founding order, 1836 to 1885

x: The Landholders' Society was founded in 1838 to represent zamindar interests, with Dwarkanath Tagore, Prasanna Kumar Tagore and Radhakant Deb among its founders.
George Thomson
founded the Bengal British India Society along with Dwarkanath Tagore, Chandra Mohan Chatterjee and Parmananda Maitra.
Pherozeshah Mehta and K.T. Telang
established the Bombay Presidency Association in 1885 to promote political thinking among western Indian youth.

secs.t: Pre-Congress associations → founders and founding order, 1836 to 1885 — Key associations

x: Sisir Kumar Ghosh
founded the India League in 1875 for the political education of the masses.
Gazula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty
is credited with being the first to spread national ideas in Andhra.
The Indian Association was the most important pre-Congress body and organised national conferences before the foundation of the INC.

secs.t: Founders and officials → roles: Hume, Dufferin and the British founders

x: All four statements describe the background of A.O. Hume as given: his ICS career, clash and demotion under Lytton, retirement and settlement at Shimla, and influence of Ripon's local self-government policy.
Lord Dufferin
(1884-88) was Viceroy in 1885 (UPPSC 2025); he at first encouraged Hume's idea of an annual forum and later mocked the Congress as a 'microscopic minority'.

secs.t: Founding of the INC, 1885 — origins, first session, demands

x: The session met at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, under Viceroy Lord Dufferin.
The first session demanded simultaneous ICS examinations, elected councils, opposition to the annexation of Upper Burma and reduction of military expenditure.
The private meeting followed the December 1884 Theosophical Convention, Hume's Indian National Union preceded the Congress, the first session was held in 1885, and the second in 1886.

secs.t: Scholars → statements on the safety-valve theory

x: R.P. Dutt gave the conspiracy interpretation, while Bipan Chandra criticised the theory as a colonial myth and described Hume as a lightning conductor; Gokhale made the related point about official hostility.

The safety-valve view presents the Congress as an outlet for discontent, while the lightning-conductor view presents Hume as a British intermediary who protected the infant organisation from official suppression.

secs.t: INC sessions 1885–1917 → presidents, venues and FIRSTs

x: "first Muslim/Englishman/woman" statement pairs.
“Vande Mataram” was first sung at the Calcutta session of 1896, presided over by Rahimtulla M. Sayani; Rabindranath Tagore sang it.

Naoroji presided at Calcutta 1886 (the 1885 session was at Bombay under W.C. Bonnerjee - the APPSC 2023 key's 'Calcutta 1885' is a trap), Tyabji at Madras 1887 as the first Muslim president, Yule at Allahabad 1888 as the first English president, and Wedderburn at Bombay 1889.

secs.t: INC presidents → titles, multiple presidencies, women and youngest

x: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
became the youngest Congress president at the age of 35 at the special Delhi session of 1923.
Surendranath Banerjee presided at Poona in 1895 and Ahmedabad in 1902; Rash Behari Ghosh at Surat in 1907 and Madras in 1908; Pherozeshah Mehta at Calcutta in 1890.
Dadabhai Naoroji
, the Grand Old Man of India, presided three times - Calcutta 1886, Lahore 1893 and Calcutta 1906 (APPSC-GS 2025).

secs.t: INC sessions by region and the 1920s → venue and president

x: Sarojini Naidu presided at Kanpur in 1925, R.N. Mudholkar at Bankipore in 1912, C.R. Das at Gaya in 1922 and Maulana Azad at Ramgarh in 1940.
The presidents were Badruddin Tyabji in 1887, Alfred Webb in 1894, Ananda Mohan Bose in 1898 and Lalmohan Ghosh in 1903.
Rash Behari Ghosh presided in Madras in 1908, Bhupendranath Basu in 1914, M.A. Ansari in 1927 and Maulana Mohammad Ali at Kakinada in 1923.

secs.t: Andhra and the early INC — delegates, Nagpur 1891, Madras 1914, Kakinada 1923

x: Ponaka Kanakamma
is identified as the first Telugu woman to attend an Indian National Congress session.
Although 256 Andhra delegates attended the Madras session in 1914, none obtained a Working Committee seat.
Ponaka Kanakamma
led the women's wing at the Kakinada session in 1923.
Anandacharlu (Chittoor) presided at Nagpur in 1891, the first Andhra/Telugu president (APPSC G2 2008 key).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The early nationalists made a major contribution by developing an economic critique of colonial rule, particularly the drain theory.
The safety-valve versus lightning-conductor debate concerns interpretations of the circumstances and purpose of the Congress’s formation.
P. Anandacharlu
presided over the 1891 session and is identified as the first Telugu INC President.
Neel Darpan was written by Dinabandhu Mitra, whereas Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Anandamath.

rows.title: Moderate phase (1885-1905) - leaders, methods, demands and achievements; economic critique of colonialism
sub: Group-II S1-80: Moderate phase - leaders, methods, demands and achievements

secs.t: Moderate leaders → titles, works and associations

x: Surendranath Banerjee wrote *A Nation in Making*. *The Bengalee* was associated with Banerjee, *Rise of the Maratha Power* with Ranade, and *Economic History of India* with R.C. Dutt.
M.G. Ranade was a
judge, economist and social reformer associated with the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha
Dinshaw Wacha was a drain-theory economist who presided over the INC at Calcutta in 1901.

secs.t: Dadabhai Naoroji and Gokhale → contributions

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2019 keyed "Naoroji founded the INC with Hume and Wacha" as wrong - Hume is the founder.
In 1892, Dadabhai Naoroji was elected from Central Finsbury as a Liberal Party candidate.
Gokhale presided at Banaras in 1905, condemning the partition and backing Swadeshi, and he was Gandhi's political guru.

secs.t: Societies and committees → founders, years and aims

x: The London Indian Society was established in 1865, the East India Association in 1866, his election took place in 1892 and he served on the Welby Commission in 1895.
Set up in 1893 by Wedderburn and W.S. Caine with Naoroji, it was a group of sympathetic MPs whose aim was to
agitate for Indian political reforms in the House of Commons

secs.t: Moderate methods — beliefs, 3 Ps, limitations and official attitude

x: Faith in British justice, the 3 Ps, and a two-pronged strategy (opinion in India + persuading Britain).
The
Partition of Bengal in 1905
exposed the limitations of the Moderate faith in British justice and fair play.
Lord Curzon made this remark in 1900 while expressing his hostile attitude towards the Congress.

secs.t: Moderate demands — councils, ICS, military expenditure, tax relief, civil rights

x: The Moderates demanded cuts in military expenditure, along with lower land revenue, abolition of the salt tax and tariff protection for Indian industries.
The Moderates demanded simultaneous examinations, a higher ICS age limit and separation of the judiciary from the executive.
Holding the examination in India as well as England was intended to make entry into the higher services more accessible to Indians and promote Indianisation.

secs.t: Acts, commissions and achievements of the Moderates

x: The Moderates fostered national identity, economic critique and democratic training, but they did not achieve complete independence.
The Welby Commission of 1895 dealt with
Indian expenditure
and was regarded as one of the gains associated with Moderate pressure.
The INC called the 1892 Act inadequate because there was no direct vote, the councils kept an official majority, and the budget could only be discussed, not amended.

secs.t: Economic critique of colonialism — drain of wealth and books → authors

x: Exam angle: APPSC-GS 2018 - author of Poverty and Un-British Rule in India = Naoroji (not R.C. Dutt).
*The Rise and Growth of Economic Nationalism in India* was written by
Bipan Chandra
and was published in 1966.
The drain operated through Home Charges, salaries and pensions, unequal trade and British monopoly.
The drain idea was linked to the devastation after 1857 and was later taken up by the Extremists and Gandhi.

secs.t: Andhra leaders in the early Congress → roles and sessions presided

x: (Vaijayanti/People's Magazine; Rajabahadur and Padyavinoda; Congress General Secretary).
Mocherla Ramachandra Rao
was described as the “Gokhale of South India.”.
After 1908,
Konda Venkatappayya and B.N. Sarma
came to the forefront among the Andhra Moderates.
P. Anandacharlu served as Secretary of the Madras Mahajana Sabha in 1884 and was the first Telugu President of the INC.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Although the Moderates were criticised for relying on petitions, their supporters argued that this approach created realistic political groundwork for the later national struggle.
The Kakinada Literary Association submitted memorandums relating to the Indian Civil Service during 1884–1885.
Gopal Krishna Gokhale
advised Gandhi in connection with his return to India.

rows.title: Growth of the nationalist movement in Andhra, 1885-1905
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-172

secs.t: Andhra spokesmen and leaders → demands and roles, 1885 to 1905

x: The INC opposed the annexation of Upper Burma.
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
presented the data-led drain critique at the 7th Andhra Mahasabha in Guntur in 1919.
The Andhra opposition to the transfer of Ganjam to Orissa was regarded as the
first victory
of the Andhra political movement.
Paidah Ramakrishnayya
served as the municipal president of Kakinada.

secs.t: District associations of Andhra → places and years

x: The Krishna District Association was formed on the lines suggested at the first session of the INC.
Nyapathi Subbarao
presided over the Krishna District Association conference, which attracted approximately 223 delegates.
The order is Krishna (1892), Vizag (1893), Nellore (1908) and Kurnool (1914).
The Krishna District Association (1892) was the first in the Madras Presidency (APPSC-GS 2021).

secs.t: Early nationalist newspapers of Andhra → founders and FIRSTs

x: The pairing of Andhra Prakasika with
P. Anandacharyulu
is accepted as correct.
Nyapathi Subbarao was associated as editor with the monthly publications
Vyjayanti and People's Magazine
These journals criticised administrative failures and helped spread nationalism and democratic ideas.
Andhra Prakasika was the first political magazine in Andhra (APPSC 2012).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Moderate leaders, district associations and nationalist newspapers collectively built Andhra's political base before the Vande Mataram phase of 1905.
The order is
B, A, C, D
: the Madras Mahajana Sabha was founded in 1884, the first INC session met in 1885, the Krishna District Association was formed in 1892 and Krishna Patrika appeared in 1902.

rows.title: Partition of Bengal 1905, Swadeshi and Boycott Movement; techniques and impact
sub: Group-II S1-81: Extremist phase - Partition of Bengal, Swadeshi and Boycott, Surat Split

secs.t: Partition of Bengal 1905 — dates, division, motives and annulment

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2022 A-R - 1911 Durbar true; Edward VII's coronation (celebrated at the 1903 Durbar ) is not its explanation.
Administrative convenience was the stated reason, while the actual policy sought to weaken Bengali nationalism and divide Hindus and Muslims.
The partition was annulled on 12 December 1911 at the Delhi Durbar of King George V. The capital was simultaneously transferred from Calcutta to Delhi.

secs.t: Persons → statements and contributions (Bengal)

x: The Moderates’ campaign from 1903 to 1905 was associated with S.N. Banerjee, K.K. Mitra and Prithwishchandra Ray, and used petitions and meetings.
Lord Curzon
described Bengal as “the nerve centre of Indian nationalism,” reflecting the political significance he attached to the province.
S.N. Banerjee and A.M. Bose raised
for the Swadeshi cause.

secs.t: Swadeshi and Boycott — launch, techniques and phases

x: On 7 August 1905,
the boycott resolution was passed at Calcutta Town Hall and Swadeshi was formally proclaimed
The boycott targeted foreign cloth, salt and sugar;
indigenous handloom products
were encouraged through the Swadeshi programme.
Jatras, folk songs, melas, volunteer corps and physical-training institutions such as akharas and lathi clubs were all used for mobilisation.

secs.t: Institutions and Swadeshi enterprises → founder

x: Bengal Chemicals was founded by
Acharya P.C. Ray
as a Swadeshi enterprise.
V.O. Chidambaram Pillai established the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company at Tuticorin in 1906.
The National Council of Education was established on
15 August 1906
and later became associated with Jadavpur University.
Munagala Raja’s textile unit at Vijayawada, established in June 1906, was the first of its kind in the Madras Presidency.

secs.t: Art, literature and science → figure and work

x: Rabindranath Tagore
wrote ‘Amar Sonar Bangla’, which later became Bangladesh’s national anthem.
Bankim Chandra Chatterjee wrote ‘Bande Mataram’, which became the anthem of the Swadeshi movement. ‘Desher Katha’ was written by S.G. Deuskar.
S.G. Deuskar’s ‘Desher Katha’ warned against
the British ‘hypnotic conquest of the mind’
Abanindranath Tagore’s Bharat Mata represented nationalist art and marked a break with Victorian naturalism.

secs.t: Extremist leaders → region, title, journals and trials

x: Aurobindo Ghosh, Bipin Chandra Pal and Ashwini Kumar Dutt were associated with Bengal.
Syed Haider Raza
was identified with the Swadeshi movement in Delhi.
Bal Gangadhar Tilak served a six-year imprisonment at
Mandalay
Bipin Chandra Pal undertook an Andhra tour in 1907 and was subsequently arrested.
Chirol called
Bal Gangadhar Tilak
(Lokmanya, of Maharashtra) the Father of Indian Unrest.

secs.t: Andhra Swadeshi — beginnings, Bala Bharati Samiti, Pal's tour (place → host) — Beginnings

x: S.N. Banerjee's arrest in 1906 set off protests at Rajahmundry, Kakinada, Vizianagaram and Gooty under the slogan 'Vandemataram - Manade Rajyam'.

secs.t: Andhra Swadeshi — beginnings, Bala Bharati Samiti, Pal's tour (place → host) — Bipin Chandra Pal's tour → place, date, host

x: Exam angle: the APPSC 2025 key paired Pal's tour with July 1907 and the Kakinada riots case with April 1907; APP dates Pal's tour to April 1907 - learn the key's pairing for that match.
The Bala Bharati Samiti was formed at Rajahmundry in February 1907 by local youths and was supported by Karanam Guneswara Rao.
Kompalle Hanumantha Rao
was Pal's host at Machilipatnam (APPSC 2008 key), where the Young Men's Swarajya Samithi was formed.

secs.t: Andhra incidents and trials → date, place, FIRSTs

x: Mark Hunter banned Vandemataram badges, 138 of 222 students were suspended, and the incident began student participation in Andhra.
Nyapati Subbarao
defended the accused in the Kakinada Riot Case.
The Kakinada case followed the assault of Kompelli Krishna Rao by Dr Kemp after the boy shouted Vande Mataram, after which the European Club was attacked.
The Kotappakonda police clash occurred near Narasaraopet; Chinnappa Reddy was hanged and the incident was associated with the only death sentence in India during the movement.

secs.t: Events → date (partition to annulment, 1905-1916)

x: The sequence is 7 August 1905, 16 October 1905, 15 August 1906 and 12 December 1911.
In December 1906, the Muslim League was formed at Dacca and the Calcutta Congress under Dadabhai Naoroji adopted Swaraj.
The Home Rule Leagues and the Lucknow Pact are associated with 1916.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sumit Sarkar authored
The Swadeshi Movement in Bengal
, dealing with the 1905 partition and its movement.
Japan’s victory over Russia in 1904–05
inspired Asian and Indian nationalist sentiment and contributed to anger against the partition.
The movement was regarded as the first mass movement, fostered mass nationalism and popularised boycott, Swadeshi and national education as methods of struggle.

rows.title: Swadeshi and Vandemataram movement in Andhra - Bipin Chandra Pal's tour, student participation
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-173

secs.t: Vandemataram movement in Andhra — name, phase, trigger, slogan

x: In Andhra, the Swadeshi-related agitation was popularly known as the
Vandemataram Movement
The protesters raised the slogan “
Vandemataram - Manade Rajyam
,” meaning that self-rule belonged to them.
“Vande Mataram” became a popular greeting as well as a political expression.

secs.t: Andhra leaders → roles, journals, songs and regions

x: Hinduvulara ennaall ee gati

' by Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham, the first Telugu national poet, is the first Telugu national song. 'Bharata khandambu chakkani paadi yaavu' was his poem composed on the spot during Pal's tour; 'Vandemataram - Manade Rajyam' was a protest slogan; Matru Murthi was Pal's final speech at Machilipatnam.

secs.t: Bipin Chandra Pal's tour, April 1907 — town → host / organiser

x: Exam angle: pairing a town with its host or organising body.

Kattiventi Perraju presided at Kakinada (17 Apr), Gadicherla welcomed Pal at Rajahmundry (19-24 Apr), Munagala Raja (with Nayani Venkata Rangarao) hosted him at Vijayawada (24 Apr), and Kompalle Hanumantha Rao hosted him at Machilipatnam (27 Apr; APPSC 2008 key).

secs.t: Swadeshi bodies and national institutions → place, year, founder

x: Nyapathi Subbarao and K. Venkataramana Rao
toured Andhra to popularise Swadeshi activities.
The National College (Andhra Jateeya Kalasala) came up at Machilipatnam in 1910, with the foundation stone laid by Pal in 1907.
Japan's victory over Russia inspired many young Andhras to seek industrial training in Japan and influenced Munagala Raja, the play Japaniyam and Adipudi Somanatha Rao's Japan Charitra.

secs.t: Incidents, riots and cases → date, place, outcome — Rajahmundry college student incident, 1907

x: Mark Hunter, principal of the Rajahmundry Arts and Teachers Training College, banned Vandemataram badges and the slogan in April 1907.
Gadicherla defied Principal Mark Hunter by presenting an address to Bipin Chandra Pal.
A total of
138 students were debarred from examinations for two years
after the incident.
The incident marked the active entry of Andhra students into the freedom struggle.

secs.t: Incidents, riots and cases → date, place, outcome — Riots, sedition and bomb cases, 1907-1909

x: Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
started the Telugu weekly Swarajya in 1908.
His article Viparita Buddhi led to a sedition charge and a sentence of
three years
' rigorous imprisonment.
The accused were
Chukkapalli Ramaiah, Lakkaraju Basavaiah and K. Venkatarayudu
T. Prakasam
successfully secured the release of the accused in the Tenali bomb case.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The movement was connected with national education, Swadeshi stores and student politics.
The movement fed into the Andhra Mahasabha era and the Home Rule branches led by the same men, including Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao and Konda Venkatappaiah.
Chinnapa Reddy
is identified with the only death sentence in India associated with this movement; he was connected with Kotappakonda.

rows.title: Extremists - Lal-Bal-Pal and Aurobindo; ideology; Surat Split 1907

secs.t: Moderates vs Extremists — classification and ideology

x: The three principles of self-reliance, self-sacrifice and strong will characterised the Extremists, not the Moderates.
The Moderates were generally pro-reform, while the Extremists were comparatively orthodox; Tilak opposed the Age of Consent Bill.
For the Extremists, Swaraj meant
complete freedom from British control
, not merely colonial self-government.
Spiritual nationalism represented the nation as
a mother goddess
, an idea expressed through symbols such as Bande Mataram and Bhavani Mandir.

secs.t: Extremist leaders → region and title (called as / known as)

x: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
was popularly known as ‘Lokmanya’, meaning ‘beloved of the people’.
Chirol used the phrase in his book
Indian Unrest
, published in 1910.
Aurobindo Ghosh
was regarded as the chief ideologue of the Extremist wing.
The Maharashtra extremist group was led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak; Bengal was associated with Pal and Aurobindo, and Punjab with Lala Lajpat Rai.

secs.t: Extremist leaders → careers and contributions

x: Tilak transformed Ganesh Utsav into a public festival in 1893 and Shivaji Jayanti in 1895.
Tilak worked with Agarkar in establishing the New English School, and the Deccan Education Society founded Fergusson College; the standard dates are 1880 and 1884.
Tilak received 18 months in the 1897 sedition trial, six years in Mandalay in 1908, and was acquitted in the 1916 case.
Bipin Chandra Pal was arrested in 1907
for refusing to testify in the Bande Mataram case

secs.t: Extremist leaders → newspapers, books and slogans

x: Tilak published
Kesari
in Marathi and Mahratta in English; both newspapers began in 1881.
Aurobindo Ghosh was the editor of Bande Mataram and wrote New Lamps for Old.
Bipin Chandra Pal
is commonly identified with Aurobindo Ghosh as a co-editor of Bande Mataram.
The Arctic Home in the Vedas was written by
Bal Gangadhar Tilak

secs.t: Sessions — Calcutta 1906 and Surat Split 1907 → president, issues, outcome

x: The Surat clash centred on the four resolutions passed at Calcutta in 1906 (Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education): the Extremists wanted them kept and the boycott extended to all India, while the Moderates wanted them dropped.
Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta represented the Moderates, while Bal Gangadhar Tilak represented the Extremists in the Surat conflict.

secs.t: Acts and repression 1907-1910 → year

x: Bipin Chandra Pal was arrested in 1907 for refusing to testify in the Bande Mataram case; he was not deported to Mandalay.
By 1910, Tilak was in jail, Aurobindo had retired to Pondicherry, Pal had been arrested and Lajpat Rai had left.
The correct order is 1907 deportation of Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh, 1908 deportation of Tilak, Aurobindo's acquittal in 1909 and his retirement to Pondicherry in 1910.

secs.t: Events → year (Swadeshi to Lucknow Pact and Home Rule, 1905-1916)

x: The Swadeshi Movement was launched on 7 August 1905, following the partition of Bengal.
Tilak began his league on 28 April 1916, Besant’s in September, and the reunion and Lucknow Pact occurred in December.
The sequence is Swadeshi Movement in 1905, Surat Split in 1907, Morley-Minto Reforms in 1909 and Lucknow Pact in 1916.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Extremists broadened nationalism into a mass movement and placed Swaraj at the centre of the political goal.
The Extremists were criticised for using religious symbolism that alienated Muslims and for being socially orthodox.
Students of the Machilipatnam National College wore
Besant lockets
after Annie Besant was arrested on 15 June 1917.
Gadicherla was called Andhra Tilak, and Andhra had 52 Home Rule branches by 1917.

rows.title: Morley-Minto Reforms 1909; formation of the Muslim League 1906; Lucknow Pact 1916

secs.t: Persons → positions held and roles

x: Lord Minto II was Viceroy from 1905 to 1910, during which the Muslim League was formed in 1906, the Surat Split occurred in 1907, and the Newspapers Act and Muzaffarpur case occurred in 1908.
Lord Minto
is associated with the title 'Father of the Communal Electorate' because the Morley-Minto Reforms introduced separate electorates for Muslims.

secs.t: Simla Deputation and the All India Muslim League, 1906

x: Exam angle: statement-type - "founded under the leadership of the Aga Khan, the Nawab of Dhaka..." - check each name/date/role carefully.
The Simla Deputation, led by Aga Khan III, met Lord Minto on
1 October 1906
The early League aimed at loyalty to the British Empire, protection of Muslim political interests and separation from the Congress; immediate armed revolt was not one of its stated aims.

secs.t: Indian Councils Act 1909 — name, aim and provisions

x: The 1909 Act enlarged the Central Legislative Council (additional members up to 60) but kept an official majority at the Centre, and gave the provinces a non-official majority that the Governor's veto left powerless in practice.
Morley and Minto sought to
rally the Moderates and reward Muslim loyalty
through limited constitutional concessions and separate electorates.

secs.t: Lucknow session and Lucknow Pact 1916 — terms

x: The 1916 session marked the reunion of Moderates and Extremists, Tilak's return and the Congress-League alliance represented by the Lucknow Pact.
Under the Lucknow Pact's communal veto, no bill affecting a community could be passed if
three-fourths
of that community's members in the legislature opposed it.
The Pact was negotiated by Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Muhammad Ali Jinnah with the Muslim League's Young Party.

secs.t: Acts → electoral feature introduced (1909, 1919, 1935)

x: Exam angle: "Which Act introduced the communal electorate?" → Morley-Minto 1909; match-the-list of Acts with separate electorates / dyarchy / federation / provincial autonomy.

The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in the provinces and bicameralism with direct elections at the Centre, and the 1935 Act prescribed an All-India Federation (along with provincial autonomy and dyarchy at the Centre).

secs.t: Events → year (Surat Split to Swaraj Party; League's two-nation milestones)

x: Muhammad Iqbal
proposed the idea of a Muslim state in the North-West in his Allahabad Address of 1930.
Chaudhry Rahmat Ali coined the name “PAKISTAN” in 1933 in the pamphlet
Now or Never
At the Delhi Durbar (12 December 1911) the partition was annulled, announced through King George V, and the capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The year 1909 is associated with the legal start of separate electorates, whereas 1916 is regarded as the high point of Congress-League unity.
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao and Bodi Narayana Rao
were arrested on 18 July 1908 for a Swarajya article during the Minto-Morley repression - the first Telugu political prisoners.

rows.title: Revolutionary nationalism - first phase: Anushilan Samiti, Yugantar, Alipore and Kakori-era cases, Savarkar
sub: Group-II S1-82: Revolutionary movements in India and abroad - first and second phases

secs.t: Revolutionary societies → founder, place, year

x: Pulin Behari Das was associated with the Dhaka branch, Yugantar was an offshoot of Anushilan Samiti, and Bharat Mata Society was associated with Ajit Singh and Lala Lajpat Rai.
Many early revolutionary groups grew out of akhadas or gymnasiums and secret societies such as Anushilan and Atmonnati Samiti.
Shyamji Krishna Varma founded India House in London in 1905, and the Ghadar Party's headquarters was Yugantar Ashram, San Francisco.
Sachindranath Sanyal, Jogesh Chatterjee and Ram Prasad Bismil were associated with the founding of the Hindustan Republican Association.

secs.t: Assassinations and bomb actions → target, place, date

x: Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki targeted
Magistrate Douglas Kingsford
at Muzaffarpur.
Basanta Kumar Biswas
physically threw the bomb, while Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal were among those who planned the attack.
Vanchi Aiyar shot Robert Ashe at Maniyachi on 17 June 1911 and was linked with the Bharata Matha Association (and V.O. Chidambaram Pillai's Swadeshi Steam Navigation agitation).
The Saunders killing was planned in retaliation for the lathi-charge on
Lala Lajpat Rai
during the anti-Simon Commission protest.
Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw the bombs against the Public Safety and Trade Disputes Bills.

secs.t: Conspiracy cases → year, accused, verdict

x: Chittaranjan Das, popularly known as
C.R. Das
, defended Aurobindo Ghosh in the Alipore Bomb Case.
The assassination of A.M.T. Jackson by Anant Kanhere led to Savarkar’s implication and sentence to life imprisonment in the Andamans.
The Ghadar revolt in Punjab was fixed for
21 February 1915
, but the plan was betrayed and many participants were hanged under the Defence of India Act.
The Lahore Conspiracy Case of 1929–30 resulted in the execution of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru on 23 March 1931.

secs.t: Revolutionaries abroad → events and bodies (1905-1915)

x: Raja Mahendra Pratap, Barkatullah and Obaidullah Sindhi were associated with the Provisional Government of India established at Kabul in 1915.
The Komagata Maru carried 376 mainly Sikh passengers, who were refused entry into Canada and forced back to India.
The Budge Budge firing killed 22 people and contributed to the radicalisation of the Ghadar movement.

secs.t: Revolutionaries → contributions, birth and fate

x: Chandrashekhar Azad reorganised the Hindustan Republican Association into the
Hindustan Socialist Republican Association
after Bismil’s death.
Jatin Das died after
63 days
of hunger strike in Lahore jail in 1929 and was regarded as the first martyr of that strike.
Azad shot himself at
Alfred Park, Prayagraj
, on 27 February 1931.

secs.t: Revolutionary writings and journals → author / editor

x: Savarkar wrote 'The Indian War of Independence, 1857' (1909) and 'Hindutva' (1923). 'Mukti Kon Pathe' (1906) was Barindra Kumar Ghosh's revolutionary manual.

The Tenali Bomb Case (6 April 1909) belongs to the Vande Mataram phase; the Kakinada bomb case is linked with Prativadi Bhayankaracharyulu, who spent 14 years in the Andamans (Andaman Jeevitam); and Darshi Chenchayya wrote the Ghadar memoir Nenu Naa Desam.

secs.t: Revolutionaries in Andhra → Alluri Sitarama Raju and other cases

x: Raju’s contact with Bengal revolutionaries preceded his leadership of the Rampa Rebellion against the Muttadari system and forest laws.
Gam Mallu Dora and Gam Gantam Dora
were associated with Alluri Sitarama Raju as lieutenants.
The first attack was on
Chintapalli
police station on 22 August 1922; Krishnadevipeta and Rajavommangi were attacked after it.

secs.t: Chronology of revolutionary events → year (1897-1931)

x: Kesari was started in 1881, Khudiram was executed in 1908, Curzon Wyllie was killed in 1909 and Al-Hilal was started in 1912.
The Chapekars killed Rand in 1897, the Muzaffarpur Bomb Case occurred in 1908, the Nasik case in 1909 and the Hardinge attack in 1912.
The sequence is 1908 Muzaffarpur and Alipore cases, 1909 killing of Curzon Wyllie, 1912 Hardinge bomb and 1915 Ghadar revolt and Singapore Mutiny.

Gandhi's rural development approach was reflected in the initiative known as
Samagra Gramseva

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gandhian ideas influenced the Directive Principles, the panchayat framework associated with the 73rd Amendment and policies supporting cottage industries.
Tummala Sitaramamurthy
wrote *Sarvodaya Ganam*, inspired by Vinoba, and translated Gandhi's autobiography into Telugu.
Gandhian trusteeship has been cited in connection with owners funding fire-safety systems, while Gandhian civil resistance has been credited as an influence in the Baltic freedom struggle.

rows.title: Gandhi on caste, untouchability, religion, women and education (Nai Talim)

secs.t: Gandhi's views — untouchability, women, religion

x: Gandhi's approach combined
moral persuasion, temple entry, funds, schools and hostels, and constructive work
After 1937, Congress ministries provided free education to Harijans as part of their social reform measures.
Women picketed liquor shops, made salt and faced lathis.
Gandhi opposed
purdah, child marriage and dowry
, and supported the remarriage of child widows.
Sarva dharma samabhava means
equal respect for all religions

secs.t: Harijan Sevak Sangh, 1932 → founder, name, work

x: The Sangh worked for access to wells, schools and temples, and promoted schools, hostels, cooperatives, inter-dining and inter-caste marriage.

secs.t: Persons → role in Harijan work, women's work and Nai Talim

x: B is the intended key: Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao was president of the Vijayawada branch (the Andhra branches were at Hyderabad and Vijayawada, 1932).
Kolla Tayaramma led Harijan schools and hostels at Tenali, while Alladi Annapurna Devi was associated with similar work at Nellore.
Durgabai Deshmukh
collected Rs 5,000 at Kakinada in April 1921 for the Tilak Swaraj Fund.

secs.t: Harijan weekly and Harijan tours → dates

x: Gandhi's Harijan tour ran from November 1933 to July 1934, covered about 20,000 km, began from the Wardha Ashram and collected funds for the Harijan Sevak Sangh.
Gandhi adopted the term ‘Harijan’, meaning ‘children of God’, from the Gujarati saint
Narsi Mehta
Gandhi toured Andhra extensively for Harijan uplift and anti-untouchability work, visited Machilipatnam for Swaraj Nidhi and was associated with Ponduru khadi.

secs.t: Nai Talim → Wardha Scheme and Zakir Hussain Committee (1937)

x: Gandhi's Basic Education was vocational and craft-centred, sought to make villages self-sufficient and aimed to dignify manual labour.
The scheme was adopted in 1937, drafted by the Zakir Hussain Committee, and envisaged seven years of free and compulsory education.
Nai Talim emphasised the mother tongue, productive craft and dignity of manual labour; it did not prescribe
exclusive reliance on classical languages

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gandhi's campaign made untouchability a national issue, and Article 17 of the Constitution abolished untouchability.
Ambedkar and Dalit leaders rejected the term ‘Harijan’ and criticised what they regarded as caste-Hindu paternalism.
Potti Sriramulu undertook temple-entry fasts in Nellore in 1946.

rows.title: Champaran, Ahmedabad Mill and Kheda Satyagrahas
sub: Group-II S1-84: Gandhian era - Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad; Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh

secs.t: Gandhi before 1917 — South Africa, return, journals, ashrams, titles

x: Indian Opinion
was the journal associated with Gandhi’s South African period.
He returned on 9 January 1915, marked as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas.
The Satyagraha Ashram at Kochrab was established in 1915, Sabarmati Ashram in 1917 and Sevagram in Wardha in 1936.
Rabindranath Tagore
is credited with giving Gandhi the title ‘Mahatma’.

secs.t: Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda → year, place, issue, outcome — Champaran (1917)

x: Under the
Tinkathia system
, Champaran peasants were compelled to grow indigo on three-twentieths of their land.
Gandhi defied the official order to leave Champaran and toured villages with his lawyers to record complaints against forced indigo cultivation.
The Bengal Indigo Revolt of 1859
preceded and served as an important precursor to the later indigo-related mobilisation in Champaran.

secs.t: Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda → year, place, issue, outcome — Kheda (1918)

x: Exam angle: arrange Champaran - Ahmedabad - Kheda - Rowlatt; Gandhi returned to India in 1915.
The 1918 movement occurred in Kheda, Gujarat; peasants resisted revenue payment despite threats, and Vallabhbhai Patel gave field leadership.
Champaran came first (1917), then the Ahmedabad Mill Strike (Feb-Mar 1918), then Kheda (1918), and the Rowlatt Satyagraha hartal on 6 April 1919.

secs.t: Persons → role in Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda

x: Exam angle: statement pairs on "who invited" and "which state" (Champaran is in Bihar, not Gujarat).
Exam angle: APPSC 2019 - Champaran was the first mass movement (1917) but in
Bihar
, not Gujarat.
Rajkumar Shukla was a
local indigo cultivator
and agriculturist of Champaran who persuaded Gandhi to investigate the peasants’ condition.
The
Kheda Satyagraha
of 1918 marked the start of the Gandhi–Patel alliance, with Vallabhbhai Patel as field commander.

secs.t: Terms → meaning — tinkathia, tawan, plague bonus

x: Sharahbeshi was enhanced rent, while tawan was lump-sum compensation extracted when indigo became less valuable.
The Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association, or Majoor Mahajan Sangh, was founded in 1920 by
Anusuya Sarabhai with Gandhi’s guidance

secs.t: Champaran Agrarian Committee and Act, 1918

x: The Champaran Satyagraha began in 1917, and the Bihar and Orissa government appointed the Champaran Agrarian Enquiry Committee later that year after Gandhi's inquiry.
The recommendations led to the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918, which abolished Tinkathia and secured a partial refund—25 per cent—of illegal exactions.

secs.t: Jallianwala Bagh massacre, 13 April 1919 — officials, casualties, renunciations

x: Damaraju Pundarikakshudu
wrote the Telugu play ‘Panchala Parabhavam’ on Dyer.
Tagore renounced his Knighthood, C. Sankaran Nair resigned from the Viceroy's Executive Council, and Gandhi returned the Kaiser-i-Hind medal.
Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal
were arrested for organising anti-Rowlatt protests.
The massacre occurred at Amritsar, Lord Chelmsford was Viceroy, and Sir Michael O'Dwyer was Punjab's Lieutenant Governor.
O'Dwyer handed Amritsar to Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer, who banned assemblies before the firing.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Champaran, Ahmedabad and related struggles between 1917 and 1919 established Gandhi as a national leader and Satyagraha as an important method of anti-colonial struggle.
The Champaran movement of 1917 and the Kheda movement of 1918
inspired peasant movements in Andhra
The peaceful hartal was observed on 6 April in Vizag, Rajahmundry, Guntur, Vijayawada and Nellore.

rows.title: Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh; Hunter Committee

secs.t: Rowlatt Act, 1919 → committee, provisions, repeal

x: That was its official name.
Statements 1, 2 and 4 are provisions: arrest and detention without warrant or trial, in-camera trials by a three-judge High Court panel, and suspension of habeas corpus.
The Rowlatt legislation extended the extraordinary powers earlier provided under the
Defence of India Act, 1915

secs.t: Committees and inquiries → members and findings

x: The committee censured Dyer, who was relieved of command, but he did not receive real punishment.
The Punjab Sub-Committee included Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, Abbas Tyabji, M.R. Jayakar and Gandhi.
The Congress inquiry condemned Dyer's firing as inhuman and considered the martial law measures
disproportionate
; it demanded action against Dyer.

secs.t: Rowlatt Satyagraha and Punjab, 1919 → events and dates

x: The Rowlatt Satyagraha was the first all-India mass strike and was urban-centred, although it later became violent in Punjab and Ahmedabad.
The movement turned violent in Punjab and Ahmedabad, prompting Gandhi to call it a Himalayan blunder and withdraw it on 18 April 1919.
The order was imposed in the Amritsar lane where
Marcella Sherwood, an English woman missionary
, had been assaulted.

secs.t: Persons → role in the Rowlatt agitation

x: Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Madan Mohan Malaviya and Mazhar-ul-Haq resigned in opposition to the Rowlatt legislation.

secs.t: Slogans and terms of 1919 → meaning; Andhra response

x: The Rowlatt Act was passed on
10 March 1919
The phrase expressed opposition to the denial of ordinary legal safeguards under the
Rowlatt Act
, popularly called the Black Act.
Gandhi visited Vijayawada on 8 April 1919, and
Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao
translated his speech.

secs.t: Chronology — Swadeshi to Quit India

x: Exam angle: APPSC G1 2003 key - Swadeshi, Jallianwala Bagh, Dandi, Quit India.
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was concluded in 1931.
The Simon Commission arrived in 1928.
Swadeshi Movement 1905, Jallianwala Bagh 1919, Dandi March 1930, Quit India 1942 (APPSC G1 2003 key).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The massacre severely damaged Indian faith in British justice and contributed directly to the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements.
Prakasam demanded fundamental rights at the Nellore meeting in September 1919.
The Prime Minister recalled C.
Sankaran Nair
's resignation from the Viceroy's Executive Council on the 106th anniversary in April 2025.
K. Kamaraj joined the freedom struggle after the
Jallianwala Bagh massacre

rows.title: Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement - programme, spread, Chauri Chaura and withdrawal
sub: Group-II S1-85: Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement

secs.t: Khilafat and NCM — aims, background, launch and FIRSTs

x: The movement aimed to restore the Ottoman Sultan as Khalifa and preserve the territorial integrity of the Ottoman Empire after the First World War.
The
Treaty of Sevres
, signed in May 1920, threatened the territorial integrity of the Ottoman Empire and intensified the Khilafat agitation.
The abolition of the Caliphate by Turkey in 1924 removed the central institutional issue around which the Khilafat agitation had developed.

secs.t: Leaders → role in Khilafat, NCM and after

x: Motilal Nehru, Jawaharlal Nehru, C.R. Das, C. Rajagopalachari, Vallabhbhai Patel, Asaf Ali, T. Prakasam and Rajendra Prasad were among the lawyers who gave up practice.
Peasants joined no-tax campaigns, forest users opposed pullari, women participated in large numbers, and Desasevikalu was an Andhra organisation of women volunteers.
The Moplah uprising occurred in August 1921, the Prince of Wales boycott on 17 November 1921, Chauri Chaura in February 1922 and the Swaraj Party was formed in 1923.

secs.t: Sessions and conferences → president and decision

x: The sequence was the failed deputation in February 1920, the Allahabad conference in June 1920, the Karachi conference in July 1921 and abolition of the Caliphate in 1924.
Gandhi presided over the All-India Khilafat Conference at Delhi in November 1919 and first proposed non-violent non-cooperation there.
The Nagpur session unanimously ratified the programme, defined Swaraj in peaceful and legitimate terms, and reorganised Congress units on linguistic lines with committees extending to village level.
Konda Venkatappayya
initially opposed the resolution but subsequently resigned from the Madras Legislature.

secs.t: NCM programme — boycott and constructive items

x: Surrender of titles was a boycott item, non-payment of taxes was the final stage, and khadi/charkha was constructive work.
Surrender of titles, boycott of government educational institutions and replacement of government courts by panchayat courts formed part of the programme.
Boycott of foreign cloth was a boycott measure, and promotion of khadi and the charkha was part of the constructive programme.

secs.t: National institutions → founding year and founder

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2023 - of Jamia, Kashi Vidyapith and AMU, only Jamia and Kashi Vidyapith are NCM-era.
Jamia Millia Islamia
was founded at Aligarh in 1920 and later shifted to Delhi.
Aligarh Muslim University developed from the MAO College, established in 1875 by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan.
Kashi Vidyapith, Gujarat Vidyapith and Bihar Vidyapith were founded in 1921, 1920 and 1921 respectively, during the movement.

secs.t: Parallel struggles, 1920–25 → place and feature

x: The Prince of Wales landed at Bombay on
17 November 1921
, leading to hartals and clashes in the city.
The Moplah uprising took place in Malabar, Kerala, and began as an agrarian conflict involving Muslim tenants and Hindu landlords before turning communal.
The Akali Movement of 1920–25 sought reform of Sikh gurdwaras and culminated institutionally in the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925.

secs.t: Andhra in the NCM — Vijayawada AICC, events, works → authors

x: Viplava Parivarthanam was written by Gollapudi Sitarama Sastri, Veeragandhamu Techhinaramu by Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary, and Makoddi Telladoratanam by Garimella Satyanarayana.
With the Congress boycotting the November 1920 elections, the Justice Party won 63 of 98 seats and the first ministry was formed under A. Subbarayalu Reddiar on 17 December 1920.

secs.t: Andhra no-tax and forest struggles → place and leader

x: Unnava Lakshminarayana and Madabhushi Vedanta Lakshmi Narasimhachari were arrested during the Palnadu forest satyagraha.
The satyagraha was led by Kanneganti Hanumanthu and involved refusal of the grazing tax, boycott of forest officials and the stated arrests.
Kanneganti Hanumanthu led the Palnadu forest satyagraha, Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya led Chirala-Perala, and Parvataneni Veeraiah Chowdary led the Pedanandipadu no-tax movement.
Parvataneni Veeraiah Chowdary, leader of the Pedanandipadu no-tax campaign, founded the Shanti Sena.

secs.t: Chauri Chaura and the withdrawal — date, place, reactions

x: Exam angle: statement pairs - NCM made nationalism a mass movement (true); withdrawn after Jallianwala (false - after Chauri Chaura).
Bhagwan Ahir
was among those beaten by the police before the crowd attacked and burnt the Chauri Chaura police station.
On 4 February 1922 (some sources say 5 Feb) at Chauri Chaura, Gorakhpur district, the crowd burnt the police station and 22 policemen were killed.

secs.t: Gandhi's arrest and the Great Trial — date, charge, judge

x: In April 1919 Gandhi was stopped and detained at
Palwal
while proceeding towards Punjab; the incident contributed to riots.
Gandhi’s 1922 Ahmedabad trial concerned sedition under Section 124A in relation to his Young India articles and resulted in a six-year sentence.
The trial before Judge C.N. Broomfield on 18 March 1922 was called the Great Trial; Gandhi pleaded guilty and requested the highest penalty.

secs.t: Swaraj Party — founders, strategy, Andhra branch

x: The Andhra branch had Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao as president and Unava Lakshmi Narayana as secretary.
The Swarajists entered the councils to expose them as sham parliaments and obstruct their functioning from within, a strategy expressed as “End or Mend.”.
The Gaya session occurred in December 1922, the party was announced on 31 December 1922, it was formally founded on 1 January 1923, and the Delhi special session followed in September 1923.

secs.t: NCM chronology — event → date

x: The Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh belong to 1919; the Treaty of Sevres was signed in May 1920; the Prince of Wales boycott occurred on 17 November 1921; and the Bardoli resolution was adopted on 11–12 February 1922.
The order is the Prince of Wales boycott (17 November 1921), the Bardoli resolution (11–12 February 1922), Gandhi's arrest (March 1922) and the Swaraj Party (1923).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The sudden withdrawal after Chauri Chaura was criticised by Subhas Chandra Bose, M.N. Roy and C.R. Das.
The Marxist interpretation argued that Gandhi halted the movement to prevent it from taking a radical anti-landlord direction.
Vijayawada, Pingali Venkayya, Chirala-Perala, Pedanandipadu and Palnadu
are the Andhra-related references highlighted for this period.

rows.title: Andhra in the Home Rule Movement and the Non-Cooperation Movement
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-195

secs.t: Bezawada (Vijayawada) AICC, 1921 — decisions, targets, flag

x: At the 1921 AICC meeting at Vijayawada, political leaders accepted Gandhi's leadership of the national struggle.
The targets (by 30 June 1921) were 1 crore members, Rs 1 crore for the Tilak Swaraj Fund and 20 lakh charkhas.
The January 1921 APCC meeting at Vijayawada established Congress committees at the
district, taluk and village levels

secs.t: Andhra persons → role in the NCM

x: Duvvuri Subbamma, Ponaka Kanakamma and Unnava Lakshmibayamma
emerged as women leaders during this phase of the movement.
Tanguturi Prakasam
gave up his lucrative legal practice as part of the boycott of courts.
Unnava Lakshmi Narayana and Madabhushi Vedantam Narasimhachari studied and backed the movement.
Unnava Lakshmi Narayana
wrote the play *Nayakuralu* while he was in jail.

secs.t: Andhra places → NCM event

x: The April coastal tour covered Kakinada, Rajahmundry, Eluru, Machilipatnam, Chirala and Nellore.
The Seethanagaram Ashram was located near Rajahmundry and is now known as Kasturba Ashram.
Ponduru
became famous for its Khadi during the nationalist movement.
The Eluru National College and Duggirala's Andhra Vidyapeetha Goshthi at Chirala were among the national educational institutions established during the movement.

secs.t: Palnad forest (Pullari) satyagraha, 1921–22 — place, grievance, action

x: Forest reservation, corrupt forest officials and the fodder shortage caused by failed 1921 rains intensified the grievance against the Pullari system.
The satyagrahis boycotted officials at Macherla, drove 300 cattle into the forest without paying Pullari and had the cattle impounded at Minchalapadu.
Kanneganti Hanumanthu was shot dead during
the cattle-rescue action at Minchalapadu
on 26 February 1922.

secs.t: Chronology — Home Rule to the suspension of the NCM

x: The Delhi AICC of 5 November 1921 permitted provinces to launch
civil disobedience, including no-tax campaigns
Subhas Bose called the suspension a national tragedy, like "sprinkling cold water"; M.N. Roy blamed weak leadership; and Jawaharlal Nehru reacted with "amazement and consternation".
Gandhi suspended the NCM at Bardoli (11-12 February 1922) after a mob burnt a police station at
Chauri Chaura
in Gorakhpur district, UP.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Prime Minister paid tribute to Pingali Venkayya on 3 August 2026, marking his 150th birth anniversary.
Konda Venkatappaiah was known as Desabhakta, Duggirala as Andhra Ratna, Prakasam as Andhra Kesari, and Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao as Desoddharaka.
The withdrawal after Chauri Chaura dismayed Andhra satyagrahis in the middle of the struggle, particularly in the context of Pedanandipadu and Palnadu.

rows.title: Swarajists and No-Changers; constructive programme in the 1920s

secs.t: Swarajist leaders → role, national and Andhra

x: The Nationalist Party brought together the
Swarajists, Jinnah’s Independents and Malaviya’s group
Vithalbhai Patel
became the first elected Indian President of the Legislative Assembly in 1925.
Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was President, Unnava Lakshminarayana Secretary, Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao Treasurer and V. Ramadas an additional associated leader.
B. Venkataratnam, P. Anjaneyulu and P.V. Venkatapathiraju were elected to the Madras council.

secs.t: Assembly, Bills, committees and sessions → year

x: The Nationalist Party used its numerical strength to outvote the government and block the Finance Bill.

The Swarajists were weak on peasant issues in Bengal and became urban and legislature-bound, they did poorly in the 1926 elections, and they walked out of the councils in 1930 after the Lahore session.

secs.t: No-Changers' constructive programme — components

x: The constructive programme included khadi and spinning, removal of untouchability, Hindu-Muslim unity, prohibition, national schools and village panchayats.
Ponduru in
Srikakulam
was nationally famous for khadi.
Women in Andhra participated in
picketing and prohibition work
as part of the constructive programme.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Swarajists kept the national movement active through council work, while the No-Changers sustained constructive work.
The Swarajists favoured entry into the councils, while the No-Changers concentrated on constructive work and continued the boycott.
Belgaum 1924 was the only INC session presided over by Gandhi, and it reunited the Swarajists and No-Changers.

rows.title: Civil Disobedience Movement - Lahore Session and Purna Swaraj, Dandi March, spread and phases
sub: Group-II S1-86: Civil Disobedience Movement - Dandi March, Round Table Conferences, Poona Pact

secs.t: Lahore Session, 1929 — background, resolutions and FIRSTs

x: Bulusu Sambamurthy
of East Godavari was associated with the first district-level Purna Swaraj resolution in Andhra Pradesh.
Lord Irwin
was the Viceroy of India during the Lahore Session of December 1929 and during the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
The Nehru Report demanded Dominion Status, and the one-year ultimatum issued at Calcutta in 1928 had expired.

secs.t: Dandi March, 1930 — demands, date, route, marchers, remarks

x: Abolition of the salt tax
was a central demand in Gandhi's eleven-point letter to Viceroy Irwin.
Yerneni, also written Erneni, Subrahmanyam of Krishna district was the only Telugu marcher among Gandhi's followers in the Dandi March.
Salt was consumed by both rich and poor, and the salt tax and monopoly made it a visible symbol of colonial economic exploitation.

secs.t: Salt Satyagraha beyond Dandi — centres, incidents → leader

x: The Khudai Khidmatgars, or Red Shirts, led non-violent protests in Peshawar and the North-West Frontier Province.
The Qissa Khwani firing in Peshawar occurred in
April 1930
during the non-violent protests of the Khudai Khidmatgars.
Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
was popularly known as the ‘Frontier Gandhi’ and was associated with the Khudai Khidmatgars.
The Garhwal Rifles, associated with Chandra Singh Garhwali,
refused to fire on the crowd at Peshawar

secs.t: Women in the CDM → role, national and Andhra

x: Sarojini Naidu led the raid at the
Dharasana Salt Works
after Gandhi's arrest.
The Civil Disobedience Movement marked the first occasion on which women participated in massive numbers.
Paturi Balasaraswatamma
was the first woman arrested in Nellore in connection with the national movement.
Duvvuri Subbamma was an Andhra woman leader from East Godavari who was jailed during the Civil Disobedience Movement.

secs.t: Salt Satyagraha in Andhra — dictator, camps, centres → leader

x: Pattabhi Sitaramayya
suggested the organisation of one satyagraha camp, with a dictator and war council, in each district.
Tanguturi Prakasam and Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao
led the first salt squad from the Swarajya office at Madras on 13 April 1930.
Rayalaseema had no coast
, so Kalluri Subbarao led the activity at Bellary instead of a coastal salt-making centre.

secs.t: Patriotic songs of the CDM → authors

x: Jagganna Sastri
wrote ‘Bharata Swarajya Yuddham’.
Adavi Bapiraju wrote patriotic songs while in jail.
The APPSC 2012 key ties the song to the
Civil Disobedience Movement

secs.t: Gandhi-Irwin Pact and Karachi session — date, mediators, terms

x: Tej Bahadur Sapru and M.R. Jayakar
acted as mediators in the negotiations leading to the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
Irwin agreed to release non-violent political prisoners, remit fines, return unsold lands and permit limited salt-making.
A major criticism was that the Pact did not secure commutation of the death sentences of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru, causing disillusionment among the youth.

secs.t: Chronology — Simon Commission to withdrawal of CDM

x: The Simon Commission was appointed in November 1927, the Lahore Session was held in December 1929, 26 January 1930 was observed as the first Independence Day, and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931.

The Nehru Report was prepared in 1928, the Dandi March took place from 12 March to 6 April 1930, the First Round Table Conference was held in November 1930, and the Civil Disobedience Movement was withdrawn in 1934.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Civil Disobedience Movement was significant as the first movement to break laws openly on a mass scale, with participation by women, peasants, tribals and merchants.
The movement brought women and the
North-West Frontier Province
into the struggle, in addition to its wider mass participation.
K. Kamaraj's first imprisonment came during the
Rajaji-led Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha

rows.title: Andhra in the Civil Disobedience Movement and the Salt Satyagraha
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-197

secs.t: Andhra CDM organisation and programme — dictator, war councils, camps

x: Konda Venkatappaiah
was appointed as the Dictator for Andhra and became the first leader of the Civil Disobedience Movement in Andhra.
The camps included Guntur in Guntur, Pallepadu Ashram in Nellore, Bellary in Rayalaseema, and Vedavanam at Prakasam's house in Madras.
The programme included making salt, picketing foreign-cloth shops, cutting toddy palms, picketing toddy and arrack shops, and raiding salt depots.

secs.t: Salt Satyagraha centres in Andhra → district and leader

x: Tenneti Viswanatham
led the Salt Satyagraha at Visakhapatnam and Bhimunipatnam.
Thota Narsayya
, popularly known as “Jenda Narsayya”, was injured while raising the flag at Tilak Chowk in Machilipatnam.
Venneti Satyanarayana was subjected to a lathi charge at
Rajahmundry
Bulusu Sambamurthy led at Chollangi near Kakinada and Kasi Viswanadham at Vadarevu (APPSC 2023 key; option B makes the known swap).

secs.t: Women in the Salt Satyagraha in Andhra → role

x: Durgabai Deshmukh
led twenty women in making salt at the High Court beach in Madras.
Duvvuri Subbamma
was among the first participants at Chollangi and was jailed in Nellore.
Achanta Rukmini Lakshmipathi was the first woman graduate in Andhra and the first woman arrested in the Salt Satyagraha.
Unnava Lakshmibayamma
ran the Swarajya Lakshmi Vratam door to door on Ugadi in Guntur.

secs.t: Salt marches outside Andhra → region and leader

x: K. Kelappan led the Salt March in Malabar.
Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
led the movement in the NWFP through the Khudai Khidmatgar organisation.
C.
Rajagopalachari
led the Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha after marching from Trichinopoly.
Sarojini Naidu led the Dharasana march, where volunteers took unarmed beatings, and Webb Miller of United Press reported it.

secs.t: CDM chronology and Viceroys — event → date

x: Gandhi wrote to Irwin on 2 March 1930, the Dandi March took place from 12 March to 6 April 1930, the pact was concluded in March 1931, and the movement revived in January 1932.
Thota Narsaiah
hoisted the flag at Machilipatnam on 26 January 1930, which was observed as the first Independence Day.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Achanta Rukmini Lakshmipathi
was the first woman arrested in the Salt Satyagraha and was also the first woman graduate in Andhra.
The Mahad Satyagraha was led by Ambedkar in 1927, so its centenary falls in 2027; it was compared with the Dandi March in March 2026.
C. Rajagopalachari
(Rajaji) is associated with the Vedaranyam salt march of 1930, and K. Kamaraj was first jailed in it.

secs.t: Karachi Session, March 1931 — president, endorsements, resolution provisions

x: The Karachi resolution included civil liberties, universal adult franchise, religious neutrality and free primary education.
The Karachi programme included rent and revenue cuts, debt relief and
state control of key industries
The Congress admired the courage of the three revolutionaries but disapproved of political violence as a method.
Vallabhbhai Patel presided and Jawaharlal Nehru drafted the Fundamental Rights and National Economic Programme resolution.

secs.t: Second RTC, 1931 — participants → represented

x: Gandhi was the sole Congress representative, Sarojini Naidu represented Indian women, Muhammad Iqbal the Muslims, and Malaviya, Ambedkar, Jinnah and the Aga Khan also attended RTC-2 (1931).
V.V. Jogayya Pantulu
went to assist Gandhi at RTC-2, and the separate-Andhra resolution was handed to Gandhi there.
The resolution adopted at the 1931 special Andhra Sabha in Madras was handed to Gandhi for
the Second Round Table Conference

secs.t: Resumption and final withdrawal of CDM, 1932-1934 — event → date

x: After Gandhi returned from the Second Round Table Conference, the movement was resumed in January 1932; Gandhi was arrested, the Congress was banned and repressive ordinances were issued.
Individual satyagraha continued after the suspension of mass action, and the Congress later revived the council-entry line.
The Civil Disobedience Movement was revived in
January 1932
, during the period of repression under Viceroy Willingdon.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Karachi resolution on Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme foreshadowed
Part III and the Directive Principles of State Policy
The Poona Pact is regarded as a historical root of the reservation of seats reflected in
Articles 330 and 332
of the Constitution.
Bharat Swarajya Yuddham was written by Jagannadh Shastry, while Navayuga Gandhi was written by Damaraju Pundarikakshudu.
