rows.title: Individual Satyagraha, August Offer, Cripps Mission

secs.t: Events → month / year — 1939 to 1946

x: The sequence was resignation of Congress ministries in October–November 1939, Ramgarh session in March 1940, August Offer in August 1940 and Cripps Mission in March–April 1942.
The sequence is August Offer in August 1940, Individual Satyagraha in October 1940, Tenali events in August 1942, and the RIN Mutiny in February 1946.

secs.t: Persons → role / statement

x: In Bihar, the 1940 Individual Satyagraha was led by
Shyam Narayan Singh
Gandhi called the Cripps offer a 'post-dated cheque' and Nehru added
'on a crashing bank'
(some sources give the whole phrase to Gandhi, with 'failing bank'). 'Dead as a doornail' was Nehru's verdict on Dominion Status in the August Offer; the other two phrases are not tied to Cripps.

secs.t: August Offer vs Cripps Mission — proposals — August Offer, 1940

x: The August Offer responded to the Ramgarh Congress position that support for the war could be extended if a provisional national government were formed at the Centre.
The mission was sent by Winston Churchill's Government under pressure from United States President Franklin Roosevelt and China's Chiang Kai-shek.
Japan's entry into the war, the overrunning of Malaya and Singapore, and the fall of Rangoon created the immediate military background to the mission.

secs.t: August Offer vs Cripps Mission — proposals — Cripps proposals

x: Exam angle: month/year (March 1942), Cripps's party (Labour), what the plan offered (Dominion Status after the war).
The provincial lower houses formed an electoral college and elected one-tenth of their size by proportional representation.
The proposal allowing unwilling provinces to form separate unions conceded the principle that later supported the demand for Pakistan and created the risk of balkanisation.

secs.t: Individual Satyagraha — satyagrahis, place, aim, Andhra

x: Exam angle: assertion-reason on why it was "limited" (October 1940).
Acharya Vinoba Bhave was the first satyagrahi, Jawaharlal Nehru the second and Brahma Dutt the third (chosen for moral conviction, not political prominence).
Tanguturi Prakasam was associated with Madras, Pattabhi Sitaramayya with Bandar, Suryadevara Annapurnamma with Nandigama and Chilukuri Sattireddy with Tiruvuru.

secs.t: Responses, failure and results

x: Congress rejected the August Offer, and Nehru described dominion status as 'dead as a doornail'.
The failure of the Cripps Mission directly contributed to the launch of the
Quit India Movement
in August 1942.
The Muslim League opposed the proposed single Indian Union and wanted Pakistan to be explicitly conceded rather than left as an indirect possibility through the provincial option.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The August Offer marked the first acceptance of a post-war constitution-making body.
Rumours of Japanese bombing of Vizag and Kakinada during the Cripps Mission led Gandhi to use the phrase ‘Quit India’ in Harijan in April 1942.
The Cripps Mission’s concession that provinces could opt out of the proposed union was regarded as the germ of
the Partition of India

rows.title: Quit India Movement 1942 - causes, course, underground activity, repression, significance

secs.t: Causes → effects and dates

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2013 - Quit India was launched in response to the Cripps Proposals.
The Japanese advance generated rumours of bombing at
Vizag and Kakinada
, adding to the sense of wartime insecurity in India.
The CWC resolution was passed at Wardha on 14 July 1942, and the AICC ratified it at Bombay on 8 August 1942.

secs.t: Quit India resolution — names, demands, Gandhi's instructions

x: The Wardha resolution empowered Mahatma Gandhi to lead a non-violent mass movement against British rule.
The resolution demanded the immediate end of British rule, envisaged a provisional government after withdrawal and authorised mass civil disobedience under Gandhi.
Government servants were told to stay in service but pledge loyalty to the Congress.

secs.t: Slogans and papers → coiner

x: Gandhi suggested the phrase in Harijan in April 1942, whereas Yusuf Meherally is generally credited with coining it.
Mahatma Gandhi
said it in his Gowalia Tank speech of 8 August 1942, the same speech in which he gave the call "Do or Die".

secs.t: Repression — Viceroy, operations, detention places

x: Operation Zero Hour was the pre-dawn operation through which Congress leaders were arrested on 9 August 1942.
The repression involved approximately 10,000 deaths, flogging, collective fines and military control of cities.
Gandhi undertook a 21-day fast at the Aga Khan Palace from February 1943 in protest against state violence, and three members of the Viceroy’s Executive Council resigned in this context.

secs.t: Persons → underground role

x: Jayaprakash Narayan was an underground leader who organised sabotage and formed the Azad Dasta; he was not a member of the Viceroy’s Executive Council.
Underground activists sabotaged
bridges, railway tracks and telegraph lines
, particularly in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

secs.t: Places → parallel governments

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2016 asked where "Prati Sarkar" was formed - Satara.
The Ballia parallel government was led by Chittu Pandey in August 1942 and lasted approximately one week.
The Satara Prati Sarkar was associated with Y.B. Chavan and Nana Patil and functioned from mid-1943 to 1945.
Satara’s Prati Sarkar developed
Nyayadan Mandals and village libraries
and also promoted prohibition and “Gandhi marriages”.

secs.t: Quit India in Andhra — circular, persons, places, fines

x: Tenali witnessed firing on 12 August and the burning of the Madras–Puri passenger train; Guntur witnessed firing on 13 August; Bhimavaram witnessed firing on 17 August and an attack on the Collectorate; and Kakinada lawyers demanded Gandhi’s release.
The underground paper titled “Quit India” circulated the message “
Rahasya Udyamam Saginchandi
Pattabhi Sitaramayya was imprisoned at
Ahmednagar Fort
and wrote ‘Feathers and Stones’ there.

secs.t: Parties → attitude to Quit India

x: The Communists opposed the Quit India Movement because, after the Nazi attack on the Soviet Union, they backed the British war effort.
The Communist Party of India lost heavily in the 1945–46 elections.
The Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha and princely states stayed away, while Muslims generally sheltered activists and there were no communal clashes.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In the Andhra context, the Quit India Movement is regarded as the
final, decisive event of the freedom struggle in Andhra
Tanguturi Prakasam
emerged as a leading figure in Andhra during the Quit India Movement.

sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-200

secs.t: Events → date — 1939 to 1942

x: Mahatma Gandhi was detained at Aga Khan Palace in Pune, while Congress Working Committee members were detained at Ahmednagar Fort.
The AICC met at
Gowalia Tank, Bombay, on 8 August 1942
and gave the call 'Do or Die'.
Police firing at
Tenali
railway station on 12 August 1942 reportedly caused about nine deaths.

secs.t: Andhra Circular (Kurnool Circular) — author, contents, fate

x: The Andhra Circular was also called the
Kurnool Circular
because it was seized by the police at Kurnool.
The Andhra Provincial Congress Committee met at Machilipatnam under
Pattabhi Sitaramayya
during the phase in which the Andhra Circular was issued.
Kala Venkata Rao
authored the Andhra Circular dated 29 July 1942 (APPSC 2019 key).

secs.t: Andhra persons → role in 1942

x: Unnava Lakshmi Narayana was jailed again in 1942, not for the first time.
The Andhra University protest was associated with Mamidipudi Venkatarangayya, and Kakinada lawyers also passed a resolution demanding Gandhi’s release.
Chitturi Annapurna Devi was arrested at Guntur for distributing pamphlets and picketing.
Vanamamalai Varadacharyulu wrote or popularised the song beginning “Paradesiyulu tolagandi...”.

secs.t: Places → mass action

x: Police firings:.
Tenali (12 Aug)
- about
nine
dead.
Guntur (13 Aug)
Bhimavaram (17 Aug)
Students:
Andhra University resolution;
Kakinada
lawyers passed a similar one.

secs.t: Communist stance vs Congress Socialists

x: The Communists suffered crushing defeats in the 1945 and 1946 elections; Pillalamarri Venkateswara Rao was the only winner from Andhra in 1945.
The Congress Socialist leaders associated with the national underground were
Jayaprakash Narayan, Rammanohar Lohia, Aruna Asaf Ali and Usha Mehta
After the ban was lifted on 23 July 1942 the CPI backed the British war effort and opposed Quit India, losing public support.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: R.P.G.V. Govindan Chettiyar had been jailed for six months during
Individual Satyagraha
and was honoured under Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav in June 2025.
K. Kamaraj, who spent three years in jail during the Quit India Movement, was paid tribute on
17 July 2026
After the CPI ban was lifted, the Communists supported the British war effort and consequently opposed Quit India, leading to a loss of public support.

rows.title: Subhas Chandra Bose - Tripuri crisis, Forward Bloc, escape, Azad Hind Government, INA campaigns
sub: Group-II S1-87: Quit India Movement 1942; Subhas Chandra Bose and the INA

secs.t: Bose — life events → year

x: Bose criticised the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement as '
sprinkling cold water on the spirits of the people
After resigning from the ICS in 1921, Bose joined the Congress and worked under
C.R. Das
, his political guru.
Bose escaped from Calcutta in January 1941, travelled through Peshawar, Kabul and Moscow, reached Berlin, and later reached Singapore in July 1943.

secs.t: Congress sessions and the Tripuri crisis

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2018 asked whom Bose defeated at Tripuri - Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
Gandhi stated, “Pattabhi's defeat is my defeat,” after Dr. Pattabhi Sitaramayya lost the presidential election to Subhas Chandra Bose.
The National Planning Committee was set up by the Congress in 1938 under Bose, with
Jawaharlal Nehru
as its chairman.
Bose defeated Dr. Pattabhi Sitaramayya (1,580 to 1,377) at Tripuri, 1939 (APPSC 2018).

secs.t: Organisations → founder / place

x: The Forward Bloc was initially formed within the Congress to unite radical, left-wing and anti-imperialist forces after Bose's resignation.
Madduri Annapurnaiah and Peta Bapayya
were associated with the Andhra branch of the Forward Bloc.
Madduri Annapurnaiah was popularly referred to as “
Andhra Netaji
” because of his association with Bose and the Forward Bloc.
The Rani of Jhansi Regiment was an all-women combat unit commanded by Captain Lakshmi Sahgal.

secs.t: Indian National Army — phases and persons

x: The first INA was organised in
South-East Asia
from Indian prisoners of war with Japanese assistance.
The INA hoisted its flag at Moirang, Manipur, on
14 April 1944
during the Imphal campaign, before retreating.
The INA maintained mixed units of Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs, including common kitchens, reflecting its secular character.
Bhulabhai Desai led the defence; Sapru, Nehru, Asaf Ali and K.N. Katju assisted.
Abid Hasan 'Safrani'
translated the Hindustani version of 'Jana Gana Mana' that served as the INA anthem.

secs.t: Azad Hind Government — places, recognition, Andaman

x: The government was proclaimed at Singapore on 21 October 1943; Rangoon was where the INA headquarters later moved.
The islands were handed over by Japan, not Germany.
Japan, Germany, Italy and their allies, including Thailand, recognised the Provisional Government of Free India.

secs.t: Andhra persons — Madduri Annapurnaiah

x: Madduri Annapurnaiah ('Andhra Netaji') was jailed 18 months for the article 'Chicharapidugu', spent 4 years in jail as a Forward Bloc member during WWII, and later edited Jai Bharat, Navashakti and Velugu.

secs.t: Wartime context — August Offer, Individual Satyagraha, Quit India

x: The municipality of Ongole condemned the arrests of those involved in the Individual Satyagraha Movement.
The AICC passed the Quit India resolution at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay on
8 August 1942
Jayaprakash Narayan, Rammanohar Lohia, Sucheta Kripalani and Biju Patnaik were associated with the underground network.
Kanaklata Barua was aged 15 and Matangini Hazra was shot while leading a flag procession.

secs.t: Commissions on Bose's death

x: Bose was reportedly killed in a plane crash at Taipei on
18 August 1945
All three pairs are correctly matched.
The Shah Nawaz Committee and Khosla Commission accepted that Bose died in the crash.

secs.t: Titles and slogans → person

x: Exam angle: "Do or Die" is asked repeatedly - answer Gandhi, not Bose.
'Ittefaq, Itmad, Qurbani', meaning unity, faith or agreement and sacrifice, was the motto of the
Indian National Army
The phrase 'Quit India' was coined by
Yusuf Meherally
Bose popularised 'Jai Hind', used 'Dilli Chalo' as the INA war cry and gave the famous blood-for-freedom exhortation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The INA trials and the RIN Mutiny demonstrated that the British could no longer rely confidently on the loyalty of the Indian armed forces.
In January 2026, the Prime Minister marked the
82nd anniversary
of Bose’s hoisting of the tricolour at Port Blair.
Madduri Annapurnaiah
, called "Andhra Netaji", led the Andhra Forward Bloc together with Peta Bapayya.

rows.title: INA trials and the naval mutiny of 1946; impact on British decision to quit

secs.t: Events → date, 1934 to 1947

x: Students protested against the INA trials in
Calcutta
on 21 November 1945, and police firing killed two persons.
The RIAF strike came in January 1946, the RIN revolt began on 18 February 1946, and the post and telegraph strike followed in July 1946.
The RIAF strike occurred in January 1946, the Jabalpur Army Signal Corps action in February 1946, and the post and telegraph strike in July 1946.

secs.t: INA trials — accused, defence, verdict

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2018 - Bhulabhai Desai was counsel, not an accused; UPSC 2021 - the three were INA officers.
Sahgal (Hindu), Shah Nawaz Khan (Muslim) and Dhillon (Sikh) were tried together as a symbol of unity.
Bhulabhai Desai
was the lead counsel of the INA Defence Committee, and this was regarded as his last major contribution.

secs.t: RIN mutiny — ship, city, numbers, leaders

x: Vallabhbhai Patel and Muhammad Ali Jinnah
persuaded the ratings to surrender.
The ratings struck over poor food, low pay and racial discrimination.
About 20,000 personnel, 78 ships and 20 shore establishments were involved.
M.S. Khan
served as president of the Naval Central Strike Committee.
Congress, the Muslim League and the Communists united in support of the INA accused.

secs.t: Impact on the British decision to quit — factor → effect

x: Sections of the Royal Indian Air Force and the Army also showed disaffection during the period of the RIN revolt.
The British depended on the 2.5-million-strong Indian Army as their coercive instrument.
Attlee regarded Gandhi's role in the immediate transfer of power as minimal compared with the loss of loyalty in the armed forces.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The events are debated as either a ‘mutiny’ or a ‘revolt’: officials emphasised breakdown of discipline, whereas historians have seen a broader nationwide uprising.
The
Royal Indian Navy revolt
of 1946 was revisited at the 80th Independence Day as a factor that hastened British withdrawal, because the Raj's armed forces had cracked.

secs.t: Titles and honours → person

Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928
Mannathu Padmanabhan was associated with the title Bharatha Kesari, founded the NSS and participated in the Vaikom and Guruvayur Satyagrahas.
Prakasam earned 'Andhra Kesari' in the Simon boycott at Madras, Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya was 'Andhra Ratna' and Konda Venkatappayya was 'Deshabhakta'.

x: The Discovery of India was written by Nehru, Annihilation of Caste by Ambedkar and Sarvodaya was Gandhi’s Gujarati rendering of Ruskin’s Unto This Last.
Jawaharlal Nehru wrote ‘The Discovery of India’ in
Ahmednagar Fort jail
Jana Gana Mana was written by
Rabindranath Tagore
(APPSC 2025).
Sarvodaya was Gandhi's Gujarati rendering of
John Ruskin's 'Unto This Last'

x: Albert Einstein
made this statement in tribute to Mahatma Gandhi.
Gandhi made the first two observations, while Subhas Chandra Bose made the comparison concerning the Dandi March.
Nehru said 'The light has gone out of our lives' on Gandhi's death.

secs.t: Institutions and organisations → founder

x: Khaksars were founded by Allama Inayatullah Khan Mashriqi, Bal Charkha Sangh by Indira Gandhi, Servants of the People Society by Lala Lajpat Rai and the Independence for India League by Jawaharlal Nehru.
The Harijan Sevak Sangh was founded in 1932 and had branches at Hyderabad and Vijayawada, whose Vijayawada branch was headed by Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao.

secs.t: Positions held — Congress presidents and the National Liberal Federation

x: Annie Besant
presided over the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress in 1917.
Gandhi presided at Belgaum in 1924, Sarojini Naidu at Kanpur in 1925, M.A. Ansari at Madras in 1927 and Nehru at Lahore in 1929.
The Moderates left the Congress in 1918-19, not 1928-29.

secs.t: Leaders by region — Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Punjab, Assam, Rajasthan; peasants and tribes

x: Lala Lajpat Rai belonged to Punjab, formed part of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio and presided over the Congress in 1920.
VOC founded the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Co. at Tuticorin and Kelappan was the 'Kerala Gandhi' of the Guruvayur satyagraha.
Birsa Munda led the Munda Ulgulan, Alluri Sitarama Raju was associated with the Rampa movement, Komaram Bheem with the Gond movement and Sahajanand Saraswati with the Bihar Kisan Sabha.

secs.t: Women freedom fighters — region and contribution

x: Sarojini Naidu was associated with Hyderabad, the Dharasana raid of 1930 and became the first woman Governor of Uttar Pradesh.
Durgabai Deshmukh stopped Nehru without a pass at the Vijayawada AICC meeting in 1921.
The correct sequence is 1780, 1907, 1921 and 1942: Rani Velu Nachiyar, Bhikaiji Cama, Durgabai Deshmukh and Aruna Asaf Ali.

secs.t: Leaders from Andhra — contributions

x: Prakasam participated in the Simon boycott in Madras, led the salt satyagraha at Devarampadu and became the first Chief Minister of Andhra State in 1953.
The Constituent Assembly adopted the present national flag on 22 July 1947, with the Ashoka Chakra replacing the
charkha
The Rampa rebellion of 1922–24 was connected with opposition to the
Madras Forest Act of 1882 and forced labour

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The comparative assessment is that
southern leaders such as Rajaji, Prakasam and EMS had less national presence than Gandhi, Nehru, Bose and Patel
Events marking Tanguturi Prakasam’s 154th anniversary were held at
Visakhapatnam and Ongole
in August 2026.
The Chief Minister recalled Alluri Sitarama Raju and Pingali Venkayya on the 80th Independence Day.

rows.title: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel - Bardoli Satyagraha, organisational role, Deputy Prime Minister

secs.t: Patel — FIRSTs, posts and the civil services

x: Patel chaired the
Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities, Tribal and Excluded Areas
, as well as the Provincial Constitution Committee.
Patel stated that if the civil service steel frame bends, the whole structure will collapse, stressing its importance to national administration.
Patel addressed the first IAS probationers at Metcalfe House, Delhi, on
21 April 1947
; the date is now observed as Civil Services Day.

secs.t: Titles → who conferred them and when

x: The title ‘Sardar’ became associated with Patel at Bardoli in 1928; accounts variously credit the women and peasants, Sarojini Naidu and the masses, or Gandhi.
Patel is popularly called the Iron Man of India for his role in integrating approximately 565 princely states.
The description refers to Patel’s role in creating the All India Services and supporting their importance in administration.

secs.t: Peasant satyagrahas → year, issue, outcome

x: Exam angle: "who led Bardoli" and "which satyagraha was not led by Gandhi".
The 6 per cent cut after the Maxwell-Broomfield inquiry belongs to Bardoli (1928); Kheda ended with revenue suspended for poor peasants and confiscated property returned.
Patel organised a disciplined no-tax campaign and maintained a village intelligence network during Bardoli Satyagraha.

secs.t: Organisational role → Congress bodies and the 1937 elections

x: As head of the Congress Parliamentary Board Patel ran the 1937 provincial elections held under the Government of India Act 1935 and supervised the Congress ministries' discipline, elections and finances.
The statement contrasts Gandhi’s moral vision with Patel’s strong organisational and administrative machinery within the Congress.
Patel served as President of the Gujarat PCC for
over two decades

secs.t: Patel vs Nehru → Kashmir, Hyderabad, China

x: Nehru referred the Kashmir issue to the UN, influenced by idealism and Mountbatten’s advice, while Patel was sceptical and preferred a military solution.
Patel pressed for and ordered Operation Polo in September 1948 after diplomacy failed to resolve the Hyderabad issue.
Patel warned Nehru about China after Tibet in his letter of
7 November 1950

secs.t: Commemoration → monument, day and award

x: National Unity Day is observed on 31 October, the birth anniversary of Vallabhbhai Patel, who was born on 31 October 1875 at Nadiad.
Instituted in 2019, the award recognises unity and integrity; it includes a medal and citation, carries no cash, and is limited to not more than three recipients annually.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The two-year commemoration of Patel’s 150th birth anniversary was launched on 31 October 2024 at the Statue of Unity and includes the ‘Amrit Parampara’ festival series.
Rashtriya Ekta Diwas (National Unity Day) honours
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
, the unifier of India; its 2025 observance fell within the two-year commemoration of his 150th birth anniversary.

secs.t: Organisations and movements → founder, year, leaders

x: Swami Ramananda Theertha
led the Join Indian Union movement through the Hyderabad State Congress.
Vijay Singh Pathik was associated with Rajasthan, Sewa Singh Thikriwala with Punjab, Sarangadhar Das with Orissa, and Swami Ramananda Tirtha with the Hyderabad State Congress.
Jawaharlal Nehru
became President of the AISPC (founded 1927) in 1939; Pattabhi Sitaramayya also served as president.
The unrest and Razakar violence in Hyderabad contributed to the Indian military intervention known as Operation Polo in 1948.

secs.t: Acts, agreements and Congress policy → year, provision

x: Congress first followed non-interference in the 1920s, adopted the Haripura position in 1938, and at Tripuri in 1939 openly backed the movements in the states.
The standard account identifies
Kashmir, Hyderabad and Junagadh
as the states that had not signed accession by 15 August 1947.
Rajpramukhs were the heads of
Part B states
, which consisted of former princely states or unions.
The 26th Amendment Act, 1971 (Indira Gandhi) abolished privy purses and royal titles.

secs.t: Persons → role in integration

x: The States Department used persuasion and patriotic appeals, along with the threat of popular uprisings or force where necessary.
Mir Osman Ali Khan was the seventh Nizam, the ruling house was Asaf Jahi, and Asaf Jah I founded it in 1724.
Moin Nawaz Jung
led the Nizam’s delegation to the United Nations Security Council in 1948.
Operation Polo (Hyderabad, 13-17 Sept 1948) was led by Maj.

secs.t: Princely states → ruler, method and timing

x: Shah Nawaz Bhutto
was the Dewan of Junagadh under Nawab Mahabat Khanji III.
Manipur and Tripura signed merger agreements and merged with India in October 1949.
Dewan C.P. Ramaswami Iyer declared Travancore’s independence, partly in the context of its thorium wealth.
Jammu and Kashmir acceded to India on
26 October 1947

secs.t: Hyderabad State — dynasty, data and dates

x: Mir Osman Ali Khan wanted Hyderabad to remain independent or accede to Pakistan, while India suspected secret dealings between Hyderabad and Pakistan.
The Nizam’s government banned Indian currency, imported arms from Pakistan and sought an independent Dominion of Hyderabad.
On 1 November 1956, the Telugu-speaking districts were transferred to Andhra Pradesh, Marathwada to Bombay State, and Raichur and Gulbarga to Mysore State.

secs.t: Operations → date, commander, result

x: Exam angle: "Operation Polo" vs Blue Star/Meghdoot/Vijay; Asaf Jahi vs Qutb Shahi; Razakar leader = Kasim Razvi.
Exam angle: Operation Vijay (Goa 1961) vs Operation Polo (Hyderabad 1948) - both asked by APPSC.
Operation Polo was conducted from 13 to 17 September 1948, ending with the surrender and accession of the Nizam.
France possessed Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam and Chandernagore, which were handed over in 1954.

secs.t: Consolidation — Menon's four phases, Part A-D states and terms

x: Menon’s four phases were extinction, consolidation into unions, democratisation and finally abolition of privy purses.

Part A comprised former Governor’s provinces; Part B comprised former princely states or unions headed by Rajpramukhs; Part C included former Chief Commissioners’ provinces and some princely states; Part D consisted of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Junagadh was resolved through a plebiscite, Hyderabad through police action, and Kashmir through an Instrument of Accession followed by war.
The Hyderabad police action removed a hostile state located in the heart of India and was followed by closer Andhra–Telangana relations.
Yanam is a French-origin enclave located inside Andhra Pradesh’s Godavari delta, but it is administered as part of the Puducherry Union Territory.

rows.title: Wavell Plan and Simla Conference; Cabinet Mission Plan 1946; Interim Government
sub: Group-II S1-90: Towards independence - Cripps Mission, Cabinet Mission, Mountbatten Plan and Partition

secs.t: League demands, formulas and pacts (1943-45) → author and proposals

x: The C.R. Formula proposed a plebiscite and joint agreements after separation, but Jinnah demanded that only Muslims should vote and that there should be no common centre.
Bhulabhai Desai was a Congress leader in the Central Legislative Assembly and negotiated with Liaquat Ali Khan for the Pact.
The Gandhi-Jinnah talks (Bombay, 9-27 Sept 1944) were held on the basis of the C.R. Formula, which proposed a post-war plebiscite in contiguous Muslim-majority areas of the north-west and north-east.

secs.t: Wavell Plan and Simla Conference, 1945 → proposals and failure

x: The Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief were exceptions, so the Executive Council was not entirely an elected body without a special Viceroyal position.
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad represented the Congress, while Muhammad Ali Jinnah represented the Muslim League at the Simla Conference.
Jinnah insisted that all Muslim members should be nominated only by the Muslim League, denying the Congress and Punjab Unionists the right to nominate Muslim members.

secs.t: Cabinet Mission, 1946 → members, provisions and grouping — Origin & members

x: The Cabinet Mission was sent by
Clement Attlee
's Labour Government after the Second World War.
Because it consisted of three British Cabinet Ministers, the Cabinet Mission was known as the
Ministerial Trio Mission
The Mission aimed to establish machinery for framing India's Constitution and to arrange an Interim Government.
The proposed Union had a deliberately weak Centre responsible only for
Defence, Foreign Affairs and Communications

secs.t: Cabinet Mission, 1946 → members, provisions and grouping — Other provisions

x: The plan envisaged an Indian Interim Cabinet with minimum Viceroy interference and recognised India's right to leave the Commonwealth.
The Congress considered grouping optional, while the Muslim League insisted that it should be compulsory.
On 10 July 1946, Jawaharlal Nehru stated that Congress could modify the scheme through its majority in the Constituent Assembly.

secs.t: Constituent Assembly and Interim Government → composition and portfolios

x: Exam angle: "The Constituent Assembly was formed under which plan?" -
Cabinet Mission Plan
(not Cripps, not Mountbatten). "Not a member" questions list a fake name.
The Constituent Assembly was not directly elected by universal adult franchise; its provincial members were indirectly elected by provincial assemblies.
M.N. Roy's demand dates to 1934, the Congress adopted it in 1935, the August Offer accepted it in 1940, and the Cabinet Mission Plan was announced in 1946.
Patel held Home and Information and Broadcasting; Rajendra Prasad held Food and Agriculture; Baldev Singh held Defence; and Jagjivan Ram held Labour.

secs.t: Persons → role and stand

x: Gandhi walked from village to village in Noakhali from
November 1946 to March 1947
to promote peace, though he could not stop the violence completely.
As Finance Member, Liaquat Ali Khan introduced the 'poor man's budget' in 1947, which heavily taxed Indian business and embarrassed Congress members.
Sir Cyril Radcliffe
, a British lawyer unfamiliar with Indian conditions, chaired both Boundary Commissions.

secs.t: Elections and events (1945-46) → date and result

x: The Red Fort trials began in November 1945 (INA Day 12 Nov) and the Rashid Ali Day protests were in Calcutta on 11 February 1946.
The Muslim League observed 16 August 1946 as Direct Action Day, which resulted in the
Great Calcutta Killings
The League called for Direct Action on
29 July 1946
; Direct Action Day followed on 16 August 1946.

secs.t: Provinces → method of partition decision

x: Exam angle: "referendum" provinces are only
NWFP and Sylhet
Referendums were held in the North-West Frontier Province and Sylhet.

secs.t: Chronology 1940-1947 → sequence of plans for revision — Sequence of events (1944-1946)

x: The Red Fort trials began in November 1945, the RIN revolt began on 18 February 1946, the Cabinet Mission arrived on 24 March 1946, and the Plan was issued on 16 May 1946.
Cripps Mission (March 1942) -> Wavell Plan (1945) -> Simla Conference (June-July 1945, which discussed the Wavell Plan) -> Cabinet Mission (1946) (UPPSC 2025).

secs.t: Chronology 1940-1947 → sequence of plans for revision — Plans compared

x: The August Offer accepted the demand for an Indian-framed constitution after the war.
The Cabinet Mission Plan proposed a weak Union, provincial groupings, a Constituent Assembly and an Interim Government.
The
Dickie Bird Plan
proposed independent successor states for the provinces and was rejected by Nehru as a plan for Balkanisation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Wavell's concessions at Simla were criticised for handing Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League an effective veto in the negotiations.
The ambiguity regarding the compulsory nature of provincial grouping created conflicting interpretations and contributed substantially to the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan.
The hastened transfer of power and Radcliffe's boundary award were widely criticised in relation to partition violence.

rows.title: Direct Action Day, Mountbatten Plan, Indian Independence Act 1947; partition and its consequences

secs.t: Events → date: Direct Action Day and Gandhi, 1946-48

x: The Muslim League called for Direct Action on 29 July 1946 after withdrawing its acceptance of the Cabinet Mission Plan.
Jinnah condemned
Wavell’s invitation to the Congress to form the interim government
, in the context of the League’s Direct Action call.
Gandhi spent 15 August 1947 at Beliaghata in Calcutta, fasting and praying, rather than attending the Delhi celebrations.

secs.t: Plans and schemes of 1947 → author, date, provisions — Attlee's Statement (20 February 1947) (CDX)

x: The Attlee Statement of 20 February 1947 declared that British rule would end by
30 June 1948
, even if no agreement among Indian political parties was reached.
The statement fixed 30 June 1948 as the outer deadline, hinted at transfer to provincial governments and was followed by Mountbatten replacing Wavell.
The sovereign undivided Bengal proposal was a separate United Bengal plan advanced by Sarat Chandra Bose and H.S. Suhrawardy.

secs.t: Plans and schemes of 1947 → author, date, provisions — Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan), 1947

x: The plan accepted the demand for Pakistan to avoid
civil war and administrative collapse
Congress accepted partition to avoid Balkanisation, establish a strong Centre and bring an end to communal bloodshed.
The Khudai Khidmatgar movement boycotted the referendum, but the North-West Frontier Province joined Pakistan.
Power was transferred on the basis of the
Government of India Act, 1935
, while the armed forces were also divided.

secs.t: Indian Independence Act 1947 → dates

x: The Indian Independence Bill was introduced in the House of Commons on
4 July 1947
Attlee's declaration was made on 20 February 1947, the Mountbatten Plan was announced on 3 June, royal assent was given on 18 July, and the dominions came into being on 15 August.

secs.t: Indian Independence Act 1947 → provisions

x: With the lapse of paramountcy, the 565 princely states were free to accede to India or Pakistan.
The
Government of India Act, 1935, as adapted
, continued to govern the dominions until their new constitutions were framed.
The Act transferred power to the two dominions but left the framing of their constitutions to their respective Constituent Assemblies.
The Constituent Assemblies had sovereign constitutional authority; they were not required to retain British laws permanently.

secs.t: Persons → statements and roles

x: Lord Mountbatten
described Gandhi as a ‘one-man boundary force’ because of his efforts to restrain communal violence.
V.P. Menon
suggested immediate transfer of power on dominion status without waiting for a new constitution.
Sir Cyril Radcliffe was a British lawyer who lacked knowledge of Indian conditions beyond the map when he chaired the Boundary Commissions.

secs.t: Partition → boundaries, assets and consequences

x: The Radcliffe Line award was announced on 17 August 1947, after independence.
The award was ready on 12 August 1947 but was published on
17 August 1947
An estimated
10–15 million
people crossed the new borders during Partition.
The UN ceasefire in the first Kashmir conflict came into effect on
1 January 1949

secs.t: Heads at independence → person (FIRST / LAST)

x: J.B. Kripalani
was the Congress President at the time of Indian independence.
M.A. Jinnah
became the first Governor-General of Pakistan in August 1947.
Lord Mountbatten was Governor-General during Kashmir’s accession in October 1947 and Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination on 30 January 1948.
C. Rajagopalachari
(June 1948 - Jan 1950) was the last and only Indian Governor-General.

secs.t: Partition accounts → author

x: India Divided was written by Rajendra Prasad; India Wins Freedom by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad; Freedom at Midnight by Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre; and Train to Pakistan by Khushwant Singh.
India Divided was written by Rajendra Prasad (APPSC-GS 2025); Azad wrote India Wins Freedom.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Dominion status enabled India and Pakistan to become free before their constitutions were written.
The haste associated with advancing the date of transfer and the late announcement of the Radcliffe Award are criticised as factors that aggravated Partition violence.
Rajaji, as Governor-General, gave assent on 2 April 1949.

rows.title: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar - life, Mahad and Kalaram Satyagrahas, writings, Round Table Conferences

secs.t: Ambedkar — birth, degrees, titles and FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: APPSC-GS 2025 asked the honorary D.Litt of 1953 -
Osmania University
Ambedkar studied at Columbia University, where he obtained an M.A. and Ph.D. Gray’s Inn awarded the qualification of Barrister-at-law, while Osmania University conferred an honorary D.Litt.
Ambedkar studied at the
London School of Economics
and obtained the MSc and DSc qualifications; his thesis was related to The Problem of the Rupee.

secs.t: Journals and organisations → year, aim

x: Mooknayak was founded by
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
Bahishkrit Bharat
was founded by Ambedkar in 1927 and focused on Dalit rights and social reform.
Samata Samaj was founded in 1927 to promote
coordination between Dalits and caste Hindus
The Independent Labour Party worked for the rights of
labourers, Dalits and peasants

secs.t: Satyagrahas and movements → date, place, feature

x: The Mahad Satyagraha was organised by the
Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha
, Ambedkar’s organisation founded in 1924.
Ambedkar and his followers drank water from the Chavdar Tank, making the event known as the Water Satyagraha.
Ambedkar compared the Mahad Satyagraha with
the French National Assembly of 1789
Bole Resolution 1923, Manusmriti Dahan 25 December 1927, Kalaram Temple Satyagraha 1930, Independent Labour Party 1936.

secs.t: RTCs, Communal Award and Poona Pact → year, persons, provisions — Round Table Conferences

x: Ambedkar demanded
separate electorates
for the Depressed Classes at the Second Round Table Conference, leading to a clash with Gandhi.
Both are correct: Ambedkar attended the 1930, 1931 and 1932 RTCs for the Depressed Classes, while Gandhi attended only the second, in 1931, where they clashed over separate electorates.

secs.t: RTCs, Communal Award and Poona Pact → year, persons, provisions — Poona Pact - Yerwada fast, signatories, seats, electorate

x: Ambedkar criticised Gandhi’s approach, including in Annihilation of Caste, and rejected the term ‘Harijan’. ‘Modern Manu’, ‘Messenger of Dalits’ and ‘Educate, Agitate, Organise’ are associated with him.
British Prime Minister
Ramsay MacDonald
announced the Communal Award on 16 August 1932, giving the depressed classes separate electorates and 71 provincial seats.

secs.t: Books → year and theme

x: The Problem of the Rupee
, published in 1923, contained ideas that formed the basis for Ambedkar’s thinking behind the Reserve Bank of India.
Who Were the Shudras?
, published in 1946, examined the origin of the Shudras.
The Buddha and His Dhamma was written by Ambedkar and published in 1957.
Annihilation of Caste
(1936) criticised Hindu orthodoxy and Gandhi.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The comparative formulation associated with Mahad is that water came before salt, highlighting the earlier importance of access to water in the struggle for social equality.

Gandhi launched temple entry at Siddantham in Krishna district on 17 December 1933. ⚠ Sources differ: Census 2011 lists a Sidhantham in Penugonda mandal, West Godavari; the 1933 tour chronology puts the 17 Dec 1933 Siddhantam visit among Krishna district stops.

rows.title: Ambedkar's contribution to the making of the Constitution - Drafting Committee and key interventions

secs.t: Drafting Committee → members, dates, numbers

x: Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar was a jurist, while K.M. Munshi chaired the Order of Business Committee and was originally the only Congress member of the Drafting Committee.
Before Partition, Ambedkar was elected from Bengal’s Jessore-Khulna area with the support of Jogendra Nath Mandal.
The Jessore-Khulna districts, from which Ambedkar had been elected, went to East Pakistan after Partition, causing him to lose that seat.

secs.t: Articles and provisions → Ambedkar's view

x: Ambedkar considered the Directive Principles equally important for social and economic justice and described them as a novel feature resembling instruments of instructions.
Ambedkar expressed the hope that Article 356 would remain a ‘
dead letter
’, indicating that it would not be used routinely.
Ambedkar advocated a Uniform Civil Code but suggested that it could initially be voluntary, applying to persons who declared themselves willing to be governed by it.

secs.t: Ambedkar → statements and warnings in the Assembly

x: In his speech of 4 November 1948, Ambedkar defended the adaptation of tested provisions and said that there was no need to apologise for such borrowing.
Ambedkar borrowed the term from George Grote and stated that constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment but one that has to be cultivated.
Ambedkar warned against violent and extra-constitutional methods, hero-worship in politics, and the failure to establish social democracy.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Munshi-Ayyangar formula was adopted on
14 September 1949
The constitutional framework embedded a social revolution through rights, reservation and the abolition of untouchability.
The Constitution was criticised as a 'lawyers' paradise' and a 'copy of the 1935 Act'.

rows.title: Ambedkar's social thought - annihilation of caste, state socialism, conversion to Buddhism

secs.t: Ambedkar → statements on caste, village and religion

x: Ambedkar described inter-caste marriage as the real remedy because fusion of blood would create kinship and weaken caste barriers.
The statement is
B.R. Ambedkar
's (APPSC-G1 2018), in line with his call in Annihilation of Caste (1936) to destroy the whole caste system, not just untouchability.
In the Constituent Assembly on 4 November 1948 he called the village 'a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism'.

secs.t: Books → theme

x: The Jat-Pat Todak Mandal organisers cancelled the session because they objected to the contents of Ambedkar's address.
The Buddha and His Dhamma was published posthumously in 1957 and provided Ambedkar's rational and social interpretation of Buddhism, forming the basis of Navayana.
States and Minorities was a 1947 memorandum submitted to the Constituent Assembly on behalf of
the Scheduled Castes Federation

secs.t: Ambedkar vs Gandhi and Congress — caste, electorates, village

x: Ambedkar later felt that the Pact made Dalits dependent on caste Hindus, although he had accepted joint electorates during the negotiations.
Ambedkar rejected Gandhi's ideas of Gram Swaraj and trusteeship, favouring a strong, centralised constitutional democracy to protect minorities.
Gandhi favoured reform of Hinduism from within and decentralised Gram Swaraj, whereas Ambedkar left Hinduism for Buddhism and advocated a strong Centre.

secs.t: State socialism, women, labour and education → proposals

x: The proposals included state ownership of key industries and agricultural land, collective farming through village collectives and nationalised insurance.
Ambedkar resigned in 1951 when the
Hindu Code Bill
, which dealt with inheritance, marriage and divorce, stalled.
“Educate, Agitate, Organise” was Ambedkar's well-known slogan expressing the importance of education and organised social and political action.

secs.t: Conversion to Buddhism → date, place

x: Ambedkar made the Yeola declaration at the Depressed Classes Conference in Yeola on 13 October 1935, declaring that although he was born a Hindu, he would not die a Hindu.
The conversion took place at Nagpur with his wife and approximately five lakh followers, mostly Mahars, and included 22 prescribed vows.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The ruling held that conversion out of
Hinduism, Sikhism or Buddhism
leads to immediate loss of Scheduled Caste status under Clause 3 of the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950.
The significance lay in moving the anti-caste struggle from reform within Hinduism to rights, law and the possibility of religious exit.

rows.title: Constituent Assembly - composition, Objectives Resolution, committees, working and adoption

secs.t: Constituent Assembly — origin of the idea and FIRSTs

x: The sequence is 1895, 1934, 1935 and 1940: attribution to Tilak, proposal by M.N. Roy, official INC demand and acceptance in principle through the August Offer.
The Cripps Proposals of 1942 carried forward the proposal after the British had accepted the demand in principle through the August Offer of 1940.

secs.t: Composition and first session → features, numbers

x: The first sitting, held on 9 December 1946, was attended by 211 members.
The Constituent Assembly was partly elected and partly nominated, and it included 15 women members, among them Durgabai Deshmukh, Sarojini Naidu and Hansa Mehta.
After Partition, Muslim League members from territories that became part of Pakistan withdrew, reducing the strength from 389 to 299.

secs.t: Persons → posts and roles

x: H.C. Mukherjee was Vice-President (later also V.T. Krishnamachari), B.N. Rau was Constitutional Adviser (later ICJ judge) and B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.

B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya chaired the House Committee; N. G. Ranga was a peasant leader; Durgabai Deshmukh founded the Andhra Mahila Sabha; and M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar later became Deputy Speaker and Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

secs.t: Acts, status and criticisms

x: The
Socialist Party
demanded dissolution of the Constituent Assembly and its re-election through adult suffrage.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Although the Dhar Commission and JVP Committee were cautious about linguistic states, the Andhra exception paved the way for the SRC and broader linguistic reorganisation.
The sequence was Dhar Commission in 1948, JVP Committee in 1948–49, Wanchoo in 1953 for Andhra, and the Fazal Ali SRC in 1953–55 for all India.
The period 1913–1920 was the propaganda phase, with four broad objectives: Andhra State, Andhra University, Telugu development and cultural revival.
Repeated resolutions and memorandums ensured that the Andhra problem remained before national political authorities until Andhra State was formed in 1953.
Nidadavolu in 1912 saw the first formal resolution, Bapatla in 1913 was the first numbered Andhra Conference, and Vijayawada in 1914 was the first session called Andhra Mahasabha.
Factional divisions between regions and leaders, notably Circars versus Rayalaseema and Prakasam versus Pattabhi, repeatedly weakened the movement.
The struggle over Andhra University helped build a distinct Telugu intellectual identity and is regarded by many as a forerunner of the Andhra State movement.
The loss of Madras left the new Andhra State administratively and economically weak, requiring it to use the relatively undeveloped town of Kurnool as its capital.
Andhra University’s centenary covers 1926–2026, and the State announced ₹500 crore to help it enter the global top 100.
Cattamanchi Ramalinga Reddy was the founding Vice-Chancellor of Andhra University, not the first Governor of Andhra State.

rows.title: Wanchoo Committee and the problems of the new Andhra State
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-212

secs.t: Committees and officers → member, date, mandate

x: Exam angle: "Wanchoo = single member, Rajasthan HC Chief Justice, 1953". Remember his Madras recommendation was
not
accepted.
The
Partition Committee
of 1949–50 was first entrusted with working out the division of assets between Andhra and residual Madras.
The Partition Committee of 1949–50, associated with administrative arrangements for the new state, was chaired by
Kumaraswamy Raja

secs.t: Capital and Madras city → stand of each body

x: Because Andhra lacked capital infrastructure, Wanchoo recommended that the Andhra Government work temporarily from Madras city for three to five years.
The Andhra PCC demanded half of Madras town, while Wanchoo recommended Madras as the temporary headquarters for three to five years.
The JVP Committee held that Andhra could be formed only if the Telugus relinquished their claim to Madras.

secs.t: Problems of the new state → finances, assets, services

x: The new state lacked both developed capital infrastructure and a commercial centre and was described as administratively and economically orphaned.

secs.t: Places → High Court, Bellary taluks and Tungabhadra

x: The Sreebagh Pact promised priority for irrigation in Rayalaseema and Nellore on the
Tungabhadra, Krishna and Penna
for ten years or as needed.
The Pact provided priority
for ten years or as needed
, rather than prescribing either a permanent arrangement or a fixed five-year period.
After Bellary was divided, the Tungabhadra works became shared between Andhra and Mysore.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Sheela Bhide Committee dealt with Schedule IX institutions, the Kamalanathan Committee with employees, and a separate Section 6 expert committee examined the capital issue.
Assets were divided by location, whereas debts were divided by population.
The Centre planned a high-level committee to address Tungabhadra water disputes involving Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka.

rows.title: Role of the press and newspapers in the Andhra Movement - Krishna Patrika, Andhra Patrika, Andhra Prabha, Zamin Ryot
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-212

secs.t: Telugu press — FIRSTs and "only"

x: Satyadoota
, established in Bellary in 1835, was the first Telugu newspaper and was run by Christian missionaries.
Hitavadi
, associated with Edmund Park and dated 1841, was the first Telugu newspaper printed in Andhra.
Jaya Bharat was the first Telugu journal published after independence.
Andhra Mata
was the paper of the Home Rule movement (APPSC G2 2017 key).

secs.t: Early Telugu newspapers → year, place, founder (1835-1905)

x: Vrutantini dates from 1838 and was associated with Mandigala Venkataraya Sastri.
Vartamana Tarangini was a weekly begun at Madras in 1842 by Syed Rahamatullah, the first Telugu paper started by a Muslim, and later passed to Puvvada Seshagiri Rao.
Purushartha Pradayini carried articles both for and against widow remarriage.

secs.t: Nationalist newspapers → founder / editor, year, place

x: Andhra Prabha was associated with the Indian Express group and Ramnath Goenka; Narla Venkateswara Rao was a noted editor.
Krishna Patrika was founded on 1 February 1902 by
Konda Venkatappaiah and Dasu Narayana Rao
at Machilipatnam.
Mutnuri Krishna Rao
was Krishna Patrika's second and most famous editor and was largely responsible for its success (APPSC GS 2024).

secs.t: Journals and magazines → editor

x: Vivekavardhani began in 1874, Hasyasanjivani in 1876, Sati Hitabodhini in 1883 and Satyasamvardhini in 1891.
Veeresalingam had his own press from 1876.
Bharati, a literary monthly started in 1924, was associated with
Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao
Andhra Bhasa Sanjivani was associated with Kokkonda Venkataratnam, who introduced the editorial column.
Gurajada Appa Rao attempted
Prakasika

secs.t: Newspapers → movement, and press laws

x: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878, popularly called the Gagging Act, was repealed by Ripon in 1882.
The Vandemataram/Swadeshi movement was supported by Krishna Patrika, Swarajya, Desamata, Andhra Kesari and Navayuga.
Hindu Sundari was associated with the year 1902, while Sri Savitri was associated with 1904.

secs.t: Papers → statements on the separate-Andhra demand

x: The article reported 56 non-Andhras to 8 Andhras in the civil services and 19 non-Andhras to no Andhras in the judiciary.
Krishna Patrika
made this statement on 30 November 1912 in support of the Andhra movement.
The cartoon depicted Rayalaseema as an iceberg blocking the ship labelled 'Andhra Movement'.
Desabhimani urged Telugu papers to focus on Andhra affairs rather than world politics.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The press performed a dual role: it spread the national movement and also built support for the separate-Andhra demand.
Newspapers gave rise to reading rooms and libraries.
Andhra Prakasika (1885) was the first political journal in Telugu.

secs.t: Editors → papers

x: Mutnuri Krishna Rao made Krishna Patrika a political weekly and a hub for freedom fighters, which made it a centre of political awakening (1, 2 and 4).
The Sreebagh Pact was signed on 16 November 1937, not 1935.
Navayuga of Chilakaluripet
was shut down by government restrictions.
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
edited Swarajya (1907).

completed and published the catalogue of printed Telugu books begun by Velidanda Hanumantha Rao.
The Granthalayodyama Trimurthulu included Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao, Ayyanki and
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
, along with Kaderbad Narasinga Rao, founded the Edward Corporation Library at Nandyal, now known as the Victoria Reading Room.

secs.t: Events and places → dates (1907 tour to 1937 pact)

x: Bipin Chandra Pal
toured Andhra in April 1907 (Kakinada on 17 April, Rajahmundry 19-24 April) after Andhra leaders invited extremist leaders.
Chilukuri Veerabhadra Rao co-founded the Bala Bharati Samithi at Rajahmundry in February 1907 with Gante Laxmanna and Unguturi Sriramulu.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The feature film is titled
Viswadata
and is being made in connection with Nageswara Rao Pantulu’s 160th birth anniversary.
These editors made journalism an instrument of political awakening while also funding and publicising the library movement.
Filmmaker
Sivalenka Pavani Prasad
is making Viswadata.

sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-212

secs.t: Library movement — FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: statement sets built on Grandhalaya Sarvasvam 1915, Andhra Patrika 1908, SKDABN 1901 in Hyderabad (not Kovvur 1916), and the 1918 boat library.
The Andhra Desa Library Association was founded in 1914 at Vijayawada and is regarded as the first state-level library association in India.

secs.t: Libraries → place, year, founder (1890-1922)

x: The respective libraries and their places and years are Hyderabad 1901, Rayakuduru 1894, Rajahmundry 1898 and Ongole 1890.
Vijnana Chandrika Mandali was founded by Komarraju Venkata Lakshmana Rao at Hyderabad in 1905 (APHQ says 1906), not at Vijayawada.
Komarraju Venkata Lakshmana Rao
founded the Sri Krishnadevaraya Andhra Bhasha Nilayam at Hyderabad in 1901, the first Telugu library; he also founded the Vijnana Chandrika Mandali.

secs.t: Andhra Desa Library Association → 1913 conference, 1914 founding, journals

x: Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya and Suri Venkata Narasimha called for the conference through
Andhra Patrika
Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya and Nalam Krishnarao were the secretaries.
After closing, Grandhalaya Sarvasvam was revived in January 1948 as the Telugu-English quarterly
Andhra Granthalayam
Only a is correct: Dharma Granthalaya was Yatagiri Lakshmi Venkataramana's journal (Kakinada).

secs.t: Library innovations → pioneer

x: Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya
pioneered the library pilgrimage, consisting of village tours.
Pathuri Nagabhushanam
pioneered the boat library on the Bank Canal during 1935–1942 and also undertook a Buckingham Canal tour.
Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao
undertook the 1918 boat tour or padava yatra in West Godavari.
Tents at fairs and markets, home delivery of books to women, night schools and training camps were activities of the movement.

secs.t: Library laws → year, mover, provision

x: The Act was influenced by the Andhra movement, created local library authorities and used a library cess for funding.
The Andhra Pradesh Public Libraries Act, 1960 created district library bodies known as Zilla Grandhalaya Samsthas.
Pathuri Nagabhushanam
served on the drafting committee of the Andhra Pradesh Public Libraries Act, 1960.
Vavilala Gopalakrishnayya
drafted and moved the Madras Public Libraries Bill, 1938 (APPSC GS 2022).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The National Mission on Libraries functions under the Ministry of Culture, has RRRLF as its nodal agency, and aids one State Central Library and one District Library in each State or Union Territory.
Libraries served as legal centres of political education under colonial curbs and helped build Telugu identity, which supported the demand for statehood.

x: The concept of the library pilgrimage was conceived by
Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya
Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya received the title Granthalaya Pitamaha from the
Maharaja of Baroda
Andhra University
conferred the title Kala Prapoorna on Paturi Nagabhushanam in 1975.
Karunasri, the pen name of Jandhyala Papayya Sastri, gave Paturi Nagabhushanam the titles “University of Humanity” and “Walking Library.”.

secs.t: Leaders → life, institutions and contributions — Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya

x: Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya was born on 24 July 1890 and died in 1979.
Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya was associated with the journal
Grandhalaya Sarvasvam
, published in 1915.
Paturi Nagabhushanam
started the Bala Saraswati Bhandaramu library in his village while he was still a schoolboy.
Komma Sitaramayya
donated the building that was named Sarvottama Bhavan in honour of Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao.

secs.t: Leaders → life, institutions and contributions — Other leaders, patrons and publishers

x: Komarraju Venkata Lakshmana Rao
founded the Vijnana Chandrika Mandali at Hyderabad.
Komarraju Venkata Lakshmana Rao founded the
SKDABN
Vavilala Ramaswamy Sastrulu & Sons and Nageswara Rao’s Andhra Granthamala supported libraries by supplying books and free copies.
Velaga Venkatappayya
was known as the “Library Gandhi” and conducted village tours in Bhimavaram, Tadepalligudem, Kovvur and Guntur.

secs.t: Library innovations and laws → pioneer (PYQ)

x: Paturi Nagabhushanam operated the boat library service on passenger boats on the Bank Canal for seven years, from 1935 to 1942.
Paturi Nagabhushanam was a member of the committee that drafted the
AP Public Libraries Act

secs.t: Gadicherla → newspapers, jail, "Rayalaseema", Sreebagh

x: Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao was imprisoned for editorials such as “Veerabali” published in
Swarajya
The renaming of Dattamandalam as Rayalaseema took place in 1928.
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
renamed the Ceded Districts "Rayalaseema" in 1928 (APPSC G2 2011, 2012); he also signed the Sreebagh Pact for Rayalaseema.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Ayyanki Venkataramanaiah built institutions, Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao mobilised people, and Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao provided financial and political backing.
Ayyanki Venkataramanaiah's 136th birth anniversary was celebrated at the Tagore Library on Bandar Road in Vijayawada.
Ayyanki Murali Krishna
, the grandson of Ayyanki Venkataramanaiah, recalled the slogan “Public libraries are temples of knowledge.”.

sub: Group-II S1-92: Reorganisation within the country - Andhra State 1953, SRC and the States Reorganisation Act 1956
Group-II M1-A-104: States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali Commission) - appointment and terms of reference
Group-II M1-A-105: SRC recommendations on Andhra and Telangana and the reaction to them

secs.t: Andhra and Visalandhra movement → events by year (1913-1956)

x: Bayya Narasimheswara Sarma
presided over the first Andhra Mahasabha at Bapatla in 1913.
Suravaram Pratapa Reddy
led the first Nizam Andhra Mahasabha at Jogipet in 1930.
The Gentlemen’s Agreement was concluded on
20 February 1956
at Hyderabad House in New Delhi.
The Congress sub-committee comprised Jawaharlal Nehru, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and G.B. Pant.

secs.t: Commissions and committees → year, members, finding

x: The JVP Committee comprised Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
The JVP Committee rejected language as the immediate basis of reorganisation and advised postponement.
The S.K. Dhar Commission (June-Dec 1948) favoured
administrative convenience
over language, which caused resentment.
Justice K. N. Wanchoo later reported on the financial and administrative consequences of separating Andhra from Madras.

secs.t: Commissions and committees → year, members, finding — SRC — setting up

x: The Commission was announced on 22 December 1953, formally constituted on 29 December 1953, submitted its report in 1955, and the States Reorganisation Act came into force on 1 November 1956.
Nehru announced the SRC in the Lok Sabha on 22
December 1953
, and it was formally constituted by Home Ministry resolution on 29 December 1953. 'August 1953' and '1954' are wrong dates found in some sources; 1 October 1953 was the formation of Andhra State.

secs.t: Commissions and committees → year, members, finding — SRC members

x: Exam angle: Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru was
not
a member (RPSC trap).
Exam angle: chairman (Fazl Ali) and the three-member set are asked most; the RPSC trap adds Tej Bahadur Sapru.
The SRC had three members: Syed Fazl Ali (Chairman, then Governor of Odisha), H.N. Kunzru (member, Council of States) and K.M. Panikkar (diplomat).

secs.t: Persons → roles and statements

x: Potti Sriramulu died on
15 December 1952
after fasting for 58 days for a separate Telugu state.
Burgula Ramakrishna Rao, then Chief Minister, acted
on the direction of the Congress High Command
to reduce Telangana's apprehensions.
In 1956 Nehru likened the merger to a matrimonial alliance, adding that there could be a provision for divorce if the partners could not get along.

secs.t: Andhra State 1953 and Andhra Pradesh 1956 → formation facts and FIRSTs

x: Exam angle: G2 2025 key "Andhra State formed on 1 October 1953" (not 1 Nov 1956).
All three were recognised arguments in favour of linguistic states: governance in the people's language, preservation of cultural identity and easier administration.
The arguments against linguistic states included fears regarding unity, regionalism, border disputes and minority disputes.

secs.t: Pacts and agreements → terms

x: The pact provided for irrigation priority, university centres and equal legislative representation for Rayalaseema, but it did not provide for the
immediate merger of Telangana with Andhra
All four statements correctly describe safeguards agreed upon by the Andhra and Telangana leaders under the Gentlemen’s Agreement.

secs.t: SRC principles → factors of reorganisation

x: The S.K. Dhar Commission preferred administrative convenience, the JVP Committee rejected language as the basis, and the States Reorganisation Commission treated language as important but not the sole factor.
The SRC considered administrative efficiency, economic and financial viability, geographical contiguity, national unity and security, and the welfare of people and the national plan.

secs.t: SRC report (1955) → recommendations for India

x: The Commission recommended retaining Bombay as a bilingual state consisting of Gujarati- and Marathi-speaking areas.
The Commission submitted its report on
30 September 1955
; it was made public on 9 October 1955.
The report was submitted in 1955 and proposed 16 states and 3 Union Territories along with abolition of the Part A, B and C classification.

secs.t: SRC on Hyderabad State → chapters, paras and Telangana

x: Exam angle: "two-thirds" and "after 1961 elections" are the testable numbers.
Raichur and Gulbarga were assigned to Mysore, Marathwada to Bombay, and the Telugu districts were to remain as a separate Hyderabad State.
Paragraph 386 recommended that Telangana initially function as a separate state to be called Hyderabad State.
After the 1961 general elections the Telangana Legislative Assembly could reconsider merger.

secs.t: Arguments for and against Visalandhra

x: The SRC regarded Hyderabad as a common capital that could solve the capital problem faced by Andhra State.
Protection of Telangana's revenue surplus was an apprehension of opponents of immediate merger, not an advantage of Visalandhra.
The SRC observed majority support for Visalandhra among Telangana legislators but gave serious consideration to grievances relating to
finance and education

secs.t: Data → memorandums, Assembly votes and resolutions

x: Of the members who voted, 103 supported Visalandhra, while 29 opposed it and 15 remained neutral.

secs.t: States Reorganisation Act 1956 and the Seventh Constitutional Amendment

x: The
Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956
abolished the Part A, B, C and D classification and created the categories of States and Union Territories.
Articles 350A and 350B
concern mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage and the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities, respectively.
The SR Act 1956 and the Seventh Amendment gave effect to
14 states and 6 Union Territories
(UPSC).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Linguistic reorganisation raised concerns about national unity, but improved administration through people's languages; disputes such as Belgaum nevertheless continued.
The departure from
paragraph 386
was identified as a central grievance in the Telangana movements of 1969 and 2001-14.
BRS leader
K. T. Rama Rao
invoked the Fazal Ali Commission recommendation in January 2026 while criticising the Congress over the merger.

Group-II M1-A-107: Formation of Andhra Pradesh, 1 November 1956 - the first government and the new capital
Group-II M1-A-108: Political developments in Andhra Pradesh, 1956-2014 - chief ministers and major turning points

secs.t: Visalandhra — meaning, roots and FIRSTs

x: Visalandhra, or Greater Andhra, envisaged one state for Telugu-speaking people living in the Madras region and Nizam’s Hyderabad.
The early proposal emerged in 1912, covered the three specified regions, and was advanced further at the second Andhra Mahasabha in 1914.
The correct sequence is 1912 proposal, 1914 Andhra Mahasabha proposal, 1936 manifesto and 1946 publication of Sundarayya’s book.
The correct sequence is Dhar Commission (1948), Visalandhra Mahasabha (1949), Swami Sitaram's fast (1951), and Andhra State (1953).

secs.t: Persons → role in the Visalandhra movement

x: All three apply: Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao founded the Visalandhra Mahasabha at Vijayawada on 26 Nov 1949, raised the demand at the 1951 Bangalore Congress manifesto meeting, and resigned when no decision came.
All four—Swami Ramananda Tirtha, Burgula Ramakrishna Rao, Mandumula Narsing Rao and Pandit Narendraji—supported Visalandhra.
Mahadev Singh
of the PSP was an opponent of the Visalandhra proposal.
K.V. Ranga Reddy
initially supported Visalandhra but later supported separate Telangana after becoming president of the Telangana Congress.
Mir Mohammed Ali Khan was a Deputy Mayor and, along with Makhdoom Mohiuddin and Mehdi Nawaz Jung, helped educate Muslim opinion in Hyderabad.

secs.t: Communist Party, press and books → authors — Communist Party role

x: The Communist Party started the Visalandhra movement, won many seats in both regions in 1952 and expected to secure a majority in a united state.
The Communists propagated Visalandhra and supported the integration of Telugu-speaking areas.
Sundarayya started the Visalandhra paper and became the first General Secretary of the CPI(M) in 1964.

secs.t: Communist Party, press and books → authors — Books, pamphlets and poems → authors

x: Puchalapalli Sundarayya
coined the expression ‘Visalandhra’ and authored Visalandhralo Prajarajyam.
The press-literary contribution included the Communist daily Visalandhra, Narayana Rao’s book, Ramanuja Rao’s pamphlets and Sri Sri’s presidency of the 1954 Mahasabha.
Kodati Rajalingam, Hayagrivachari, Devulapalli Ramanuja Rao and Paga Pulla Reddy
explained the benefits of Visalandhra through books, pamphlets and tours.

secs.t: Mahasabhas and party resolutions → date and venue

x: The 1950 position treated Madras as temporary and Hyderabad as permanent, while the 1953 Kurnool meeting demanded Visalandhra with Hyderabad as capital under Neelam Sanjiva Reddy’s association.
The Warangal meeting was on 8 July 1954, the Chief Ministers met at Hyderabad House on 22 October 1955, and the agreement was signed on 20 February 1956.

In June 1953 the Hyderabad Congress Committee proposed three divisions; in 1954 that resolution was rejected; on 8 July 1954 the PCC delegation met the SRC; and in November 1955 Harishchandra Heda supported separate Telangana.

The Visalandhra Mahasabha was founded in 1949; the APCC Kurnool resolution occurred on 30 September 1953; the Hyderabad PCC delegation met the SRC on 8 July 1954; and the Telangana convention took place in November 1955.

secs.t: Burgula Ramakrishna Rao → posts and change of stand

x: Exam angle: "In which year did Burgula change his stand?" - key answer 1954.
Burgula Ramakrishna Rao
headed the first elected ministry of Hyderabad State, which assumed office in 1952.
B. Ramakrishna Rao changed his position in 1954 and advocated the early merger of Telangana with Andhra; he later kept Delhi informed in favour of Visalandhra.

secs.t: Telangana background — Mahasabha, Hyderabad State and Mulki rules

x: The Mulki rules belong to the Nizam's era: they date from 1888 and were tightened by the Nizam's farman of 1919, allowing only residents of about 15 years to get local jobs.
The Nizam Andhra Mahasabha became a vehicle for Telugu cultural and political awakening in the Nizam’s State and later divided along moderate and Communist lines.

secs.t: Arguments for and against Visalandhra

x: Swami Ramananda Tirtha
argued that Telangana would develop within Visalandhra and that a separate Telangana would be weak.
The Communist agrarian argument held that unification could promote land reform and weaken feudal structures.
The apprehensions concerned the use of Telangana’s revenue surplus, widening regional disparities and weakening of local employment protections.
The argument for separate Telangana was based on its higher per capita income and revenue compared with Andhra State, making it economically viable on its own.

secs.t: Wanchu Committee, Andhra State 1953 and Pataskar Award

x: Justice K.N. Wanchoo, CJ of Rajasthan HC, headed it, and it was appointed on 7 Feb 1953 after Potti Sriramulu died in Dec 1952.
Its mandate was to
identify the financial and administrative problems of forming Andhra State
(PYQ, APPSC G2 2012); its March 1953 report fixed the new state's districts.

secs.t: States Reorganisation Commission → recommendations and Assembly vote

x: The SRC recommended that Telangana remain separate initially, that the issue be reconsidered after the 1961 elections, and that merger require a two-thirds majority in the Telangana legislature.
Nehru announced the Commission on 22 December 1953; it was constituted on 29 December 1953; its report came in 1955; and the Visalandhra Mahasabha was founded in 1949.

secs.t: Gentlemen's Agreement — date, place and signatories

x: The Gentlemen's Agreement's Regional Committee for Telangana was given constitutional backing through Article 371(1) (inserted by the Seventh Amendment, 1956) and the Andhra Pradesh Regional Committee Order, 1958.
Burgula Ramakrishna Rao served as Governor of Kerala from 1956 to 1960 and later as Governor of Uttar Pradesh from 1960 to 1962.

Eight leaders signed, four from each region: Bezawada Gopala Reddy, Neelam Sanjiva Reddy, Gouthu Latchanna and Alluri Satyanarayana Raju for Andhra; Burgula Ramakrishna Rao, K.V. Ranga Reddy, Marri Chenna Reddy and J.V. Narsing Rao for Telangana.

secs.t: Gentlemen's Agreement → safeguards for Telangana

x: The agreement provided proportionate sharing of common expenditure, exclusive use of Telangana's surplus in Telangana and a review after five years.
The agreement protected existing educational facilities and provided Telangana students admission priority or at least one-third of the seats in technical institutions, whichever was more favourable.
The services safeguard provided for recruitment according to population ratio under domicile rules and proportionate retrenchment from both regions.
The agreed safeguard referred to Mulki or domicile rules requiring
12 years
of residence for recruitment in Telangana.
The Andhra Assembly resolution supported Telangana priority and population-based allocations in
jobs, education, irrigation and development

secs.t: Regional Committee, Deputy CM post and violations

x: The Committee represented Telangana legislators, included Telangana ministers other than the Chief Minister ex officio, referred disputes to the Centre and was subject to review after ten years.
The Committee was extended for five years in 1968 and was subsequently wound up after the 32nd Amendment in 1973 removed Andhra Pradesh from Article 371(1).
The alleged method of bypassing the Mulki rules was to reclassify local posts as state-cadre or unreserved posts.
The alleged violations, especially concerning employment, domicile and revenue surplus, contributed to the
Jai Telangana agitation of 1969

secs.t: Articles, Amendments and Orders → provisions

x: Article 371(1) gave constitutional footing to the
Regional Committee

Article 371D, inserted by the 32nd Amendment (1973) to implement the Six-Point Formula, provides equitable opportunities in public employment and education, local cadres and the AP Administrative Tribunal.
The 1975 Presidential Order was the AP Public Employment (
Organisation of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment
) Order.

secs.t: Formation of Andhra Pradesh, 1 November 1956 — basis, name, capital

x: Andhra Pradesh was formed by merging the 11 districts of Andhra State with the nine Telugu-speaking districts of Hyderabad State, while the Kannada and Marathi areas went to Mysore and Bombay respectively.
The SRC noted that Hyderabad could solve Andhra's permanent-capital problem, and it was the largest city with ready administrative infrastructure.
The draft Bill used 'Andhra Telangana' and the Communists proposed 'Visalandhra', but the Seventh Amendment Bill in the Lok Sabha (10 Aug 1956) settled on 'Andhra Pradesh'.

secs.t: First government, legislature and High Court → first holders

x: Neelam Sanjiva Reddy became the first Chief Minister and C.M. Trivedi was the first Governor of Andhra Pradesh after its formation in 1956.
Puchalapalli Sundarayya
was the first Leader of the Opposition in the newly formed Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly.
The Congress had 40 seats from Hyderabad in 1952 and 119 from Andhra in 1955, giving a total strength of 159.
The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council was constituted in 1958 with
90 members
during the tenure of N. Sanjiva Reddy.

secs.t: Chief Ministers of Andhra Pradesh → tenure and FIRSTs

x: The Telugu Desam Party was founded on 29 March 1982 during the tenure of
Bhavanam Venkatarami Reddy
Kotla Vijaya Bhaskara Reddy
served from 20 September 1982 until January 1983, immediately before N.T. Rama Rao became Chief Minister.
Nadendla Bhaskara Rao served 31 days (16 Aug-16 Sep 1984), the shortest tenure.
Jalagam Vengala Rao assumed office in 1973, followed by M. Chenna Reddy in 1978, T. Anjaiah in 1980 and Bhavanam Venkatarami Reddy in February 1982.
Damodaram Sanjivayya
, the second CM of Andhra Pradesh, became India's first Dalit CM on 11 January 1960 and later became AICC President.
Sanjivayya (1960), Kasu Brahmananda Reddy (1964), P.V. Narasimha Rao (1971), T. Anjaiah (1980).

secs.t: Elections, party splits and Panchayat Raj, 1957-1989

x: Indira Gandhi
formed Congress (I) on 1 January 1978, while Brahmananda Reddy led the rival Reddy Congress.
The three-tier Panchayat Raj system was implemented in Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1959 under
N. Sanjiva Reddy
The Balwant Rai Mehta report, considered by the National Development Council in 1958, was associated with the three-tier Panchayat Raj system.
NTR introduced the Mandal system from 1985 and, in 1983, permitted a simple majority for no-confidence motions against Zilla Parishad vice-chairmen instead of the earlier two-thirds majority.

secs.t: Telugu Desam Party and NTR → initiatives and the 1984 crisis — Founding and 1983 victory

x: The Telugu Desam Party won 202 seats in the 1983 election and formed the first non-Congress government in Andhra Pradesh.
Nadendla Bhaskara Rao
served as Deputy Chief Minister in N.T. Rama Rao’s initial cabinet.
N. Vittal
was the first holder of the Dharma Mahamatra office associated with the anti-corruption initiative.
The TDP was founded on 29 March 1982, not 29 May (a known misprint).

secs.t: Telugu Desam Party and NTR → initiatives and the 1984 crisis — The 1984 crisis — event → date

x: The dismissal by Governor Ram Lal led to Nadendla Bhaskara Rao’s short-lived ministry and NTR’s restoration after Nadendla resigned.
Nadendla Bhaskara Rao was sworn in on 16 August 1984, Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October, mid-term polls were held on 28 December, and NTR was sworn in again on 9 March 1985.

secs.t: AP leaders → national office

x: Neelam Sanjiva Reddy was President of India, P.V. Narasimha Rao was Prime Minister, Damodaram Sanjivayya was AICC President, and N.T. Rama Rao was Chairman of the National Front.
Neelam Sanjiva Reddy was the only Janata candidate to win in Andhra Pradesh in the 1977 election.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Gentlemen's Agreement followed the Sribagh Pact's approach of addressing regional fears through a moral and political understanding rather than through a constitutional settlement.
The Deputy Chief Minister provision, protection of surplus funds and the Mulki rules were among the safeguards regarded as inadequately enforced.
The Six-Point Formula of 1973 was also part of the subsequent regional-safeguard framework, making statement 2 false.
K. T. Rama Rao made the criticism in January 2026, while Tejasvi Surya's April 2026 remark drew protests in Telangana.
The current Andhra Pradesh capital is Amaravati, and the Governor and Chief Minister are S. Abdul Nazeer and N. Chandrababu Naidu respectively.
The 1984 dismissal is cited as a classic instance of gubernatorial discretion being misused, and it contributed to later debate examined by the Sarkaria Commission.
In June 2026, N. Chandrababu Naidu was Chief Minister heading the NDA coalition, with K. Pawan Kalyan as Deputy Chief Minister.
